title: HOW TO KNOW IF YOU'RE ACTUALLY GROWING OR JUST GETTING OLDER
excerpt: The uncomfortable signs that you're moving through life and not actually growing through it.
content:
You have more responsibilities than you did five years ago. Better vocabulary for your problems. A calmer face in situations that used to wreck you. But if you are honest, you still react the same way to the same kind of person, still fall into the same argument you swore you'd never repeat, still make the decision you already know the ending to.

Age changed. Something underneath it didn't. That gap is what this is about. Walk with me.

THE TRAP OF LOOKING GROWN

It's easy to mistake the props of adulthood for actual growth, a job title, a wedding, a new city, a more polished way of talking about your feelings. These things are real, but they are not proof of anything. You can accumulate every marker of a "put together" life and still handle conflict exactly like you did at nineteen. Yes that's true. Growth is not what you have collected. It's what you have stopped repeating.

THE TEST NOBODY TELLS YOU ABOUT

Here's a sharper way to check, think of the last time someone disappointed you, or the last time you were wrong about something. Not what you said about it afterwards, what you actually did in the moment. Did you get defensive the same way you always have? Did you go quiet and punish with distance, the way you did years ago? Did you apologize, or did you wait for the other person to go first, like usual? That moment tells you more than any birthday could. Growth shows up in the reflex, not the reflection.

WHY THIS IS HARD TO SEE IN YOURSELF

Nobody experiences their own patterns as patterns. You experience each one as a fresh, justified reaction to a unique situation. It's other people, the ones who have known you for years, who can tell you "you always do this" while you are still convinced this time was different. That's the quiet danger of aging without growing, you get better and better at explaining your reactions, and worse at noticing they are the same reaction wearing a brand new outfit.

THE UNCOMFORTABLE TRUTH

Real growth is often invisible to the person doing it, because it rarely feels like an achievement. Those moments you feel you're not doing enough, that's growth. It feels like discomfort, staying in a hard conversation instead of leaving it, admitting fault before you are cornered into it, choosing the version of honesty that costs you something instead of the one that keeps the peace. If your personal growth has only ever felt good, it's worth questioning whether it's growth or just a more comfortable performance of yourself. The stuff that actually changes you rarely feels like main character energy while it's happening.

WHAT ACTUALLY CHANGED BEHAVIOUR LOOKS LIKE

It's smaller than people expect. It's apologizing without adding a "but." Yes you heard me. It's noticing you're about to repeat an old pattern and interrupting it mid sentence, even clumsily. It's letting a relationship end instead of performing the version of yourself that keeps people around out of guilt. None of this photographs well. Nobody posts "I finally didn't ghost someone when things got uncomfortable." But that's usually closer to real growth than anything that fits in a caption.

So Are You Actually Growing, or Just Getting Older? Maybe stop asking the question in general terms and get specific. Pick one pattern, the one you already know the answer to, the one you have been calling "just how I am" and ask if it's changed even slightly in the last year. If it hasn't, that's not a failure. It's just information. And now you have it, which is more than most people are willing to sit with long enough to find out, are you willing to work on it?

Remember, growth is painful but necessary in every area of life. I'm rooting for you.

Share your opinion in the comment section.

Don't forget to Like. Follow. Share. Comment.

title: It took less time than it takes to read this sentence for the Emirates to fall silent — then 89 minutes for it to roar back
excerpt: The 77-Second Lead: How Chelsea's Fastest Start of the Season Became Their Cruelest Defeat
content:
Arsenal came from behind to beat Chelsea 2-1 at the Emirates — a game that says more about resilience than talent, and a reminder that fast starts don't guarantee finishes.

Seventy-seven seconds. That's all it took. Chelsea hadn't even settled into their shape, Arsenal fans hadn't finished their first chant, and the ball was already in the back of the net. A gorgeous, first-time volley that sent the away end into delirium and the home crowd into stunned silence. For a moment, it looked like Xabi Alonso's Chelsea were about to hand Mikel Arteta his first defeat of the season on his own turf. Then Arsenal did what champions do. They didn't panic. They didn't rush. They simply took the game apart, piece by piece, until the scoreline read exactly the opposite of how it started. By full time, this had turned into one of the most gripping 90 minutes London football has produced all season — and a match that says a lot about what actually wins games.

*Reason: The perfect start can lull you into a false sense of security.*

Chelsea's opening goal was as good as it gets — a slick move finished with real quality. But football has a cruel habit of punishing teams who mistake an early lead for a finished job. Arsenal barely blinked. They spent the rest of the half figuring out Chelsea's shape, testing their spaces, and probing for the equalizer that felt, even at 0-1, somehow inevitable.

*Reason: Championship-level teams respond, they don't retreat.*

Kai Havertz leveled things midway through the first half — fittingly, against his former club — and from there Arsenal's control of the game only grew. Pedro Neto rattled the post for Chelsea right before the break, a reminder they were still very much alive in this one. But Arsenal came out of halftime with intent, and five minutes into the second period, Martin Ødegaard finished off a gorgeous dummy from Havertz to make it 2-1.

*Reason: The best games are won in the moments that don't show up on the scoresheet.*

What made this one special wasn't just the goals — it was everything in between. Emiliano Martínez pulling off a wonder save to deny Bukayo Saka. David Raya somehow doing him one better to keep out a certain goal. Chelsea refusing to fold, pushing men forward, giving their manager's first away test against a title rival everything they had, right up to the final whistle.

Arsenal walk away still perfect through three games, level on points with Manchester City at the top. Chelsea leave with nothing but the frustrating knowledge that for 76 minutes, they were the better story — and for the final 14, they weren't.

*The takeaway:*in football, as in most things worth watching, it's never about who starts fastest — it's about who's still standing when the final whistle blows.

title: What If the AI's Answer Isn't the Only Thing You Should Be Worried About?
excerpt: You ask an AI a question.It gives you an answer.You read it, decide whether you like it, and move on.Simple enough.But here's a question I hadn't really thought…
content:
You ask an AI a question.

It gives you an answer.

You read it, decide whether you like it, and move on.

Simple enough.

But here's a question I hadn't really thought about before:

What happens to everything the AI does before that answer reaches you?

And more importantly

what if someone found a way to see parts of it that were never supposed to be visible?

That is the uncomfortable question behind a recent piece of AI security research involving models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

And no, this does not mean that someone can currently open your ChatGPT conversation and read everything the AI was "thinking." The researchers reported the vulnerability to the affected companies, and mitigations were subsequently deployed.

But what they found is still worth paying attention to.

The part of AI we don't see

Modern AI systems can perform internal reasoning before producing a final response.

You see the answer.

You don't necessarily see everything that happened behind it.

To protect those hidden reasoning traces, AI providers use technical safeguards, including encryption.

The researchers described a way of taking an encrypted reasoning payload produced by one model and replaying it through another model from the same provider, under certain conditions, to recover the hidden reasoning in readable form.

It sounds extremely technical.

But the basic idea is surprisingly simple:

Something that was supposed to stay hidden could potentially be made visible by sending it somewhere it wasn't supposed to go.

And that's where this story becomes more than just another technical vulnerability.

Because what is inside those hidden traces?

This is the part that made me stop.

According to the report, researchers examined 6,708 publicly available AI-agent transcripts and recovered hundreds of pieces of sensitive information from reasoning blocks, including personally identifiable information and hardcoded credentials such as API keys and passwords.

Think about that for a moment.

We're used to thinking about cybersecurity in terms of things like:

passwords → protect them.

emails → protect them.

files → protect them.

credit card information → protect it.

But AI is changing the picture.

We're increasingly giving AI systems access to our documents, emails, code, research, business information and personal data.

So now there's another question we have to start asking:

What happens to information while the AI is working with it?

The problem isn't necessarily the AI giving you a bad answer.

That's what makes this interesting.

We've spent a lot of time talking about AI hallucinations.

We ask:

"Can I trust this answer?"

But security researchers are increasingly asking a different question:

"Can I trust what happens behind the answer?"

Those are not the same thing.

An AI could give you a perfectly normal-looking response while something problematic is happening somewhere underneath the surface.

And as AI systems become more capable and begin acting as agents that can access tools, files, websites and other systemsthat distinction becomes increasingly important.

So, are we all in trouble?

Not exactly.

The research was disclosed to the affected providers, and the reported vulnerabilities were addressed through server-side mitigations.

That's important because headlines about AI vulnerabilities can easily make it sound as though millions of people are currently exposed.

That's not what this story tells us.

What it does tell us is something more useful:

AI security is still evolving.

We're building systems that can reason, remember, access information and perform tasks on our behalf.

And we're still learning how to secure all the things happening underneath.

That's probably going to be one of the biggest challenges of the AI era.

We've learned to protect the front door.

Now we have to think about the rooms inside.

When you log into your email, you know you have to protect your password.

When you receive a suspicious link, you know you should be careful.

When you connect to public Wi-Fi, you know there are risks.

But AI introduces another layer.

You may not even know what information is being processed, where it is stored, what systems it touches, or what could happen if a vulnerability is discovered somewhere along the chain.

And that's why I think cybersecurity is going to become increasingly inseparable from AI literacy.

You don't necessarily need to become a cybersecurity engineer.

But if you're going to use AI to work, study, build businesses, write code, analyze documents or handle sensitive information, you should eventually start asking better questions.

What am I giving this system?

Where does that information go?

What permissions does it have?

What happens if something goes wrong?

Because AI isn't just becoming a tool we ask questions.

It's becoming a tool we trust with things.

And the more we trust it with, the more important security becomes.

Maybe that's the uncomfortable lesson here.

We've spent so much time learning how to get better answers from AI.

Perhaps we also need to start learning how to understand what happens behind them.

Because sometimes, the part of the system we can't see is the part we should be paying the most attention to.

This story is based on research reported by Cyber Security News. The reported vulnerabilities were disclosed to the affected providers, who subsequently deployed mitigations.

Full story: https://cybersecuritynews.com/top-ai-models-apis-flaw-exposes-hidden-reasoning/

title: Not the end, but a part of the journey
excerpt: Death is one of the few things in life that every human being will eventually face, yet it remains one of the greatest mysteries we struggle to understand. No m…
content:
Death is one of the few things in life that every human being will eventually face, yet it remains one of the greatest mysteries we struggle to understand. No matter how different people are in their beliefs, backgrounds, dreams, or circumstances, death reminds us that our time on earth is not unlimited. We spend much of our lives planning for tomorrow, chasing dreams, building relationships, seeking success, and imagining all the things we will accomplish someday. But death quietly reminds us that someday is never guaranteed. That truth can be frightening, but it can also make life more meaningful. Knowing that our time is limited encourages us to appreciate the moments we often overlook—the conversations with people we love, the laughter shared with friends, the opportunities to learn, the dreams we are brave enough to pursue, and even the ordinary days that seem unimportant while we are living them. Death may be the end of a person's physical life, but the existence of that person does not simply disappear from the memories, lessons, love, and influence they left behind.

The thought of death can also change the way we understand what truly matters. Many things that seem enormous today may become surprisingly small when viewed against the limited time we have. Arguments, jealousy, pride, unnecessary hatred, and the desire to constantly prove ourselves can consume years that we can never recover. We sometimes act as though we have endless time to apologize, forgive, reconnect, express gratitude, or pursue the things that genuinely matter to us. But life does not make that promise. This is why the awareness of death should not only make us afraid; it should make us more conscious of how we use the time we have. It can teach us to love people while they are still here, to speak honestly when our words can still be heard, and to stop allowing temporary problems to control our entire existence. Death is painful because people matter, and the emptiness left by someone's absence can remind us just how deeply a human life can affect another. Yet even after someone is gone, their kindness can remain in another person's heart, their teachings can continue through others, and their story can become part of the lives they touched.

Perhaps the deepest lesson death gives us is not about dying, but about living. Because we know that our time is limited, every day carries a value that we cannot completely measure. We do not know how many mornings we will see, how many songs we will hear, how many dreams we will accomplish, or how many conversations remain ahead of us. That uncertainty is part of what makes existence so precious. We cannot control everything that happens in life, and we cannot know exactly when our journey will end, but we can choose what we do with the time we have now. We can create instead of destroying, love instead of constantly holding onto hatred, learn instead of remaining trapped in ignorance, and pursue meaningful dreams instead of allowing fear to decide our future. Death may be inevitable, but the way we live before it arrives is still within our hands. In that sense, the shadow of death can make the light of life easier to recognize. We are here for a limited time, and perhaps the goal is not to live forever, but to make the life we are given meaningful enough that something good remains in the world because we were here.

title: I'm a Believer!!
excerpt: How one ordinary night on a hospital bench changed everything I thought I knew about God.
content:
Jeff never had a problem with God. He just never had a reason for Him either. Growing up, church was something other people did. His parents weren't churchgoers, and by the time he was old enough to make his own choices, faith felt like a box he'd simply never opened — not out of anger, just indifference. To Jeff, prayer was for people going through something. And nothing in his life had ever felt big enough to pray about. Until one Tuesday night, it did.

The Call

Jeff was twenty-three, halfway through a bag of chips and a rerun of some show he wasn't even watching, when his phone rang. It was his sister. Their dad had collapsed at work. He was in the ER. They didn't know yet if he'd make it through the night. Jeff doesn't remember grabbing his keys. He doesn't remember the drive. He remembers the waiting room — the fluorescent lights, the stiff plastic chairs, the smell of hand sanitizer — and he remembers, for the first time in his life, not knowing what to do with his hands.

The Bench

Somewhere around 2 a.m., Jeff found himself outside on a bench near the hospital entrance, the cold air doing nothing to clear his head. His sister was inside, crying quietly. His mom hadn't said a word in an hour. And Jeff, who had never once in his life felt the urge to pray, found himself whispering into the dark. It wasn't eloquent. It wasn't even really a sentence — more like a plea with no punctuation. Please. Please let him be okay. I don't know You, but please. He didn't feel lightning. He didn't hear a voice. But something in him went quiet in a way it hadn't been quiet all night. Not certainty exactly — just the sense that he wasn't sitting on that bench alone.

The Morning After

His dad made it. The doctors called it close — closer than they were comfortable saying out loud. Jeff sat with that word for days afterward: close. Close enough that a few different choices, a few different minutes, could have gone another way entirely. He couldn't shake the feeling that something — someone — had been holding the line that night. He didn't have theology for it. He just had the bench, the whisper, and the quiet that answered it.

The Search

In the weeks that followed, Jeff did something he never expected to do: he started asking questions. Not out of guilt, not because anyone told him to, but because he wanted to understand what he'd felt. He talked to a coworker who happened to be a quiet, steady kind of Christian — the kind who never pushed, just answered honestly when Jeff finally asked. He started reading, slowly, skeptically, a few verses at a time. He visited a church on a Sunday he almost talked himself out of. Nothing about it was instant. But piece by piece, the indifference that had defined Jeff's whole life gave way to something he'd never expected to feel: belief.

Today

Jeff still remembers exactly what the bench felt like — cold metal, three in the morning, a prayer with no punctuation. He tells people now that God didn't wait for him to have the right words. He just waited for Jeff to say something at all. Jeff isn't the boy who never had a reason to believe anymore. He's the man who found one on the worst night of his life — and never let it go. I wasn't looking for God. But on the night I needed Him most, He was already there, waiting for me to notice.

title:
PART FOUR

WHEN EVERYTHING FELL APART
excerpt: After the funeral, everything she knew began to disappear.
content:
After her father’s burial, she thought the hardest part was over. She was wrong.

When her father died, the family didn’t realize just how many lives he had touched until the day of his burial.

People came from different places to mourn him. Among them were schoolchildren—children her father had helped with transportation money on their way to school. Some of them cried so deeply that it shocked the family.

They were not his biological children.

But he had made a difference in their lives.

That was when she began to understand how respected and well-known her father had truly been.

By the grace of God, the family did everything they could to give him a proper burial. But the burial itself came with another burden.

They had already spent a lot of money during his illness. Properties had been sold. Loans had been taken. Debts had accumulated.

After he was buried, the family had to face those debts.

And that was when everything began to fall apart.

While her father was alive, his presence had commanded a certain level of respect. People were careful about how they treated the family.

After his death, that changed.

People began to disrespect them.

People started gossiping.

Some began taking advantage of the family.

Things people would never have dared to do while her father was alive suddenly became normal.

Her father’s mother also began experiencing difficulties. When she became sick, the family took her to the hospital and spent money on her treatment.

But even outside the hospital, she was no longer treated with the same respect.

Village meetings became difficult.

There were times she would go for meetings and people would lock her in.

There was gossip, humiliation and accusation.

It was as if everyone knew that the man who had once stood between his family and the world was gone.

And without him, they believed the family could be pushed around.

Meanwhile, her father’s third wife was left trying to manage the shop and take care of the younger children.

Her brothers were also trying to survive.

The family had lost the person who had held so many things together.

Thankfully, her father had left one important thing behind—the borehole.

He had opened it so water could be pumped and sold, and it became one of the things helping the family survive.

But even that became difficult to maintain after his death.

There was no longer anyone to handle things the way he used to.

And while all of this was happening, she decided to leave home and look for a way to survive.

She thought she was simply going out to hustle.

She didn’t know she was stepping into another chapter of suffering.

After her father’s burial, a friend approached her.

The friend told her about a place where there was money and assured her that she would be fine.

She trusted her.

She followed her.

She had no idea that decision would become the beginning of another painful chapter of her life.

She began doing whatever work she could find.

She sold akara.

She sold pure water.

She hawked.

She did anything she could to survive.

Eventually, the friend who had taken her there disappeared.

She was left alone.

And once again, she had to figure out how to survive by herself.

She worked as a waitress.

She worked as a farmer .

She worked as a cleaner.

She worked in cafés and canteens.

She took whatever honest work came her way.

Little by little, she began saving money.

Eventually, she was able to rent a place of her own.

For the first time in a long time, she felt that she was beginning to build a life for herself.

But life had not finished testing her.

She had another friend staying with her.

She trusted this friend enough to accommodate her.

Then she had to return to the village for the prayers and ceremonies connected to her father’s death.

While she was away, the friend disappeared with her belongings.

When she came back, she was left with almost nothing.

Once again, she had to start from the beginning.

Another loss.

Another betrayal.

Another chapter of survival.

But she kept going.

Because by then, she had learned something life had been trying to teach her since her father’s death:

Sometimes, the person you expect to save you will be the person who leaves you behind.

And sometimes, the only person left to save you is yourself.

There were still many things she had not told anyone.

There were things that happened while she was working and struggling to survive—things that would eventually become some of the darkest memories of her life.

But those memories would come later.

For now, she was still trying to survive.

And her story was far from over.

title: My Crush Has Mouth Odor
excerpt: Fine Boy, Why Na?
content:
To Rita, Louis was not just a guy; he was a masterpiece walking the halls of the university. Tall, light skinned, and sleekly built, he moved with an effortless poise. With his almond eyes, sharp nose, perfectly contoured pink lips, and subtle, elf-like ears, he looked like he had stepped right out of a high-fantasy novel.

He was quiet, almost ghostlike yet his aura dominated every room he entered. Nobody really knew what his voice sounded like, though rumors claimed a lucky few had heard him speak.

"Louis is the one for me," Rita declared proudly, resting her chin on her hands as she watched him cross the courtyard.

Martha, her roommate looked up from her notebook with a slight smirk. "Hmm. Rita, small-small o. Have you ever actually spoken to him?"

"Not yet. But I have a plan."

"What if he snubs you?" Martha asked.

"He won't," Rita said confidently. "He’s just reserved."

"Toh, go get him then," Martha chuckled. "Though, word on the street is that a couple of girls used to crush on him hard before they suddenly dropped him and ran."

Rita waved a hand dismissively. "Doesn't matter, Martha. I know what I want."

Rita launched her full-scale campaign. She tried approaching him after class, but he glided away effortlessly. Undeterred, she began slipping handwritten love letters into his bag. When she finally managed to get his WhatsApp number, her enthusiastic paragraphs were met with ice-cold single-word replies: "Ok," "Alright," and the occasional thumbs-up emoji.

Then came the gifts. She left him sleek pens, notebooks, silver chains, woven bracelets, and designer beanies.

Soon, coursemates started whispering, sending anonymous messages taunting her desperation. Rita ignored them all. She was goal-oriented, and Louis was the target.

Her persistence paid off on a hot Thursday afternoon. A text popped up on her screen:

"Passageway behind Faculty of Engineering. 3:00 PM.”

Rita’s heart leaped. The moment had finally arrived. She practically flew to the venue.

When she reached the quiet passageway, Louis was waiting, leaning casually against the concrete pillar.

"Thank you for meeting me," Rita gushed, her heart doing backflips. "I hope you've been getting my messages and gifts. I really just want us to vibe, you know? You're always so isolated."

Before she could finish her sentence, Louis stepped forward and pulled her into a tight, sudden embrace. Rita froze, her cheeks burning as their hearts beat in sync.

Then the first sign hit her. A sharp, sour odor wafted from his armpits, cutting through the warm afternoon air. It’s just sweat, Rita reasoned quickly, trying to stay calm. He's been in lectures all day.

Without warning, Louis leaned down and pressed his lips to hers.

What was supposed to be a romantic moment ended instantly. Rita jerked backward, gasping for air as her eyes widened in complete horror.

As he stood there, completely unbothered by her reaction, he began to speak. His voice was shockingly deep, a low rumble that sounded almost completely inaudible like a faint reverberation coming from deep inside his chest.

"I see how much effort you put in for me," he mumbled, his deep tones barely reaching her ears. "I think we should be together. By the way, my real name isn't Louis... it's Brombromlagwe."

Rita could barely hear the words, nor did she care to. She was completely paralyzed not by the kiss or his muffled, deep voice, but by the overwhelming wave of stench that erupted with every quiet syllable.

It tasted metallic, sour, and heavy, like something rotting deep within his gut. Beneath those pristine pink lips, his tongue was coated in a thick white layer of bacteria, and the smell was pure, unadulterated halitosis.

Before he could take another step toward her, Rita turned on her heel and sprinted back to her hostel.

The moment she burst into her room, she scrubbed her teeth until her gums bled, used half a bottle of mouthwash, and flossed repeatedly. Still feeling utterly contaminated, she tore open a fresh pack of mints and shoved three into her mouth at once.

When Martha walked in later that evening, she found Rita sitting on her bunk, aggressively chewing through a mountain of mint wrappers.

"What's with all the mints?" Martha asked, raising an eyebrow.

"My crush has terrible mouth odor. And body odor," Rita gagged, holding her chest. "It’s not normal odor, Martha, it’s coming straight from his internal organs! And he kissed me!"

Martha stared at her for a second before bursting into hysterical, breathless laughter.

"Is it not what you wanted?" Martha wheezed, clutching her stomach. "You said you didn't care!"

"Gosh, I feel so dirty!" Rita whined, tossing another mint into her mouth. "He even told me his real name is Brombromlagwe! I couldn't even process it!"

Martha laughed so hard she nearly fell off her stool.

Rita sank back against her pillow, staring blankly at the ceiling. "No wonder all those other girls ran away."

"So..." Martha grinned, wiping a tear from her eye. "Is your love not unconditional anymore?"

"It was never love o!" Rita cried out. "It was just pure foolishness. Omo, I have moved on!"

What would you do if you were Rita?

~ Dorothy Kaankuka

title: It hurts more than it heals
excerpt: Hatred is one of the strongest emotions a human being can carry, and unlike anger, which may disappear after a moment, hatred can remain quietly for years. It c…
content:
Hatred is one of the strongest emotions a human being can carry, and unlike anger, which may disappear after a moment, hatred can remain quietly for years. It can begin with something small—a betrayal, rejection, misunderstanding, humiliation, jealousy, disappointment, or pain that was never properly healed. Sometimes people hate because they were hurt by someone they trusted, while other times hatred grows from assumptions, fear, or things people were taught to believe about others. The dangerous thing about hatred is that it can slowly become part of the way a person sees the world. When someone carries hatred for too long, they may begin to see enemies everywhere, interpret every action negatively, and remember every wrong while forgetting every good thing. Hatred can make a person believe that holding onto resentment gives them power, when in reality it can keep them emotionally connected to the very person or situation they desperately want to escape. A person may move forward physically while their mind remains trapped in something that happened long ago.

Hatred also has a way of spreading. One person's pain can become another person's anger, and anger can eventually become a cycle that continues from one generation to another. People who have been treated badly sometimes convince themselves that hurting others is the only way to protect themselves from being hurt again. But pain does not become justice simply because it is passed to someone else. Hatred can destroy friendships, families, communities, and even a person's relationship with themselves. It can make forgiveness feel impossible and make peace seem like weakness. Yet forgiveness does not necessarily mean pretending that something wrong never happened or allowing someone to hurt you again. Sometimes forgiveness simply means refusing to allow the past to control your future. You can remember what happened, learn from it, create boundaries, and still choose not to let hatred become the person you are. There is strength in walking away from unnecessary conflict, strength in choosing peace, and strength in refusing to become cruel simply because someone else treated you cruelly.

Perhaps the greatest victory over hatred is not defeating the person you hate, but refusing to let hatred destroy the person you could become. Life is already difficult enough without carrying the weight of every insult, betrayal, disagreement, and disappointment forever. There will always be people who misunderstand you, people who dislike you without knowing you, people who disappoint you, and people whose actions leave scars on your memories. You cannot control every person's heart, but you can decide what you allow to live inside yours. Sometimes the best response to hatred is growth—to become wiser without becoming bitter, stronger without becoming cruel, and more careful without becoming completely closed off. Hatred may feel powerful, but peace has its own kind of power. A person who learns to release unnecessary hatred is not surrendering; they are choosing freedom. Because at the end of the day, you only have one life to live, and it is too valuable to spend all of it carrying emotions that were never meant to become your permanent home.

title: THE PRESSURE TO LOOK SUCCESSFUL BEFORE YOU ACTUALLY ARE
excerpt: Performing a Life You Haven't Built Yet
content:
You posted the new bag before you finished paying for it. Smiled through the photo while doing quiet math on rent in your head. Said "I'm good" to the group chat asking how business is going, while the business have not made a real profit in months. None of this felt like lying at the time. It felt like keeping up. You begin to feel you're living the life.

If you have ever managed the appearance of a life you have not actually built yet, this one's for you.

THE ORDER GOT SWITCHED

It used to be that you built something worthwhile, then it showed. Now the showing often comes first, the aesthetic, the captions, the "soft launch" of a success that has not fully landed and the actual substance is expected to catch up quietly, in private, while nobody's watching. Really? That reversed order is exhausting in a specific way, you are not just working toward something, you're simultaneously maintaining a performance of already having it.

WHY THIS IS NOT JUST VANITY

It's easy to dismiss this as shallow, just people wanting to look good. But underneath it is something more understandable, nobody wants to be the person still "figuring it out" in a world where everyone else appears to have arrived. Looking like you are behind feels riskier than actually being behind, because people react to appearances long before they know the real story. That's the kind of world/society we happened to find ourselves in this recent times. So the performance is not vanity. It's often protection, a way of buying time and dignity while the real thing is still under construction.

THE COST NOBODY MENTIONS

Here's what rarely gets said, maintaining the appearance of success takes real resources such as money you don't have, energy you need elsewhere, honesty you can't afford to give your closest people. You end up financing an image instead of financing the actual goal, which means the real thing takes even longer to arrive, because you're too busy paying for the illusion of having already arrived. The performance doesn't just fail to help. It actively competes with the progress it's supposed to be covering for.

The Uncomfortable Truth

Some of the people who look most "together" online are further behind privately than the people who never bothered performing at all. Looking successful and being successful are sometimes inversely related, the more energy goes into the image, the less is often left for the substance behind it. This is not a reason to judge anyone. It's a reason to ask yourself honestly which one you're actually building.

WHAT THIS ACTUALLY REQUIRES

Not silence about your goals, and not full public disclosure of every struggle either. Just an internal honesty, knowing, privately, where you actually stand, so the performance doesn't start replacing the plan. Let people think what they think. Just don't let your own image fool you into believing you're further than you are. The pressure to look successful will always be there. Whether you build quietly underneath it, or spend everything maintaining it, is the actual choice.

Which one are you choosing today?

Let us know in the comments.

Like. Follow. Share. Comment

title: The only risk worth taking
excerpt: Love is one of the most powerful things a human being can experience. It is more than words, promises, or the excitement that comes when someone makes your hear…
content:
Love is one of the most powerful things a human being can experience. It is more than words, promises, or the excitement that comes when someone makes your heart feel different; it is the feeling that makes another person's happiness matter to you, the willingness to understand someone even when they are difficult to understand, and the decision to care even when life becomes complicated. Love can make ordinary moments feel unforgettable—a simple conversation, a shared laugh, a quiet moment together, or the feeling of knowing that someone genuinely cares about your existence. It can give people courage when they feel weak and hope when everything around them seems uncertain. But love also requires vulnerability because to truly care about someone is to accept that they have the ability to affect your emotions. That can be frightening, because love does not come with a guarantee that everything will always work out. Still, people continue to love because the possibility of experiencing something genuine can be worth the risk of opening their hearts.

Real love is not always perfect, and it is not supposed to be. People make mistakes, misunderstand each other, change, grow, and sometimes disappoint one another. Love is tested not only during beautiful moments but also during disagreements, difficult seasons, and moments when patience is required. It means learning how to communicate instead of assuming, listening instead of immediately judging, and respecting another person's feelings even when you see things differently. Love should never require someone to lose themselves, constantly prove their worth, or accept being treated badly. Healthy love allows two people to grow while still respecting each other's boundaries, dreams, individuality, and dignity. It is not about possession or control; it is about connection. It is being able to celebrate someone's happiness without jealousy, support their dreams without trying to own them, and remain honest even when the truth is uncomfortable. Sometimes love means staying and working through problems, while other times it means recognizing that letting someone go is healthier than forcing something that no longer brings peace.

Perhaps the most beautiful thing about love is the way it can continue to exist through the memories and lessons people leave in each other's lives. Not every person we love will remain beside us forever, and not every relationship will have the ending we imagined. Some people arrive for a season and teach us something we carry for the rest of our lives. Others become lifelong companions who stand beside us through countless changes. Either way, love can leave a person different from who they were before they experienced it. It can teach patience, compassion, courage, forgiveness, and the importance of appreciating people while they are still present. In a world where people can be quick to judge, abandon, or hurt one another, choosing to love genuinely is an act of courage. Love reminds us that we are not meant to experience everything alone, that kindness can matter more than pride, and that sometimes the greatest thing we can give another person is simply the assurance that they are seen, heard, respected, and valued. Love may not make life perfect, but it can make the journey feel more meaningful—and sometimes, that is more than enough.

title: Feedback
excerpt: What it feels like to hear the truth about yourself and not run from it
content:
I just got off the phone with someone pretty close to me
and I’ve been left with a well of mixed emotions.

I feel sorry
and misunderstood at the same time.

So I’ll try to articulate my thoughts
without boring you in the process.

For context, I have this thing where I like to use my name as a verb, not a noun.
Call it ego, call it self-worth…
I just know it has been a kind of spice in my journey
out of really messy situations.

But now I’m starting to question it.

Because I’ve always believed I was emotionally intelligent.

But with this person…
I haven’t been able to connect my intentions to my actions.

And that gap?

It might have made them feel small.
Or even stupid.

Yeah… I’m trying to hide the gender here 🤣

But continuing on this little road to enlightenment,
I’ve come face to face with something uncomfortable.

Truth.
Accountability.

And if I’m being honest…

I think I’ve been a shitty person.

Maybe even borderline horrible.

That’s not easy to admit.
But it feels necessary.

Because one thing I’m grateful for, even in all of this,
is the gift of communication.

Nothing builds resentment faster than silence.

Unspoken things have a way of growing teeth.

So the fact that this was said out loud…
even if it hurt…
means something.

It gives me something to work with.

Not just communication though.

Feedback.

Real feedback.

The kind that doesn’t massage your ego
but forces you to sit with yourself.

So now, I’ll process.

I’ll sit with it.
I’ll understand it.

And I’ll come back with an apology
that isn’t just words,
but actions.

For now, I’m trying to make things right with myself first.
To actually work with what I’ve been told
instead of defending against it.

Because it’s crazy when you think about it.

Someone can laugh with you,
be around you,
share moments with you…

and still carry a completely different version of you in their head.

And you’d never know.

Sometimes I wish I could hear
what people really think about me
when I’m not there.

When there’s no need to perform.
No need to filter.

Just raw, honest perception.

Maybe then I could fix every misunderstanding.
Explain every version of me
that got lost in translation.

But that’s not how it works.

I’m learning that I can’t control
how I’m perceived.

I can only take responsibility
for how I show up.

And maybe that’s enough.

For now, I’m sitting with two things.

Apology…
and gratitude.

Because as uncomfortable as it feels,

feedback is still a gift.

And I just received one.

title: 20s And It's Pressure
excerpt: I swear, the moment you turn 20,omo  everybody starts acting like you've been sent the PDF of your life. 😭"So... what's the plan?( Maybe ask my mum 😔)"When ar…
content:
I swear, the moment you turn 20,omo everybody starts acting like you've been sent the PDF of your life. 😭

"So... what's the plan?( Maybe ask my mum 😔)

"When are you graduating?(In six years silly)

"What do you want to do with your life?(I wan become dokinta)

"Where do you see yourself in five years?(Probably in my final year)

Omo... I don't even know what I'm eating tomorrow. 🧍🏽‍♀️😂

One minute I'm stressing over assignments. 📚

The next minute I'm refreshing my Substack to see if one more person subscribed. 👀

Then I'm searching for remote writing jobs, calculating dollar rates, and convincing myself that this writing thing will pay my bills one day. 💻🥲

It's like everybody expects you to have your whole life mapped out already.

Meanwhile, I'm just trying not to panic. 🐸

Then you open TikTok... mistake. 😭

One person my age just relocated. ✈️

Another one is tweeting about making their first $10k. 💸

Someone is engaged. 💍

Someone bought a car. 🚗

Someone else is already calling themselves a CEO. 👩🏽‍💼

Meanwhile, my biggest achievement this week was submitting an assignment before the deadline ,remembering to drink water and my stir fry pasta coming out edible 😭

You start asking yourself,

"Am I behind?"

Honestly... I ask myself that too 🥹 A lot.

But maybe we're asking the wrong question. 🤍

Maybe 20 isn't the age to have everything figured out.

Maybe it's the age to try things. 🌱

To start again.

To change your mind.

To discover what actually makes you happy. 🦋

A few weeks ago, I started sharing my writing online. 💚

I didn't know if anybody would read it.

Then people started liking it.

Commenting.

Subscribing.

Every new subscriber genuinely makes me smile because it reminds me that maybe... just maybe... I'm building something. 🥹✨

For one minute I feel like, "Yeah, I think I'm on the right path."

Then the next morning I'm questioning every life decision I've ever made. 😭🐥

That's literally what being 20 feels like.

You're motivated on Monday. 💪🏽

Confused by Wednesday. 🤡

Feeling like the main character on Friday. 💅🏽

Having an identity crisis by Sunday night. 😭

It's actually a full-time job. 😂

So if you're reading this and you also feel like everyone else has life figured out except you...

This is your reminder that social media is a highlight reel, not the whole movie. 🎬

You're not failing.

You're not late.

You're not the only one figuring things out.

You're just growing. 🌱🐢

And maybe that's what 20 is supposed to look like.

No blueprint.

Just tiny steps.

Tiny wins.

Lots of questions.

A little faith.

And enough courage to keep showing up anyway. 💚✨

We'll figure it out.

Maybe not today.

Maybe not tomorrow.

But we will. 🦋🤍

title: The Power of Starting Small
excerpt: Big dreams are built through the steps we often miss.
content:
Sometimes we ignore the start because it does not look impressive. We want the moment. The big chance. The time when everything suddenly changes.

We want to wake up one day and see the results of all our work.

Most important things in life do not begin with a big moment.

They begin quietly.

With one choice.

One try.

One small step.

A writer does not become a writer after publishing a bestseller. They begin with a page and a single sentence.

A business owner does not build an empire overnight. They begin with one idea, one customer and one decision to start.

A person does not change their life in one day. They begin with choices done over and over.

The problem is that we often think beginnings are not important because they do not show us we are moving forward.

We look at our chapter and compare it to someone else’s finished book.

We look at our steps and compare them to someone else’s whole journey.

Then we think what we are doing is not enough.

Every great thing you admire now was once small.

A tree was once a seed.

A building was once a plan.

A dream was once a thought hidden inside someone’s heart.

Small does not mean not important.

Small means something is beginning.

We Wait for the Perfect Time

We tell ourselves we will start when we feel ready.

When we have time.

When we have money.

When we know more.

When life finally slows down enough for us to breathe.

So we wait.

We wait for the version of ourselves that feels completely ready forgetting that preparation grows because we started.

It is not something that arrives before we begin.

The perfect time is often a story we tell ourselves to make the fear of starting feel okay.

There is no time.

There is the moment we are in now. Not perfect not certain, full of unknowns. And the choice to keep going anyway.

The people who build the things we admire did not wait until they felt ready.

They started with what they had where they were, before they felt ready.

They became ready by continuing.

You do not need permission to begin.

You do not need conditions.

You need one step, taken today exactly as you are.

Celebrating Progress Nobody Sees

Some of the important progress in your life will happen where no one is watching.

No praise.

No audience.

No proof to show the world.

Just you, showing up again on a day when it would have been easier not to.

We are taught to celebrate finish lines. Launches, promotions, publications and achievements that tell everyone we have arrived somewhere.

Long before any finish line exists there is a quieter kind of progress.

The version of you who kept practicing after the excitement faded.

The version of you who kept trying after the first attempt failed.

The version of you who returned to the task even when it felt unimportant.

That version of you deserves to be celebrated.

Not always with a crowd. With your own support.

A quiet note that says:

"I am becoming something even if I cannot see it yet."

The seed does not stop growing just because no one is watching it beneath the soil.

Neither should you.

Consistency Over Speed

We like speed because it is easy to see.

But it is consistency, not speed that builds things that last.

Speed is a run.

Consistency is a habit.

Speed asks, "How fast can I get there?"

Consistency asks, "Can I still be doing this a year from now?"

A single burst of energy can carry you for a week.

It cannot carry you for a lifetime.

What carries you for a lifetime is something steadier than energy.

It is discipline. The choice to keep showing up on days you do not want to do the thing again just because you know it is important.

The people who build lasting things are rarely the fastest.

They are the ones who refuse to stop.

One sentence a day becomes a book.

One repetition becomes strength.

One conversation becomes a relationship.

One small effort, repeated without giving up becomes a life you're proud of.

It is not about how you move.

It is about whether you keep moving all.

Trusting the Process

There will be a time in the middle of anything building where it feels like nothing is happening.

The early excitement has gone.

The results have not come yet.

All that remains is the hard work of continuing anyway.

This is the part where many people give up.

Not because they lack skill.

Not because the dream was wrong.

Because they think the quiet middle is a dead end instead of seeing it for what it is. The space between starting and becoming.

Trusting the process means keeping watering the seed when the soil looks the same as it did yesterday.

It means believing that roots are growing even when you cannot see them.

Because results are always the thing to appear, never the first.

The process was never broken because it was slow.

It was just working below the surface.

Where Small Beginnings Lead

One day you will look back at where you started.

It will look impossible small compared to where you are now.

You will remember the page before the book.

The first customer before the business.

The first small decision before the life it created.

You will realize that none of it happened suddenly.

It happened one step at a time.

Most of those steps were so quiet that you barely noticed you were making progress.

That is how everything meaningful is built.

Not with one jump but with thousands of small starts. Each one too small to seem impressive on its own yet each one completely needed.

So if all you have today is one step, take it.

Not because it will change everything tomorrow.

Because it is the only way anything has ever changed.

Start small.

Stay consistent.

Trust what you cannot yet see.

The beginning was never supposed to look like the ending.

It was only meant to be the step toward becoming who you are meant to be..

title: IF I COULD GO BACK TO THE VERY FIRST DAY I MET YOU…
excerpt: The Other Family
content:
“Kunle, what else is there?”

He looked at me for a moment before shaking his head.

“Bola, Teni is trying to destroy my life.”

I stared at him.

“Then why does she keep saying you haven’t told me the truth?”

“Because she wants you to believe whatever she says.”

I picked up my phone and opened Teni’s chat.

Me: What truth are you talking about?

Her reply came almost immediately.

Teni: I need to show you something.

Before I could respond, Kunle spoke.

“Bola, please. You don’t understand what you’re getting yourself into.”

I looked up at him.

“Then help me understand.”

He said nothing.

My phone buzzed.

Teni had sent a picture.

I opened it.

And just like that, I felt my entire world shift.

It was Kunle.

Standing beside a woman, his arm wrapped around her. Two children stood in front of them, smiling at the camera.

I zoomed in.

It was definitely him.

The caption read:

Happy Father’s day to amazing husband and the best daddy to our babies. We love you.

I checked the date.

Three months ago.

My hands began to shake.

I turned the phone towards him.

“Kunle… who are these people?”

He glanced at the picture.

For a moment, he didn’t say anything.

Then he reached for my phone.

“Give me that.”

I pulled it away.

“No. Answer me first.”

“Bola, give me the phone.”

“Who is that woman? Who are those children?”

He grabbed my wrist.

“Stop this!”

I froze.

Not because of what he said, but because of the way he was holding me.

“Kunle. Let go of me.”

He held on for another second before releasing me.

I stepped back, staring at him.

He looked at my wrist, then at me.

“Bola, I didn’t mean to—”

“Don’t touch me.”

The room went quiet.

This was the man who always asked if I had eaten. The man who checked on me, who made sure I got home safely, who could never go a day without telling me how much he loved me.

And now, I was standing in front of him, afraid of what he might do next.

My phone buzzed again.

Teni: That’s not even the worst part.

I swallowed.

Me: What do you mean?

Her reply came.

Teni: There are two children. And that woman isn’t the first one.

I stared at the message.

There were two children.

And apparently, there had been other women.

I looked at Kunle, who was now pacing around the room.

“Is there anything else you want to tell me?”

He rubbed his face.

“Bola, please. Just let me explain.”

“Explain what? That you have another family? That you were married to Teni when you married me? Or that there are even more women I don’t know about?”

He didn’t answer.

I picked up my bag.

“Where are you going?” he asked.

“Somewhere I can think.”

“Bola, don’t do this.”

I walked past him.

This time, he didn’t stop me.

⸻

I spent the night at my friend’s place.

I barely slept.

Every time I closed my eyes, I saw that picture.

Kunle. Another woman. Two children.

A whole life I knew nothing about.

At some point in the night, my phone lit up.

It was Teni.

She had sent a screenshot.

I opened it.

It was a conversation between her and Kunle from before my wedding.

I read it once.

Then again.

Kunle: Just keep quiet about Bola. I’ll handle everything.

I stared at the screen.

He knew.

He knew about me. He knew what he was hiding. And he had made sure Teni kept quiet.

I thought about the wedding day.

I remembered Teni.

The way she had looked at me. The way she had tried to warn me about Kunle, even when I didn’t understand what she was talking about.

Back then, I thought she was just another woman from his past, someone who couldn’t let him go.

Kunle had given me an explanation, and I had chosen to believe him.

Now, I was looking at proof that he had been hiding an entire life from me.

I didn’t know what hurt more—the lies, the other family, or the fact that I had defended him when someone tried to warn me.

I locked my phone and stared into the darkness.

For the first time since I met Kunle, I wasn’t wondering how to save my marriage.

I was wondering how much of my life with him had ever been real.

To be continued…

title: WHY SO MANY YOUNG NIGERIANS FEEL LIKE THEY'RE RUNNING OUT OF TIME (And What's Actually Going On)
excerpt: Following the manual the society drafted
content:
Have you been in that position whereby you check your phone, someone from secondary school just posted their traditional wedding. Another just got a Canada visa. Someone you used to be better than at everything now has a house project on ground. And you're still here, refreshing job portals, doing the math on your age, wondering when exactly you fell behind and whether everyone else got a memo you missed.

If you have ever lain in bed at 11pm doing silent calculations, if I get a job by next year, and I save for two years, and I meet someone in year three....this one is for you.

WHY AM I STILL "NOT THERE YET" WHILE MY MATES ARE GETTING MARRIED, RELOCATING, OR LANDING BIG JOBS?

It rarely hits you all at once. It creeps in through small moments, a group chat announcement, a "congratulations" comment section you scroll through twice, a cousin's introduction party you attend with a smile that doesn't reach your eyes.

The truth nobody says out loud, you're not comparing your whole life to theirs. You're comparing your behind-the-scenes, the rejected applications, the business that has not picked up, the relationship that ended quietly to their highlight reel. That's not a fair fight, and it never was.

IS IT NORMAL TO FEEL BEHIND AT 24, 26, 28?

Yes. Painfully, boringly normal. Almost everyone in their twenties in Nigeria right now is running some version of this math in their head, salary versus rent, age versus "settling down," CV versus classmates who japa'd.

What's not normal is treating this feeling as evidence. Feeling behind is not proof that you are behind. It's proof that you were handed a timeline nobody actually agreed to, and you're now grading yourself against it in private, without telling anyone the rules feel impossible.

THE WHAT'SAPP STATUS EFFECT: How Social Media Quietly Convinced You That You're Failing

Here's what's actually happening when you scroll, you are watching curated announcements from hundreds of people, compressed into a single feed, with none of the boring middle parts included. Nobody posts the eighteen months before the wedding when the relationship almost ended. Nobody posts the three failed businesses before the one that worked. Nobody posts the loan.

Your brain wasn't built to process that many "wins" from that many people in one sitting. It was built for a village of maybe 150 people, where you'd know the full story behind every milestone. Now you get the milestone with none of the story, on a loop, every day.

Nobody Tells You This, the Timeline You're Chasing Was Never Real. Here's the part that stings a little: the "normal" timeline: degree by 22, job by 24, marriage by 27, house by 30 was not handed down by God. It was assembled from your parents' generation, church expectations, extended family pressure, and now, social media's highlight reel, all mixed together into something that feels universal but was never actually agreed on by anyone.

Your uncle who "made it" by 30 was working in a completely different economy. Your parents got married young in a system where that made more financial sense than it does now. The timeline you're panicking about missing was built for conditions that no longer exist.

Why "I Should Have Figured Life Out By Now" Is a Lie Your Environment Sold You

Motivation is not your biggest problem. Your environment might be. Think about it honestly, if you are surrounded by people constantly announcing engagements, relocations, and promotions, of course you'll feel like you're standing still even while you are actually moving. The comparison is not coming from inside you first; it's coming from what you're marinating in daily. Change what you're consuming, the accounts, the group chats, the conversations that leave you anxious and watch how much of that "I'm behind" feeling was actually just noise.

HOW TO STOP MEASURING YOUR LIFE WITH SOMEONE ELSE'S CALENDAR

You don't need a new year. You need a system. Track your own inputs, not their outputs. You can't see what someone did to get their result, only the result. Focus on what you are actually doing weekly, applications sent, skills practiced, money saved. That's the only data that's real to you. Set a personal timeline, on paper, that only you can see. Not to please anyone but to give your brain a target that is not borrowed from a wedding album. Mute what makes you spiral. Muting isn't jealousy. It's protecting your peace so you can actually think straight about your own life.

WHAT ACTUALLY HELPS WHEN THE PRESSURE FEELS LIKE IT'S CRUSHING YOU

Talk to someone, a friend, not just the group chat where everyone's performing. Say the quiet thing out loud: "I feel like I should be further than this." You'll be surprised how many people carrying the exact same weight have just been too ashamed to say it first. You're not late. You're not behind. You're on a timeline nobody else can see and that's exactly how it's supposed to be.

If this sounds like your 11pm thoughts, drop a comment, you're not the only one doing this math in your head. Share this with the friend who keeps saying "I should be further by now."

title: Apple Finally Launches Its First Foldable iPhone — Here’s Everything You Need to Know about
excerpt: Apple has finally entered the foldable smartphone market with the launch of the iPhone Duo, its first foldable iPhone.The company unveiled the device on Septemb…
content:
Apple has finally entered the foldable smartphone market with the launch of the iPhone Duo, its first foldable iPhone.

The company unveiled the device on September 9, 2026, introducing a new design that combines the portability of a regular smartphone with the larger screen of a tablet.

The launch is a major step for Apple, which has stayed out of the foldable phone market while companies such as Samsung, Huawei and Xiaomi have continued to develop the technology.

With a starting price of $1,999, the iPhone Duo is clearly positioned as a premium device. But beyond its high price, Apple is hoping its combination of design, performance, artificial intelligence and productivity features will convince consumers that foldable phones are ready for the mainstream.

The iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone. Unlike traditional iPhones, the device opens horizontally like a small book.

When closed, it has a 5.4-inch outer display that allows users to handle everyday tasks without opening the phone. When unfolded, it reveals a much larger 7.6-inch inner display.

Apple says the inner screen is the largest display ever used on an iPhone and is designed for activities such as gaming, watching videos, browsing the web and multitasking.

The company has also redesigned iOS 27 to take advantage of the foldable design. Apps and content can adjust as users open, close or reposition the device.

A Design Built for Portability and Productivity

One of the biggest selling points of foldable phones is the ability to carry a large screen without carrying a large device.

Apple is taking the same approach with the iPhone Duo.

When folded, the phone is compact enough to fit into a pocket while still providing a usable outer display. When opened, the 7.6-inch screen provides considerably more space for reading, entertainment and work.

Apple has also introduced multitasking features that allow users to place two apps side by side.

For example, someone could browse the web while taking notes, respond to messages while viewing a document, or use one side of the screen for information while working on the other.

This could make the iPhone Duo particularly interesting to students, professionals, content creators and people who regularly work from their phones.

The iPhone Duo features two Super Retina XDR displays.

The outer screen measures 5.4 inches, while the inner foldable screen measures 7.6 inches.

Apple says the inner display is 50% larger than the display on the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Both screens use the same aspect ratio so content can transition more naturally between the two displays.

The inner screen also uses a nano-texture finish designed to reduce glare and reflections.

The display supports ProMotion and Always-On functionality, while Apple says it can reach up to 3,000 nits of peak outdoor brightness.

Apple has also designed the folding display with additional protective layers and structural support aimed at improving durability.

Under the hood, the iPhone Duo is powered by Apple's new A20 Pro chip, the same processor used in the iPhone 18 Pro models.

The chip is built to handle demanding tasks, including gaming, multitasking and artificial intelligence workloads.

Apple says the A20 Pro has a six-core CPU and seven-core GPU, while its new Neural Engine is designed to provide significantly more processing power for on-device AI.

The phone also features an advanced thermal management system with a custom vapor chamber. This is important because foldable phones need to manage heat while running demanding applications across a larger display.

Artificial intelligence is another major part of Apple's strategy with the iPhone Duo.

The phone comes with Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, allowing users to interact with Apple's AI features while using other applications.

For example, users can ask Siri to help edit text while continuing to view content on another part of the screen.

Apple has also integrated AI into some of the phone's camera features. One example is Smart Take, which uses on-device AI to analyse a scene and automatically capture a photo when subjects are ready.

This shows how Apple is attempting to combine the foldable hardware with its growing AI ecosystem rather than simply creating a phone with a flexible screen.

Apple has also redesigned some camera experiences specifically for the Duo.

The phone comes with a 48MP Fusion Main camera and a 48MP Fusion Ultra Wide camera. It can record video in 4K at up to 120 frames per second with Dolby Vision.

One interesting feature is the ability to use the rear cameras to take selfies while using the outer screen as a preview.

This means users can take selfies using the higher-resolution rear cameras instead of relying only on a traditional front-facing camera.

The foldable design also allows users to prop the phone up for hands-free photography and video calls.

Apple is also bringing Apple Pencil support to the iPhone Duo.

According to Apple, support for Apple Pencil with USB-C is expected later this year. Users will be able to use it for activities such as taking notes, sketching and marking up documents on either display.

This adds another productivity feature to a device that Apple is already positioning as more than just a conventional smartphone.

The iPhone Duo uses a dual-battery architecture alongside Apple's new thermal management system.

Apple says the device is designed to provide all-day battery life while maintaining strong performance during demanding activities.

The A20 Pro chip is also designed to sustain performance during gaming, multitasking and AI processing.

For people who use their phones heavily for work or content creation, sustained performance could be one of the most important aspects of the device.

Apple is offering the iPhone Duo in several storage configurations.

The device starts with 256GB of storage, with higher-capacity options including 512GB, 1TB and 2TB.

The 2TB option is particularly aimed at users who store large amounts of photos, videos and other files on their devices.

How Much Does the iPhone Duo Cost?

The biggest concern for many potential buyers may be the price.

The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 in the United States for the 256GB model.

Apple is also offering higher-storage configurations, with the most expensive version reaching $3,199, according to Reuters.

For Nigerian buyers, the actual cost would likely be considerably higher after currency conversion, import costs, taxes and retailer margins.

That makes the iPhone Duo a luxury smartphone rather than a device aimed at the average smartphone buyer.

When Will the iPhone Duo Be Available?

Apple has announced that preorders for the iPhone Duo will begi o.n on October 16, 2026.

The phone will officially become available on October 23, 2026.

The device will initially be offered in two colours: Star White and Night Sky.

Apple vs Samsung in the Foldable Phone Market

Apple's entry into the foldable market comes several years after Samsung introduced its first Galaxy Fold in 2019.

Samsung currently has considerable experience in the category and has released multiple generations of foldable smartphones.

The competition is therefore going to be interesting.

Samsung's latest Galaxy Z Fold8 starts at $1,899, making Apple's $1,999 starting price even more noticeable.

Apple, however, has something Samsung cannot easily replicate: its enormous iPhone user base and tightly connected ecosystem of hardware and services.

The question is whether existing iPhone users will be willing to pay a significant premium to switch to a foldable model.

Apple's entry could have a major impact on the foldable smartphone industry.

For years, foldable phones have remained a relatively small part of the wider smartphone market because of high prices, durability concerns and limited consumer demand.

Apple's reputation and massive customer base could help bring more attention to the category.

The company has also had the advantage of watching other manufacturers develop foldable technology before entering the market.

Instead of being the first, Apple is entering at a time when the technology has already gone through several generations of development.

Is the iPhone Duo Worth $1,999?

That will ultimately depend on what a user needs from a smartphone.

For someone who wants a large screen, strong performance, AI features, advanced cameras and the convenience of Apple's ecosystem, the iPhone Duo could be an attractive option.

However, its $1,999 starting price is difficult to ignore.

For many users, a conventional flagship smartphone combined with a tablet could offer a similar large-screen experience for less money.

The iPhone Duo is therefore likely to appeal most to technology enthusiasts, professionals, Apple fans and early adopters who are willing to pay for a completely different smartphone experience.

The iPhone Duo marks a significant change for Apple.

The company has finally moved into a smartphone category that competitors have been developing for years. Rather than simply copying existing foldable designs, Apple is combining its foldable hardware with iOS 27, Apple Intelligence, the A20 Pro chip and new multitasking features.

Whether the iPhone Duo becomes a mainstream success remains to be seen.

But one thing is already clear: Apple's entry has made the competition in the foldable smartphone market much more interesting.

With preorders beginning October 16 and sales starting October 23, consumers will soon have the opportunity to decide whether Apple's first foldable iPhone is worth its premium price.

title: Self-Teaching Without The Setup: What Nobody Talks About
excerpt: IntroductionHave you ever tried learning a skill and once you begin it feels like you’ve got this Vast ocean of knowledge staring back at you? This analogy is t…
content:
Introduction

Have you ever tried learning a skill and once you begin it feels like you’ve got this Vast ocean of knowledge staring back at you? This analogy is to portray how vast nature of self-studying. Guides on how to self-study are more of, just open that book, open that laptop… but what if you don’t have that laptop or that book or the constant internet or no power supply or a guided plan or that necessary resource?

Hurdles in self learning

Unlike traditional school where you’ve got a curriculum or a guided lesson, self-studying has this vast world of knowledge with no guidebook or a plan to navigate your way, you’re left to figure out what works best like; find a well explained course, course availability or even course approach. Let’s dive deeper and examine together the hurdles of self-studying.

1.    Low or no availability of resource tools: Most self-studying learners have this as their first hurdle, most have to figure ways around it and often without a structured plan. Common problems include, power supply, program tools, or device issues; not having a phone, laptop or internet. In a scenario where you need to learn SQL and you don’t have a laptop to perform, or not able to access an online course. This scenario makes it difficult for you to keep learning and put a strain to effective studies.

2.    Too much information and no clear starting point: Due to the vast amount of information on a program or course, most self-taught students take a strain in finding the right material for the right program or course. You can see course that contradicts each other and you can’t figure which to trust or learn from.

3.    Financial constraints: Most well explanatory course with a guided track plan mostly in premium package and then self-studying learners are now forced to finding the perfect free course or program. Apps like Coursera, Udemy, LinkedIn learning  for example needs you to have monthly subscription or purchasing the course or program individually and it’s believed that this platform gives the best course but because of low financing, self-studying learners are have to find free resources which comes with there own setbacks.

4.    Slow or no visible progress: This has been my major hurdle, speaking personally, I can’t seem to learn without seeing progress in what I learnt. Imagine  sitting for months and still not know how to navigate and apply what you’ve learnt. Apparently, application leads to better outcomes, like how generative AI needs to be fine-tuned for better outcome that’s ow the human brain needs to apply knowledge to increase understanding and knowledge of a subject.

Navigating these hurdles.

I cannot say there’s a pre-determined navigation of this hurdle but with a consistent mind and active believe we can make a light shine inside a the tunnel without waiting for the light at the end of the tunnel. Let’s look at what can potentially be done to pave way in this hurdles;

1.    Financial support: This is the hardest but one thing I can’t take of this list. If you’ve got a financial support there’s a way to get professional learning process that doesn’t only make a structured plan but gives you a medium to track growth. I engage my self now in a learning while earning goal for me to save up to create funding for my advance learning.

2.    Setting up bit size goals: In a long run bit goals helps to accomplish broad objectives. By setting up bit size goals you can overcome the hurdles of Too much information and no clear starting point. As you accomplish one goal it affects the other and that’s what I want to start doing now,

3.    Constant practice: I fall short here as each time I want to practice I lose the ability to think of a project but I got to find out after seeing how messy my learning life is, I want to take my time by constantly practicing with the little I know, the more you practice the faster your mastery. This isn’t an easy part but it’s here because a lot of self-studying learners have a hard time practicing themselves, and that’s is why we need a built plan  for study and practice.

Conclusion

I'm flawed in every way but I believe there may be learners who experience what I'm experiencing and it would be nice sharing my experience. You can make everything work, is all I can say to myself and everyone who's like me right now, and I urge you not to give up in the pursuit of knowledge. I don't have it figured out yet but I'm still here, still learning, still showing up with whatever I've got that day. After hearing the testimony of self-taught data analyst Alex Freberg, known on YouTube as Alex The Analyst, I found inspiration in what he achieved. I admire him and hope to make the breakthrough in my career like he did. If that's you too then keep going.

title: Did Apple Just Enter Samsung's Game?
excerpt: The foldable phone race just got a little more interesting.
content:
Apple finally has a foldable iPhone. And honestly, I can't help but wonder: did Apple just enter Samsung's game?

Samsung has been making foldable phones for years. We watched the company experiment with the Galaxy Fold, improve it with every generation, and slowly make foldable phones feel less strange.

Now Apple has joined the party. What's interesting is that Apple is usually the company people associate with setting trends. But with foldable phones, Samsung got there first. Samsung has been doing this since 2019, while Apple is only just stepping in.

And Samsung has noticed.

The company has already taken a few playful shots at Apple, basically reminding everyone that it has been folding phones for years. It's funny, but it also shows how seriously Samsung is taking Apple's arrival.

Because let's be honest, once Apple enters a category, people start paying even more attention to it.

Suddenly, it's not just about having a foldable phone anymore. It's Apple versus Samsung. Which one looks better? Which one is actually worth the money? Which company did it better?

But I'm more curious about something else. Does Apple really need to be first to win?

Probably not.

Samsung has the head start and years of experience with foldables. Apple has something different: the iPhone name, a massive user base and an ecosystem that keeps people coming back.

So maybe this isn't really about who invented the foldable phone first. Maybe it's about who can make people look at their current phone and suddenly feel like they need a new one.

And if there's one thing Apple has always been good at, it's that.

So, who do you think has the upper hand: Apple or Samsung?

title: 100MB for Every Student, Says Nigerian Government
excerpt: NCC Partners Ministry of Education to Launch Free Daily Data for Students From October 1
content:
Come October 1, millions of Nigerian students will no longer have to choose between buying data and studying online the Federal Government says it's picking up part of that bill.

The Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC), working with the Federal Ministry of Education, has announced the Initiative for Zero-Rated Access to Educational Platforms and Content in Nigeria , a plan to give eligible students 100 megabytes of free data every single day, at no cost, to access approved learning platforms. Here's everything you need to know.

Who is it for?

The first phase targets students in public senior secondary schools and public tertiary institutions. Officials say it will later expand to cover other categories of learners, though no specific age limit has been publicly announced eligibility is tied to being enrolled in a covered public institution, not age itself.

What exactly are students getting?

100MB of zero-rated data daily meaning it won't be deducted from a student's regular data bundle or charged at all but only for use on whitelisted educational platforms approved jointly by the NCC and the Ministry of Education. It is not general purpose internet data.

When does it start?

October 1, 2026 is the official commencement date, announced by the Minister of Education, Dr. Tunji Alausa, at the initiative's launch in Abuja.

Where does it apply?

Nationwide, rolled out through participating network operators, with coverage expected to expand progressively beyond the initial phase.

Why is the government doing this?

To remove data cost as a barrier to digital learning particularly for students from low-income households and underserved communities who may own a smartphone but can't consistently afford data to use it for schoolwork.

How will it work and how do students register?
