Participating mobile network operators MTN Nigeria, Airtel Nigeria, and Globacom will provide the daily 100MB allowance under what the NCC calls an "operator consult model." However, no official registration portal or application process has been released yet. Students are advised to watch for guidance from their schools, the NCC, and the Ministry of Education and to be wary of anyone requesting payment, since the government has confirmed there is no registration fee.

title: Why Does the “Igbo Woman” Conversation Keep Coming Back?
excerpt: A conversation about abuse, househelps, culture and the uncomfortable stereotypes we keep repeating.
content:
Another disturbing video involving a woman and her child has been making the rounds, and, as expected, the conversation quickly moved beyond the woman herself.

It became: “Igbo women again.” and honestly, I have been thinking about that.

Because this is not the first time Nigerians have had this conversation. We have seen disturbing stories involving Igbo women and their house helps, domestic workers and, sometimes, their own children. Then there are cases involving women from other parts of Nigeria too.

So what exactly are we looking at here? Are Igbo women really more abusive, or have we created a stereotype from a number of highly publicised cases?

I don't think it is fair to say that Igbo women are naturally more wicked or abusive. That is an entire group of women being judged because of the actions of individuals.

But I also don't think the answer should be to shut down the conversation whenever someone brings up the pattern, because there is something worth talking about.

In some Nigerian homes, especially when it comes to house helps, there is a disturbing difference between “this child works for me” and “this child is still a human being.”

A house help can be shouted at for everything, beaten for things your own child would probably get a warning for, overworked and treated like they are lucky to even be in the house.

And sometimes, we call it discipline, sometimes we call it culture, we even simply say, “That's how we were raised.”

But not everything we were raised with deserves to be passed down, and this conversation shouldn't stop at Igbo women either.

Why do some parents become extremely harsh with children they didn't give birth to? Why are some people kinder to strangers outside their homes than to the vulnerable people living under their roof? Why do neighbours and relatives sometimes see things and decide it is “family matter”?

And perhaps most importantly, why does it take a viral video before everybody suddenly cares?

I think we can have this conversation without pretending every Igbo woman is abusive and without pretending there isn't a problem worth examining.

There are good Igbo women. There are abusive Igbo women. There are good Yoruba women, Hausa women, Efik women, and abusive ones too.

A person's tribe does not determine whether they have empathy, but if a particular stereotype keeps resurfacing, maybe instead of immediately shouting “tribalism,” we should at least ask why people have formed that perception in the first place.

The goal shouldn't be to drag Igbo women. It should be to get to a point where “Igbo woman and house help” stops being a story Nigerians already expect to hear.

Life is one of the greatest mysteries we will ever experience. We enter this world without knowing why we are here, where we are going, or what the future has prepared for us. We simply begin, surrounded by people who teach us how to walk, speak, dream, and understand the world around us. As we grow older, we slowly discover that life is not always the beautiful journey we imagined as children. There are days when everything feels possible, and there are days when even getting out of bed feels like a battle. There are moments filled with laughter, love, excitement, and hope, but there are also moments filled with disappointment, confusion, loneliness, and fear. Yet somehow, through all of these experiences, we continue moving forward. Perhaps that is one of the most powerful things about being alive: even when we do not understand the journey, something inside us keeps telling us to take another step.

Life teaches us lessons that no classroom can fully explain. Sometimes we learn through success, but many of our deepest lessons come through failure. We learn what matters when we lose something we once took for granted. We learn the value of people when someone genuinely stands beside us during difficult times. We learn about ourselves when the people we expected to stay suddenly walk away. There are moments when we may feel like we are falling behind everyone else, especially when we look around and see people achieving things we are still dreaming about. But life does not move according to one universal timetable. Someone may find success early, while another person may spend years searching for their direction before finally discovering it. Comparing our journey to someone else's can make us forget that our story is still being written. A chapter that looks empty today may become the foundation of something extraordinary tomorrow.

Comparing our journey to someone else's can make us forget that our story is still being written. A chapter that looks empty today may become the foundation of something extraordinary tomorrow.

One of the hardest truths about life is that not everyone will understand you. Some people will judge you based on what they see without knowing what you have survived. Some will laugh at dreams they cannot imagine achieving themselves. Some people will only recognize your value after you have already proven what you were capable of. That is why learning to believe in yourself is so important. You cannot build your entire life around the approval of other people because people change, opinions change, circumstances change, and sometimes even the people closest to you may not understand the vision inside your heart. This does not mean you should ignore advice or believe you are always right. It means you should learn to listen, think, grow, and still have enough courage to follow a path that genuinely matters to you. Your life belongs to you, and while other people may influence your journey, they should not be allowed to completely define it.

Time is another part of life that we often fail to appreciate until we realize how quickly it disappears. Yesterday eventually becomes a memory, today becomes yesterday, and tomorrow arrives before we are ready for it. We spend so much time worrying about what people think, regretting things we cannot change, and fearing things that have not happened yet that we sometimes forget to actually live. There is nothing wrong with planning for the future, but the future should not become a place where we postpone everything that makes life meaningful. Appreciate the people who care about you. Chase the dreams that matter to you. Learn new things. Make mistakes and learn from them. Laugh when you can. Create memories. Tell people you appreciate them while you still have the chance. One day, many of the things that seem extremely important today may become insignificant, while the small moments you barely noticed may become the memories you treasure most.

Dreams are another reason life is worth fighting through its difficult seasons. A dream does not guarantee an easy road. In fact, sometimes the bigger the dream, the more difficult the road becomes. There will be moments when you question whether you are talented enough, strong enough, prepared enough, or even meant to succeed. You may start something with confidence and later find yourself wondering whether you should quit. But progress is rarely as dramatic as we imagine. Sometimes progress is simply waking up and trying again. Sometimes it is practicing when nobody is watching, studying when nobody is praising you, creating when nobody is listening, or continuing after disappointment. The world may not recognize your effort immediately, but that does not make the effort meaningless. Every skill begins with someone being a beginner. Every achievement begins with an attempt. Every great story begins somewhere, often long before anyone knows the person's name.

In the end, life may not be about having everything figured out. It may be about becoming the person you were capable of becoming while experiencing everything the journey places in front of you. There will be people you meet who change your life, and there will be people you lose who leave lessons behind. There will be victories that make you proud and failures that humble you. There will be seasons when you feel unstoppable and seasons when you have to rebuild yourself quietly. But none of those seasons lasts forever. The important thing is to keep learning, keep growing, keep your heart open to meaningful experiences, and keep moving toward the future you want to create. You do not need to know every step today. Sometimes you only need enough courage to take the next one. title: The Truth Was Always Watching
excerpt:
I used to think losing my mother was the worst thing that could ever happen to me.

I was wrong.

The worst thing was believing that, after losing her, I had lost my father too.

I was only ten when my mother's blood stained the floor beneath me.

I remember the cupboard.

I remember the darkness.

And I remember the sound of gunshots.

Bang!

Bang!

Bang!

Each shot tore through the room, followed by my mother's cry. I pressed both hands over my mouth, terrified that even the slightest sound would give away my hiding place.

I could see her through the narrow opening between the cupboard doors.

She staggered backwards.

Another gunshot rang through the house.

My mother clutched her chest, blood spreading across her clothes. Her knees weakened, and she slowly sank to the floor.

Then her eyes found mine.

For one terrible second, everything became still.

She knew where I was.

Her lips parted, but no words came out.

Tears slipped down her cheeks as she stared at me, and somehow, even with death taking the strength from her body, I knew what she was telling me.

Stay hidden.

Don't come out.

I bit down on my hand to stop myself from screaming.

My mother's eyes slowly closed.

She was gone.

But the men did not leave.

They searched the entire house, throwing things aside and opening every door. Their footsteps grew closer to the cupboard, and I could barely breathe.

One of them stopped.

My heart nearly stopped with him.

He opened another cabinet.

Then another.

But he never opened mine.

When they found nothing, they poured something across the floor.

A moment later, flames rose.

The house was burning.

Smoke filled the cupboard, and my lungs began to tighten. I could no longer feel my fingers. My body trembled uncontrollably as the heat grew stronger.

I was going to die there.

Just like my mother.

Then, through the smoke, I heard someone shouting my name.

"Julian!"

My father's voice.

The cupboard door was ripped open.

My father pulled me into his arms and carried me out of the burning house.

I remember looking over his shoulder.

I remember seeing my mother's body disappear behind the flames.

Then everything went black.

When I opened my eyes again, I was in my grandmother's house.

There was no hospital.

My grandmother treated me herself.

And when I was strong enough to ask for my father, he was already gone.

He never came back.

Not once.

Flowers arrived.

Gifts arrived.

Letters sometimes arrived.

But my father never did.

As the years passed, I began to wonder whether he blamed me.

Maybe he thought I should have protected my mother.

Maybe he thought I had failed her.

Maybe he simply didn't want me anymore.

"Grandma," I cried whenever the loneliness became too much. "I want to see my dad."

She would hold me tightly, but she never gave me the answer I wanted.

Instead, she trained me.

I learnt how to fight before I fully understood why I needed to.

I learnt how to move quickly, how to defend myself and how to use a gun.

My father had assigned a kung-fu master to train me.

Another man taught me how to handle firearms.

I was being raised like a warrior while everyone around me pretended it was normal.

Even my identity was kept hidden.

At ten years old, I did not understand any of it.

I only understood that my mother was dead.

And my father was gone.

For years, I hated him for it.

Then, on my eighteenth birthday, everything changed.

A package arrived from my father.

My heart jumped when I saw his name.

For the first time in years, I thought he was finally coming for me.

Instead, there was an envelope.

Inside it was a flash drive and a handwritten note.

My father's handwriting.

I stared at it for a long time.

He had promised that one day he would explain everything.

Why my mother died.

Why he had stayed away from me.

Why he had sent me to my grandmother.

Why he could only love me from a distance.

But I never opened the note.

I was angry.

If my father had something to say to me, he should say it to my face.

I didn't want an explanation written on a piece of paper.

I wanted him.

So I left.

I went looking for my father.

I didn't know that the moment I stepped out of my grandmother's house, someone was already watching me.

The news reached my father before I could get very far.

His daughter was gone.

He immediately began searching for me.

But by the time I reached the train station, I had a much bigger problem.

They found me first.

The men stepped out from different directions.

Black clothes.

Covered faces.

Guns in their hands.

My blood ran cold.

I knew those masks.

I had seen them once before.

Ten years ago.

The night my mother died.

One of them raised his gun.

I moved before he could pull the trigger.

My body reacted almost instinctively.

I ducked.

The bullet flew past my head.

I kicked the gun from his hand and drove my elbow into his chest.

Another man rushed towards me.

I turned.

Blocked his attack.

Then struck him hard enough to send him crashing to the ground.

Another came.

Then another.

There were too many of them.

But I had spent years preparing for this moment without even knowing it.

One by one, they fell.

By the time I heard hurried footsteps behind me, most of the men were already on the ground.

I turned.

My father stood several feet away.

He stared at me.

For the first time in my life, I saw something I had never seen in his eyes before.

Pride.

A small smile appeared on his face.

He walked towards me.

I wanted to remain angry.

I had spent years telling myself that I hated him.

But the moment he opened his arms, all those years of anger suddenly felt fragile.

I had missed him.

More than I wanted to admit.

I stepped into his arms.

He held me tightly.

And for the first time since my mother's death, I felt like I had my father back.

Then I heard it.

Bang!

My father's body jerked in my arms.

His weight suddenly collapsed against me.

"Dad?"

I caught him before he hit the ground.

Blood spread across his back.

My eyes widened.

A sniper.

The security officers at the station immediately sprang into action. Some ran towards the direction of the shot while others surrounded us.

My father gripped my arm.

"Run," he whispered.

"What?"

"Run, Julian."

"No!"

"Leave no trace."

I shook my head violently.

"No, Dad. You need a hospital."

"They'll find you."

"Who?"

His breathing became weaker.

"They're all..." He coughed, blood staining his lips. "They're all in..."

"In what?"

His eyes struggled to remain open.

"The letter."

My heart stopped.

"The letter?"

He nodded faintly.

"They're... in the letter."

"Dad, please. Save your strength. You can tell me everything later."

His fingers tightened around mine.

"I love you, sweetheart."

Tears filled my eyes.

"Don't say that. You're going to be fine."

"Don't... try saving me."

"There is no way I'm letting you die."

I screamed towards the security officers.

"Call an ambulance!"

For a few seconds, everything became a blur.

Then the sound of the ambulance siren pierced through the station.

"Please!" I shouted as the paramedics rushed towards us. "Over here! My father has been shot!"

They placed him on a stretcher.

I followed them, still holding his bloodstained hand.

But as they lifted him into the ambulance, his eyes suddenly opened.

He looked directly at me.

There was fear in his eyes.

Not for himself.

For me.

"Julian..."

"I'm here."

His lips moved, but the words were barely audible.

"Whatever you do..."

He swallowed painfully.

"Don't let them get you."

The ambulance doors slammed shut.

And as the siren began to fade into the distance, I finally understood one thing.

My father hadn't stayed away from me because he hated me.

He had been running from someone.

Someone who had been hunting my family for ten years.

And whatever was inside that letter...

was the reason they had finally found me.
content: Julian thought her father abandoned her after her mother's murder. But when she finally goes looking for him, the same masked men who killed her mother come after her. After a sniper shoots her father, Julian is forced to uncover the dangerous secret hidden in the letter she refused to read.

title: Copy of It took less time than it takes to read this sentence for the Emirates to fall silent — then 89 minutes for it to roar back
excerpt: The 77-Second Lead: How Chelsea's Fastest Start of the Season Became Their Cruelest Defeat
content:
Arsenal came from behind to beat Chelsea 2-1 at the Emirates — a game that says more about resilience than talent, and a reminder that fast starts don't guarantee finishes.

Seventy-seven seconds. That's all it took. Chelsea hadn't even settled into their shape, Arsenal fans hadn't finished their first chant, and the ball was already in the back of the net. A gorgeous, first-time volley that sent the away end into delirium and the home crowd into stunned silence. For a moment, it looked like Xabi Alonso's Chelsea were about to hand Mikel Arteta his first defeat of the season on his own turf. Then Arsenal did what champions do. They didn't panic. They didn't rush. They simply took the game apart, piece by piece, until the scoreline read exactly the opposite of how it started. By full time, this had turned into one of the most gripping 90 minutes London football has produced all season — and a match that says a lot about what actually wins games.

*Reason: The perfect start can lull you into a false sense of security.*

Chelsea's opening goal was as good as it gets — a slick move finished with real quality. But football has a cruel habit of punishing teams who mistake an early lead for a finished job. Arsenal barely blinked. They spent the rest of the half figuring out Chelsea's shape, testing their spaces, and probing for the equalizer that felt, even at 0-1, somehow inevitable.

*Reason: Championship-level teams respond, they don't retreat.*

Kai Havertz leveled things midway through the first half — fittingly, against his former club — and from there Arsenal's control of the game only grew. Pedro Neto rattled the post for Chelsea right before the break, a reminder they were still very much alive in this one. But Arsenal came out of halftime with intent, and five minutes into the second period, Martin Ødegaard finished off a gorgeous dummy from Havertz to make it 2-1.

*Reason: The best games are won in the moments that don't show up on the scoresheet.*

What made this one special wasn't just the goals — it was everything in between. Emiliano Martínez pulling off a wonder save to deny Bukayo Saka. David Raya somehow doing him one better to keep out a certain goal. Chelsea refusing to fold, pushing men forward, giving their manager's first away test against a title rival everything they had, right up to the final whistle.

Arsenal walk away still perfect through three games, level on points with Manchester City at the top. Chelsea leave with nothing but the frustrating knowledge that for 76 minutes, they were the better story — and for the final 14, they weren't.

*The takeaway:*in football, as in most things worth watching, it's never about who starts fastest — it's about who's still standing when the final whistle blows.

title: The Champions League Is Back, and It Already Feels Like Magic
excerpt: Two nights, twelve matches, and that unmistakable Tuesday-night (well, midweek) feeling returns to Europe
content:
There's a specific kind of electricity that comes back every September — the anthem, the flags unfurling around the stadium bowl, the sense that for the next nine months, nothing on a football calendar matters quite as much as a Champions League night. This week, it returned in full force. Over two matchdays, Wednesday and Thursday, the competition reminded everyone why it's the most romanticized stage in club football.

The story of Wednesday: Barcelona and PSG remind us why they're feared

Barcelona put on a show at home, beating Feyenoord 5-1, with Raphinha weaving through defenders off a Lamine Yamal assist as the highlight of the rout. Across the continent, Paris Saint-Germain — chasing a third straight crown — were even more ruthless, hammering Slovan Bratislava 6-1 to announce, again, that they intend to be the team to beat. Liverpool ground out a tighter 2-1 win over Atlético Madrid, the kind of gritty European night Anfield specializes in, while Sporting CP saw off Galatasaray 3-1 and Stuttgart handled Viking 3-1. The upset of the night belonged to Arsenal, who traveled to Napoli and stole all three points with a slender 1-0 win — the sort of result that can define a European campaign in hindsight.

The story of Thursday: goals, goals, and more goals

If Wednesday was about the giants flexing, Thursday was chaos and cutting edge. Bayern Munich obliterated Bodø/Glimt 5-0, Manchester United put four past Sabah without reply, and Como — yes, Como — put four past RB Leipzig in a 4-1 statement win that nobody saw coming. Elsewhere, the drama was tighter: Fenerbahçe and Roma shared the points in a 1-1 draw, PSV Eindhoven and Shakhtar Donetsk did the same, and Lens came from behind to beat Slavia Prague 3-2 in the day's best late twist.

Why this matters for the season ahead

Two matchdays in, the league-phase format is already doing what it was built to do: every match carries weight, every table position matters, and there's no room to hide. The giants (PSG, Barcelona, Bayern, Liverpool) have served early notice, but the so-called smaller sides — Como, Lens, Arsenal away at Napoli — have already shown that shock results are part of the competition's DNA. That's the beauty of it: on paper, it's the best 36 teams in Europe, but on the pitch, September nights have a habit of humbling anyone.

The joy of it all!!!

There's something almost ritualistic about the Champions League's return — the same clubs, the same rivalries reignited, but always new heroes emerging from nowhere. It's not just about who wins; it's about the feeling. The nervous energy of a last-minute winner. The away days in cities most fans will never otherwise visit. The shared, collective gasp when a team like Como scores four against a European heavyweight. Every September, football fans get handed the same gift: nine months of stories nobody could have scripted, building toward a single final that decides who becomes part of the competition's history. The Champions League doesn't just bring back football — it brings back the feeling that anything can happen on any given night. And two matchdays in, it's already delivering.

title: When You Stop Explaining Yourself To Everyone
excerpt: Not everyone needs to understand your choices for them to be right for you
content:
There was a time when I thought I had to explain myself.

If I said no, I needed to explain why.

If I changed my mind, I needed to explain what happened.

If I made a decision that someone didn't agree with, I felt almost obligated to make them understand.

Sometimes, I wasn't even looking for advice.

I just wanted them to understand me.

I wanted them to know that I wasn't being difficult. I wasn't trying to hurt anyone. I wasn't making a careless decision.

So I explained.

And explained.

And sometimes, even after explaining everything I could, I still felt misunderstood.

Looking back, I realize how exhausting that was.

Because there comes a point where you're no longer explaining yourself.

You're trying to convince someone that you're allowed to make your own choices.

And those are two very different things.

Why Do We Feel the Need to Explain Everything?

I think a lot of it comes from wanting to be understood.

Nobody enjoys being misunderstood, especially by people we love.

When someone gets the wrong idea about us, our first instinct can be to correct the story.

"That's not what I meant."

"You don't understand."

"Let me explain what really happened."

And sometimes, explaining is necessary.

There are moments when communication matters. We have responsibilities. We make mistakes. We hurt people. When our actions affect someone else, we should be willing to talk about them.

But there is a difference between explaining because communication matters and explaining because you're afraid someone won't approve of you.

That difference can be difficult to recognize.

Sometimes we keep talking because we're hoping that if we give someone enough reasons, they'll finally say, “Okay, I understand. You're right.”

But what happens when they don't?

You explain a little more.

Then a little more.

Until you're exhausted from defending a decision that you had already thought through before anyone questioned it.

You Can Explain Yourself and Still Be Misunderstood

This is one of the hardest things to accept.

You can choose your words carefully.

You can tell the whole story.

You can explain your intentions.

You can answer every question.

And someone may still misunderstand you.

Not because you explained badly.

Sometimes, people simply see your life through their own experiences, expectations, and beliefs.

Someone who would never make the choice you're making may struggle to understand why you made it.

Someone who values security may not understand why you chose uncertainty.

Someone who fears change may not understand why you're willing to take a different path.

And that's okay.

Understanding doesn't always have to be mutual.

You can respect someone's perspective without allowing their perspective to dictate your life.

Sometimes people have already decided what they think about you before you finish speaking.

And when you realize that, you stop trying so hard to control how everyone sees you.

You begin to understand something important:

Being misunderstood is uncomfortable, but it isn't always something you need to fix.

The Exhaustion of Seeking Approval

Imagine making a decision about your own life and immediately thinking about how everyone else will react.

"What will my friends say?"

"What will my family think?"

"Will people judge me?"

"What if they don't understand?"

You haven't even made the decision yet, but you're already preparing your defense.

That's exhausting.

You shouldn't have to hold a meeting in your head every time you make a personal choice.

Sometimes, you simply know that something is right for you.

You may have thought about it for weeks.

You may have prayed about it.

You may have considered the consequences.

You may have struggled with the decision before finally making it.

But someone who only sees the final decision may not know any of that.

And you don't always have to give them the entire history just to earn their approval.

Your decision doesn't become valid because someone else agrees with it.

It's Okay If Someone Doesn't Understand

There is a strange freedom that comes from accepting this.

Not everyone will understand you.

Some people will misunderstand your silence.

Some will misunderstand your boundaries.

Some will misunderstand your ambition.

Some will misunderstand why you walked away.

Some will misunderstand why you stayed.

And some people will create an explanation for your choices because they don't have the real one.

You can spend hours trying to correct every assumption.

Or you can accept that people are allowed to have their opinions.

Their opinion is theirs.

Your life is yours.

That doesn't mean you should become insensitive to how your actions affect others. It simply means you don't have to make yourself miserable trying to control every person's perception of you.

Accountability Is Not the Same as Over-Explaining

This distinction is important.

Choosing not to explain yourself doesn't mean you should become careless.

If you hurt someone, apologize.

If you make a mistake, own it.

If your actions affect someone else, communicate.

That's maturity.

But you don't have to defend every personal decision simply because someone doesn't like it.

There is a difference between saying:

“I understand that my actions affected you, and I'm willing to take responsibility.”

and saying:

“Please understand why I did this. Please understand why I chose this. Please understand that I'm not a bad person.”

The first is accountability.

The second can become a desperate search for approval.

Learning that difference can change the way you communicate with people.

You can take responsibility without begging to be understood.

You can apologize without abandoning your boundaries.

You can listen without automatically changing your decision.

Sometimes Peace Looks Like Saying Less

There comes a point where you realize that not every conversation needs to be won.

Not every misunderstanding needs a ten-paragraph explanation.

Not every opinion deserves a response.

Not every person needs access to every detail of your life.

Sometimes the healthiest response is simply:

“This is what I've decided.”

And then you leave it there.

No argument.

No essay.

No desperate attempt to convince someone.

Just peace.

At first, that kind of silence can feel strange if you're used to explaining yourself.

You may even feel guilty.

You might wonder whether you're being rude or selfish.

But there is a difference between being disrespectful and simply refusing to argue about your own life.

You can be kind and still have boundaries.

You can be respectful and still say no.

You can love someone and still make a decision they don't agree with.

Peace doesn't always come from being understood. Sometimes it comes from no longer needing to be.

You Don't Owe Everyone Access to Your Life

There are parts of your life that belong to you.

Your dreams.

Your boundaries.

Your fears.

Your healing.

Your plans.

Your next chapter.

You can share them with people you trust, but you don't have to put every personal decision on trial.

Not everyone who asks a question is entitled to the full answer.

That's something many of us learn slowly.

Sometimes we overshare because we feel that if people know the entire story, they'll judge us less.

But privacy isn't dishonesty.

You are allowed to keep some things to yourself.

You are allowed to say, “I'd rather not talk about that.”

You are allowed to change the subject.

You are allowed to protect something simply because it is personal.

There Is Freedom in Trusting Yourself

The goal isn't to become someone who doesn't care what anyone thinks.

That's not confidence.

We are human. We care about people. We value relationships. We listen when someone we trust gives us honest advice.

The goal is to become secure enough to listen without losing yourself.

To hear someone's opinion without immediately changing your decision.

To accept criticism without assuming you're wrong.

To admit when you've made a mistake without believing you're a failure.

And to make a choice simply because, after thinking it through, you believe it is right for you.

That's confidence.

Not having everyone agree with you.

But being okay when they don't.

Maybe You Don't Need to Explain Yourself This Time

Maybe you've been carrying the weight of someone's misunderstanding for too long.

Maybe you've been trying to convince someone that your intentions were good.

Maybe you've been explaining a decision you've already made over and over again.

Maybe you're tired of trying to prove that you're not the person someone has decided you are.

Take a breath.

Ask yourself:

“Am I explaining because this person deserves communication, or because I need their approval?”

The answer may tell you everything you need to know.

You are allowed to communicate.

You are allowed to apologize.

You are allowed to listen.

But you are also allowed to say less.

You are allowed to protect your peace.

You are allowed to make choices that others wouldn't make.

And you are allowed to walk away from the exhausting need to prove that your life makes sense.

Because at the end of the day, you are the one who has to live it.

Not everyone needs to understand your choices.

Not everyone needs to agree with them.

And not everyone needs a front-row seat to the reasoning behind them.

Sometimes, it is enough that you understand yourself.

Sometimes, choosing yourself means accepting that someone may never fully understand you.

And sometimes, the moment you stop explaining yourself to everyone is the moment you finally start listening to yourself.

You don't need permission to live a life that feels right to you. ✍️🤍

title: "You're getting older": the silent pressure to get married in Nigeria
excerpt: For many young women, questions about marriage can turn from casual family conversations into a source of anxiety, shame, and emotional exhaustion.
content:
“So, when are you getting married?”

For some Nigerian women, this sounds like an ordinary question.

For others, it is a question that becomes heavier every time they hear it.

It may come from a parent during a family gathering, an aunt at a wedding, a friend who recently got married, or even a stranger who believes marriage should already be part of a woman's life.

At first, she may laugh.

“Soon, by God's grace.”

But sometimes, behind that smile is anxiety, frustration, or even fear.

When a Simple Question Becomes Pressure

Marriage is an important part of life for many Nigerians. Many women genuinely want to get married, build a family, and share their lives with someone they love.

The problem is not necessarily the desire for marriage.

The problem begins when marriage becomes a deadline.

A woman may be working hard to build her career, trying to become financially independent, recovering from a difficult relationship, supporting her family, or simply trying to understand what she wants from life.

Yet, at family gatherings, the question remains:

“When will you marry?”

After a while, she may begin to feel that everything else she has achieved is being ignored because she is not married.

She can have a job.

She can have goals.

She can support her parents.

She can be educated, hardworking, kind, and successful.

But sometimes the question still becomes:

“You are doing all these things, but when are you bringing a husband home?”

The Comparison Trap

Social media can make the pressure even stronger.

One woman announces her engagement.

Another posts beautiful wedding pictures.

Someone else shares pictures of her newborn baby.

Before long, a woman who is still single may begin comparing her life with everyone else's.

She may start asking herself:

“Am I behind?”

“Is something wrong with me?”

“Why is everyone moving forward except me?”

But what we see online is usually only a small part of someone's life.

A beautiful wedding photograph does not show what happened before the wedding.

A smiling couple does not automatically mean they have a perfect relationship.

And being single does not mean that someone's life has stopped.

Everyone's journey has a different timeline.

The Danger of Marrying Just to Please People

Constant pressure can sometimes influence people to make decisions before they are ready.

A woman may begin considering a relationship not because she genuinely believes the person is right for her, but because she is afraid of getting older without a husband.

She may ignore warning signs because she thinks:

“At least I'm getting married.”

She may stay in an unhealthy relationship because leaving would mean starting over.

She may even accept a marriage that does not give her the emotional safety, respect, or compatibility she needs.

But marriage is a major life decision.

It should not be treated as a competition where the person who gets married first wins.

What About the Parents?

It is also important to understand that family pressure does not always come from a place of hatred or bad intentions.

Many parents worry about their daughters.

Some believe marriage provides companionship, family, security, or stability. Others grew up in environments where marriage was considered an essential part of adulthood.

Some parents may also worry about what society will say.

But good intentions can still create pressure.

Instead of repeatedly asking a woman why she is not married, families can ask different questions:

“How are you doing?”

“Are you happy?”

“How can we support you?”

“What are your plans for the future?”

These questions allow a woman to feel valued as a complete person rather than as someone waiting for marriage.

A Woman's Life Is Bigger Than Her Marital Status

Being married can be beautiful.

Being single can also be a meaningful part of life.

A woman's worth should not be measured by whether she has a husband.

She can build a career.

She can start a business.

She can care for her family.

She can develop her talents.

She can serve her community.

She can pursue her dreams.

And if she chooses marriage, she deserves the opportunity to enter it because she is ready—not simply because everyone around her is asking when it will happen.

Perhaps the question we should be asking young Nigerian women is not:

“When are you getting married?”

Maybe we should ask:

“What kind of life are you trying to build?”

Because marriage can be part of a woman's story.

It does not have to be the entire story.

What Do You Think?

Do you think young Nigerian women face too much pressure to get married?

Or do you believe that questions about marriage are simply part of Nigerian family and cultural expectations?

Share your thoughts in the comments.✨

title: The Scariest Thing Isn't Failing. It's Realizing You Never Tried.
excerpt: Nobody talks about the opportunities we lose because we were afraid.Not the ones we failed at.The ones we never even attempted.The application you almost submit…
content:
Nobody talks about the opportunities we lose because we were afraid.

Not the ones we failed at.

The ones we never even attempted.

The application you almost submitted.

The business idea sitting in your notes app.

The message you typed and deleted.

The article you wrote but never published because you thought, "Who would even read this?"

Fear is quiet like that.

It doesn't always tell you to quit.

Sometimes it simply tells you to wait.

"Start next month."

"Learn a little more first."

"Someone else can do it better."

And before you know it, months have turned into years.

Here's something I've learned.

Confidence doesn't come before action.

It comes because of action.

Nobody wakes up one morning magically believing in themselves.

They become confident by doing the scary thing over and over again until it no longer feels impossible.

The people you admire didn't begin because they had everything figured out.

They began because they were tired of wondering, "What if?"

Maybe you've been waiting for the perfect moment.

Maybe you've been waiting to feel ready.

Maybe you've convinced yourself that everyone else is somehow more talented.

They aren't.

The difference is that they started.

Today, someone will post their first video.

Someone will publish their first article.

Someone will launch a business with nothing but hope and determination.

And six months from now, people will call them "lucky."

They won't see the fear.

They'll only see the results.

So if there's something you've been putting off, don't ask yourself whether you're ready.

Ask yourself this:

How much longer are you willing to regret not trying?

Maybe today isn't the day everything changes.

But it could be the day you decide to change everything.

What is one thing you've been afraid to start? Share it in the comments. You never know who your story might encourage.

title: Hammertime at 24
excerpt: My first attempt at writing a normal non-bounty piece since I turned 23.
content:
Chainstellar said to have a core story, a beautiful story to tell, and it will guide and influence the quality of the work throughout.

He said it’s what works for him.

I do not think my story is beautiful. It’s a core story, but beautiful?

Nah! I don’t think so. “Beautiful” is relative. Also, I could say that not one thing in the universe is beautiful in itself. A thing is beautiful because something makes it beautiful.

Is there something in my story that’s beautiful? Who knows?

Well, in this piece, I am not trying to tell a beautiful story. I am putting down what happened - from when I turned 23 till now - and trusting that the pattern reveals itself.

That being said, I want you to have two closing lines in mind - by the time you’re done reading, you can pick which one is more suitable as the last line for this piece;

  1. “Remember who you are, mate”

  2. “Hogwarts, it’s Hammertime” (A duplicate of “Lewis, it’s Hammertime” - I’m sorry if you’re not familiar with Formula 1)

In the past five months, I've found several things interesting. One of them is genetic engineering, and how humans in a certain estate can “work” the brains of humans in a lesser estate to shape how they behave, what they do, and the resolve they create in their hearts.

I’ve seen sci-fi movies and shows, and watched how people get triggered by “something” they see in a place, which, when investigated, we find out they grew up in an environment where that “something” was prevalent.

The interesting part is that this is not fiction - I have seen it with my own eyes. The environment a person grows up in does not just shape their memories - it shapes the wiring of their brain, the chemicals their body learns to produce, and the instincts they carry into adulthood without ever questioning where those instincts came from.

Imagine walking with a lady, you both hear gunshots down the street, and the first thing she does is to remove her shoes and hold them in her hands… She’s seen things.

A child raised in lack learns to think small. Not because they chose to, but because the environment did the choosing for them. I know some of these things happen by accident, but joining the NYSC made me see and think that these things can also happen by someone’s design. Those in power have always known, even without the science to explain it, that you do not need chains to control a person if you can control what they believe about themselves.

In the strict biological sense, we agree that NYSC is not genetic engineering, but in the social engineering sense, NYSC is a plausible environment for what I am writing about. See this:

  • NYSC takes you at a post-adolescent age and puts you in a controlled, structured environment with uniforms, schedules, authority, and collective ritual.

  • Being deployed away from home causes you to lose your familiar anchors, making you more open to absorbing new norms. values, and loyalties.

  • The camp experience - drills (I only marched once), the anthem, the parades, and communal living - is textbook conditioning. It is designed to produce a particular emotional relationship with national identity.

  • It exposes corps members to poverty, unfamiliar cultures, and institutional dysfunction in ways that can either awaken consciousness or suppress it, depending on how the person processes the experience.

Your mind and behaviour are shaped - some leave at the end of the program with the mindset to change things. Optimism, etc. Others leave with the mindset of “every person for himself”.

Speaking of humans and behaviours, I have also noticed that, in the last five months, when I am on the road, I think of people’s outlook.

Some time ago, on the road, I saw a man who looked sick, dirty, and probably had mental issues, and the thought that came to mind was, “So God created this man in His own image, too.”

That same phrase has come to mind in other scenarios - I see a lady saying trash on the street, same thought. I see a child looking like he has no one to care for him in this world, same thought. I see someone behaving like God can’t do a thing about where he is, same thought. I see someone beautiful like the lady at the pharmacy in FMC Yenogoa, someone well-dressed, cultured, and I think the same thing: So, God created this person in His own image too.

The last time this happened, I was on my way back from Market Square in Yenogoa, and I think I saw a fat lady, or a terrible-looking guy (Facially), and the same thought waltzed through… “So God created this person in His own Image”.

I am a Christian, and I agree with the dignity of human life such that, regardless of how broken, lost, or difficult a person is, they were created…

…and a created being capable of the non-good things I have seen can do some moral common good, and by Grace, some divine good.

Another thing that I tend to think, closely related to what I have mentioned earlier, when I see someone is: Where did they grow up, what have they been exposed to, and how did it make them up to be this person who acts this way?

Two big things were happening when I turned 23 last year. First was Senior’s wedding on June 19, and the second was me wooing someone, someone I will get married to soon.

Two things that were evident back then were God's providence and the wisdom from good elders. God came through + I had plenty of little money back then.

Then, Greed Academy’s blockchain class and Turbin3 came in. I am not sure I enjoyed Greed Academy’s play at stake, lock, and earn, but I really loved my time at Turbin3. My capstone project for Turbin3 revolved around assessing the quality of smart contracts audits done by companies like Hacken, etc. I created a framework, did my demo (I remember the demo day - we were told that we’d talk for five minutes each, but while panicking, I had set a 5hr timer instead of 5 minutes and was so focused that I could not see Jeff’s cue to stop. I think I spoke for up to 20 minutes.)

After Turbin3, I had a different approach to writing and research. Then the PMF bounty came + I got on 1, 2 calls with Danny of NectarFi back then, checking out the product and leaving feedback.

Then I resigned from the agency I was working for, and I ran out of cash. It was quite interesting living as an unemployed personnel in Senior’s house, until the NYSC call-up letter came in.

Mogbe! Where will I see money from?

And somehow, I won a bounty before I left for camp in October. That money helped. All in all, I have been learning, enjoying God’s mercy and provision, and to this day, I am grateful to God that OUTIS made a tweet about Antigravity on X - that IDE makes me feel like Thanos with a 6-stoned infinity gauntlet in both hands.

Concerning work and Antigravity, I have done a number of things, and I do remember the event that happened in February, I think… Some of my colleagues had their Substack accounts reported and blocked, including Ral’s. Ral’s pained me, and I can’t place why I like Ral. Maybe it’s because he’s as tall as OUTIS, or because he came at a good time to our space. There was a scenario that played out in May in Project Sinan’s research cohort group, on TG: Ral had asked us to use the given criteria for team selection and adhere to them to avoid turning him “into a wicked village uncle”. Efe picked it up and threw it back at him later, and it became our in-house joke - even Spade jokingly calls Ral “wicked Uncle”.

The Substack occurrence + Josip Volarevic’s statement led me to start working on Solscribe. I am building my own publishing platform that will be limitless, accept crypto payments, and include regulations that make it less likely for people to report my friend’s account and cause a loss of publication for them.

Aside from Solscribe (not sure if that’s what it’d be called when it goes live), I also worked on gospellens.site, a Christian content aggregator, a platform focused on giving people access to content, without having them juggle multiple apps and platforms. There’s Vela - a Real-world asset yield aggregator on Solana (I need funding to continue that), and there’s my teaching schedule with the boys in Bishop Dimaeri Grammar School, Yenogoa, Bayelsa State.

The school is my Place of Primary Assignment (PPA), an all-boys day and boarding government school, and the boys all have unique characters. For example, Doubeni Difference likes to show off (took my laptop one evening and wanted to take a picture to post on TikTok/Snapchat as HK proof). Onyekwere David doesn’t take things seriously. Frank and his friends are more concerned about my CODM account than they are about their academics. Tonbie and 80% of SS2A are money-minded - Yahoo, business, OnlyFans, TikTok. Someone mentioned today in class (15th June) that his mentor includes Geh-Geh and VeryDarkMan - It threw me off. Charles Henry tends to ask questions revolving around choosing money or pleasing God - the class always erupts when I give my answers.

These boys are more exposed than I was when I was in SS2.

There’s also Tonye and Funkebi Godswill, who tend to misbehave when they see girls. Wisdom is intelligent and quiet. Corson thought he’d be the next senior prefect, but he was appointed as sanitation prefect.

Unique characters. right?

Well, my class is a functional sample size that can be studied to understand what’s happening to us at the big stage - greed, pride, bad governance, wrong mindset, selfishness, etc.

I am a Christian, and I hope they come to find and know what is true. For their sake, and for the ones that will come after them.

About my lady, she’s adorable. I look forward to getting married and having babies.

Yesterday, I sent three video notes to my significant other - she was surprised. I never send videos, and I have a thing for not sharing my pictures.

I do think I am love-struck, and I do think I am learning. Underneath the happiness and the impulse to pick up my phone and send the video notes was a feeling of GRATITUDE.

I am not sure I can remember everything that happened from June 16, 2025 till now, but I am alive and grateful.

I can’t say that I hit every one of the goals I set for myself when I turned 23. Nah! I messed up at some point, had sour thoughts, played the wrong cards, did not meet one-tenth of my money and skill goals (kept postponing my Blueshift.gg session), did not read as much as I wanted to, but I did try.

I am still trying.

From 23 till now, I have worked on different things, passed out on three occasions, and laughed in the face of death like Puss in Boots.

There’s a lot to look forward to. Not looking forward to social engineering as a recipient, but I am looking forward to learning how these guys use it to hack protocols. I am also looking forward to seeing how everyone turns out in the future, especially Tonbie, Tonye, and Wisdom - They will all grow. Some of them will never leave the walls of Bayelsa, some will, and it’s all a function of design.

What I know for certain is that there is someone I live for, and I intend to live for Him fully - not partially, not when it’s convenient.

That’s what 24 looks like from the inside.

Now you be the judge — “Remember who you are, mate”, or “Hogwarts, it’s Hammertime”.

title: Hammertime at 24
excerpt: My first attempt at writing a normal non-bounty piece since I turned 23.
content:
Chainstellar said to have a core story, a beautiful story to tell, and it will guide and influence the quality of the work throughout.

He said it’s what works for him.

I do not think my story is beautiful. It’s a core story, but beautiful?

Nah! I don’t think so. “Beautiful” is relative. Also, I could say that not one thing in the universe is beautiful in itself. A thing is beautiful because something makes it beautiful.

Is there something in my story that’s beautiful? Who knows?

Well, in this piece, I am not trying to tell a beautiful story. I am putting down what happened - from when I turned 23 till now - and trusting that the pattern reveals itself.

That being said, I want you to have two closing lines in mind - by the time you’re done reading, you can pick which one is more suitable as the last line for this piece;

  1. “Remember who you are, mate”

  2. “Hogwarts, it’s Hammertime” (A duplicate of “Lewis, it’s Hammertime” - I’m sorry if you’re not familiar with Formula 1)

In the past five months, I've found several things interesting. One of them is genetic engineering, and how humans in a certain estate can “work” the brains of humans in a lesser estate to shape how they behave, what they do, and the resolve they create in their hearts.

I’ve seen sci-fi movies and shows, and watched how people get triggered by “something” they see in a place, which, when investigated, we find out they grew up in an environment where that “something” was prevalent.

The interesting part is that this is not fiction - I have seen it with my own eyes. The environment a person grows up in does not just shape their memories - it shapes the wiring of their brain, the chemicals their body learns to produce, and the instincts they carry into adulthood without ever questioning where those instincts came from.

Imagine walking with a lady, you both hear gunshots down the street, and the first thing she does is to remove her shoes and hold them in her hands… She’s seen things.

A child raised in lack learns to think small. Not because they chose to, but because the environment did the choosing for them. I know some of these things happen by accident, but joining the NYSC made me see and think that these things can also happen by someone’s design. Those in power have always known, even without the science to explain it, that you do not need chains to control a person if you can control what they believe about themselves.

In the strict biological sense, we agree that NYSC is not genetic engineering, but in the social engineering sense, NYSC is a plausible environment for what I am writing about. See this:

  • NYSC takes you at a post-adolescent age and puts you in a controlled, structured environment with uniforms, schedules, authority, and collective ritual.

  • Being deployed away from home causes you to lose your familiar anchors, making you more open to absorbing new norms. values, and loyalties.

  • The camp experience - drills (I only marched once), the anthem, the parades, and communal living - is textbook conditioning. It is designed to produce a particular emotional relationship with national identity.

  • It exposes corps members to poverty, unfamiliar cultures, and institutional dysfunction in ways that can either awaken consciousness or suppress it, depending on how the person processes the experience.

Your mind and behaviour are shaped - some leave at the end of the program with the mindset to change things. Optimism, etc. Others leave with the mindset of “every person for himself”.

Speaking of humans and behaviours, I have also noticed that, in the last five months, when I am on the road, I think of people’s outlook.

Some time ago, on the road, I saw a man who looked sick, dirty, and probably had mental issues, and the thought that came to mind was, “So God created this man in His own image, too.”

That same phrase has come to mind in other scenarios - I see a lady saying trash on the street, same thought. I see a child looking like he has no one to care for him in this world, same thought. I see someone behaving like God can’t do a thing about where he is, same thought. I see someone beautiful like the lady at the pharmacy in FMC Yenogoa, someone well-dressed, cultured, and I think the same thing: So, God created this person in His own image too.

The last time this happened, I was on my way back from Market Square in Yenogoa, and I think I saw a fat lady, or a terrible-looking guy (Facially), and the same thought waltzed through… “So God created this person in His own Image”.

I am a Christian, and I agree with the dignity of human life such that, regardless of how broken, lost, or difficult a person is, they were created…

…and a created being capable of the non-good things I have seen can do some moral common good, and by Grace, some divine good.

Another thing that I tend to think, closely related to what I have mentioned earlier, when I see someone is: Where did they grow up, what have they been exposed to, and how did it make them up to be this person who acts this way?

Two big things were happening when I turned 23 last year. First was Senior’s wedding on June 19, and the second was me wooing someone, someone I will get married to soon.

Two things that were evident back then were God's providence and the wisdom from good elders. God came through + I had plenty of little money back then.

Then, Greed Academy’s blockchain class and Turbin3 came in. I am not sure I enjoyed Greed Academy’s play at stake, lock, and earn, but I really loved my time at Turbin3. My capstone project for Turbin3 revolved around assessing the quality of smart contracts audits done by companies like Hacken, etc. I created a framework, did my demo (I remember the demo day - we were told that we’d talk for five minutes each, but while panicking, I had set a 5hr timer instead of 5 minutes and was so focused that I could not see Jeff’s cue to stop. I think I spoke for up to 20 minutes.)

After Turbin3, I had a different approach to writing and research. Then the PMF bounty came + I got on 1, 2 calls with Danny of NectarFi back then, checking out the product and leaving feedback.

Then I resigned from the agency I was working for, and I ran out of cash. It was quite interesting living as an unemployed personnel in Senior’s house, until the NYSC call-up letter came in.

Mogbe! Where will I see money from?

And somehow, I won a bounty before I left for camp in October. That money helped. All in all, I have been learning, enjoying God’s mercy and provision, and to this day, I am grateful to God that OUTIS made a tweet about Antigravity on X - that IDE makes me feel like Thanos with a 6-stoned infinity gauntlet in both hands.

Concerning work and Antigravity, I have done a number of things, and I do remember the event that happened in February, I think… Some of my colleagues had their Substack accounts reported and blocked, including Ral’s. Ral’s pained me, and I can’t place why I like Ral. Maybe it’s because he’s as tall as OUTIS, or because he came at a good time to our space. There was a scenario that played out in May in Project Sinan’s research cohort group, on TG: Ral had asked us to use the given criteria for team selection and adhere to them to avoid turning him “into a wicked village uncle”. Efe picked it up and threw it back at him later, and it became our in-house joke - even Spade jokingly calls Ral “wicked Uncle”.

The Substack occurrence + Josip Volarevic’s statement led me to start working on Solscribe. I am building my own publishing platform that will be limitless, accept crypto payments, and include regulations that make it less likely for people to report my friend’s account and cause a loss of publication for them.

Aside from Solscribe (not sure if that’s what it’d be called when it goes live), I also worked on gospellens.site, a Christian content aggregator, a platform focused on giving people access to content, without having them juggle multiple apps and platforms. There’s Vela - a Real-world asset yield aggregator on Solana (I need funding to continue that), and there’s my teaching schedule with the boys in Bishop Dimaeri Grammar School, Yenogoa, Bayelsa State.

The school is my Place of Primary Assignment (PPA), an all-boys day and boarding government school, and the boys all have unique characters. For example, Doubeni Difference likes to show off (took my laptop one evening and wanted to take a picture to post on TikTok/Snapchat as HK proof). Onyekwere David doesn’t take things seriously. Frank and his friends are more concerned about my CODM account than they are about their academics. Tonbie and 80% of SS2A are money-minded - Yahoo, business, OnlyFans, TikTok. Someone mentioned today in class (15th June) that his mentor includes Geh-Geh and VeryDarkMan - It threw me off. Charles Henry tends to ask questions revolving around choosing money or pleasing God - the class always erupts when I give my answers.

These boys are more exposed than I was when I was in SS2.

There’s also Tonye and Funkebi Godswill, who tend to misbehave when they see girls. Wisdom is intelligent and quiet. Corson thought he’d be the next senior prefect, but he was appointed as sanitation prefect.

Unique characters. right?

Well, my class is a functional sample size that can be studied to understand what’s happening to us at the big stage - greed, pride, bad governance, wrong mindset, selfishness, etc.

I am a Christian, and I hope they come to find and know what is true. For their sake, and for the ones that will come after them.

About my lady, she’s adorable. I look forward to getting married and having babies.

Yesterday, I sent three video notes to my significant other - she was surprised. I never send videos, and I have a thing for not sharing my pictures.

I do think I am love-struck, and I do think I am learning. Underneath the happiness and the impulse to pick up my phone and send the video notes was a feeling of GRATITUDE.

I am not sure I can remember everything that happened from June 16, 2025 till now, but I am alive and grateful.

I can’t say that I hit every one of the goals I set for myself when I turned 23. Nah! I messed up at some point, had sour thoughts, played the wrong cards, did not meet one-tenth of my money and skill goals (kept postponing my Blueshift.gg session), did not read as much as I wanted to, but I did try.

I am still trying.

From 23 till now, I have worked on different things, passed out on three occasions, and laughed in the face of death like Puss in Boots.

There’s a lot to look forward to. Not looking forward to social engineering as a recipient, but I am looking forward to learning how these guys use it to hack protocols. I am also looking forward to seeing how everyone turns out in the future, especially Tonbie, Tonye, and Wisdom - They will all grow. Some of them will never leave the walls of Bayelsa, some will, and it’s all a function of design.

What I know for certain is that there is someone I live for, and I intend to live for Him fully - not partially, not when it’s convenient.

That’s what 24 looks like from the inside.

Now you be the judge — “Remember who you are, mate”, or “Hogwarts, it’s Hammertime”.

title: Copy of The Girl Who Kept Going
excerpt: There was a girl who kept telling herself, “I’ll try again tomorrow.”Not because she was lazy.Not because she didn’t have dreams.She was simply tired.Tired of s…
content:
There was a girl who kept telling herself, “I’ll try again tomorrow.”

Not because she was lazy.

Not because she didn’t have dreams.

She was simply tired.

Tired of starting things and wondering if they would work out. Tired of watching other people move forward while she felt like she was standing in the same place. Tired of pretending she had everything figured out when, deep down, she was still trying to find her way.

But there was something she refused to do.

Give up.

Some mornings, she woke up with confidence. Other mornings, she woke up with questions.

Am I good enough?

Will things ever change?

What if I fail again?

Still, she got up.

She learned something new.

She wrote another page.

She applied for another opportunity.

She tried again.

And slowly, she began to understand something important:

Progress doesn't always look like success.

Sometimes, progress is simply refusing to stop.

The girl didn't know exactly where her journey would take her. She didn't have all the answers. She didn't even know how long it would take.

But she knew she wanted a different life.

So she kept going.

One word.

One lesson.

One opportunity.

One day at a time.

Maybe that's what courage really is not being certain that everything will work out, but choosing to continue even when you're not sure.

And perhaps, somewhere along the way, the girl will look back and realize that all those small steps she almost dismissed were actually taking her somewhere.

She just had to keep going.

Winny ✍🏽

title: Nigeria’s Tech Growth in 2026​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​
excerpt: Nigeria’s digital economy is no longer just expanding rapidly it’s becoming more structured. Fresh legislation, a flagship regional tech expo, and advancing AI …
content:
Nigeria’s digital economy is no longer just expanding rapidly it’s becoming more structured. Fresh legislation, a flagship regional tech expo, and advancing AI oversight are helping the country cement its role as the digital hub of West Africa.

Digital Economy Projected to Reach $18.3 Billion
Industry forecasts put Nigeria’s digital economy revenue at $18.3 billion this year, fueled by rising AI use, a more mature fintech landscape, growing cloud services, and broader 5G and broadband coverage. Experts view 2026 as a pivotal year: the focus is moving from rapid but unstructured expansion toward steadier, higher-value innovation, backed by stronger legal foundations for the sector.

A key piece of that foundation is the National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill, which is expected to become law this year. Once enacted, it would elevate the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) to a central “super-regulator” role empowering it to categorize AI systems by risk level, mandate algorithmic transparency, and certify AI auditors. This would complement the work of the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, creating a dual regulatory layer for technology.

Telecoms already accounted for more than 9% of real GDP last year, a share likely to rise further as fibre to the home networks expand and mobile access improves. Internet penetration is forecast to approach 60% this year, largely thanks to Nigeria’s mobile-first user base.

GITEX Nigeria 2026 Heads to Abuja and Lagos
West Africa’s premier tech, AI and startup gathering, GITEX Nigeria, takes place from 31 August to 3 September across Abuja and Lagos, with the backing of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. Organizers describe the event as evidence that Nigeria and the wider region are prepared to convert innovation into tangible economic gains, creating platforms for partnerships, investment and collaboration across the digital economy.

Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy Minister Bosun Tijani emphasizes that the ambition goes beyond importing technology: Nigeria aims to develop a digital economy in which Africa creates AI and digital solutions rather than merely using them.

Africa’s Frontrunner in Responsible AI
Recent assessments show Nigeria leading African countries in responsible AI governance. Policy frameworks, however, are only the starting point. The greater task is expanding real-world AI adoption across sectors while strengthening infrastructure, skills and regulatory systems. Nations that convert solid governance into measurable productivity and broad-based growth will capture the greatest long-term benefits from AI.

Growing Regional Ties
Nigeria and Ghana are examining joint digital innovation projects, with the National Agency for Science and Engineering Infrastructure (NASENI) central to Nigeria’s industrial shift. Information Minister Mohammed Idris notes that initiatives under the Renewed Hope Agenda are delivering concrete results jobs, projects and innovation in areas such as local manufacturing, renewable energy, agri-tech and digital skills training.

The Bottom Line
Nigerian tech in 2026 is less about isolated headline launches and more about infrastructure finally matching ambition. Sharper regulation, leading AI governance, expanding telecoms and broadband, plus a major regional showcase in Lagos and Abuja, are all aligning. Should the digital economy bill pass and GITEX meet expectations, 2026 may be the year Nigeria moves from “emerging” tech market to established player.
