title: You’re 3 States Away and Your Dad Is in Front of Your Hostel? (Part 2)
excerpt: The lie got bigger. Then I opened his door.
content:
I tried to calm myself down by thinking of my boyfriend. I pictured the cute reaction—the hugging, the emotional moment, the “I can’t believe you are here”. You know that moment you’re day dreaming and smiling to yourself like a fool only to look beside you and realize someone has been looking at you? Yeahhhh, I quickly adjusted myself and continued being optimistic. No one will spoil my joyyy….lolll🤧🙂

When I got to his city, I carried my bag like someone going to her husband's house. I ordered a ride straight to his place. My stomach was doing excitement, not knowing it should have been doing warning.

I reached his door and didn't knock. I wanted to set up my phone for the surprise video. I positioned the camera small, patted my face. I rehearsed my smile.

I wish someone slapped me at this point. Like one hot slap instantly because...Kai... God Ahbeg🥲

I opened the door—thankfully, it was unlocked. And I didn't see my boyfriend initially sef.

Like "Everywhere first blurrrrr."

Then I looked again

The first thing I saw...

Legs...

Legs in the air....

Legs doing activities my own legs had never done. Ehnnnn???

I just stood still. I was trying to process what I am seeing. I mean, I’ve got eye issues so that might not be my boyfriend, right? —first stage: denial.

I dropped my bag and I just stood like that. My boyfriend turned, saw me and shouted like he just saw a ghost.

The girl jumped up and behaved like I was the intruder. She said, "Can't you knock?" I said, "On my boyfriend's door?" She said, "YOUR what?"

Oh the pain I was feeling was indescribable.

My boyfriend was begging, kneeling, trying to touch me. He kept saying the girl meant nothing. But the girl was shouting that she was his real girlfriend and I was the side chick.

I just wanted to leave there but this goat was still holding me down, begging.

My dad’s message came in to my phone saying he’s sending my uncle to the hotel we are “staying” and that he will be around for the competition to cheer me on.  All the color drained from my body at that moment. I wasn’t even in Lagos State to start with, I just lied that I was there🤧😭.

Can you see how complicated it is now?Omooo God punish you Olaaaa😭.

I managed to free myself from the stupid boy and I stepped outside. Then, it started raining heavily. My boyfriend followed me, still trying to beg, while my dad kept texting that he was sending my uncle to verify my location.

My life was crashing before my eyes. In HD. In 4k. I was whirling in disgrace. My uncle is on his way to a hotel I was never even in.

What will you do if you were me???🥹 I need a story asapppp.

To Be Continued.

title: Equality? That's a false narrative
excerpt: Would  a father who killed his children and claimed insanity get this kind of sympathy?    Well, i hate to burst your bubble but the answer is No. Take the case…
content:
Would a father who killed his children and claimed insanity get this kind of sympathy?

Well, i hate to burst your bubble but the answer is No. Take the case of Timothy Ray Jones Jr as a reference. The contrast with Lindsay Clancy is not subtle. Both parents admitted causing the deaths of their young children and advanced mental-illness defenses. The public and media responses have been strikingly different

Timothy Ray Jones Jr., a divorced software engineer and primary custodial parent, killed his five children on August 28, 2014, in their Lexington County, South Carolina, home. After one of the children died during harsh physical punishment for breaking electrical outlets, Jones strangled the other four (two with his hands, two with a belt). He then drove their bodies around the Southeast for eight or nine days before dumping them in garbage bags on a rural Alabama road. He used synthetic marijuana. His defense pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, citing family history of schizophrenia, possible brain damage from a teenage car accident, stress as a single father, religious turmoil, and voices, including a “demonic gremlin.”

A court-appointed psychiatrist diagnosed substance-induced psychosis from Spice, concluded Jones knew right from wrong, and suggested he may have exaggerated symptoms to live with what he had done. A jury rejected the insanity claim in 2019, convicted him of five murders, and recommended death. The South Carolina Supreme Court upheld the conviction and sentence in 2023. There were no pink-shirt vigils, no mass identification campaigns, and no comparable fundraising wave. Coverage treated the crime as “obscene” and “outrageous.” Jurors later described lasting trauma. Jones’s own father expressed personal guilt over not intervening sooner, but the dominant public frame was of a father who panicked after one death and then methodically finished the rest.

Cultural scripts still treat maternal filicide as a possible medical catastrophe and paternal filicide as a failure of character or simple evil. Andrea Yates, who drowned her five children in 2001 and was eventually found not guilty by reason of insanity, is frequently compared to Clancy; Jones is not. That difference in narrative power, not just the facts of each crime, explains why one parent’s insanity claim generated identification and the other’s generated a death sentence. The dead children in both families received no second chance to benefit from either story.

It's such a crazy world we live in. I hear a mistrial has been declared already. Such a shitty society.

3enchnad

title: The Night We Played Truth or Dare
excerpt: What started as a game slowly became something else
content:
It was a few minutes past 10 p.m. My eyes were still wide open despite having a stressful day in school. I'd finished all my chores so I could use my mum's phone without interruption.

I got chatting with my stranger friend, and everything was going smoothly until he asked if we could play Truth or Dare. I agreed because I'd always heard my friends talk about their funny dare experiences.

After all, I wanted the experience too.

We started with truth. The questions were harmless.

"What's your favourite colour?"

"Who's your celebrity crush?"

"Have you ever had a boyfriend?"

We laughed through every answer, and somehow it made us even more comfortable with each other. Then we switched to dares.

"Change your profile picture for five minutes."

"Send a random emoji."

Easy enough.

But as the game went on, the dares became more personal. He asked me to send a picture. At first, it sounded innocent, so I did. Then another. Then another. Before I knew it, the requests became uncomfortable. He kept saying things like, "Come on, it's just a game," or, "Don't you trust me?"

I remember staring at my screen, wondering why I suddenly felt uneasy. I didn't want to seem rude or boring, but deep down I knew I didn't want to do what he was asking.

That was the first time I realised that people don't always cross your boundaries all at once. Sometimes they do it little by little until saying "no" feels harder than saying "yes."

I eventually refused, and the atmosphere changed immediately. The friendly guy I'd been talking to disappeared. He became cold, dismissive, and eventually stopped talking to me altogether.

For a while, I blamed myself. I wondered if I'd overreacted or ruined the friendship. But with time, I realised something important.

A genuine friend will never make you feel guilty for protecting your boundaries. Anyone who walks away because you said "no" wasn't staying because they valued you, they were staying because they hoped to get something from you.

Looking back now, I'm actually grateful that happened. It taught me that not everyone who is kind to you has good intentions. Some people earn your trust first before testing your limits.

That stranger didn't just become my friend. He became one of the biggest lessons of my life.

title: Everyone has an excuse.
excerpt: People create justifications that let their side off the hook. We do it constantly. Once we pick a team mothers, mental-health advocates, “tough on crime” types…
content:
People create justifications that let their side off the hook. We do it constantly. Once we pick a team mothers, mental-health advocates, “tough on crime” types, whoever we start collecting reasons why our people aren’t really at fault. The facts get rearranged so the people we identify with come out looking more sympathetic, more victimized, or more reasonable than they actually were. The Lindsay Clancy case is a brutal example of this habit in action.

On January 24, 2023, Lindsay Clancy strangled her three children with exercise bands in the basement of their house in Duxbury, Massachusetts. Then she cut her wrists and neck and jumped out a second-story window. She survived, paralyzed from the waist down. She has never denied doing it. Her defense is that she was in the grip of postpartum psychosis and should not be held criminally responsible. Prosecutors say she planned it: she sent her husband out for takeout and medicine so she would have the house to herself, then acted methodically. The trial has stretched on for weeks. As of early September 2026 the jury is still deliberating and has already told the judge they are deadlocked.

That is the core of what happened. Everything after that is people choosing sides and then inventing stories that make their side look better.

One large group of people mostly other mothers, mental-health advocates, and a surprising number of conservative women treat Clancy as the real victim. They point to the months she spent seeking help, the revolving door of doctors, the long list of medications, the hospital stay that ended only weeks before the killings. They say the system failed her. They wear pink T-shirts outside the courthouse. Online they post “I am Lindsay” or “same, Lindsay” next to pictures of their own kids. The implication is clear, any of us could have snapped if the doctors had treated us this badly. The justification lets an entire category of people off the hook. Motherhood is hard, the medical system is broken, society doesn’t support women therefore the woman who actually killed three children is not the main problem. The problem is everyone else.

The other side does the same thing in the opposite direction. They focus on the planning. She texted her husband to leave. She chose a quiet moment. She used objects already in the house. She told the children “go to God, baby” while she did it. To this group, postpartum psychosis is either rare enough to be almost irrelevant or being stretched into an all-purpose excuse. Some commentators went further and suggested a lot of postpartum talk is just selfishness women who don’t want to sacrifice their old lives. That version lets a different tribe off the hook: the people who believe in personal responsibility, who think “mental illness” has become a get-out-of-jail-free card, who are tired of seeing children’s deaths treated as a talking point about healthcare. If you start from that worldview, Clancy is simply a murderer who happened to have a convenient diagnosis.

Both versions require ignoring pieces of the story. The first side downplays how organized the afternoon looked. The second side downplays how long Clancy had been describing intrusive thoughts, insomnia, and a sense that she was losing control and how many professionals saw her and still sent her home. Neither side likes holding both ideas at once: that she was severely ill and that three children are still dead because of what she did.

You can see the same pattern in smaller ways. Some people decided the husband must have done it, even though Clancy has admitted the acts and the 911 call is public. Others decided the doctors should be in prison instead of her. Each theory exists because it protects a preferred narrative. If the husband is the villain, then the story becomes one about men who don’t help enough. If the doctors are the villains, then the story becomes one about a broken medical system. The actual sequence of events is less convenient for either team.

This is not unique to this case. People have always done it. We just have more platforms now, so the justifications get louder and more detailed. The Clancy trial happens to be a clean illustration because almost nothing about the basic facts is in dispute. She killed the children. She tried to kill herself. She had been unwell for months. The argument is only about what those facts mean and meaning is where the justifications start.

The uncomfortable part is that most of us would do the same thing if the person involved belonged to our group. We would look for the details that make our side look less responsible and the other side look more so. We would call it “context” or “nuance.” It is just ordinary tribal thinking with better vocabulary. Three children are still gone either way. The justifications do not change that. They only make it easier for the rest of us to keep our preferred story intact.

Until humans begin to take responsibility of their actions i see no difference between us humans and animals. Yes i said that and that is my own view.

title: SWITCH: THE FINAL TRIAL AND ERROR, THEN RESULTS.
excerpt: SWITCH: THE FINAL TRIAL & ERROR, THEN RESULTSI am the best at my craft and I am confident in my skillsMy product is so great and I am sure if people k…
content:
SWITCH: THE FINAL TRIAL & ERROR, THEN RESULTS

  • I am the best at my craft and I am confident in my skills

  • My product is so great and I am sure if people know about it they’ll line up.

  • Five posts a week on Linkedin, Instagram, X and Facebook and I should make those sales.

And yet, 

  • No leads

  • No sales

  • Random “congratulations on the new role” on linkedin on a brand/business you just started.

Yeah, this may be you. You need something, and right now you may not really know exactly what it is you need but you just know there’s something missing. Frankly, I am not here to be a Mr. Genie swooshing out of a lamp to give you solutions to your problems but I can hold your hand and we can figure things out together.

You want visibility, sales, traction/traffic, more likes, more views, growth, better marketing strategies, and to be respected in your industry. You need these;


Feel it to understand it.

It is in frustration, that is where problems are identified. In today’s world, we avoid the things that make us uncomfortable and we seek comfort in quotes about failure and watch videos on how to cope with failure and, here’s the really sad one, “flop proud”.  Emotion is a variable that cannot be removed from progress in any form, how you feel doesn’t just portray what you go through in a period of time, it also dictates your next step. It says, “are you just going to fail and start from square one or are you going to break down the information you have from failing and fix the problem?” 

  Disregarding public opinion, the “don’t be too hard on yourself”, YOU should dissect your own actions and strategies and chastise yourself for mistakes, unavoidable or not. That way there’s room for HOW DO I GET THIS RIGHT? In your chain of thoughts. 

You have to think; I am not visible enough, my work/effort are not aligned with my goal, I got too greedy, too hasty, too comfortable, or a hundred and one other issues in order to MAKE IT WORK. A banner and random post/video not clearly telling your story or mission is not enough.

Let these stay with you for an hour or two and no more. For in that agonizing comes the hard truth that sets you free, and once you are free and see clearly, nothing can stop the next step.


Game board it

Being a business or brand owner is synonymous to being a chess master, your strategy must be future oriented. You must at all times, use the data in front of you to predict the world around you as well as move strategically, thereby positioning yourself where opportunity meets you.

This is where you draw a mind and road map based on information retrieved and information acquired, and then you SWOT. 

S- strength (what you currently do very well or excel at)

W-weaknesses  (chinks and loopholes)

O- opportunities  (what you stand to gain)

T- threats  (potential situations that may lead to losses)

Now, find a way to use your strengths to grab opportunities and curtail threats. And prevent observed threats by plugging weaknesses. The aim is to have at least a semblance of structure and a plan. It is a BEING UNTOP OF IT line of thought. Basically, a new way of thinking/problem solving. 


SYSTEMIZE IT 

So now you’ve reached the tricky, fun, delicate part. Building a system.  Coming up with a stable system with guaranteed results and flexibility capable of accommodating any scenario/situation. This requires patience, and an understanding of yourself and the living entity you’ve built and dubbed “business”.

title: Broken Mirror, Smile Face 2
excerpt: The house on Douglas Road was the kind of house that had opinions. Adaeze had felt it the first time she walked through its door as a young bride, twenty-four a…
content:
The house on Douglas Road was the kind of house that had opinions. Adaeze had felt it the first time she walked through its door as a young bride, twenty-four and luminous with the specific hope of a woman who believes she has chosen well — the high ceilings, the dark wood banister worn smooth by other hands, the way the afternoon light came slanting gold through the parlor windows like something out of an old photograph. Chidi had bought it from an aging widower who wept when he handed over the keys, and she had thought, then, that a house loved that much by its previous owner must hold something good inside its walls. Some residue of tenderness in the plaster.

She had been wrong, or she had been right and the house had simply absorbed too much else in the years since — arguments swallowed whole by the thick old walls, apologies that were never really apologies, silences stretched taut across dinner tables until they hummed. Houses remember. She believed that now, in the way she believed few things anymore, with the flat certainty of someone who has stopped needing anyone else to agree with her.

In the weeks after Chidi left, the house grew stranger. Not haunted — she didn’t believe in haunted, not in the cinematic sense, not in the sense of things that rattled chains and moved cutlery in the night. But inhabited, somehow, by the residue of who she had been inside it. She would walk past the study and feel, for just a moment, the ghost of her younger self standing in the doorway asking permission to speak. She would pass the broken mirror — she had never had it replaced, had in fact instructed the housekeeper never to touch it — and catch her own face looking back at her from seven different angles, seven different women, none of whom she entirely recognized.

That was the strangest part. Not the loneliness — she had expected the loneliness, had steeled herself for it the way you steel yourself for cold water, knowing the shock will pass. What she hadn’t expected was the stranger in the glass. Some mornings the woman looking back seemed harder around the eyes than Adaeze remembered being. Some mornings she seemed impossibly young, undone, a girl playing dress-up in her mother’s jewelry. And some mornings — the worst mornings, the ones that left her sitting on the edge of the bathtub with her face in her hands — the woman in the mirror seemed to be waiting. For something. As if the breaking hadn’t been an ending at all, but the opening of a door that had been locked for a very long time.

title: Dangote Refinery Goes Public Today: What Nigerians Need to Know About the ₦2.15tn IPO
excerpt: Dangote Refinery IPO Opens Today as Nigerians Get Chance to Own Stake in Africa’s Biggest RefineryThe Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals has opened i…
content:
Dangote Refinery IPO Opens Today as Nigerians Get Chance to Own Stake in Africa’s Biggest Refinery

The Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals has opened its highly anticipated initial public offering (IPO), giving Nigerians and other eligible investors an opportunity to become shareholders in Africa’s largest oil refinery.

The public offer opened on Monday, September 14, 2026, as Dangote Group seeks to raise about ₦2.15 trillion from the sale of 4.1 billion shares. The shares are priced at ₦525 each.

The refinery, owned by Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote, is offering the shares as part of plans to raise additional funds for expansion. The company plans to increase its refining capacity from about 700,000 barrels per day to 1.4 million barrels per day over the coming years.

The public offer has been promoted as an “IPO for the People,” with the company seeking to make ownership accessible to ordinary Nigerians and retail investors.

Eligible investors can subscribe for as little as 10 shares, costing ₦5,250 at the offer price, although investors are advised to read the offer documents and understand the risks before investing.

The refinery, located in the Lekki Free Zone in Lagos, began operations in 2024 and has a processing capacity of about 700,000 barrels of crude oil per day. Its operations have helped Nigeria move from relying heavily on imported refined petroleum products toward becoming an exporter of refined products.

The IPO represents a major development for Nigeria’s capital market. If fully subscribed, the ₦2.15 trillion offer would rank among the country's biggest public share offerings and give retail investors an opportunity to participate in the ownership of a major Nigerian industrial asset.

The refinery is also seeking to strengthen its position in the African energy market. Its planned expansion to 1.4 million barrels per day would significantly increase its ability to supply refined petroleum products to Nigeria and other African markets.

However, investors should remember that buying shares does not guarantee profit. The value of shares can rise or fall, while dividends are only paid when declared by the company. The official IPO information also warns investors to consider the risks before subscribing.

The Dangote Refinery public offer is scheduled to close on October 13, 2026, according to the company's official IPO information.

With strong interest from Nigerian retail investors, the Dangote Refinery IPO is expected to be closely watched as a major test of investor appetite and participation in Nigeria's capital market.

title: Dancing With The Devil
excerpt: Because when you're desperate enough to take the devil's hand, you don't realize you're walking yourself straight into the fire.
content:
I was so tired of drowning that I didn't care who pulled me out.

The ballroom was quiet; only the melody of a cello playing a tune that felt boring.

I have lived my entirely life watching other people live, watching doors slam shut in my face, and counting every single money left in my pocket. When the walls are closing in, you stop looking for angels.

The world had made it abundantly clear that it was completely done offering me mercy.

That’s when he showed up. No horns, no scary monster face, just a warm smile, and an easy way out. He looked like the answer to a prayer whispered at midnight when you're completely out of options.

"You look like someone who is tired of losing," he whispered into my ear.

"I am," I said, my voice shaking.

"Then let me lead," he said, offering his hand.

And without thinking, without pausing for even a second to know the cost, or to wonder why an escape route was being handed to me so easily, I placed my palm right into his.

The moment our fingers locked, the music swelled. He pulled me straight into the center of the floor, and for a brief, blinding second, it felt like true grace. The weight of everything and desperation left my shoulders.

He spun me effortlessly, catching me every time I stumbled. The floor beneath us turned into clear, fragile glass, revealing a roaring furnace deep down below, but he just smiled at me, his gaze locking into mine. “Don't look down,” he said. “Just look at me.”

So I did. I let myself get completely lost in the rhythm. I loved the speed of it, the sudden, rush of power, the dangerous thrill of feeling important to someone, even if that someone was the devil.

And then, right in the middle of a spin, the music stopped.

I looked down at our joined hands, his hand split wide open, and underneath wasn't skin at all; it was monstrous, hot and burning my own hands, eating away at my flesh. The sudden pain didn't even shock me. What truly broke me, was when I finally stopped spinning and looked around the ballroom.

I wasn't a guest at a masquerade ball at all.

Everyone there were in chains and on their knees, weeping. There were monsters all around them, whipping their backs. They had a mark; some had on their foreheads while some, on their necks. I looked at my hand that was still holding his and noticed the mark was at the back of my right hand.

I started feeling hot; I was burning up. That was when I realized that the floor underneath our feet was shattering and before long, we went down. I thought I was taking his hand to escape the fire not knowing all along, I was walking deeper into it.

Then he left my hands and I finally saw the monster that was hiding all along in him. He began to laugh and then before long, I was in chains like the others and on my knees.

And just like that, I had created hell for myself.

title: How to Manage a High-Performing Remote Team in 2026
excerpt: Remote and hybrid work are now established ways of working for millions of professionals. Managing people across locations, though, takes more than video calls, project-management software, and a busy…
content:
Remote and hybrid work are now established ways of working for millions of professionals. Managing people across locations, though, takes more than video calls, project-management software, and a busy Slack channel.

The real challenge is building a system where people understand their priorities, communicate well, collaborate across time zones, and stay accountable without feeling micromanaged. In 2026, AI adds another factor. It is increasingly used for meeting summaries, reporting, research, and task management, which changes how managers can spend their time. Meanwhile, Gallup data shows that among U.S. employees whose jobs can be done remotely, 52% work hybrid and 26% work fully remotely.

So how do you build a remote team that actually performs? These eight practices are a good place to start.

1. Start With Clarity

Remote teams can't rely on overheard conversations or a quick word at someone's desk, so expectations have to be explicit. Every team member should be able to answer six questions:

What are our priorities?

What am I responsible for?

What does success look like?

Who owns each task?

When is the work due?

Where is information stored?

If people can't answer these, adding more software won't help. Clarity comes before technology. When goals, responsibilities, and deadlines are clear, employees can make decisions on their own instead of waiting for a manager to respond, which matters most when your team spans several time zones.

2. Build a Strong Remote Culture

Culture doesn't disappear when people leave the office. It has to be designed more deliberately. Start by agreeing on team norms for:

Communication channels and etiquette

Working hours and time-zone overlap

Expected response times

What counts as urgent

Documentation habits

Then add simple rituals: a weekly team update, a monthly retrospective, and regular recognition of good work. The goal isn't to force people to socialize online. It's to create an environment where they feel connected, trusted, and included. Small, consistent gestures, such as publicly crediting a colleague's contribution, do more for remote culture than an occasional virtual happy hour.

3. Make Communication "Async First"

Not everything needs a meeting. A project update that takes two minutes to read shouldn't cost 30 minutes of everyone's time.

For routine updates, use asynchronous communication with a consistent format:

Project: Website redesign

Completed: Homepage

In progress: Mobile version

Blocked by: Final copy approval

Next step: Complete testing

A shared template like this lets colleagues in any time zone catch up quickly and spot problems early. Save live meetings for what they do best: discussion, decision-making, brainstorming, and relationship building. Drawing this line clearly can dramatically reduce unnecessary meetings and gives people longer stretches of uninterrupted time.

4. Make Meetings Outcome-Driven

Before scheduling any meeting, ask one question: what needs to be different when this meeting ends? If you can't answer, you probably don't need the meeting.

Every meeting that does go ahead should have:

A clear purpose

A shared agenda

Decisions that need to be made

Assigned action items

Deadlines for those actions

Keep routine meetings short and record important decisions afterward in a place everyone can find. A meeting should produce an outcome, not simply consume time. Circulating notes and owners within a day also gives absent colleagues, often those in other time zones, the same information as everyone else.

5. Use AI as a Productivity Assistant

AI shouldn't replace leadership, but it can remove a significant amount of administrative work. A remote manager can use it to:

Summarize team updates

Prepare meeting agendas

Extract action items from meeting notes

Draft weekly reports

Flag overdue tasks

Organize research

Create onboarding resources

Try this workflow. At the end of each week, collect your team's updates and ask an AI assistant: "Summarize these updates into three key wins, three challenges, unresolved issues, and the top priorities for next week." Instead of reading several separate reports, you get a structured overview that helps you focus on decisions. Review the output before acting on it, as AI summaries can miss context or nuance.

Microsoft's Work Trend Index has highlighted the growing role of AI agents and human-AI collaboration at work. The principle for managers is simple: use AI to reduce administrative friction, not to replace human judgment.

6. Measure Results, Not Online Activity

One of the biggest mistakes in remote management is confusing being online with being productive. Someone can spend eight hours logged in and accomplish very little, while another person completes their most important work in four focused hours.

Instead of tracking:

Online status

Message counts

Hours spent in meetings

Keyboard activity

focus on outcomes such as:

Projects completed

Deadlines met

Customer satisfaction

Sales generated

Response times

Quality of work

Progress on strategic milestones

When expectations are clear, employees need less surveillance. Trust-based management also tends to attract and keep stronger people, because capable professionals rarely thrive under constant monitoring.

7. Protect People From Digital Overload

Remote work has a side effect: the workday can start to feel endless. Microsoft's research has described the "infinite workday," in which employees increasingly check messages and email outside traditional working hours.

Leaders can push back by:

Protecting blocks of focus time

Reducing unnecessary meetings

Defining what counts as urgent, and how to escalate it

Encouraging people to disconnect

Avoiding after-hours messages unless truly necessary

Managers set the tone here. If you send messages at 10 p.m., people will feel they need to reply at 10 p.m. Productivity isn't about keeping people busy every minute. It's about helping them do meaningful work without unnecessary friction, and sustainably enough to keep doing it.

8. Keep Developing Your Team

Technology is changing quickly, so employees need ongoing chances to build new skills. The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 lists AI and big data, technological literacy, creative thinking, resilience, and leadership among the skills shaping the future of work.

Build learning into the team's routine through:

Short training sessions

Peer learning and knowledge sharing

Mentorship

AI skills training

Quarterly career conversations

Remote employees can feel invisible when it comes to growth, so making development an explicit, scheduled part of the job matters. A high-performing team isn't just productive today. It becomes more capable over time.

The Remote Team Manager's Checklist

Before each week begins, ask yourself:

Are our priorities clear?

Does everyone know what they own?

Are unnecessary meetings being eliminated?

Are important decisions documented?

Are we using AI where it genuinely saves time?

Are we measuring outcomes rather than activity?

Is the workload sustainable?

Are people learning and developing?

If you can answer "yes" consistently, you're building the foundations of a strong remote team.

Final Thoughts

Managing a high-performing remote team in 2026 isn't about keeping everyone online. It's about clarity, communication, coordination, capability, and trust. Technology and AI can make the system faster, but leadership still determines how well it works.

The best remote leaders don't simply monitor work. They design better ways of working.

Start small: identify one process that wastes your team's time, fix it, document it, and then look for a way to automate part of it with AI. Small improvements in how a team works add up to significant gains over time.

For more practical insights on AI workflows, executive productivity, digital tools, and the future of work, follow Dennis Njoku on Echo Gist.

Sources

  • Gallup: Hybrid Work and Remote Work Trends

  • Microsoft: Work Trend Index

  • Microsoft: The "Infinite Workday"

  • World Economic Forum: Future of Jobs Report 2025

title: WE'RE LOSING THE ABILITY TO BE BORED
excerpt: The Elevator Test You Didn't Know You Were Failing
content:
You are in a lift for eleven seconds. Phone's out before the doors even close. You're standing in a queue, waiting for water to boil, sitting in a parked car waiting for someone and in every single one of those gaps, your hand has already found your phone before your brain even registered there was a gap to fill.

If you can't remember the last time you did nothing, on purpose, for more than thirty seconds, this is for you.

BOREDOM USED TO BE A WAITING ROOM, NOT AN EMERGENCY

There was a version of life, not even that long ago, where waiting meant actually waiting, staring at a wall, watching people, thinking about nothing in particular until a thought eventually wandered in. Boredom was uncomfortable, sure, but it was tolerable. It was just a normal texture of being alive. Now boredom registers almost like a malfunction, something to fix immediately, the second it starts. The gap between feeling under-stimulated and reaching for your phone has shrunk to almost nothing. Most people don't experience boredom anymore. They intercept it.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS IN AN UNFILLED MOMENT

Here's what's easy to forget, boredom was never actually empty. It was your brain's background processing time, sorting through the day, connecting ideas that had nothing to do with each other, occasionally producing the exact insight or idea you'd been stuck on for days, except it arrives at 2pm in a queue, not at your desk while you are trying to force it. Constant stimulation does not just remove discomfort. It removes the raw material creativity actually runs on, unstructured, undirected thinking time that can't be scheduled, only allowed to happen.

WHY THIS IS HARDER TO NOTICE THAN IT SOUNDS

Nobody feels the absence of an idea they never had. That's what makes this loss so quiet, you don't experience "I would have thought of something interesting just now if I hadn't filled the gap." You just fill the gap, move on, and never know what didn't get to surface. The cost is invisible precisely because it's a cost of something that never happened. That's very different from, say, tiredness, which announces itself. This one doesn't. It just slowly narrows what your mind produces, without ever telling you it's happening.

THE TRUTH YOU NEED TO KNOW

A lot of what feels like "I'm just not that creative" or "I never have good ideas anymore" is not actually a personality trait. It's a symptom of never giving your mind the unfilled time it needs to wander somewhere useful. You can't out scroll your way into insight. The two are, in a fairly direct sense, in competition with each other.

It's also worth admitting, reaching for the phone in these gaps is not really about entertainment most of the time. It's about avoiding the mild discomfort of being alone with your own thinking, even for eleven seconds in a lift. That discomfort used to be tolerable. Now it barely gets the chance to start before it's interrupted.

WHY "JUST PUT THE PHONE DOWN" DOESN'T ACTUALLY WORK

Telling yourself to simply resist reaching for it treats this as a willpower problem, when it's closer to a withdrawal problem. The urge to fill silence is not really about wanting content. It's the discomfort of an under-stimulated brain that's been trained, through years of instant intercepts, to expect input constantly. Removing the phone without addressing that trained expectation usually just leads to restlessness, not reflection.

WHAT REBUILDING BOREDOM TOLERANCE ACTUALLY LOOKS LIKE

Not a dramatic digital detox. Smaller, more repeatable interruptions to the automatic reach:

- Let one small wait go unfilled on purpose: the queue, the lift, the kettle and notice how uncomfortable even that short a gap feels at first.

- Keep a place to catch the thoughts that show up in those gaps: They're often oddly specific and easy to lose the moment you distract yourself again.

- Treat restlessness as a normal part of the process, not a sign you're doing it wrong: The discomfort fades with repetition; it doesn't disappear immediately.

SO WHAT NOW? AS I ALWAYS ASK

Next time you feel that reflex, the reach for your phone before you have even registered why, pause for just a few seconds before you do it. Not forever. Just long enough to ask what your mind might have done with that moment if you'd let it.

You'll probably never know what you have been missing until you start leaving the gaps open long enough to find out.

I hope you find this helpful.

Don't forget to like. Share. Follow. Comment

Shalom!

title: 5 Digital Skills Every Nigerian Youth Needs to Make Money in 2026
excerpt: Practical digital skills you can learn and turn into income opportunities, even as a beginner.
content:
Nigeria’s job market is changing quickly. A university degree is still valuable, but having practical digital skills can open additional opportunities for young Nigerians.

From writing and designing to managing social media and using artificial intelligence, many services can now be delivered online to businesses and clients in Nigeria and abroad.

The Nigerian government is also putting increasing attention on digital skills and the digital economy. In 2026, the Federal Government launched initiatives aimed at expanding digital skills, employment and opportunities for Nigerians to work with international clients.

The good news is that you don’t need to learn everything at once.

Here are five digital skills worth considering in 2026.

1. Content Writing

If you can research a topic and explain it clearly, content writing can become a useful skill.

Businesses need written content for websites, blogs, newsletters, social media pages, product descriptions and other platforms. Writers can also work with individuals who need articles, scripts, captions or other forms of written communication.

A beginner can start by learning:

  • Blog writing

  • SEO writing

  • Copywriting

  • Social media captions

  • Script writing

  • Product descriptions

The important thing is not simply learning how to write. You also need to understand your audience, research information properly and produce content that solves a problem.

How to start: Pick one type of writing, create three to five sample pieces and use them as your portfolio when approaching potential clients.

2. Social Media Management

Almost every business wants an online presence, but many business owners don’t have enough time to manage their social media accounts.

That’s where social media managers can help.

A social media manager may create posts, write captions, schedule content, respond to comments, research trends and analyse the performance of a page.

You can begin by learning how platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, Facebook and LinkedIn work.

You should also learn basic content strategy. Posting randomly is not enough. You need to understand who the audience is, what they want and what type of content makes them take action.

How to start: Choose a small business, create a sample seven-day content plan for it and use that as part of your portfolio.

3. Graphic Design and Canva

You don’t necessarily need expensive design software to begin learning graphic design.

Tools such as Canva allow beginners to create social media graphics, flyers, presentations, thumbnails, posters and other visual content.

Graphic design can become particularly useful when combined with another skill. For example, someone who understands both social media management and design can offer a business a complete content package instead of only creating individual graphics.

How to start: Learn basic principles such as typography, spacing, alignment and colour combinations. Then practise by recreating different types of professional designs.

Your goal should eventually be to create original work rather than simply relying on templates.

4. Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools

AI is becoming an important part of many digital jobs.

However, learning AI doesn’t necessarily mean becoming a computer scientist.

For many beginners, the useful skill is learning how to use AI tools to research ideas, brainstorm content, analyse information, improve workflows and complete repetitive tasks more efficiently.

The key is to combine AI with another valuable skill.

For example:

Writing + AI = faster content production

Design + AI = faster creative workflows

Marketing + AI = faster research and content planning

Don’t think of AI as a replacement for learning. Think of it as a tool that can make your existing skills more productive.

5. Digital Marketing

Digital marketing brings several skills together.

It includes areas such as search engine optimisation (SEO), social media marketing, email marketing, online advertising, content marketing and analytics.

Businesses need people who can help them attract potential customers online and turn attention into sales.

You don’t have to master everything immediately. Start with one area and gradually expand your knowledge.

For example, Google currently offers a Digital Marketing & E-commerce Career Certificate designed for beginners, covering areas including social media marketing, search, email, e-commerce and analytics.

Where Can You Learn These Skills?

One of the biggest advantages of learning digital skills today is the number of online resources available.

You can start with free educational videos on YouTube and practise what you learn immediately.

There are also structured learning opportunities. For example, Nigeria’s government-backed Digital Training Academy says it provides access to free digital and professional training through partnerships with platforms including Coursera and Pluralsight.

MTN Nigeria also operates its Digital Skills for Digital Jobs initiative, which provides curated learning resources aimed at helping young Nigerians develop digital skills for employment and entrepreneurship.

The most important thing is to avoid becoming a professional course collector.

You don’t need 20 certificates before you start.

Learn → practise → build a portfolio → look for clients.

How Can You Start Making Money?

Learning a skill is only the first step.

The next step is turning that skill into a service that somebody is willing to pay for.

For example, instead of saying:

“I know Canva.”

You could offer:

“I create social media graphics for small businesses.”

Instead of saying:

“I can write.”

You could offer:

“I write SEO-friendly blog articles for businesses.”

This difference is important because clients usually pay for solutions, not simply for someone’s knowledge.

Start small. Create sample work, build a simple portfolio and approach businesses, creators and potential clients who could benefit from your service.

You can eventually explore freelance platforms, direct outreach, social media and professional networks to find opportunities.

Final Thoughts

You don’t need to master all five skills.

In fact, trying to learn everything at once can slow you down.

Pick one skill.

Spend the next 30 days learning and practising it. Create real examples of your work, build a portfolio and start looking for opportunities.

As your experience grows, add complementary skills.

Nigeria’s digital economy is creating new opportunities, but opportunity alone isn’t enough. You need a skill that can solve a real problem.

The best time to start building that skill is before you need it.

content:
The mirror had hung in that house for eleven years before Adaeze ever raised a hand against it, and even then, she hadn’t meant to.

It happened on a Tuesday — she would remember that detail long after she forgot the color of the walls, the smell of the hallway, the sound her own voice used to make before it learned to whisper. A Tuesday, ordinary as bread, the kind of day that asks nothing of you and receives nothing in return. She had been standing in front of the mirror doing something so mundane it embarrassed her later to recall it: pinning her hair back, tilting her chin, deciding whether the woman looking back at her still deserved to be looked at.

And then Chidi’s voice had come up the stairs, low and even, the way it always was right before it wasn’t. Adaeze. Just her name. Nothing more. But she knew, the way a house knows a storm is coming before the first drop falls — some pressure change in the air, some tightening behind the ribs — and her hand had closed into a fist before she’d told it to, and the fist had found the glass, and the glass had found seven ways to break.

She stood there afterward with blood beading along her knuckles like small red stars, and she did not cry. That was the thing she would think about for years — she did not cry. She simply looked at the wreckage of her own reflection, fractured into panes of light and shadow, and felt something in her chest exhale for the first time in longer than she could remember.

He never came up the stairs that day. She would learn later that he’d simply turned around and walked back out to the car, as if her silence — her refusal to answer, her refusal to make herself small and available for whatever was coming — had confused some internal calculation he’d relied on for years. As if the woman who broke mirrors instead of apologizing was a woman he no longer recognized, and didn’t know how to want.

He left three weeks after that. Not because of the mirror. Because of everything the mirror had let loose in her.

title: AI Isn’t Taking Your Job — But Someone Who Knows How to Use It Might
excerpt: A few years ago, knowing how to use a computer was an advantage.Today, knowing how to use AI might be becoming one.Everywhere you look, artificial intelligence …
content:
A few years ago, knowing how to use a computer was an advantage.

Today, knowing how to use AI might be becoming one.

Everywhere you look, artificial intelligence is changing the way people work. It can write, research, analyse information, generate ideas, create images and even help people learn new skills.

And naturally, people are worried.

Will AI take our jobs?

Maybe that’s not the question we should be asking.

A more uncomfortable question is:

What happens when someone who knows how to use AI competes for the same job as someone who doesn’t?

AI is becoming more than a chatbot

For many people, AI still means opening a chatbot and asking it a question.

But the technology is moving beyond that.

AI is increasingly being used to handle repetitive tasks, assist with research, analyse information and help businesses get work done faster.

Think about a content writer.

One writer might spend hours researching a topic, creating an outline and working through a first draft.

Another might use AI to brainstorm ideas, organise research and improve their draft.

The second writer hasn’t necessarily become a worse writer.

They may simply have more time to focus on the things that require a human touch: creativity, judgment, personality and understanding their audience.

That’s where the real advantage begins.

The workplace is changing

It’s easy to imagine AI as a machine whose only purpose is to replace humans.

But that’s not necessarily how this transition will happen.

Some jobs will change, and some tasks will become automated. At the same time, new roles and new ways of working will emerge.

We’ve seen this happen before.

Technology has always changed the workplace. The people who adapt to those changes often find themselves with new opportunities.

AI may be doing the same thing.

The question isn’t whether your current job will look exactly the same in five years.

It probably won’t.

The question is whether you’ll be willing to learn as it changes.

But AI still needs you

Here’s something people sometimes forget:

AI can be wrong.

It can give you information that sounds convincing but isn’t true. It can misunderstand what you want. It can produce something generic when what you really need is creativity or human understanding.

That’s why knowing how to use AI isn’t the same as letting AI do everything for you.

The valuable skill is knowing when to use it, what to ask it, what to verify and what to do yourself.

So, should you learn AI?

You don’t need to become a programmer.

You don’t need to understand every technical detail behind artificial intelligence.

Start with your own field.

Ask yourself:

What part of my work takes too much time?

What tasks are repetitive?

Where could AI help me research, organise or generate ideas?

Then learn how to use it responsibly.

Because the goal isn’t to become dependent on AI.

The goal is to become better at what you already do.

Maybe the future of work isn’t humans versus AI.

Maybe it’s humans who know how to work with AI versus those who refuse to learn.

AI might not take your job.

But someone who knows how to use it might become better prepared for the opportunities you both want.

title: 100MB.. Is It Enough
excerpt: The government announced 100MB of free daily data for students like it was a scholarship. Like it was rent paid, like it was a laptop, like it was anything clos…
content:
The government announced 100MB of free daily data for students like it was a scholarship. Like it was rent paid, like it was a laptop, like it was anything close to what "digital learning" actually requires. I did the math before I did the gratitude.

100MB is one video call, if you turn your camera off. It's a handful of PDF downloads, if they're not scanned images pretending to be PDFs.

I'm not ungrateful for gestures. I've lived here long enough to know something is technically better than nothing, and I know somewhere a student with zero data now has a little more than zero. That matters, even at this size. But I'm tired of being asked to celebrate the shape of help instead of the substance of it.

And of course it's election season again. Funny how the announcements multiply right when the votes are about to matter data today, maybe light tomorrow, a scholarship scheme by December. I'm not saying the timing is deliberate. I'm saying I've seen this calendar before, and I know what month it usually stops being generous.

Meanwhile, the man who oversaw a decade of our elections just landed an ambassador post in Doha. So Yakubu will manage. The rest of us will get 100MB.

This is the pattern, not the exception. Light comes back for two hours and it's a "restoration." A road gets one lane resurfaced and it's a "commissioning." A scholarship covers registration but not tuition and it's still called a scholarship. We've been trained to receive announcements as if they were outcomes, to clap at the press release before anyone's checked whether the thing actually works.

I think about what 100MB says about who they think we are students who'll be moved by the sound of "free" more than the fact of "enough." It's not malice, I don't think. It's just cheaper to announce data than to fix electricity, cheaper to whitelist a few platforms than to make the internet actually affordable, cheaper to give us a headline than a system.

So I'll take the 100MB. I'm not too proud to use what's offered. But I'm also not going to pretend it solves what it claims to solve, or thank anyone like it did. There's a difference between gratitude and amnesia, and I'd rather stay a little ungrateful than forget, every single time, what we actually needed.

We are handed peanuts to sway us. Laughable, honestly. And the maddening part isn't even the peanuts it's that they're not wrong to try it. It's worked before.

title: Health is wealth. But we only learn that the expensive way.
excerpt: Think about the last time you told yourself "I'll rest later." Did later ever actually come? For most of us, it doesn't, because we keep pushing it down the lis…
content:
Think about the last time you told yourself "I'll rest later." Did later ever actually come? For most of us, it doesn't, because we keep pushing it down the list until our body makes the decision for us, usually in the form of a headache that won't quit, a cold that lingers too long, or an exhaustion that sleep alone can't fix anymore. That's the thing about rest, it's not negotiable, and it's definitely not something that should be postponed. Listen to your body, go for regular checkups, and add rest into your routine the same way you'd add anything else that matters.

Health is wealth, they say, but it's quite a bit to understand until you actually fall ill. Sickness can be avoidable, but only with a proper routine, one that includes eating healthy, exercising regularly, going for checkups, and yes, resting.

But there's one thing people skip the most, and that's rest. We wear tiredness like a badge of honor, as if pushing through exhaustion means we're winning at life, when really it just means we're running on borrowed time. Your body isn't a machine that runs forever on empty, it's a system that needs downtime to keep working properly, and the moment you start ignoring that, everything else begins to slip.

While you sleep, your muscles repair themselves, your cells regenerate, and your immune system quietly rebuilds its defenses, which is why skimping on rest leaves you more vulnerable to illness than you'd expect. It also sharpens your mind in ways you don't notice until it's missing, because everything feels harder when you're exhausted, focus fades, memory slips, and a tired brain ends up making tired choices. Your heart feels it too, since chronic lack of rest has been linked to high blood pressure and added strain, proving that your heart needs the slowdown just as much as your muscles do. Even your mood depends on it more than people realize, as irritability, anxiety, and low spirits often trace straight back to poor rest, while a well rested mind simply handles stress better. And perhaps most importantly, rest is what stands between you and burnout, because constant hustle without recovery doesn't make you more productive, it only speeds up the crash, and rest is what makes consistency possible in the first place.

So don't wait until your body forces you to stop. Build rest into your routine the same way you'd build in exercise or meals, take the naps, sleep the full hours, take the day off when you need it, because it isn't laziness, it's maintenance. In the end, a body that's well rested is a body that's well prepared, for work, for life, for everything.
