title: What Happened After Heartbreak?
excerpt: So, they left you. And what happened next? Did the world stop spinning? Did the sun refuse to rise the next morning because the person you loved was no longer i…
content:
So, they left you. And what happened next? Did the world stop spinning? Did the sun refuse to rise the next morning because the person you loved was no longer in your life? Did their departure somehow put your own life on hold? Of course not. Their life continued, and whether you like it or not, yours continued too. The only question is: what are you going to do with the life that continued after they left?

Maybe you think their life will be paused because they left you. Maybe you think their light will stop shining because they walked away. Perhaps you are sitting somewhere waiting for their life to fall apart, hoping that one day they will finally realize what they lost and come running back to you. Then think again. Someone leaving you does not automatically mean their destiny will be denied, just as your heartbreak does not mean yours has been cancelled. Life does not pause because a relationship ended.

And honestly, some of us need to stop watching the person who left us and start watching ourselves. We spend so much time checking whether they are happy, whether they have found someone else, whether they are struggling, or whether karma has finally arrived at their doorstep. We become spectators in someone else's life while our own life is waiting for us to participate in it. You are sitting there waiting for karma to deal with someone while your own dreams are waiting for you to deal with them. You must be a comedian.

Yes, you were disappointed. Yes, you may have been hurt. Maybe you genuinely believed that person was going to be part of your future, and suddenly you had to imagine your life without them. Give yourself permission to acknowledge that. You don't have to pretend that nothing happened or force yourself to be fine the next morning. But there has to be a point where disappointment stops being an experience and starts becoming a lifestyle. You cannot keep building your identity around the person who left you.

Sometimes, the space created by someone's absence can become the space where you finally start doing things for yourself. Maybe you have been putting off that business because you were too occupied with the relationship. Maybe there is a skill you have always wanted to learn but never made time for. Maybe you have always wanted to write, design, study, create content, start a small business, improve your career, or simply become more disciplined with your life. Now you have time. What are you going to do with it?

This is where many people get it wrong. They say, "I am going to become successful so that they will regret leaving me." But why should your success still revolve around the person who left? Why are they still the centre of your plans? Build because you want to build. Learn because you want to grow. Start the business because you have something to offer. Improve yourself because you deserve to become better, not because you are waiting for someone to notice the difference.

And please, don't turn your entire healing process into a competition with someone who may not even know they are competing with you. You don't need to become richer than them, prettier than their new partner, more successful than their friends, or more visible on social media just to prove a point. That is still allowing their existence to control your decisions. The real win is when you stop asking, "Will they see what I have become?" and start asking, "What kind of person do I want to become?"

There is also something we don't talk about enough: sometimes people leave at a time when we desperately needed a change. That doesn't necessarily mean they left for our benefit, because we cannot always know another person's reasons for leaving. But their departure can still become an opportunity if we choose to use it. A closed door can leave you standing outside complaining about the door, or it can make you look around and realize there are other doors you have never tried to open.

Imagine spending six months waiting for someone to regret leaving you when you could have spent those six months building something. Imagine checking their page every morning while someone else is spending those same mornings learning a skill that will change their income. Imagine hoping they will come back while the life you said you wanted is sitting untouched because you are still waiting for the past to give you permission to move forward.

Don't do that to yourself.

Let the relationship end if it has ended. Let the disappointment be real, but let it have an expiry date. Pick yourself up and look at the things you have neglected. What did you stop doing? What dream have you postponed? What skill have you always wanted to develop? What business idea have you been talking about for years? What kind of person have you always wanted to become? Start there.

Maybe you can start small. You don't need a huge amount of money or a perfect plan before you begin. You can start with what you already have. If you can design, design. If you can write, write. If you can bake, bake. If you know how to sell, sell. If you have a talent that you have been hiding because you were too busy worrying about a relationship, bring it back to life. Your next chapter does not have to begin with something dramatic. Sometimes it begins with one decision to stop wasting your own potential.

And don't be surprised if your life starts looking different after you make that decision. You may discover abilities you never knew you had because you finally have the time and freedom to explore them. You may meet new people, learn new things, make mistakes, start again, and eventually build something you are genuinely proud of. The person who left may never see any of it. They may see it and say nothing. They may hear about it years later. They may even come back. But none of those possibilities should determine whether you move forward.

Because your life cannot be built around the hope that someone who left will one day return.

One day, you may look back and realize that the biggest thing you gained after that relationship was not another person. It was yourself. You became more intentional with your time. You learned to make decisions without constantly seeking someone's approval. You became better at recognizing what you want and what you will no longer accept. You built something. You failed at something and tried again. You became more confident. You discovered that there was a whole life waiting for you outside the relationship you thought was your whole world.

That is why you shouldn't be afraid of the question, "What happens after heartbreak?"

Something happens after heartbreak.

Life happens.

Bills still need to be paid. Dreams still need to be pursued. Opportunities still come. New skills can still be learned. Businesses can still be started. Books can still be written. Careers can still grow. Friendships can still be made. There are still places you haven't visited, things you haven't learned, people you haven't met, and versions of yourself you haven't discovered.

So don't sit around waiting for the person who left you to lose their light. Their light is not your responsibility, and neither is their destiny. Your responsibility is what you do with yours.

Maybe they left you at a chapter you thought was supposed to last forever. Fine. Turn the page.

Don't let them meet you where they left you.

Let them meet a person who kept going. Better still, don't spend your life hoping they meet you at all. Build a life so meaningful that whether they return, regret leaving, or never look back becomes irrelevant.

Because heartbreak may have ended something, but it does not have to end you.

So, what happened after heartbreak?

That depends on you.

Did you see the end of a relationship and mistake it for the end of your life?

Or did you look at the empty space it left behind and say, "Alright. What can I build here?"

title: You Don't Have To Have Your Life Figured Out Yet
excerpt: Why feeling behind doesn't mean you're actually behind.
content:
Have you ever looked at your life and wondered, "What am I even doing?"

You open social media and someone your age has graduated. Someone has landed their dream job. Someone is starting a business. Someone is getting married. Someone is traveling to places you have only seen in pictures. And then there's you.

Still trying to figure things out.

Sometimes, it can make you feel like everyone received a manual for life except you.

You start asking questions you don't even have answers to.

Am I falling behind?

Why does everyone seems to know what they want except me?

If you ever felt this way, I want you to know something:

You are not necessarily behind.

You may simply be on a different part of your journey.

Life Isn't a Race

Growing up can sometimes feel like there is a deadline for everything. You are supposed to finish school at a certain age. Get a job. Become financially stable. Find love. Get married. Build a home. Become successful.

And somehow, you are expected to accomplish all of these things according to a timeline that nobody actually gave you.

But who decided that everyone's life has to follow the same schedule?

Some people find their passion when they're young. Others spend years trying different things before discovering what truly makes them happy.

Some people get their dream job immediately after school.

Others have to apply again and again before someone finally gives them a chance.

Some people know exactly what they want.

Others are still discovering themselves.

Neither person is automatically doing better.

Different doesn't mean behind.

Social Media Doesn't Show You The Whole Story

This is something I have had to remind myself of too.

When you look at someone's social media page, you're actually seeing the part of their life they chose to show you. You see the graduation picture. You see the car. You see the engagement announcement. You see business launch. You see the Vacation.

But you don’t see the uncertainty that came before those moments.

You don't see the applications that were rejected. You don't see the night they questioned themselves. You don’t see the mistakes.

You don't see the moments when they wondered whether they were making the right decisions.

You're comparing your behind-the-scenes to someone else's highlight reel.

And that's an unfair comparison.

So celebrate people when good things happen to them. Be happy for them. But don't turn their achievements into evidence that you're not doing enough.

Someone else's progress does not cancel yours.

You Are Allowed to Change Your Mind

Maybe you once thought you knew exactly what you wanted to do with your life.

Then things changed.

Maybe the career you imagined for yourself no longer feels right. Maybe the dream you had years ago doesn't excite you anymore. Maybe you started something and realized you wanted something completely different.

That's okay.

You are growing. And growth sometimes changes your perspective. You are allowed to say: "This isn't what I want anymore".

You're allowed to start over.

You are allowed to try something new.

You are allowed to take a different path.

Changing direction doesn't automatically mean you wasted your time. Sometimes the wrong road teaches you enough to recognize the one.

Start With What You Have

One of the biggest mistakes we make is waiting until we have everything figured out before we begin. We tell ourselves:

"I'll start when I'm ready".

"I'll do it when I have enough money."

"I'll begin when I know exactly what I'm doing".

But sometimes, readiness comes after you start.

Write the first page.

Take the course.

Send the application.

Start the small business.

Make the phone call.

Try the thing you've been thinking about.

It doesn't have to be perfect.

It just has to begin.

You don't need to see the entire staircase before taking the first step

Give Yourself Time

Not every season of your life will look impressive.

Some seasons are loud.

Some are exciting.

Some are full of achievements.

But some seasons are quiet.

They are the seasons where you are learning, making mistakes, discovering yourself and slowly becoming stronger.

And just because nothing exciting seems to be happening doesn't mean you're not growing.

Think about a seed.

When you first put it into the soil, there is nothing impressive to look at.

For a while, it seems like nothing is happening.

But underneath the surface, something is taking place.

Roots are forming.

Growth is happening where nobody can see it.

Maybe you're in that kind of season right now.

Maybe your progress is simply happening quietly.

Don't give up on yourself just because your growth isn't visible yet.

So, What If You Don't Have It All Figured Out?

Honestly?

That's okay.

You don't need to know exactly where you'll be five years from now.

You don't need to have every answer today.

You don't need to become everything at once.

Focus on the next step.

Learn what you can.

Try what interests you.

Make mistakes.

Start again when you need to.

And give yourself permission to grow at your own pace.

One day, you may look back at this confusing season and realize that you were not actually lost.

You were learning.

You were growing.

You were becoming the person you were meant to be.

So the next time you feel like everyone is moving ahead while you're standing still, remember this:

You are not running their race.

Your journey is yours.

Your timing is yours.

And your story is still being written.

Don't judge your entire life by a chapter that hasn't finished yet.

title: WHY NIGERIAN INTERNET DRAMA GETS MORE ATTENTION THAN IMPORTANT CONVERSATIONS
excerpt: We react to everything. But are we paying attention to what matters?
content:
A serious thread about the naira, or fuel prices, or a bill that will actually affect your life gets just three retweets, maybe a sigh emoji, just maybe. A celebrity's ex posts a cryptic story at 2am and by morning it's a full trending topic, with think pieces, screenshots, and strangers arguing in your mentions about a relationship they have no stake in.

You have noticed it. You have probably even taken part in it, I know. Not because you are shallow but because the drama was simply built better than the conversation.

It's Not That People Don't Care.

The easy explanation is that Nigerians on the internet are more interested in gossip than substance. That's lazy, and it's not even true. People care deeply, you can see it in how quickly a fundraiser moves when it's framed right, or how fired up a comment section gets when a real issue is presented as a story instead of a statistic.

The difference is not the caring. It's the packaging. Drama arrives pre-loaded with characters, stakes, a villain, and a cliffhanger. A policy issue arrives as a paragraph you have to work to understand. One asks nothing of you but your attention. The other asks for effort you may not have left after a full day of surviving Lagos, or Abuja, or wherever you're doing your own version of surviving.

THE ALGORITHM IS NOT NEUTRAL, IT'S A CO-AUTHOR

Here's the part most people skip over, you are not just choosing drama over depth. Something is choosing it for you, repeatedly, until it feels like your own preference.

Engagement: not truth, not important, is what gets rewarded. A screenshot of someone's messy breakup will always outperform a thread explaining subsidy removal, because outrage and curiosity are cheaper to trigger than understanding. The apps are not asking "what does this person need to know." It's asking "what will keep this person scrolling for four more minutes." Those are rarely the same question.

THE UNCOMFORTABLE PART

Here's what stings a little, drama gives you something real conversations often don't, a clear villain, a clean side to take, and the satisfying feeling of having an opinion without the responsibility of holding it for long. Tomorrow there will be a new scandal, and today's outrage will be forgotten with no consequences to you. But a real issue, insecurity, unemployment, a failing system does not resolve by tomorrow. It just sits there, asking you to keep caring long after it stopped being entertaining. Drama is a story with an ending. Real life rarely gives you one.

SO WHAT DO YOU ACTUALLY DO WITH THIS?Not "log off" that advice rarely survives past the weekend. You know what I'm talking about.Try noticing instead. Before you engage with the next trending topic, ask what it's actually asking of you, your attention, or your outrage, or nothing at all. That one second pause does not make you above it. It just makes the choice yours again, instead of the algorithm's.

Maybe the goal was never to care about the important things and ignore the noise completely. Maybe it's learning to tell, in real time, which one you're actually being handed, the story, or the thing that was trying to look like one.

How relatable is this to you?

We are eager to hear from you at the comment.

Like. Share. Follow. Comment.

title: Should You Call Your Boss by His First Name? Tony Elumelu Video Has Nigerians Divided
excerpt: She said “Good morning, Tony.” He replied that she should call him “Mr Elumelu” or “TOE.” Now Nigerians are debating something bigger than the viral video: if your workplace teaches you to use first names, should that rule still apply when you're speaking to the chairman?
content:
A young UBA trainee’s “Good morning, Tony” greeting to Tony Elumelu has sparked a wider debate about respect, workplace hierarchy and whether first-name culture belongs in Nigerian offices.

A brief exchange between United Bank for Africa (UBA) Group Chairman Tony Elumelu and a young graduate trainee has turned into a much bigger conversation about how Nigerians should address senior colleagues and bosses.

The incident happened during the graduation ceremony of UBA’s Graduate Management Accelerated Programme (GMAP), where a trainee addressed Elumelu simply as “Tony” while speaking during an interactive session. UBA itself confirms that the 2026 GMAP graduation ceremony involved more than 700 young professionals in Lagos. 

Elumelu appeared to initially mishear the greeting, asking whether the trainee had said “Toyin.” When she clarified that she had said, “Good morning, Tony,” he stopped her and told her to address him as “Mr Elumelu” or “TOE.” 

The exchange was brief, but the question it raised has proved anything but simple: when you work for an organisation that encourages first-name communication, does that mean you should address the chairman by his first name too?

The Viral Moment

In the video circulating online, the young woman stands to interact with Elumelu and begins her greeting with “Good morning, Tony.”

Elumelu initially appears to think she said “Toyin.” She repeats herself and makes it clear that she is addressing him as Tony.

He then corrects her.

According to multiple reports of the video, Elumelu tells her she should call him “Mr Elumelu” or “TOE,” rather than Tony. He also says he does not subscribe to what he describes as “Oyinbo life.” 

The trainee subsequently addresses him as “Mr Elumelu” before continuing with her question.

There is no indication from the available reporting that the exchange developed into a serious confrontation. What happened afterward, however, was largely outside the room.

The clip went viral.

Why Did a Simple Greeting Become Such a Big Deal?

For many Nigerians, the answer is obvious.

How you address someone can communicate much more than their name.

In traditional Nigerian settings, calling an older person “Sir” or “Ma” is often considered basic courtesy. Senior executives may be addressed as “Chairman,” “Boss,” “Oga,” “Mr [surname]” or by a professional title.

That is particularly true when there is a significant difference in age or status.

So, to some Nigerians watching the video, hearing a young trainee address one of the country's most prominent businessmen simply as “Tony” sounded unnecessarily casual.

But there is another side to the story.

What If Your Workplace Teaches You to Use First Names?

This is where the situation becomes more complicated.

Some people who have worked in Nigerian banks and corporate organisations have come forward to argue that the trainee may not have intended any disrespect.

One business leader, Modupe Okeowo, said in a reaction shared on X that she understood the woman to be a new recruit and suggested that her training may have contributed to the situation.

Okeowo said new employees can be taught to address people within an organisation by their first names and suggested that the woman may simply have carried that practice into the interaction with Elumelu. 

Other former bank employees have made similar arguments, saying first-name culture can be deliberately built into corporate training.

And this is important because the woman was not simply a random member of the public approaching a billionaire on the street.

She was reportedly a graduate trainee participating in a UBA programme.

That changes the context.

Is Calling Your Boss by His First Name Actually Disrespectful?

Not necessarily.

In some modern workplaces, using someone's first name is completely normal.

It can make communication feel less hierarchical and encourage employees to speak more freely. Some companies deliberately adopt this culture because they want employees to feel comfortable approaching senior executives.

And there is evidence that first-name culture has existed within parts of the Nigerian banking industry for years.

So, if an organisation tells its employees, “Call everyone by their first name,” would it really be fair to accuse an employee of disrespect for following that culture?

That is where the debate gets interesting.

But There Is Also a Difference Between Company Culture and Personal Preference

There is another reasonable argument.

Even if a company encourages informal communication, an individual may still have a personal preference about how they want to be addressed.

In this case, Elumelu made his preference clear.

He did not tell the trainee that she could not speak to him. He simply told her what he preferred to be called in that setting.

And once someone has clearly stated a preferred form of address, there is a strong argument for respecting it.

The disagreement, therefore, may not really be about whether “Tony” is inherently disrespectful.

It may be about knowing when a general workplace rule meets an individual's personal preference.

The Nigerian Workplace Is Changing

This incident also exposes a larger generational shift.

Older Nigerians generally grew up in environments where age and position carried significant weight.

You did not casually call your teacher by their first name.

You did not call your parents' friends by their first names.

And calling an older person without a title could easily be interpreted as poor home training.

But younger professionals are entering workplaces that increasingly operate differently.

They are working in multinational companies, startups, and modern corporate environments where CEOs can sit with junior employees, encourage them to challenge ideas, and even ask to be addressed by their first names.

The result is an interesting collision between traditional Nigerian respect culture and modern corporate culture.

Neither side necessarily has to be completely wrong.

What Are Nigerians Saying?

The reactions to the Elumelu video have reflected this divide.

Some Nigerians believe the trainee should have known better and addressed Elumelu as “Sir,” “Chairman” or “Mr Elumelu.”

Others believe she was simply following the culture she had been taught during her training and that the incident should not have become a public spectacle.

Some former bank employees have particularly defended the young woman, arguing that first-name communication is not unusual in the financial sector. 

Others have taken a more nuanced position: first-name culture may be acceptable inside an organisation, but employees should still learn to read the room when dealing with a very senior executive at a formal event.

That may be the most practical lesson from the entire incident.

So, Who Was Right?

Perhaps the better question is not whether Tony Elumelu was right or whether the young woman was wrong.

It is whether respect should depend on a person's name, their tone, the workplace culture or the preference of the person being addressed.

Imagine working in a company where everyone, from the newest recruit to the CEO, is called by their first name.

You finish your training and walk into a room where the company's chairman is standing in front of you.

Do you automatically switch back to “Sir”?

Or do you assume that the company's first-name culture still applies?

There is no universal answer.

The safest approach is to understand the culture of the organisation, pay attention to the setting and, most importantly, respect the individual's stated preference.

Because while “Good morning, Tony” may sound perfectly normal in one office, it may produce a very different reaction in another.

And perhaps that is the real lesson from this viral moment: professional etiquette is not always about knowing the right word. Sometimes, it is about knowing the room.

If your boss told you to call him by his first name, would you actually do it?

title: Looks premeditated to me.
excerpt: When prosecutors argue that an act was premeditated rather than the result of a sudden mental break, they rely on evidence of sequence, timing, and deliberate c…
content:
When prosecutors argue that an act was premeditated rather than the result of a sudden mental break, they rely on evidence of sequence, timing, and deliberate choice. In the case of Lindsay Clancy, arguments that the deaths of her three children were planned center on specific, documented steps taken on the evening of January 24, 2023.

The core argument for premeditation rests on the creation of a guaranteed, uninterrupted window of time. Prosecutors highlighted that Clancy sent her husband on two specific errands picking up a prescription at a pharmacy and getting takeout from a restaurant further away in a neighboring town. Digital records from her phone showed she checked the restaurant's route and travel duration on Apple Maps just before asking him to go. Prosecutors contend this search was a deliberate calculation to confirm she would have roughly 45 to 50 minutes alone in the house.

Additionally, prosecutors pointed to the physical execution of the acts and her demeanor immediately beforehand. Retrieving exercise bands and using them sequentially required deliberate choice and sustained effort over several minutes, which meets the legal definition of reflection prior to action. Furthermore, during a brief phone call with her husband while he was out, her tone was described as completely calm and ordinary an interaction prosecutors interpret as a conscious attempt to avoid raising alarm or causing him to return early.

Conversely, defense attorneys and mental health experts argue that these structured actions do not rule out severe mental illness. They contend that individuals suffering from acute postpartum psychosis or severe depressive delusions can still execute multi-step tasks and display outward calm while entirely detached from reality. Whether these actions reflect cold, conscious calculation or the internal logic of a profound psychotic breakdown remains the central point of contention in the case.

title: YOU'RE TIRED ALL THE TIME? IT MAY NOT JUST BE LAZINESS
excerpt: The Exhaustion That Sleep Doesn't Fix
content:
You slept eight hours. You still feel like you fought someone in your dreams. You get up, and within an hour, you are already counting down to when you can lie back down. Somewhere along the way, someone, a parent, a boss, your own inner voice, labeled this "laziness," and you believed it, because it was easier than asking what was actually going on. If rest has not been fixing your tiredness in a while, this is for you. Journey with me.

THE GUILT BEFORE THE QUESTION

Most people don't start by asking "why am I this tired." They start by asking "what's wrong with me that I can't just push through like everyone else." The exhaustion gets buried under self judgment before anyone even considers a cause. That order matters. Guilt makes you hide the tiredness, powered through meetings, fake energy in conversations, blaming your own discipline instead of actually investigating it. You end up managing the shame of being tired more than the tiredness itself.

IT'S RARELY JUST ONE THING

Fatigue is almost never a single clean cause, which is part of why it's so easy to dismiss. It's the combination of broken sleep from a mind that won't switch off, meals skipped or grabbed in a rush, a body that has not moved properly in weeks, and a nervous system that's been quietly running on alert for months without a real break. Each piece alone might seem manageable. Stacked together, they add up to a tiredness that no amount of "sleeping earlier tonight" can undo. I'm sure you're getting my point.

WHY REST DOESN'T ALWAYS FIX IT

Here's something people don't say enough, sleep and rest are not always the same thing. I hope you are not surprised? You can get hours of sleep and still be in a state of stress the entire time, jaw tight, mind racing, body never actually relaxing. That's sleep without recovery, and it explains why you can wake up from a full night feeling like you barely closed your eyes. Real rest requires your nervous system to believe it's safe to slow down. If you are carrying unresolved stress, unspoken worry, or a body that's been running on adrenaline, sleep alone will not reach that.

THE UNCOMFORTABLE TRUTH

Calling yourself lazy is, in a strange way, easier than asking whether something in your life or your body needs attention. Laziness has a simple fix, try harder. A deeper cause means facing something that might take longer to sort out, cost money, or require admitting you have been ignoring your own warning signs for a while. It's worth asking honestly, is this actually a discipline problem? or have I been quietly running on empty for longer than I have let myself notice?

WHEN IT'S WORTH PAYING CLOSER ATTENTION

Occasional tiredness after a rough week is normal. But fatigue that doesn't lift after real rest, that comes with other changes in your body, mood, or ability to function, that's not something to keep explaining away with willpower. That pattern is worth taking to a doctor, not just a better sleep schedule.

So What Now?

Stop asking how to be less lazy, and start asking what your tiredness has actually been trying to tell you about your sleep, your stress, your body, or all three. The answer is not always comfortable, but it's more useful than another pep talk about discipline. Sometimes tired is not a character flaw. Sometimes it's information you've been too busy pushing through to read.

title: 5 AI-Powered Services Beginners Can Sell Online in 2026
excerpt: You don't need to build an AI model to make money with AI. You can use existing tools to solve problems people already pay for.
content:
5 AI-Powered Services Beginners Can Sell Online in 2026

When people hear “making money with AI,” they often imagine building the next big AI company.

But you don't need to build an AI model to start earning from the technology.

A simpler approach is to use AI to help you deliver a service that people already need.

Businesses still need content. They need social media posts. They need videos, research, designs and customer support.

AI can help you do some of that work faster.

The important part is understanding that the AI tool itself isn't what clients are paying for.

They are paying for the result.

Here are five services a beginner can start exploring.

1. AI-Assisted Content Writing

Businesses and creators constantly need captions, blog posts, product descriptions, emails and other written content.

AI can help with research, brainstorming and first drafts, while you provide editing, fact-checking and the human touch.

You could offer services such as:

• Social media captions

• Blog articles

• Product descriptions

• Email newsletters

• Website copy

The goal isn't to copy and paste whatever AI produces.

The value comes from turning that first draft into something accurate, useful and appropriate for the client.

2. AI-Assisted Social Media Management

Many small businesses struggle to consistently create content for their social media pages.

AI can help generate content ideas, captions, content calendars and variations of posts.

You can combine that with tools such as Canva to create graphics and help a business maintain a consistent online presence.

You don't necessarily need hundreds of followers yourself.

You need to understand what the business wants to communicate and create content that fits its audience.

3. AI-Assisted Video Content

Short-form video has become an important part of online marketing.

AI tools can help with tasks such as generating scripts, creating captions, removing unnecessary sections and speeding up parts of the editing process.

A beginner could offer services such as:

• Short video editing

• TikTok or Reels scripts

• Captions and subtitles

• YouTube Shorts preparation

• Promotional videos

You still need to understand storytelling and what makes a video worth watching.

AI simply helps you work faster.

4. AI-Assisted Research and Data Work

AI can read, summarize and organize large amounts of information much faster than doing everything manually.

That can be useful for businesses that need research.

For example, you could help organize competitor information, summarize documents, collect publicly available information or prepare research reports.

But accuracy matters.

AI can make mistakes, so anything delivered to a client should be checked before it is presented as fact.

5. AI-Powered Business Support

This is where things can become more interesting.

Businesses are increasingly using AI inside their existing workflows.

Upwork's 2026 research shows growing demand for people who can apply AI to existing work, including AI integration, chatbots, data work and other specialized services. 1

That means you don't necessarily have to sell “AI” as the product.

You can sell the result.

For example, instead of saying:

“I know how to use ChatGPT.”

You could say:

“I can help you create a weekly social media content system.”

That is a much clearer service.

Don't Try to Sell Everything

One mistake beginners make is trying to become an expert in every AI tool at once.

You don't need to.

Choose one service.

Learn the tools needed for that service.

Create two or three sample projects.

Then start looking for people who might need the service.

Your first samples don't have to come from paying clients.

You can create examples for imaginary businesses or improve sample projects to demonstrate what you can do.

AI Doesn't Remove the Need for Skill

There is an important warning here.

AI has made producing basic content easier, which also means basic AI-generated work is becoming easier for everyone to produce.

Upwork's recent research found that demand is increasingly shifting toward people who can improve, refine and finish AI-generated work rather than simply generate an output. 2

So learning how to press a button isn't enough.

You need to learn how to judge the result.

Edit it.

Improve it.

Fact-check it.

And understand what the client actually needs.

Start Small

You don't need an expensive AI subscription to begin experimenting.

Start with tools you can access.

Pick one service.

Build a few samples.

Find potential clients.

And improve with every project.

The opportunity isn't really about asking:

“How can AI make me money?”

A better question is:

“What problem can I solve faster or better with AI?”

Because clients don't pay for AI.

They pay for solutions.

What AI-powered service would you try first?

title: Google Is Increasing Its Prices in Nigeria Tomorrow — Here's How Much You Will Now Pay
excerpt: If you pay for Google One in Nigeria, your next renewal could cost significantly more. The 100GB plan is moving from ₦1,900 to ₦2,950, while 200GB rises to ₦4,400. But the exact date depends on how you subscribed. Here’s what you need to know before your next payment.
content:
Google One subscribers in Nigeria are facing higher storage costs, with the new rates taking effect for certain renewals from August 26. Here is what is changing and what users need to know before their next payment.

Google is increasing the price of its Google One cloud-storage plans in Nigeria, with existing subscribers on Google Play and annual Apple App Store subscriptions being charged the new rates when they renew on or after August 26, 2026. Apple App Store monthly subscribers began moving to the new rates from August 23. 

For Nigerian users, the increase means the popular 100GB plan moves from ₦1,900 to ₦2,950 per month, while the 200GB plan rises from ₦2,900 to ₦4,400 per month. 

That means some Nigerians who use Google Photos, Gmail or Google Drive for their everyday storage will soon have to decide whether the additional space is still worth the higher monthly bill.

Google One Prices Are Going Up in Nigeria

Google One gives users additional cloud storage that can be used across Google Drive, Gmail and Google Photos. A standard Google Account comes with up to 15GB of storage at no charge, while paid Google One plans increase that capacity. 

The latest Nigerian prices are:

Google One 100GB
Old price: ₦1,900/month
New price: ₦2,950/month
Increase: ₦1,050/month (55.3%)

Google One 200GB
Old price: ₦2,900/month
New price: ₦4,400/month
Increase: ₦1,500/month (51.7%)

The 100GB plan therefore costs ₦12,600 more per year at the new monthly rate, while the 200GB plan costs ₦18,000 more per year.

The current Nigerian App Store listing also shows the new monthly prices of ₦2,950 for 100GB and ₦4,400 for 200GB. 

When Does the New Price Actually Start?

This is where Nigerian subscribers need to pay attention.

The new prices are not necessarily charged to every existing subscriber on August 26.

Google says new members in affected countries, including Nigeria, have been able to subscribe at the updated prices since July 27, 2026. For existing members, however, the timing depends on where the subscription was purchased. 

For Google Play subscriptions, the new price applies to renewals on or after August 26.

For Apple App Store annual subscriptions, the new price also applies to renewals on or after August 26.

For Apple App Store monthly subscriptions, the new price started applying to renewals on or after August 23. 

So if your Google One subscription does not renew on August 26, that does not necessarily mean you will be charged the new price on that exact day.

Google says existing subscribers receive advance notification of the price change by email, while a banner notification can also appear when they log into Google One on the web or through the Android or iOS app. 

Why Is Google Increasing the Price?

Google has confirmed the price increase but its official notice does not provide a specific Nigeria-focused explanation for why the prices are being raised. It says the increase affects selected countries and that the amount varies according to the plan and local currency. 

That means users should be careful about attributing the increase specifically to inflation, exchange rates, taxes, artificial intelligence costs or any other factor unless Google directly confirms it.

For now, the important fact for Nigerian subscribers is simply that the new prices have been announced and are being introduced according to the relevant subscription and renewal dates.

What Is Google One and Why Do Nigerians Use It?

Google One is essentially an expanded storage subscription for Google's ecosystem.

Your storage is shared across services including:

  • Google Drive

  • Gmail

  • Google Photos

A normal Google Account comes with up to 15GB of free storage shared across these services. Once that space becomes insufficient, users can purchase Google One to increase their storage capacity. 

For someone who regularly backs up photos and videos, stores documents in Drive and keeps years of Gmail messages, the subscription can become difficult to give up.

What Happens If You Cancel Google One?

Cancelling does not immediately wipe out your Google One storage or benefits.

Google says users who cancel retain their paid Google One benefits until the end of their current billing cycle. After that, their storage returns to the amount available under their account's free storage allowance. 

The important issue comes if you are using more storage than your free allowance.

For example, someone with 80GB of data on a 100GB Google One plan would be above the free 15GB limit after cancellation.

In that situation, Google says restrictions can affect Gmail, Google Drive and Google Photos. Users may be unable to send or receive Gmail messages, upload or sync new files in Drive, or back up new photos and videos until they reduce their storage usage or purchase additional storage. 

So cancelling is not as simple as pressing a button and forgetting about the account. Users should first check how much storage they are actually using.

Should You Cancel or Keep Your Google One Subscription?

There is no universal answer.

If your Google account contains thousands of photos, important documents, large files and years of emails, paying for additional storage may still be worthwhile.

The question becomes more difficult for someone who is barely using their current storage allowance.

If you are considering cancelling, first check whether you can:

  • Delete unnecessary photos and videos.

  • Remove large files from Google Drive.

  • Clear old emails and attachments.

  • Empty your Gmail and Drive trash.

  • Move important files to another reliable storage location.

Google provides storage-management tools to help users see what is consuming their space. 

How to Check How Much Google Storage You Are Using

Before deciding whether the new price is worth paying, check your current storage usage.

You can open Google One while signed into the relevant Google Account and check the storage section. Google also provides storage-management tools that break down usage across services. 

This is particularly useful because some people may be paying for 100GB without realising that they are using only a small portion of it.

On the other hand, someone who is already close to the 100GB limit may find that cancelling would create problems.

Is Google One Still Worth It at the New Price?

The answer largely depends on how much you rely on Google's ecosystem.

At the old ₦1,900 monthly price, a 100GB subscriber spent about ₦22,800 over 12 months if billed monthly.

At ₦2,950 per month, the same plan costs about ₦35,400 over a year.

For the 200GB plan, the annual monthly-billing cost rises from approximately ₦34,800 to ₦52,800.

That is a significant difference for Nigerian consumers, particularly at a time when many households are already watching their monthly expenses closely.

But for someone whose Google account is effectively their digital filing cabinet, the additional cost may still be preferable to losing convenient access to cloud storage.

The smarter approach is therefore to check your actual storage usage before deciding.

What Nigerian Google One Subscribers Should Do Now

If you are an existing subscriber, check the email or notification Google sent you and look at the renewal date attached to your account.

Google's official schedule says Google Play subscriptions and annual Apple App Store subscriptions renewing from August 26 will be charged the new price, while Apple monthly subscriptions have already moved to the new rate. 

If you do not want to continue at the higher rate, Google says eligible existing members who do not want to renew at the new price can cancel by August 25; Apple monthly subscribers had an earlier August 22 deadline. 

The important thing is not to cancel blindly. Check your storage first.

If you are already above the free storage limit, make a plan for where your files, photos and other data will go before your paid storage expires.

The Bigger Question

For years, ₦1,900 a month made Google One's 100GB plan relatively easy to overlook as a small digital expense.

The new ₦2,950 price changes that calculation.

A user who barely needs the extra storage may decide that it is time to clean up their account. Someone whose entire digital life is stored across Google Photos, Drive and Gmail may decide that the convenience is still worth paying for.

Either way, Nigerian subscribers now have a reason to look at exactly how much space they are using before their next renewal.

Will you keep paying for Google One at the new price, or are you considering cancelling?

title: The Old Clock That Thought Me Patience
excerpt: Some things are not broken; they are simply taking the time they need to become whole
content:
The first thing Elena noticed when she stepped into her grandfather's house that summer was the silence. Not the peaceful kind of silence that settles over a house at rest. The strange hollow silence of something missing. The kind you don't notice until it's gone.

It took her a moment to realize what it was.

The clock.

For as long as she could remember her grandfather's house had been filled with the steady comforting tick of the old grandfather clock that stood in the hallway between the kitchen and the living room. It had ticked through her childhood. Through birthday parties, rainy afternoons, summer evenings when she and her cousins would sit on the porch steps and listen to it chime through the open window. It had always been so constant that she had stopped hearing it the way you stop hearing a river once you've lived beside it long enough.

Now it stood silent, its hands frozen at twenty minutes past three as if time itself had simply given up somewhere in that hallway and decided to stay forever.

"Grandpa," Elena called, setting her bag down by the door. "Your clock stopped."

Her grandfather, Antonio looked up from the armchair where he'd been reading his glasses pushed low on his nose. 

"I know, " he said and returned to his book.

"For how long?"

" three months now."

Elena walked over to the clock and studied it. Dust had settled faintly along the top of its case and when she opened the small glass door at the front she could see the pendulum hanging motionless caught in mid-swing forever. It looked, she thought, a little sad. Like something that had once had a purpose and had quietly lost it.

"Why haven't you thrown it out?" she asked. "You could get one. A nice digital. Something modern. This old thing is just taking up space now."

Her grandfather set down his book with the patience of a man who had never once in his life been in a rush to finish a sentence. He looked at her for a moment the way he always did when he was about to say something he wanted her to actually hear.

"Some things " he said, "are not broken. They are simply taking the time they need to become whole."

Elena frowned. "That clock hasn't moved in three months Grandpa. That's broken."

"Or it's waiting for someone enough to fix it properly " he said and smiled the small knowing smile that had frustrated and comforted her in equal measure her whole life. "Come. I'll show you."

That evening after dinner Antonio brought out a wooden toolbox that Elena had never seen before. Worn at the corners the brass latches tarnished with age. He set it on the table beside the clock and began, piece by piece to take the clock apart.

Elena pulled up a chair to watch out of politeness rather than real interest at first. She had errands to think about, messages to answer a life waiting for her on the phone in her pocket.. There was something about the way her grandfather worked that slowly pulled her attention away from all of it.

He didn't rush. He lifted the pendulum free. Set it down with the same gentleness he might have used to lift a sleeping child. He removed the small brass gears one at a time laying each one on a cloth in the exact order he'd taken them out so that putting them back would be no different than reading a sentence from left to right.

"This one " he said, holding up a gear no bigger than a coin "is worn down. See how the teeth here are smoother than they should be? That's why the clock kept losing time before it stopped completely. It wasn't sudden, you know. It didn't just die one day. It had been struggling for a while before anyone noticed."

Elena leaned in. "I didn't even know clocks could struggle."

"Everything struggles before it fails, " Antonio said. "The failing is loud. The struggling is always quiet."

He set the gear aside and reached for a small tin of oil, applying it with careful unhurried drops to each joint and spring inside the mechanism. He worked in silence for a while. Elena found herself simply watching his hands. Hands that had built furniture, fixed radios repaired the roof after storms and now moved just as carefully over pieces of brass so small they seemed almost imaginary between his thick fingers.

"You could have just bought a clock, " she said, again softer this time.

"I could have, " he agreed. ". This clock was for your grandmother before it was mine. It has kept time through fifty-two years of this house. A new clock would tell the hour as well.. It wouldn't have kept any of this." He gestured, not at the clock exactly. In the room around them. The worn armchair, the photographs on the wall, the quiet weight of decades that seemed to live inside the house itself. "Some things are worth repairing or replacing, Elena. Not because they're perfect. Because of what they carry."

They worked on the clock together for three evenings. Elena found herself looking forward to it in a way that surprised her. Coming home earlier than she needed to putting her phone away without being asked, pulling her chair to the table eagerly.

In the evening as her grandfather cleaned a small spring with a soft brush Elena finally said the thing she had been carrying since she arrived.

"I feel like that clock, Grandpa."

He didn't look up but she could tell he was listening the way he always listened. Fully without hurry.

"I'm twenty-six " she continued. "I thought by now I'd have. I don't know. A career I was proud of. A place of my own. Something that looked like progress. Instead I feel like I'm just... Stuck. Frozen at twenty past three like the clock. Everyone around me seems to be moving and I'm just standing still gathering dust."

Antonio set down his brush. Looked at her for a long moment. Then he picked up the gear from earlier and held it out to her in his palm.

"Do you see this?" he said. "This gear was working when the clock was slowing down. It didn't stop trying. It kept turning and kept doing its part even as it wore thin even as it struggled more each day than the day before. The clock didn't fail because this gear gave up. It failed because it needed rest and repair and someone was patient enough to notice what was happening underneath the surface."

He closed her fingers gently around the brass piece.

"You are not frozen, Elena. You are being repaired. There is a difference. A frozen thing has given up. A thing being repaired is simply being tended to piece by piece in an order that makes sense to the one doing the tending. Even if that order doesn't make sense to the one being fixed."

Elena felt her throat tighten unexpectedly. ". How do you know when the repair is almost done? How do you know it's not just... Broken for good?"

"You don't always know, " he admitted. "That's the part. You keep going. You keep cleaning the gears, oiling the joints, checking each piece when the whole thing still looks silent and useless from the outside.. One day —" he shrugged, the simplest gesture in the world "— one day you wind it back up and it starts ticking again. Not because you rushed it. Because you didn't."

In the evening the clock was finally whole again. Every gear cleaned, every worn piece either repaired or carefully replaced, every joint oiled and patient under her grandfather's steady hands. He lifted the pendulum. Hung it back in its place and then with the same unhurried calm he'd shown through the entire process he gave it a gentle push.

For a moment nothing. Elena's heart caught in her chest the way it had when she was small and terrified something wouldn't work.

Then the pendulum swung.

The clock began to tick.

Not loudly. Not dramatically. Just a soft steady sound, the sound that had filled this house for fifty-two years returning now as though it had never truly left. As though it had simply been resting somewhere deep inside the mechanism waiting for someone patient enough to bring it back.

Elena sat still listening. Tears rose in her eyes before she understood why.

"It's working, " she whispered.

"It never stopped being worth fixing, " her grandfather said. "It just needed time."

He looked at her then. There was nothing else he needed to say. She understood.

Elena stayed at her grandfather's house for two weeks that summer and every evening she sat beside the old clock and listened to it tick feeling something, in her own chest slowly loosen with each steady beat. She thought of the gear resting now among the others doing its quiet work again, no longer straining, simply turning at its own pace exactly as it was meant to.

She thought of herself the way. Not frozen, not broken, not failing. Just being repaired, piece by piece in a way that would make sense in time even if it didn't make sense yet.

Years later, long after she had built the career and the life she once thought she was failing to reach Elena would still remember that clock whenever things felt slow or uncertain or unfinished. She would remember her grandfather's hands moving without hurry over pieces small to rush and his voice steady, as the ticking itself:

Not everything that is delayed is denied. Some things need time, care and patience before they work again.

Somewhere quietly she would begin to tick forward again too.

Lesson:

Not everything that is delayed is denied.

Some things need time, care and patience before they work again.

Healing is not the absence of brokenness. It is the presence of tending.

Keep showing up for the parts of yourself that are still being repaired.

title: Can You Go to Prison for Beating a Suspected Thief? What Nigerian Law Says
excerpt: You catch someone you believe has stolen from you. Everyone around you starts shouting “thief!” and someone suggests beating the person. But where does the law draw the line? A recent warning from IGP Tunji Disu has raised an important question every Nigerian should understand.
content:
A recent warning from the Inspector-General of Police has put a serious question back in the spotlight: if you catch someone you believe is stealing, are you legally allowed to beat them?

The answer is not as simple as “yes” or “no”. Nigerian law recognises circumstances in which force may be legally justified, particularly self-defence, but being angry at someone you suspect of stealing does not give you the automatic right to punish that person.

The issue has gained fresh attention after Inspector-General of Police Tunji Disu ordered police commissioners across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory to treat cases of mob action as homicide and investigate them accordingly. 

The Police Warning That Has Nigerians Talking

Disu delivered a strong warning against what Nigerians commonly call jungle justice.

In his statement, the IGP said: “Jungle justice is murder. It is not justice.” He stressed that Nigeria operates under the rule of law and that no citizen, community or group has the authority to try, sentence or execute another person. 

He also pointed to Sections 33, 34 and 36 of the 1999 Constitution, saying that suspects retain rights to life, dignity and fair hearing.

According to reports of the statement, Disu said suspicion, allegations, photographs, videos or rumours cannot replace proper police investigation and judicial proceedings. 

The warning is particularly significant because the police chief has directed commissioners of police nationwide to investigate mob action as homicide and pursue those who participated in such attacks. 

So, what does that mean for an ordinary Nigerian who catches someone allegedly stealing?

So, Can You Go to Prison for Beating a Suspected Thief?

Yes, potentially.

But it is important to understand what that actually means.

There is no rule saying that every person who gets into a physical confrontation with a suspected thief will automatically be sent to prison. Criminal liability depends on the circumstances, what happened during the incident, the injuries caused, the person's intention and the applicable law.

However, the fact that someone is suspected of stealing does not give members of the public a free licence to assault or punish that person.

That distinction is crucial.

If someone is accused of stealing a phone, money or another item, the allegation still has to be investigated. The person does not become legally guilty simply because someone shouted “thief” or because a video appears to show something suspicious.

The IGP specifically warned that suspicion and allegations cannot replace investigation and a court's determination of guilt. 

What Is the Difference Between Arrest and Assault?

This is where the situation can become confusing.

There is an important difference between bringing a suspected offender to the attention of law enforcement and punishing that person yourself.

The police warning is essentially that members of the public cannot become the police, prosecutor and judge simply because they believe someone has committed a crime.

Once a person is caught, the appropriate response is to involve law enforcement rather than turning the situation into a punishment session.

The Constitution also protects the right to life and provides exceptions involving lawful use of force, including certain circumstances involving defence and lawful arrest. 

That does not mean every physical act carried out during an alleged arrest is automatically lawful.

The circumstances matter.

What If the Suspected Thief Attacks You First?

This is where self-defence becomes important.

Nigerian law does recognise self-defence in appropriate circumstances.

Section 286 of the Criminal Code provides that where a person is unlawfully assaulted and has not provoked the assault, the person may use force that is reasonably necessary to defend against the assault. The provision also places limits on the use of force, with different considerations where there is a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm. 

The key idea is defence, not revenge.

For example, there is an obvious legal difference between trying to protect yourself from an ongoing attack and continuing to beat someone after the immediate danger has ended.

Nigerian courts have also considered whether force used in alleged self-defence was reasonably necessary in the circumstances. 

So if someone attacks you, the existence of self-defence as a legal principle does not mean that every response will automatically be protected.

The facts matter.

What If a Suspected Thief Is Beaten and Dies?

This is where the consequences can become extremely serious.

The IGP has specifically warned that people involved in mob killings can face murder charges. Reports of his statement also indicate that he referenced Section 319 of the Criminal Code and Section 221 of the Penal Code when discussing the severe punishment attached to unlawful killing. 

Under Section 319 of the Criminal Code, a person convicted of murder is subject to the prescribed punishment of death, subject to the provisions of the section. Nigerian courts have upheld murder convictions under the Criminal Code where the prosecution established the necessary elements of the offence.

But there is an important distinction:

Being involved in a fight that results in death does not automatically mean a person is guilty of murder.

The prosecution still has to establish the offence under the applicable law. Nigerian Supreme Court authority has, for example, identified elements that must be proved for a murder conviction, including the death of the victim, causation and the required intention or knowledge regarding death or grievous harm. 

That is why it is dangerous to reduce every mob-related death to a simple slogan.

The exact circumstances matter legally.

Why Do Nigerians Still Take Matters Into Their Own Hands?

If the law is clear that mob justice is unlawful, why does it continue to happen?

There is no single explanation.

Distrust of the justice system can play a role. So can fear of criminals, frustration with crime, anger after an alleged theft and the belief that suspects will escape punishment.

There is also the power of crowds.

A person who might not attack someone alone may behave differently when surrounded by dozens of angry people.

Phones can make the situation even worse. Someone starts recording. Another person shares the footage. More people arrive. Before the allegation has been properly investigated, the crowd can begin treating it as established fact.

But none of these factors turns an allegation into a conviction.

What Should You Do If You Catch Someone You Suspect Has Stolen Something?

The safest approach is to involve the appropriate authorities rather than administer punishment yourself.

If there is evidence relating to the alleged offence, preserve it and provide it to law enforcement.

If the situation is dangerous, prioritise the safety of yourself and others and contact the police or relevant emergency authorities.

Most importantly, avoid turning an accusation into a physical punishment.

The IGP has specifically directed police commanders to identify, arrest and prosecute people involved in mob attacks, including those who plan, incite, encourage or otherwise participate in such actions. 

Why Being a Suspect Is Not the Same as Being Guilty

The word “suspect” is perhaps the most important word in this entire discussion.

A suspect is someone who is suspected of committing an offence.

That is not the same thing as being convicted.

Section 36 of the Constitution protects fair hearing, and the IGP specifically emphasised that suspects are entitled to these constitutional protections. 

This matters because mistakes happen.

Someone can be accused because of a misunderstanding.

Someone can be wrongly identified.

A video can leave out important context.

A crowd can believe something that later turns out to be false.

And once violence begins, correcting a mistake may become impossible.

The Bigger Problem With Mob Justice

Mob justice does not only create a danger for suspected criminals.

It creates danger for everyone.

An innocent person can be killed because of a false accusation. Someone attempting to intervene can become a victim. And people who participate in unlawful violence can potentially expose themselves to criminal prosecution.

The Uromi killings of 16 travellers in Edo State in March 2025 remain one of the cases cited by Disu while discussing the dangers of mob justice. 

The broader lesson is simple: an accusation is not evidence, and a crowd is not a court.

What the IGP's Warning Really Means

Disu's warning is not simply about people who kill suspects.

It is also about changing the way Nigerians respond when they believe someone has committed a crime.

His position is that the determination of guilt belongs to the legal system, not to an angry crowd.

That does not mean Nigerians have to ignore crime or allow themselves to be attacked.

It means the response to suspected criminal activity must remain within the boundaries of the law.

Self-defence, where legally applicable, is different from revenge.

Reporting a suspected thief is different from beating one.

And an allegation is different from a conviction.

The Bottom Line

So, can you go to prison for beating a suspected thief in Nigeria?

You potentially can, depending on the circumstances and the offence established.

The fact that someone is suspected of stealing does not by itself give you the legal right to punish that person.

And if a confrontation escalates into serious injury or death, the potential criminal consequences can become far more severe.

The safest principle is straightforward: if someone is suspected of committing a crime, report the matter and allow the authorities and courts to determine what happens next.

If you caught someone you believed had stolen from you, would you hand the person over to the police or would you be tempted to take matters into your own hands?

title: I No Go Gree
excerpt: The Cost of A Plate
content:
"How far na? I wan come your shop on Saturday make I come charge my phone," Jacko said, leaning against the wooden frame of the kiosk. "You know say light no dey ever dey on Saturdays."

"Omo, true," Malo replied, wiping down his counter. "But I get wedding to attend."

Jacko’s eyes lit up slightly. "Wedding? Ah, I go fit go?"

"Yes, you fit," Malo said with a casual shrug.

To anyone else, a wedding was a celebration of love. To Jacko, it was a guarantee of a warm meal, something that could sustain him for the entire day. His daily routine had long devolved into a forced fast, enduring empty mornings and hollow afternoons just to eat a single meal at night.

Tall, lanky, and visibly malnourished, his bones practically pressed against his faded shirt.

Whenever the hunger reached a breaking point, Jacko would show up at Malo’s shop. On good days, Malo would offer him a bowl of soaked garri or whatever leftovers he had to spare.

Being an undergraduate had become a slow, painful endurance test. His coursemates had repeatedly advised him to drop out, pointing out that the financial burden was destroying him.

Surviving on a ruthless budget of three thousand Naira a month, he trekked long, grueling miles to campus and back every single day.

His grades were slipping under the fog of exhaustion, but he kept showing up. He crashed church programs, claiming to be a first-time guest just to get the free refreshment packages.

He would follow almost anyone who offered to buy him a few pieces of hot awara or buns.

He had even attempted to date, hoping a girlfriend might cook for him, but no one wanted a guy who could barely afford to feed himself.

When Saturday arrived, Jacko didn't care about the music, the decor, or the couple. He immediately began hovering around the catering staff, trailing the waiters before the ceremony had even reached the refreshment phase.

His desperate, jittery movements made him look suspicious, like a thief scoping out a target, when all he was really hunting for was jollof rice.

Malo was across the grand hall, deep in conversation with a few guests, when a sudden commotion shattered the music.

Near the catering station, Jacko was in a fierce tug-of-war, wrestling a heavy thermal cooler away from a frantic waitress.

"Shey una go still share the food?!" Jacko screamed, his voice cracking with rage and starvation. "Greedy people! I say I wan chop now! I dey hungry! Wicked people!"

Mortified, Malo stepped back into the crowd, completely pretending not to know him to escape the second-hand embarrassment.

The shouting grew so chaotic that it drew the attention of the entire room. The music cut out as the bride and groom rushed over to quell the scene. But as the groom stepped forward, Jacko froze.

His grip on the cooler loosened, and his hollow eyes locked onto the man in the tailored suit.

"Odoba?!" Jacko gasped, his voice turning icy. "Na you be this?!"

The groom's face drained of color.

"So you leave us dey suffer!" Jacko roared, stepping past the waitress. "When time come for you to settle us, you run... now you wan marry?!"

The truth hit the room like a physical blow. Odoba wasn't just a wealthy groom, he was Jacko’s elder brother. Years ago, he had gathered money from Jacko and their struggling siblings under the promise of investing it to lift the family out of poverty, only to disappear with every last kobo to build a lavish new life.

Years of starvation, humiliation, and bone-deep agony snapped inside Jacko all at once.

Before anyone could react, Jacko moved like a whirlwind of pure wrath. He tore down the sheer fabric decor, kicked over the floral arrangements, and lunged toward the head table.

With a furious shove, he sent the elaborate three-tiered wedding cake crashing to the floor in a heap of ruined icing. He marched over to the catering line and flipped the very food coolers he had been fighting for, spilling jollof rice and meat across the shiny tiles.

Panic erupted. Guests scrambled out of the hall, whispering and gasping in total disarray as the event unraveled in minutes.

The wedding was officially over.

Malo stood frozen by the entrance, his jaw dropped, watching the destruction in utter shock.

In the center of the ruined hall, surrounded by spilt food and crushed cake, Jacko stood towering over his trembling brother, his chest heaving.

"Tell your wife who you really are!" Jacko shouted, tears of rage cutting through the dust on his face. "Kai! I don suffer... I no go gree!"

What would you do if you were Malo?

Would you have done worse if you were Jacko?

title: You’re 3 States Away and Your Dad Is in Front of Your Hostel?
excerpt: The one time I decided to misbehave, and the universe made sure I regretted it.
content:
I traveled interstate to surprise my boyfriend on his 27th birthday. No heads-up, no "I'm coming", nothing. As an undergraduate with strict parents who never allowed you to go anywhere, this was like my breaking of the shell thing. Also, it is going to be very cuteeee and romantic for my baby and I🥹.

But life had other plans…

Not long after I left the hostel, my parents kept calling me. At first, I thought it was their usual check ins- I still didn’t pick up. The calls were getting much tho as if it was a loan app calling one of their debtors. I had already entered the bus by this time. Like... we had even gone far already. I was settling into the trip, eating groundnut and minding my business, when my dad's name popped up on my phone again, he was calling and this time, I picked up.

At first it was normal check-up. "Where are you? Hope you're okay?" I said I was fine and I’m in my hostel. It’s not the first time he will be asking me these questions so I answered without thinking too much of it. My voice was shaking small tho and I was trying to sound like someone in the hostel, not someone currently on the road. I think he bought it because he said okay and hung up.

30 minutes later, this man called again. But this time he said, "I'm in your school. Come outside. I'm standing in front of your hostel"

My spirit left my body. Everything inside me scattered. How do I explain to my dad that I am no where near the hostel after telling him few minutes ago that I am in the hostel????

Helppppp. What do I say? What do I do? Should I say lie that I don’t where I am and act like I was kidnapped and had a memory loss? Why me, God? Why today? Any day but today???? No nawwww!!! I’ve been a good girlll just this one timeee🤧.

I told him calmly, “Daddy, I’m…um…I’m on my way to Lagos State for the AIC competition. I was shaking so bad hoping he will believe it.

There was a long pause. Then he said, “Without telling me or your mother?”. I said, “It was sudden. Very important!. Out of those selected to go, one of them fell ill and I was asked to replace her. Everything was last minute”. Then, he said “Okay”. I heaved a sigh of relief.

“Send me the location and all the details”, my dad said. At that point, my soul left me quietly. Is he planning to travel down to Lagos or what? I quickly texted my friend, Bola, who was actually selected to go for the competition.

-Oh, that part of the competition is actually true, just that I was not selected. I’m not a liar🌚

Bola got back to me with the details and location and was wondering what’s going on but I just told her I’ll fill her in later. By this time, I was sweating like someone that had different problems in life. I sent them my dad and he said okay and wished me luck.

Phew,free at last….or so I thought. Little did I know that the real wahala hadn’t even started yet.

title: Zero-Downtime Database Migrations: Safe Schema Changes in Production
excerpt: How to safely rename columns, add NOT NULL constraints, and migrate large PostgreSQL tables without locking rows or interrupting active users.
content:
Zero-Downtime Database Migrations: Safe Schema Changes in Production

In high-availability web services, locking tables during database migrations causes user-facing downtime and request timeouts. Implementing safe, multi-phase migration patterns guarantees zero downtime.

The Expand-and-Contract Migration Pattern

  1. Expand: Add the new column or table alongside the old one without removing the old column.
  2. Dual-Write: Update application code to write to both the old and new columns simultaneously.
  3. Backfill: Run a background worker to copy historical data in small batches.
  4. Read Switch: Update application queries to read exclusively from the new column.
  5. Contract: Deprecate and drop the old column once all systems are verified.

title: The Japa syndrome
excerpt: There's a word every young Nigerian knows without a dictionary. “Japa” Yoruba for "to flee." It's become the name for a generation's desperate urge to leave Nig…
content:
There's a word every young Nigerian knows without a dictionary. “Japa” Yoruba for "to flee." It's become the name for a generation's desperate urge to leave Nigeria by any means, for anywhere that will have them. That urge just sparked a heated online argument, a popular creator publicly told a friend not to attempt the Libya route to Europe, and what should've been a private conversation exploded into a public fight some insisting no hardship is worth risking your life or body for, others arguing Libya is just a "closer," faster shortcut than waiting years for a proper visa.

Both sides are talking about the same road, but not the same risk. IOM's counter-trafficking data shows Nigerians make up over half of all identified trafficking victims in Libya the largest single nationality by far, ahead of Libyans and Somalis with victims most commonly funneled into forced labor, sex trafficking, and kidnapping for extortion. By early 2026, Nigeria remained one of the top nationalities among the roughly 936,000 migrants IOM counted moving through Libya, and in Europe, a 2022 snapshot found Italy home to over 120,000 Nigerians is the single most significant destination for Nigerian trafficking victims specifically. Between 2014 and 2016 alone, IOM recorded a nearly 600% spike in potential sex-trafficking victims arriving in Italy via that same Mediterranean crossing.

Someone's cousin really did make it through and is now sending money home. Someone's neighbor really did disappear on that same road. Both stories are true, and that's exactly why the argument won't die.

Japa syndrome won't be solved by a viral thread or a warning from a well meaning friend it's a symptom of an economy that keeps pushing its most ambitious people outward, and a legal migration system too slow and expensive for the people most desperate to use it. But the numbers aren't ambiguous, even when the feelings are, for a lot of people, the Libya route isn't a shortcut to Europe, it's a pipeline into exploitation. So is the Libya route ever worth the risk for a shot at a better life, or is no hardship in Nigeria worth those odds?
