title: How to Stop Procrastinating: Practical Strategies
excerpt: Four, that’s the number of books I’ve been working on. Two should have been completed at least a year ago, but I never seem to be able to put the words down......
content:
Four, that’s the number of books I’ve been working on. Two should have been completed at least a year ago, but I never seem to be able to put the words down. What’s stopping me from becoming a published author? Writer’s block or maybe the feeling of inadequacy? Nah, PROCRASTINATION: the dominant act of delaying that which needs to be done. That’s what stopping me. I keep delaying, and holding myself back.

So how do we get over this?

What is procrastination?

Procrastination is simply the act of delaying important tasks you need to finish. It usually involves doing less strenuous activities despite potentially negative consequences.

In most studies, it has been said that Procrastination can have a detrimental effect on both you and your work. It increases the feelings of guilt and anxiety. It also reduced work performance.

The fear of failure is usually the leading cause of procrastination, because as human beings we often postpone tasks because we fear making mistakes.

Ways to Stop Procrastinating

Break your work into steps

One of the reason we procrastinate is that we find the work too overwhelming for us, so breaking it down into little parts, and then focusing on one part at a time makes it easier to do the task step by step. If you still procrastinate on the task after breaking it down, then break it down more.

Prioritize tasks

Make a list of what you have to do on a daily or weekly basis. Then spend a few minutes figuring out what needs to be done and what doesn’t, so you can identify, prioritize and work accordingly.

Change your environment

This really worked for me. After finishing my degree and moving to another state, I realized the new environment have an impact on my productivity. So by changing or finding a better and different environment, you can focus more on what’s before you.

Minimize distractions

Limit distractions when you commit to focusing on a task that could cause you to procrastinate. You can turn off your phone or stay away from social media.

Clarify your goals

If you’ve been procrastinating for too long, it show there’s a misalignment between what you want and what you are currently doing. So take a break from your work and use the time to regroup yourself.

Move with people who inspire you to act

Identify individuals who trigger you and hang out with them more often. Soon you will emulate their drive and spirit too.

I, personally joined a writing community whereby most of the members are published authors. This pushed me further because I want to join the clique of published authors.

Get a motivational friend

Having a companion makes the whole process much easier and more fun. Your friend should be someone who has his/her own set of goals. Both of you will hold each other accountable to your goals and plans.

My good friend Ekundayo Femi was the one for me (No homo). I’m sure he’s going to read this and smile.

Give yourself a break

Finally, don’t be too hard on yourself if you are having a tough time beating procrastination. Just reschedule and get back on track later.

Beating procrastination is not exactly a walk in the park, but with dedication, you can do it.

title: Atiku Abubakar, presidential candidate of ADC has vowed to review Nelfund and introduce debt relief for qualifying Nigerian students if elected in 2027.
excerpt: Atiku Abubakar, Nigeria's former Vice President (1999–2007) and presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) for the 2027 election, has inten…
content:
Atiku Abubakar, Nigeria's former Vice President (1999–2007) and presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) for the 2027 election, has intensified his campaign against President Bola Tinubu by targeting the administration's signature economic reforms. Central to his pitch is the Atiku Economic Recovery Plan (AERP) 2027, under which he has pledged to replace Nigeria's old fuel-import subsidy with what his campaign describes as a capped, transparently budgeted, and independently audited production subsidy tied to domestic refining. Atiku has framed this as distinct from the pre-2023 subsidy regime, arguing that support would flow to Nigerian refineries rather than importers, with crude supplied at preferential rates in exchange for verified production and consumer benefits, and a built-in sunset clause as local capacity grows. He has also called for a review of the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), including debt forgiveness for students, as part of a broader critique of economic hardship, insecurity including violence in Benue State and what he characterizes as Tinubu's mismanagement of subsidy-removal savings.

Beyond economic policy, Atiku's team has taken legal action challenging Tinubu's eligibility to contest the 2027 election, alleging that the NYSC discharge certificate Tinubu submitted to Nigeria's electoral commission (INEC) bears the name "Tinubu Bola Adekunle" rather than his official name, "Bola Ahmed Tinubu," and that the document amounts to forgery. The Federal High Court in Abuja, presided over by Justice Inyang Ekwo, adjourned the matter to September 28, 2026, after Atiku's legal team was unable to personally serve Tinubu with the originating summons a procedural dispute that has stalled substantive arguments for now. On the regional front, Atiku has also called for reviving the ECOMOG model as a way to restore unity and collective security within ECOWAS, framing it as part of a broader vision for regional stability alongside his domestic reform agenda.

title: The Real Battle Isn't the Device. It's the Interface.
excerpt: For two decades, the tech industry's biggest wars were fought over hardware and platforms  who made the best phone, who owned the app store, who controlled the …
content:
For two decades, the tech industry's biggest wars were fought over hardware and platforms who made the best phone, who owned the app store, who controlled the browser. That era is ending. The next battleground is the layer that sits between humans and their machines, the AI system you talk to, delegate tasks to, and increasingly trust to act on your behalf. Whoever controls that layer doesn't just sell a product they become the default intermediary for how people access information, make decisions, and get things done.

This is why Apple, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are no longer just competitors in their traditional categories. They're all racing toward the same prize becoming the operating system of human intention.

Each player is approaching this from a different angle, which makes the competition more interesting than a simple feature race. Apple holds the distribution advantage a billion pockets and the operating system those pockets run on but has moved cautiously on building its own frontier AI, leaning instead on partnerships to fill the gap while it protects its walled garden.

OpenAI has consumer mindshare and a head start in making AI feel like a default habit, but lacks Apple's hardware reach and Google's data pipes. Anthropic has staked its position on being the trusted, safety conscious choice for developers and enterprises betting that reliability and alignment become the deciding factor as AI takes on more consequential tasks.

Google has the broadest reach of all search, Android, Workspace, and a research engine that rivals anyone's, giving it the rare ability to embed AI into products people already use daily without asking them to switch anything.

What makes this fight existential rather than incremental is that the AI layer, once entrenched, is remarkably sticky. A search engine can be swapped with a new tab, an AI assistant that knows your calendar, your writing style, your preferences, and your history is much harder to walk away from.

That's why the real contest isn't about who ships the flashiest demo this quarter it's about who becomes the assumed default that people route every question, task, and decision through.

The company that wins that position doesn't just gain a product line. It gains a foothold in nearly every digital interaction that follows, which is exactly why Apple, Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic are treating this moment with the same intensity once reserved for the smartphone wars except this time, the stakes are the interface to everything.

title: Your bar soap grew hair overnight. Has to be your village people at work right?
excerpt: Microchemistry in a layman's fashion
content:
Your bar soap grew hair overnight.

No, it is not mold.

No, it is not cotton fibers.

No, it is not your village people. 😄

It is chemistry, happening right on your bathroom counter.

I was supposed to get ready for an outing and I wanted to grab a quick bath.

But then as I reached for my white Premier bar soap, I noticed it had grown white hair.

Worrisgoingonhere!! 😂

Sharpally, I picked up my Redmi Note 14 and took some sharp shots that inspired this fine piece you are reading right now.

Here is what was actually going on 👇

When soap gets wet and dries slowly in a humid bathroom, dissolved sodium ions migrate to the surface through capillary action.

Capillary action? What is that?

Don't worry — I got you!

The independent ability of fluids to flow into narrow spaces without the help of external forces like gravity is called capillary action.

Simple!

Those ions, remember the dissolved sodium ions, they hit the air.

They react with carbon dioxide.

They crystallize into tiny fibrous needles.

The result?

A fine, white, woolly coat of sodium carbonate growing right along the edge of your soap.

This is called soap efflorescence.

Or soap bloom.

And here is the fascinating part.

It happens most dramatically on thin slivers of soap, not fresh bars.

(Check the attached picture 📸)

Don't check "slivers" in the dictionary — I have got you as always.

It simply refers to those small, flat, leftover pieces of bar soap.

That time when the soap is almost completely used up?

Yes. Exactly that.

But why does it happen on slivers specifically?

As a bar soap wears down, its surface-area-to-volume ratio increases exponentially.

All I mean is it becomes far more exposed to evaporation and air activity, especially when left out in the open, compared to when it was still new and fresh.

The ions have less distance to travel.

The crystals form faster.

The bloom is more dramatic.

Is it dangerous?

Not at all.

Run it under warm water and the crystals dissolve instantly.

Your soap is perfectly fine to use.

You have probably seen this dozens of times and never knew what it was.

Now you do.😊

What did you think it was the first time you saw it?

As a chemist, do you think this explanation is without corrections?

Repost — someone in your network needs to know this today.

#ScienceCommunication #Chemistry #EverydayScience #ScientificWriting #Microbiology #Nigeria

title: The Stranger Who Became My Friend
excerpt: The conversations that made a stranger feel like home
content:
I said that was only the beginning because who would have thought that a random stranger I met on Facebook one cold Tuesday evening would become my friend?

We started chatting, and for a girl who didn't know much, at least not yet, he filled a void I didn't even know existed.

You could tell how excited I was every time we texted. It didn't feel like I was talking to a stranger anymore. We just clicked.

The conversations flowed effortlessly. The energy was there, the vibe was unmatched, and talking to him felt like I'd known him my whole life.

I didn't mind if my Mum's old android phone, which lagged almost all the time, wasn't available. I'd gladly pick up my Dad's button phone and spend what felt like forever trying to connect to Facebook. On a bad day, it could take ages. On a good day, it loaded just fast enough to keep me smiling.

I didn't even mind the stress of typing by pressing the same button over and over just to get the right letter.

And I definitely didn't enjoy the heartbreaking moments when I accidentally pressed the cancel button and watched my carefully typed message disappear.

None of it mattered.

Not the slow internet.

Not the lagging phones.

Not the frustration of starting a message all over again.

As long as I could talk to my stranger.

Back then, all I saw was a friend.

I had no idea that this friendship would eventually teach me one of the biggest lessons of my life.

To be continued...

title: Starting Was Never the Hard Part
excerpt: What nobody tells you about staying when the excitement wears off.
content:
I remember the excitement that comes with starting something new.

That feeling when an idea suddenly makes sense in your head.

You start imagining what it could become. You tell yourself, “This time, I’ll actually do it.”

Maybe you even see someone else doing something similar and suddenly, you want to start too.

You create the account.

You write the first post.

You make the first sale.

You publish the first video.

And for a little while, everything feels exciting.

Then reality happens.

The excitement wears off.

The numbers aren't moving the way you imagined. Nobody seems to be noticing. The thing you were so excited about yesterday suddenly feels like another responsibility today.

And that's when you realise:

Starting was never the hard part.

Nobody talks about how easy it is to start a thing.

Nobody talks about how often we want to start a thing.

Sometimes, all it takes is seeing someone else doing what we've always wanted to do. Suddenly, we're inspired. We want the momentum. We want to experience the feeling of “I'm finally doing something with this.”

But nobody talks enough about what happens after the excitement.

When you have to show up even when you don't feel inspired.

When you have to keep building when nobody is clapping.

When you have to keep learning because what you thought would work isn't working.

When you have to look at what you've built so far and still believe it can become something bigger.

That's where the real work begins.

Consistency is not always glamorous.

Sometimes, consistency is publishing the post that gets three views.

Sometimes, it's trying again after something you were sure would work doesn't.

Sometimes, it's choosing to believe in the process when there is very little evidence that the process is working.

And perhaps that's why so many things never get to become what they could have been.

Not because people couldn't start.

But because they couldn't stay.

Because starting gives you a rush.

Building requires patience.

And growing requires you to remain optimistic even when the results haven't caught up with your effort yet.

I think we're too fascinated by beginnings.

We celebrate the announcement, the first post, the launch, the new idea.

But there is something beautiful about the person who quietly keeps going long after the excitement is gone.

Maybe the real question isn't, “What do I want to start?”

Maybe it's:

“What am I willing to keep building when starting no longer feels exciting?”

title: ChatGPT Is Not Your Friend
excerpt: ChatGPT is not your friendBut hear me out.You can give it a name. You can tell it about your terrible day. You can ask it for advice at 2 a.m. You can even have…
content:
ChatGPT is not your friend

But hear me out.

You can give it a name. You can tell it about your terrible day. You can ask it for advice at 2 a.m. You can even have it talk to you like your best friend and after a while, it can start feeling strangely personal but ChatGPT doesn't actually know you the way your best friend does.

It doesn't worry about you when you disappear for three days. It doesn't laugh because it remembers that embarrassing thing you did in secondary school. It doesn't sit around wondering whether you're okay.

It's an AI and I think remembering that is important.

Not because ChatGPT is bad. Actually, it's one of the most useful tools I've personally come across.

You can use it to explain something you don't understand, brainstorm ideas when your brain is completely empty, help organize your thoughts, practice for an interview, create study questions, improve your writing, or simply help you figure out where to start when you have absolutely no idea what you're doing but useful doesn't mean human, and that's where we sometimes get carried away.

We can become so comfortable talking to AI that we forget to question what it tells us.

ChatGPT can be wrong.

It can misunderstand you.

It can give you an answer that sounds incredibly confident and still be completely incorrect.

So please don't let a beautifully written paragraph convince you that something must be true.

And maybe don't hand over every private detail of your life either. Be careful of what you share with it. Your AI doesn't need your passwords, financial information, or deeply sensitive personal details just because you're having a late-night conversation.

Use it.

Question it.

Learn from it.

Let it help you but don't forget that there's a difference between having a useful tool and having a human relationship.

So no, ChatGPT isn't your friend.

But it can be a pretty damn useful companion when you know how to use it and yes, before you ask,

I still love ChatGPT.

title: 7 Things Nigerians Can Use ChatGPT For That Could Actually Save Them Money
excerpt: ChatGPT isn’t only for answering questions. If you use it properly, it can help you spend less, learn faster, and even find new ways to make money.
content:
With the rising cost of everyday expenses in Nigeria, many people are looking for ways to make their money go further. At the same time, AI tools like ChatGPT are becoming easier to access.

But instead of using AI only for school assignments, captions, or random questions, you can use it as a practical tool for managing your money and making better decisions.

Here are seven useful ways Nigerians can start using ChatGPT today.

1. Use ChatGPT to Plan Your Budget

You don’t always need a complicated spreadsheet to understand where your money is going.

Give ChatGPT your income and regular expenses, and ask it to help you create a realistic budget.

For example, you could write:

“I earn ₦100,000 per month. My transport is ₦20,000, food is ₦30,000, data is ₦10,000, and other expenses are ₦15,000. Help me create a budget and show me where I can reduce spending.”

It can organize your expenses and help you identify areas where you may be spending more than necessary.

The important part is to give it real numbers rather than guessing.

2. Find Cheaper Alternatives Before You Buy

Before spending money on something, ask ChatGPT whether there are cheaper alternatives.

For example, if you need software, a study resource, a design tool, or another digital service, you can ask:

“What free alternatives can I use instead of this paid tool?”

You can then research the alternatives yourself and compare their prices, features, and limitations.

This doesn’t mean ChatGPT will always know the cheapest option. Prices change, so verify current prices before buying anything.

But it can give you a starting point instead of immediately reaching for your wallet.

3. Use It to Learn Skills for Free

One of the biggest advantages of AI is that you can turn it into a personal tutor.

Instead of paying for a course immediately, you can ask ChatGPT to teach you a skill step by step.

For example:

“Teach me copywriting from beginner to advanced. Give me a 30-day learning plan and practical exercises every day.”

You can do the same with graphic design, coding, digital marketing, Excel, content writing, or many other skills.

You still need practice and real-world experience, but AI can help you understand concepts and get feedback while you’re learning.

4. Improve Your CV and Job Applications

Applying for jobs can be exhausting, especially when you keep sending the same CV everywhere.

ChatGPT can help you improve your CV for a particular position.

Instead of saying:

“Make my CV better.”

Try:

“Here is my CV and here is the job description. Identify the skills the employer is looking for and help me rewrite my CV to clearly show my relevant experience. Don’t invent experience I don’t have.”

You can also use it to prepare for interviews, generate practice questions, and improve your answers.

That can save you time and potentially help you submit stronger applications.

5. Help a Small Business Create Marketing Content

You don’t have to own a large company to benefit from AI.

If you sell clothes, food, cosmetics, digital products, or services, ChatGPT can help you create marketing ideas.

For example:

“I sell handmade perfumes in Nigeria. Give me 10 Instagram content ideas that can attract potential customers without sounding too salesy.”

You can also ask for product descriptions, captions, promotional ideas, email messages, and content calendars.

And there’s another opportunity here.

If you become good at using AI for these tasks, you could eventually offer content-writing or social-media services to businesses instead of only using AI for yourself.

6. Turn Your Existing Knowledge Into a Service

You don’t necessarily need to learn an entirely new skill before trying to earn online.

Think about what you already know.

Maybe you’re good at writing. Maybe you understand social media. Maybe you can edit videos, design simple graphics, tutor students, translate languages, or do research.

You can ask ChatGPT:

“I know how to [insert your skill]. Give me 10 simple services I could offer online, who would pay for them, and examples of what I could deliver.”

AI can help you turn a vague skill into a specific service.

For example, instead of saying:

“I am a writer.”

You could offer:

“I write social-media captions and short promotional posts for small businesses.”

A specific service is often easier for a potential client to understand.

7. Use ChatGPT to Avoid Bad Spending Decisions

One of the simplest uses of AI is asking it to challenge your purchase before you make it.

Suppose you want to buy something expensive.

Ask:

“I want to spend ₦80,000 on this item. Give me five questions I should ask myself before buying it.”

You can also ask it to create a simple need vs. want comparison.

For example:

Need: Something essential for school, work, or daily life.

Want: Something you would enjoy having but can live without.

This doesn’t mean ChatGPT should decide what you buy. You should make the final decision based on your own financial situation.

The Bigger Opportunity

The real value of ChatGPT isn’t simply getting free answers.

It’s learning how to use AI to do useful work faster.

Someone might use ChatGPT to write a random poem.

Someone else might use it to build a study plan, improve their CV, organize a business, create marketing content, research an idea, or develop a service they can sell.

The difference isn’t necessarily the tool.

It’s how you use it.

And you don’t need to become an AI expert overnight.

Start with one problem you already have.

Ask ChatGPT to help you solve it.

Check the information it gives you.

Make your own decisions.

Then repeat the process.

Final Thought

With the cost of living putting pressure on many Nigerians, saving ₦1,000, ₦5,000, or ₦10,000 where possible can matter.

At the same time, learning how to use AI effectively could help you become more productive and potentially create new income opportunities.

So don’t just ask ChatGPT:

“What can you do?”

Ask:

“What problem can you help me solve?”

That question can lead to much more useful answers.

title: "Is It Not Just Food?"
excerpt: Fool Me Once
content:
Living off a student budget means every single naira counts. Tired of watching her allowance vanish into the pockets of campus food vendors, Amaka spent her Saturday afternoon in the kitchen.

She cooked enough to survive the brutal stretch of upcoming lectures and assignments ahead.

A rich, fragrant batch of chicken stew and a thick, well-seasoned pot of egusi soup.

Living in a shared apartment with two other girls, she took no chances. She neatly portioned the food into plastic bowls, bolded her name across every lid with a permanent marker, and stacked them securely in the communal fridge.

By Tuesday evening, the stew looked suspiciously light. "Maybe I ate more than I remembered", she thought, brushing it off.

By Wednesday, half her egusi soup was outright gone. There was no denying it now; someone was helping themselves.

Amaka stood by the fridge, her blood pressure rising. She immediately called out to her two roommates, demanding to know who had been raiding her shelf. Both met her gaze with wide, exaggerated eyes of innocence, swearing on their lives they hadn't touched her food.

Then came Thursday.

When Amaka opened the fridge, her stew and egusi soup were completely gone and the containers sat empty, licked clean, and left unwashed. It wasn't just theft anymore; it was pure disrespect.

She didn't bother asking twice. She threw open the bedroom door and confronted them point-blank. Cornered by the sheer fury in her eyes, the roommates finally abandoned their denials and copped to the crime, though their defense was nothing short of tragicomedy.

"Haba, Amaka, why are you vexing over ordinary food?", standard guilt-tripping from Chidinma the vocal one.

"Is it not just food?", Chidinma said rolling her eyes as if Amaka was the unreasonable one. "You should pity us naw. You know my father lost all his shop capital recently, so things have been tight. We've been starving."

Amaka stared at her in utter disbelief. Only forty-eight hours earlier, Chidinma had strutted into the room wrapped in a brand-new bone-straight wig, clutching a designer shopping bag, with a fresh bottle of Hennessy resting on her study table. Starving, indeed.

Instead of shouting, Amaka let out a cold, quiet breath. She didn't yell. She didn't threaten. She simply nodded and walked away.

Friday evening, she went back to the kitchen. She whipped up a fresh, delicious batch of stew, labeled it with her name just like before, and slid it into the fridge.

Only this time, the secret ingredient wasn't rosemary, it was a heavy-handed dose of medical-grade laxatives, thoroughly blended into the rich, spicy sauce.

She didn't have to wait long. Chidinma and her co-conspirator didn't just eat the stolen stew; they treated it like a weekend buffet, inviting an unsuspecting friend over to help them finish it.

When Amaka returned from her evening classes, she walked into a lively room. The three girls were sitting together, gisting and laughing loudly, completely unbothered by her presence. Amaka didn't say a word about the food. She simply grabbed her bag, casually stepped out into the hallway, and locked the bedroom door securely from the outside with a heavy padlock she had bought just for the occasion.

Not two minutes later, the first rumble sounded.

What started as a frantic knock quickly escalated into desperate, frantic pounding against the wood. Screams of panic pierced the air as the chemical time bomb detonated simultaneously inside three digestive tracts.

With the single bathroom trapped on the other side of the locked bedroom door, total and catastrophic chaos erupted.

By the time Amaka strolled back to the room an hour later, the noise had died down to pathetic, muffled whimpers.

She unlocked the door and pushed it open. The room smelled like a biological hazard zone. Three broken, defeated girls sat in absolute silence, staring at the floor, utterly stripped of their pride.

Amaka leaned casually against the doorframe, her expression entirely deadpan.

"Let this be a permanent lesson," she said smoothly. "Never touch what doesn't belong to you. Next time, the consequences won't be flushed away."

With that, she left the door wide open for them to figure out their own cleanup, turned on her heel, and walked out into the evening breeze.

What would you have done if you were Amaka?

title: He Saw People Getting Paid. Then He Sent ₦50,000.
excerpt: What looked like an opportunity turned out to be an expensive lesson.
content:
My friend thought he had found an easy way to make money.

He had been seeing people participate in this online "fast fingers" challenge. Someone would drop a word or phrase, and whoever typed it first could win money.

People were posting screenshots.

People were celebrating.

Someone he knew was even participating and appearing on the winners' list.

So, naturally, it started looking real.

Then came the bigger opportunity.

Money doubling.

Send ₦50,000.

Get much more back.

It sounded almost too good to be true.

But he'd already seen the screenshots.

So he tried it.

He went to the bank, made the transfer and sent the receipt.

The response was simple:

“I've received it. Wait for your payment.”

He waited.

One hour.

Then another.

Nothing.

Eventually, he realized the ₦50,000 wasn't coming back.

And then he learned something even more interesting about the whole thing.

Some of the "proof" people had been seeing wasn't proof at all.

Screenshots could be manipulated.

Conversations could be carefully selected.

Even identities could be used to make the opportunity look more trustworthy.

And suddenly, the whole thing made sense.

The scam wasn't just asking people for money.

It was first giving them a reason to believe.

That's what makes online scams so dangerous.

We often think we'll recognize a scam because it'll look suspicious.

But what if it doesn't?

What if there's a screenshot?

What if other people appear to be getting paid?

What if someone you know is participating?

What if the account looks like someone you already trust?

At that point, you're no longer asking:

“Is this real?”

You're asking:

“How much should I send?”

And that's the part we need to be careful about.

A screenshot isn't proof.

A testimonial isn't proof.

A crowded WhatsApp group isn't proof.

And someone looking successful online doesn't automatically make their offer legitimate.

Before you send your money, verify what you're being shown.

Because sometimes the most convincing part of a scam is not the promise of getting rich.

It's the fake evidence that makes you believe everyone else already did.

And my friend?

He learned that lesson for ₦50,000.

title: WHY WE CAN'T LOOK AWAY FROM OTHER PEOPLE'S MESS
excerpt: It's Not Gossip. It's Something Older Than That.
content:
You told yourself you were not going to click on it. Then you clicked on it. Then you watched the screen recording twice, read every quote tweet, checked if there was a part two, and somehow ended up more emotionally invested in two strangers' breakup than in your own unanswered messages. You know this feeling, I'm sure you do. Everyone does. Nobody quite admits how often they engage in it.

THE MESS YOU DON'T HAVE TO CLEAN There's a specific relief in watching someone else's disaster unfold, you get all the drama, the stakes, the emotional charge, with none of the consequences. You don't have to apologize to anyone tomorrow. You don't have to live with the fallout. It's conflict with the safety rail on, and that combination is almost impossible to resist.

Compare that to your own unresolved situations, the friend you are avoiding, the decision you keep postponing. Those come with real weight. A stranger's scandal comes with none. Of course the second one is easier to sit with.

WHAT YOU'RE ACTUALLY WATCHING FOR It's rarely really about the specific celebrity or the specific fight. It's about permission, permission to feel a strong emotion (outrage, judgment, secondhand embarrassment) without having earned it through your own mess. Watching someone else's public unraveling lets you feel intensely without being exposed yourself. That's the quiet trade happening every time a scandal goes viral, millions of people borrowing someone else's chaos to feel something, safely, from a distance.

THE COMPARISON NOBODY SAYS OUT LOUD

Here's the part that doesn't get admitted enough, watching someone else fall apart publicly makes your own private mess feel smaller by comparison. If someone's entire reputation can collapse over a leaked voice note, your unpaid bill or unfinished project suddenly feels almost manageable. It's a strange, unspoken comfort, not because you wish anyone harm, but because someone else's public disaster quietly recalibrates what "doing badly" looks like, and you come out of the comparison feeling slightly less alone in your own. True or false?

THE UNCOMFORTABLE TRUTH

Some of the loudest reactions to a scandal come from people who recognize a piece of themselves in it and are relieved it's someone else's name attached instead of theirs. The intensity of the judgment is sometimes a measure of how close it hit, not how far removed the viewer actually is.

That does not make the outrage fake. It just means it's rarely only about the person being dragged. It's also about what their mess reflects back.

WHY THIS IS NOT ACTUALLY ABOUT BEING A BAD PERSON

It's tempting to read all of this as evidence that people are cruel or shallow. That's too simple. Curiosity about other people's lives is old, older than the internet, older than celebrity culture. What changed is the volume and speed. You used to hear about someone's business weeks later, filtered through a few people. Now you get it live, raw, and endlessly replayable, with a comment section pushing you to react immediately instead of just observing quietly.

The fascination is not new. The infrastructure around it is what makes it feel inescapable now.

WHAT TO ACTUALLY DO WITH THIS

Not guilt, and not forced detachment either, pretending you don't care about any of it usually doesn't last. Just a small honest check: notice what a scandal makes you feel before you comment on it. Relief that it's not you? Recognition of something you've done yourself, quietly?

That question won't stop you from watching. It just stops you from mistaking watching for something more innocent than it is.

Maybe the real story was never really about them, yes. Maybe it's about what their unraveling gave you permission to feel, and what that says about what you've been sitting on all this while.

Think about it for a while, is it really about them?

Shalom!

Don't forget to like. Follow. Share. Comment

title: We Don't Have an Information Problem. We Have a Trust Problem.
excerpt: A screenshot felt like proof.
content:
A few years ago, if someone showed you a video, you probably believed what you were seeing.

A screenshot felt like proof.

A voice recording sounded like evidence.

And if something came from a familiar-looking news page, you probably didn't think twice before sharing it.

But things have changed.

The internet has become very good at showing us things that look real.

And sometimes, that's exactly the problem.

You wake up.

Someone sends a message to the group chat.

"Have you seen this?"

There's a screenshot.

Maybe a video too.

It looks serious.

You read it, react to it, perhaps send it to someone else.

Then later, you discover that it wasn't true.

Maybe the picture was generated.

Maybe the video was edited.

Maybe the person in the audio never actually said those words.

And you find yourself thinking:

How was I supposed to know?

That's the difficult part.

Sometimes, you weren't supposed to know immediately.

The content was made to look believable.

We used to trust what we could see.

If someone told you something happened, you might ask for a picture.

"Send me proof."

And if they sent you a screenshot, that often settled the argument.

But a screenshot can be created.

A picture can be changed.

A video can be manipulated.

A voice can be generated.

And now AI makes creating convincing content easier than it used to be.

This doesn't mean that everything you see online is fake.

It means something has changed:

Seeing is no longer enough.

But here's the part we don't talk about enough.

The problem isn't only that people create false information.

It's that we've become very comfortable believing things that feel right.

If a story confirms something we already believe, we're more likely to accept it.

If everyone in our WhatsApp group is talking about it, it feels true.

If the person sharing it is someone we trust, we don't always question it.

If there's a screenshot, we think:

"There. That's the evidence."

Sometimes, we don't even realize we've stopped checking.

We're no longer asking:

"Is this true?"

We're asking:

"Does this look true?"

And those are two very different questions.

So what do we do now?

I'm not saying you should become suspicious of everything.

That would be exhausting.

You don't need to investigate every WhatsApp message like you're solving a crime.

But maybe we need to develop a small habit:

Pause before you believe.

Who posted this?

Where did it originally come from?

Can I find the same story somewhere else?

Does the original source actually say what this screenshot claims?

And perhaps the hardest question:

Am I believing this because it's true, or because I want it to be true?

Sometimes, that question is enough to stop us from spreading something we haven't actually verified.

The internet has given us access to more information than any generation before us.

We can learn almost anything.

We can hear from people on the other side of the world.

We can see events almost as they happen.

AI can help us create, research and understand things faster than ever.

But with all that access comes another responsibility.

We have to become better at deciding what deserves our trust.

Because we don't have an information problem.

We have a trust problem.

And perhaps one of the most important digital skills we can develop isn't learning how to find more information.

It's learning when to stop, question what we're seeing, and decide whether it deserves to be believed.

title: A Splash of Color
excerpt: If love was always perfect, it would probably mean a lot less.
content:
A friend once called me and asked,

“Can you be faithful to one woman all your life?”

Four years ago, I wouldn’t even think twice.

Of course.

Back then, I really thought I understood love.
Lowkey felt like I had it figured out.

But now I know better.
You can’t be a master at something you’ve barely experienced.

Then she asked something deeper.

Why does God allow certain things to happen?

And honestly, the first thing that came to my mind was simple.

A splash of color.

Imagine this for a second.

You meet the right person the very first time.
No heartbreak. No confusion. No wrong choices.

Just straight love.
Clean. Easy. Perfect.

You meet, you click, you marry.
End of story.

Sounds nice, right?

But if you really think about it…

that kind of life would be boring.

Too smooth.

Like a painting with just one color.

Because love as we know it doesn’t come like that.

It’s built in contrast.

In the ups and downs.
In the moments that excite you and the ones that break you a little.

The confusion.
The disappointment.
The “what is even going on” phases.

That’s what gives it depth.

Even the parts we hate,
betrayal, mistrust, heartbreak,

they’re not from God.

But somehow, they still shape us.

Because in those moments, you’re forced to decide who you are.

You choose to be kind, not because life has been kind to you,
but because you want to be.

You choose to forgive when everything in you is saying don’t.

And that choice?

That’s where things get real.

That’s where you meet yourself.

Not the version your parents raised.
Not the one shaped by rules or expectations.

But the one that shows up
when you have every reason to do wrong
and you still choose right.

So maybe life without all this,

without the chaos,
without the uncertainty,

would actually be missing something.

Because certainty sounds nice
until it becomes your entire life.

Then it starts to feel empty.

Predictable.

Like you already know how everything ends.

And where’s the fun in that?

So maybe the goal isn’t to avoid the chaos.

Maybe it’s to step into it.

To experience it fully.

To learn from it without letting it define you.

Because somewhere inside all that mess,

you might just find your answer
to why.

P.S I later said yes, please I don’t cheat 🤣

title: Comfort is a slow trap
excerpt: When you stop chasing and start settling without realizing it
content:
Comfort

Comfort used to mean something different.

It was what our parents chased. Stability. Safety. A life that didn’t constantly feel like survival. And somehow, that desire got passed down to us.

But somewhere along the line, something changed.

Because now, comfort doesn’t always feel like safety.

Sometimes, it feels like a cage.

I try to imagine how it started. Maybe they didn’t set out to raise people who would settle. Maybe they were once like us. Young. Certain. Full of dreams. Talking about the future like it was guaranteed.

So what really went wrong?

Let me paint it simply.

Between 15 and 25, almost everyone is a dreamer. It doesn’t matter if you’re rich, average, or below. You have ideas. Big ones. You see a version of your life that feels possible.

But here’s the truth.

Most people dream.
Very few act.

Then comes 25 to 30.

Reality starts to tap you on the shoulder. Some of your mates are already living the life you imagined for yourself. And you’re left with two choices.

You either sink…
or you push.

But even when you try to push, something fights you.

Your brain.

People don’t talk about this enough.

Your brain doesn’t understand dreams. It understands patterns.

Its job is simple. Keep you alive.

And to do that, it resists change.

Because change feels like risk. Risk feels like danger. And danger is something your brain is wired to avoid.

So what does it do?

It creates comfort.

Not real comfort.
False comfort.

Procrastination becomes its best tool. Delay. Avoid. Stay where it’s safe.

And slowly, without even realizing it, you settle.

That’s where the real danger is.

Because comfort, when left unchecked, becomes the beginning of decline.

You start to justify things.

You call it being “realistic.”
You tell yourself certain levels of success aren’t for you.

And before you know it, you’re no longer chasing anything.

You’re just… maintaining.

Living hand to mouth. Surviving instead of building.

I call that the second fall.

But I’m not here to preach doom.

Because there’s good news.

Your brain can be rewired.

Not overnight. Not with one big decision. But with small, consistent actions.

Micro moves.

Doing something, no matter how small, that moves you forward. Then doing it again. And again.

It won’t feel easy. In fact, it will feel unnatural at first.

That’s the point.

You’re breaking a pattern.

And if you really want to go further, build structure around yourself.

Put yourself around people who are ahead of you. People who won’t clap for your excuses. People who will call you out when you start slipping.

Because growth doesn’t happen in isolation.

And comfort, left alone, will always win.

The ages I mentioned are just examples.

Change isn’t tied to time.

It’s tied to action.

So no matter where you are right now…

Start.

Even if it’s small.

Especially if it’s small.

title: Why Nobody Is Reading Your Content — How to Get Your First 1,000 Readers as a Beginner Content Writer
excerpt: Starting a career as a content writer can be exciting, but the early stages are rarely easy.You may have good writing skills, plenty of ideas and the motivation…
content:
Starting a career as a content writer can be exciting, but the early stages are rarely easy.

You may have good writing skills, plenty of ideas and the motivation to create content, yet still struggle to get people to read your work. Sometimes, you can spend hours researching and writing an article only to get a handful of views.

This can be discouraging, especially when you see other writers posting content that receives hundreds or thousands of views.

But getting traffic is not only about being a good writer. It also requires understanding your audience, choosing the right topics, promoting your work and consistently creating content that people actually want to consume.

If you are a beginner wondering why your content is not getting enough attention, here are some common challenges you may face and practical steps you can take to grow your audience.

Challenges Content Writers Face in the Early Stages

1. Getting Your First Readers

One of the biggest challenges for a new content writer is getting people to read their work.

When you are just starting, you may not have an established audience on your blog or social media platforms. Search engines may also take time to discover and rank your content.

This means that even a well-written article can remain almost invisible.

The solution is not to give up. You need to actively put your content in front of the people who are most likely to find it useful.

2. Not Knowing What to Write About

Another common problem is choosing topics.

Some writers write about whatever comes to mind without first considering whether anyone is interested in the subject.

Writing about your interests is important, but if your goal is to attract traffic, you also need to understand what your target audience is searching for, discussing and struggling with.

A topic that solves a real problem will usually have more potential than a random topic that provides little value.

3. Comparing Yourself With Established Writers

Social media can make the early stages of writing feel harder than they actually are.

You may see another writer with thousands of followers, viral posts and major publications and wonder why your own content is not performing the same way.

What you may not see is the amount of time that person has spent building their audience.

Instead of comparing your beginning to someone else's progress, study what successful writers are doing and learn from their strategies.

4. Inconsistent Content Creation

Many beginners start with enthusiasm.

They publish several articles in their first few weeks and then stop when the expected traffic does not come.

Building an audience takes time. People need to see your work repeatedly before they become regular readers.

Consistency does not necessarily mean publishing several times every day. It means creating a realistic schedule and sticking to it.

5. Poor Content Promotion

Publishing an article and waiting for people to find it is rarely enough.

Even excellent content needs distribution.

A new writer may have a useful article on their website but fail to share it on LinkedIn, Facebook, X, WhatsApp communities, Reddit or other platforms where potential readers spend time.

Promotion should therefore be treated as part of content creation, not an afterthought.

6. Writing for Everyone

Trying to appeal to everyone can make your content less useful to anyone.

A beginner writer should have a clear understanding of who they are writing for.

For example, instead of simply writing about "technology," you could focus on technology for Nigerian students, AI tools for freelancers, digital skills for young professionals or remote-work opportunities for Africans.

The more clearly you understand your audience, the easier it becomes to create relevant content.

How Content Writers Can Build Huge Traffic and a Strong Audience

There is no secret button that guarantees thousands of visitors overnight. However, there is a process that can significantly improve your chances of attracting consistent traffic.

Here is a step-by-step approach.

Step 1: Choose a Clear Niche

Start by deciding what you want people to know you for.

Your niche could be:

- Technology

- Artificial intelligence

- Education

- Remote work

- Career development

- Business

- Digital marketing

- Personal finance

- Lifestyle

- Health and wellness

You do not have to limit yourself to one subject forever. However, having a clear direction makes it easier to attract a specific audience.

For example, a writer who consistently publishes useful information about AI tools and remote work may gradually become known by people interested in those areas.

Step 2: Understand Your Target Audience

Before writing an article, ask yourself:

Who am I writing this for?

Then think about their problems.

What are they searching for?

What questions do they ask?

What information do they struggle to find?

What would make them click on your article?

For example, if your audience consists of Nigerian graduates, topics such as "How to Find Remote Jobs From Nigeria," "Best Digital Skills to Learn in 2026" or "Free Online Courses With Certificates" may be more relevant than a general article about technology.

The closer your content is to your audience's actual needs, the better your chances of attracting them.

Step 3: Find Topics People Are Already Searching For

Do not always start with a blank page and simply ask yourself what to write.

Research first.

Look at Google search suggestions, Google Trends, social media discussions, news developments, forums and questions people are asking online.

You can also examine what established websites in your niche are publishing.

The goal is not to copy them.

Instead, identify gaps.

If people are searching for an answer but existing articles are confusing, outdated or incomplete, that could be an opportunity for you.

Step 4: Create Strong Headlines

Your headline is often the first thing a potential reader sees.

A weak headline can make people scroll past even when the article contains valuable information.

Compare:

"Remote Work Skills"

with:

"7 High-Income Skills You Can Learn in 2026 to Start Working Remotely"

The second title immediately tells the reader what they will get from the article.

Good headlines should be clear, specific and interesting without making false promises.

Step 5: Make Your Introduction Count

Once someone clicks your article, the introduction has an important job: convince them to continue reading.

Avoid starting every article with a long, generic introduction.

Instead, quickly establish the problem and explain what the reader will gain.

For example:

«Finding a remote job can be difficult when you do not know which skills employers are looking for. The good news is that several digital skills can be learned online and turned into income opportunities.»

The reader immediately understands what the article is about.

Step 6: Focus on Solving Problems

People do not visit websites simply because someone has published an article.

They visit because they want something.

They want an answer, solution, explanation, recommendation, idea or piece of information.

Therefore, before publishing, ask:

What problem does this article solve?

If you cannot answer that question clearly, the article may need more work.

Useful content is more likely to be saved, shared, recommended and revisited.

Step 7: Learn Basic SEO

Search engine optimization, commonly known as SEO, can help people discover your content through search engines.

You do not need to become an SEO expert before publishing your first article.

Start with the basics.

Use the main topic naturally in your:

- Title

- Introduction

- Subheadings

- Body of the article

- Meta description

- Image alt text, where appropriate

You should also create clear URLs and link to relevant articles on your own website.

Most importantly, do not fill your article with keywords simply to manipulate search rankings. Write for humans first.

Step 8: Create Content Around Topics, Not Just Individual Articles

One article may bring a visitor to your website.

A collection of related articles can keep that visitor there.

For example, if you write about remote work, you could create several connected articles:

Main topic: Remote Work

Supporting articles:

- Best Skills to Learn for Remote Work

- How to Create a Remote Work Portfolio

- Where Beginners Can Find Remote Jobs

- Common Remote Job Application Mistakes

- How to Prepare for a Remote Job Interview

You can then link these articles to one another.

This creates a content network that helps readers discover more of your work.

Step 9: Promote Every Article

Do not stop after clicking "Publish."

Share your article across platforms where your audience is active.

You can promote it through:

- LinkedIn

- Facebook

- X

- WhatsApp

- Telegram communities

- Relevant online communities

- Email newsletters

However, avoid repeatedly dropping links without context.

Instead, write a short post explaining why the article is useful and give people a reason to click.

For example, rather than saying:

"Read my new article: [link]"

you could say:

"Many beginners want remote jobs but don't know which skills employers are actually looking for. I broke down seven skills that can help you get started and where you can learn them."

Then direct interested readers to the full article.

Step 10: Build an Email Audience

Social media followers are useful, but building an email list gives you a direct way to reach people who want your content.

Offer readers a reason to subscribe.

You could provide:

- A free guide

- Writing tips

- Weekly career opportunities

- Remote job updates

- AI tool recommendations

- Industry news

- Exclusive articles

Send useful emails consistently rather than filling people's inboxes with constant promotions.

Over time, your email list can become one of your most valuable traffic sources.

Step 11: Turn One Article Into Multiple Pieces of Content

You do not always have to create something completely new for every platform.

One detailed blog post can become several pieces of content.

For example, a blog about "How to Get Your First Remote Job" can become:

- A LinkedIn post

- Five short social media posts

- An Instagram carousel

- A short video script

- An email newsletter

- A discussion topic

- A list of interview tips

This strategy allows you to reach different audiences without starting from scratch every time.

Step 12: Build Relationships With Other Creators

You do not have to build your audience alone.

Connect with other writers, bloggers, creators, professionals and businesses within your niche.

Comment thoughtfully on their posts.

Join relevant conversations.

Share useful insights.

Collaborate when possible.

Networking can introduce your work to people who would never have discovered it otherwise.

Step 13: Study Your Analytics

Do not rely only on likes and comments to decide whether your content is successful.

Look at your website and social media analytics to understand what is actually happening.

Pay attention to:

- Page views

- Search traffic

- Click-through rate

- Time spent on pages

- Returning visitors

- Most popular articles

- Traffic sources

If one topic consistently performs better than others, investigate why.

You may discover that your audience wants more content around that subject.

Step 14: Update Your Best Articles

Getting traffic is not only about publishing new content.

Older articles can continue bringing visitors if they remain useful.

Review your best-performing articles periodically.

Update outdated information, improve the introduction, add useful sections, replace broken links and make sure the article still answers the reader's question.

An article published months ago can sometimes become more valuable after a good update.

A Simple 30-Day Traffic-Building Plan

If you are completely new to content writing, you can start with a simple plan.

Week 1: Find Your Direction

Choose your niche.

Identify your target audience.

Research at least 20 questions or topics your audience is interested in.

Choose five strong topics from your research.

Week 2: Create Valuable Content

Write two or three detailed articles.

Focus on solving specific problems instead of simply trying to hit a word count.

Make your headlines clear and interesting.

Apply basic SEO to each article.

Week 3: Promote Your Content

Share your articles across your active social platforms.

Turn each article into smaller posts.

Join relevant conversations and communities.

Start connecting with other people in your niche.

Week 4: Study and Improve

Check your analytics.

Identify which articles received the most attention.

Look at where your visitors came from.

Study which headlines and topics performed best.

Then use what you have learned to plan your next month's content.

Don't Chase Viral Traffic Alone

One mistake new writers make is believing that going viral is the ultimate goal.

Viral traffic can be exciting, but thousands of visitors who never return may not be as valuable as a smaller audience that regularly reads, shares and recommends your work.

The real goal should be to build consistent traffic and a loyal audience.

One reader who discovers your article today could become a subscriber, client, customer or regular reader tomorrow.

That is how an audience grows.

The beginning of a content writing career can feel frustrating.

You may write articles that receive little traffic, struggle to find clients, question your ability and wonder whether anyone is paying attention.

Those challenges are normal.

What separates writers who eventually build an audience from those who give up is often their willingness to keep learning and improving.

Do not focus only on writing more.

Learn how to research better topics, understand your audience, write useful content, optimise it for search, promote it effectively and study your results.

Traffic does not usually happen overnight. It is built through valuable content, consistency, distribution and patience.

Start with one audience. Solve one problem at a time. Keep improving your writing and your strategy.

With time, the few people reading your content today can become the larger audience you are working toward tomorrow.

title: The Things Nigerian Parents Never Say but Somehow Expect You to Understand
excerpt: What was your experience like growing up with your parents?
content:
Growing up Nigerian means learning a lot of things nobody actually teaches you.

There was no conversation. No explanation.

You just… knew. For example, visitors.

If someone comes to the house, my mum didn't have to say, “Please go inside.” She'd just give us that sign.

And we understood immediately. Everybody disappears.

No questions, no complaints. You just enter inside and continue whatever you were doing there.

Same thing when you're watching a film and suddenly a “corrupt” scene comes on. Nobody says, “leave the room.”

You already know. You stand up and go inside, and you stay there until the scene is over. If your mum is in a good mood, she might call you back.

If not, well… congratulations. You've been dismissed for the rest of the movie. 😭

Then there's the look. Nigerian parents don't need to shout every time, and it's always our mother.

Sometimes your mum just looks at you, That's it.

You immediately remember every questionable thing you've done since January. And when she calls your full name?

Just start preparing your defence.

Another thing we somehow learned was how to behave when adults were around. You could be making noise five seconds ago, but the moment an adult enters the room, suddenly you're sitting properly like you've never made a sound in your life.

And greeting?... You better greet, because apparently, someone can see you every day and still be offended that you didn't greet them properly. You can imagine that.

The funniest part is that none of these rules were ever formally explained. You just picked them up along the way.

A hand gesture meant come here, certain look meant don't even try it.

Your name being called twice meant this is serious, and sometimes, “Go inside” wasn't even said. You just knew.

Maybe that's one of the funniest parts of growing up Nigerian. Our parents didn't always explain the rules.

They just expected us to understand them, and somehow…

we did.

What was your experience like growing up with your parents? What are those unspoken rules you somehow just knew? Share yours with us in the comments.

content:
In a village not too far away from the city, there lived a dedicated, focused, God fearing and skillful young man whose name is Andrew. Andrew was very dedicated and set his heart to do anything he wanted to do which he did it with all his might.

You could refer to Andrew as every lady’s spec. This is because not only was he very God fearing, diligent and skillful, he was quite handsome just like Absalom who was described as a very fine young man in the scriptures.

Although, Andrew was the most handsome young man in his village, there was something missing, Andrew wanted more, he wanted to make it quick, explore the city, chill with those he assumed as high and mighty.

He truly wanted to show his village people that he was a fine boy in every sense, and not just a local champion wasting his life in a village settlement with no good water, good roads or beautiful infrastructure. He decided to put it to God in prayers concerning his desire to move to the city.

He wept as he prayed, he said, “God I want to go to the city, I need to be part of the “what's up gang.” Then God replied, “Is that the only reason you want to go to the city? Is it to join the high and mighty? How about staying in this village for a little while, equip yourself the more, soak yourself in me, gain roots in my word deeply and when it is time, you will begin to bear much fruits that people from all over the world will begin to call your name.

You will travel to nations and continents and not just the city, it is then you will know that it is I who has announced you. By then you will become UNSTOPPABLE because the oil upon your head will begin to overflow.”

Did Andrew stay back or he decided to travel?
