title: Consistency is the magic
excerpt: Don’t underestimate what can happen when you keep showing up day after day, even when the results feel invisible and the effort seems thankless. Quiet consisten…
content:
Don’t underestimate what can happen when you keep showing up day after day, even when the results feel invisible and the effort seems thankless. Quiet consistency compounds in ways you rarely notice until suddenly everything shifts.

The very thing you’re struggling with today, the frustration, the doubt, the slow progress, might be the exact process that transforms your life months from now. What feels like resistance right now is often the forge that’s shaping the version of you who can handle the breakthrough when it arrives.

So keep going. Trust the work you’re putting in, even when you can’t yet see the payoff.

title: Ehm.
The Things We Learn Too Late
excerpt: Some lessons only make sense after life has already taught them to us.
content:
There are some lessons we wish we had learned earlier.

Not because someone didn't try to tell us.

Not because we weren't warned.

But because some truths are difficult to understand until life places us in a moment where we finally see them for ourselves.

Someone can tell you to appreciate time, but you may not truly understand it until a moment you wish you could have back.

Someone can tell you not everyone is meant to stay, but you may not accept it until you watch someone you thought would always be there walk away.

Someone can tell you to be kinder to yourself, but you may not understand it until you look back and realize how hard you were on a younger version of yourself who was simply trying to survive.

Life has a way of teaching lessons slowly.

And sometimes, the lessons that arrive late become the ones we remember forever.

We Learn That Time Is More Valuable Than We Realize

When we are younger, we often believe there will always be more time.

More time to call someone.

More time to visit.

More time to say the things we should have said.

We postpone moments because we assume they will still be waiting for us.

"I'll do it next week."

"I'll visit when I'm less busy."

"I'll call when I have more time."

But life doesn't always wait for our perfect timing.

There are people who have looked back and wished they had spent more evenings with loved ones instead of chasing things that seemed urgent at the time.

They realize that the message they delayed sending, the conversation they avoided, or the moment they ignored was actually more valuable than they understood.

The truth is, time is one of the few things we spend without knowing how much we have left.

We often chase achievements, money, and success while forgetting that some of the most meaningful moments are the simple ones.

A conversation.

A laugh.

A meal together.

A memory created with someone we love.

Sometimes, the things we think are ordinary today become the things we miss tomorrow.

We Learn That Not Everyone Is Meant to Stay

One of the hardest lessons life teaches us is that some people are only meant to be part of a chapter, not the entire story.

And accepting that can hurt.

There are friendships we thought would last forever.

Relationships we thought would never change.

People we imagined growing old with.

But sometimes, people leave.

Sometimes, we outgrow each other.

Sometimes, the person who once felt like home becomes someone we no longer recognize.

At first, it can feel like a loss.

You wonder what went wrong.

You replay conversations.

You think about what you could have done differently.

But with time, you begin to understand something:

Not every goodbye is a punishment.

Some endings create space for growth.

Some people enter our lives to teach us something.

They teach us about love.

They teach us about boundaries.

They teach us about ourselves.

And even though we may wish certain chapters had ended differently, we can still be grateful for what those chapters gave us.

A person leaving does not mean the relationship had no value.

Sometimes, something can be meaningful and still not be permanent.

We Learn That We Should Have Been Kinder to Ourselves

Many of us are much kinder to others than we are to ourselves.

We forgive other people's mistakes.

We encourage others when they feel lost.

We remind people that they are doing their best.

But when it comes to ourselves, we often become our biggest critics.

We remember every mistake.

Every failure.

Every moment we wish we had handled differently.

We tell ourselves we should have known better.

We should have done more.

We should have been further ahead.

But the person you were years ago was making decisions with the knowledge, experience, and strength they had at that time.

You cannot judge your past self using everything you know today.

Growth means becoming wiser.

It means learning.

It means changing.

And sometimes, the person you need to forgive the most is yourself.

You were learning.

You were trying.

You were becoming.

Give yourself the same grace you freely give to others.

We Learn That Chasing Approval Can Make Us Lose Ourselves

There is a quiet exhaustion that comes from constantly trying to make everyone happy.

Trying to be accepted.

Trying to meet expectations.

Trying to become the version of yourself that makes everyone else comfortable.

Many people spend years making choices based on what others will think.

They choose careers because they want approval.

They hide parts of themselves because they fear judgment.

They stay in situations that make them unhappy because they are afraid of disappointing people.

But eventually, many people learn a difficult truth:

You can spend your entire life trying to please everyone and still not be enough for some people.

Someone will always have an opinion.

Someone will always have advice.

Someone will always see things differently.

And that is okay.

Your life was not created for you to constantly perform for an audience.

There comes a time when you have to ask yourself:

“Am I living a life that feels true to me, or am I living a life that makes everyone else comfortable?”

We Learn That Small Moments Are Actually Big Moments

Sometimes, we spend so much time waiting for big moments that we forget to appreciate the small ones happening around us.

We wait for the perfect day.

The perfect opportunity.

The perfect season.

But life is mostly made up of ordinary moments.

The morning conversations.

The random laughter.

The quiet moments when everything feels peaceful.

The people who check on us.

The little victories nobody else notices.

One day, we may realize those moments were not small at all.

They were the things that made life meaningful.

Happiness is not always found in the biggest achievements.

Sometimes, it is hidden in the simple things we were too busy to notice.

We Learn That Healing Takes Time

Another lesson life teaches us is that healing cannot be rushed.

We often want to move on quickly.

We want to forget the pain.

We want to wake up one day and feel completely okay.

But healing is not always a straight line.

Some days are better than others.

Some memories return when we least expect them.

Some wounds take longer than we thought they would.

And that's okay.

Healing is not about pretending something never happened.

It is about learning how to carry your story without allowing it to control your future.

You are allowed to take your time.

You are allowed to rebuild slowly.

You are allowed to become whole again.

The Lessons We Learn Are Often the Ones We Needed Most

Looking back, many of us realize that the moments we thought would break us were also the moments that shaped us.

The disappointment taught us strength.

The loss taught us appreciation.

The mistakes taught us wisdom.

The endings taught us acceptance.

Life rarely gives us lessons in the way we expect.

Sometimes it teaches through unexpected changes.

Sometimes through difficult seasons.

Sometimes through experiences we would never choose.

But every lesson adds something to our story.

Maybe there are things you wish you knew earlier.

Maybe there are mistakes you wish you could undo.

Maybe there are moments you wish you had handled differently.

But remember this:

You were learning.

You were growing.

You were becoming.

And even the lessons that arrived late still arrived at the right time.

Because the person you are today exists because of everything you have experienced.

So be patient with yourself.

Appreciate the people who matter.

Protect your peace.

Say the words you need to say.

Create the memories you don't want to lose.

And never stop learning.

Because life is a story, and every chapter — even the difficult ones — is teaching you something worth knowing.

Some lessons come late, but they still have the power to change everything. ✍️

title: Broken Mirror, Smile Face 4
excerpt: She didn’t sleep well that night, or many nights after. She would lie awake in the wide bed that had once held two people and now held only her and the shape of…
content:
She didn’t sleep well that night, or many nights after. She would lie awake in the wide bed that had once held two people and now held only her and the shape of her own thoughts, and she would listen to the house breathe around her — the settling of old wood, the far-off hum of the refrigerator, the wind finding every gap in the window frames it had found for eleven years running. And she would think about the woman in the mirror. The seven women, really. The one who had smiled too easily for too long, agreeing before she’d even heard the question. The one who flinched at raised voices in other rooms, other houses, other lives that weren’t even hers. The one — this was the one that frightened her most — who had, for one clean and terrible second, wanted to put her own fist through more than glass.

She was not a woman who had ever thought of herself as capable of rage. That was the story she’d told herself for thirty-one years: that she was patient, accommodating, easy to love because she made so little demand on the world’s affection. But rage, she was discovering now, doesn’t announce itself politely. It doesn’t ask if this is a convenient time. It simply arrives, sudden as broken glass, and shows you a version of yourself you’d spent a lifetime carefully not becoming.

The question that kept her awake, night after night, staring at the ceiling fan’s slow rotation, was not why did I break it. She knew why. The question was quieter than that, and far more dangerous:

Which one of these women is actually me.

title: The Little Seed That Almost Gave Up
excerpt: Sometimes the greatest growth happens in places no one can see
content:
Every morning before the sun had fully climbed over the rooftops Mia walked to the corner of her garden with a watering can. She knelt beside the patch of soil where she had planted her seed. Gave it enough water to darken the earth.

Days passed.

Then weeks.

Nothing happened.

The soil looked the same. The garden looked the same. The roses bloomed, the tomatoes climbed their stakes and butterflies visited every flower except the patch in the corner. Mia started to believe her seed would never grow.

One evening as the sky turned orange and the crickets began to sing she sat down beside the patch of soil. She pulled her knees to her chest. Whispered, "Maybe I was wasting my time."

Her grandfather, who was trimming the hedges nearby, heard her. He set down his shears, walked over and lowered himself onto the grass beside her with a groan.

“Just because you cannot see something happening " he said, "doesn’t mean nothing is happening."

Mia looked at him confused.

“Grandpa, I’ve watered it every day. There’s nothing."

He smiled the way he always did when he knew something she didn’t. Not to tease her. Because he remembered being her age and not knowing it too.

“Some of the important growth happens where nobody can see it, " he said. "Under the ground in the dark a seed is working harder than it will above the soil. It’s growing roots before it ever shows a leaf. Roots take patience."

Mia didn’t fully understand.. Something in his voice made her want to try one more day.

The morning she filled her watering can again and returned to the same patch of soil even though her heart wasn’t quite sure it mattered anymore.

A day later she noticed something

A tiny green leaf, no bigger than her fingernail had pushed through the soil.

She dropped to her knees, careful not to touch it.

“Grandpa! Grandpa, come look!"

He walked over slowly, peered down at the leaf and nodded like he had expected it all along.

“There it is, " he said. "It was never doing nothing. It was just doing the kind of work you can’t see."

From that day Mia watered the seed with a different kind of patience.

Not the anxious waiting kind. The quiet trusting kind.

Weeks turned into months. The leaf became a stem. The stem grew taller and stronger and one morning Mia woke up to find a bud had formed at its tip.

Not after the bud opened into the most beautiful flower in the entire garden. Bright, full and unlike anything growing there.

Mia sat beside it. Finally understood what her grandfather meant.

Growth is not always visible at the beginning.

Sometimes before life shows the results it is building something underneath. Something patient, something real.

The seed did not grow because Mia watered it once.

It grew because she kept showing up even when she saw no evidence of change.

Sometimes our lives are the same.

The work happening inside us may be invisible today. That does not mean it is not happening.

The dreams we are building, the lessons we are learning and the person we are becoming are all growing in ways we may not see yet.

Lesson:

Do not give up on yourself just because you cannot see progress yet.

Some seasons are for growing.

Keep showing up. Keep learning. Keep trying.

Your roots are growing, even when nobody can see them.

title: Jaded
excerpt: Some things don’t end when you leave them behind…
content:
Five months later, I was still lying on my bed, staring at the ceiling, unable to sleep or feel much of anything.

Why did he do that to me?

I had asked myself the question so often it no longer sounded like one. It was simply another thought living in my head.

My phone’s harsh cry broke through the silence.

I had forgotten to put it on silent.

I reached for it and saw the name on the screen.

Beatrice.

Of course.

She had been calling every day since I returned from Lagos. Sometimes I answered. Most times I didn’t.

She was worried I might harm myself.

Once, after I ignored her calls for a few days, she came banging on my door.

“Rapu! I know you are in there! You will open this door this minute, ozigbo, ozigbo! You don’t have to be doing this to me and yourself!”

That was Beatrice.

Loud. Dramatic. Full of life.

The kind of person who could walk into a room and make friends with everyone before she had even found a seat.

We were opposites in almost every way.

Beatrice was boisterous. I was quieter.

She could argue with a wall and somehow win. I preferred to smile, observe and let people think I wasn’t listening.

Yet somehow, we worked.

We were girls’ girls.

Lunch dates. Staycations. Long phone calls. Talking about jobs. Making fun of men. Swearing off men. Then meeting men and forgetting everything we had said.

Beatrice used to complain that people noticed me without me doing anything.

“You just stand there looking pretty and people come to you,” she would say. “Meanwhile, I have to do all the work.”

I would laugh.

I couldn’t really argue with her.

I wasn’t the loudest person at parties, but once I settled in, I could become the life of the party. I loved good music, good food and good company. I liked making people laugh. I liked making people feel comfortable.

I was also embarrassingly romantic.

Beatrice hated that about me.

She thought I was too soft.

“Rapu, you will enter one man’s car because he called you beautiful three times and then come and tell me he has a good heart.”

She was always saying things like that.

I would roll my eyes.

“You’re just jealous because nobody is calling you beautiful.”

“Please, I don’t need a man to validate me.”

“You need one.”

“I need Jesus.”

We would laugh until our stomachs hurt.

I miss those days.

Today, however, I wasn’t in the mood for Beatrice’s drama.

I picked up my phone to put it back on silent, but then I noticed the missed calls.

Beatrice.

And Marcus.

A message from Marcus sat beneath the calls.

Dear, I hope all is well? Remember we have a date by 5 PM and I have been trying to reach you.

I sighed.

Marcus.

I had completely forgotten about the date.

He had always liked me.

Scratch that.

Loved me.

And still did.

Marcus had been there before Frank.

Before everything.

Before Lagos.

Before the hospital.

Before I learned that sometimes the person you trust to hold you together is the very person who tears you apart.

I met Frank during the period I was having issues with my former boyfriend.

I had recently lost my remote job and was spending most of my days sending applications, attending virtual interviews and refreshing my email like an offer might magically appear if I stared at it long enough.

It was frustrating.

I hated being idle.

I hated having to explain to people that I was job hunting when I didn’t even know what job I was going to get next.

It was on one of those difficult evenings that I found myself outside Salivate Restaurant, waiting for a cab after a long argument with Ebuka, my boyfriend.

The weather wasn’t promising at all. The heavens were rumbling, ready to cry their eyes out for my predicament.

I stood there with my arms tightly clasped around my bosom, trying to shield myself from the cold.

Frank drove past me.

Then he reversed.

He wound down his window.

“You’re going to stand here until the rain carries you away?”

I laughed despite my pain.

“I’ve been waiting for a cab.”

“You can enter. I’ll drop you somewhere you can get one.”

I hesitated for barely a second.

I didn’t need much convincing.

Frank was charming.

Tall. Handsome. Chocolate-skinned with nice biceps, exactly how I liked them.

But it wasn’t his looks that got me.

It was the conversation.

He was a good conversationalist, and somehow, talking to him felt easy. Before we reached our destination, I was telling him about Ebuka and the problems in my relationship.

He listened.

He didn’t interrupt.

He didn’t tell me what I should have done.

He just listened.

When he dropped me off, he asked if he could call me.

I said yes.

That was how it started.

Weeks later, I was able to get over Ebuka with Frank by my side.

I started a relationship with him a few weeks after I called things off with Ebuka.

Frank was the perfect man.

At least, he knew how to make himself look like one.

He sent good morning texts.

He called to check if I had eaten.

When I was job hunting, he became almost as invested in my applications as I was.

“Send me your CV,” he’d say.

Then he’d send me links.

Try this one.

This company is hiring.

Apply here too.

Sometimes, he would call and ask, “Have you checked your email today?”

He stocked my fridge when I complained about being too tired to go shopping.

He stocked my kitchen.

He remembered things I forgot.

Once, I casually mentioned that I needed a new phone charger. I completely forgot about it.

Two days later, he showed up with one.

“You said you needed it.”

I remember looking at him and smiling like an idiot.

It was the kind of thing that made me feel seen.

And I loved being seen.

Frank remembered little things.

My favourite snacks.

How I liked my eggs.

The song I played when I was sad.

The perfume I once pointed out in a shop window and said was too expensive.

He remembered everything.

He was also always there when I wanted to talk.

I could yap for hours, jumping from one topic to another, and Frank would listen.

Sometimes he’d laugh.

Sometimes he’d tell me I was overthinking.

Sometimes he’d just hold me.

It was everything I thought love was supposed to be.

Or so I thought.

There were, however, things Frank said that I didn’t pay enough attention to.

He didn’t like how close Beatrice and I were.

Not openly.

Never openly.

He was too calculated for that.

“You know I love that you and Beatrice are close, right?” he would say.

Then he’d pause.

“But you don’t have to tell your friends everything we do.”

I’d laugh.

“Why?”

“Nothing. I just think some things should stay between us.”

Another time, he said, “I see how close you both are, and that’s beautiful. Just remember that not everybody is happy when they see someone else doing well.”

I frowned.

“Beatrice is happy for me.”

“I didn’t say she wasn’t.”

He kissed my forehead.

“I’m just saying, be careful. Sometimes people can love you and still be jealous of you.”

I dismissed it.

That was Frank.

Every body in my corner was not happy for me, in his words.

He simply planted little doubts and watered them occasionally.

I didn’t notice.

I was too busy falling in love.

Life with Frank went smoothly until one night when I was at his house.

Frank’s elder brother came in with another relative of theirs.

They were both cold towards me, and Frank wasn’t home at the time.

Jide, Frank’s elder brother, paced around the house for a while before walking over to where I was seated, attending to my nails.

“You need to get out of this house now!”

I was gobsmacked by his outburst.

I looked up, chuckled and continued with what I was doing.

Jide grew red with anger.

He snatched my manicure set from me and shouted, “I paid for this house, and so I have the right to ask you to leave!”

His other relative intervened at that point and took him out of the house.

I was furious.

I felt humiliated.

I packed my bag to leave, but I met Frank at the exit.

After I narrated what had happened, he apologized and confronted his brother about the ownership of the house.

He called Jide’s bluff and, to make up for what had happened, promised us a trip to Lagos.

I was excited.

I needed a new air.

The airport was bustling with people.

We managed to move past the busy crowd and made our way to the exit to get a taxi to convey us to Frank’s house.

Yes.

His house.

Frank had boasted a lot about his magnificent house in Lagos, so I couldn’t wait to get there and relax from work.

The first taxi we approached was too expensive, so we opted for another that conveyed us to the estate.

We got to the apartment and were welcomed by his friend.

After settling in, I looked around the apartment.

Something felt different.

It looked like a rented apartment.

Again, I confronted Frank.

He got so offended that he shouted at me for not believing him.

That night, we had a big fight.

The next morning, I woke up before him.

Fortunately for me, his phone was unlocked.

Frank was always selfish with his phone, and now I had an opportunity to go through it.

I went through his texts, and my suspicions were confirmed.

The apartment was rented.

I also found out that Frank was a big casanova and a leech.

When he woke up, we had another bout of argument.

After a while, he apologized about the apartment.

He convinced me that he truly had an apartment but had not taken me there because he was unsure of me and whether I was with him for his money.

I loved Frank so much that I foolishly believed him.

But I had my reservations.

I suggested that we move to a cheaper apartment to save money, since I already knew that the one we were staying in wasn’t his.

Living with Frank in that apartment opened my eyes to a lot of red flags.

The man who used to send me good morning texts began yelling at me.

The man who remembered my favourite snacks began hitting me.

The man who listened to me yap for hours began kicking and hissing at me.

He didn’t even care about my well-being when I was sick.

I received a series of calls from different people and vendors asking me to tell Frank to pay what he owed them.

Frank had even borrowed money from a microfinance bank and used me as a guarantor without my knowledge.

Whenever I confronted him, he always had an explanation.

There was always a reason.

There was always someone else to blame.

When I couldn’t take it anymore, I searched for Frank’s ex-girlfriend online and sent her a message asking about him.

As I feared, she confirmed my suspicions.

She told me that targeting pretty, young women who were well-to-do and leeching off them was Frank’s modus operandi.

My heart shattered.

Everything suddenly made sense.

The attention.

The gifts.

The listening.

The way he seemed to know exactly what I needed before I even asked.

I wondered how much of it had been real.

Frank wasn’t at the hotel after I reached out to his ex-girlfriend.

I was feeling feverish, so I went to the hospital.

The result came out.

I was a month and two weeks gone.

My heart skipped as soon as I saw the word POSITIVE boldly written in red.

I was devastated.

I sat there staring at the result.

Pregnant.

There was a strange mixture of fear and disbelief in me.

I thought about Frank.

I thought about the baby.

I thought about everything I had imagined my life would become.

Frank was still not back when I returned to the hotel.

He finally came back late that night, reeking of alcohol.

He pounced on me immediately I opened the door for him.

With each blow that landed on me, he muttered, “You think you are special, eh? You think?”

He stopped, took off his shorts, dragged me by my hair to the ground and tore my pants amidst my wailing and pleading.

A heavy slap landed on my face each time I tried to push him off me.

“You are going around asking people about me, you stupid girl. I’ll show you what you are looking for today!” he cussed.

I gathered enough strength to tell him I was pregnant because I thought it would make him stop.

I was wrong.

That was the last thing I could remember.

I woke up the next day not knowing what had happened.

I believe I had passed out from the beatings after I told him I was pregnant.

There was a knock at the door.

The knock from the receptionist and security man resuscitated me.

I was a mess.

The room was a mess too, and it smelled of old blood.

I managed to open the door.

They told me that we had been owing for two weeks.

I was bewildered.

Frank had been borrowing money from me to pay, claiming that there was an issue with his bank account that he needed to rectify.

Frank wasn’t in the room.

I looked for my phone to call him but couldn’t find it.

That was when I realized it.

Frank was GONE.

None of his belongings was in the room, and I had no way of reaching him.

I was escorted to the hotel lobby to stay there until I could clear the bill.

There, I borrowed one of the staff’s phones and logged into my social media accounts.

I tried contacting Frank.

He had blocked me.

I reached out to Beatrice.

She called immediately.

I couldn’t say anything.

I just whimpered and handed the phone to the receptionist to speak with her.

I felt terrible.

I hadn’t listened to Beatrice when she warned me about Frank.

And now she was the one picking up the pieces.

She cleared my debt and booked the next flight for me to return home.

It has been five months since that ugly experience, but I still haven’t gotten over it.

It is too much for me.

Mourning the murder of my unborn child by his own father is another weight I don’t know how to carry.

Beatrice wasn’t gentle with me when I got back.

Not at first.

She was angry.

Furious, actually.

“I warned you, Rapu.”

I remember sitting there quietly while she cried.

“I told you.”

She wasn’t trying to make me feel worse.

She was hurt.

She had watched me walk straight into something she had tried to protect me from.

And now she had to watch me suffer through it.

I knew Beatrice meant well.

I knew she wanted me to start living again instead of wallowing in misery.

But I just couldn’t.

I felt so dead inside.

I wanted to stay on my bed and cry.

Some days, I couldn’t even bring myself to shower.

Some days, I stared at my phone for hours without replying to anyone.

Marcus kept checking on me.

That was another thing I couldn’t bear.

He had always been there.

Before Frank.

During Frank, even when I didn’t realize how much I needed him.

And now, after everything, he was still there.

That was exactly why I didn’t want to see him.

I felt guilty.

Out of all the people who had loved me, I had chosen someone else.

Marcus had been there, and I had chosen Frank.

I didn’t want Marcus to look at me with pity.

I didn’t want him to see what was left of me.

I didn’t want him to look at me and think, I told you so.

Even if he never would.

I simply couldn’t bear it.

I didn’t want to have anything to do with men again.

Not now.

Maybe not ever.

My phone rang again.

Beatrice.

I stared at her name for a few seconds before answering.

“Hello?”

“Rapu?”

“Hmm.”

“Have you eaten?”

I smiled faintly.

Same old Beatrice.

Always asking if I had eaten.

“Yes.”

“Liar.”

I laughed.

It was small.

Barely there.

But it was a laugh.

There was silence on the other end.

Then she said, “Come out with me.”

“I don’t want to.”

“I didn’t ask if you wanted to.”

I smiled again.

“Where?”

“My favourite lounge.”

I looked around my room.

It was a mess.

My clothes were scattered everywhere. Empty bottles sat on the table. The curtains had barely been opened in days.

I sighed.

“I need to clean up first.”

“Good.”

“And then?”

“And then you will meet me.”

I shook my head.

“You’re so annoying.”

“I know.”

The call ended.

I stared at the phone in my hand.

For five months, I had been waiting to feel like myself again.

Maybe that was the problem.

Maybe I was waiting for the old Rapu to come back.

But perhaps she wasn’t coming back.

Perhaps I had to become someone else.

Someone who knew that surviving something didn’t mean pretending it hadn’t happened.

I got out of bed.

Slowly.

I picked up the first piece of clothing from the floor.

Then another.

It wasn’t much.

But it was movement.

And for now, that was enough.

Tonight, I would meet Beatrice at her favourite lounge.

Not because I was healed.

Not because I was ready to fall in love again.

Not because everything was suddenly okay.

Just because, for the first time in five months, I wanted to leave my room.

Maybe surviving is not always about becoming the person you were before.

Maybe sometimes, it is simply deciding to get out of bed.

Sometimes you outgrow people without warning

He Ignored the First Warning. Then It Happened Again.
excerpt: The first notification didn't scare him.He was on his laptop, going about his day, when a Google security prompt appeared.Was this you trying to sign in?He igno…
content:
The first notification didn't scare him.

He was on his laptop, going about his day, when a Google security prompt appeared.

Was this you trying to sign in?

He ignored it.

Maybe it was nothing.

Maybe it was just one of those random security notifications that show up every now and then.

Then it happened again.

That's when he stopped.

Something wasn't right.

Someone or something was trying to access his Gmail account.

And this wasn't an account he could afford to lose.

It was his main work account. The one connected to important information, documents, accounts, and other things he had built around his work.

So he didn't wait to find out what would happen next.

He started securing everything.

He changed his password.

He checked his account.

He strengthened his two-factor authentication.

He went through his security settings and made sure he could lock down the account before the situation became worse.

And thankfully, he was online when it happened.

That part stayed with me.

Because what if he wasn't?

The notification we almost always ignore

Think about how many security notifications we receive.

"New sign-in detected."

"Is this you?"

"Someone is trying to sign in to your account."

"We've noticed unusual activity."

After seeing enough of them, they can start to feel like background noise.

You look at your phone.

You see the notification.

You think:

"I'll check it later."

And swipe it away.

But sometimes, that notification isn't just an inconvenience.

It's the warning.

Someone could be trying to get into your account right now.

And the difference between an attempted takeover and a successful one might simply be whether you noticed the warning in time.

Your email account is more important than you think

There's something else this experience made me think about.

We often treat our email like it's just another app.

It isn't.

Your main email address can be connected to your social media accounts, work platforms, cloud storage, financial services, subscriptions, documents, and countless other accounts.

And when you forget a password?

Where does the reset link usually go?

Your email.

That means your primary email can become something of a master key to your digital life.

If someone gets control of it, the problem may not stop with your inbox.

They could potentially use access to your email to attempt to take over other accounts connected to it.

That's why protecting your main email isn't something you should put off until you have time.

And here's the uncomfortable part

My friend ignored the first notification.

I don't blame him.

I probably would have wondered if it was just another random security alert too.

That's what makes this story so relatable.

Cybersecurity isn't always about someone sitting in a dark room writing complicated code.

Sometimes, it's much less dramatic.

Sometimes it's someone trying to sign into your account while you're busy doing something completely unrelated.

And sometimes, the only thing standing between them and your account is a notification you haven't decided whether to take seriously.

So what should you do?

You don't need to become a cybersecurity expert overnight.

But there are a few things you shouldn't keep postponing.

Turn on two-factor authentication.

If someone somehow gets your password, 2FA gives your account another layer of protection.

Don't approve a login request you didn't initiate.

If your phone asks whether you're trying to sign in and you're not, don't approve it just to make the notification disappear.

Use a unique password for your primary email.

If you reuse the same password everywhere, one compromised account can create problems elsewhere.

Pay attention to security alerts.

Especially unexpected ones.

Check recent sign-ins and devices connected to your account if something doesn't look right.

And perhaps most importantly:

Don't wait until something happens before taking your account security seriously.

My friend's account wasn't taken over.

He noticed the warning.

He acted quickly.

And the story ended there.

But it made me think about how many people might see that first notification, swipe it away, and continue with their day.

Maybe nothing happens.

Or maybe the next notification never comes.

Because the person trying to get in already succeeded.

Sometimes cybersecurity starts with something as simple as noticing the warning and not ignoring it.

title: Am I Weird? How I Screwed My First Date (4)
excerpt: Turns out, the date wasn't the embarrassing part.
content:
I spent the rest of that evening thinking about everything I'd said.

Every laugh.

Every awkward silence.

Every answer I probably should have worded differently.

And especially that one question.

Do you like me?

Why did he even ask me that?

Why did I answer the way I did?

Why couldn't I just behave like a normal human being?

I checked my phone.

Nothing.

I put it down.

Picked it up again.

Still nothing.

Put it down.

Picked it up.

Nothing.

At this point, I was no longer waiting for a text. I was conducting an investigation.

Then, finally, my phone buzzed.

His name.

My heart jumped.

I opened the message.

“I had a really nice time today.”

I stared at it.

Then smiled.

Then immediately started overthinking again.

Was he just being nice?

Before I could convince myself that the entire date had been a social experiment, another message came in.

“Can I see you again?”

And just like that, all the embarrassment I'd been carrying around disappeared.

I smiled at my phone.

Maybe I hadn't screwed up the date after all.

Maybe I'd been too busy worrying about how I looked, what I said and whether he liked me to actually enjoy the fact that someone wanted to spend time with me.

So I replied.

“Yes.”

Simple.

No overthinking.

No rehearsing.

Just yes.

Except...

That wasn't the end of the story.

Because the second date was where I discovered that screwing up a first date and screwing up a relationship are two completely different things.

And if you think I was awkward on the first date...

You haven't heard anything yet.

The End.

title: Peter Obi Endorses Fellow Presidential Candidate Seyi Makinde.
excerpt: Peter Obi, the former Anambra governor and 2023 Labour Party presidential candidate now running for president in 2027 under the Nigeria Democratic Congress with…
content:
Peter Obi, the former Anambra governor and 2023 Labour Party presidential candidate now running for president in 2027 under the Nigeria Democratic Congress with running mate Rabiu Kwankwaso, made a notable show of cross party solidarity on September 7. He appeared in Abuja at the launch of Seyi Makinde's campaign office for the Allied Peoples Movement and told the crowd that Makinde was qualified to become president, calling him his "dear brother" and urging Nigerians to make their own free choice at the polls. The gesture wasn't a withdrawal from his own race both men remain active presidential candidates on separate party platforms, with Obi framing the appearance as a call for opposition figures to set aside rivalry and unite around free, fair elections rather than personal ambition.

The same day, Obi pushed a doubt from within his own former camp, rejecting a claim from ex running mate Datti Baba-Ahmed that no opposition leader is capable of fixing Nigeria and pointing instead to his record governing Anambra State. The pushback came against the backdrop of a busy campaign swing through Port Harcourt, Kogi, Benue, and Enugu, and just days after he struck a defiant tone on social media, declaring on September 4 that he remains willing to risk everything, even his life, for the country's future. Together, the Makinde endorsement, the rebuttal to Baba-Ahmed, and the multi-state tour paint a picture of an increasingly assertive Obi trying to position himself as a unifying figure in a crowded and fractious opposition field ahead of 2027.

title: A US Newsroom Wants African Voices in the AI Policy Debate — And Will Pay $10,000 for a Year of Work
excerpt: A year-long, $10,000 remote fellowship for journalists, researchers and policy professionals working on tech and democracy — with African and Global Majority applicants specifically encouraged. Applications close 24 September 2026.
content:
Most conversations about how artificial intelligence and technology should be regulated happen without much input from Africa. Tech Policy Press is trying to change that with its 2027 Fellowship, a paid, year-long programme for journalists, researchers and policy professionals — remote, and open to applicants worldwide. Applications close 24 September 2026.

What Is the Fellowship, Exactly?

What does Tech Policy Press actually do?

Tech Policy Press has run this fellowship since 2023, and says it has supported 25 fellows from 11 countries so far, producing work on AI governance, digital rights, and the relationship between governments, corporations and technology. The 2027 cohort is the next round of that programme.

What will a fellow actually spend the year doing?

Each selected fellow pursues an independent reporting or research project sitting at the intersection of technology and democracy — not a fixed curriculum, but a self-directed body of work built around one issue the fellow chooses. Tech Policy Press has specifically flagged interest in work covering regions and communities usually left out of global tech-policy debates, which puts African and Nigerian-focused proposals squarely in scope.

What could that work actually look like for a Nigerian applicant?

The organisation doesn't hand fellows a prescribed topic list, but plausible directions include how AI is being adopted inside government services, data protection and digital identity policy, surveillance technology, platform regulation, technology's role in elections, or the effect of automation on African workers. The through-line has to be technology's relationship to democracy and society — the specific angle is up to the applicant to define and defend.

Who Should Actually Apply?

Is this only for tech people?

No. Tech Policy Press is explicit that this isn't aimed at software developers. It's built for mid-career journalists, researchers, and public policy professionals — including lawyers working in tech policy, digital-rights researchers, and writers who cover technology's social impact. What matters more than job title is a demonstrated track record on a specific policy issue or geography.

Do you need to move to the United States?

No. The fellowship is remote and part-time, meaning a Nigerian journalist or researcher can take part without relocating or stepping away from existing work. Tech Policy Press specifically encourages applicants from the Global Majority and from communities underrepresented in media.

Is this realistic for someone new to the field?

Not really — and it's worth being honest about that upfront. Applicants need existing, publicly accessible published work to point to. This fellowship is built for people who can already show they know how to report or analyse a technology issue, not a starting point for someone new to the space.

What Does the Money Actually Cover?

What is the $10,000 for?

It's a stipend supporting the fellow's work over the year, not a training fee or tuition payment. Fellows work as independent contractors, using the funding to sustain a year of reporting and analysis on their chosen issue.

What else comes with it, beyond the stipend?

Fellows get editorial guidance directly from Tech Policy Press, a cohort of international peers working on related issues, monthly group sessions, and monthly one-on-one editorial check-ins — structured enough to push the work forward, without being a rigid course.

What Does the Fellowship Actually Expect in Return?

Is this a light commitment?

No. Fellows are expected to produce at least monthly analysis or reporting tied to their focus area, attend a mandatory monthly cohort meeting, and complete a monthly check-in with the editorial team, for the full twelve months. Anyone hoping for an occasional workshop and a certificate at the end should look elsewhere — this fellowship expects real, ongoing output.

How Do You Actually Apply?

What does the application require?

Four things: a CV or résumé, a cover letter no longer than two pages, links to previously published work, and two professional references. The cover letter carries real weight — it needs to explain what the applicant intends to investigate, why the issue matters, and why they're positioned to do that work, not just restate their résumé.

Is there a way to learn more before applying?

Tech Policy Press is running two online information sessions for prospective applicants: 9 September 2026 at 8:00 a.m. EDT, and 16 September 2026 at 7:00 p.m. EDT. Registration is required for both.

What happens after you submit?

Applications close 24 September 2026. Tech Policy Press says selected applicants will be notified in early December 2026, with some candidates invited to an online interview as part of the review. The selected cohort begins its twelve-month term in January 2027.

Why This One Is Worth the Effort

Submitting an application here is not a guarantee of selection — the process is competitive, and the strength of the proposed work matters as much as past experience. But for a Nigerian journalist or researcher already working around technology policy, this isn't just a stipend. It's a rare, fully backed year to pursue one issue in depth, with editorial support and an international network behind it — and a direct route to putting Nigerian and African tech-policy questions in front of a much wider global audience.

title: Love as a business?
excerpt: When your heart is the currency, losses feel different.
content:
Love

For most of my life, I approached love like an entrepreneur.

Personal relationships and friendships felt like investments.

Time, energy, care. I put them in and expected returns.

And for a while, business was good.

I was getting results.

People showed up.

The returns made it feel worth it.

And there is nothing wrong with wanting to be treated the way you treat people.

That is human.

But at some point, it started to feel like I was expecting a turtle to jump for me just because I jumped for it.

Then I came across something that changed everything.

People do not love you based on how lovable you are.

They love you based on their capacity to love.

The limit of what someone can give you is not what you deserve.

It is what they have.

And if you are not careful, you start defining your worth

through the way other people show up for you.

That realization destroyed my entire business model.

Because recently, some of my biggest investments failed.

I am talking about years of effort.

Time, care, presence.

And it all came crashing down.

I tried to fix it.

Tried to piece things back together.

For a moment, it looked like things were stabilizing.

But the cracks never really held.

And the pieces kept falling apart.

I am not saying everything has been bad.

There were seasons where the returns were incredible.

But when your heart is the currency,

losses feel different.

They do not just affect your portfolio.

They shake your existence.

Would I do it again?

Maybe.

Would I advise someone else to?

Probably not.

It is not that I do not care anymore.

If I am being honest, I would still subconsciously take a bullet for the people I love.

But it hurts when what you give and what you receive feel worlds apart.

And I am learning to accept that.

Because loving is not the same as expecting.

And that has been my mistake.

I thought I was loving,

but I was measuring.

Now, I am trying to love because I can.

Even though somewhere deep down,

there is still a part of me that hopes it will be returned.

I just try not to let that part lead anymore.

And if you are judging my business skills at this point,

let me be clear.

There were profits.

Massive ones.

Other areas of my life were thriving.

But in all of that,

I gave myself the least investment.

I neglected myself while pouring into everything else.

So now, I am shifting.

I will become my own best investment.

And from what I build within myself,

I will give to others.

Not the other way around.

title: Broken Mirror, Smile Face
excerpt: Part Two: The Widower’s Daughter
content:
It was the housekeeper, Mama Nkechi, who first mentioned the widower’s daughter — offhand, the way people mention things they assume you already know, while she wrung a cloth over the kitchen sink and Adaeze sat at the table pretending to read a newspaper she had no intention of finishing.

“That mirror,” Mama Nkechi said, not looking up, “it was hers. Papa Obinna’s daughter. The one who died.”

Adaeze set the newspaper down slowly. “Died? Chidi never told me anyone died in this house.”

“Ah, Madam Adaeze.” Mama Nkechi’s hands stilled over the basin. “Chidi does not know. He bought the house from Papa Obinna in a hurry — the old man wanted to be rid of it fast, before he changed his mind, before the memory got its claws in deeper. He didn’t tell young Oga the whole story, and young Oga didn’t ask. Men like that never ask. They only see good bones and a fair price.”

The kitchen had gone very quiet. Outside, the harmattan wind pushed dust against the window glass in soft, insistent waves, and somewhere upstairs a loose shutter knocked twice against its frame, like knuckles on a door.

“Tell me,” Adaeze said.

Mama Nkechi dried her hands on her wrapper and sat down across from her, the chair creaking beneath the shift of her weight, and for a long moment she said nothing at all, as though deciding how much of the past a woman standing at the edge of her own unraveling could safely be given.

“Her name was Chiamaka,” she said finally. “Papa Obinna’s only daughter. Beautiful girl — too beautiful, people said, the kind of beautiful that makes other women’s husbands forget themselves. She was engaged to be married. A good man, everyone said. Rich man. And then, one week before the wedding, she was found in the room upstairs — your room now — in front of that same mirror. They said her heart simply stopped. Young and strong and her heart simply stopped, as though something had frightened the life clean out of her.”

Adaeze’s fingers had gone cold around the edge of the newspaper. “What frightened her?”

“Nobody knows, Madam. Papa Obinna never spoke of it again after the burial. He kept her room exactly as she left it for years — the mirror, the bed, her books — until finally the silence in that room became too heavy even for a grieving father to carry, and he sold the house rather than walk past that door one more day.” Mama Nkechi’s eyes, when she finally lifted them to meet Adaeze’s, were older than her face. “Some houses hold on to things, Madam. Some rooms remember the last face they saw.”

title: A place for all.
excerpt: They say writing is the description of your soul.But these days, it’s been so much more for me.It has become a medium. A way to process things. A way to underst…
content:
They say writing is the description of your soul.

But these days, it’s been so much more for me.

It has become a medium. A way to process things. A way to understand how life, in all its complexity, has shaped me. Sometimes, it’s not even about me. It’s about the stories of people around me. The way I see their struggles, the way I try to make sense of their experiences. And if I could play God for a moment, I’d probably rewrite parts of their lives just to make things better.

Recently, I started writing on Echo Gist, and it has been more than I expected.

At first, it was the community. We all crave belonging, that feeling of finding “our people.” And Echo Gist gives you that. But what surprised me the most was something deeper.

It was seeing people relate.

Seeing someone read something I wrote and feel understood. Having people reach out to say, “This made me feel less alone.” That feeling is beyond fulfilling. The idea that something as simple as words can shift someone’s perspective, or even give them hope, is something I don’t take lightly.

Now, when ideas come to me and I don’t write them down, or when I leave drafts sitting in my notes, I feel a certain kind of guilt. Because maybe, just maybe, that piece could have been someone’s ladder out of a dark place. Or the reassurance they needed to know they’re not alone.

And the beautiful thing is, it doesn’t have to be emotional or motivational writing.

At Echo Gist, there’s space for every kind of writer.

Whether you’re into business, tech, comics, or you enjoy reviewing books and movies, there’s a place for you to grow. It’s not just about writing. It’s about finding your voice and building something meaningful with it.

Echo Gist is more than a blog.

It’s a community that supports growth. A space where you don’t have to be perfect to start. You just have to begin.

We believe in you exactly as you are right now.

And we want to see you grow into everything you can be.

So if you’ve been holding onto an idea, a story, or a thought…

Share it.

Join us at echo-gist.com

We’ve believed in you, even before you clicked subscribe.

title: In Arcadia
excerpt: Reading In Arcadia by Ben Okri made me question my own existence. I found myself asking, What is my purpose? What am I truly afraid of? What is my own Arcadia? …
content:
Reading In Arcadia by Ben Okri made me question my own existence. I found myself asking, What is my purpose? What am I truly afraid of? What is my own Arcadia? At first, I didn’t think the novel was for me, but as I read on, its psychological and philosophical reflections completely changed my perspective.

What struck me most was the journey of the characters. Each of them is searching for something different, and through their conversations and experiences, I found myself reflecting on happiness, fulfilment, and death. Why are we so afraid of death? If we all leave this world one day, what does it really mean to continue existing? The novel also changed the way I see art. A painting is never just a painting; it carries a message that can outlive its creator. Nicolas Poussin’s Et in Arcadia Ego reminded me that even in paradise, death is always present, yet so is the legacy we leave behind.

My biggest takeaway was that our struggles do not always define us. Sometimes the life we imagine for ourselves is different from the purpose we eventually discover. I finished the book asking myself, What if my disappointments are not failures, but directions toward my own Arcadia? If you enjoy books that challenge the way you think about life, purpose, and existence, In Arcadia by Ben Okri is well worth reading.

title: The Girl He Chose
excerpt: By the time Ethan made me his favourite person in school, I had already become the favourite target of every girl who wanted him. And there were plenty of them. Ethan was handsome, effortlessly charmi…
content:
By the time Ethan made me his favourite person in school, I had already become the favourite target of every girl who wanted him.

And there were plenty of them.

Ethan was handsome, effortlessly charming, and, according to the endless whispers that followed him through the corridors, one of the richest boys in school. Girls found excuses to sit beside him in class. They waited outside his lectures. Some even fought over the smallest attention from him.

Yet somehow, he kept coming back to me.

My mother had warned me from the beginning.

“Never take advantage of that boy,” she had said. “And whatever you do, don't let your guard down.”

I tried.

I really did.

Especially after Kate cornered me one afternoon.

She folded her arms and looked me up and down, her expensive perfume lingering in the air between us.

“Stay away from my man,” she said. “You should know your place.”

I said nothing.

What could I possibly say?

Kate came from one of the wealthiest families in school. She was beautiful, confident, and accustomed to getting whatever she wanted.

I was no match for her.

But Ethan didn't seem to care.

The more I avoided him, the closer he came.

If I changed seats, he found me during break. If I left the lecture hall early, he was waiting outside. If I ignored his messages, he would simply appear beside me the next morning with that irritating smile on his face.

And in front of everyone, he made one thing painfully clear.

I was the girl he had chosen.

That afternoon, the library was unusually quiet.

I sat opposite Ethan, pretending to read while he worked on his laptop. The soft turning of pages and occasional tapping of his keyboard were the only sounds around us.

Then I felt it.

Someone was watching me.

I slowly lifted my eyes.

Kate stood several shelves away.

She wasn't smiling.

Her eyes were fixed on me with such coldness that, for a moment, I imagined they could cut straight through my chest.

I quickly looked away.

“Ethan.”

He looked up.

“Hmm?”

I hesitated before closing my book.

“Why do you keep coming back to me?”

His brows furrowed.

“After everything?” I continued. “I've turned you down so many times. I've tried to stay away from you. So why won't you leave me alone?”

For a few seconds, he simply stared at me.

Then he laughed softly.

I frowned.

“What?”

He leaned back in his chair.

“Because you're different.”

I rolled my eyes. “That's not an answer.”

“It is.”

He closed his laptop and lowered his voice.

“I don't care about a girl's surname, her father's money, or how many people know her name.”

My fingers tightened around the edge of my book.

“I like a girl with a brain,” he continued. “Someone who can stand on her own feet. Someone humble enough to understand that money doesn't make a person better than everyone else.”

My cheeks grew warm.

His eyes never left mine.

“I don't want someone who needs people to solve every problem for her.”

He paused.

“I want you.”

My heart stumbled.

“Ethan…”

“I don't want you to be my girlfriend just because that's what people expect.”

He reached across the table, his fingers stopping just short of mine.

“I want you to be my woman.”

I forgot how to breathe.

“And I won't let anyone disrespect you,” he added. “Not even if that person thinks she can buy the whole school.”

I glanced towards the shelves.

Kate was gone.

A strange uneasiness settled in my stomach.

Ethan noticed.

“Don't worry about her.”

“You don't understand.”

“No,” he said quietly. “I understand perfectly.”

He smiled.

“That's why I'm asking you to stop running from me.”

For the first time, I didn't have an excuse.

Maybe my mother had been right to warn me.

Maybe Ethan was dangerous in ways I hadn't yet discovered.

Or maybe, for once, I had finally found someone who saw me for who I was rather than what I could offer him.

I looked at him and smiled despite myself.

“Fine,” I whispered.

His smile widened.

But as we left the library together, I couldn't shake the feeling that someone was following us.

And when I glanced over my shoulder, I saw Kate standing at the end of the corridor.

She wasn't crying.

She wasn't angry.

She was smiling.

That was the moment I realised accepting Ethan might have been the easiest part.

Keeping him might be the real battle.

title: I have it all, but at what Cost.
excerpt: An arm, a leg, and everything in between,  that's what success cost me
content:
“All my life, I have strived to have it all; wealth, power, and fame. And now, I do, all before the age of forty. I bloody have it all. Sweet, isn’t it? Yeah, it is, except for this sudden headache that started a week ago. Aspirin didn’t do anything, so I went for a checkup.

I’m waiting in the doctor’s office, staring at the calendar hanging behind his chair on his blue-colored wall. It was one of those nutritional facts calendars. Quite calming except for the   smell of the cheap antiseptic. “The best doctor in the country, but his office reeks of cheap antiseptic,” I thought to myself.

“You are sick,” the doctor said as he came back in. “You have an experimental terminal illness called ‘Ifotomime’. We’ll try our best with treatment, but full disclosure, it doesn’t look so good.”

“Ifotomime? Experimental? Who the heck named it?”

“How long do I have?” I asked.

“A couple of years, could be more, could be less, but we need to start treatment right away, sir.”

“What treatment, if it’s experimental?”

***

I  was supposed to be in Tahiti or the Bahamas now, drinking expensive wine and living luxuriously. Instead, tubes were being attached to me, and I was being poked, prodded, and stuck with all sorts of needles and tiny tubes.

“Your cells are dying faster than they can reproduce,” the doctor said.

“I know. They are being killed by your so-called bloody ‘Ifotomime’.”

***

Six months of scientific treatment and these needles-wielding butchers were failing. “Screw this, I’m done with this bullcrap called science,” I told the useless doctor and had myself discharged.

I left to look for other alternatives: spirituality, and religion, I even smoked weed and bounced like a Rastaman. “Well, I wouldn’t call it bouncing, with the life-threatening illness and all that”. Still, nothing worked.

And when everything seemed bleakest, I found it: a tiny light at the end of the tunnel. But the bloody track was filled with broken glass and thorns. I met an Oungan in New Orleans, and he said to me in a voice as deep as a grave: “You made a deal with the devil.”

“What?… Damn,” I remembered. I had signed a contract with a joker in a black robe eleven years ago. He told me I would have everything, literally everything, but I might not enjoy it. “F**k it,” I said, and I did it. He didn’t tell me it was real, that it would take me nine years to achieve everything I wanted, and just two years to enjoy it before I died, minus the enjoyment.

“What’s the solution?” I asked the voodoo doctor.

Bring me a newborn,” he said. “I will use the newborn’s life to extend yours.”

“Will it be okay?” I asked.

“Meh. You will have to…” he replied.

“No, I can’t do that. I just can’t. No way am I doing that cannibalistic deed, not to a newborn,” I said and left him.

***

It’s been a year now. I’m shrinking in size, my skin is paler than chalk, I freaking shit blood, and to make matters worse, these useless doctors told me I only had less than a month to live. I’ve got no friends to talk to, no family to turn to, and no wife or children to look to. The only ones close to me are freaking vultures who want to nibble on my carcass and wealth. They’d rather let me die.

“Damn, I don’t want to die. I want to live. I’ll do it.”

I paid a greedy nurse to get me what the voodoo man asked for.

I took it back to him, he prepared some rituals and says some strange incantations. Perhaps, it was a weird sermon, who knows? He placed the infant in my arms and asked me to..., the baby didn't cry, it smiled at me. I want to cuddle it so bad but I had to do it. I did what he asked. It was horrible, I know, but I had no choice.

The voodoo man then gave a sinister laugh, sounding like a hyena cackling at its prey. He abruptly stopped and shook his head pitifully, saying, “What a shame. Human beings and vanity.”

“What do you mean?“ I asked. “You asked me to do it.”

“You could have refused and died with a little dignity and a lot less sin,” he replied.

“Wha..” I felt dizzy and drowsy, and then I blacked out. When I regained consciousness, it was silent - awfully silent. I was inside a giant tube filled with a transparent liquid that burned but didn't char, with a breathing tube shoved down my throat. I tried to move, but I couldn't. I attempted to shout, but my voice wouldn't cooperate. I could only tilt my head and glance to my left and right, seeing hundreds or even thousands of tubes like the one I was in, each containing a human being. The tubes were filled with a liquid that resembled water but wasn't water, and all of them had numerous wires attached to them in every direction.

I locked eyes with the woman in the tube beside me, but we couldn't communicate. “Hello,” I said, or at least thought I did. The expression on her face was one of hopelessness, regret, and despair. I tried to fathom why, but I was in a similar situation.

The breathing tube retracted, and the liquid rushed in. I drowned, blacked out, and died. When I awoke, I uttered, “What's happening?” or thought I did. It was déjà vu all over again. I opened my eyes, looked left and right, and saw many people in my doomed situation. The breathing tube retracted once more. I tried to hold my breath, but it was pointless. The liquid rushed in, causing excruciating pain. I drowned, blacked out, and died.

It happened hundreds, thousands, perhaps millions of times - all over again and again and again. It was silent, deathly silent, until I heard it; music to my ears, literal music, echoing in my ears:

“We ain't nothin' but mammals

Well, some of us are cannibal

Who cut other people open like cantaloupes”

Eminem had never sounded so good. And then it stopped.

“Hello,” a booming and gruff voice said. “You might be wondering where you are and what is happening. You are all now the property of AYOCORP, a science company aiming to clean our society of all kinds of filth by all means necessary. You all agreed to participate in an illusion-induced experiment that tests your reactions to unique situations, and you all failed. As per the contract you signed, you will be here until you are all reformed or until we run out of electricity. So don't fight it, just go with the flow.”

“No!”I screamed or thought I did, but it didn't stop. The agony continued, happening all over again."

 

 Note: No AI was used in writing this short story

title: My family's secret
excerpt: My family's secret should have been kept secret. Some things are never meant to see the light of day.
content:
First of five I was. Born in poverty, but wasn't my parents’ fault. Blame life for that.

We strived, all of us, but the cosmos always seems to be against us. I wanted to become a writer so I wrote, about lots of things: “strange new world”, “a deal with the devil”, “how to make it in a not so legal way”, “my family's secret that should be kept secret”, “a unicorn that can jump through time”, and many more. All, fiction, of course except for “my family's secret that should be kept secret”. 

43 years of age, I am now, my mother, 70, father, 72, siblings, two years after the other.  Strived, we did, but our conditions never seem to improve; although our family size did, we are no longer 7 members; now we are 18. We should have been way more, but we're 18.

And then I got it, a publishing contract with a company, one of the biggest in our country. All my works, they rejected except for my “family’s secret that should be kept secret”. 

I was gonna consider it with some variations of course. But they refused. They wanted the raw story. “6 figures, they offer me, hell, a movie deal might also come in”. I’ll get rich but it’ll cost me a lot if I go through with this. Why did I even submit this manuscript, I asked myself but I couldn’t come up with an answer. If this get published in its raw form, it will ruin us.

My family secret should be kept secret. What’s this secret you might ask. Let’s just say, the world frown upon it, even the law is against it.

My family, I loved, my dream, I also loved. I don’t know what to do but I must make a decision. And yes, I made it. It was tough but I choose myself and my dream. 6 figures upfront, I got. My book hit, millions of people read, but some made the connections quickly.

They figure out why we never marry outsiders And why our extended family never seems to get bigger despite the fact we give birth to several children each year,  and why we all look so much alike.

My family got arrested. Their Fate, you can guess. I went underground, disappeared completely, and moved to a town nobody has heard of. Yes, I was selfish and left my family to a terrible fate, but any one of you would have done the same.

“Did I enjoy my life?” No, I didn’t because eight months afterwards, I was hit by a truck and got paralysed. Whoever did it, nobody knows.

title: Skin Tone, Like Volume Control
excerpt: Brightening not Bleaching
content:
Think of your skin the way you think of a song playing through your headphones. Some days you want it soft and low.

Some days you turn it up just a notch. You are not trying to change the song—you are just adjusting the volume until it sits right in the room.

That is what brightening should feel like: practical, measurable, and completely in your control. You do not need to bleach the melody out of your skin. You do not need to tone your face into a stranger’s face. You only need to turn the dial a little.

If you are dark-skinned and want to deepen into a warm, even brown glow, treat it like raising the volume from three to five, not from three to ten. Start with a whitening soap that cleanses gently and lifts dullness without stripping your natural color. Let it do the daily work of clearing dead skin, sweat, and the grayish film that makes your tone look tired. Then leave the heavy brightening creams alone. Creams that promise three shades in three weeks are usually doing the work of bleach in a prettier jar, and they come with a price: thin skin, dark patches, stretch marks, and regret.

Instead, moisturize with something simple and nourishing. Protect yourself from the sun, because the sun is the static that distorts your song. Drink your water. Sleep. Exfoliate with patience. Brightening is maintenance, not transformation. You are not becoming someone new. You are simply making sure your own skin sounds clear.

So turn the dial slowly. Listen to your body. A shade or two of radiance is enough when the radiance is healthy. The goal is not to disappear into another color. The goal is to glow, confidently, in the one you already are.
