title: Dream bigger, sis!”  Adeife Adeoye’s bold call to Nigerian women.
excerpt: There's a growing conversation online about whether young Nigerians, especially women, are being told to "dream bigger" in ways that ignore the ground they're a…
content:
There's a growing conversation online about whether young Nigerians, especially women, are being told to "dream bigger" in ways that ignore the ground they're actually standing on. When public figures encourage people to look beyond familiar career paths, government jobs, tech, even fields like aviation or space science, the advice is often well intentioned. Nobody wants young women boxed into a narrow set of "acceptable" jobs simply because that's what's always been done. But intention and impact aren't always the same thing, and a lot of people online feel that ambition without context can come off as tone deaf.

The pushback isn't really about discouraging big dreams. It's about the gap between motivational language and lived reality. In a country wrestling with double digit inflation, currency devaluation, and a job market that hasn't kept pace with population growth, telling someone to "aim for the stars" can land very differently depending on who's saying it and what safety net they have. Critics argue that real empowerment isn't just about expanding what people believe is possible, it's about acknowledging the actual barriers (cost of education, lack of infrastructure, limited opportunities) that stand between a dream and its execution. Otherwise, the advice risks sounding like it's coming from a place of privilege rather than solidarity.

At the same time, defenders of this kind of messaging make a fair point too, expectations shape outcomes, and if young girls are only ever told to aim for "safe" or traditional roles, that ceiling becomes self fulfilling. Somebody has to be the first Nigerian woman in a given field, and that person needed someone to plant the idea before the resources ever lined up. The real tension seems to be less about whether to dream big, and more about whether the people encouraging that dream are also doing the work of showing a realistic path there.

What do you think, is this kind of "dream beyond your zone" messaging genuinely motivating, or does it gloss over the real economic walls young Nigerians are up against?

title: Production Dockerization: Multi-Stage Builds, Security Hardening, & Best Practices
excerpt: How to craft ultra-slim, secure production Docker containers with multi-stage builds, non-root user execution, and layer caching optimization.
content:
Production Dockerization: Multi-Stage Builds, Security Hardening, & Best Practices

Containerizing full-stack applications is the standard for modern deployment pipelines across Kubernetes, AWS ECS, and cloud hosts. However, naive Dockerfiles often produce bloated images (1GB+) riddled with unnecessary build tooling and security vulnerabilities.

1. Multi-Stage Builds for Node.js / Next.js

Multi-stage builds allow you to use heavy compilation tools (like TypeScript and native C++ build bindings) in a builder stage, and copy only the compiled artifacts into a lightweight production runtime image.

# Stage 1: Base Dependencies
FROM node:20-alpine AS deps
RUN apk add --no-cache libc6-compat
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci

# Stage 2: Application Builder
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY . .
ENV NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED 1
RUN npm run build

# Stage 3: Production Runner
FROM node:20-alpine AS runner
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV production
ENV NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED 1

# Security: Create and use non-root system user
RUN addgroup --system --gid 1001 nodejs &&     adduser --system --uid 1001 nextjs

COPY --from=builder /app/public ./public
COPY --from=builder --chown=nextjs:nodejs /app/.next/standalone ./
COPY --from=builder --chown=nextjs:nodejs /app/.next/static ./.next/static

USER nextjs
EXPOSE 3000
ENV PORT 3000

CMD ["node", "server.js"]

2. Essential Security Hardening Rules

  • Never Run as Root: Always create a dedicated non-root application user (UID 1001) to prevent container breakout exploits.
  • Leverage .dockerignore: Exclude .git, .env.local, and node_modules from the build context.
  • Scan Images for CVEs: Integrate automated vulnerability scanners like Trivy or Docker Scout into your CI/CD pipeline.

title: It Was Never Really About the Stranger
excerpt: Some people leave your life, but the version of you they met doesn't leave with them.
content:
If you had asked JSS3 me what changed me, I probably would have pointed at the stranger.

I would have told you about the friendship that came out of nowhere, how exciting it was, how quickly everything happened, the game that ruined it, and the day I told my classmates about it only to have them laugh.

Back then, it felt like a big deal.

It was one of those experiences I thought I would remember forever.

But life moved on.

School continued.

Break times came and went.

There were new conversations, new people and new things to get excited about.

Eventually, I stopped thinking about the stranger as much.

We never became friends again.

There was no dramatic reunion.

No big conversation where we finally explained everything to each other.

Nothing.

The friendship simply ended.

And maybe that's why, looking back now, I don't think the stranger was the most important part of the story.

What stayed with me was everything that came after.

I was young.

I was curious.

I wanted to explore the things my classmates talked about.

I wanted to make friends.

I wanted to feel seen.

And I was still figuring out what all of that meant.

The stranger was just one chapter in that process.

A very strange chapter, yes.

But still just a chapter.

Funny how some people enter your life for such a short time and somehow leave you with a story you can still remember years later.

I don't know what became of him.

I don't even know if he remembers me.

But I remember that girl.

The JSS3 girl who was just trying to find her way through friendship, social media, curiosity and growing up.

And maybe that's who I was really trying to understand all along.

Not the stranger.

Me.

title: Architects of Our Own Crisis
excerpt: How Collective Responsibility Can Defeat Antimicrobial Resistance
content:
Part Two: The prescription pad is part of the battlefield

We have spent years telling patients not to misuse antibiotics.

Don't self-medicate.

Don't demand antibiotics for every illness.

Don't stop treatment unnecessarily.

Don't share your antibiotics.

All of that matters.

But there is an uncomfortable question we also need to ask:

What happens on the other side of the prescription?

If patients have a responsibility in the antimicrobial resistance crisis, are healthcare providers completely free from responsibility?

Of course not.

Antimicrobial resistance is too complex to be reduced to a single group of people.

Patients can misuse antimicrobials.

Healthcare professionals can prescribe them inappropriately.

Health facilities can lack diagnostic capacity.

Agricultural systems can use antimicrobials improperly.

Pharmaceutical and regulatory systems can have gaps.

And weak surveillance can allow the problem to grow without us fully seeing it.

If the damage is collective, then the repair must also be collective.

And this is where one of our most important weapons against antimicrobial resistance enters the conversation:

Antimicrobial Stewardship

Antimicrobial stewardship programmes are designed to improve how antimicrobials are selected, prescribed, administered and monitored.

The goal is not simply to use fewer antibiotics.

The goal is to use them intelligently.

That distinction matters.

A patient who genuinely needs an antibiotic should receive the appropriate treatment.

The problem begins when antimicrobials are used when they are unnecessary, when the wrong drug is selected, when the dose is inappropriate, when treatment continues longer than necessary, or when therapy is not reassessed as new information becomes available.

A practical way to think about this is through the 5 Ds: Diagnosis, Drug, Dose, Duration and De-escalation.

1. Diagnosis: Is an antimicrobial actually needed?

Before the prescription comes the question:

What are we actually treating?

Not every fever is bacterial.

Not every cough requires an antibiotic.

Not every infection-like symptom means that an antibacterial drug is appropriate.

Whenever feasible, antimicrobial treatment should be guided by appropriate clinical assessment and diagnostic testing.

There are, of course, situations where treatment cannot wait for laboratory confirmation.

A critically ill patient cannot always afford to wait several days for a culture result.

That is why empirical therapy exists.

But empirical treatment should not become an excuse for abandoning diagnosis altogether.

And this is where I have a message for the healthcare professional who says:

“Doctor, I've been prescribing this way for 30 years.”

With all due respect, experience matters.

But the microorganisms aren't exactly newcomers either.

Bacteria have been evolving and adapting for billions of years.

Run the appropriate tests whenever the clinical situation allows it.

The question is not whether experience is valuable.

The question is whether experience should replace evidence.

It shouldn't.

2. Drug: Is this the right antimicrobial?

Once an antimicrobial is considered necessary, the next question is:

Which one?

The strongest antibiotic is not automatically the best antibiotic.

Treatment should target the confirmed or most likely pathogen while minimizing unnecessary effects on the patient's normal microbiota.

This is particularly important when broad-spectrum antibiotics are used.

Think about it this way:

Using a broad-spectrum antibiotic for every infection is like using a sledgehammer to swat a fly on a glass table.

Yes, you may kill the fly.

But you might also destroy the table.

Broad-spectrum antimicrobials have important clinical uses, particularly when the pathogen is unknown or the patient is seriously ill.

The problem is not that broad-spectrum drugs exist.

The problem is using them when a narrower, appropriate option would do the job.

Antimicrobial stewardship therefore asks:

  • What organism are we trying to treat?

  • What is the likely susceptibility pattern?

  • Is there a narrower agent that would be effective?

  • Can unnecessary antimicrobial exposure be avoided?

Precision matters.

3. Dose: Is the amount appropriate for this patient?

Antimicrobial dosing is not simply a matter of memorizing a number.

The appropriate dose can depend on factors such as:

  • the type and severity of infection;

  • the site of infection;

  • the patient's age and weight where relevant;

  • kidney function;

  • liver function;

  • the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of the drug; and

  • other patient-specific considerations.

Giving everyone the same dose without considering these factors is like putting the same quantity of fuel into every vehicle and expecting every engine to perform perfectly.

Some may receive too little.

Some may receive too much.

And some may experience avoidable toxicity.

There is another important point here:

The drug needs to reach the infection at an effective concentration.

Treating an infection is not simply about putting an antimicrobial into someone's bloodstream.

The drug must reach the relevant site of infection in sufficient concentration while remaining safe for the patient.

The brain, lungs, bones, urinary tract and other tissues do not all present the same pharmacological challenges.

So the question isn't merely:

“What dose kills the organism?”

It is:

“What exposure will effectively treat this infection in this particular patient?”

4. Duration: How long should treatment continue?

This is where one of the most persistent assumptions about antibiotics needs to be challenged:

Longer does not automatically mean better.

Antimicrobial stewardship promotes treatment durations supported by evidence for the specific infection and clinical circumstances.

Continuing therapy unnecessarily exposes patients to additional antimicrobial pressure and potential adverse effects without necessarily providing additional benefit.

Imagine leaving a fire hose running for three days after the flames have already been extinguished.

You're not making the building safer.

You're just flooding it.

The same principle applies to antimicrobial therapy.

Once an appropriate evidence-based treatment period has been completed, continuing “just to be safe” is not automatically safer.

The appropriate duration depends on the infection, the antimicrobial, the patient and the clinical response.

Therefore:

The right duration is not necessarily the longest duration.

It is the duration supported by evidence for that clinical situation.

5. De-escalation: Now that we know more, can we narrow the treatment?

This may be one of the most important moments in antimicrobial stewardship.

A patient may initially present with a serious infection where the causative organism is unknown.

In such a situation, empirical therapy may need to cover several possible pathogens.

But the clinical picture does not remain static.

The laboratory may return culture and antimicrobial susceptibility results.

The patient's condition may improve.

The suspected pathogen may become known.

And suddenly, the question changes.

It is no longer:

“What could possibly be causing this?”

It becomes:

“Now that we have more information, what is the most appropriate treatment?”

That is where de-escalation comes in.

Can the broad-spectrum antimicrobial be narrowed?

Can an unnecessary antimicrobial be stopped?

Can treatment be changed from intravenous to an appropriate oral option?

Can therapy be adjusted according to susceptibility results?

Imagine continuing to call in an airstrike after the target has already been identified and contained.

More force does not necessarily mean better treatment.

Sometimes, precision is the stronger weapon.

De-escalation is therefore not “weakening” treatment.

It is using new information to make treatment more precise.

The laboratory is not a side character

There is an important lesson running through all five Ds:

Antimicrobial stewardship cannot function effectively without diagnostics.

The prescriber needs information.

The laboratory provides information.

The pharmacist contributes expertise in antimicrobial selection, dosing and interactions.

Nurses monitor administration, response and patient factors.

Infection prevention teams address transmission.

Hospital leadership provides the systems and resources that allow all of this to happen.

This is why effective antimicrobial stewardship is not simply about giving doctors another guideline and telling them to “prescribe responsibly.”

It requires multidisciplinary collaboration.

AMR is bigger than the hospital

And this brings us to the bigger picture.

Antimicrobial resistance does not exist exclusively inside hospitals.

It does not belong exclusively to doctors.

It does not belong exclusively to patients.

It does not even belong exclusively to human medicine.

Antimicrobial resistance moves across interconnected systems involving people, animals and the environment.

That is why the response must be grounded in a One Health approach.

Healthcare institutions need the capacity to support antimicrobial stewardship through:

  • trained multidisciplinary teams;

  • reliable diagnostic services;

  • evidence-based prescribing guidelines;

  • antimicrobial-use surveillance;

  • regular audit and feedback;

  • infection prevention and control;

  • continuing professional education; and

  • institutional accountability.

At the same time, medical, pharmacy, nursing and other health-professional programmes need to prepare future healthcare workers to understand antimicrobials as a finite and shared resource.

The conversation must also extend beyond hospitals.

Agriculture matters.

Veterinary medicine matters.

Environmental contamination matters.

Public policy matters.

Regulation matters.

Public awareness matters.

And education matters.

We cannot educate our way out of AMR alone

One of the easiest things to do in the AMR conversation is to blame the patient.

“People buy antibiotics without prescriptions.”

“People stop taking antibiotics when they feel better.”

“People share medication.”

All of these behaviors deserve attention.

But stopping there would be a mistake.

We cannot educate our way out of AMR while leaving healthcare systems, prescribing practices, diagnostics, agriculture, regulation and environmental pathways untouched.

Similarly, we cannot simply blame healthcare professionals while ignoring the pressures under which healthcare systems operate.

AMR is a systems problem.

And systems problems require systems solutions.

We are architects of the crisis. We can also be architects of the solution.

Antimicrobial resistance is often presented as though humanity is simply waiting for bacteria to defeat our medicines.

But there is another way to look at it.

Every unnecessary prescription creates antimicrobial pressure.

Every poorly targeted treatment creates an opportunity for selection.

Every preventable infection creates another reason to use antimicrobials.

Every missed opportunity for diagnosis makes precision more difficult.

Every failure to de-escalate wastes information that could have improved treatment.

And every effective stewardship intervention represents an opportunity to preserve antimicrobial effectiveness.

The solution therefore does not rest on one profession.

It does not rest on one laboratory.

It does not rest on one new antibiotic.

And it certainly does not rest on blaming patients alone.

It requires collective discipline.

Better diagnosis.

Better prescribing.

Better stewardship.

Better infection prevention.

Better surveillance.

Better regulation.

Better agricultural practices.

Better public understanding.

And better collaboration across the One Health spectrum.

The future of antimicrobial therapy will not be protected by a miracle drug alone.

It will be protected by the millions of decisions we make before, during and after that drug is prescribed.

We are, in many ways, architects of our own crisis.

And that means we have an opportunity to become architects of the solution.

We may not need a miracle drug to save the medicines we already have.

We need the collective discipline to protect the miracles we already have.

Part Two of the series on antimicrobial resistance.

title: We Have Made Life Look Like We Only Came Here to Find Money and Die
excerpt: When I was little, I thought growing up was going to be beautiful.I didn’t really understand money then. I didn’t know you needed money to keep the lights on, p…
content:
When I was little, I thought growing up was going to be beautiful.

I didn’t really understand money then. I didn’t know you needed money to keep the lights on, pay rent, eat, move around, buy data, fix things when they broke, or basically exist without constantly calculating your next expense.

I just thought you grew up.

You made money.

You were happy.

You had friends.

You went out.

You had a nice house.

And you lived.

Simple.

Nobody told me that somewhere between growing up and actually becoming an adult, life would become this endless cycle of find money, pay bills, complain about money, find more money.

And somehow, everybody is tired.

People wake up, go to work, come back exhausted, pay bills, sleep, and do it all over again.

Then when you ask them to hang out, they say they don’t have money.

Ask them to visit you, they say they are busy.

Ask them when last they saw their friends, and they genuinely have to think about it.

And I sometimes wonder, is this really what we thought adulthood was going to be?

Because we are working so hard to afford life that we barely have the time or energy to actually live it.

I know money is important. Very important, actually.

Especially in Nigeria.

Let’s not pretend.

Nigeria is hard.

Things are expensive. Rent is expensive. Food is expensive. Transportation is expensive. The value of the naira keeps falling, and even when you finally find a job, sometimes the salary barely survives the journey from your employer’s account to your bank account.

You earn ₦300,000 and before you know it, transport has taken some, food has taken some, data has taken some, skincare has taken some, bills have taken some.

What is left?

You start wondering if you were actually paid at all.

And jobs? Finding a good-paying job sometimes feels like finding a needle in a very large, very frustrating haystack.

So yes, people need money.

I need money.

You need money.

We all need money.

But somewhere along the line, I think we started confusing having money with being allowed to live.

And those are not the same thing.

We started telling ourselves that we would enjoy life when we have enough money.

When we get the better job.

When we move into the nice apartment.

When we can afford to travel.

When we buy the car.

When we get the perfect body.

When we can afford the expensive restaurant without checking the menu prices first.

When we finally “make it.”

And before you know it, your entire life becomes a waiting room.

Wait.

Just wait.

Things will be better soon.

And I understand why.

We are scared of slowing down.

Because everybody keeps telling us that the time to make money is when you’re young. So you work while you’re young, save while you’re young, sacrifice while you’re young, so that when you’re old you can finally enjoy yourself.

Because who knows what will happen later?

The care culture is dying too.

There was a time when your neighbour could be your brother. When people looked out for each other. When seeing someone struggling could actually move you to help them.

Now you can practically be dying on the road and people will walk past you.

Everybody is trying to survive.

Everybody is trying to secure themselves because, honestly, who knows who will be there for you tomorrow?

So people hustle.

And hustle.

And hustle.

But then something happens.

You become so busy securing your future that you stop experiencing your present.

And I don’t think we’re meant to live like that.

I also think social media has made this worse.

Because now it’s not enough to live a good life.

Your life has to look good.

You have to look like you’re living.

You need the latest phone.

The expensive hair.

The nice apartment.

The restaurant pictures.

The vacation pictures.

The perfect body.

The perfect outfit.

The perfect lighting.

And then, of course, you need the perfect picture to prove that you have all these things.

Nobody wants to post a real picture anymore.

Everybody is waiting for that one picture where they look like a baddie.

The picture where the stomach is flat, the hair is laid, the face is giving, the lighting is perfect and everything looks expensive.

And honestly, I get it.

Who doesn’t want to look good?

But sometimes I wonder when we stopped using social media to share our lives and started using it to present evidence that our lives are worth envying.

We used to post nonsense.

Real nonsense.

A stupid picture of your friend.

A blurry picture.

A joke that only five people understood.

Something embarrassing that happened during the day.

You could make a dumb post and your friends would laugh at you in the comments.

People weren’t trying so hard to look perfect.

We were just having fun.

Now everybody is so serious.

Even our silliness has been curated.

And the likes matter too.

People take pictures, edit them, spend money on hair, clothes, photographers and sometimes even gadgets, then sit down refreshing the post to see how many people liked it.

And sometimes the picture doesn’t even do well.

So you’ve spent all that money trying to create a moment that will impress people, and three hours later, the algorithm has swallowed it.

I know a girl who spent most of her money preparing for her birthday pictures.

Hair.

Makeup.

Outfit.

Pictures.

Everything.

She wanted the birthday pictures.

And she got them.

Beautiful pictures.

But by the time the birthday was over, she didn’t have money for a bedframe.

And I don’t even say this to make fun of her.

Because honestly, I understand her.

We’ve all been sold this idea that certain things make you look like you’re doing well.

And sometimes we spend money trying to look like we are living a beautiful life while the actual life underneath the picture is struggling.

That is the part that worries me.

And I’m not even going to sit here and act like I have figured it out.

I haven’t.

I postpone happiness too.

Many times.

Sometimes I want to buy a bottle of wine or get something small for myself and I’ll start calculating.

“If I buy this now, when it finishes, my money will be gone.”

Sometimes I’m exhausted and I just want to take a ride home instead of entering a bus.

Then I check the price.

“For what?”

And I enter the bus.

Sometimes I want to see my friends but I don’t have money for transport.

Sometimes I want to take a picture but I don’t have the hair I think I need for the picture, so I tell myself I’ll take it later.

When?

When I get the hair.

When I have the money.

When things are better.

And that’s the exact thing I’m talking about.

We keep waiting.

The funny thing is, I think I’m actually a very low-maintenance girl.

I hate admitting it because the internet has made it seem like every woman must be a particular kind of “baddie” to be considered desirable.

But honestly?

Sometimes I just want to live.

I can wear my natural hair.

I can do all-back and be fine.

I love wigs. I love nice hair. I love beautiful things. But I can survive without them.

I don’t need a new gadget every time something new comes out.

Give me food in my house.

Give me money in my account.

Give me data.

Let me work out.

Let me have somewhere comfortable to sleep.

Let me have people I love around me.

Honestly, I’m good.

And maybe that’s not enough for Instagram.

But it can be enough for life.

You are also allowed to get excited over small things.

I think we have forgotten that.

A good cup of coffee.

Clean sheets.

A meal you’ve been craving.

Getting home after a long day and taking off your bra.

A quiet weekend with absolutely nothing planned.

Seeing someone you haven’t seen in a long time.

Sitting with your friends in someone’s house, nobody looking at their phone, everybody talking rubbish and laughing.

Making fun of one another.

Remembering something stupid you did years ago and laughing about it all over again.

These things don’t sound impressive.

You probably can’t make a “soft life” TikTok out of most of them.

But they are still life.

And sometimes happiness is just noticing the little things that are still there.

I was talking to a friend recently, and she told me she had been feeling depressed because she didn’t know how her life was going.

She doesn’t have an apartment of her own.

And the funny thing is, I was actually admiring her.

This girl had started learning hair installation. She’s also learning makeup.

Meanwhile, I’m sitting here thinking, this babe is doing something with herself.

And she’s sitting there thinking her life is going nowhere.

It made me realize how strange we are.

We are constantly looking at somebody else’s life and thinking they are doing better, while that person might be looking at us and thinking the exact same thing.

Everybody is tired.

Everybody thinks they’re behind.

Everybody thinks they haven’t done enough.

Maybe sometimes we need to stop and look at what is actually happening.

Maybe your life isn’t as empty as you think it is.

I learned something about this when I was dealing with my own health problems.

When you’re healthy, you don’t wake up and say, “Thank God, I can eat without pain today.”

You just eat.

You don’t say, “I’m grateful that I woke up feeling normal.”

You just wake up.

You don’t think about how beautiful it is to sit with your family, laugh with your friends, walk around freely, or simply feel okay.

Until something takes that normality away from you.

Then suddenly, the things you thought were ordinary become precious.

And maybe we don’t have to wait for something to go wrong before we notice what is going right.

This isn’t me saying we should stop working.

Please.

Make your money.

Get the job.

Build the business.

Save.

Invest.

Buy the house.

Travel.

Get the nice hair.

Buy the iPhone if you want it.

Do all the things you’ve dreamed about.

Wanting more is not a bad thing.

But maybe we need to stop making more the entry fee for happiness.

You can want a better life without hating the one you currently have.

You can be ambitious and still rest.

You can be broke and still laugh.

You can be working towards something and still enjoy a random Tuesday.

You can wear your natural hair and take the picture anyway.

You can post the silly picture.

The ugly picture.

The picture where you weren’t posing.

The picture that only makes sense to you and your friends.

You don’t have to look like a baddie every day to prove that you’re living.

And maybe we should start going to our friends’ houses again.

Not every hangout needs a restaurant.

Not every gathering needs drinks and a photographer.

Sometimes everybody can bring whatever they have.

Someone cooks.

Someone brings a drink.

Someone brings absolutely nothing but their presence.

And you sit down.

You talk.

You laugh.

You remember old stories.

You make new ones.

And for a few hours, nobody is thinking about rent.

Nobody is thinking about Instagram.

Nobody is checking how many likes their last picture got.

You’re just there.

Alive.

Maybe this is the part we’ve forgotten.

Life is not only the big things.

It is also the little things happening while you’re waiting for the big things.

The coffee.

The friends.

The laughter.

The food.

The clean sheets.

The breeze coming through an open window.

The random phone call.

The stupid joke.

The good news.

The quiet evening.

The ability to wake up and try again.

We have become so obsessed with building a life worth living that we’ve forgotten to live while we’re building it.

So yes, make the money.

Please make the money.

But don’t spend your entire youth preparing for a future where you finally get to be happy.

Call your friend.

Go and see them.

Sit somewhere and talk nonsense.

Post the picture.

Open the windows.

Eat the food.

Laugh too loudly.

Take the ride home once in a while if you’re too tired for the bus.

Buy the small thing that makes you happy sometimes.

Let yourself be excited about something that will not change your life.

Because maybe happiness was never supposed to be this grand thing we finally unlock after we’ve achieved everything.

Maybe sometimes it is just realizing that, despite everything, there are still good things here.

And maybe that’s enough reason to live a little.

title: My Brother Used to Beg for Everything — So I Taught Him a Very Expensive Lesson
excerpt:
He never stopped begging until one bottle of 7up changed everything.

A childhood sibling rivalry escalates into one unforgettable prank involving a bottle of 7up and it is not fiction.
content:
Disclaimer: don’t try this at home, we were unserious children 😭

My younger siblingcan beg. I mean, beg beg. Most especially, my younger brother. He can beg for your eyessss.

When we were much younger, my brother begged for everything even if we were both given the same thing. He’d make sure to finish his own first, then watch me until I started eating mine, before stretching his hand out and saying, “Come and give me.” If you refused, he’d start crying, and your mum would have to come out and say, “Give him now, don’t be stingy.” It always made me so annoyed and frustrated. Eventually, I’d have to give him.

I had had it up to hereeeee. So one day, I decided enough was enough.

I bought a bottle of 7up — the plastic bottled one. My brother bought his own, Fanta. As usual, he didn’t even wait for food before bubbling his all up. I drank a little out of mine and kept it in the fridge after eating, with a serious warning that no one should touch my 7up.

Tell me why I went back there later and the quantity I left was no longer the same. Someone had taken my 7up🥹. I was livid. I knew it was no other person but my brother.

“Tobi,” “Tobiiiiii,” I called my brother.

When he came, I asked, “Did you drink my 7up?”

He said, “Ahnnn, why will I do that? Someone drank your 7up?” Feigning ignorance too. Mehnnnn, smoke was coming out of my nose from all the anger.😡

I poured my remaining 7up somewhere else and devised a plan. I went inside the kitchen, poured kerosene into the 7up bottle, and cleaned the outside. Then I went back to where I’d kept my remaining drink, poured a little of it into the kerosene-filled bottle, and coated the mouth with 7up too, so it wouldn’t give off any smell.

I dropped it on the table and called my brother to get me snacks — acting like I wanted to eat the snacks with the drink. As usual, he first grumbled. Then he agreed, on the condition that I’d give him some of it. I said no problem.

When he got back, I gave him a little of the snacks, then specifically said, “The drink is already small, so make sure you drink small out of it.”

He collected it, unsuspecting of anything, and as the greedy person that he is, instead of sipping it small small, he gobbled a big chunk of the 7up mixed with kerosene.

He screameddddd and dropped the whole drink, then started crying.

Oh, the joy that gave me. Is this how criminals are birthed?🌚

The noise attracted my parents, who came to the scene almost immediately, asking what happened. None of us could explain, but my brother was pointing at the drink while fainting.

Ahhhh, fainting ke? Modaran. This was not part of the plan nowwww.

My mum sniffed the drink and immediately knew what had happened. By this time, people were already gathering and offering solutions. They quickly gave him palm oil which was apparently some kind of antidote. I think it worked, because he opened his eyes a few minutes later. I was legit scared I had killed my brother.

After everything had died down, I was given the beating of my life, but my brother also learned the lesson of his life. So, win-win, yeah?🌚😌

Oh, and this is not fiction, btw.

title: WHY "SOFT LIFE" BECAME MORE THAN A TREND (AND WHY SO FEW PEOPLE ARE ACTUALLY LIVING IT)
excerpt: The dream of ease, the pressure to afford it, and the reality nobody posts about.
content:
She posted a video sipping tea by the window, captioned "choosing peace this season." Ten minutes later, she was back on three client calls, an unpaid invoice, and a landlord message she had not answered in four days. That's soft life now, not the absence of stress, but the art of hiding it well. If you've ever posted a calm, glowing picture of your life while your chest was tight with anxiety the whole time, you already know exactly what this article is about.

WHY DOES EVERYONE SUDDENLY WANT A "SOFT LIFE"?

It didn't come from nowhere. An entire generation grew up watching their parents work themselves into exhaustion and call it responsibility. The aunty who worked two jobs and still fainted from stress, the uncle who "provided" but was never around, the quiet understanding that suffering equals maturity. Soft life is the loud, public rejection of that story. The desire underneath it is real, people are genuinely tired of proving their worth through struggle. The problem is what happened to that desire once it hit the internet, it got packaged, filtered, and sold back as a lifestyle you could buy into with the right skincare routine and the right caption.

Have you wondered if Soft Life Is Real, or Is It Just Good Lighting and a Caption?

Both. That's the uncomfortable answer, yes you read right.

For a small number of people, soft life is genuinely funded by money, by privilege, by circumstances that remove the daily grind most people can't opt out of. For a much larger number of people online, it's a fifteen-second clip of the one peaceful hour in an otherwise chaotic day, posted because that hour is the only part worth showing anyone. You're not seeing a lie exactly. You're seeing a highlight reel of someone's best moment, presented as if it were their whole life. And you're comparing it to your entire, unfiltered day.

AM I THE ONLY ONE WHO CAN'T AFFORD TO "CHOOSE PEACE"?

No. And this is the part nobody wants to admit out loud, because it sounds like complaining, peace costs money, and rest requires a level of financial and emotional stability that a lot of young Nigerians simply don't have yet.

You can want to "choose yourself" all you want, the rent still needs paying, the family still calls with needs, the job still doesn't care how tired you are. Feeling locked out of soft life is not a personal failure to manifest calm. It's a fairly accurate read of your actual circumstances.

IS IT NORMAL TO FEEL LIKE YOU'RE FAILING AT RELAXING?

Yes, and it's one of the strangest side effects of this trend. People are now stressed about not being relaxed enough. Rest became a performance metric. Instead of resting because you're tired, you rest so you can post that you rested, and somehow that turns relaxation into another task on the list. If your "self-care Sunday" feels more exhausting than your actual work week, that's not you doing soft life wrong. That's soft life, as currently sold to you, being a bit of a trap.

Nobody Tells You This: Soft Life Was Never About Doing Less, It Was About Doing Less Loudly

Here's the hard truth, a lot of what gets called soft life online isn't rest. It's rest with an audience. The tea by the window only counts if someone sees it. The "day off" only registers if it's documented. Real rest, the kind that actually restores you, usually looks boring, unposted, and slightly unglamorous, sleeping in without telling anyone, sitting in silence with no caption, saying no to something and never explaining why. The version that goes viral is rarely the version that's actually working.

HOW TO BUILD AN ACTUAL SOFT LIFE (NOT JUST POST ONE)

You don't need a new aesthetic. You need boundaries nobody can see. Protect one unposted hour a day. Something that's just for you, with no camera and no caption. If it feels strange to keep something private, that's worth noticing. Separate rest from performance. Ask yourself honestly: am I doing this because I need it, or because I need people to see me doing it Build the softness before you advertise it. Save quietly. Set the boundary quietly. Let the calm be a byproduct of real changes, not the opening scene of a story you have not lived yet. Soft life is not fake. But most of what's sold to you under that name is a photo of a destination, not a map to get there. The real version is slower, less photogenic, and unlike the trend, actually sustainable. Be honest, is your soft life real, or is it just your best camera angle?

Tell us in the comments. And send this to the friend who's been "resting" since January but hasn't stopped hustling for a day.

title: The Rude Bus Driver
excerpt: The Mutiny
content:
Travelling by road?

There is an undeniable charm to road trips in Nigeria.

The rhythmic hum of the engine, the refreshing breeze cutting through the open window, the vibrant energy of roadside hawkers thrusting plantain chips and cold drinks through the glass, and the endless stretch of green scenery, it was almost enough to make Diana forget her severe motion sickness.

Almost.

She was traveling home to visit relatives, settled into a middle seat of a commercial bus. But any hope of a peaceful journey was shattered before they even cleared the city limits, courtesy of the driver.

He was a bitter, abrasive man who treated his weathered vehicle like a pristine luxury vehicle and his passengers like stray livestock.

"Abeg, make una eat carefully o!" he barked into the rearview mirror, his voice dripping with venom as he glared at a middle-aged woman carefully holding a takeaway container. "Kai! Madam, no go stain my seat with that beans!"

The woman paused mid-bite, her spoon hovering in the air. "Haba, driver! I no fit chop again? Why you dey talk to me like this?"

The driver only grunted, continuing his barrage. A few rows back, a young student leaned his head backward against the headrest, trying to sleep off the heat.

"Hey! You!" the driver shouted. "Adjust your head! Before you go drool come stain my car seat!"

The young man snapped his eyes open, thoroughly unimpressed. "This your ajepako car wey dey cry for help? Na him you dey pride yourself on top?"

By noon, the bus was a battlefield of loud arguments and back-to-back insults. But nobody clashed with the driver quite like the mother of three sitting near the front.

"You are extremely bad at driving, rude, and completely mannerless!" she yelled over the engine roar.

"And you, this unmarried woman with plenty children," the driver sneered back, "don't even try me. Go and control your noisy kids!"

"Who told you I'm not married?!" she fired back, pulling out her phone. "In fact, I will call my husband now! He’s in the army, and he will deal with you at the next checkpoint!" She dialed furiously, but the highway signal was dead.

Realizing her threat was falling flat, the woman resorted to pure malice. Diana watched in utter disbelief as the woman covertly induced vomit in one of her young children, deliberately letting the mess spill onto the floor mat just to spite the driver.

When the driver noticed, he lost his mind. He slammed on the brakes, pulling over to the shoulder, and began screaming at the terrified child until the kid burst into tears.

"Don't you dare speak to my child like that!" the mother roared, shielding her crying kid.

With a final curse, the driver shoved the bus back into gear and tore down the road. An hour later, when another one of the woman's children whimpered that he needed to pee, the driver stubbornly refused to pull over, speeding past every safe stop.

The noise inside the bus reached a boiling point. Everyone was shouting at once. That was when Diana, unable to take the chaos any longer, raised her voice over the noise.

"If you know you are this frustrated and sparkling neat," Diana called out, "why are you driving us, the dirty passengers?"

That was the final straw.

The driver swerved hard onto the dirt shoulder, cutting the engine right in the middle of a dense, isolated forest stretch. He threw open his door, stepped out, and crossed his arms.

"All of you should come out of my car!" he shouted through the open windows. "I am not moving again! Walk to where you are going!"

A sudden, tense silence fell over the passengers. Pride urged them to step down and leave the arrogant man behind, but reality quickly set in. They were stranded in an insecure bush area with no network, no towns in sight, and zero passing commercial vehicles. Leaving the bus meant putting their lives at risk.

The passengers began whispering among themselves, gathering in a quick, urgent consensus. This driver was an unhinged safety risk to every single person on board.

"I know this road," a calm voice called out from the back. A young man stood up. "And I have a valid license. I can drive us."

Before the driver could comprehend what was happening, three male passengers stepped off the bus, grabbed the driver by his shirt, and forcefully bundled him into the back row.

"What are you doing?!" the driver screamed, his arrogance suddenly turning to panic. "This is my car! I will have all of you arrested for kidnapping and carjacking!"

"Shut up there!" a passenger barked, landing a light slap on the side of his head as they pinned him down. Even the mother of three leaned over to throw a firm slap of her own for good measure.

"Nobody is stealing your precious car," Diana said coldly as the new driver started the ignition and put the bus in drive. "We are only taking ourselves to our destination. When we get there, you can have your sparkling clean vehicle back."

The bus rolled smoothly back onto the highway, leaving the former king of the road trapped in his own backseat, forced to endure the rest of the trip in complete, humiliated silence.

title: My Crush Has Mouth Odor
excerpt: The Illusion of Perfection (Comedic)
content:
To Rita, Louis was not just a guy; he was a masterpiece walking the halls of the university. Tall, light skinned, and sleekly built, he moved with an effortless poise. With his almond eyes, sharp nose, perfectly contoured pink lips, and subtle, elf-like ears, he looked like he had stepped right out of a high-fantasy novel.

He was quiet, almost ghostlike yet his aura dominated every room he entered. Nobody really knew what his voice sounded like, though rumors claimed a lucky few had heard him speak.

"Louis is the one for me," Rita declared proudly, resting her chin on her hands as she watched him cross the courtyard.

Martha, her roommate looked up from her notebook with a slight smirk. "Hmm. Rita, small-small o. Have you ever actually spoken to him?"

"Not yet. But I have a plan."

"What if he snubs you?" Martha asked.

"He won't," Rita said confidently. "He’s just reserved."

"Toh, go get him then," Martha chuckled. "Though, word on the street is that a couple of girls used to crush on him hard before they suddenly dropped him and ran."

Rita waved a hand dismissively. "Doesn't matter, Martha. I know what I want."

Rita launched her full-scale campaign. She tried approaching him after class, but he glided away effortlessly. Undeterred, she began slipping handwritten love letters into his bag. When she finally managed to get his WhatsApp number, her enthusiastic paragraphs were met with ice-cold single-word replies: "Ok," "Alright," and the occasional thumbs-up emoji.

Then came the gifts. She left him sleek pens, notebooks, silver chains, woven bracelets, and designer beanies.

Soon, coursemates started whispering, sending anonymous messages taunting her desperation. Rita ignored them all. She was goal-oriented, and Louis was the target.

Her persistence paid off on a hot Thursday afternoon. A text popped up on her screen:

"Passageway behind Faculty of Engineering. 3:00 PM.”

Rita’s heart leaped. The moment had finally arrived. She practically flew to the venue.

When she reached the quiet passageway, Louis was waiting, leaning casually against the concrete pillar.

"Thank you for meeting me," Rita gushed, her heart doing backflips.

"I hope you've been getting my messages and gifts. I really just want us to vibe, you know? You're always so isolated."

Before she could finish her sentence, Louis stepped forward and pulled her into a tight, sudden embrace. Rita froze, her cheeks burning as their hearts beat in sync.

Then the first sign hit her. A sharp, sour odor wafted from his armpits, cutting through the warm afternoon air. It’s just sweat, Rita reasoned quickly, trying to stay calm. He's been in lectures all day.

Without warning, Louis leaned down and pressed his lips to hers.

What was supposed to be a romantic moment ended instantly. Rita jerked backward, gasping for air as her eyes widened in complete horror.

As he stood there, completely unbothered by her reaction, he began to speak. His voice was shockingly deep, a low rumble that sounded almost completely inaudible like a faint reverberation coming from deep inside his chest.

"I see how much effort you put in for me," he mumbled, his deep tones barely reaching her ears. "I think we should be together. By the way, my real name isn't Louis... it's Brombromlagwe."

Rita could barely hear the words, nor did she care to. She was completely paralyzed not by the kiss or his muffled, deep voice, but by the overwhelming wave of stench that erupted with every quiet syllable.

It tasted metallic, sour, and heavy, like something rotting deep within his gut. Beneath those pristine pink lips, his tongue was coated in a thick white layer of bacteria, and the smell was pure, unadulterated halitosis.

Before he could take another step toward her, Rita turned on her heel and sprinted back to her hostel.

The moment she burst into her room, she scrubbed her teeth until her gums bled, used half a bottle of mouthwash, and flossed repeatedly. Still feeling utterly contaminated, she tore open a fresh pack of mints and shoved three into her mouth at once.

When Martha walked in later that evening, she found Rita sitting on her bunk, aggressively chewing through a mountain of mint wrappers.

"What's with all the mints?" Martha asked, raising an eyebrow.

"My crush has terrible mouth odor. And body odor," Rita gagged, holding her chest. "It’s not normal odor, Martha, it’s coming straight from his internal organs! And he kissed me!"

Martha stared at her for a second before bursting into hysterical, breathless laughter.

"Is it not what you wanted?" Martha wheezed, clutching her stomach. "You said you didn't care!"

"Gosh, I feel so dirty!" Rita whined, tossing another mint into her mouth. "He even told me his real name is Brombromlagwe! I couldn't even process it!"

Martha laughed so hard she nearly fell off her stool.

Rita sank back against her pillow, staring blankly at the ceiling. "No wonder all those other girls ran away."

"So..." Martha grinned, wiping a tear from her eye. "Is your love not unconditional anymore?"

"It was never love o!" Rita cried out. "It was just pure foolishness. Omo, I have moved on!"

title: The Girl They Thought Would Never Rise
excerpt: PART TWO: WHAT SHE BUILT IN SILENCE
content:
For seconds neither woman moved.
Meera stood in the doorway with one hand resting on the glass handle.

Nora looked at her from behind the desk.

There was something about seeing a person from your past standing in front of you after so many years. They could look the same and somehow feel like a stranger.

Meera was the first to speak.

“You own this company?”

Nora closed the folder in front of her.

“Yes.”

Meera looked around the office as if the answer might be hiding somewhere.

The large windows overlooked half the city. There were framed designs on the walls shelves filled with packaged products and employees moving quietly outside the glass doors.

This was not the girl Meera remembered.
The girl she remembered had always been in the kitchen. Always carrying something. Always apologizing. Always waiting.

Meera looked back at her.

“How?”

Nora almost smiled.

It was a question.

It took her back years.

How?

She had asked herself the question many times. How was she supposed to survive? How was she supposed to pay rent?
How was she supposed to build anything when she had started with nothing?

The answer had never been one moment.

There were hundreds of them. Most of them nobody had seen. After leaving home Nora worked at the diner during the day. Studied at night. The room above the laundromat became her classroom.

She borrowed books from the library and watched lessons on a secondhand computer whenever she could afford the electricity to charge it.

She studied business. Marketing. Design. Accounting. Customer service. Anything that might help her build a life. She didn't have anyone to explain things to her so she taught herself.

Some nights she was so tired that she would fall asleep with her head on a book. Nights she couldn't sleep at all. Those were usually the nights when memories of home came back.

Priya's birthday. Her fathers silence. Meera's voice. The school she had been forced to leave.

The life she might have had if someone had simply decided that she was worth investing in. Sometimes she cried. Quietly.

She had learned how to cry without making noise.

Every morning she still got up. The diner needed her. The rent was due. Nobody was coming to save her.

She had eventually learned that the hardest part of being alone wasn't having nobody to hold your hand.

It was having nobody to tell you that you were doing okay. So she learned to tell herself.

“You're doing okay Nora.”

When she wasn't sure she believed it.

The first course she paid for was supposed to help her get into the design industry.

She saved for months.

Every week she put money aside and refused to touch it. When she finally had enough she enrolled. The course was nothing like she had expected.

The lessons were rushed. The materials were incomplete. Whenever she asked questions the instructor acted as though she was wasting his time.

Still Nora kept attending. She needed that certificate. She needed something she could put on a résumé.

When the course ended she realized she had learned little. When she complained the instructor told her she had misunderstood what she was paying for.

Nora knew she hadn't. Knowing she had been cheated didn't give her the money back.

She walked home that evening with the envelope containing what remained of her savings pressed tightly inside her bag.

When she got to her room she emptied the money onto the mattress. Counted it.

Then she counted it again. She sat there for a time. She could have cried. Instead she pulled out her notebook. On a page she wrote:

What did this teach me?

She stared at the question. Eventually she wrote:

Don't pay for promises. Pay for proof.

She closed the notebook. It wasn't the lesson she wanted. It was one she would never forget.

A year later Nora found a job helping a small clothing business manage its orders. It wasn't much. She was grateful.

The owner told her she would be paid at the end of every week. For the few weeks Nora worked harder than anyone had asked her to.

She wrote product descriptions. Answered customers. Organized orders. Took photographs. Updated the business page. Sometimes she stayed until midnight because she wanted the business to succeed.

It did.

Orders started coming in. Customers returned. The owner seemed pleased. Then payday came. Nothing. Nora waited. The following week came. Still nothing. She called. No answer. She sent messages. No response.

Eventually she went to the shop. The shutters were down. She called again. This time the owner answered.

“I'll pay you when things improve, " he said.

Nora stared at the shop.

“You told me you'd pay me every week.”

“I know.”

“. I've done all the work.”

“I said I'll pay you.”

The call ended. He never did.

Nora walked home angry enough to cry. The money he owed her wasn't a fortune to him. To her it was rent. Food. Electricity. A little breathing room.

That night she sat on the floor beside her mattress and cried. Not because she was weak.

Because she was tired of having to fight for things other people received without thinking.

In the morning she went back to work at the diner. She couldn't afford to stay in bed and be angry.

Bills didn't care that she had been cheated. Hunger didn't care that she was heartbroken.

So she kept moving. The rejections came too. Nora applied for design jobs at agencies and larger companies. She sent applications until she could predict the rejection emails before opening them. Some companies responded. Most didn't.

During one interview a man looked through her portfolio. Asked where she had trained.

“I taught myself, " Nora said.

He looked up.

“Do you have anyone in the industry who can recommend you?”

“No.”

“Any connections?”

Nora shook her head.

He gave her a smile.

“We'll get back to you.”

They didn't.

A week later she found out someone else's had gotten the position.

It hurt.

After a while Nora stopped asking why life wasn't fair. Fairness wasn't going to pay her rent. She needed something. She needed a way forward.

So she started with what she had. A small table. A secondhand computer. A few design tools. The skills she had picked up along the way.

Her first products were simple. Handmade journals. Gift boxes. Small accessories. Custom packaging.

Nothing that looked impressive from the outside. She made them in the room above the laundromat. She took photographs beside the window because that was where the light was best.

Then she posted them online. For two days nothing happened. Nobody ordered. Nobody even asked a question.

On third day a woman bought a journal. Nora stared at the payment notification. She checked it twice. Then a third time.

It was real.

Someone had actually paid for something she had made. She smiled. It wasn't an amount of money. It felt huge to her.

She wrapped the journal carefully in paper and tied it with the nicest ribbon she had.

That month she barely made a profit. After buying materials and paying for deliveries almost everything was gone.

The second month was better.

The third month was better, than the past two months. Then someone asked her to make gift boxes for an office event. Nora agreed before she had figured out how she was going to make them.

She spent most of the night working. The order wasn't perfect. One box was the size.Several labels had to be redone.

The customer loved them. They recommended her to someone else. That was how it started. One customer. Then another. Then another.

Nora learned as she went. She learned that making something beautiful wasn't enough. She had to know how much it cost.

She had to know how much to charge. She had to keep records. She had to deal with suppliers. She had to answer customers without losing her temper.

She made mistakes. A few of them cost her money. One time she sent an order to the wrong address.

Another time a supplier delivered the materials and Nora had to replace everything herself.

There were weeks when she wondered whether she was making progress at all. She kept going. The business slowly grew.

First it was Nora.

Then she hired one person to help with packaging. Later, another person joined.

She moved from the room above the laundromat into a workspace behind a printing shop.

It wasn't beautiful. The walls needed painting. The roof leaked whenever it rained.

The first time Nora unlocked the door in the morning and realized the place was hers she stood there smiling.

She had a business.

A real one.

She registered the company. Spent an entire evening trying to decide what to call it.
Eventually, she chose one

Still Rising.

When someone asked why she simply said, "It reminds me to keep going.”

She didn't tell them about the bus station. She didn't tell them about the notebook. She didn't tell them about the girl who had once believed she would never become anything.

That part of her life belonged to her.

Rising grew slowly. Then it grew quickly. People began recommending Nora's work. A few businesses started placing orders.

Someone wrote about her products online. Another customer shared her work. Nora hired people. For the time she had employees depending on her. It scared her.

She remembered what it felt like to depend on people who didn't care whether she succeeded. She promised herself she would never make her employees feel that way.

Then came Daniel. He joined the company when it was still small. He was good with clients. Understood the business. Importantly he believed in Nora.

At least she thought he did.

He had seen the company when it had a handful of orders and a lot of uncertainty. He had seen Nora working late. He had seen her struggle.

So when Daniel told her "One day people are going to know your name " she believed him. She trusted him. That trust would cost her.

The biggest opportunity Still Rising had ever received came from a luxury hotel group.

They wanted a company to handle custom gift packages and branded products for several of their properties.

It was the kind of contract that could change everything. Nora spent weeks preparing. She worked on designs until two in the morning. She revised proposals. She made samples. She attended meetings.

Daniel helped manage the account.

When the client finally said they wanted to move Nora sat in her office after the meeting and stared at the email.

She read it again. Then she laughed. Not loudly. Just a small disbelieving laugh. They had made it. Not completely.

Enough to know that they were going somewhere. A day later Daniel stopped answering his phone. Then the client stopped responding.

Nora became worried. She sent emails. Nothing. She called. Nothing. Then one morning she saw a photograph online.

Her stomach dropped. The same designs. The same presentation. The same concept she and her team had spent months creating.

But the company listed underneath wasn't Still Rising. It was Daniels' company. Nora sat still. She called him. This time he answered.

“How could you do this?”

There was a pause.

Then Daniel said, "It's business, Nora.”

“You took my work.”

“I improved it.”

“You took my client.”

“You weren't moving enough.”

Nora could barely speak.

“You knew how much this meant to me.”

“I knew how much it meant to the company.”

The call ended.

Nora put the phone down. For minutes she just stared at the wall. Then the cancellations started. Two clients left. Then another.

A few employees followed Daniel. The money began disappearing when it came in.

For the time since she had left home Nora wondered if she had finally reached the end of what she could survive.

That evening she stayed in the office long after everyone had gone. The building was quiet. The machines were off. The lights above her desk buzzed softly.

Nora opened the company's account. The numbers were frightening. She opened her email. More cancellations. Then she opened her notebook. The old one.

The one she had carried from home. The cover was bent now. Some pages were stained. She turned through it until she found the sentence she had written years ago.

This is not where my story ends.

Nora stared at it.

She remembered the bus station. The cold bench. The flickering light. The bag against her chest.

She remembered being eighteen and having no idea what would happen next. That girl had been scared too. She had still walked into the diner.

She had still taken the job.

She had still bought the notebook.

She had still tried.

Nora wiped her face.

“You didn't come this far to stop now " she whispered.

In the morning she called her lawyer. Then she called the people who had stayed. They rebuilt. It wasn't quick. It wasn't easy.

Slowly the company began recovering. Nora became more careful. She stopped trusting people simply because they said the things. She learned to put agreements in writing. She learned to protect her work.

Importantly she stopped being afraid of starting again. Then, months later, something happened that Nora wasn't prepared for.

A major lifestyle company discovered, Still Rising.

They had seen one of her products at an event. They wanted to meet. Nora thought it was a mistake at first. She checked the email three times.

It wasn't.

They wanted to discuss a partnership. For the time in years Nora allowed herself to hope without immediately telling herself to be careful.

The meeting went well.

Very well.

A week later the partnership was confirmed. Orders came in faster than Nora could process them. People who had never heard of Still Rising were suddenly talking about it.

Her team celebrated.

Nora stood quietly in the middle of the office. Watched everything happening around her. She thought about the girl above the laundromat. The girl who had sold one notebook. The girl who had once counted coins before buying food.

She wished she could go back and tell her:

Keep going.

That night Nora stayed late. She was about to leave when her phone rang. An unfamiliar number. She almost ignored it. Instead she answered.

“Hello?”

There was silence.

Then a mans voice came through.

“Nora?”

Her heart stopped. She knew that voice. She hadn't heard it in years. Her fathers voice. Nora sat slowly in her chair.

“Where did you get this number?" she asked.

“I saw your name in the newspaper.”

She said nothing.

“I saw what you've built.”

Still Nora said nothing.

Her father cleared his throat.

“I wanted to call.”

Nora looked around her office.

At the company name on the glass wall.

STILL RISING.

At the people who now depended on the thing she had built. At the life she had created without him.

“I don't know what to say " her father admitted.

Nora looked down at her mothers ring hanging around her neck. There had been a time when she would have given anything to hear those words from him.

A time when she would have waited by the phone. A time when one call from her father could have made her feel chosen.

That girl was gone.

“I just wanted to know how you are " he said.

Nora took a breath.

“I’m fine.”

Another silence.

Then he asked the question she had never expected to hear.

“Can we meet?”

Nora looked toward the window.

The city lights stretched across the darkness. For years she had imagined what it would feel like to stand in front of her father after becoming successful.

She had imagined proving him wrong. She had imagined him regretting everything. Now the moment had finally come.

Strangely she wasn't sure she wanted it anymore.

“I'll think about it, " she said.

Her father exhaled.

“I understand.”

The call ended.

Nora remained in her chair. She didn't cry. She didn't smile. She simply sat there staring at the phone. Because for the time she realized something.

Her father had finally come looking for her. She wasn't the girl who had been waiting anymore.

Nora had no idea what would happen when she finally opened that door.

title:
Breaking news!!!
Tragic Fire Engulfs Calabar SPAR Mall as Traders Watch Fortunes Go Up in Flames
excerpt: In a heartbreaking incident that has left the city of Calabar in shock, the popular SPAR Mall (also referred to as Calabar Mall) was engulfed by a devastating f…
content:
In a heartbreaking incident that has left the city of Calabar in shock, the popular SPAR Mall (also referred to as Calabar Mall) was engulfed by a devastating fire in the early hours of Saturday, August 22, 2026.

The blaze reportedly started inside a section of the shopping complex that houses several businesses, including a pharmacy, clothing store, perfumery, and phone shop. The mall, widely regarded as the main (and for many, the only major) modern shopping destination in Calabar, Cross River State, also anchors the multinational SPAR supermarket chain alongside other outlets. What began in one wing quickly spread from shop to shop, overwhelming the mall’s internal fire hydrant system and leaving firefighters struggling to contain the flames.

Eyewitness accounts and circulating videos paint a painful picture, distressed shop owners and traders stood outside, some weeping uncontrollably, as their hard earned goods worth millions of naira were reduced to ashes.

Despite the Calabar Fire Service being reportedly just a short drive described by some as a mere three minutes from the mall, initial reports indicated that only one fire service truck was on the scene in the early stages, battling an already spreading blaze. Subsequent footage showed additional firefighters and police personnel arriving to manage the crowd, restore order, and prevent attempted looting by some bystanders. Law enforcement agents worked to clear the area as the flames continued their destructive path.

As of the latest updates, the exact cause of the fire remains unknown, and no official confirmation of casualties has been issued by the Cross River State Government or emergency authorities. The full extent of structural damage and total financial losses is still being assessed, but the human cost is already clear, livelihoods destroyed, years of investment wiped out in hours, and a community left questioning the state of emergency preparedness.

This tragedy has reignited longstanding concerns about infrastructure and emergency response capacity in Calabar and across Nigeria. In a well functioning system with adequate equipment, rapid deployment, functional hydrants, and sufficient fire trucks, such a blaze so close to a fire station might have been contained far more quickly, limiting the scale of destruction. Instead, traders are left wailing over irreplaceable losses while the city watches one of its key commercial hubs burn.

Residents, shop owners, and observers continue to call for thorough investigations into the cause, stronger investment in firefighting resources, and better preventive measures in commercial facilities. For now, the focus remains on bringing the fire fully under control and supporting those whose businesses and dreams have been reduced to smoke and rubble.

The people of Calabar deserve better. This avoidable scale of loss serves as a painful reminder of the urgent need for improved public safety systems.
