title: The Gift of Loving and Being Loved
excerpt: Not all love is romantic, and some of the most important love never is.
content:
Romantic love is beautiful.

It’s loud.

It’s intense.

It’s the one everyone talks about like it’s the main event.

And somehow, every other kind of love becomes background noise.

But I don’t think it should be that way.

Because the friend you call when everything feels off…

the one who somehow makes things lighter without even trying…

the one who listens and makes you feel seen, not judged…

or the one that steps in and makes sense of the chaos when your head is all over the place…

That kind of love?

It’s powerful.

The collection of people like that in your life

honestly beats a love that is only fueled by desire…

or what we now casually call love but is really just lust.

And sometimes, I feel a slight pang of pity.

When someone says, “I’m in a relationship,”

and then slowly disappears into it.

Everything becomes about one person.

One source of warmth.

One source of validation.

One source of companionship.

It sounds sweet at first…

but it’s almost like the blueprint for suffocation.

My friends would probably hear this and come for me immediately,

saying this is coming from someone who has been single since the break of dawn 🤣

But I promise you, it’s not that.

I’m not against having your person.

In fact, I hope everyone experiences that kind of connection.

The one you think about when you close your eyes.

The one that somehow sits behind your heartbeat 🤣

That kind of love is real.

But so is this one.

The quiet, consistent, everyday love

that comes from your people.

The ones you call over the smallest discomfort

and it doesn’t feel weird.

It feels normal.

The ones you share deep, personal things with

without second-guessing yourself.

And yes… the money bags too 🤣

The ones who show up when life is squeezing you,

who make sure you’re good in ways that go beyond words.

Even the ones that call you out of nowhere

and somehow make you feel like the most important person on earth in that moment.

That is love too.

And it’s something we should invest in.

Because at the end of the day,

no one person should have to carry the weight

of being everything to you.

It’s not fair to them.

And it’s not healthy for you.

So yes, fall in love.

Have your person.

But don’t neglect the people

who have been loving you in ways

that didn’t need romance to feel real.

I probably don’t say this enough…

especially since it’s spread across both genders

and guys like to act weird about these things 🤣

But I genuinely love you all.

And I feel privileged

to have access to that kind of love.

title: Rock, Paper, Scissors
excerpt: Sometimes, life doesn't give you the option to choose the perfect move.
content:
Rock.

Paper.

Scissors.

Three simple choices.

You pick one, hoping it beats whatever the other person picked.

Sometimes you win.

Sometimes you lose.

And sometimes, you both pick the same thing and have to start again.

Funny how life works almost the same way.

There are days when you feel like you've figured everything out. You have a plan. You know what you're doing. You make a decision, convinced it is the right one.

Then life throws something completely different at you.

And suddenly, your carefully planned rock meets someone else's paper.

You lose.

Not because you were foolish.

Not because you didn't try hard enough.

You simply made a move that didn't work this time.

And that's one thing nobody really prepares us for: sometimes, the right decision can still produce the wrong outcome.

You can be hardworking and still not get the opportunity.

You can love someone genuinely and still lose them.

You can prepare for something for months and still fail.

You can do everything you know to do and still find yourself staring at a result you didn't expect.

It doesn't always mean you chose badly.

Sometimes, it just means life played scissors when you brought paper.

And perhaps that's why the game doesn't end after one round.

You don't throw your paper on the table, see that you've lost, and decide you'll never play again.

You simply laugh, reset your hand, and try again.

Maybe that's the part we forget.

Losing one round isn't the same as losing the game.

So, if today feels like one of those days where everything you chose seems to have worked against you, take a breath.

Reset.

Pick again.

Rock.

Paper.

Scissors.

Whatever comes next, don't let one bad round convince you that you were never meant to win.

title: The Internet Made Everyone a Creator, Now Everyone Is Tired
excerpt: Nobody warned us that being online would eventually feel like a job.You wake up, check your phone, and before you’ve even brushed your teeth, you’re already con…
content:
Nobody warned us that being online would eventually feel like a job.

You wake up, check your phone, and before you’ve even brushed your teeth, you’re already consuming somebody else’s life.

Then you remember you’re supposed to post too.

Your business needs content.

Your personal page needs content.

Your brand needs content.

And apparently, even your breakfast needs to be content.

So you take the picture.

You record the video.

You write the caption.

You post.

Then you wait.

Why only 47 views?

Maybe I should delete it.

Maybe the picture isn’t good enough.

Maybe I should have used a trending sound.

Maybe I’m not posting enough.

And suddenly, something that was supposed to be fun starts feeling like work.

There was a time when being online was just… being online.

You opened Instagram to see what your friends were doing. You watched a few videos. Maybe you posted a picture once in a while.

Nobody expected you to have a content strategy.

Now?

Everyone is a creator.

You’re expected to have a personal brand. A niche. A content calendar. Good lighting. Good pictures. Good captions. And somehow, you’re supposed to “show up consistently.”

Even when you’re tired.

Even when nothing interesting happened that day.

Even when you’re just trying to survive.

The internet turned ordinary people into brands.

Your hobby can become content. Your morning routine can become content. Your business can become content. Your relationship can become content.

Sometimes, even your struggles become content.

And at first, it felt exciting.

Everyone suddenly had a voice.

You didn’t need a television station, a publishing company or a huge audience to tell your story. You could simply pick up your phone and speak.

But somewhere along the way, creating stopped feeling like creating.

It started feeling like a job.

We have become so obsessed with being visible that we rarely give ourselves permission to disappear for a while.

If you haven’t posted in three days, you start feeling guilty.

If your business page is quiet, you worry that customers will forget you.

If you don’t post your achievements, it almost feels like they didn’t happen.

We’re constantly documenting our lives while barely having time to live them.

And perhaps the strangest part is that the internet never actually said everyone had to become a creator.

We just started believing it did.

You don’t have to turn every experience into a post.

You don’t have to build a personal brand around every part of your life.

You don’t have to be interesting every single day.

Sometimes, you can just exist.

No content.

No strategy.

No perfectly edited video.

Just you, living your life without wondering how it would perform on the internet.

Because maybe the next big thing isn’t creating more.

Maybe it’s learning when to put the phone down.

If you made it to the end, thank you for reading. ❤️

Kindly share this with someone who might enjoy reading it too.

title: 🇳🇬 October 1, 1960: The Day Nigeria Became Her Own
excerpt: Before the coups, before Biafra, there was October 1, 1960.
content:
Imagine waking up in Nigeria in 1960.

The country you knew had spent decades under British colonial rule. Decisions about government, administration and the country’s future had largely been shaped within a colonial system.

Then came October 1, 1960.

Nigeria became an independent nation.

But independence was not simply about lowering one flag and raising another. It was the beginning of a completely new chapter—and one that would eventually lead Nigeria through political crises, military coups and, only seven years later, a devastating civil war.

So, how did Nigeria become independent, and what was the country like on that historic day?

Before Independence

Before 1960, Nigeria was under British colonial rule.

The territory had been brought together under British administration over time, and by the mid-20th century, Nigerian political movements were increasingly demanding greater self-government.

Nigerian politicians and nationalists pushed for greater representation and eventually complete independence.

Among the prominent political figures of the period were Nnamdi Azikiwe, Obafemi Awolowo and Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, who represented different political movements and regions of the country.

Nigeria’s political system had also developed around three major regions: the Northern Region, Western Region and Eastern Region. Each had considerable autonomy, while the federal government at the centre had more limited powers than it would have in later decades.

The road to independence was therefore not simply a single event. It was the result of years of political negotiations, constitutional changes and growing demands for self-government.

🇳🇬 October 1, 1960

Then came the historic day.

On October 1, 1960, Nigeria gained independence from Britain. The United Nations records Nigeria as having attained independence that day, while the Nigerian government formally applied for UN membership on the same date.

The country’s new government operated under a parliamentary system.

Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa became Nigeria’s Prime Minister, while Queen Elizabeth II remained the country’s head of state, represented in Nigeria by a Governor-General.

Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe would later become Governor-General in November 1960.

So although Nigeria was now independent, the country initially remained within the Commonwealth and retained the British monarch as its constitutional head of state.

This is an important detail that is sometimes forgotten when we talk about independence.

Nigeria was sovereign, but it did not immediately become a republic.

That happened three years later.

The Man Who Spoke for the New Nigeria

At the centre of the independence celebrations was Nigeria’s Prime Minister, Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa.

Balewa delivered the country’s independence speech on October 1, 1960. The National Library of Nigeria preserves a photograph of him delivering that historic speech.

His words reflected the hopes of a newly independent country.

Nigeria was entering the international community as a sovereign state, and its leaders wanted the country to establish friendly relationships with other nations while contributing to the development of Africa.

Just six days later, on October 7, 1960, Balewa addressed the United Nations General Assembly in New York as Nigeria’s Prime Minister.

Nigeria was admitted as the 99th member of the United Nations that same day.

In his speech, Balewa emphasized Nigeria’s desire for peaceful relations with other countries and its intention to work with other African nations.

It was a significant moment.

Nigeria was no longer speaking to the world as a British colony.

It was speaking as Nigeria.

What Changed After Independence?

Independence meant that Nigerians could now take control of their own government.

The new constitution established a federal system with elected institutions, including a Prime Minister and Parliament. The three major regions retained substantial powers of their own.

But independence did not magically solve Nigeria’s problems.

The country was incredibly diverse, with different ethnic groups, languages, religions, political interests and regional identities.

The challenge was now clear:

Could all these different groups successfully build one united nation?

For a while, Nigeria continued under civilian democratic rule.

But political tensions increased over the following years.

In 1963, Nigeria took another major constitutional step.

The country became a republic, ending the British monarch’s role as head of state. Nnamdi Azikiwe became Nigeria’s first President.

Nigeria had moved from colony, to independent federation, to republic in just three years.

But Independence Was Only the Beginning

Looking back today, October 1, 1960 can feel like the beginning of modern Nigeria.

And in many ways, it was.

But the optimism of independence would eventually collide with serious political and ethnic tensions.

In January 1966, Nigeria experienced its first military coup.

The country’s political crisis deepened.

In 1967, the Eastern Region declared itself the independent Republic of Biafra, leading to the Nigerian Civil War, which lasted until 1970.

Thousands of lives were lost, and millions of Nigerians were affected by the conflict.

So when we celebrate October 1, we are not simply celebrating a date.

We are remembering the beginning of a journey that has included hope, political struggles, military rule, war, democracy, setbacks and remarkable resilience.

🇳🇬 The Meaning of October 1

On October 1, 1960, Nigeria became independent from Britain.

The British colonial era had ended, and Nigerians took control of their own national government.

The country was still young.

Its leaders had enormous responsibilities ahead of them.

And the people had enormous expectations.

They had inherited a country with enormous cultural diversity, natural resources and human potential.

The question was whether Nigeria could transform that potential into a peaceful and prosperous nation.

More than six decades later, that question is still part of Nigeria’s story.

Because October 1, 1960 wasn’t the end of Nigeria’s history.

title:
Lionel Messi Retires from Argentina National Team
After 20 Years.
excerpt: Lionel Messi has closed one of the most extraordinary chapters in football history. Twenty years after first pulling on the Argentina jersey, the 39 year old an…
content:
Lionel Messi has closed one of the most extraordinary chapters in football history. Twenty years after first pulling on the Argentina jersey, the 39 year old announced on Monday that he is retiring from international duty, following the emotional heartbreak of losing this summer's World Cup final to Spain and, more recently, the passing of his father, Jorge. In a handwritten note shared to Instagram, Messi revealed he had first written the words on July 21st, just two days after that final but it was grief and reflection in the weeks since that made him certain the time had finally come to say goodbye.

What Messi leaves behind is staggering, 125 goals in over 200 caps, a World Cup title in 2022, and Copa América glory in both 2021 and 2024. But beyond the numbers lies the story of a boy from Rosario who carried a nation's hopes through years of heartbreak before finally delivering. He didn't just win trophies for Argentina, he healed a complicated relationship with a country that once doubted him and, in the end, adored him completely.

The tributes have poured in from teammates, CONMEBOL, FIFA, and fans across the globe, with the phrase "Gracias eternas, Leo" eternal thanks, Leo echoing across social media as a nation says farewell to its favorite son. Messi won't disappear from football entirely, he'll continue turning out for Inter Miami, and he's already promised to watch future tournaments from the stands, cheering for the very team he once carried on his back. It's a bittersweet ending, but also a fitting one a champion stepping aside not in defeat, but in peace, leaving the door open for the next generation to carry the torch he lit two decades ago.

title: People feel safe around you when you stop being impressive
excerpt: People don’t actually want impressive people. They want people they can feel safe being imperfect around. Think about who you actually remember, it’s rarely the ones who had it all together. It’s the…
content:
People don’t actually want impressive people.

They want people they can feel safe being imperfect around.

Think about who you actually remember, it’s rarely the ones who had it all together. It’s the ones who made you feel comfortable just being around them.

The moment you start acting like you know it all, like you never make mistakes, you’re not being impressive. You’re just performing perfection.

And pride always shows. People can feel it. Nobody stays fully comfortable around someone who thinks they’re the best at everything.

At first, they’ll admire you. They’ll want to copy what you do, try to move the way you move.

But give it days, weeks, months, and they’ll start pulling away. That's Because you never taught them the basic steps. You just laughed when they got it wrong.

So they go back to the people who make them feel safe being imperfect. People don't stay because you are perfect, they stay when they feel comfortable.

title: 10 opportunities where you can LEARN, BUILD EXPERIENCE and GET PAID 💰
excerpt: Not every opportunity is a job.Some will train you.Some will give you real work experience.Some will fund your research.And some will actually put money in your…
content:
Not every opportunity is a job.

Some will train you.

Some will give you real work experience.

Some will fund your research.

And some will actually put money in your pocket.

I went digging through opportunities that are currently open as of September 9, 2026. Here are 10 worth checking:

1. IAPS AI Policy Fellowship — up to $24,000

Interested in AI, technology, policy, research or governance?

The Institute for AI Policy and Strategy is accepting applications for its 3-month AI Policy Fellowship.

Fellows receive $18,000, while Senior Fellows receive $24,000. There is also additional support for fellows based in Washington, D.C. or London.

📅 Deadline: September 27, 2026

🌍 Remote, London or Washington, D.C.

🔗 Apply: https://www.iaps.ai/fellowship

This is one of the strongest opportunities on this list if you're serious about building a career around AI policy and research.

---

2. Africa's Data Future Fellowship — $1,500

A 3-month remote fellowship focused on Africa's data governance future.

You learn about digital rights, data sharing, digital public infrastructure, data sovereignty and more.

Selected fellows can receive up to US$1,500 after successfully completing the fellowship.

📅 Deadline: September 18, 2026

🌍 African countries

🔗 Apply: https://openopportunities.org/opportunities/2026-africas-data-future-fellowship/

⚠️ This one requires a postgraduate degree and relevant professional engagement, so check eligibility before applying.

---

3. Creative Changemakers Fellowship — monthly stipend

If you're a Nigerian writer, filmmaker, photographer, content creator, spoken-word artist or other creative, pay attention.

The CivicHive fellowship combines training, mentorship, creative labs and hands-on production around civic and social issues.

Fellows receive a monthly stipend, and outstanding fellows can also receive a soft grant.

📅 Deadline: September 15, 2026

🇳🇬 Nigerian creatives

🔗 Apply: https://civichive.org/

This is especially interesting if you want to turn creative work into social impact.

---

4. Iliad AI Safety Fellowship — $6,000/month

This is not your average beginner fellowship.

Iliad is looking for strong researchers in mathematics, physics, theoretical computer science and related fields to work on mathematical approaches to AI safety.

The fellowship provides a $6,000/month travel-and-housing allowance.

📅 Next Fall 2026 cohort deadline: September 21, 2026

📍 London or San Francisco Bay Area

🔗 Apply: https://www.iliad.ac/fellowship

If you're already a serious technical researcher, this is a big one.

---

5. LASR Labs AI Safety Research — £15,000 stipend

Want to work on AI safety research?

LASR Labs runs a 13-week research programme where participants work in small teams with experienced researchers and take projects from proposal through to publication.

The programme provides a £15,000 stipend, plus food, office space and travel support.

📅 Deadline: September 20, 2026

📍 London

🔗 Details: https://www.lasr.org/

This one is aimed at people with strong quantitative/technical ability, so don't apply just because "AI" is in the title.

---

6. Princeton in Africa Fellowship — paid 12-month experience

Want real work experience in Africa, not another certificate?

Princeton in Africa places fellows with organisations across the continent for 12 months.

Fellows receive a living/housing stipend, with packages varying by placement.

📅 Deadline: October 26, 2026

🌍 African continent

🔗 Apply: https://www.princetoninafrica.org/applicants/how-to-apply/

African graduates from locally accredited African universities can apply through the Nexus route.

---

7. KAUST Global Fellowship — $75,000/year

For early-career researchers, this is on another level.

The KAUST Global Fellowship supports independent research in areas including AI, food, water, energy, health and marine science.

Global Fellows receive a $75,000 annual stipend, plus housing, healthcare, relocation and other benefits, alongside research funding.

📅 Application window: October 1, 2026 – January 15, 2027

🌍 International

🔗 Apply: https://kgfp.kaust.edu.sa/fellowship

⚠️ This is primarily for exceptional postdoctoral/early-career researchers—not an entry-level opportunity.

---

8. African Plant Nutrition Outreach Fellowship — $5,000

This one is for African scientists, extension specialists and educators working on agricultural and plant-nutrition challenges.

Selected applicants can receive US$5,000 to support education, training and communication projects around plant nutrition and soil fertility.

📅 Deadline: September 21, 2026

🌍 African countries

🔗 Apply: https://www.apni.net/outreach-fellowship-apply/

Not for students—but potentially excellent for researchers and educators already working in the field.

---

9. Young Africa Innovates — training + incubation + funding pathways

If you're a young Nigerian building a startup, product or solution, look at this.

UNDP and the Mastercard Foundation's Young Africa Innovates programme is currently recruiting innovators aged 18–35 in selected Nigerian states.

You get bootcamp training, technical mentorship, product refinement, business advisory, incubation and exposure to funding and investors.

📍 Abia, Akwa Ibom, Cross River, Katsina, Niger, Plateau & Taraba

📅 Applications open August–September 2026

🔗 Apply: https://www.youngafricainnovates.ng/

This isn't a "salary for attending a course" opportunity. Think learn → build → incubate → access capital.

---

10. Sahara CodeSwitch Africa Challenge — $10,000 prize pool

For the builders.

Sahara is challenging developers, researchers, startups and product teams across Africa to build real-world applications using voice AI that can handle code-switching.

Think education, healthcare, agriculture, fintech, public services and more.

🏆 $10,000 total cash prize pool

📅 Deadline: September 15, 2026

🌍 Africa

🔗 Details & application: https://www.intron.io/compete/

This is particularly interesting if you want to build something real and have a chance of getting paid for it.

Here's the part people miss:

You don't always have to choose between learning and earning.

Sometimes the smarter move is finding opportunities where the two happen at the same time.

A fellowship can give you research experience.

An internship can give you your first serious line on your CV.

A challenge can force you to build something.

A funded programme can introduce you to people who can change your career.

So don't search only for:

"Jobs hiring now."

Search for:

Fellowships.

Paid internships.

Research programmes.

Incubators.

Competitions.

Apprenticeships.

Accelerators.

Your next opportunity might not look like a job.

Save this post. Share it with someone looking for their next opportunity.

And please check the eligibility requirements and deadline on the official application page before submitting anything—the opportunities landscape changes quickly.

title: NOBODY TALKS ABOUT HOW LONELY IT CAN FEEL TO OUTGROW PEOPLE
excerpt: The uncomfortable loneliness of changing priorities, setting boundaries, and realizing some friendships belong to an older version of you.
content:
There is a strange kind of loneliness that comes with becoming a different person. You may still have friends. You still reply to messages, attend birthdays, laugh at jokes and show up when someone needs you but something feels different. The conversations don't hit the same. The things you used to enjoy together no longer excite you. You find yourself explaining choices you never had to explain before and sometimes, you leave a hangout wondering why you felt lonely while surrounded by people.

Nobody necessarily did anything wrong. You just grew and that's the part people don't talk about enough. You can love someone and still outgrow them. Outgrowing someone doesn't mean you stopped loving them. Maybe you used to spend every weekend together, but your priorities have changed. Maybe you once talked for hours about relationships, parties and other people's lives, but now you find yourself wanting conversations about money, career, health, purpose or the future. Maybe you have simply become more protective of your time and peace. That doesn't make your old friend a bad person. It doesn't make you a better person either.

It simply means you're no longer standing in the same place. Some friendships are deeply meaningful without being permanent and accepting that can hurt.

SOMETIMES YOUR PRIORITIES CHANGE BEFORE YOUR FRIENDSHIPS DO

Growth often starts quietly. You begin saying no to things you used to say yes to and you become more serious about your work. You stop spending money just because everyone else is spending. You start caring about your health. You become intentional about where your time goes.

Then someone says:

"You've changed."

Maybe you have.

But change is not automatically betrayal. At the same time, personal growth doesn't give you permission to become arrogant. You can change without judging people who haven't changed in the same direction. Your growth is yours. It doesn't have to become a ranking system.

THE LONELINESS COMES WHEN YOU NO LONGER BELONG WHERE YOU USED TO

This may be the hardest part. There is a period between leaving your old life and finding your new one. You don't quite fit where you used to, but you haven't found your new people yet. So you exist somewhere in the middle. You might sit alone on a Friday night and wonder: "Where did everybody go?" Sometimes nobody went anywhere. You simply stopped meeting each other in the same place. You may miss the friendship without wanting the old version of it back. You miss the inside jokes. The random calls. The familiarity.

But you know returning to that dynamic would not feel right anymore. That's a painful truth.

BOUNDARIES CAN MAKE YOU FEEL LIKE THE DIFFICULT ONE

When you start protecting your time, some people will interpret it as rejection. When you stop tolerating disrespect, you're "too sensitive." When you stop being constantly available, you're "distant. "When you say no, you're suddenly "different." And if you have always been the person who keeps everyone happy, boundaries can feel like guilt. But boundaries are not supposed to punish people.

They're supposed to create clarity.

You can care about someone and still say:

"I can't do that."

"That doesn't work for me anymore."

"I need some time to myself."

You don't owe everyone unlimited access to you just because they had it before.

NOT EVERYONE IS SUPPOSED TO COME WITH YOU

We love the idea that the right people will grow with us. Sometimes they do. Sometimes they don't. You may become more ambitious while your friend wants a quieter life. You may become more private while they love being constantly social. You may develop completely different priorities. Different doesn't automatically mean incompatible. But sometimes the differences become too significant to ignore. You don't have to make a dramatic announcement. You don't have to turn them into a villain. Sometimes the relationship simply becomes less frequent, less intimate or eventually ends. And that's okay. You can say, "We became different people," without saying, "You were holding me back."

DON'T USE "GROWTH" TO AVOID ACCOUNTABILITY

This matters too. Not every friendship you struggle with is a friendship you've outgrown. Sometimes you are avoiding a difficult conversation. Sometimes you are using "protecting my peace" as an excuse to avoid accountability. Sometimes you have become so focused on improving yourself that you have forgotten how to show up for others. Growth should make you more self aware, not self important. You don't need everyone around you to become like you. Your friend can have different ambitions, interests and priorities and still be a good friend. Sometimes what needs to change is not the friendship. It's your expectation of what the friendship should look like.

SO WHAT DO YOU DO WITH THE LONELINESS?

First, do not run back simply because you are lonely. Familiarity can make unhealthy relationships look comforting. Allow yourself to grieve what changed. Friendship breakups deserve grief too. You lost routines, memories and someone who once occupied a particular place in your life. Then make room for new connections. Join something. Start conversations. Reconnect with people you naturally click with. Be willing to be the new person somewhere. Because sometimes the loneliness is not proof that you made the wrong decision. It's simply the space between who you were and who you're becoming.

And yes, some nights will still feel lonely. You may miss old conversations. You may scroll through pictures and wonder when everything changed but don't abandon yourself just to feel included again. Not every person you lose is a loss and not everyone you miss needs to come back. Sometimes growing up means accepting that someone can have been important to your life without being meant to remain in every chapter of it. That doesn't erase what you shared. It simply means the story changed.

And sometimes, becoming someone new requires learning how to be comfortable with the silence that comes before you find people who understand who you've become.

Have you been in this situation before? What was your experience like? Share your thoughts in the comment.

title: Why Erling Haaland’s Movement Off the Ball Matters More Than His Goals
Olu Jacobs: The Lion of Lufodo Takes His Final Bow
excerpt: For generations of Nigerians, Olu Jacobs was more than an actor. He was a familiar presence on their screens, a commanding voice, a distinguished face, and the …
content:
For generations of Nigerians, Olu Jacobs was more than an actor. He was a familiar presence on their screens, a commanding voice, a distinguished face, and the man who was the perfect actor for the role of a King.

Today, that voice has gone silent.

Veteran Nigerian actor Oludotun Baiyewu Jacobs, popularly known as Olu Jacobs, has died at the age of 84. His family announced his death on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, bringing to an end a remarkable acting career that spanned more than five decades.

His family described him as “The Lion of Lufodo”.

But who was the man behind the legendary voice and unforgettable characters?

Born on July 11, 1942, Jacobs spent part of his childhood in Kano. His interest in acting grew after he watched one of Chief Hubert Ogunde’s travelling theatre productions.

He eventually travelled to Britain, where he trained at the prestigious Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (RADA) in London.

Before becoming one of Nollywood’s most recognizable faces, Jacobs had already built an international acting career, appeared in British television productions and worked in theatre, while also taking roles in international films including The Dogs of War and Pirates.

When Jacobs returned to Nigeria, he became one of the defining actors of the country’s film industry.

He appeared in more than 100 Nigerian films and became particularly associated with roles that demanded presence and authority. Kings, fathers, chiefs, politicians and elders were among the characters he brought to life.

His voice alone could make an ordinary line sound like a decree, but Jacobs’ contribution to Nigerian entertainment did not stop at acting.

Together with his wife, actress Joke Silva, he co-founded the Lufodo Group, which became involved in film production, distribution and the development of performing arts. The couple also established the Lufodo Academy of Performing Arts.

In 2011, he received the Nigerian national honor of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic (MFR) for his contribution to the arts.

Jacobs’ later years were marked by declining health and a gradual retreat from the public eye.

In 2021, Joke Silva revealed that her husband had been living with Lewy body dementia, after years of public speculation and false reports about his health.

However, his family has not stated a cause of death and have asked for the public to respect their privacy. What has been confirmed is that Jacobs died on September 16, 2026, at the age of 84.

After more than five decades in the profession, one of Nigeria’s most recognizable actors has taken his final bow.

The Lion of Lufodo has left the stage. He will be greatly missed!!

title: Before I Was Forgotten
excerpt: She spent twenty-three years making sure everyone else's plate was full. Nobody checked if hers was.
content:
Chapter One

The Empty Kitchen

Zainab stood over the pot of egusi, stirring long after it needed stirring.

She did that sometimes.

Let her hands continue with something when her mind had nowhere else to go.

The house was quiet in a way that still surprised her, even after all these years of slowly becoming this way.

Not the peaceful kind of quiet.

The kind that used to be full.

Full of Halima's laughter carrying from the sitting room. Full of Yusuf arguing with his brother over the remote. Full of Ahmad's voice calling from the study to ask if dinner was ready yet, as though he could smell it from three rooms away.

Tonight, there was only the soft scrape of the ladle against the bottom of the pot.

Zainab lowered the flame.

She had made enough for five.

There would be two.

Ahmad had called at half past six to say he would be late.

A client dinner.

Nothing urgent.

Don't wait up.

He had said it kindly, the way he said most things to her now. Kindly and from a distance, like a man speaking to someone he respected but no longer quite knew.

Halima was at her fiancé's family house again, helping with wedding preparations. Something about fabrics that couldn't wait until morning.

Yusuf hadn't called at all.

These days, that was its own kind of answer.

Zainab turned off the cooker and covered the pot.

She looked at the dining table.

Eight chairs.

She had bought it when the children were still young enough to fight over who sat where.

She could still remember Yusuf dragging one chair closer to the television because he wanted to see the screen while he ate.

She could remember Halima complaining that he was blocking her view.

She could remember Ahmad laughing at both of them.

Now, most evenings, the table held more chairs than people.

She went to the kitchen sink and washed her hands.

Then she returned and set two plates.

She paused.

After a moment, she took one away.

There was no reason to set Ahmad's plate when he had already said not to wait.

She served herself.

The food was good.

She knew it was.

She had made it herself.

Zainab sat at the table and whispered, “Bismillah.”

The first few mouthfuls were quiet.

Halfway through the meal, she looked up.

Her reflection stared back at her from the dark window.

She had not noticed the grey at her temples until recently.

There was more of it now.

She touched the side of her face without thinking.

Then she lowered her hand.

She looked away.

Her phone was beside her plate.

She checked it.

Nothing.

She opened the family group.

There were messages from earlier.

Halima had sent pictures of fabric.

Yusuf had reacted with a laughing emoji.

Someone had asked whether the tailor had finished the outfits.

Zainab scrolled through them slowly.

She had not said anything.

She typed:

Beautiful.

Then deleted it.

She put the phone down.

The egusi was getting cold.

She ate anyway.

After dinner, she carried the plate to the sink.

She washed it.

Dried it.

Put it away.

Then she wiped the table, even though there were only a few crumbs on it.

She had always done that.

There was something comforting about returning things to their proper place.

She wiped the chair where she had been sitting.

Then the chair beside it.

She stopped.

She looked at the empty seat.

For a moment, she could almost hear Halima saying, Mummy, give me meat.

Zainab smiled before she realized she was smiling.

The smile disappeared.

She picked up the cloth.

By the time she finished cleaning the kitchen, it was almost nine.

She switched off the light and walked towards the sitting room.

Then she turned back.

She had forgotten the pot.

She checked it.

Covered.

Fine.

She laughed softly at herself.

“Old woman,” she murmured.

The words sounded strange in her own voice.

She went upstairs.

Ahmad wasn't in the bedroom.

His side of the wardrobe was still half-open.

His slippers were beneath the chair.

His Qur'an rested on the bedside table.

Everything about him was familiar.

Everything about the room was familiar.

Zainab changed into her nightdress and sat before the mirror to remove her earrings.

She had worn them all day.

She couldn't remember when she had stopped dressing for herself.

She couldn't remember if she had ever started.

She placed the earrings in their little dish.

One.

Then the other.

She looked at her reflection again.

Not old.

Not sick.

Not unhappy, exactly.

Just tired in a place sleep couldn't reach.

She turned off the light.

Ahmad came home sometime after eleven.

She heard the front door downstairs.

His footsteps.

The bathroom tap.

The wardrobe opening.

She kept her eyes closed.

A few minutes later, the mattress shifted.

He got into bed carefully so he wouldn't wake her.

“Zainab?”

She didn't answer.

He waited.

Then he whispered, “You sleeping?”

She opened her eyes.

“Yes.”

“Oh.”

Silence.

She could hear him breathing beside her.

After a while, his hand rested briefly against her shoulder.

A small touch.

Familiar.

Almost automatic.

Then he turned away.

Zainab remained awake.

She stared into the darkness and realized she had been so good at being needed, she no longer remembered the last time anyone wondered where she was.

She didn't yet know that in a box at the back of her wardrobe, wrapped in an old wrapper she hadn't worn in decades, a twenty-three-year-old version of herself was still waiting to be found.

Author's Note: Thank you so much for reading Chapter One of Before I Was Forgotten.

Zainab's quiet isolation is a reality many mothers and wives experience but rarely speak about.

Have you ever witnessed someone you love like a mother or aunt slip into this quiet, background role?

Let me know your thoughts in the comments below.

Your feedback means the world to me.

Make sure to hit the Follow button on my profile right now so you don't miss Chapter Two when Zainab finally opens that box!

title: A stupid mistake
excerpt: One thing is for sure, I’m never trying that shit again
content:
We had been walking in this desert for hours and very tired. Oyin had lost her shoes and her feet cut. Kunle had lost his will and his hope waned. How we got into this, I barely remember.

‎I only get flashes of the accident. I was driving on the long highway. Death valley, Texas, they called it. I saw a squirrel and tried to avoid hitting it. A couple of minutes later, we were deep into the desert, how we survived that tumbling was a mystery. We managed to pry ourselves out of the crumbled vehicle and we kept walking.

‎For whatever reason we just keep walking. We didn't slow down. It's felt like days now. The sun never stopped shining, our energy waned, no food or water but we kept walking.

‎Then suddenly we saw a village in front of us. I knew we were saved.

‎”Thank the gods” Oyin said as we tried to pick up the pace but the longer we walked, the farther the village seems.

“What the hell is going on” Kunle said

“Oh geez, I think we are having a shared hallucination. We never should have drank the cactus juice”

“No fool, you shouldn’t have gone to that rave or taken the damn drugs!” I heard my mum’s voice

I turned around and saw a man…..,doctor standing over me with a clipboard in his hand. I was on an hospital bed, and I’m pretty sure it wasn’t as a result of an accident.

“Last night was wild, huh” the doctor said with a smirk on his face

I couldn’t say a word, but I damn sure won’t truly drugs again. What a stupid mistake that was.

 

Note: Not AI generated

title: What Actually Happens When You Ask ChatGPT a Question?
excerpt: A simple question goes in. What happens inside the machine before an answer comes back?
content:
What Actually Happens When You Ask ChatGPT a Question?

You type a sentence.

A few seconds later, an answer appears.

It feels like you’re talking to something that knows what you’re asking.

But here’s the strange part:

ChatGPT doesn’t read your question the way you do.

It doesn’t sit there thinking, “Okay, Ezekiel wants to know why the sky is blue. Let me remember the answer.”

Something much more interesting is happening.

Your sentence first gets broken down into small pieces called tokens.

Those tokens are converted into numbers that a neural network can process. Your words aren’t being treated as little dictionary entries sitting inside a computer. They’re represented mathematically, allowing the model to detect relationships between words and the context surrounding them.

Then comes the part that makes ChatGPT feel almost magical.

The model looks at the context of your prompt and calculates what should come next.

Then the next piece.

Then the next.

And the next.

One prediction at a time.

That’s why when you ask:

“Why do I feel tired after sleeping for eight hours?”

the model isn’t pulling a finished paragraph from a hidden folder labelled Tired After Sleep.

It’s generating a response based on patterns it learned during training and the context of your conversation.

And this is where things get really interesting.

ChatGPT doesn’t actually “know” that you’re right.

It can produce an incredibly convincing explanation while still being wrong.

That’s because producing a fluent answer and verifying that answer are two different problems.

A model can be extremely good at predicting what a useful-sounding answer looks like without having the same relationship with truth that a human researcher does.

Think about that for a second.

The machine can sound certain without being certain.

That’s one of the most important things to understand about generative AI.

The impressive part isn’t simply that ChatGPT can write an essay in seconds.

It’s that we’ve built systems capable of turning mathematical patterns learned from enormous amounts of data into something that feels like a conversation.

And we’re still figuring out what that actually means.

Because the more natural these systems become, the easier it is to forget that underneath the conversation is mathematics, probability, computation and an astonishing amount of training.

So the next time you ask ChatGPT a question and get an answer in two seconds, remember:

It didn’t open a book.

It didn’t “think” like you do.

It predicted its way into an answer.

And somehow, that is only the beginning.

title: Someone Asked to Use My Hotspot. Could Their Crime Come Back to Me?
excerpt: Most times being too good can become your nightmare.
content:
Imagine you're sitting at a mall.

Someone walks up to you.

“Please, can I use your hotspot? I don't have data.”

You probably wouldn't think much of it.

Maybe you'll say yes.

Maybe you'll say no.

But here's the question I want you to think about:

If that person uses your hotspot to do something illegal, whose internet connection does it look like they were using?

Yours.

And suddenly, that harmless little favour becomes a cybersecurity question.

Your hotspot isn't just sharing data

When you turn on your hotspot, you're essentially allowing another device to use your phone's internet connection.

Their phone connects to yours.

Your phone connects to your mobile network.

And when they browse the internet, the websites and services they access may see the public IP address associated with your internet connection.

That's where the confusion begins.

Because your IP address is often described as your device's "address on the internet."

That's a useful way to understand the concept, but it isn't your digital identity.

An IP address can tell a service where a connection appears to be coming from.

It doesn't automatically tell them:

“This specific person committed this specific action.”

That's an important distinction.

So, can someone commit a cybercrime using your hotspot?

Yes, they can use your connection to access the internet.

And if they do something malicious, their traffic could initially appear to come through the same public IP address you're using.

But that doesn't mean you automatically become responsible for their actions.

An investigation wouldn't necessarily stop at an IP address.

Depending on the situation, investigators could look at other evidence such as account activity, device information, timestamps, service-provider records, authentication logs and other digital evidence.

So the viral advice that:

“If someone commits a cybercrime on your hotspot, it's you that committed the crime.”

is far too simplistic.

But there's still a lesson worth taking seriously.

You're giving someone access to your connection

This is the part we shouldn't overlook.

When you share your hotspot, you're allowing another device to use your internet connection.

You may not know what they're doing with it.

You may not know what they're downloading.

You may not know what websites or services they're accessing.

And you definitely shouldn't assume that everyone who asks for your hotspot has harmless intentions.

This doesn't mean you should start treating everyone who asks for data like a cybercriminal.

It simply means:

Be conscious of what you're sharing.

There's another thing people rarely think about

Your hotspot also has a password.

And if you're constantly sharing that password with different people, there's a simple question worth asking:

Who still knows it?

Maybe you gave it to a friend last month.

Then your cousin.

Then someone at work.

Then someone else asked for it yesterday.

At some point, you may not even remember who has access.

That's why changing your hotspot password occasionally isn't a bad habit.

And when you don't need your hotspot?

Turn it off.

Simple.

But here's where I disagree with the viral post

We shouldn't be scared into cybersecurity.

The internet is already complicated enough without turning every small action into a disaster story.

Someone using your hotspot doesn't automatically mean they're going to frame you for a cybercrime.

Your IP address isn't a magic fingerprint that proves who was holding the phone.

And you don't need to stop helping people because someone on the internet told you that “anything they do becomes your crime.”

That's not how digital investigations work.

But you should understand what you're actually sharing.

Because cybersecurity isn't only about hackers breaking into computers.

Sometimes it's simply about understanding what happens when you press:

“Turn on hotspot.”

So, should you share your hotspot?

You can.

Just share wisely.

Use a strong hotspot password.

Don't leave the hotspot open unnecessarily.

Turn it off when you're done.

And if you don't know or trust the person asking, it's perfectly okay to say no.

Because being helpful online doesn't mean you have to be careless.

The next time someone asks, “Please, can I use your hotspot?”

You don't have to panic.

But maybe take a second to think about what you're actually giving them access to.

title: HOW TO KNOW WHEN STRESS IS  NO LONGER "JUST STRESS"
excerpt:
You tell people you are  "just stressed" the same way you tell them you are "fine."
It's the answer that ends the conversation, not the one that's true.
content:
Most times you just want to end the conversation and avoid saying the truth.You have said it in the group chat. You have said it to your mother when she asked why your voice sounds different. You have said it to yourself, lying awake at 1 a.m. doing math you didn't ask your brain to do, your rent, that email you haven't replied to, why your chest feels tight for no reason. I'm just stressed. It's the most dangerous sentence in your vocabulary, because it's the one that lets you keep going without ever asking what's actually happening to you.

Here's the truth nobody tells you, stress has a job. It's supposed to spike, help you handle the thing in front of you, then leave. What you're describing, the version that doesn't leave, that's been living in your shoulders for eight months, is not stress doing its job anymore. It's your body sending a different message entirely, and you've been translating it wrong.

THE SIGNS YOUR BODY SENDS BEFORE YOU "BURN OUT"

Burnout doesn't announce itself. It arrives disguised as small, forgivable things. You put the milk in the cupboard. You reread the same paragraph four times and retain none of it. You say "I'm fine" to your partner in a tone that makes them ask if you're actually fine. None of these feel like a crisis on their own, that's exactly why they are dangerous. You are not falling apart in one dramatic moment; you're leaking, quietly, one forgotten name and one skipped meal at a time.

AM I THE ONLY ONE WHO FEELS LIKE THIS?

You're not, and that's not a comforting cliché, it's the part nobody says out loud because everyone's too busy performing "handling it." Your colleague who always seems composed has cried in her car in the office parking lot.

That friend who posts the productive morning routine has also lain on his bathroom floor at 11 p.m. because getting up felt like too much. Normal stress doesn't make you Google "why do I feel like crying for no reason" at your desk. If you're here, reading this, you already know which category you're in.

IS IT NORMAL TO SNAP, FORGET, OR FEEL NUMB?

Occasionally, yes. Constantly, no, and the difference is duration, not intensity. It's normal to snap at your partner once during a brutal week. It's not normal when snapping becomes your default setting and you don't recognize your own tone anymore. It's normal to forget a name under pressure. It's not normal to walk into a room and forget why, three times in one day. And feeling numb, not sad, not angry, just flat, like you're watching your own life through glass is one of the quietest signs, because it doesn't look like suffering. It looks like coping. It isn't.

HOW TO TELL THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN STRESS AND SOMETHING DEEPER

Ask yourself one question: does it end? Real stress has an off switch, the deadline passes, the exam ends, and your body comes back down. What you might be dealing with doesn't come back down. You finish the project and you're still tight in the chest. You get through the week and Monday still arrives with dread instead of relief. That persistence, not the intensity of any single bad day, is the actual signal. Stress is a reaction to something. What you're describing has started reacting to nothing, on its own schedule, without your permission.

WHY "I'M JUST STRESSED" KEEPS YOU STUCK Here's what nobody tells you, minimizing it is not resilience, it's avoidance wearing resilience's clothes. Every time you say "just stressed," you give yourself permission to skip the harder, more honest question, why has this been going on for so long, and why haven't I told anyone the real number of weeks? Naming it accurately is not dramatic. It's the only thing that actually gets you help instead of more coping mechanisms stacked on top of the original problem.

WHAT TO DO ONCE YOU NOTICE THE SHIFT You don't need a full breakdown to justify getting support, that's the trap. Waiting for it to get "bad enough" is how people end up in the parking-lot-crying stage before they say anything to anyone. The move is smaller and less dramatic than you think. Tell one person the real version, not the "I'm fine" version. Ask a doctor to check the physical side, sleep, hormones, thyroid because chronic stress mimics and masks other things. And stop measuring whether you deserve help by comparing your life to someone who "has it worse." You don't need permission to take this seriously. You just need to stop calling it something smaller than it is.

title: Chasing Validation
excerpt: Sometimes, the things we run from have a way of finding us in another form.
content:
The game we played changed something between us.

I really don't know all he had in mind, but I was grateful I didn't succumb to all the requests disguised as dares.

And yes, it changed a lot.

I lost the vibe.

The excitement that came with chatting with strangers disappeared. I wasn't interested in meeting new stranger friends anymore, and I promised myself I would never play such a game again.

I wasn't interested in any conversation that would lead me into doing something against my own wish.

So, I decided to just have fun.

I started chasing something else—validation.

Likes.

Comments.

Friend requests.

Back then, I didn't have my own phone, so I still used my mum's phone whenever I had the chance.

The moment she handed it to me or left it with me for a while, I'd quickly log into Facebook.

I'd dress up, go behind the curtain where the lighting was just right, and take those trendy pictures everyone seemed to be posting back then.

I'd upload one, close the app, then open it again a few minutes later.

One new like.

Three comments.

Five friend requests.

I can't even explain the excitement.

It made me feel seen.

It made me feel like I mattered.

Whenever my pictures got the attention I wanted, my day felt complete.

But whenever they didn't...

I found myself checking again and again, hoping the numbers would somehow change.

Maybe people hadn't seen it yet.

Maybe Facebook didn't show it to enough people.

Maybe...

Without realizing it, those little numbers had started deciding how I felt about myself.

I told myself I was just having fun.

I didn't know I was slowly measuring my worth with likes, comments and friend requests.

And the scary part?

It didn't even feel like a problem.

It felt normal.

To be continued...

title: A Dive Into Baby Mama/Baby Daddy Culture
excerpt: As having children across multiple relationships becomes increasingly common, are we creating family trees so tangled that future generations may struggle to know who they’re connected to?
content:
What Happens When Everybody Has Everybody’s Children?

I’ve been thinking about something lately, and I’m not sure if I’m the only person who has ever thought about it.

What happens to family trees when everybody starts having children with everybody?

Before you misunderstand me, this isn’t an argument against single mothers, single fathers, divorcees, or people who have children outside marriage. Life happens. Relationships fail. People move on. People make different choices.

I’m thinking about something much further down the line.

Something that might not even concern us, but could concern the generations after us.

Let’s say I have a child with Paul.

Paul and I don’t work out.

I move on and meet Charles. I have another child with Charles. That relationship ends too. I meet Emmanuel and have another child. Then Samuel, and another child.

Now I have four children by four different men.

Nothing unusual about that anymore.

But Paul also moves on.

He has children with five different women.

Charles has children with other women. Emmanuel does the same. Samuel does the same.

Now imagine that all those children grow up.

They have children.

And their children grow up and have children with other people who also come from increasingly complicated family trees.

At some point, the branches start crossing.

My child could meet Paul’s other child.

They don’t share a surname.

They didn’t grow up together.

They may not even know the other person’s mother.

They meet at university, at work, at a party, online. They like each other. They start dating.

But they share a biological father.

And neither of them knows.

Now take it one generation further.

Maybe they aren’t half-siblings.

Maybe they’re cousins.

Maybe their parents are half-siblings and nobody knows because the connection runs through a parent who had children with several different people.

Suddenly, the person you’re dating isn’t simply “someone from another family.”

They might be connected to your family in a way neither of you knew.

And this is the part that makes me wonder where we’re heading.

Because there was a time when family structures were easier to trace.

You knew your siblings.

You knew your cousins.

Your parents knew their siblings.

Your grandparents knew their children and grandchildren.

Families had their own histories, and those histories were often passed down.

But what happens when one person has children with four people, those four people have children with several others, and those children repeat the same pattern?

The family tree doesn’t just grow.

It spreads.

One person can create biological connections across several different families, communities, cities and even countries.

And then those families continue multiplying.

We talk a lot about the freedom adults have to choose who they love and who they have children with. And they absolutely have that freedom.

But I wonder if we’re thinking enough about the collective consequence of those choices over several generations.

Because eventually, it isn’t just about one man having children with five women.

It’s about those five women having children with other men.

And those men having children with other women.

And everybody’s children eventually meeting other people’s children.

Imagine a future where you’re getting married and somebody says:

“Wait. Your grandfather had a child with my grandmother’s sister.”

Or:

“Your father and my mother have the same father.”

Or:

“Hold on. We’re actually related.”

And you didn’t know.

Imagine discovering that after you’ve already fallen in love.

Or after you’ve already had sex.

Or, even worse, after you’ve already had children together.

That’s the part I find fascinating.

Not because I think everyone should be forced into marriage.

Not because I think children born outside marriage are somehow less valuable.

And certainly not because I think people who have children with different partners are automatically bad parents.

It’s because biological relationships don’t disappear simply because we stop organising our lives around them.

The child still has a father.

The father still has other children.

Those children still have children.

And those children will eventually enter the dating pool.

That’s where things get complicated.

Maybe I’m thinking too far ahead.

Maybe technology, DNA testing and better record keeping will make this easier to navigate.

Maybe future generations won’t care about biological connections in the same way we do today.

But maybe they will.

And if the number of children being born across multiple overlapping relationships keeps increasing, I can’t help wondering whether we’re creating family trees so tangled that future generations will have a much harder time knowing where they connect.

Marriage used to be one of the structures that helped organise families.

One man. One woman. One household. Their children.

Of course, reality has never been that neat. People cheated. People had children outside marriage. People divorced and remarried. Families have always been complicated.

But the structure existed.

And today, even marriage doesn’t necessarily provide that structure anymore.

A man can marry one woman and have children with another.

A woman can marry one man and have children with another.

People can marry, divorce, remarry and have children in each relationship.

Again, I’m not saying people shouldn’t.

I’m asking whether we have stopped to consider what happens when this becomes the dominant pattern rather than the exception.

Because children don’t remain children forever.

They grow up.

They date.

They marry.

They have children.

And they enter a world filled with other people whose biological connections are becoming increasingly difficult to map.

Maybe the future will be perfectly fine.

Maybe this is simply what the evolution of family looks like.

Or maybe, one day, knowing someone’s surname, hometown or family name won’t tell you much at all about whether you’re biologically connected to them.

Maybe the question before marriage won’t just be:

“Who are your parents?”

Maybe it will be:

“Okay… but who exactly are your parents’ other children?”

And perhaps that’s something we should start thinking about now.

Are we simply creating more flexible families, or are we slowly creating generations of people whose family trees are so interconnected that they could unknowingly become romantically involved with someone they’re biologically related to?

What do you think?

title: Ten Men, One Goal, Three Points.
excerpt: How Manchester City silenced Old Trafford on derby day.
content:
Old Trafford has seen its share of chaos, but Sunday's Manchester derby delivered a script nobody in blue would have written on purpose — and City still walked away with everything.

The Reason: In just the 23rd minute, Phil Foden was sent off for kicking out at Bruno Fernandes, who had caught him with a kick of his own moments earlier. Suddenly, City were down to ten men for the remaining 67 minutes of the biggest fixture on the calendar, away from home, against a United side desperate for a signature win. On paper, this was the kind of moment that swings derbies. Instead, it became the moment City proved something.

The Response: Rather than retreat into damage control, City tightened up and waited for their chance. It came through the man who always seems to find one against United — Erling Haaland, whose finish stood after a VAR review into an offside call involving Enzo Fernández, who was ruled to have not touched the ball. United threw bodies forward in search of an equalizer, hitting the woodwork twice through Marcus Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo, but couldn't turn their numerical advantage into a goal. In the dying seconds, Gianluigi Donnarumma produced a stunning point-blank save to deny Bryan Mbeumo and keep the clean sheet intact.

The Result: Manchester United 0, Manchester City 1. A first derby win for Enzo Maresca as City boss, a perfect start to the league campaign extended to four straight wins, and a statement that this City side doesn't need eleven men to beat their biggest rivals on their own turf.

The Takeaway: Champions find ways to win the ugly ones. City didn't need the full XI, the friendly bounce of the ball, or a stress-free afternoon — they needed one moment of quality and the discipline to hold on, and that's exactly what they got.

title: Nobody Is Coming to Save Your Career, And That’s Actually Good News.
excerpt: Nobody is coming to hand you the perfect job, the perfect opportunity, or the perfect career path.And honestly? That might be good news.It means your future doe…
content:
Nobody is coming to hand you the perfect job, the perfect opportunity, or the perfect career path.

And honestly? That might be good news.

It means your future does not have to depend entirely on someone discovering you.

Whether you are a student, fresh graduate, job seeker, or young professional, you have more control over your career than you may realize.

You can start building yourself before the opportunity arrives.

1. Stop Waiting for the Perfect Opportunity

Many young people spend months waiting for the right job, internship, connection, or opportunity.

There is nothing wrong with wanting a good opportunity. The problem begins when waiting becomes your only strategy.

While you are waiting, you can be learning.

You can be improving your communication skills, taking courses, reading, practising your craft, or working on small projects.

The opportunity may not be here yet, but preparation can begin today.

2. Build Skills Before You Need Them

One of the best things you can do for your career is develop skills before someone asks you to use them.

Interested in writing? Write.

Interested in digital marketing? Learn how campaigns work and practise creating content.

Interested in technology? Start learning the basics.

You don't need to master everything at once.

Choose one useful skill, learn it consistently, and practise it.

Skills become valuable when you can actually use them.

3. Create Proof of What You Can Do

Saying “I can write” is different from showing someone your writing.

Saying “I understand digital marketing” is different from showing them a campaign, content strategy, or project you worked on.

This is why personal projects matter.

Write an article.

Create a social media campaign.

Build a small portfolio.

Analyse a brand.

Volunteer for a project.

Document what you are learning.

These things can become evidence of your ability.

You may not have years of professional experience yet, but you can start building proof of work.

4. Put Yourself Where Opportunities Can Find You

Sometimes opportunities don't come because people don't know you exist.

Build your professional presence.

Share what you're learning.

Talk about your interests.

Connect with people in your field.

Apply for opportunities.

Join relevant communities.

Ask thoughtful questions.

You don't have to pretend to be an expert. You can simply show that you are learning, building, and willing to contribute.

Your online presence can become part of your professional identity.

5. Don't Let Silence Convince You to Stop

This is probably one of the hardest parts.

You may post something and nobody reacts.

You may apply for a job and receive no response.

You may start learning a skill and feel like nobody notices.

That doesn't automatically mean you're failing.

Sometimes you're simply building before people start paying attention.

The first article may get very few readers.

The first application may be rejected.

The first project may not be impressive.

Keep improving.

Every piece of work gives you experience. Every rejection can teach you something. Every new skill increases what you can offer.

Your Career Is Something You Can Start Building Now

You don't have to wait until graduation to take your career seriously.

You don't have to wait until you have a perfect CV.

You don't have to wait until someone gives you permission to start.

Start with what you have.

Learn something useful.

Practise it.

Create something.

Share it.

Connect with people.

Look for opportunities.

Then repeat.

Nobody may be coming to save your career but you don't need to sit around waiting to be saved.

You can start building it yourself, one skill, one project, and one opportunity at a time.

Your Turn

What is one skill you're currently learning that you believe could change your career in the future?

Share your answer in the comments. Someone reading your response might be learning the same skill, and your experience could help them.

title: WHY INTERNET CELEBRITIES FEEL LIKE PEOPLE WE ACTUALLY KNOW
excerpt: You've Never Met Them, But You'd Recognize Their Voice Anywhere
content:
You found out your favorite YouTuber got engaged before some of your actual friends knew. You felt genuinely happy for them, the real kind, the kind that makes you smile at your phone alone in a room. You have never spoken to this person. They don't know you exist. And yet somehow, their good news landed like it belonged to someone in your actual life.

If that has ever confused you a little, this is for you.

IT'S NOT DELUSIONAL, IT'S DESIGN

The instinct to dismiss this as unhealthy or embarrassing misses what's actually happening. Your brain didn't evolve to distinguish between someone talking to a camera and someone talking to you directly. Repeated eye contact, casual tone, daily updates about their life, their bad days, their opinions on things, all of it mimics the exact ingredients that build real friendships. Familiarity does not require mutual awareness. It just requires repeated exposure that feels personal.

So when a creator says "hey guys" and tells you about their morning, some part of your brain genuinely registers it the same way it would register a friend texting you. That's not weakness. That's the software running exactly as built.

WHY IT FEELS MORE COMFORTABLE THAN REAL FRIENDSHIP

Here's the part that's harder to admit, parasocial relationships come with none of the risk that real ones carry. I bet you would agree with me on that. The creator can not reject you, misunderstand you, get tired of you, or need something from you at an inconvenient time. You get closeness without the vulnerability that closeness usually requires. For a lot of people, especially the ones who have been burned or exhausted by real relationships, that one directional safety is genuinely appealing, not because they don't want real connection, but because this version doesn't demand anything back. Not at all.

THE REALITY WE WOULD RATHER AVOID

Some of the emotional investment people put into internet personalities is investment they have quietly withdrawn from the actual people around them. It's easier to feel deeply about someone who will never ask you to show up for them at 2am, never need you to apologize first, never require the ongoing, mutual effort that real relationships cost. That's not a moral failing. But it is worth noticing if the emotional energy going toward a stranger on a screen has started to outweigh the energy going toward people who could actually reciprocate it.

WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THE ILLUSION CRACKS

Watch what happens when a favorite creator does something disappointing, or turns out to be different from their persona. The reaction is often disproportionate, genuine grief, a sense of personal betrayal, the specific ache of a relationship ending, except nothing was ever actually there to end. That intensity is real, even if the relationship producing it was always one sided. The heartbreak is not fake just because the connection was never mutual.

WHY THIS IS NOT ACTUALLY ABOUT THE CREATOR

The specific person matters less than what they represent, consistency, familiarity, someone who "shows up" daily in a world where a lot of real relationships feel inconsistent or effortful. People are not really attaching to individuals as much as they're attaching to the reliability of the format itself, same time, same face, same tone, every day, no negotiation required.

That reliability is rare in real relationships. It's manufactured, deliberately, in this one.

SO WHAT DO YOU ACTUALLY DO WITH THIS?

Not guilt, and not forcing yourself to "stop caring" about people whose content genuinely adds something to your day. Just an honest check: is this connection sitting alongside your real relationships, or quietly replacing the effort you used to put into them?

You're allowed to enjoy the version of connection that asks nothing of you. Just don't let it become the only version you're still willing to try.

title: The tenant in Room 7
excerpt: SHE KNEW HER NAME
content:
By morning, she was exhausted.

She got ready for work without thinking too much about it. She avoided looking towards the locked room as she walked out, but just before she opened the main gate, she heard something.

Knock.

She stopped.

Knock. Knock.

Her heart dropped.

The sound was coming from inside the house.

She slowly turned around.

She stared at the door of the room for a few seconds before forcing herself to leave.

When she returned from work that evening, she noticed something immediately.

The landlord was standing outside Room 7.

He was holding a bunch of keys.

Amara slowed down.

“Good evening, sir.”

He looked at her.

Then at Room 7.

Then back at her.

“Good evening.”

There was an awkward silence.

Amara wanted to ask what he was doing there, but something about his expression made her keep quiet.

As she walked past him, she heard him lock the door again.

That night, Amara couldn’t stop thinking about it.

Why would the landlord go near the room if nobody was allowed inside?

Around 1:17 a.m., she woke up to the sound of footsteps.

Slow footsteps.

Coming down the corridor.

Amara held her breath.

The footsteps stopped directly outside her door.

She waited.

Nothing.

Then came three soft knocks.

‘’knock” “knock” “knock”

Her entire body went cold.

She didn’t move.

Then she heard a woman’s voice.

“Amara…”

She covered her mouth.

The voice came again.

Saying “ Please Don’t let him open the door”

Amara’s eyes was filled with tears

She wanted to scream but she couldn’t.

Then the voice whispered something that made her blood run cold.
