title: A WAY BACK ~a halal love story~
content:
Chapter 1

(Love at first sight isn't real until it's the first time you raise your forever lowered gaze just to land onto the face you can't take off your mind)
---

"Just go back home Zahra your aunty is going to get mad if you delay!" complained a girl in a pink Shalwar Kameez set with a tight tied hijab around her head and a veil falling off her shoulders her tote bag almost falling off her shoulder running behind another girl who held her hand softly tight leading the way in a runny way

"Ooh... my Nay.. that's my problem not yours.... As for now let's enjoy!" said Zahra still pulling her hand further to the park
Naysal sighed not angry exactly "Where are you taking me?"
"Just follow me quietly.... And I will show you the wonders of the world... right here in Lahore!"

Naysal rolled her eyes dramatically but still followed suit "Come ishq.... Come!" added Zahra still in the running mode
then finally they reached the center of the park, too quiet and peacefully beautiful just the singing birds against the blowing wind that flowers fell from that tree making the ground look miraculously eye catching

"Wow... zaza... this place is quite beautiful!" Her amusement took over as her eyes scanned the whole place
"As it should be!" She muttered circling the earth like the princess she felt, her hands widely opened her shoulder veil blowing with wind with her hijab neatly kept, facing the sky as if silently grateful to the heavens

"Close your eyes Nay.... You are going to enjoy this!" insisted Zahra with her eyes closed the wind brushing he beautifully maintained face with the perfect skin she never worked onto, Naysal did the same copying her friend

From a distant a man sat quietly busy doing the dhikr with his fingers, until the voices of girls reached his ear drums

"To find peace is impossible nowadays" he sighed upset as he stood up to leave trying to find a quick way to avoid the ladies whose voices he just heard

"And yes ... there is a pond there Nay... let me show you!" She grabbed Naysal's hand again pulling her towards the direction where the pond is
"This is beautiful I swear.... How did you find this place Zaza?"

Upon arrival Naysal's eyes where mesmerized by the beauty it carried flowers on the edge of the pond from the other side and the other side left freely, trees at the other end, flowers of different type decorating the other end while the other side presented with well arranged paving

"Mmh..... guess!"
"those little friends huh?" her brows pulled up questioningly
"Yeah!" She winked playfully

As the echoes spread rapidly the man didn't know where exactly the sound came from he just hoped that he was walking away from the girls avoiding them completely, with his gaze fixed on the ground, it went silent now, hopping the girls left, he led his way out of the park

"Maybe they left!" convincing himself as he walked towards the pond the easiest exit for him, with gaze lowered, he kept on with that dhikr again, he walked alongside the pond so close to the edge just one wrong step he swims

With his lowered gaze his eyes landed on a reflection in the pond,, the pair of doe eyes , pink full lips, the jawline straight and sharp enough to cut your evil thought....
he was supposed to lower his gaze, he did but still he saw it.. a beautiful face he wasn't supposed to see, Zahra.... The innocent soul in such a cruel world

His eyes widened.... He knew he wasn't supposed to be looking but the view was too beautiful to avoid.
His feet glued on the ground no more step taken, never his life has ever seen such a beauty or maybe it's because his gaze has always been lowered

While the girls sat at the edge of the pond enjoying the soft wind it produced suddenly Zahra did an abrupt movement her hand ran towards her chest as soon as she gazed the other side ending up finding a tall standing figure she didn't know was there
"Subhaan-Allah!" she said terrified, startling her friend beside her "Zaza!" lamented Naysal lightly slapping Zahra on her shoulder "You almost killed me!" she added gazing towards the figure briefly before she looked away

"I'm very sorry..... I... I terrified you!" He muttered not even looking up... he already saw the reflection he doesn't get any to increase the sins by seeing the real one now

"It's..... it's okay!" her tone stuttered like his
He took a few steps to walk away. But missed a step and then splash... he fell into the pond water splashed on Zahra and Naysal
"Subhaanaallah!" They muttered in unison, as the girls stood straight quickly in response

In the pond he struggled to pull himself out but the slippery edges said something else, the girls stood there watching him while swallowing back their chuckles over the view of how he looked during his scramble from the pond process,

Naysal almost chuckled but swallowed it back as her friend secretly pinched her, As his struggles didn't pay off he finally gave up he just stood in there the pond water reaching by his waist, he ran his hands from his hair to the face trying to wipe them dry

Zahra calculated what to do then a thought crossed her mind, she took her Veil that was resting on her shoulders it wasn't a problem her hijab was long enough she bent her back giving him her veil to hold onto with that he got to see her whole face clearly now

"hey hold this... and pull up!" she muttered as her one sided dimple showing as she spoke
instead of holding the veil, he kept on standing still staring in those eyes like they were a sacred thing he wanted to lose himself into
"hold this!" she repeated snapping him from the beautiful thought then he held the veil
"Come help me Nay!"
"Hold still!" a command

He held the veil tightly as he pulled himself out while the girls pulled harder as they could "Aaah ... so heavy.... Pull Nay pull!" She muttered, and for a moment it looked cute seeing her beautiful face wrinkling is such cuteness
"Aah... Subh-haana-Allah!.... I'm breaking my hands here.... Pull Zaza pull!" as they emphasized each others they pulled using all the energy they had even that they inherited from their ancestors till they pulled the man out
"Aaah ...... Alhamdulillah we did it, we did it Ishq!" Zahra jumped off excitement like a little kid celebrating her little wins

"Aah .. thank you!" Fighting the urge to look again, his curiosity telling him he needs to see how she looks again when she is excited but he ignored his own thoughts
"You're welcome ..... Marhabaa!" muttered Naysal
"You're welcome!" she paused holding Naysal's hand "and bye!" She started running and Naysal followed and just like that they disappeared.

Leaving the man's heart pounding in fear but of what? being sinful or?...Never in his life has his heart pounded this much he could tell that it's about to escape his ribcage, but yes also it's his first time falling into the pond that's definitely the reason his heart is racing it's way out of his ribcage, Maybe

he put his hand on his chest closing his eyes hardly regaining his composure shaking his head chasing away any wild thought trying to cross his mind whispering dhikr with his hand on his chest
"Subhaanaallah, Alhamdulillah, Allahu Akbar!" He repeated a few times more and finally his heart rate stabilized

--

Sliding into the back seat of a dark shaded Maybach where a man in a black suit with glasses was seating
"Let's go home Salman!" with that one statement the driver started the engine

Waqas stared at the man beside him with that questioning look that sent questions without his lips moving
Salim stared at him like he was looking at a crazy and dumb person who didn't know he was "Why..... are you that wet"
"I fell in the pond!" explained Waqas curtly
Salim almost chuckled before he questioned again "Pond?....!" He raised a brow demanding for more explanations that Waqas didn't give he just looked away like his face was frustrating to look at

"Salman.... Your friend is now blind that he didn't see the ponds .. so he fell!"
Salman chuckled lightly
"And he has been visiting that place for long enough to walk with his eyes closed without falling!"
"it happened accidentally!" Waqas shot back his tone full of the annoyance the two caused

"Or maybe you saw something terrifying so you fell huh?" Teased Salim
"Ooh Come on Salim.... What would scare the Waqas Yazid Mirza huh?" Added Salman the annoying tease he knows Waqas hates
"Can you two.... Stop talking nonsense... or maybe each of you should focus on his own issues!" muttered Waqas fixing himself properly on the seat and he rolled his eyes away

"Fine.... Fine!" Salim chuckled "Let's not get far with this yet!" added Salim as Salman just chuckled seeing the annoyed Waqas

With his eyes closed he rested his head on the car seat, accompanied with Salman's gentle and smooth driving peace found its way towards his mind, he crossed his hands around his bosom enjoying the fresh air that hit his face like a drop of hope.

Then it came again, her face, her eyes the way they looked terrified when he fell on the pond, her voice echoed in his eardrums like it was just now, then again how excited she was after finally saving him..

"how can someone be so happy just for saving someone's life"... The way she jumped out of joy, a smirk escaped his lips before he even managed swallowing it back
"Do you mind sharing what makes you smile alone... Mr...!" teased Salim
Without even a single word, Waqas turned his gaze to Salim gave him a stare that was enough to shut his mouth
"So arrogant!" muttered Salim dramatically

Minutes later the car made the entry in a mansion, luxury by reality and looks but broken by foundation, He scrambled out of the car
"See you tomorrow!" muttered Waqas to his driver who stays with the car then drives his way here to take him for work

"In-Shaa-Allah!" responded both Salim and Salman in unison, before their regular argument between them started
"Let's go Salman!" Muttered Salim adjusting himself on the front passenger seat,
Salman turned towards him looking like he was overly annoyed
"There you go again... commanding me!"
"You should be obedient to your elders isn't it?" Salim shot back mockingly as usual

Salman rolled his gaze away from him "Or maybe you should walk home!"
"Saying that in your boss' car?" his brows pulled up
he gazed at him again his gaze narrowing towards him "Or our boss?"
"Just drive now.... Don't start the drama!"
"who is starting the drama here.... Or do I have to remind you always that you aren't my boss!"
"But I'm your brother!"
"That doesn't glorify you commanding me!"
"I found this job for you.... You remember that" teased Salim
"still that doesn't justify you.... Acting like my boss here!" he shot back
" okay ...take me home I'm tired yaaar!"
Salman frowned over his brother's tease but drove away anyways, or else they wouldn't reach home any sooner and their argument wouldn't end either

title: The Future of Work Isn’t About Jobs
excerpt: The workplace is changing. Here are the skills you need to prepare for what comes next.
content:
The world of work is changing faster than most people realize.

The future of work will not be defined only by the jobs you have. It will be defined by the skills you can bring to those jobs.

Artificial intelligence is transforming how tasks are completed. Remote and hybrid work are changing how teams collaborate. Automation is taking over repetitive processes, while new technologies are creating roles that did not exist a few years ago.

But there is a bigger shift happening beneath all of this:

A job title may get you through the door. Your ability to adapt, learn and create value will determine how relevant you remain.

According to the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025, technological skills are expected to grow in importance faster than any other category of skills through 2030. AI and big data rank among the fastest-growing skills, followed by networks and cybersecurity and technological literacy. The report also highlights creative thinking, resilience, flexibility, agility, curiosity and lifelong learning as skills rising in importance.

LinkedIn's Work Change Report adds another important perspective: it estimates that 70% of the skills used in most jobs will change by 2030, with AI acting as a major catalyst.

So, as we move toward 2027 and beyond, what should professionals be paying attention to?

1. AI Literacy

You don't necessarily need to become an AI engineer.

But you need to understand how AI works, what it can do, where it fails and how to use it responsibly.

AI literacy involves more than knowing how to write a clever prompt. It includes knowing how to:

Write effective prompts

Validate AI-generated information

Recognize AI limitations

Protect sensitive information

Use AI responsibly and ethically

Integrate AI into everyday workflows

In total, AI Prompt Engineering.

This distinction is becoming increasingly important.

Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index found that among AI users surveyed globally, quality control of AI output and critical thinking were identified as the two most important human skills as AI takes on more work.

In other words, the advantage will not necessarily go to the person who uses AI the most.

It may go to the person who knows when to use it, how to evaluate its output and when human judgment should take over.

AI should not replace your judgment.

It should strengthen it.

2. Digital Collaboration

The modern workplace is no longer restricted to people sitting in the same office.

Teams can be spread across cities, countries and time zones. Meetings happen virtually. Projects are managed through digital platforms. Communication increasingly happens asynchronously.

That means digital collaboration is becoming more than simply knowing how to join a video call.

It involves knowing how to:

Communicate clearly online

Work effectively across time zones

Manage remote or distributed teams

Document information properly

Use collaboration and project-management tools

Work asynchronously

Maintain productivity without constant supervision

The broader transformation of work reinforces the importance of these capabilities. LinkedIn reports that the skills required for many jobs are already shifting, even for professionals who remain in the same role.

The implication is clear:

Your ability to work effectively in a digital environment can become just as important as your technical expertise.

3. Continuous Learning

Perhaps the most valuable skill of all is the ability to keep learning.

Technology will continue to change. Tools will become outdated. Some roles will evolve, while entirely new roles will emerge.

This means yesterday's expertise cannot guarantee tomorrow's relevance.

The World Economic Forum specifically identifies curiosity and lifelong learning among the skills expected to rise in importance through 2030.

LinkedIn's research also shows that professionals are increasingly adapting and upskilling as the skills required for work change.

But continuous learning doesn't mean collecting certificates endlessly.

It means developing the habit of asking:

“What do I need to learn next?”

That could mean taking a short course, learning a new digital tool, reading a book, attending a webinar, experimenting with AI or building a practical project.

You don't have to learn everything.

You simply need to keep learning what matters.

The Real Career Advantage

There is a dangerous assumption that the future belongs only to people who are highly technical.

It doesn't.

The future belongs to people who can combine technology with uniquely human abilities critical thinking, communication, creativity, leadership, empathy, decision-making and problem-solving.

AI can generate an answer.

But someone still needs to determine whether that answer is accurate, useful and appropriate.

A digital tool can organize information.

But someone still needs to understand what deserves attention.

Automation can complete a task.

But someone still needs to decide whether the task should be done in the first place.

Microsoft's latest research makes this point particularly relevant: as AI and agents take on more execution, humans gain more responsibility for directing work, making decisions and owning outcomes.

Technology may change the way we work, but human judgment remains valuable.

Don't Wait for the Future

One of the biggest mistakes professionals can make is waiting until a skill becomes essential before learning it.

By then, the competition may already be ahead.

The evidence suggests this transition is already happening. LinkedIn estimates that 70% of the skills used in most jobs could change by 2030.

That means the question isn't whether work will change.

It is whether you will change with it.

Start small.

Choose one skill you believe will make you more valuable in your current or desired career.

Spend just 30 minutes a day learning it.

Take a short course. Watch a tutorial. Read an article. Experiment with an AI tool. Build something. Practice what you've learned.

Thirty minutes may not feel significant today.

But repeated consistently, it can dramatically change your capabilities over the next year.

The Question You Should Be Asking

Instead of asking:

“Will AI take my job?”

Perhaps a better question is:

“What skills do I need to develop so I can remain valuable in an AI-powered workplace?”

That question puts you back in control.

The future of work is already being built.

And the people who prepare for it now will have more choices when it arrives.

Don't wait for the future to demand new skills from you. Start building them today.

Your Action This Week

Pick one skill: AI literacy, digital collaboration or continuous learning and block 30 - 60 minutes daily this week to start developing it.

Your future career may depend less on the job you have today and more on the skills you decide to build tomorrow.

title: Toddler Romance?
excerpt: Society's Subtle Pressure
content:
Rakeem Ayomide Mkambala, the son of Priscilla Ojo and Juma Jux, turned one on Monday, August 24, 2026, and his parents threw him a vibrant cowboy-themed birthday party on Saturday, August 29, 2026.

The guest list read like a red-carpet star reunion: Priscilla’s mum Iyabo Ojo came through matching the energy alongside Enioluwa, the bestie while Johnny Drille showed up looking like the ultimate dad with his two-year-old daughter, Amaris. Veekee James made it a full family affair with her husband, their four-month-old baby girl, and her ten-month-old niece with her mum. Lateef Adedimeji and his wife brought their usual charm, joined by May Yul-Edochie and her kids, Mohbad’s wife and son, Mercy Aigbe, and Chioma of Good Hair. And of course, Toke Makinwa was right there in the middle of it all with her one-year-old daughter, Yaya.

Online, people have jokingly paired little Rakeem and baby Yaya as a "couple." But at the party, cameras caught Rakeem staring completely spellbound at Johnny Drille’s daughter, Amaris. Naturally, the internet went wild with jokes, teasing that Rakeem was already "cheating" on Yaya.

I found the clips hilarious and took them in good fun. But watching it also unlocked a memory from my own childhood.

When I was just four or five years old, adults in my circle would constantly pair me with a male friend simply because our families were acquainted.

They would routinely refer to me as "our wife." I hated it back then, and honestly, I still dislike the concept today. It isn't the flex people think it is.

To be clear, I don't view baby Yaya and baby Rakeem through that heavy lens. When they grow up, they can be friends, partners, or whatever they choose.

What bothers me is the broader adult habit of imposing romantic labels and future marriage expectations on young children instead of encouraging healthy, genuine friendships.

Why are we so eager to remind children about marriage from such a tender age?

Before a child even learns how to spell their own name, society is already hinting that their final boss in life is becoming somebody's spouse.

It subtly sends a message that no matter what tantrums you throw or what you accomplish while growing up, your ultimate destination in life is to get married just to earn societal respect.

Let children build pure, unburdened friendships, and let them just be kids.

title: Politics in Practice: What Does Politics Actually Look Like in Real Life?
excerpt: When we hear the word politics , what usually comes to mind? • Politicians. • Elections. • Political parties. • Campaign posters. • Long speeches. • Arguments on X. Maybe even those family discussions…
content:
When we hear the word politics, what usually comes to mind?

• Politicians.

• Elections.

• Political parties.

• Campaign posters.

• Long speeches.

• Arguments on X.

Maybe even those family discussions where someone mentions politics and, before you know it, everybody has become a political analyst.

For many of us, politics feels like something that happens somewhere else. In government offices. In political meetings. During elections. Among people whose names we see on posters.

But what if politics starts much closer to home?

What if politics is not only about the people making decisions in government, but also about how people make decisions with one another?

Think about something as simple as deciding where a group of friends should eat.

One person suggests a place. Someone else doesn’t like it. Another person has a different idea. Someone starts convincing everyone. Somebody compromises. And eventually, after going back and forth, a decision is made.

It seems like an ordinary conversation.

And it is.

But look a little closer.

There were different interests. There was influence. There was negotiation. There was disagreement. And there was a decision that affected everyone involved.

Now, choosing where to eat with your friends is obviously not the same thing as running a government. But some of the ideas we associate with politics : power, influence, interests, negotiation and decision-making, don’t suddenly appear when politicians enter the room.

They exist in our everyday lives too.

How I started seeing politics differently

And I didn’t always see politics this way.

When I was preparing to enter college, I honestly didn’t know what I wanted to study. I eventually chose Political Science, not because I had always dreamed of studying politics or had some amazing plan to become a politician.

I simply didn’t know what else I wanted to do.

And, if I’m being honest, I thought I knew what Political Science was about - I knew it was connected to Government (the subject that was taught in high school so since I liked government in school, I decided to go for the course )

Politics.

Politicians.

Government.

Elections.

Basically, everything that seemed to happen far away from my everyday life.

But while studying Political Science, I slowly began to realise that I had been looking at politics through a very small window.

One of the first ideas I encountered was Aristotle’s description of human beings as “political animals.”

At first, it sounded like one of those statements you learn because you know it is probably going to appear in an exam.

But the more I studied, the more I understood it differently.

Politics wasn’t only happening in government.

It was happening in the way people interacted with one another.

In our discussions.

In our disagreements.

In the moments when we try to convince someone to see things from our point of view.

In negotiations.

In deciding who gets to do what.

In figuring out what happens when two people want completely different things.

Even within a family, there can be questions of authority, influence, compromise and decision-making.

Suddenly, politics didn’t feel so distant anymore.

And that’s when I began to understand that politics is not simply about politicians.

IT IS ALSO ABOUT PEOPLE

So what does politics actually look like?

Think about your family…. When an important decision has to be made, who usually gets the final say? Is it necessarily the person who speaks the loudest? Not always.

Sometimes it’s the person everyone respects. Sometimes it’s the person paying the bills. Sometimes it’s the person with the most experience. Sometimes it’s the person who knows exactly how to convince everybody else.

That’s influence.

Now think about school or work.

There may be someone who doesn’t have the highest position in the room but somehow manages to influence what everyone does.

There may also be someone with the official authority to make a decision, but whose decision still depends on getting other people on board.

That’s another interesting part of how power works.

And then there is the community.

People want different things.

Different groups have different interests.

Everyone has an opinion about what should happen.

But eventually, somebody has to decide.

How do we get there?

• Through conversations.

• Through persuasion.

• Through negotiation.

• Through compromise.

• Sometimes through disagreement.

• And sometimes, unfortunately, through the people with the most power simply getting their way.

These are not exactly political campaigns or elections, but they help us understand some of the same ideas that shape political life.

Politics begins when people have to decide together

Perhaps this is why politics can feel so complicated.

We attach it so strongly to politicians and government that we forget the human interactions underneath it.

Before politics becomes policies, elections and political institutions, there are people.

People with different interests.

People trying to influence one another.

People trying to protect what matters to them.

People trying to reach agreements.

People disagreeing about what should happen next.

And people trying to decide how they should live together.

That is what made Political Science more interesting to me.

I went into the course thinking I was going to study politics. I didn’t realise I was also going to study people. And perhaps that is the part of politics we don’t talk about enough.

Politics doesn’t begin at the ballot box. It begins wherever people have to live, communicate, negotiate, make decisions and share power with one another.

And today, we are celebrating independence.

Today is October 1, Nigeria’s Independence Day.

And every year, we are reminded to celebrate. But alongside the celebrations, there are also conversations about the state of the country and whether we have enough to celebrate.

I think both conversations can exist.

We can celebrate Nigeria while still being honest about the things that need to change.

Because independence is not just a date we remember every year. It is also a reminder that we are participants in the society we live in.

And if politics begins wherever people have to communicate, negotiate, make decisions and live together, then perhaps building Nigeria begins there too.

In our homes.

In our communities.

In the way we participate.

In the questions we ask.

In the way we use whatever influence we have.

Independence may have been declared at the level of a country, but the responsibility that comes with it is lived out by people.

Maybe that is what politics in practice really looks like.

And perhaps, on a day like today, that is worth remembering.

Happy Independence Day, Nigerians.

title: The Child Beneath the Rainbow
excerpt:
“Adora, you will be a star. One day, the whole world will see you.”

Mama always said it with that wide smile of hers, the kind that made her eyes shine.

I would giggle and bury my face against her chest.

“I pray so, Mama.”

She would kiss my forehead.

“You will see.”

I had heard that story so many times that I could almost recite every word before she spoke it.

But I never grew tired of it.

It was the story of the day I was born.

The day an entire village wanted me dead.

The day my mother chose to die with me rather than let them take me.

“When you were born,” Mama once told me, “the midwives refused to touch you.”

She had been lying on the cold floor of the birthing hut, exhausted and trembling, yet she had pulled me tightly against her chest.

“They looked at your eyes and screamed.”

She paused.

“‘Witch!’ they cried.”

Outside, the villagers gathered.

“Kill her!”

“Stone the child!”

“She is a curse!”

Mama tightened her arms around me.

“You will have to kill me first,” she had shouted.

Her voice had shaken the walls.

“She is mine.”

For years, Mama had prayed to the goddess for a child.

And when she finally had one, the village called her child a curse.

But Mama never believed them.

To her, I was a blessing.

And perhaps the goddess had been listening.

Because while the villagers screamed for my death, something strange was happening beyond the village walls.

My father, King Anyanwu, was away at war.

His warriors were losing.

Their enemies had surrounded them, and defeat seemed certain.

Then I was born.

According to my father, the sky suddenly changed.

A rainbow stretched across the heavens, brighter than anything he had ever seen. The wind grew still. Even the birds seemed to fall silent.

And then, without warning, strength surged through his warriors.

Men who had been too weak to lift their swords suddenly fought as though the gods themselves had entered their bodies.

They turned the battle.

They won.

My father always believed it was no coincidence.

He said that the goddess of nature appeared only when a child of great destiny was born.

And on the day I entered the world, she had come.

Perhaps she had come to protect me.

Perhaps she had come to warn them.

But while my father fought for his kingdom, my mother fought for my life.

The villagers dragged her into a dark room and locked the door.

No food.

No water.

No one was allowed to enter.

They called her the Curse Queen.

For three days, she remained there with me pressed against her breast.

She should have been weak.

She should have been starving.

Yet she never stopped feeding me.

“I would rather die,” she whispered to me, “than let them take you.”

Three days passed.

Then the sound of drums rolled through the village.

The warriors had returned.

My father was home.

The moment he heard that his queen had given birth, joy filled his face.

But that joy vanished when the elders told him what had happened.

“You cannot see her yet, Your Majesty,” one of them said.

My father's eyes narrowed.

“Why?”

The elders exchanged frightened glances.

“The child is a bad omen.”

Silence.

Then my father walked towards the room where my mother was being held.

The elders tried to stop him.

He pushed them aside.

The door was locked.

My father lifted one foot.

Bang!

The door flew from its hinges.

My mother was sitting on the floor, her clothes torn, her hair tangled, her face pale from three days without food or water.

My father stared at her.

Then his eyes darkened.

“Who did this?”

His voice thundered through the room.

No one answered.

The midwives slowly stepped forward.

They began explaining.

They spoke of my eyes.

Of the villagers' fear.

Of the elders' orders.

My father listened.

Then he drew his sword.

The room fell silent.

Before anyone could understand what he intended, the midwives fell.

One after another.

The sword returned to its sheath.

My father turned towards the elders.

“You punished my wife without hearing her.”

His voice was cold now.

“You condemned my child without seeking the word of the chief priest.”

He looked down at me.

“And yet this child brought victory to my army.”

Then, as though the goddess herself had been waiting for that moment, the doors of the palace burst open.

The chief priest entered.

Everyone froze.

He walked slowly into the room, his staff striking the floor with every step.

“Curse be upon those who refuse to welcome the goddess of peace.”

Every person in the room dropped to their knees.

The priest's gaze travelled across the frightened faces.

“The princess is her replica.”

A murmur swept through the palace.

“She came to you, and instead of welcoming her, you raised your hands against her.”

The elders bowed until their foreheads touched the ground.

“Mercy, Chief Priest.”

“Please, forgive us.”

The priest closed his eyes.

For a moment, he said nothing.

Then his head turned slowly, as though he were listening to a voice no one else could hear.

When he opened his eyes again, the room seemed to grow colder.

“You have already chosen your punishment.”

The elders trembled.

“All your first daughters shall die a mysterious death.”

A cry escaped the room.

The priest turned away from them.

Then he faced my father.

“Take care of her.”

His voice softened.

“For your days of suffering have ended. The goddess has blessed your house with one of her children.”

He looked at me.

“She shall be your pride and your strength.”

My father held me closer.

“Let her be loved,” the priest continued. “For she will bring no shame to your name.”

Then his expression hardened.

“But hear me well.”

Everyone lifted their heads.

“Whoever treats this child with cruelty shall die before the sunset of the following day.”

The palace fell utterly silent.

“But whoever treats her with love shall live in abundance.”

He raised his staff.

“She will bring more children into your household. The queen's years of barrenness are over.”

He struck the floor once.

“So let it be written.”

Another strike.

“So let it be done.”

And with that, the chief priest turned and walked away.

That same day, my mother was carried into her chamber.

They bathed her.

They dressed her in clean clothes.

They placed her in a warm bed.

And for the first time in three days, she slept without fear.

As for me, my father took me into his arms.

He stared into my strange, unfamiliar eyes.

Then he smiled.

“Adora.”

The name meant that I had come not only for him, but for his people.

That was the day the village stopped calling me a curse.

The day they bowed before me.

The day they learnt to fear the child they had once tried to kill.

And perhaps Mama had been right all along.

I was born beneath a rainbow.

The goddess had announced my arrival.

And the whole world had not yet seen me.

But one day, it would.

title: Copy of The Gift of Loving and Being Loved
excerpt: Not all love is romantic, and some of the most important love never is.
content:
Romantic love is beautiful.

It’s loud.

It’s intense.

It’s the one everyone talks about like it’s the main event.

And somehow, every other kind of love becomes background noise.

But I don’t think it should be that way.

Because the friend you call when everything feels off…

the one who somehow makes things lighter without even trying…

the one who listens and makes you feel seen, not judged…

or the one that steps in and makes sense of the chaos when your head is all over the place…

That kind of love?

It’s powerful.

The collection of people like that in your life

honestly beats a love that is only fueled by desire…

or what we now casually call love but is really just lust.

And sometimes, I feel a slight pang of pity.

When someone says, “I’m in a relationship,”

and then slowly disappears into it.

Everything becomes about one person.

One source of warmth.

One source of validation.

One source of companionship.

It sounds sweet at first…

but it’s almost like the blueprint for suffocation.

My friends would probably hear this and come for me immediately,

saying this is coming from someone who has been single since the break of dawn 🤣

But I promise you, it’s not that.

I’m not against having your person.

In fact, I hope everyone experiences that kind of connection.

The one you think about when you close your eyes.

The one that somehow sits behind your heartbeat 🤣

That kind of love is real.

But so is this one.

The quiet, consistent, everyday love

that comes from your people.

The ones you call over the smallest discomfort

and it doesn’t feel weird.

It feels normal.

The ones you share deep, personal things with

without second-guessing yourself.

And yes… the money bags too 🤣

The ones who show up when life is squeezing you,

who make sure you’re good in ways that go beyond words.

Even the ones that call you out of nowhere

and somehow make you feel like the most important person on earth in that moment.

That is love too.

And it’s something we should invest in.

Because at the end of the day,

no one person should have to carry the weight

of being everything to you.

It’s not fair to them.

And it’s not healthy for you.

So yes, fall in love.

Have your person.

But don’t neglect the people

who have been loving you in ways

that didn’t need romance to feel real.

I probably don’t say this enough…

especially since it’s spread across both genders

and guys like to act weird about these things 🤣

But I genuinely love you all.

And I feel privileged

to have access to that kind of love.

title: They All Laughed. I Didn’t Get the Joke.
excerpt: I thought I was about to tell them a story. I didn't know I was about to become one.
content:
It felt normal because I wasn't the only one doing it.

During break time, we'd sit together and talk about our latest posts, likes and comments. We'd check who had gotten the most likes, laugh over funny comments and talk about new friend requests.

It was just what we did.

Then someone asked, “You get gist?”

My heart skipped a bit.

I wasn't sure if I wanted to tell them about my gone-too-soon friendship. I thought about it for a few seconds, wondering if I should just keep it to myself.

But eventually, I decided to drop the gist.

I told them everything.

From when we first got talking, how quickly we became friends, how much I enjoyed having someone new to talk to, and how one game managed to ruin everything.

I explained how I had refused some of the dares and how things became awkward afterwards. I told them how I eventually lost interest in the friendship.

I thought I was making sense.

I thought they would understand why it mattered to me.

Instead, someone laughed.

Then another person joined.

Soon, everyone was laughing.

I looked at them, confused.

What was funny?

Then someone asked,

“So you actually stopped talking to him because of that?”

And they laughed again.

To them, it was probably just a funny story about two young people who met online, played a silly game and couldn't remain friends afterwards.

To me, it wasn't funny.

I smiled because I didn't know what else to do.

Maybe they simply didn't see it the way I did.

The bell rang shortly after, and everyone went back to class.

Just like that, my gone-too-soon friendship became another break-time gist.

But for some reason, I kept thinking about that conversation.

Not the friendship.

The laughter.

title: Are We Living Our Lives or Creating Content About Them?
excerpt: In a world where everything can become content, what happens to the moments that are just for us?
content:
Sometimes I wonder if we actually know how to enjoy things anymore without showing someone.

You go somewhere nice and before you even settle down, your phone is already out. You take a picture of the place, record the food, take a video of yourself, maybe do another one because the first angle wasn't giving what you wanted. Then you post it, check who viewed it, check the likes and move on.

And I'm not judging because, honestly, I do it too. Most of us do.

Social media has become such a normal part of our lives that documenting what we're doing doesn't even feel unusual anymore. If something exciting happens and nobody knows about it, sometimes it almost feels like it didn't happen.

That's the part I've been thinking about lately. When did we start experiencing our lives through the eyes of an audience?

Think about going on a trip. You finally get to that beautiful place you've been looking forward to, but instead of just looking around, you're already thinking about the pictures you're going to take. You see a nice view and immediately think, This would make a good post. You eat something that looks good and your first instinct is to reach for your phone.

There's nothing wrong with taking pictures. We take pictures because we want to remember things. We want to look back years later and remember what we wore, where we went and who we were with.

But sometimes I think we've moved beyond remembering. We're now documenting almost everything.

Your birthday isn't just your birthday anymore. It's a photo dump. A new job becomes a LinkedIn announcement. A relationship becomes couple pictures. A breakup can become a storytime. A new hobby becomes a content series. Even going through a difficult period can become something to post about.

And the funny thing is that we're not always doing it because we want to. Sometimes there's this quiet pressure to share.

You get good news and immediately think about how you're going to announce it. You buy something you've wanted for a long time and start thinking about the picture. You go somewhere your followers would love and feel like you have to show them.

It's almost as if we're not just living experiences anymore. We're also producing them.

And I think the creator economy has made this even more complicated.

We're constantly being told to monetise our interests. Turn your hobby into a business. Build your personal brand. Document your journey. Post consistently. Create a community. Don't just enjoy something,find a way to make money from it.

Again, there's nothing wrong with that. People have built real careers from creating content, and that's amazing. Social media has given people opportunities that didn't exist for previous generations.

But sometimes I wonder if we've forgotten that it's okay to do something and not turn it into a brand.

You can enjoy cooking without starting a food page, dress nicely without taking pictures of every outfit, travel without making a travel vlog.

Read a book without posting a review, have a good day without proving to anyone that you had one, and maybe I'm just getting tired of the idea that everything has to be shareable.

There are some moments I don't want an audience for. Some conversations are better when nobody is recording them. Some memories are actually more special because they exist only in your head.

And I think there's something beautiful about that.

The internet has made us so used to sharing that privacy can sometimes feel like we're missing out. You see other people's birthdays, vacations, relationships, achievements and seemingly perfect lives every day. Then you look at your own life and start wondering why yours doesn't look as exciting.

But what we forget is that we're comparing our actual lives to other people's edited versions of theirs.

Nobody posts the boring Tuesday afternoon, the argument they had before the cute couple picture, the ten failed attempts before the perfect Instagram photo, or posts themselves staring at the ceiling wondering what they're doing with their life.

We see the content, not the whole life behind it. Maybe that's why we're so obsessed with making our own lives look interesting too.

We want proof that we're doing something. We want memories. We want attention. We want to feel seen. Sometimes we simply want people to say, “Wow, your life looks amazing.”

And there's nothing wrong with wanting to be seen, but I don't think we should get to the point where we can't enjoy something unless someone else sees it.

So maybe the answer isn't to stop posting or suddenly become one of those people who says they don't use social media. That's unrealistic for most of us, especially when social media is also where we work, communicate, discover things and make money.

Maybe it's just about remembering that our phones don't have to be part of every moment. Sometimes you can go out with your friends and not record the funniest part of the conversation, eat your food while it's still hot instead of photographing it from six different angles, accomplish something and tell the people you love instead of the entire internet.

And sometimes, something wonderful can happen to you and you can keep it. Not because you're hiding, not because you're anti-social media.

Just because it belongs to you. We're living in a time where almost anything can become content. Our homes, relationships, jobs, bodies, struggles, hobbies and even our healing can be turned into something for an audience.

Maybe that's not necessarily a bad thing,but I think we should be careful not to become so focused on documenting our lives that we forget to actually live them.

Because when the phone goes away, the likes disappear and nobody is watching, there still has to be a life there.

And maybe that life doesn't always need to be posted.

title: I Asked Myself: If AI Can Do This Task, What Should an Executive Assistant Actually Be Doing?
excerpt: AI can handle the tasks. But the future of Executive Assistance will depend on who can provide the judgment behind them.
content:
AI can schedule meetings, summarize emails, draft documents and organize information. So where does that leave the Executive Assistant?

I recently found myself asking a question that I think more Executive Assistants need to ask:

If AI can do this task, what should I actually be doing?

It's an uncomfortable question.

Artificial intelligence can already draft emails, summarize meetings, organize information, conduct research and automate repetitive workflows.

And the technology is moving quickly.

The International Labour Organization reports that clerical occupations remain among the occupations with the highest exposure to generative AI. Yet its research also suggests that most jobs are more likely to be transformed than completely eliminated, because human involvement is still required.

That distinction matters.

Because an Executive Assistant is not simply a collection of administrative tasks.

A great Executive Assistant understands the person behind the tasks, the business behind the calendar, the relationships behind the emails and the priorities behind the deadlines.

So perhaps the question isn't whether AI can do parts of the job.

It can.

The better question is:

What becomes more valuable for an Executive Assistant when AI can handle more of the routine work?

The job is changing

For years, Executive Assistance has involved responsibilities such as:

  • managing calendars;

  • coordinating meetings;

  • handling emails;

  • preparing documents;

  • organizing information;

  • taking notes;

  • following up on tasks.

Many of these activities can now be assisted or partially automated by AI.

But that doesn't necessarily make the Executive Assistant less valuable.

It changes where the value comes from.

Microsoft's recent Work Trend Index describes an emerging workplace where humans and AI agents increasingly work together, with people directing work, managing AI and taking responsibility for outcomes.

That points toward an important shift:

The future Executive Assistant may spend less time simply completing tasks and more time deciding which tasks should be done, how they should be done and what should happen afterward.

1. Protect the executive's time not just the calendar

AI can find an available time slot.

But an Executive Assistant should be asking:

Does this meeting deserve the executive's time at all?

That's a different question.

A calendar is not just a schedule. It is a reflection of priorities.

A strong Executive Assistant should understand when an executive needs:

  • a meeting;

  • preparation time;

  • uninterrupted thinking time;

  • travel time;

  • recovery time;

  • or simply fewer commitments.

AI can help organize the calendar.

The human should help protect what goes into it.

2. Don't compete with AI on speed. Compete on judgment.

If AI can summarize a 60-minute meeting in seconds, there is little value in spending another 30 minutes manually summarizing it.

The value shifts to what happens next.

An Executive Assistant can ask:

  • What decisions were made?

  • Who is responsible for each action?

  • What wasn't resolved?

  • What needs to be escalated?

  • What should the executive know before the next meeting?

That's the difference between recording information and creating value from information.

AI can produce the summary.

The Executive Assistant can turn that summary into action and accountability.

3. Become a systems builder

This may be one of the biggest opportunities for Executive Assistants.

Instead of asking:

“How do I complete this task faster?”

Start asking:

“Why does this task keep happening manually in the first place?”

Imagine an executive spends hours every week coordinating meetings.

A task-focused assistant might become faster at scheduling.

A systems-focused assistant might create:

  • scheduling rules;

  • priority categories;

  • automated reminders;

  • meeting templates;

  • briefing documents;

  • follow-up workflows.

Now the assistant isn't simply completing today's task.

They're improving the system that produces tomorrow's results.

That's a much more valuable contribution.

4. Learn to work with AI not against it

I don't think the answer for Executive Assistants is to resist AI.

It is to learn how to use it intelligently.

Microsoft's research describes a growing model of human-agent teams, where AI increasingly handles execution while humans provide direction, judgment and oversight.

Think about the possibilities.

AI could:

Prepare a meeting brief.

Summarize previous conversations.

Identify scheduling conflicts.

Draft routine communications.

Organize information.

The Executive Assistant can then:

Review.

Interpret.

Prioritize.

Decide.

Follow up.

The goal isn't to compete with AI.

The goal is to become the person who knows how to direct it.

5. Human skills become more important

There is something AI still doesn't automatically give you:

context.

Imagine an important client sends an email.

AI can summarize it.

It can draft a response.

It may even suggest a tone.

But an experienced Executive Assistant might know that:

  • the client has been frustrated recently;

  • the executive promised something three weeks ago;

  • this relationship is strategically important;

  • the issue should be handled personally;

  • or the email contains something that shouldn't be automated.

That's where human judgment matters.

The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 highlights skills such as analytical thinking, creative thinking, resilience, flexibility, leadership and collaboration alongside technological skills as important in the changing workplace.

Technology may process information.

People still provide context, judgment and trust.

So, what should an Executive Assistant actually be doing?

If I had to simplify it, I'd say:

Protect time.

Make sure the executive's attention goes where it creates the most value.

Manage priorities.

Help distinguish what is urgent from what is actually important.

Anticipate needs.

Don't wait for the executive to ask about everything.

Build systems.

Turn recurring tasks into efficient processes.

Manage relationships.

Understand the people and context behind the communication.

Handle exceptions.

Know when automation works and when human intervention is necessary.

Use AI intelligently.

Let technology handle what it does well while retaining human oversight.

Create leverage.

The ultimate goal isn't simply to make the executive's life easier.

It's to make the executive more effective.

The future isn't “AI vs Executive Assistant”

Maybe we've been asking the wrong question.

The debate often sounds like:

“Will AI replace Executive Assistants?”

But I think a more useful question is:

“What kind of Executive Assistant becomes more valuable because of AI?”

That person isn't trying to compete with a machine.

They're learning how to work alongside one.

They're not simply managing tasks.

They're managing priorities, systems, relationships and outcomes.

They're not waiting for instructions.

They're anticipating what comes next.

And they're not measuring their value by how many tasks they personally complete.

They're measuring it by how much better the executive can operate because they're there.

That's a very different definition of an assistant.

And perhaps that's where the profession is heading.

In Conclusion

AI may eliminate some tasks.

It may automate others.

It may even fundamentally change what we call administrative work.

But that doesn't mean the human contribution disappears.

It means we have to become more intentional about what that contribution is.

So the next time you find yourself asking:

“If AI can do this task, what should I be doing?”

Don't panic.

Ask a better question:

“What can I do that creates more value because AI is handling the routine work?”

That may be the mindset that separates the Executive Assistant of yesterday from the Executive Assistant of tomorrow.

title: I Thought I Was Too Late to Learn
excerpt: I Thought I Was Too Late to LearnGrowing up, there was one thing that always made me feel left out: football.Whenever people around me started talking about foo…
content:
I Thought I Was Too Late to Learn

Growing up, there was one thing that always made me feel left out: football.

Whenever people around me started talking about football, I felt like I was in a different world. They talked about clubs, players, matches, goals, and everything that was trending. I would listen, but I barely understood what they were saying.

Instead of asking questions or trying to learn, I simply told myself, “I’m already late. Everyone knows this except me.”

And because I thought I was too late, I never really tried.

Now, about 15 years later, I sometimes think about it differently.

What if I had simply listened back then? What if I had asked someone to explain the game to me? What if I had accepted that it was okay not to know something and started learning anyway?

Maybe today, I would be the one passionately discussing football with everyone else.

It taught me something bigger than football:

Sometimes, we are not actually too late. We only become too late when we allow the fear of being behind to stop us from starting.

You don't have to know everything before you begin.

Start where you are. Ask questions. Listen. Learn.

Because being late is not the same as being incapable.

title: The Convenient Husband (Part 1)
excerpt: My hands trembled as I pressed myself against the wall, fighting to breathe, fighting to understand what I'd just witnessed. Nathan. Sienna. Together. In ways t…
content:
My hands trembled as I pressed myself against the wall, fighting to breathe, fighting to understand what I'd just witnessed. Nathan. Sienna. Together. In ways that siblings should never be.

It was supposed to be the happiest day of my life. My graduation day. After years of hard work, sleepless nights, and countless blood donations for Sienna's mysterious illness, I had finally earned my degree. I'd kept it simple, just close family and friends, exactly how I liked it. No surprises, no fuss. Nathan knew me well enough to let me plan it myself, or so I thought.

Everything had been perfect until the baker stopped answering my calls. The cake was late, my guests would be arriving soon, and I couldn't have my graduation party without it. So I'd driven to the exclusive bakery myself, the one that only served the elite of the country. I knew my way around the place from previous visits.

The shop was empty when I arrived, eerily quiet except for a faint sound coming from the back. As I moved toward the kitchen, the sounds grew clearer. Moans. Passionate, unmistakable moans. My feet froze mid step.

A mirror hung on the side wall, angled toward the kitchen entrance. I didn't mean to look. God, I wish I hadn't looked. But there, in the reflection, I saw him. Nathan. My fiancé. The man I was supposed to marry tomorrow. His hands were tangled in long dark hair, his mouth pressed against bare skin, his body moving in rhythm with someone else's.

My heart stopped before my mind could catch up. That woman, it couldn't be. But when she turned her head, laughing breathlessly, I saw her face clearly. Sienna. His sister. The girl I'd given my blood to for ten years. The girl I'd loved like family.

"Thank you for always choosing me over her," Sienna's voice drifted through the doorway, breathy and satisfied. "My blood transplant is almost complete. We won't need her anymore. No more pretending we're related.

The words hit me. I bit down hard on my hand to keep from gasping, tasting copper as my teeth broke skin. What did she mean, pretending? They'd told me they were siblings. For fifteen years, I'd believed it.

Nathan's response made my blood run cold. "After tomorrow, we'll finally be free. Once she's arrested, you won't need her blood to survive anymore. She's useless anyway, not smart like you, not beautiful like you. Just a convenient blood bag."

My vision blurred with tears, but I couldn't tear my eyes away from the mirror. Sienna laughed again, a sound that had once brought me comfort now twisted into something cruel. "Did the baker include the substance in her favorite cupcakes? The drug test needs to come back positive. It's the only way to get her out of our lives permanently."

The room spun. They were framing me. After everything I'd sacrificed, every pint of blood I'd given, every time I'd put Sienna's needs before my own, they were going to destroy me.

I stumbled backward, my legs barely supporting my weight as I found my way to the door. Couldn't feel anything except the crushing weight of betrayal pressing down on my chest.

Somehow, I made it to my car. Drove to a nearby park. Collapsed against the steering wheel as fifteen years of memories crashed over me like waves.

I'd been seventeen when I lost my family in the war. The chaos, the explosions, the screaming, it all blurred together in my mind. One moment I had parents who loved me, a home, an identity. The next moment, I was alone in a foreign country. Every search had ended in failure.

Then Nathan found me. Kind, gentle Nathan with his warm smile and promises. His parents had taken me in without hesitation. Sienna had hugged me tight and called me sister. They'd given me a home when I had nothing, loved me when I was lost. Or so I believed

For ten years, I'd been Sienna's personal blood donor. Her rare blood disorder required regular transfusions, and I was the only match they could find with type O negative. I'd never questioned it. Never hesitated. How could I, when they'd given me so much?

But it was all a lie. Every moment of kindness, every gesture of love, had been planned. They'd never wanted me. They'd only wanted what flowed through my veins.

The sun was beginning to set when I finally dried my tears and started the car. I had a party to attend. Guests who expected to see me smile. A fiancé who expected me to eat poisoned cupcakes and disappear from his life in handcuffs.

I checked my reflection in the rearview mirror, wiped away the mascara streaks, and painted on a smile. They wanted to play games? Fine. But they'd made one critical mistake: they'd underestimated me.

When I arrived at the venue, I went straight to a private room to compose myself. I couldn't let anyone see the cracks in my facade. Today was my graduation day. I was the top student in my department though I'd asked them not to announce it publicly. I'd earned this moment through blood, sweat, and tears. Literally.

"Mila! There you are!" Nathan's mother rushed over as I emerged, her face etched with concern that now seemed fake. "We've been looking everywhere for you. Are you alright?"

"Just a headache from all the stress," I lied. "Needed some fresh air."

Nathan and Sienna walked in at that moment, carrying my cake between them like it was precious cargo. My stomach turned. Sienna bounced over and kissed my cheek, her smile bright. "Happy graduation day, Mila! I'm so proud of you."

"Sienna, did you remember to bring Mila's favorite cupcakes?" Nathan's mother asked, right on cue.

I watched them all, seeing them clearly for the first time in fifteen years. They all knew. Every single one of them was in on this conspiracy. But why? What crime were they covering up that required my destruction?

"Mila, are you sure you're okay?" Nathan's voice cut through my thoughts. His hand touched my arm and I had to fight not to flinch away. "You look pale. You need to stay strong for yourself and for Sienna. She's only stable because of you."

Of course. It had always been about Sienna. Every doctor's appointment Nathan had attended, every concerned look, every gentle touch it was all for her. I'd been so blind, mistaking manipulation for love, captivity for family.

But not anymore. As I looked at the cake sitting on the table, those innocent-looking cupcakes that would seal my fate, I made a decision. They wanted to play the long game? I'd show them what patience really looked like.

I smiled at Nathan, at Sienna, at their parents. Let them think they'd won. Let them believe I was still their naive, grateful little orphan.

Because starting tomorrow, everything would change. They'd spent fifteen years setting their trap. Now it was my turn.

And I would make sure they regretted every lie.

title:
The Sky She Never Flew.

Amina had paper planes all over her room.
Dozens of them. Some folded from old WAEC past questions, some from the back of her aviation magazines, some from the brown paper her mother used to wrap suya. They hung from string on her ceiling, and every time the ceiling fan turned, they dipped and dove like a squadron.
From age 8, she would climb onto their zinc roof in Kano after Maghrib. The heat of the day would still be rising from the metal, but she didn't care. She'd stand with her arms stretched wide, face tilted up, watching the big jets carve white lines across the purple sky.
"One day," she told her little brother Yusuf, who always sat beside her with a torch, "I'm going to be up there. Not looking up. Looking down."
Yusuf would laugh. "You'll crash."
"I won't," Amina said. "Pilots don't crash. They land."
She was serious about it. While other girls in her class talked about weddings and Ankara, Amina talked about lift and drag and air traffic control. She was first in Maths and Physics three years running. She saved every naira from selling zobo and kunu after school. 500 naira here, 1000 there. It all went into a blue tin under her bed labeled Flight School.
In SS3, she got the admission letter.
Nigerian College of Aviation Technology, Zaria.
Provisional Admission.
She held it to her chest and ran to her father.
Baba looked at it for a long time. He didn't smile.
"Flying planes is men's work," he said finally. "Who will marry you if you're always in the sky?"
Two weeks later, Alhaji Suleiman came for dinner.

Are We Actually Happy,Or Are We Just Distracted
excerpt: When was the last time you sat alone with no phone, no music, no TikTok, no Instagram, and no one to talk to?Just you and your thoughts.For some of us, that sounds uncomfortable. We are constantly scr…
content:
When was the last time you sat alone with no phone, no music, no TikTok, no Instagram, and no one to talk to?Just you and your thoughts.For some of us, that sounds uncomfortable.

We are constantly scrolling, chatting, watching videos, listening to music, going out, or looking for something to keep us busy.

But sometimes I wonder…

Are we actually happy, or are we just distracted?

We laugh at memes.

We post pictures.

We say “I'm good” when someone asks.

But behind all of that, some of us are tired.

Tired of pretending.

Tired of comparing.

Tired of trying to have everything figured out.

And maybe that's why silence feels uncomfortable.

Because when everything gets quiet, we finally hear the thoughts we've been avoiding.

Being distracted isn't necessarily bad. Everyone needs entertainment and a break sometimes.

But don't become so busy escaping your feelings that you forget to understand them.

Maybe happiness isn't always about having more things to do.

Maybe sometimes it's simply being at peace with yourself.

So tonight, put your phone down for a few minutes.

Ask yourself honestly:

“Am I happy… or have I just been keeping myself busy?”

Your answer might surprise you. ❤️

title: Hilda Baci vs Seyi Vibez: How a Comment About Food Turned Into a Legal Threat
excerpt: What started as Seyi Vibez’s clash with Dapper Music took an unexpected turn after comments about Hilda Baci prompted her lawyers to demand a retraction, apology and removal of the posts.
content:
What began as Seyi Vibez’s public criticism of his former music executive, Dapper, has taken an unexpected turn, with celebrity chef Hilda Baci dragged into the controversy and her lawyers demanding that the singer remove what they described as defamatory posts.

The dispute escalated after Seyi Vibez mentioned Hilda Baci in a series of posts on X on August 14, 2026, while discussing the wider controversy surrounding Dapper Music and allegations involving artistes’ earnings and catalogue money. 

Days later, lawyers acting for Hilda Baci sent a letter to Seyi Vibez demanding that the posts be taken down, followed by a public apology and retraction. Seyi Vibez has since deleted the posts, adding another twist to an already heated entertainment-industry dispute. 

What Did Seyi Vibez Say?

Seyi Vibez entered the conversation while reacting to allegations surrounding Dapper Music, a controversy that has involved former artistes and claims concerning money, royalties and music catalogues.

In his posts, the singer criticised Dapper and said he was grateful to have left the arrangement earlier.

He also made references to alleged spiritual manipulation before turning his attention to Hilda Baci.

In one of the posts, Seyi Vibez alleged that he had eaten food associated with Hilda Baci and claimed the experience had almost killed him.

He also made a separate allegation involving Hilda Baci’s body and money allegedly connected to artistes’ catalogues.

Those claims were made publicly on X but were not independently established by the reports reviewed for this article. 

The comments quickly shifted attention away from the original dispute involving Dapper and towards Hilda Baci.

And that is where things became more serious.

Why Did Hilda Baci Take Issue With It?

Hilda Baci was not the original focus of the dispute between Seyi Vibez and Dapper, but her name became directly involved after the singer made the posts.

An entertainment lawyer who reacted publicly questioned why Hilda had been dragged into the matter, describing the comment as unfair. He also stated that Hilda was no longer in a relationship with Dapper. 

The development raised a broader question: if Seyi Vibez's grievances were primarily about his former dealings with Dapper, why bring Hilda Baci into the conversation?

That question became even more significant after Hilda's legal representatives got involved.

Hilda Baci's Lawyers Step In

On August 15, law firm Olaniwun Ajayi LP reportedly wrote to Seyi Vibez on behalf of Hilda Baci.

According to the letter's contents, the lawyers accused the singer of publishing defamatory, malicious, and false statements about their client on X. They specifically referred to two posts published on August 14.

The lawyers reportedly said the posts had reached millions of people, with the two posts collectively attracting approximately 4.3 million views, 7,100 reposts, 3,000 comments and 45,000 likes.

They also alleged that the posts had resulted in harassment and abusive messages being directed at Hilda, causing reputational harm and distress. The lawyers demanded that Seyi Vibez permanently delete the posts, issue a public apology and retraction, and ask his followers to stop harassing Hilda Baci.

Provide a written undertaking not to repeat or circulate similar allegations.

The reported letter gave the singer three days to comply and warned that further legal action could follow if he failed to do so.

Then Seyi Vibez Deleted the Posts

The latest development has added another layer to the story.

According to a report published on Thursday, August 20, Seyi Vibez has deleted the posts concerning Hilda Baci following the demands from her lawyers.

The deletion is significant because it came after the legal letter demanding that the statements be removed.

However, deleting the posts does not by itself establish that Seyi Vibez admitted wrongdoing, nor does it settle whether any further legal action will follow.

The available reports reviewed for this article do not establish that a court case has been concluded or that a court has made a finding against the singer.

How a Food Comment Became a Bigger Celebrity Dispute

What makes the controversy particularly interesting is how quickly the story moved away from its original subject.

The wider dispute involved allegations concerning Dapper Music and financial dealings with artistes. Seyi Vibez's comments brought Hilda Baci into that conversation through allegations about food and catalogue money.

The food allegation, in particular, became a talking point because Hilda Baci is known primarily for her work as a celebrity chef.

For her, therefore, a public claim suggesting that food she prepared almost caused serious harm could potentially affect how members of the public perceive her brand.

At the same time, Seyi Vibez's comments were part of a much broader public dispute involving his former music executive, meaning the Hilda Baci controversy cannot be completely separated from the larger Dapper Music saga.

What Happens Next?

For now, the most concrete development is that the controversial posts have reportedly been deleted.

Whether that will be the end of the matter remains unclear.

Hilda Baci's lawyers reportedly demanded more than just deletion. They also requested an apology, retraction, a request to followers to stop harassment, and a written undertaking not to repeat similar allegations.

The available reports do not yet establish whether all those demands have been fulfilled.

What is clear, however, is that a controversy that initially appeared to be another chapter in the ongoing dispute surrounding Dapper Music has now created a separate legal dimension involving one of Nigeria's best-known celebrity chefs.

And with Seyi Vibez's posts already reaching millions of people before their removal, the conversation is unlikely to disappear immediately.

So, what do you think? Was Hilda Baci right to involve her lawyers, or should the matter have been resolved privately?
