title: Go and Wash Again, You Still Smell Like Him
excerpt: Chinaza knew something was wrong the moment she saw the message.She had only picked up her boyfriend's phone to check the time, but the notification sitting on …
content:
Chinaza knew something was wrong the moment she saw the message.

She had only picked up her boyfriend's phone to check the time, but the notification sitting on the screen had been enough to make her stomach turn. Baby, I miss you already. Last night was amazing. She stared at it for what felt like forever, waiting for the words to rearrange themselves into something less painful. They didn't. There were more messages when she opened the chat. Pictures. Voice notes. Plans for another night together. Things he had never said to her, things she suddenly realized he had probably been saying to someone else while she was at home calling him the love of her life.

"Who is she?" Chinaza asked when he walked into the room.

He looked at her, then at his phone in her hand.

For a second, neither of them spoke.

Then he sighed. "So you've gone through my phone?"

"Who is she?"

"Chinaza, abeg."

"Who is she?"

He snatched the phone from her hand and tossed it on the bed. "She's someone I'm seeing."

The words landed harder than a slap.

Chinaza laughed, but it came out broken. "Someone you're seeing?"

"Yes."

"Since when?"

He shrugged. That shrug broke something inside her.

She cried. She shouted. She asked him what she had done wrong. She reminded him of everything they had been through, every sacrifice she had made, every time she had chosen him even when choosing herself would have been easier. He stood there looking irritated, as though her heartbreak was an inconvenience he had somewhere else to be.

That night, Chinaza sent him messages even though they were sleeping under the same roof.

Please, let's talk

I'm sorry if I did something.

Please don't do this to us.

I love you

Please.

By morning, there were paragraphs upon paragraphs on her screen. She had begged until she had no dignity left to lose.

He read them.

Then he looked at her and said, "Pack your things and leave.

She stared at him. "Where am I supposed to go?"

"Wetin concern me?"

And that was the worst part.

It wasn't the cheating.

It wasn't even the fact that he had stopped loving her.

It was knowing exactly where she would have to go if she left. Home. Her father's house.

Chinaza stood in the middle of his room with her bag in her hand for almost an hour, staring at the door. She could still hear her father's voice in her head. She could still remember the sound of her mother's cries behind the thin walls. She could remember the bruises her mother hid beneath long sleeves, the excuses she made for him, the way she always said, "It's okay, my daughter. Your father is just angry."

It was never okay.

But Chinaza had nowhere else to go, so she went home.

The compound was unusually quiet when she arrived. She pushed the door open and stepped inside.

Then she heard the shouting.

"You be good for nothing!"

Her mother's voice followed, weak and trembling. "Please..."

"Ị ga anwụ!"

Chinaza dropped her bag.

She ran into the sitting room and froze.

Her father had both hands around her mother's neck.

"Mummy!"

Her father turned.

"You again?" he spat.

"Leave her!"

"Get out of my house."

"You are killing her!"

He shoved her mother against the wall. "I regret marrying someone like you!" he screamed. "All these years, what have you given me? You no fit born male pikin for me!"

Her mother sobbed.

Something inside Chinaza snapped. She rushed forward and tried to pull him away, but her father pushed her with so much force that she stumbled backwards and hit her back against the ceramic table.

Pain shot through her body.

For a moment, everything went silent.

She heard her mother's frightened voice. "Chinaza..."

She didn't answer. She stood up slowly and walked into the kitchen, opened the drawer and came back with a knife.

Her father barely had time to turn before she moved.

One second. Two.

Then everything changed.

He staggered backwards, his hands flying instinctively to his neck. A strangled sound escaped him before his body gave way and hit the floor.

Chinaza stared at him. She couldn't hear anything anymore. Not her mother screaming.

Not even her own breathing.

She only remembered the first time her father slapped her mother. The second even the third.

The night he broke a wooden chair over her back.

The mornings her mother wore sunglasses indoors.

The nights Chinaza pretended to be asleep because she was too afraid to come out of her room.

She remembered every single one and before she realized what she was doing, she had raised the knife again.

Once. Twice. Again and again.

Her mother screamed her name, but Chinaza couldn't stop.

"Chinaza!"

Again.

"Chinaza, biko!"

Again.

"Stop!"

Her mother finally grabbed her from behind, trembling violently as she held her daughter's arm. "E don do, my child."

Chinaza's fingers loosened and the knife fell from her hand.

She looked at her mother.

Both women were crying.

Her mother pulled her into her arms.

"It's okay," she whispered, even though nothing about the room was okay.

Chinaza didn't know how long she stayed there.

Eventually, her mother gently pushed her away.

"Go and wash yourself."

Chinaza obeyed. She stood beneath the shower for what felt like hours, scrubbing her skin until it turned red. She washed her hands again and again. She washed her hair. She washed her face.

When she finally came back into the sitting room, everything looked different.

The floor was clean. The furniture had been moved.

The knife was gone and her father was no longer there.

Her mother had cleaned everything.

She had wrapped his body tightly and was standing beside it, staring at Chinaza.

There was something different in her eyes.

Something Chinaza couldn't understand.

She took one step forward. "Mummy..."

Her mother looked her up and down.

Then she said quietly, "Go and wash again."

Chinaza froze.

"You still smell like him."

title: THE HEALTH HABITS YOU KEEP POSTPONING WILL EVENTUALLY BECOME HEALTH PROBLEMS
excerpt: I'll Deal With It When It Gets Serious" Is Doing More Damage Than You Think
content:
You have felt that twinge in your knee for months and just changed how you walk instead of getting it checked. You know your blood pressure has not been tested in years but you feel "fine," so why bother. You have been meaning to fix your sleep, your diet, that persistent lower back ache, for so long that "I'll start soon" has quietly become a permanent state rather than a temporary one.

If any of that sounds like your own internal script, keep reading.

THE HABITS THAT DON'T ANNOUNCE THEIR COST

Skipping a checkup doesn't hurt today. Eating badly for another week does not hurt today. Ignoring that ache does not hurt today. That's exactly what makes these habits so easy to postpone, the consequence is not attached to the action in any way you can feel immediately. There's no instant penalty, so your brain files it as "not urgent," even when it's exactly the kind of thing that becomes urgent later, all at once. Health problems built from neglect rarely arrive as a single dramatic moment. They arrive as the sum of a hundred small postponements, each one individually reasonable, collectively expensive.

WHY "I FEEL FINE" IS NOT THE REASSURANCE YOU THINK IT IS

Here's something worth sitting with, feeling fine and being fine are not the same thing, and a lot of the health conditions people fear most develop quietly, symptom free, for years before they announce themselves. By the time something "suddenly" goes wrong, it usually was not sudden at all, it was just finally loud enough to notice. Waiting for your body to alert you before you take it seriously means outsourcing your health decisions to the moment things are already further along than you'd like.

THE REAL REASON PEOPLE POSTPONE PREVENTIVE CARE

It's rarely pure laziness. It's often a mix of cost, fear, and a strange kind of denial, if you don't get the test done, you don't have to know the answer, and not knowing feels safer than a diagnosis you're not ready to face. There's also the simple exhaustion of adult life, preventive care requires effort now for a benefit you can't see or feel, competing against a hundred other things that feel more immediately pressing. None of these reasons are irrational. They are just reasons that stop working the moment the thing you were avoiding actually shows up.

THE UNCOMFORTABLE TRUTH YOU'RE IGNORING

The version of you dealing with a manageable issue today is in a far better position than the version of you dealing with the same issue three years from now, after it's had time to become something bigger, more expensive, and harder to reverse. Early is almost always cheaper in money, in treatment options, in how much of your life it disrupts than late. Postponing is not neutral. It's actively trading a smaller, easier problem now for a larger, harder one later, even if it doesn't feel like a trade while you are making it. I'm sure you understand my point here.

WHY PREVENTION FEELS OPTIONAL WHEN IT IS NOT

Prevention does not compete well against urgency. A checkup will always lose to a deadline, a bill, a family obligation, because none of those things will punish you for skipping the checkup this week. The cost only shows up later, disconnected from the decision that caused it, which makes it almost impossible to feel the stakes in the moment you're actually choosing.

This is why "just prioritize your health" rarely works as advice. The problem is not priorities. It's that the consequence is invisible until it isn't.

What Taking This Seriously Actually Looks Like: Not a total health overhaul overnight that rarely survives past two weeks anyway. It's something smaller and more sustainable:

- Pick the one thing you have been postponing the longest: The checkup, the test, the dentist visit and book it this week, not "soon."

- Treat small, recurring symptoms as information, not inconvenience: A pain that keeps returning is trying to tell you something specific; it's not just bad luck. Check it.

- Separate "I feel okay" from "I'm actually okay": The first is a feeling. The second requires occasionally checking. Know the difference.

SO WHAT NOW?

Think of the one health habit you have been quietly postponing the longest, not the trendy one, the actual one. Ask yourself honestly what you are waiting for, and whether waiting has ever actually made it easier to deal with. Usually, it has not. It's just made the eventual conversation with yourself a little more urgent, and a little less optional.

So the better you stop postponing, the better your health would be.

title: HOW TO PROCESS YOUR AFFIDAVIT FROM THE COMFORT OF YOUR HOME
excerpt: Do you know you can process your affidavit without necessarily having to visit the court? Read the full story to find out.
content:
You may not necessarily need to visit a court physically to begin the process of obtaining an affidavit.

The Federal High Court of Nigeria has an online portal that allows applicants to initiate certain affidavit-related processes from the comfort of their homes using a smartphone or laptop.

Despite this option being available, many Nigerians are still unaware that they can start the process online.

If you need an affidavit, here is a simple step-by-step guide to getting started.

1. Visit the Federal High Court Online Portal

Go to portal.fhc.gov.ng/index and create an account.

Enter your details correctly, verify your account and log in.

2. Update Your Profile

After logging in, go to your dashboard and select Profile.

Update your personal information and ensure that the details provided are accurate before starting your application.

3. Provide Your Required Information

Complete all the required fields carefully.

You may also be required to upload documents such as your passport photograph and a valid means of identification.

Save your information once you have completed the required sections.

4. Start a New Application

Return to the homepage and select the available application option.

Choose New Application to view the affidavit services available on the portal.

Select the type of affidavit you need and follow the instructions provided to complete the application.

5. Receive Your Affidavit

After successfully completing the process and any required steps, the affidavit may be sent to the email address associated with your application.

You can then save the electronic copy or print it when a physical copy is required.

No More Unnecessary Movement?

The online process can make it easier to initiate an affidavit application without immediately having to travel to a court.

However, applicants should carefully check the requirements for the specific affidavit they need, as procedures and requirements may vary.

Have you used the Federal High Court online affidavit portal before? Share your experience in the comments.

Whether that will be the end of the matter remains unclear.

Hilda Baci's lawyers reportedly demanded more than just deletion. They also requested an apology, retraction, a request to followers to stop harassment and a written undertaking not to repeat similar allegations. 

The available reports do not yet establish whether all those demands have been fulfilled.

What is clear, however, is that a controversy that initially appeared to be another chapter in the ongoing dispute surrounding Dapper Music has now created a separate legal dimension involving one of Nigeria's best-known celebrity chefs.

And with Seyi Vibez's posts already reaching millions of people before their removal, the conversation is unlikely to disappear immediately.

So, what do you think? Was Hilda Baci right to involve her lawyers, or should the matter have been resolved privately?

title: Honestly Music Is Our Time Machine
excerpt: Through music we can turn back the hands of time
content:
The Time Machine in a song

Music is the closest thing we have to turning back the hands of time.

One song is all it takes. A melody you have not heard in years begins to play, and suddenly you are somewhere else. Not just remembering it, but feeling it. The heat of that summer. The smell of that room. The exact shape of a heartbreak you thought you had outgrown. The song does not describe the past; it reconstructs it. It rebuilds the moment around you, brick by brick, note by note, until you are standing inside it again.

That is not nostalgia. That is engineering.

A time machine does not have to move your body through years. It only has to move your consciousness. And music does exactly that. It captures time the way a photograph captures light. It freezes a feeling in a three-minute frame and stores it safely until the right pair of ears comes along to unlock it. Play an old hit, and you are not just listening. You are traveling.

So maybe the creative ones, the musicians and photographers, are the real engineers of time.

A songwriter builds a machine without knowing it. They sit in a small room with a guitar or a laptop, chasing a feeling they cannot name, and they produce something that will outlast the moment that inspired it. Years later, someone in another country, in another life, presses play and is pulled backward. The songwriter becomes an architect of memory. The producer becomes a pilot. The singer’s voice becomes the engine hum.

A photographer does the same with silence. One click, and a fraction of a second becomes permanent. A laugh that would have vanished. A street that no longer exists. A face that has since changed. The photograph does not move, but every time you look at it, you move. You return. You stand beside whoever you were when it was taken.

Both of them are building machines that bend time. Not with science, but with attention. They notice what the rest of us are too busy to preserve, then they preserve it so well that it becomes transportable.

And the beautiful thing is that we all get to operate these machines. We curate our own time travel. The song at the wedding. The album on the road trip. The photograph tucked into a wallet. We become engineers too, building private railways back to the people and places we cannot reach any other way.

So yes, it is safe to say it. Musicians and photographers are time machine engineers. They do not wear lab coats. They do not announce what they are building. But they build portals all the same, and they leave them open for the rest of us, waiting on a shuffle, hiding in a frame, ready to take us back the moment we need to go.

title: A COLD NIGHT IN LONDON
excerpt: Four strangers. One impossible job. And a fifth person who was never supposed to be there. — ( Thriller Series )
content:
PART ONE: THE INVITATION

London was freezing the night Daniel Cross decided he had made a terrible mistake.

Not the dramatic kind of freezing you see in films, where snow falls beautifully beneath streetlights.

This was worse.

This was London freezing.

Cold rain getting into your shoes. Wind finding its way through your coat. Pavements shining under orange streetlights while every sensible person was somewhere indoors, drinking something hot and pretending they had nowhere else to be.

Daniel had been standing outside a closed café in Southwark for eleven minutes.

He had counted.

Eleven minutes and thirty-two seconds, to be precise.

He checked his phone again.

Nothing.

He put it back in his pocket.

Three seconds later, he took it out again.

Still nothing.

“Brilliant.”

A couple walking past looked at him.

Daniel pretended he hadn’t spoken.

He wasn’t usually the sort of man who talked to himself.

At least, that’s what he told himself.

He looked at the building across the road.

Old brick. Black windows. Nothing remarkable.

That was the point.

The message had instructed him to meet someone there at 11:15 p.m.

No name.

No company.

No explanation.

Just an address and a sentence:

Come alone.

Daniel had immediately assumed it was a scam.

Then came the second message.

You will be paid £20,000 for one night’s work.

He had stared at it for almost a full minute.

Then he’d laughed.

Twenty thousand pounds.

For one night.

Nobody offered twenty thousand pounds for something innocent.

Well, almost nobody.

Daniel had spent the last six months trying to convince himself that his financial problems were temporary.

His landlord had stopped believing him around month four.

His bank had stopped believing him even earlier.

And tomorrow morning, unless he found £3,800 from somewhere, he was going to lose his flat.

So when the third message arrived, he read it twice.

You don’t need to know who we are. You only need to decide whether £20,000 is worth your curiosity.

Daniel had replied before he could talk himself out of it.

Where?

The answer came immediately.

The address.

11:15 p.m.

Come alone.

Now it was 11:27.

And nobody had shown up.

Daniel looked at his watch.

“I’m going home.”

He said it firmly.

Then he waited another thirty seconds.

Because apparently his principles had a thirty-second cancellation policy.

His phone vibrated.

This time, he almost dropped it.

UNKNOWN NUMBER

A message.

Don’t leave.

Daniel looked around.

The street was quiet.

Too quiet.

A bus rumbled somewhere in the distance.

A window opened above him.

Someone shouted something unintelligible.

Then the window slammed shut.

Daniel typed:

Who are you?

The reply appeared.

Someone who knows you need the money.

His jaw tightened.

He typed again.

How do you know that?

Three dots appeared.

Disappeared.

Appeared again.

Then:

Because I know what happened at Meridian.

Daniel stopped breathing for a second.

The rain suddenly seemed much louder.

Nobody knew about Meridian.

Not really.

There had been an investigation.

There had been interviews.

There had been lawyers.

And there had been a very carefully written statement that Daniel had signed after being told, repeatedly, that it was “in everyone’s best interests.”

He hadn’t thought about Meridian in months.

Or at least he had tried not to.

He stared at the message.

What do you want?

This time, there was no typing indicator.

His phone rang.

Same unknown number.

Daniel answered.

“Hello?”

A man’s voice.

Older.

Calm.

“Walk to the corner.”

Daniel didn’t move.

“Why?”

“Because the man watching you has been standing there for seven minutes.”

Daniel’s eyes moved slowly toward the opposite pavement.

A man stood beneath a shop awning.

Dark coat.

Umbrella.

Face hidden.

Daniel’s stomach tightened.

“How do I know you’re not the person watching me?”

“You don’t.”

A pause.

Then the man on the phone added:

“But if I were watching you, Daniel, you wouldn’t have noticed him.”

The call ended.

Daniel looked across the street again.

The man with the umbrella was gone.

“Wonderful.”

He rubbed his face.

“This is how documentaries start.”

He stepped away from the café.

One street.

Then another.

His phone rang again.

“Keep walking.”

Daniel stopped.

“I have questions.”

“You’ll get answers.”

“When?”

“When you’re inside.”

“Inside what?”

Silence.

Daniel heard a car approaching behind him.

Black Mercedes.

It slowed.

Stopped.

The rear window lowered.

A woman was sitting in the back.

Late twenties, maybe early thirties.

Dark hair.

Black coat.

She looked at Daniel as though she’d been waiting for him for hours.

Then she glanced at the empty pavement beside him.

“You’re Daniel?”

He hesitated.

“Yes.”

She opened the door.

“Get in.”

Daniel stared at her.

“No.”

She raised an eyebrow.

“No?”

“I don’t get into random cars.”

She looked genuinely confused.

“Then why did you come to a random address at midnight because an anonymous person offered you twenty thousand pounds?”

Daniel opened his mouth.

Closed it.

“That’s… different.”

“How?”

“I don’t know yet.”

For the first time, she smiled.

It wasn’t a warm smile.

It was the smile of someone who had just discovered something mildly entertaining.

“Get in, Daniel.”

He looked at the car.

Then at the road behind him.

Then at his phone.

£20,000.

Meridian.

Someone knew.

He got in.

The door shut.

The woman leaned forward.

“Seat belt.”

Daniel stared at her.

“Seriously?”

“Yes.”

“I thought we were committing a crime.”

“We haven’t committed anything yet.”

Daniel looked at her.

She looked back.

“Yet?”

She smiled again.

“Good. You’re paying attention.”

The car pulled away.

For several minutes, neither of them spoke.

London passed outside the window.

Wet streets.

Closed shops.

Red buses disappearing into the darkness.

The woman finally broke the silence.

“My name is Mara.”

Daniel nodded.

“Daniel.”

“I know.”

“Right.”

He looked out the window.

“Where are we going?”

Mara didn’t answer.

Instead, she took a phone from her coat pocket and checked the screen.

Daniel noticed something.

A photograph.

Four faces.

He only saw it for a second before Mara turned the phone away.

But it was enough.

There were four people in the photograph.

Mara.

Daniel.

Two strangers.

Daniel looked at her.

“You knew I’d come.”

“Yes.”

“You knew my name.”

“Yes.”

“You knew about Meridian.”

“Yes.”

“And you have photographs of me.”

Mara slipped the phone back into her pocket.

“Yes.”

Daniel stared at her.

“Should I be concerned?”

Mara considered the question.

“Probably.”

The car continued through the rain.

Daniel looked through the rear window.

For a moment, he thought he saw another car following them.

Black.

No headlights.

Then it disappeared around a corner.

He turned back.

Mara was watching him.

“You saw it too,” she said.

Daniel swallowed.

“Saw what?”

Mara smiled.

“Good answer.”

The Mercedes continued into the night.

Neither of them noticed the figure standing beneath the awning of the café they had left behind.

The figure took out a phone.

Made one call.

And said only four words:

“The first one came.”

A voice answered.

“Good.”

A pause.

Then:

“Bring me the other three.”

END OF PART ONE.

title: The Closing Hour Danfo
excerpt: The Danfo at Five-ThirtyThe conductor hanging off the blue danfo at five-thirty in the evening has a name, but nobody asks. We just call him the conductor with …
content:
The Danfo at Five-Thirty

The conductor hanging off the blue danfo at five-thirty in the evening has a name, but nobody asks. We just call him the conductor with the grey singlet, because his shirt glows against the smoke and the rust. He shouts "Obalende! Obalende! One hundre' naira!" like a song he has sung so long it has become part of his body. His palm is dusty from clutching crumpled notes. When he looks at me, his eyes do not stop working — they are still scanning for the next passenger, the next police checkpoint, the next pothole.

I squeeze between a woman selling phone chargers and a man whose lap is a filing cabinet of brown envelopes. The woman is asleep against the window, her gele tied so tight it looks like it is holding her thoughts together. The man opens one envelope, reads half a sentence, sighs, and closes it. Lagos has taught him this: not everything urgent deserves your full attention.

The danfo lurches. A container truck blocks the intersection near Iponri and the driver — a small man with a beard that does not match his face — begins to preach. Not religion. Traffic. "Na because of this kain nonsense person dey miss flight o." Nobody argues. In Lagos traffic, every driver is a philosopher, every delay is a conspiracy, and every passenger is a captive audience.

Beside me, a girl of maybe ten is peeling an orange with the patience of someone much older. She does it in one long spiral, the way my mother used to, and the smell hits me somewhere below the ribs. Suddenly I am eight again, in our compound in Ibadan, watching Mama peel oranges while she argued with her sister about a wedding that should never have happened. The air smelled of kerosene, of frying akara, of something burning three streets away that nobody would ever explain.

The girl catches me staring and offers me a segment.

"No, thank you," I say.

She shrugs and pops it into her own mouth. Good. A Lagos child knows not to trust strangers who stare too long.

We start moving again. The conductor slaps the roof of the bus twice — kpom kpom — and the driver obeys the language they have built between them. The sky above the Third Mainland Bridge is doing that thing it does in harmattan season: turning from orange to purple without asking permission, smearing the clouds like a child with access to too many crayons. Someone on the bus starts playing Fuji music from a phone speaker that has survived worse things than this evening. A woman in the front row hisses. A man in the back row laughs. Both sounds are Lagos. Both are honest.

I get down at Obalende, and the conductor does not count my change properly. He gives me fifty naira extra by mistake. I look at the coin in my palm. In this city, you do not return money to a danfo conductor — he will accuse you of witchcraft. So I keep it, but I do not spend it. It sits in my pocket like a tiny debt I owe to the evening.

The bridge lights come on, one by one, as if Lagos is remembering something beautiful and deciding, slowly, to show it.

title: WHAT HAPPENS WHEN YOU CONSTANTLY IGNORE YOUR MENTAL HEALTH?
excerpt: You don't have to completely fall apart before you admit that something isn't okay.
content:
I know you always tell yourself you are just tired. Then you add "it's just a busy season". Then it's just how adulthood feels. Somewhere along the way, "I'm not okay" got translated into a dozen more acceptable sentences, none of which actually said what was true. If you've ever caught yourself explaining away the same exhaustion for months, this is for you. Ride with me.

IT DOESN'T ANNOUNCE ITSELF

Nobody wakes up one day and decides to stop dealing with their mental health. It happens in small, reasonable sounding decisions, skipping the conversation because there's no time, numbing out with your phone instead of sitting with the feeling, telling a friend "I'm fine" because explaining felt like too much work that day. Each one seems harmless. Stacked over months, they become a pattern, the quiet, ongoing decision to postpone yourself.

THE BODY KEEPS THE RECEIPTS

Here's what people rarely connect until much later, the headaches that don't have a clear cause, the sudden irritability over small things, the sleep that never feels like enough no matter how many hours you get. That's not randomness. That's your mind sending the bill through your body because you stopped answering it directly. Ignored emotional exhaustion does not disappear. Yes it doesn't. It relocates. It shows up as snapping at someone who didn't deserve it, as dreading your own bed, as feeling flat about things that used to interest you.

THE WITHDRAWAL NOBODY TALKS ABOUT

At some point, ignoring your mental health stops being passive and starts costing you people. You cancel plans, not because you are busy, but because showing up as yourself feels like too much effort. You reply later and later to messages. You get good at being present in the room while being completely somewhere else. The dangerous part is that withdrawal feels like relief at first, fewer demands, fewer people to perform for. But isolation doesn't fix exhaustion. Trust me it doesn't at all. It just removes the witnesses to it.

THE COPING MECHANISM THAT LOOKS LIKE NOTHING

Nobody pictures the version of coping that looks ordinary, the doom scrolling until 3am because silence feels unbearable, the overworking that gets praised as ambition, raising the volume of the music to shut up the voices in your head, the constant need for noise or company because being alone with your own thoughts has started to feel unsafe. These don't look like a crisis. They look like a personality. That's exactly why they last so long, nobody, including you, questions a coping mechanism that's dressed up as a work ethic or a busy schedule.

THE UNCOMFORTABLE TRUTH

Ignoring your mental health does not make you strong. It just delays the conversation and raises the interest. The version of you that finally has to deal with it later is usually more depleted, more isolated, and further from asking for help than the version who could have addressed it earlier, when it was smaller and less tangled. Waiting for a "better time" to deal with how you're actually doing is often just fear wearing a scheduling excuse.

SO WHAT NOW? YOU MAY ASK

Not a checklist. No not that. Just this, the next time you catch yourself explaining away how you feel, "I'm just tired," "I'm just busy" pause on the sentence before you finish it. Ask what you would be saying if you weren't trying to make it sound manageable. You don't have to fix everything today. But the moment you stop translating "I'm not okay" into something smaller, something quieter starts to shift. That's usually where it actually begins.

If any part of this hit close to home, please don't carry it alone. Talk to someone you trust, or reach out to a mental health professional.

Like. Follow. Comment. Share

title: Starting Over Is  Not a Sign Of Failure
excerpt: Sometimes a new beginning is proof that you are brave enough to choose yourself.
content:
The Fear of Starting Again

There is a particular kind of fear that comes with starting over.

It can show up when the plan you were so sure about suddenly fails apart. When the job doesn't work out. When a relationship ends. When you realize the dream you've been chasing no longer feels like your dream.

And sometimes, the hardest part isn't even the change itself.

It's wondering what people will think.

You may find yourself thinking, "What will they say?"

"Won't they think I failed?"

"Am I really going back to the beginning?"

Same has a way of arriving before courage does. But starting again doesn't make you a failure. It makes you human.

Life doesn't always move in a straight line. We imagine when we were younger. Sometimes you can take a turn you never expected. Sometimes, you have to let go of something you work incredibly hard for. Sometimes, you simply outgrow a version of yourself you once thought you'd be forever.

And yes, it can hurt.

You're allowed to be disappointed. You're allowed to grieve what didn't work out.

But don't mistake disappointment for defeat.

You are still here. And that means there is still something ahead of you.

A Different Path Does Not Mean a Wrong Path

We are often taught to believe that if we change direction, we've made a mistake.

But what if we haven't?

What if we simply know more now than we knew before?

Think about it.

The person you are today has experiences that the person you were five years ago didn't have. You've learned what you can tolerate. You've discovered what drains. You've learned what you actually want - and maybe, just as importantly, what you don’t want anymore.

That isn't failure.

That's growth.

Your career may change. Your plans may change. Your relationship may change. Even the dreams you once prayed for may look different when you finally get there.

And that's okay.

Instead of asking yourself, "where did I go wrong?" try asking:

"What did this season teach me?"

Then ask :

"What do I want to do differently this time?"

Those questions don't erase what happened.

They simply help you stop living inside it.

The Lessons You Carry With You

Starting over doesn't mean starting from zero.

Youbare not the same person who began the journey the first time.

You are carrying experience with you.

Maybe you learned how to recognize red flags sooner. Maybe you discovered that you are stronger than you thought. Maybe you learned that you need netter boundaries. Maybe you finally understand the kind of environment where you actually thrive.

Those lessons matter.

Even the painful ones.

Take a moment and think about the chapter you're leaving behind. What did it teach you?

Maybe it taught you to stop abandoning yourself just to keep other people happy. Maybe it taught you that every opportunity is meant to be taken.

Whatever it is, carry it forward.

You don’t have to carry the pain forever, but you carry the wisdom.

That's one of the beautiful things about starting again: you get to begin with more knowledge than you had before.

Nobody Sees the Courage Behind a New Beginning

From the outside, starting over can look easy.

People might only see you making a new decision. They don’t see the nights you spent questioning yourself. They don’t see the tears.

They don't see how difficult it was to admit that something wasn't working anymore. They don't see the courage it took to walk away, ask for help, learn something new, apply again, or simply get out of bed and try another day.

But you know.

You know how hard it has been to get here.

So don’t wait for everyone else to recognize your progress before you recognize it yourself. Celebrate the small things.

The application you finally submitted. The difficult conversation you finally had. The morning you got up even though you didn't feel motivated.

The first step toward something new.

They may look small to someone else, but you know what they cost you.

Ams sometimes, courage doesn't look dramatic. Sometimes, courage is simply saying: "I'm going to try again."

Give Yourself Permission to Begin Again

You don't need permission frome everyone around you to start a new chapter.

You need to give yourself permission. Permission to change your mind. Permission to take a different route. Permission to admit that something isn't working. Permission to begin again without being ashamed of the fact that you had to.

You don't have to fight out your entire future today.

Start small

Give Yourself one thing to work toward this week. Read for ten minutes. Learn something new. Update you CV. Apply for that opportunity. Start the project you've been putting off. Take a walk and clear you head.

One small step is still movement.

And when that familiar voice comes back saying, "You're starting over because you failed," answer it with something kinder:

"I'm not starting over because I failed. I'm starting over because I chose myself."

You may not believe it completely at first.

That's okay.

Keep choosing yourself anyway.

Three Small Steps You Cna Take

1. Write down five lessons from your last chapter.

Don't focus only on what went wrong. Ask yourself what you learned and how that lesson can help you moving forward.

2. Give yourself a 14-day experiment.

Instead of trying to change your entire life overnight, try one new habit, routine, or small projects for two weeks. See what happens.

3. Find someone who can keep you accountable.

Tell someone you trust what you're trying to accomplish. Sometimes having someone ask, "How is it going?" Is enough to keep you moving.

You Are Allowed to Begin Again

Maybe you're not where you thought you'd be by now. Maybe your life looks completely different from the picture you once had in your head.

That can be painful.

But it doesn't mean your story is over.

Sometimes the chapter you thought was your ending is simply the chapter that teaches you how to begin differently.

So if you have to start again, start.

Start scared.

Start slow.

Start without knowing exactly how everything will turn out.

Just start

Because sometimes the ending you feared is actually the beginning you needed.

title: Do You Believe In Love At First Sight
excerpt: Or should I walk again?
content:
I really thought love at first sight didn't exist until I experienced it myself.

Grab your popcorn. Let me tell you why.

After an exhausting week at my 9–5 job, I decided I deserved a little break. So, naturally, I took myself on a solo date that weekend and when I say I was excited, I mean excited.

I stood in front of my wardrobe for almost thirty minutes before finally settling on a fitted emerald-green midi dress with a sweetheart neckline that hugged my body in all the right places. I paired it with gold earrings, a tiny handbag and stiletto heels. Then sat in front of the mirror, dabbing my face with my big makeup brush.

Admiring myself, I said “Omoh, I be better package oo.”

I headed to this Victoria suites looking like somebody's spec. My dress was sitting perfectly, my makeup was giving, and honestly, I was feeling myself.

"10/10 across the board. Clock itt."

The place was beautiful. Soft lighting, elegant interiors and the kind of atmosphere that made you temporarily forget your bank account existed.

I settled into my seat, enjoying the view as the waiter handed me the menu. After making my very important decision, he returned a few minutes later with my food and as a Gen Z baddie, obviously the first thing I did was take pictures for TikTok.

Content first. Hunger later.

I had barely started eating when a voice interrupted me.

“Hi. Please, Is that seat taken?"

I froze.

It was a deep, smooth voice, the kind that sounded like it had no business coming from someone this fine.

Slowly, I looked up and my jaw nearly dropped and hit the floor because standing in front of me was the most ethereal man I had ever seen. Dark skin. Sharp jawline. Tall. Broad shoulders.

He was dressed in a perfectly fitted black tuxedo, looking like he had walked straight out of a movie and he smiled. "Oh my God" I muttered and for a second, I genuinely forgot how to breathe.

I think I was drooling.

“Are you okay?” he asked, his lips twitching into a smile.

No, absolutely not but I wasn't about to tell him that.

“I'm fine,” I managed to say.

"And no, it's not," I added referring to the chair opposite mine.

To be continued.

title: Women! We Think We are Special
excerpt: Sometimes the signs are there. We just don’t believe they apply to us.
content:
There is this particular kind of comment I have seen so many times on social media.

A woman will post about how her boyfriend cheated on his wife. Or how he was controlling with his ex. Or how he treated the woman before her terribly.

And then, somehow, he gets another girlfriend.

And the new girlfriend is in the comments saying something like:

“He would never do that to me.”

Or:

“You people don’t know him like I do.”

Or my personal favourite:

“Maybe his ex was the problem.”

I used to see these comments and think, How do you people do this?

How do you hear what a man has done to another woman and decide that you are somehow the exception?

How do you look at a pattern and confidently place yourself outside of it?

Well.

I understand now.

Because I became one of those women.

I think one of the reasons I never really liked dating what people would call the traditional Igbo man is because of the things that come with that stereotype. The whole idea that men are supposed to be in charge, women are supposed to listen, men can do certain things that women cannot, and somehow everybody is expected to just accept it.

I’m a feminist, so naturally, that kind of thinking and I don’t always get along.

Then I met my boyfriend.

And I loved him.

That made things a lot more complicated.

Because he wasn’t some horrible man who walked around announcing that he hated women.

He was actually nice to me.

We had our arguments, obviously. And some of our arguments were about women. Sometimes I would joke that it was like I was the feminist and he was the misogynist.

But I didn’t think much of it beyond that.

I thought, Okay, we just have different opinions.

And besides, he was good to me.

That’s the part that can really mess with your head.

Because how do you reconcile someone being nice to you with them having beliefs about women that you find completely ridiculous?

I decided they were separate things.

He could have questionable opinions about women and still be a good person.

And I could have my opinions about men and still be a good person.

Fair enough, right?

Except that sometimes people’s opinions tell you more about them than you want to know.

He had told me things about the women he had been with before me.

He wasn’t really a relationship person, he said. It was mostly sex. He told me about how he had treated women in the past. There were things he had done that, if I had heard about another man doing them, I probably would have judged him immediately.

But because it was him, I had context.

There was always context.

That’s just how he was before.

He’s different now.

That’s not how he treats me.

I remember telling him about women who would go to a man’s house or hotel and then decide they didn’t want to have sex, and the man would get angry and tell them to leave.

He told me he had done something like that before.

And somehow, I didn’t see it as the warning sign it probably was.

I thought, Well, he’s a man.

And that’s honestly embarrassing to admit.

Because what exactly was I expecting?

A man tells you he has treated women badly before, and your response is to mentally put yourself in a different category?

I wasn’t just another woman.

I was me.

Surely that meant something.

Then there were the things he did with me.

He monitored me.

He wanted to know which men I was talking to. He didn’t want me visiting male friends because, according to him, all these men wanted to sleep with me.

He didn’t want me talking to people I had previously been involved with. He wanted me to block my exes.

I would argue with him about it.

I’d tell him that talking to a man doesn’t automatically mean I’m sleeping with him. That I can have male friends. That if I had decided to keep some of my exes in my life, that was my business.

He didn’t really agree.

And the funny thing was, I once went through his phone and saw that he was also talking to girls.

So there I was, being interrogated about men while he had women in his own phone.

There were always questions.

Where are you?

Who are you with?

Send evidence.

And whenever I wanted to go somewhere and there was a possibility that men would be there, his mood would change.

He wouldn’t necessarily say, “I’m angry because there will be men there.”

But I knew.

I could feel it.

Still, I stayed in the space of he loves me.

Because he did nice things too.

He could be sweet.

He could be caring.

We could be completely fine one minute, laughing and being in love, and then suddenly we were having one of those arguments where I’m wondering how two people who love each other can have such completely different ideas about certain things.

There was even a time we were discussing a rape case.

I was trying to explain to him why the man was wrong for raping the woman.

His response was basically, Why did she go to the hotel if she wasn’t ready to sleep with him?

I remember being so frustrated.

I told him that going to a man’s hotel does not mean you have consented to sex. Giving someone access to you does not mean they have access to your body.

He disagreed.

He argued that if the man had given her money, she probably wouldn’t have reported him.

And I remember thinking, Okay, so if money was the issue, then give her the money.

But that wasn’t really the point.

We argued about it. It became heated.

And again, I filed it away as one of those things we simply disagreed about.

I didn’t stop and ask myself what that opinion actually said about how he understood women.

I think that’s what I did wrong.

I kept separating the things he believed from the man I believed he was.

Until one night, I couldn’t separate them anymore.

We had a disagreement.

Actually, disagreement is making it sound more serious than it was.

I had an attitude.

He had hit me on the head, and I was angry about it. So I was giving him attitude because, in my head, if he had just said sorry, I would have gotten over it.

It was one of those normal couple things that shouldn’t have turned into anything serious.

But it did.

And at about 4 a.m., this man I thought loved me chased me out of the house.

I remember looking at him and saying,

“You’re really doing this to me?”

I genuinely couldn’t understand it.

I was waiting for him to look at me and realise what he was doing.

Like maybe something would click.

Maybe he would remember that he loved me.

Maybe he would say, Come back inside.

He didn’t.

He chased me out.

He took back the money he had given me.

And while doing it, he was talking about his friend who had just come back from a club with a girl. He was talking about how his friend had met this girl and they were already having sex.

And basically, here I was, giving him attitude.

I remember thinking, What does that have to do with anything?

But I was standing there trying to understand how we had gone from being lovey-dovey to this.

How can someone look at you, someone they claim to love, and just switch like that?

I stayed there for a while thinking maybe he would change his mind.

Maybe he would come outside.

Maybe he would say sorry.

He didn’t.

I eventually left in the morning.

And this is probably the part that makes me look the most pathetic, but I’m going to say it anyway.

I was still the one who called him.

I was still the one who begged.

He didn’t even apologise until after I eventually told him how much what he had done hurt me.

And I think that was when something in my head finally shifted.

Not because I suddenly discovered that he was capable of being toxic.

I had known.

Not because I had never seen the signs.

I had.

Not because he hadn’t told me things about how he had treated women before me.

He had.

I just never thought those things would happen to me.

And that’s the thing about being the woman who thinks she’s special.

You don’t necessarily ignore the red flags.

Sometimes you see them perfectly.

You just believe they belong to someone else.

You hear him talk about his ex and think, I’m not like her.

You hear him talk about how he used to treat women and think, But that’s before me.

You hear his opinions about women and think, That’s just his opinion. He would never treat me that way.

You see him controlling and jealous and think, It’s because he loves me.

You hear all the stories and somehow convince yourself that your presence has changed the entire pattern.

Because you’re special.

Because he loves you.

Because what you have is different.

And maybe sometimes it really is different.

People can change. People can grow. People can become better than who they used to be.

But I think there is something dangerous about needing to believe someone has changed when they have given you very little reason to believe it.

I think we sometimes listen to what a man says about other women only to find out what he thinks about us.

And that’s where we get it wrong.

We think the important thing is how he talks about us.

“You’re different.”

“I’ve never felt this way before.”

“You’re not like the other girls.”

But maybe we should pay more attention to how he talks about women when he isn’t trying to impress us.

How does he talk about his ex?

How does he talk about women who reject him?

How does he talk about women who sleep with him?

How does he talk about women who don’t?

How does he understand consent?

How does he react when a woman tells him no?

How does he behave when he is angry?

Because love can make you feel very special.

It can also make you very stupid.

And I say that with love because, honestly, I don’t think I am any better than the women I used to judge in those comment sections.

I used to wonder how they could see what a man had done before them and still believe it would never happen to them.

Now I understand.

I got my own fair share of the cake.

The same thing I had watched happen to other women, the thing I had thought, Oh, he would never do that to me, happened to me too.

And maybe worse.

Not because I was stupid.

Not because those other women were stupid.

Maybe sometimes we are just so desperate to believe that we are the exception that we forget something very simple:

A person can tell you who they are without telling you directly that they’re talking about you.

Sometimes they’re talking about their ex.

Sometimes they’re talking about another woman.

Sometimes they’re telling you a story about something they did years ago.

Sometimes they’re giving you their opinion about consent, relationships, women, loyalty, respect.

And you’re sitting there thinking,

That’s not me.

He wouldn’t do that to me.

I’m different.

Maybe we aren’t as special as we think we are.

title: Am I Weird? How I Screwed My First Date (3)
excerpt: There are some things you should never say on a first date.
content:
I knew immediately that I'd said the wrong thing.

The kind of wrong thing where you wish you could grab the words out of the air and shove them back into your mouth.

He looked at me.

I looked at him.

Silence.

That horrible, uncomfortable silence.

I wanted to disappear.

“I'm sorry,” I finally said, laughing awkwardly. “That came out wrong.”

He laughed too.

“It's fine.”

But was it?

Because now I was replaying what I'd just said in my head.

Why did I say that?

Why couldn't I have just kept quiet?

This was exactly what I'd been afraid of.

I'd spent the whole day worrying about being awkward, and now I was actively proving myself right.

I tried to change the subject.

It worked.

For approximately three minutes.

Then something happened that I didn't expect.

I started enjoying myself again.

We laughed.

We talked.

I even forgot that I was supposed to be nervous.

Maybe first dates weren't as scary as I'd imagined.

Maybe I wasn't terrible at this.

Then my brain decided to remind me that I was, in fact, terrible at this.

He asked if I was enjoying the date.

I said yes.

Then he asked the question that made my heart jump.

“So... do you like me?”

I froze.

There are questions you prepare for.

There are questions you don't.

And then there are questions that make you suddenly question every decision that brought you to that exact moment.

This was one of them.

I could have simply said yes.

I could have smiled.

I could have said, “I think you're nice.”

Instead, I panicked.

And when I panic, apparently my mouth starts working independently of my brain.

I gave him an answer.

He stared at me for a few seconds.

Then he laughed.

I laughed too, but inside, I was already regretting everything.

The rest of the date continued, but something had changed.

Not necessarily between us.

In my head.

I kept wondering if I'd ruined it.

If I'd said too much.

If I'd made myself look stupid.

If he was going to go home and tell his friends about the weird girl he took on a date.

When it was finally time to leave, he walked me part of the way.

We said goodbye.

He smiled.

I smiled.

And then I walked away pretending I was completely fine.

The moment I turned the corner, though, I pulled out my phone.

I stared at our chat.

I wanted to text him.

Did I make things awkward?

No.

Too desperate.

I had fun today.

Too obvious.

Sorry about earlier.

Absolutely not.

So I did what any perfectly rational 18-year-old girl would do.

Nothing.

I went home.

And waited.

Because if I'd really screwed up my first date...

I was about to find out.

To be continued.

title: Marriage Is Optional. Yes, I Said It.
excerpt: Marriage is optional. Yes, I said it.Now come closer, let me tell you why. Somewhere along the way, we started treating marriage like a mandatory stage of adult…
content:
Marriage is optional. Yes, I said it.

Now come closer, let me tell you why.

Somewhere along the way, we started treating marriage like a mandatory stage of adulthood.

Go to school. Get a job. Get married. Have children.

But what if someone doesn't want that life?

Marriage can be beautiful. Finding someone you love, building a home together, and growing old with them can be a wonderful thing.

But it isn't the only way to have a meaningful life.

Some people simply don't want to get married. Others would rather stay single than marry the wrong person just because they feel pressured to meet a certain age or expectation.

And honestly, I think that's okay.

Marriage shouldn't be something you do because everyone around you is doing it.

It shouldn't be something you rush into because you're afraid of being alone.

And it definitely shouldn't be treated as proof that you've finally become successful or "settled."

You can have a fulfilling career, meaningful friendships, a loving family, exciting experiences, personal goals, and a beautiful life without having a spouse.

Of course, if marriage is something you genuinely want, that's beautiful too.

The point is simply that it should be a choice.

Get married because you want to build a life with someone—not because society handed you a deadline.

And if you don't want marriage at all?

Your life can still be full.

Marriage is an option, not an obligation.
