title: The sky she never flew.
excerpt: Here's part 2.He was 53. A friend of Baba's from the market association. He owned three trucks and a house with tiles. He laughed loudly and patted Baba on the …
content:
Here's part 2.

He was 53. A friend of Baba's from the market association. He owned three trucks and a house with tiles. He laughed loudly and patted Baba on the back and called Amina "my daughter" even though they'd just met.

After he left, Baba called Amina to the parlor.

"The marriage will be in two months," he said. "It's a good match. He's a responsible man. He will take care of you."

Amina felt like the floor had dropped out.

"Baba, please. I have admission. I can pay my way. Just give me two years."

"A girl's place is in her husband's house," Baba said, not looking at her. "This pilot thing is nonsense. Finish it."

She begged her mother. She begged her aunties. She wrote a letter to the college asking to defer.

The answer came back: _Deferment not possible. Admission forfeited.

She folded the admission letter into a paper plane and threw it off the roof. The wind took it.

The wedding was loud. There was drumming, and women ululating, and men spraying money until the floor was sticky. Amina wore white lace and gele, and her henna was dark and perfect. People said, "Masha Allah, what a beautiful bride."

She smiled because that's what brides do.

Inside, she was still 8 years old on the roof, arms wide.

Alhaji's house was big and quiet. The walls were high. The driver called her "Madam." The cooks called her "Madam." No one called her Amina.

Her job was to pour tea, to greet guests, to sit still during meetings and not talk too much.

At night, after Alhaji slept, she would pull the aviation magazine from under the mattress. The pages were soft from her fingers. She would trace the diagram of a cockpit with a penlight and whisper the names of the parts to herself. _Yoke. Throttle. Altimeter.

She didn't tell anyone she was still dreaming.

Six months into the marriage, she missed her period.

The clinic was in town, 40 minutes away. Alhaji said, "These hospital people just like to collect money. My first two wives gave birth at home with Mama Rekiya. Women have been doing this for centuries."

So Amina went to Mama Rekiya. The old woman checked her pulse and smiled. "Strong baby," she said. "Eat well."

But Amina wasn't eating well. The smell of food made her sick. Her ankles swelled. Her head felt heavy.

At the mosque, one of the women noticed. "You should go to the hospital, dear. Check your BP."

Alhaji overheard and shook his head.

"She's fine. She's just pregnant." He said

In her seventh month, the dizziness started. She'd be washing plates and the kitchen was tiled .She told Yusuf, who was now 14 and came visiting on Fridays.

"You look pale, Amina," he said.

"I'm fine," she lied. Then she took his hand and pressed something into it. A small paper plane, folded from her last magazine page.

"Keep this for me," she whispered.

Labor started on a Tuesday night. Rain was falling hard.

The pains came in waves. Mama Rekiya was called. She boiled water and laid out cloths.

Hours passed. The bleeding started.

"It's too much," Mama Rekiya said, her voice going thin. "We need to go to the hospital."

The driver tried to start the car. It coughed and died.

"Battery," he said. "It's the battery."

TO be continued!

title: Am I Weird? How I Screwed My First Date (2)
excerpt: The date hadn't even started, and I was already panicking.
content:
The day of the date finally came.

And suddenly, saying yes didn't feel like such a good idea anymore.

I stood in front of my mirror for what felt like forever, changing my mind about what to wear every five minutes.

Too much.

Too simple.

Too casual.

Too I'm trying too hard.

Eventually, I picked something and decided I was just going to go.

After all, it was only a date.

Only a date.

I repeated that to myself like it was going to calm me down.

It didn't.

On my way there, I kept rehearsing possible conversations in my head.

“What do you like doing?”

I like sleeping.

No.

“What kind of music do you listen to?”

Anything.

Terrible.

“What do you want to be in the future?”

Can we please talk about something else?

I was already preparing answers to questions nobody had asked.

When I finally got there, I saw him.

And somehow, all the confidence I had managed to gather on the way disappeared.

He smiled when he saw me.

I smiled back.

At least, I think it was a smile.

It probably looked more like my face was malfunctioning.

“Hi.”

“Hi.”

And then came the most painful two seconds of silence.

I wanted the ground to open.

He asked how I was doing.

“Fine.”

Fine?

That was it?

After spending the entire journey preparing for this moment, all I could produce was fine.

He laughed.

Not in a mocking way. More like he found my nervousness funny.

That somehow made me even more nervous.

We started walking and talking.

Well, he talked.

I listened.

Then he asked me questions and I answered them with the shortest responses possible.

I wasn't trying to be rude.

I was just nervous.

Very nervous.

The kind of nervous where your brain suddenly forgets every interesting thing you've ever known about yourself.

At some point, he asked me why I was so quiet.

I laughed.

“I'm not quiet.”

He looked at me.

I looked at him.

We both knew I was lying.

And then, somehow, I started relaxing.

We talked about school. Friends. Random things. Things that didn't matter but somehow made the conversation easier.

For the first time that day, I stopped thinking about how awkward I was being.

I was actually enjoying myself.

Maybe this date wasn't going to be as disastrous as I thought.

Maybe I had worried for nothing.

Then he asked me something that completely caught me off guard.

And my response?

Let's just say...

I have no idea what possessed me to say that.

Because the moment the words left my mouth, I knew.

I had just made things awkward again.

And this time, there was no pretending it didn't happen.

To be continued.

title: My Crush Has Mouth Odor
excerpt: Fine boy, why na?
content:
To Rita, Louis was not just a guy; he was a masterpiece walking the halls of the university. Tall, light skinned, and sleekly built, he moved with an effortless poise. With his almond eyes, sharp nose, perfectly contoured pink lips, and subtle, elf-like ears, he looked like he had stepped right out of a high-fantasy novel.

He was quiet, almost ghostlike yet his aura dominated every room he entered. Nobody really knew what his voice sounded like, though rumors claimed a lucky few had heard him speak.

"Louis is the one for me," Rita declared proudly, resting her chin on her hands as she watched him cross the courtyard.

Martha, her roommate looked up from her notebook with a slight smirk. "Hmm. Rita, small-small o. Have you ever actually spoken to him?"

"Not yet. But I have a plan."

"What if he snubs you?" Martha asked.

"He won't," Rita said confidently. "He’s just reserved."

"Toh, go get him then," Martha chuckled. "Though, word on the street is that a couple of girls used to crush on him hard before they suddenly dropped him and ran."

Rita waved a hand dismissively. "Doesn't matter, Martha. I know what I want."

Rita launched her full-scale campaign. She tried approaching him after class, but he glided away effortlessly. Undeterred, she began slipping handwritten love letters into his bag. When she finally managed to get his WhatsApp number, her enthusiastic paragraphs were met with ice-cold single-word replies: "Ok," "Alright," and the occasional thumbs-up emoji.

Then came the gifts. She left him sleek pens, notebooks, silver chains, woven bracelets, and designer beanies.

Soon, coursemates started whispering, sending anonymous messages taunting her desperation. Rita ignored them all. She was goal-oriented, and Louis was the target.

Her persistence paid off on a hot Thursday afternoon. A text popped up on her screen:

"Passageway behind Faculty of Engineering. 3:00 PM.”

Rita’s heart leaped. The moment had finally arrived. She practically flew to the venue.

When she reached the quiet passageway, Louis was waiting, leaning casually against the concrete pillar.

"Thank you for meeting me," Rita gushed, her heart doing backflips. "I hope you've been getting my messages and gifts. I really just want us to vibe, you know? You're always so isolated."

Before she could finish her sentence, Louis stepped forward and pulled her into a tight, sudden embrace. Rita froze, her cheeks burning as their hearts beat in sync.

Then the first sign hit her. A sharp, sour odor wafted from his armpits, cutting through the warm afternoon air. It’s just sweat, Rita reasoned quickly, trying to stay calm. He's been in lectures all day.

Without warning, Louis leaned down and pressed his lips to hers.

What was supposed to be a romantic moment ended instantly. Rita jerked backward, gasping for air as her eyes widened in complete horror.

As he stood there, completely unbothered by her reaction, he began to speak. His voice was shockingly deep, a low rumble that sounded almost completely inaudible like a faint reverberation coming from deep inside his chest.

"I see how much effort you put in for me," he mumbled, his deep tones barely reaching her ears. "I think we should be together. By the way, my real name isn't Louis... it's Brombromlagwe."

Rita could barely hear the words, nor did she care to. She was completely paralyzed not by the kiss or his muffled, deep voice, but by the overwhelming wave of stench that erupted with every quiet syllable.

It tasted metallic, sour, and heavy, like something rotting deep within his gut. Beneath those pristine pink lips, his tongue was coated in a thick white layer of bacteria, and the smell was pure, unadulterated halitosis.

Before he could take another step toward her, Rita turned on her heel and sprinted back to her hostel.

The moment she burst into her room, she scrubbed her teeth until her gums bled, used half a bottle of mouthwash, and flossed repeatedly. Still feeling utterly contaminated, she tore open a fresh pack of mints and shoved three into her mouth at once.

When Martha walked in later that evening, she found Rita sitting on her bunk, aggressively chewing through a mountain of mint wrappers.

"What's with all the mints?" Martha asked, raising an eyebrow.

"My crush has terrible mouth odor. And body odor," Rita gagged, holding her chest. "It’s not normal odor, Martha, it’s coming straight from his internal organs! And he kissed me!"

Martha stared at her for a second before bursting into hysterical, breathless laughter.

"Is it not what you wanted?" Martha wheezed, clutching her stomach. "You said you didn't care!"

"Gosh, I feel so dirty!" Rita whined, tossing another mint into her mouth. "He even told me his real name is Brombromlagwe! I couldn't even process it!"

Martha laughed so hard she nearly fell off her stool.

Rita sank back against her pillow, staring blankly at the ceiling. "No wonder all those other girls ran away."

"So..." Martha grinned, wiping a tear from her eye. "Is your love not unconditional anymore?"

"It was never love o!" Rita cried out. "It was just pure foolishness. Omo, I have moved on!"

What would you do if you were Rita?

~ Dorothy Kaankuka

title: If Monday Was A Person, That Would Be Mallory Bellarie
excerpt: The beauty of a brilliantly written antagonist
content:
If you’ve been watching Beauty in Black, then you already know that Mallory Bellarie doesn’t just walk into a scene, she completely commandeers it.

Played with ruthless perfection by Crystle Stewart, Mallory is easily one of the most unapologetic characters on screen right now.

She has absolutely zero filter. If someone in the room is thinking something private, Mallory will say it out loud with a straight face and zero regard for the aftermath.

She moves like consequences are an abstract concept meant only for regular people, which is exactly why audiences can't look away.

On paper, Mallory is a complete nightmare. She runs over her own aunt-in-law on a private road, looks at the body, and simply drives off. She covers up cancer-causing products for the Bellarie empire, treats her husband Roy like a footstool, and routinely terrorizes her staff.

Yet, half the internet is on social media defending her, saying: "She just has a thick skin to protect herself from bad people!"

That is the beauty of a brilliantly written antagonist.

When you place a villain in a family as toxic as the Bellaries, people start viewing her cruelty as survival.

She looked at a room full of corporate sharks and decided to become the killer whale. When surrounded by predators, she chose to become the apex predator.

She doesn't care who lives or dies, she just wants her shares.

Which Zodiac Sign Owns This Level of Audacity?

The internet debate over Mallory's star sign is hilarious because every argument makes sense:

Scorpio: The secretive coldness, the obsession with control, and the total lack of remorse when she hits you where it hurts.

Sagittarius: The dangerous, unfiltered honesty. She will roast your entire life choices simply because she felt like talking.

Virgo: The ruthless perfectionism, high corporate standards, and absolute intolerance for anyone she considers weak or incompetent.

Love her or hate her, if you can’t stand Mallory, it just means Crystle Stewart is playing the role too well. We definitely need a spin-off origin story to see how she became this cold.

Which energy do you think Mallory Bellarie gives off? Unhinged corporate evil, or a woman who just adapted to the Bellarie family's madness?

title: You Don't Have to Be a Hacker to Belong in Cybersecurity
excerpt: When I tell people I'm studying cybersecurity, one of the first questions I sometimes get is:"So, are you learning how to hack?"And honestly?Not exactly.At leas…
content:
When I tell people I'm studying cybersecurity, one of the first questions I sometimes get is:

"So, are you learning how to hack?"

And honestly?

Not exactly.

At least, not yet.

I've met people who are already interested in red teaming, blue teaming, penetration testing, ethical hacking, system analysis, and all the different paths cybersecurity can take you into.

And sometimes, listening to people talk about what they're learning makes me realize just how much I still don't know.

There are concepts I'm still trying to understand.

Tools I've heard about but haven't mastered.

Things that make perfect sense to someone more experienced that I still have to sit down and break apart before they click.

And for a while, I wondered if that meant I wasn't doing enough.

Then I started looking at it differently.

Maybe I don't have to know everything yet.

I'm a cybersecurity student.

I'm still learning.

And being a student doesn't mean I have nothing to contribute.

It simply means I'm somewhere along the road.

For now, I might not be the person testing the security of a complex system.

I might not be the person sitting in a room conducting penetration tests.

I might not even know yet whether I'll eventually find myself in a red team, blue team, security analysis, API testing, or an entirely different part of the field.

And that's okay.

Because cybersecurity needs more than people who know how to break into systems.

It also needs people who can help others understand how to protect them.

That's where I've found my own little space.

I can write.

I can research.

I can take something complicated I've learned and try to explain it in a way that doesn't make someone feel like they need a technical degree to understand it.

I can share simple ways people can protect their accounts.

I can talk about things happening in the cybersecurity space.

I can keep learning and document what I'm discovering along the way.

Maybe you could call that cybersecurity advocacy.

Maybe that description will change as I grow.

I'm okay with that too.

Because I'm beginning to understand something about learning:

Your current skill level doesn't have to be the limit of your contribution.

You can share what you know while still learning what you don't.

You can teach one thing and still have a hundred things left to learn yourself.

You can start writing before you become an expert writer.

You can start building before you become an experienced developer.

You can start exploring cybersecurity before you've decided exactly which corner of cybersecurity belongs to you.

The important thing is to start somewhere.

For me, that somewhere happens to be writing about what I'm learning.

Today, I'm writing about cybersecurity.

Tomorrow, I might find myself deep into penetration testing.

Or system analysis.

Or API security.

Or something I haven't even discovered yet.

I don't know.

And honestly, I don't think I need to know yet.

What I do know is that I'm still learning.

I'm still asking questions.

I'm still unlearning things.

And I'm still finding ways to share what I discover.

So no, I don't have to be a hacker to talk about cybersecurity.

I just have to be willing to keep learning about it.

And maybe that's enough to begin.

title: You’re Using AI Wrong: 5 Mistakes Nigerians Should Stop Making With ChatGPT
excerpt: 5 common AI mistakes that could be wasting your time—and how to use ChatGPT smarter.”
content:
AI is everywhere in 2026.

Students use it for assignments. Business owners use it for marketing. Freelancers use it for writing and research. Content creators use it for ideas, scripts and captions.

But here’s the uncomfortable truth:

Many people are using AI every day and still getting poor results.

The problem isn’t always the AI. Sometimes, it’s the way we ask it to work.

If you use ChatGPT or other AI tools, here are five mistakes you should stop making.

1. Giving AI Extremely Short Prompts

One of the biggest mistakes is typing something like:

“Write a business post.”

That gives AI almost nothing to work with.

What kind of business? Who is the audience? What platform is the post for? Should it sound professional, funny, persuasive or casual?

Instead, give AI context.

For example:

“Write an Instagram post for a Nigerian small-business owner selling affordable perfumes. Target young adults aged 18–30. Make it friendly, persuasive and short, with a strong opening hook and a clear call to action.”

Notice the difference?

Better instructions usually produce better results.

2. Copying AI Answers Without Checking Them

AI can be extremely useful, but it isn’t automatically correct.

It can misunderstand your question, make mistakes or provide information that needs verification.

This is especially important when dealing with money, schoolwork, jobs, health, laws, technology or current events.

Don’t simply copy an answer because it sounds confident.

Instead, ask:

  • “Are you sure?”

  • “What assumptions are you making?”

  • “Give me the source.”

  • “Separate facts from opinions.”

  • “What could be wrong with this answer?”

And when something really matters, verify it using reliable sources.

AI should help you think and research—not turn off your brain.

3. Asking AI to Do Everything For You

AI is powerful, but using it as a complete replacement for your own thinking can hurt you.

For example, instead of asking:

“Do my entire assignment.”

Try:

“Explain this topic to me like I’m a beginner, then give me five questions to test whether I understand it.”

Instead of:

“Write my entire business plan.”

Try:

“Help me develop a business plan. Ask me the important questions first, then help me build it step by step.”

The second approach makes AI your assistant, not your substitute.

That’s a much more valuable way to use the technology.

4. Not Telling AI Who You Are Talking To

AI doesn’t automatically know your audience.

A post written for a Nigerian university student isn’t necessarily the same as one written for a corporate executive in London.

Tell AI who you’re trying to reach.

For example:

“I’m creating content for Nigerian university students who want to learn practical digital skills. Keep the language simple, use Nigerian examples where appropriate, and avoid complicated technical terms.”

Suddenly, the response can become much more relevant.

You can also tell AI about your:

Audience + goal + platform + tone + format + limitations.

The more useful context you provide, the less time you’ll spend fixing the result afterward.

5. Using AI Without Actually Taking Action

This might be the biggest mistake of all.

You can spend three hours asking AI for business ideas, content ideas, freelancing strategies and productivity tips.

But if you never actually do anything with those ideas, nothing changes.

AI can give you:

  • Ideas

  • Research assistance

  • Drafts

  • Strategies

  • Explanations

  • Brainstorming

  • Feedback

But you still have to take action.

If AI gives you ten content ideas, choose one and publish it.

If it gives you a business strategy, test it.

If it teaches you a skill, practise it.

Don’t become addicted to preparing and forget to start.

The Simple Prompt Formula You Should Try

The next time you use ChatGPT, don’t just tell it what you want.

Tell it:

ROLE + TASK + CONTEXT + AUDIENCE + FORMAT + GOAL

For example:

“Act as a social media strategist. Help me create a short LinkedIn post about using AI for productivity. My audience is Nigerian young professionals. Keep it practical and easy to understand. Start with a strong hook and end with a question that encourages comments.”

That’s much better than:

“Write a LinkedIn post about AI.”

Final Thoughts

AI isn’t magic.

The people getting the most value from it aren’t necessarily the people who know the most complicated prompts.

They’re the people who know what they want, provide useful context, check the results and actually take action.

So the next time ChatGPT gives you a disappointing answer, don’t immediately conclude:

“AI is useless.”

Try asking yourself:

“Did I actually give the AI enough information to help me?”

You might discover that the problem wasn’t the AI.

You were just using it wrong.

title: THE POWER OF PRAISE
excerpt: TEXT: 2 Chronicles 20:22
content:
INTRODUCTION

Beloved, there is a mystery in the Kingdom of God, A mystery that many believers overlook. It is the mystery of praise.

Some battles in life are not won by fasting alone, not by prayer alone, but by praise. In our text, the people of Judah were faced with a serious crisis. Three powerful nations came against them. They were outnumbered, overwhelmed, and afraid. But instead of relying on weapons, God gave them an unusual strategy: “Send singers ahead!” And the Bible says: 2 Chronicles 20:22. The victory began when they started praising.

1. PRAISE IS A SPIRITUAL WEAPON

Praise is not entertainment—it is warfare. Many people think praise is just singing songs in church. No! Praise is a weapon that provokes divine action. The Bible says in Psalm 149:6: "Let the high praises of God be in their mouth, and a two-edged sword in their hand."

This means: Praise is a weapon. Praise fights battles. Praise enforces victory. When you praise God, you are engaging in spiritual warfare.

2. PRAISE BRINGS GOD INTO THE SITUATION

The Bible tells us in Psalm 22:3 "God inhabits the praises of His people."

That means: Praise attracts God. Praise invites His presence. Praise brings heaven down. When God steps into your situation: Sickness cannot stay, Delay cannot continue, Enemies cannot prevail

3. PRAISE TURNS BATTLES AROUND

In 2 Chronicles 20:22: God caused the enemies to destroy themselves. Hear this clearly: You don’t need to fight every battle—some battles must be handed over to God through praise.

4. PRAISE BREAKS CHAINS AND OPENS DOORS

Let us look at Acts 16:25-26: At midnight: They were in pain, They were in chains, They were in prison. But instead of complaining, they praised God. Suddenly: There was an earthquake, The prison doors opened, Their chains fell off, Praise turned a prison into a place of freedom!

5. PRAISE IS FAITH IN ACTION

The Bible says in Hebrews 11:1, Praise is saying: “God, I trust You—even when I don’t see results yet.” Anybody can praise God after a miracle. But it takes faith to praise Him before the miracle.

6. PRAISE BRINGS DOWN STRONGHOLDS

In Joshua 6:20, The walls of Jericho did not fall by bulldozers. They fell by shouting and praise.

That means: Every wall in your life can come down, Every obstacle can collapse, Every limitation can break

7. PRAISE DRIVES AWAY EVIL AND BRINGS PEACE

In 1 Samuel 16:23, Whenever David played: Evil spirit departed, Peace returned

Praise has healing power: It heals the mind, It lifts depression, It restores joy

PROPHETIC DECLARATIONS: “Every battle in your life is turning around!” “Every chain is breaking right now!” “Every delay is coming to an end!” “God is giving you victory without struggle!”

PRACTICAL APPLICATION: This Month: Praise God every morning, Praise Him in difficult situations, Praise Him before expecting answers

CONCLUSION: Your praise is your weapon. Your praise is your victory. Your praise is your breakthrough. If you can praise God in advance, God will give you victory ahead of time

FINAL DECLARATION: “As you journey in this new month, may your praise bring miracles, May your praise bring breakthroughs, May your praise bring victory, In Jesus’ name!”

title: SEPTEMBER IS NOT A RESET BUTTON
excerpt: Stop Waiting for a Clean Slate That Was Never Coming
content:
Happy New Month, but don't make the mistake of abandoning everything you started just because August didn't go as planned.

You did this in January too. Made the list, felt the surge of "this time will be different," and somewhere around week three, life happened and the list quietly stopped mattering. Now it's September, and you're doing the exact same thing, new month, new energy, new promise to finally get it right. If this is starting to feel familiar, that's not a coincidence. That's a pattern worth actually looking at.

THE MONTHLY RESET IS NOT HEALING YOU, IT'S HIDING YOU

New months feel good because they let you skip the hard part, the part where you sit with what didn't work and ask why. A new month gives you permission to start over without ever finishing the conversation with your old goals. You get the relief of a fresh start without the discomfort of an honest review. That relief is real. But it's also a quiet form of avoidance beautifully dressed up as motivation.

WHAT YOU'RE ACTUALLY RUNNING FROM The uncomfortable thing is not that you fell off. Everyone falls off something. The uncomfortable thing is what falling off usually means, you didn't build a system, you built a mood. And moods don't survive contact with a bad week, a broken routine, or a version of you that's tired and unmotivated. Waiting for September, or October, or "next Monday" is really just waiting for the mood to come back, instead of building something that doesn't depend on it showing up.

THE SELF FORGIVENESS NOBODY EXPLAINS PROPERLY

Here's what gets missed, forgiving yourself for an unfinished goal is not the same as forgetting it happened. Real self forgiveness looks at the mess honestly, this is what I said I'd do, this is what actually happened, this is probably why and still chooses to continue. Not a clean slate. A continued page, with the old writing still visible underneath. That's harder than a reset. It's also the only version that actually builds something that lasts.

WHY STARTING OVER KEEPS FAILING YOU Every reset erases the data. You lose the information about what specifically broke your consistency, was it the plan being unrealistic, was it your energy, was it that you never actually wanted this goal in the first place, just the idea of having achieved it. Wipe the slate enough times, and you never get far enough to learn any of that.

Continuing, messy as it is, is the only thing that teaches you anything.

WHAT TO DO WITH SEPTEMBER INSTEAD Don't ask what you are starting fresh. Ask what you're picking back up, and what you are finally willing to look at from where it fell apart last time. That's a smaller, less exciting question than "new month, new me." It's also the one that actually moves you somewhere. You don't need September to forgive you for August. You need to stop needing a new month's permission to keep going at all

Happy New Month y'all. I'm rooting for you always.

Don't forget to like. Follow. Share. Comment.

title: Your Degree Is Not Your Only Skill
excerpt: Your Degree Is Not Your Only SkillYou can have a degree and still feel unprepared for the real world.Not because your education is useless.But because a degree …
content:
Your Degree Is Not Your Only Skill

You can have a degree and still feel unprepared for the real world.

Not because your education is useless.

But because a degree is only one part of what you bring to the table.

The world of work also requires skills like communication, writing, research, problem-solving, digital skills and the ability to learn quickly.

The good news is that you don't have to wait until graduation to start developing these skills.

5 skills every student should start building:

1. Communication

Learn how to express your ideas clearly, both in writing and when speaking.

2. Writing

Good writing is useful in almost every career. Learn how to write emails, articles, reports, social-media posts and professional documents.

3. Digital skills

Learn how to use digital tools that are relevant to the kind of work you want to do.

4. Research

Learn how to find reliable information, understand it and turn it into something useful.

5. Problem-solving

Don't only learn information. Learn how to use what you know to solve real problems.

Your university education matters, but don't let your degree be the only thing you leave school with.

Start building skills.

Start creating projects.

Start gaining experience.

Start showing people what you can do.

Your degree can open a door. Your skills can help you make something happen once you're inside.

What skill are you currently learning outside your course of study?

title: When You Call for Help and No One Answers: Nigeria's Suicide Helplines Are Failing the People Who Need Them Most
excerpt: September is Suicide Prevention Month the month we remember the lives lost, tell the grieving they're not alone, and post soft reminders online that "help is av…
content:
September is Suicide Prevention Month the month we remember the lives lost, tell the grieving they're not alone, and post soft reminders online that "help is available." Survivors mark the occasion by sharing how grateful they are that they didn't stay the same age forever. Organizations put out infographics. Hotline numbers get shared and reshared.

But what happens when someone actually dials one?

A Nigerian content creator recently tried to find out. In a video circulating online, she called several of the country's advertised suicide prevention helplines, one after another including numbers marketed as 24/7 emergency lines. The result: silence. No answer. One line, it turned out, only operates on weekdays, within a specific window of business hours as if despair keeps office hours too. Even the emergency line didn't pick up.

Sit with that for a second. If someone in the grip of suicidal thoughts had made those exact calls that night, at that exact hour, there would have been no one on the other end. Not a counselor. Not a volunteer. Not even an automated message pointing them somewhere else. Just a dial tone, and whatever they were already carrying.

This isn't a technical glitch. It's a design failure and a dangerous one. A crisis line that isn't reliably staffed isn't a safety net; it's a signpost pointing at an empty room. The entire premise of a suicide hotline is that it works in the exact moment someone can't wait. A helpline that answers "most of the time" or "during business hours" has quietly redefined itself into something else a hotline in name only.

There's a particular cruelty in the mismatch between messaging and reality. All month, the narrative has been "you are not alone" and "help is always there." Meanwhile, the actual infrastructure behind that promise the phone lines people are told to call in their worst moment isn't consistently there at all. Awareness campaigns raise expectations. Unstaffed lines then break them, at the exact moment someone is least equipped to absorb another disappointment.

To be fair, some of these organizations are under-resourced, understaffed, and running largely on the goodwill of volunteers and nonprofits stretching thin budgets across a country of over 200 million people. That context matters. But context isn't an excuse for silence when someone calls a number that says, in writing, "24/7." If a line cannot realistically be staffed around the clock, it shouldn't be marketed that way. Honesty about limited hours is safer than a false promise of constant availability at least people would know to look elsewhere sooner.

So what needs to change? A few things, urgently:

• Every number listed as a suicide or crisis helpline should be independently and regularly tested for actual pickup rates not just published and forgotten.

• Lines that can't sustain 24/7 coverage should say so clearly, and be paired with alternative numbers that can.

• Government health authorities, telecom providers, and mental health nonprofits need to treat crisis-line funding and staffing as core infrastructure, not an awareness-month afterthought.

• The public conversation needs to move past "help is available" toward "here's proof it actually answers."

Awareness without access is just noise. Telling people to reach out is only half the job someone has to be there to receive the call.

If you are struggling with suicidal thoughts after reading this, please don't wait on a number that might not pick up. Reach out to a friend, a family member, a therapist, a mental health professional, or anyone you trust, right now, in person if you can. You deserve a real response not a busy signal.

title: The Boy Whose Shadow Ran Away
excerpt:
The Boy Whose Shadow Ran Away is a magical children’s adventure story about Kelechi, a curious boy whose shadow suddenly decides it has had enough of following him everywhere. When Kelechi follows his runaway shadow into a secret city filled with independent shadows, he discovers that even the things we take for granted may have feelings, dreams, and a story of their own.

The adventure teaches children an important lesson about empathy, friendship, responsibility, and appreciating others. Kelechi learns that sometimes, we become so used to having someone or something around us that we forget to notice its value.

The biggest takeaway is simple: don't wait until something leaves before you realize how much it means to you. Treat people with kindness, listen to them, and remember that everyone deserves to feel seen and appreciated.
content:
The first time Kelechi's shadow ran away, he thought it was a joke.

It happened on a Tuesday morning.

Kelechi was brushing his teeth when he noticed something strange.

He moved his toothbrush to the left.

His shadow moved to the right.

He stopped.

His shadow didn't.

Kelechi slowly lowered his toothbrush.

His shadow raised its hand.

Kelechi's mouth fell open.

The shadow waved.

“Stop that!” Kelechi whispered.

The shadow waved again.

Kelechi stepped backward.

The shadow stepped forward.

Then it turned around…

…and ran away.

Kelechi screamed.

“MUMMY!”

His mother rushed into the bathroom.

“What happened?”

“My shadow!”

His mother looked at the floor.

There was no shadow.

She looked at Kelechi.

Then at the floor again.

“Kelechi, you need to stop watching cartoons before school.”

“But it ran away!”

His mother sighed.

“Go and wear your uniform.”

Kelechi stared at the empty floor.

“I knew it,” he whispered.

“My shadow has finally had enough of me.”

At school, everything became worse.

Kelechi tried standing in the sunlight.

Nothing.

He stood beside his friends.

Nothing.

He jumped.

Nothing.

He even danced.

Still nothing.

His friend Tobi stared at him.

“Bro.”

“Yes?”

“You look suspicious.”

“How?”

“You don't have a shadow.”

Kelechi looked around.

“Exactly!”

Tobi's eyes widened.

“So…”

“So what?”

“You're a ghost.”

Kelechi nearly fell over.

“I'm NOT a ghost!”

Tobi stepped backward.

“That's exactly what a ghost would say.”

By lunchtime, half the class had heard the story.

By break time, the whole school had heard it.

And by the end of the day, someone had started a rumor that Kelechi had become invisible.

Kelechi was furious.

“I am NOT invisible!”

His teacher looked at him.

“We can see you.”

“Exactly!”

She paused.

“But where is your shadow?”

Kelechi sighed.

“That is what I'm trying to find out.”

That evening, Kelechi followed a trail of strange little footprints behind his house.

They weren't human footprints.

They weren't animal footprints either.

They looked like…

shadow footprints.

They led through the garden.

Past the mango tree.

Behind the old water tank.

And straight into the abandoned storage room.

Kelechi pushed the door open.

It creaked.

Inside was darkness.

“Hello?”

Something moved.

Kelechi swallowed.

“Shadow?”

A tiny voice answered.

“Go away.”

Kelechi froze.

It was his shadow.

“What are you doing here?”

“I'm tired.”

“Tired of what?”

“Following you everywhere!”

Kelechi blinked.

“What?”

His shadow stepped out from behind a box.

It looked exactly like him, except completely black.

“You wake up. I wake up.”

“You eat. I stand behind you.”

“You run. I run.”

“You dance badly. I have to dance badly too.”

Kelechi frowned.

“I don't dance badly.”

The shadow stared at him.

“You danced yesterday for twenty minutes while wearing one sock.”

Kelechi looked away.

“That was different.”

“No, it wasn't.”

The shadow crossed its arms.

“I want my own life.”

Kelechi couldn't believe what he was hearing.

“You're my shadow!”

“I know.”

“You can't just leave me!”

“Why not?”

“Because…”

Kelechi stopped.

He didn't actually know.

The shadow smiled.

“Exactly.”

Then it walked away.

Kelechi followed.

“Wait!”

The shadow disappeared through a crack in the wall.

Kelechi squeezed through after it.

On the other side was something impossible.

A whole city.

A city made entirely of shadows.

Shadow houses.

Shadow trees.

Shadow cars.

Even shadow chickens.

And thousands of shadows walked around without people attached to them.

Kelechi stared.

“What is this place?”

His shadow smiled.

“Home.”

For the first time, Kelechi understood.

His shadow wasn't broken.

It wasn't lost.

It had simply been somewhere else all along.

He walked through the strange city.

Then he noticed something.

Some shadows were sitting alone.

Some were crying.

Some were hiding.

One tiny shadow sat beneath a tree, trembling.

Kelechi walked over.

“What's wrong?”

The little shadow pointed toward the city.

“I can't find my person.”

Kelechi frowned.

“Your person?”

The shadow nodded.

“She disappeared.”

Suddenly, Kelechi understood why his own shadow had run away.

Maybe shadows weren't supposed to spend their whole lives simply following.

Maybe they needed to know they mattered too.

Kelechi turned to his shadow.

“You know what?”

“What?”

“I'm sorry.”

The shadow looked surprised.

“For what?”

“For never thinking about you.”

The shadow smiled.

Then something enormous appeared behind them.

A giant shadow towered over the city.

Kelechi grabbed his shadow.

“What is THAT?”

His shadow whispered:

“The Shadow Eater.”

The creature opened its enormous mouth.

And every shadow in the city screamed.

“RUN!”

Kelechi and his shadow raced through the streets.

The Shadow Eater chased them.

Faster.

Faster.

It swallowed houses.

It swallowed trees.

It swallowed shadows.

Kelechi suddenly stopped.

“I have an idea!”

His shadow stared at him.

“Is it a good one?”

“No!”

“Wonderful.”

Kelechi ran toward the creature.

The Shadow Eater opened its mouth.

At the last second, Kelechi jumped into the sunlight pouring through a crack in the ceiling.

The giant creature stopped.

It couldn't move into the light.

Kelechi turned around.

“Everyone! Follow me!”

Hundreds of shadows rushed toward the light.

The Shadow Eater shrank.

Smaller.

Smaller.

Until it became nothing more than a tiny dark spot.

Then.....

POP!

It disappeared.

The shadow city cheered.

Kelechi's shadow walked over.

“You saved everyone.”

Kelechi smiled.

“We saved everyone.”

His shadow raised an eyebrow.

“Does that mean I have to go back to following you?”

Kelechi laughed.

“No.”

The shadow smiled.

“Good.”

“But…”

Kelechi pointed toward the doorway leading back home.

“Can you at least come back sometimes?”

The shadow pretended to think.

“Maybe.”

The next morning, Kelechi stood outside his house.

The sun rose.

And there it was.

His shadow.

Right beside him.

Kelechi smiled.

“Welcome back.”

The shadow waved.

Then Kelechi noticed something strange.

His shadow was smiling.

But Kelechi wasn't.

He stopped.

The shadow kept smiling.

“Kelechi…”

He slowly looked down.

His shadow whispered:

“I think something followed us home.”

Kelechi's smile disappeared.

Behind him, something moved.

He turned.

Nothing.

He looked at the ground.

His shadow was gone.

Again.

Then a second shadow appeared beside his feet.

It wasn't shaped like him.

It was shaped like something with three long arms.

Kelechi screamed.

And somewhere behind the house…

something laughed.

The End.

title: The "Saturated Field" Myth Why Diligence Still Beats the Crowd
excerpt: Every few years, a new wave of people insists a particular skill is "too saturated" to bother learning, coding was saturated in 2015, then digital marketing, th…
content:
Every few years, a new wave of people insists a particular skill is "too saturated" to bother learning, coding was saturated in 2015, then digital marketing, then UI/UX, and now the chorus has moved on to almost everything touched by AI. But saturation is often less about the market and more about mindset. It's easier to call a field "full" than to admit the real barrier is showing up consistently, refining your craft, and outlasting the noise. The market doesn't reward the most people in a space, it rewards the most valuable output in that space. There's always room at the top, because most people quit long before they get good.

The AI conversation deserves the same scrutiny. Yes, AI is changing how work gets done, automating repetitive tasks, speeding up first drafts, restructuring workflows. But automation replacing tasks isn't the same as AI replacing people. Every AI tool still needs someone to prompt it well, interpret its output, catch its blind spots, and apply judgment it doesn't have. The developers, designers, writers, and strategists who learn to work alongside these tools aren't being phased out, they're becoming the ones who get more done, faster, with a sharper edge over people still waiting on the sidelines for "the right time."

What actually separates people in any skill, tech or otherwise, isn't how new or "unsaturated" the field is. It's depth. Two people can learn the same skill at the same time, and five years later one is a recognized expert while the other never moved past tutorials. The difference is rarely talent or timing, it's usually just who kept building, kept shipping, kept showing up when it wasn't exciting anymore.

So if you're waiting for a field to feel empty before you jump in, you'll be waiting forever, because every valuable skill will always have people in it. The real question isn't "is this saturated," it's "am I willing to get good enough that it doesn't matter." Learn the skill. Build the portfolio. Let diligence do what excuses never will.

title: 7 Simple Ways to Reduce Hair Breakage
excerpt: For healthier, stronger hair. ✨
content:
You wash your hair today, style it beautifully, and two weeks later you're wondering, “Wait… where did all my hair go?” 😭

If you constantly find tiny pieces of hair on your comb, pillow, clothes, or bathroom floor, your hair may not be refusing to grow. It may simply be breaking faster than you can retain the length.

Here are seven simple ways to reduce hair breakage and give your hair a better chance to thrive.

1. Moisturize Your Hair — Please 😭

Dry hair is basically your hair saying, “I cannot do this anymore.”

When your strands become excessively dry, they become more fragile and easier to snap. Don't just focus on your scalp; your actual hair strands need moisture too.

Use a good moisturizing conditioner after washing, and consider adding a leave-in conditioner to your routine. If your hair feels rough, stiff, or difficult to comb, that's usually a sign that it needs more moisture and gentler handling.

2. Stop Fighting Your Hair While Detangling

If your comb is fighting for its life every wash day, something needs to change. 😂

Don't attack tangled hair from the roots like you're angry with it. Detangle gently, starting from the ends and gradually working your way up.

Using your fingers or a wide-tooth comb can make the process easier. And please, don't rush through a huge knot just because you're late. Your hair doesn't care about your appointment. 😭

3. Give Your Edges a Break

We love a good sleek ponytail, braids, cornrows and laid edges, but your edges are not supposed to be under military training 24/7.

Constant tension from very tight hairstyles can contribute to hair breakage and hair loss around the hairline.

If your hairstyle gives you a headache, causes pain, or makes your scalp feel extremely tight, that's not a sign that the hairstyle is “neat.” Your scalp is protesting. 😂

Give your hairline regular breaks and choose styles that don't constantly pull on the same areas.

4. Reduce the Heat

Your straightener does not need to know you personally. 😭

Frequent exposure to high heat from flat irons, curling irons and very hot blow-dryers can weaken the hair and make it more prone to breakage.

You don't have to completely ban heat from your life, but use it less frequently, avoid unnecessarily high temperatures and use a heat protectant when using hot tools.

5. Don't Overprocess Your Hair

Relaxer, bleach, permanent colour and other chemical treatments can change the structure of your hair.

The problem isn't necessarily using these treatments; it's overdoing them or combining too many damaging processes without giving your hair time to recover.

If your hair is already weak, dry and breaking, adding another chemical treatment because “I want to look fine this weekend” may not be the best idea. 😂

Sometimes your hair needs rest more than it needs another transformation.

6. Protect Your Hair While You Sleep

You can spend the whole day carefully treating your hair and then spend eight hours at night rubbing it against a rough pillowcase. 😭

Cotton fabrics can create friction, which may contribute to dryness and breakage.

A satin or silk bonnet, scarf or pillowcase can help reduce friction while you sleep. It also helps your hairstyle last longer, which means less manipulation the next morning.

Basically, let your hair sleep peacefully.

7. Trim Those Damaged Ends

We know. Nobody wants to hear this one. 😭

But if your ends are severely damaged and splitting, refusing to trim them won't magically make them healthy again.

Regularly removing damaged ends can help prevent splits from travelling further up the hair shaft and can make your hair look healthier.

And no, trimming your hair doesn't make it grow faster. Hair grows from the scalp, not the ends. The point is to help you retain the healthy length you're already growing.

The Bottom Line

Hair growth isn't only about making your hair grow. It's also about keeping the hair that grows.

You can have perfectly normal hair growth at your scalp, but if your strands are constantly breaking at the ends, it may feel like your hair isn't growing at all.

So moisturize it, handle it gently, protect your edges, reduce unnecessary heat and chemical damage, and give your hair a little patience.

And please… stop combing your hair like you're settling a personal disagreement. 😂

If breakage is severe, sudden, or accompanied by noticeable thinning or bald patches, it's worth speaking with a dermatologist or other qualified healthcare professional, because breakage isn't always just a hair-care issue.

title: If I Could Go Back to the Very First Day I Met You…
excerpt: I for give you one very big slap.
content:
If I could go back to the very first day I met you, I for give you one very big slap.

And no, I’m not joking.

The annoying thing is, that day, I actually thought you were a very nice person.

If somebody had told me that the man I was smiling and taking pictures with at that wedding would eventually become the biggest regret of my life, I would have laughed.

Maybe I would have even insulted the person.

Because you?

You were too sweet.

But let me not jump ahead.

Let me tell you how I met him.

It was at my friend’s wedding.

And honestly, I wasn’t even looking for a man that day.

I was looking for food.

And maybe small enjoyment. 😂

My friend had been stressing me for weeks about the wedding, so when I finally got there, my only plan was to look good, eat well, take pictures and go home.

Then my friend came to me with this guy.

“Bola, meet—”

And that was how I met him.

He smiled and stretched out his hand.

“Hi. Nice to meet you.”

I shook his hand.

“Hi.”

That was it.

Until he looked at me again and smiled.

“I don’t know why, but I have a feeling meeting you today isn’t going to be the last time I see you.”

I laughed.

“Ah-ah. So you’ve already planned our second meeting?”

He laughed too.

“Not exactly. I’m just saying… I’d like to see you again.”

Hmm.

This man had confidence o.

But somehow, it wasn’t annoying.

He wasn’t doing too much. He wasn’t trying to impress me or say those corny lines men say when they want to collect your number.

He just seemed… comfortable.

And surprisingly, a little shy.

Which was funny because from the way he carried himself, you would think he had never been shy around a woman in his life.

We talked for a few minutes before my friend dragged me away for pictures.

I didn’t think much of it.

Until I noticed him looking at me from across the hall.

Not in a creepy way.

Just… looking.

And whenever our eyes met, he would smile.

At some point, I laughed and shook my head.

My friend saw it.

“Omo. I see you.”

“See me where?”

“Don’t worry. Continue.”

“There’s nothing.”

She gave me that look.

You know that look your friend gives you when she knows something you haven’t admitted to yourself yet?

Exactly that one.

Later that evening, he came to where I was sitting.

“Can I get your number?”

I looked at him.

“You’re asking very directly.”

“I don’t like wasting time.”

I laughed.

“Okay then.”

I gave him my number.

He called immediately.

My phone rang.

I looked at the screen.

His name wasn’t saved, obviously.

I picked up.

“Hello?”

“Now you have my number too.”

“That’s not how it works. You called me.”

“So save it.”

“Who said I want to?”

He laughed.

“You will.”

I rolled my eyes.

This man.

Before he left, he said, “I’ll text you.”

“Okay.”

“And Bola?”

“Hmm?”

“Don’t disappear.”

I smiled.

“I won’t.”

And honestly, I didn’t think anything serious would come out of it.

I had met men before.

Some were sweet for two weeks.

Some were sweet until they got what they wanted.

Some would text you every morning and suddenly disappear for three days because apparently, their phone fell inside water.

So I wasn’t expecting anything.

But that night, while I was lying on my bed, my phone lit up.

Him: You got home safely?

I smiled.

Me: Yes.

A few seconds later:

Him: Good. I was wondering.

And that was the beginning.

The next morning, he texted me again.

Then the next day.

Then the next.

Nothing excessive.

Just little things.

“Have you eaten?”

“How was work?”

“Don’t forget that thing you told me you had today.”

He remembered things.

That was the first thing I noticed about him.

If I mentioned something once, he remembered it.

If I told him I had a stressful day, he would check on me later.

If I said I wasn’t feeling well, he would call.

And when we eventually started dating, it only got better.

He was the kind of man people prayed for.

He supported me.

He encouraged me.

He celebrated my little wins like they were his own.

He knew when I was upset even when I said I wasn’t.

He would randomly send food to my office because he knew I would forget to eat when I was busy.

Once, I casually mentioned that I had been wanting something for weeks.

I forgot about it.

He didn’t.

Two weeks later, he showed up with it.

I remember looking at him and saying,

“Why are you this sweet?”

He laughed.

“I don’t know. Maybe I just really like you.”

I loved hearing things like that.

And honestly?

I loved him too.

A lot.

My friends loved him.

My family loved him.

Even my mother, who normally found something wrong with every man I brought around, liked him.

She once told me,

“Bola, this one looks serious.”

I laughed.

“He is serious.”

She nodded.

“Good. Don’t lose him.”

I didn’t plan to.

I thought I had finally found my person.

The man I would marry.

The man I would grow old with.

The man I could trust completely.

And for a long time, I had absolutely no reason to think otherwise.

Until one random Tuesday afternoon…

I saw a message on his phone.

And that was the first time I realised that maybe…

I didn’t know the man I had married as well as I thought I did.

title: Abia Hubs Now Eligible to Partner with RevUp Women to Support Female Entrepreneurs
excerpt: Innovation, technology, and entrepreneurship hubs across Abia State can now apply to become implementing partners for the RevUp Women Initiative. The program focuses on strengthening female-led enterprises within the e-commerce and agribusiness sectors.
content:
Rather than providing direct business grants to individual business owners, this call targets established organizations capable of operating as regional execution partners. One hub will be selected in Abia to deliver structured training, mentor local female founders, and expand their digital market access.

Core Eligibility Criteria

To qualify as an implementing partner, applying organizations must meet specific operational standards:

  • Network Membership: Active membership in good standing with the AfriLabs network.

  • Track Record: A minimum of three years of continuous operation at a functional physical location.

  • Cohort Experience: Proven experience running business incubation or acceleration programs, backed by evidence of at least one completed cohort.

  • Sector & Gender Focus: Demonstrated engagement with tech, innovation, or entrepreneurship, alongside a history of supporting female founders particularly in e-commerce or agricultural value chains.

  • Program Infrastructure: Physical facilities and technical setup capable of hosting 12-week hybrid training sessions, backed by an established network of female mentors and investors.

Key Responsibilities of the Selected Hub

The chosen Abia hub will manage local implementation for the initiative. Primary responsibilities include:

  • Onboarding female-led businesses using informal digital tools and helping them transition to structured e-commerce strategies.

  • Conducting training, business development sessions, and mentorship connections.

  • Linking participating entrepreneurs to external funding networks and growth resources.

Required Application Documents

Hubs preparing their submission should compile the following evidence:

  • Official business registration and proof of AfriLabs membership.

  • Operational records confirming three or more years of physical presence.

  • Curricula, participant records, and case studies from past incubation cohorts.

  • Profiles of accessible female mentors and investor network partners.

  • A 12-week execution plan for delivering hybrid program activities.

Application Route

  • For Organizations (Hubs): Hub managers in Abia must submit their Expression of Interest through the official AfriLabs partner portal, attaching required facility photos, track record documents, and cohort evidence.

  • For Female Business Owners: Individual entrepreneurs should not apply to this hub call. Female founders seeking training and mentorship can register as mentees on the central RevUp Women portal during active cohort intake windows.

title: Poor Money Management: How a Good Business Can Still Fail
excerpt: Starting a business is exciting.
content:
You have a good idea, you find customers, people start buying from you, and money begins coming in. At that point, it can feel like the business is doing well.

But there is one problem many small business owners overlook: making money is not the same as managing money.

A business can have customers and still struggle if the money coming in is not properly managed.

Spending Without a Plan

One common mistake is spending business money without having a clear plan.

For example, a business owner makes ₦100,000 in sales and immediately spends a large part of it on personal needs. When it is time to buy more stock, pay for transportation, advertise the business or handle an unexpected expense, there may not be enough money left.

This can put unnecessary pressure on the business.

Mixing Business Money With Personal Money

Another problem is treating business money like personal money.

When there is no clear separation between the two, it becomes difficult to know how much the business is actually making.

You may think, “I'm making good money,” when in reality, most of the money has already gone into personal spending and business expenses.

Even a small business should have a simple way of keeping track of its income and expenses.

Not Keeping Records

You don't need to be an accountant to keep basic business records.

Write down:

How much money comes in

How much you spend

What you spend it on

How much stock you purchase

How much profit you make

How much you take out for personal use

These simple records can help you understand what is really happening in your business.

The Business Needs Money Too

Sometimes, business owners make the mistake of taking all the profit for themselves.

But a growing business needs money to grow.

Some of your profit may need to go back into the business—for example, buying more stock, improving your services, marketing your products or investing in tools that can make your work easier.

This doesn't mean you should never enjoy the money you make. It simply means you need to pay yourself while still taking care of the business.

Start Small, But Manage What You Have

You don't need millions of naira to start learning good financial habits.

Whether you're running a small food business, selling clothes, offering a service, doing affiliate marketing, or running an online business, learn to keep track of your money from the beginning.

A good business idea can bring money in, but good money management helps you know where that money is going.

Before asking, “How can I make more money?” sometimes the better question is:

“Am I managing the money I already have properly?”

What is one money-management habit you think every small business owner should develop?

title: Dangote Refinery IPO: Everything You Need to Know Before You Invest
excerpt: Africa's biggest industrial name is about to make history on the stock market. Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals the company behind the Lekki mega r…
content:
Africa's biggest industrial name is about to make history on the stock market. Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals the company behind the Lekki mega refinery, the world's largest single train facility is set to open its long awaited public share sale on 14 September 2026, closing 13 October. The offer, unveiled at a signing ceremony in Lagos on September 7, 2026, involves 4.1 billion ordinary shares priced at ₦525 each, targeting gross proceeds of roughly $1.63 billion at an implied $49 billion valuation.

What makes this different from a typical big ticket listing is the accessibility angle, everyday investors can get in with a minimum of 10 shares, costing just ₦5,250, putting ownership within reach of ordinary Nigerians, not just institutions and the wealthy.

The timing tells its own story. The refinery swung from a $476 million aftertax loss in 2025 to a $1.82 billion net income in the first half of 2026 alone, a dramatic turnaround fueled by rising output and refining margins. Proceeds from the IPO are earmarked for a massive expansion drive, part of Aliko Dangote's ambition to nearly double the plant's capacity and cement its place as the largest refinery on the planet. With SEC approval secured and the offer documents already signed, this listing is being billed as potentially the largest in African history a milestone moment for Nigeria's capital markets and a real test of how much retail and institutional appetite exists for homegrown mega companies going public.

So would you buy in? Is ₦5,250 for a slice of Africa's biggest refinery an easy yes for you, or are you waiting to see how the shares perform after listing first?

title: Your only limitation is you
excerpt: Years ago I thought the issue was that people weren’t helping me. I blamed my failures on my family, friends, and people I felt could have made my life better.…
content:
Years ago I thought the issue was that people weren’t helping me. I blamed my failures on my family, friends, and people I felt could have made my life better. I was living in denial because owning up to it felt too big.

But after some time I realized life is meant to be lived by one person, and everything you get is attributed to you. So I dropped the excuses, started building, started believing in myself, faced the work, and left the blame behind.

And today I won’t say I’m at my peak, but I am better. It made me realize sometimes life just wants you to take a chance, and then everything unfolds.

title: Wait, Is This About Me?
excerpt: Because your late-night overthinking is actually universal.
content:
Have you ever stared at your phone, frozen mid-scroll, because a random post felt less like content and more like a direct security camera feed of your inner thoughts?

You blink, double-check the username, and think: Wait, is this about me?

Relax, the algorithm isn't running a personal surveillance unit on your life. The reality is much funnier: we are all living the exact same parallel experience. We're all over-thinking minor text messages from three days ago, building entire movie plots in our heads while trying to sleep, and convincing ourselves we're the only ones winging it while everyone else has their life together.

You aren't uniquely chaotic; you're just human. We're all just passing the same universal survival blueprint back and forth.

When was the last time the internet called you out like this? Drop it in the comments.

title: Nigerians Face Another Fuel Shock as Pump Prices Approach ₦1,500 a Litre
excerpt: Fuel is now going for as much as ₦1,500 a litre in parts of Nigeria, and honestly, people are tired. Prices keep climbing while everything else, food, rent, tra…
content:
Fuel is now going for as much as ₦1,500 a litre in parts of Nigeria, and honestly, people are tired. Prices keep climbing while everything else, food, rent, transport just keeps getting harder to afford. It's not just a headline for most Nigerians. It’s the difference between getting to work or staying home, between eating three meals or two.

And when you put that next to a minimum wage of ₦70,000, the math simply doesn't work. That's barely enough to fill a tank, let alone live on for a month. Families are cutting corners just to survive, and there's a growing sense of frustration that the people making decisions aren't the ones feeling the pinch. The gap between what Nigerians earn and what it costs to just get by is stretching thinner by the day.

title: HAKDASHA 2
excerpt: Without much thought and deep reflection, Andrew left for the city the next day. Soon he remembered that he once had a primary school friend whose name is Jack …
content:
Without much thought and deep reflection, Andrew left for the city

the next day.

Soon he remembered that he once had a primary school friend whose name is Jack who was now based in the city. He immediately placed a call to his friend and told his friend of his intention to come to the city to hustle, but had nowhere to stay.

Jack was happy and surprised and then he said, “I will be happy to accommodate you.” Andrew was so happy and he told Jack that he would love to come the next day. Jack was shocked and he said to Andrew, “are you sure you don't want to take your time to really think about this? Are you really sure you want to come? The city’s life is not the way you think, it involves a lot of determination and it is sometimes risky and dangerous if not well prepared.”

Andrew felt like Jack didn't want him to come over so he got slightly offended. He said to Jack, “are you sure you want to accommodate me? Because I don't like the way you sound.” Andrew responded, “of course, I want you to come, I just want you to be aware and to be ready for anything that comes.”

Andrew shrugged and requested for his house address which Jack gave. While on the bus going to the city, the passenger who sat beside Andrew decided to engage him in a conversation.

They got talking and after some introduction, the passenger asked Andrew where exactly he was headed in the city and what he plans to do there, but Andrew couldn't provide an intelligent answer. He simply said, “God will take control when I get there.”

The passenger said, “Yes, God will take control but you should have at least asked God to show you the plans He has for you and how He wants them actualised in your life because God has amazing plans for every one of His children, but sometimes it will take patience for those plans to begin to actualize. You know His ways are different from our ways and His thoughts from our thoughts.

Proverbs 16:3 also says, Commit your actions to the Lord and your plans will succeed. You see, God didn't say we shouldn't make our own plans, but what is best is that as we are making plans, we should also be seeking the face of God concerning His plans for us, so that we don't do something opposite—which might harm us in the long run.”

“Andrew”, he continued, “did God really approve of you going to the city?” Andrew wasn't having any of that, instead he acted like he couldn't hear the passenger, but in real sense, what the passenger said cut deep into Him. Unknown to Andrew, the passenger was also sent to him by God to talk to him to go back to the village, but Andrew was bent on his fleshly desires.

Finally, Andrew arrived at the city and he was so elated! He was amazed at the beautiful buildings, infrastructures, latest models of cars, the fresh atmosphere of luxury and essence. Andrew was happy that he was set for life! “I am no longer going to that poverty stricken village till I have made it in life. I have left everything that connects me to the village and I don't mind what it will take me to become

very rich.”

“I will do anything it takes me to become rich, chill with the big guys and show my village people that I am not here to play.”

Unknown to Andrew, his predicament had just begun.
