title: Big 25
excerpt: Finally joined the ranks of old and wise
content:
For someone who just unlocked the full frontal lobe upgrade 🤣, I feel like I finally have bragging rights.

Everything that pops out of my mouth or every thought now feels like ancient wisdom 🤣.

So for someone that's joined the ranks of the old and wise, I probably have a few things to say.

The most important one?

Never live your life in anticipation.

It's easy to think: when I reach this level, or when I finally have this, then I can finally live life. For now, you just choose to exist. You think you're not worthy of some things. Or worse, you think you need all the constellations to align before you make certain moves.

(Please don't mind the grammar, it comes with the age 🤣)

I do put it to you: there's no greater time than now.

So get up from sitting on your hands. Truly grasp everything life has to offer. Make sure you milk every opportunity life throws along your way.

Learn to forgive yourself for things done to you and things you've done too. It's one of the most freeing things you can do for yourself.

I know I said I had a few things to say, and I'm probably exceeding that. But I'll round it up with this:

Don't forget to breathe.

You have no pre-existing knowledge of what life is all about. There's only one lifeline given to each of us. So as you strive to be great, still keep account of the fact that you're human.

The good thing about everything I've said is that once you scrape it's already too late from your train of thoughts and vocabulary, you get access to everything I've just said which comes with a magical boon: another chance at life. No matter your current age or situation.

In all, put God first. And I promise everything else will be added to you.

I hope you guys subscribe and follow me so you get to be the first to see my stuff and engage with it.

Thank you in anticipation.

title: If I Could Go Back to the Very First Day I Met You…
excerpt: The Man I Still Loved
content:
I wish I could tell you that after everything I found out about Kunle, I packed my things and never looked back.

But the truth is, I couldn’t leave him.

I stayed at my friend’s place for four days. Four days of staring at my phone, rereading old messages, and missing the same man who had given me every reason to walk away.

My friends kept saying, “Bola, you need to leave this marriage.”

And I would nod like I agreed.

Then, on the fifth day, Kunle texted me.

Kunle: Good morning, my love. I know you’re not ready to talk, but I’m sorry. I miss you.

I didn’t reply.

He called later.

“Please don’t hang up. I just want to hear your voice.”

“What’s left to say, Kunle?”

“I know I’ve hurt you. I’m not asking you to forget everything. I just need you to know that I still love you.”

I wanted to be angry. I really did.

But hearing his voice made me cry.

The next day, he sent another message.

Kunle: I made your favourite stew. I know you haven’t been eating properly.

It was such a small thing. But he remembered.

And I hated how much that mattered to me.

Two days later, I agreed to see him.

When I got to the house, he didn’t try to hug me or force a conversation. He just brought me water and sat beside me.

“Why did you lie to me?” I asked.

“Because I was afraid of losing you.”

“So you decided to make me marry you without knowing the truth?”

He lowered his head.

“You’re right. I was wrong, Bola. I can’t undo it, but I’m sorry.”

Then he brought out my favourite food.

And when he opened his arms, I went into them.

I cried against his chest, and he held me like he used to.

For a moment, I forgot about Teni, the other woman, and all the lies.

I just missed my husband.

My friends weren’t happy when I told them I’d seen him.

“Bola, love is not enough,” my friend said.

Teni called too.

“You don’t have to prove you love him by staying,” she warned.

I knew they were right.

But knowing I should leave and actually being able to leave were two different things.

When I returned home, Kunle had cleaned our bedroom and replaced the flowers on my bedside table.

“I know things can’t go back to how they were,” he said. “But I want to try. If you’ll let me.”

I thought about everything he’d done.

Then I thought about the man I’d fallen in love with.

“I want to try too,” I whispered.

That night, I lay beside him, his arms wrapped around me.

Maybe things could get better.

Maybe we could rebuild what we’d lost.

I know what everyone would say.

But they don’t know him like I do.

They don’t know the man I fell in love with.

And lying there beside him, I wanted so badly to believe that we could still be okay.

So I held him tighter.

To be continued…

title: I Think There Is Something Wrong With Me
excerpt: The madness of hiding who you are to survive a system built on lies.
content:
Is being perfect all just a myth or can I actually achieve that perfection everyone claims it exists?

I am human and I make mistakes but yet I don't accept all these and try to shape myself into something I am not. It's hard; it really is, yet I still reach for this perfection, knowing fully well, I'll probably end up being buried ten feet deep.

It's all just made up, isn't it? But why am I still aiming for it? Why do I need to wish for a different smile, jawline, waist, voice and appearance? Why do I hide my flaws and pretend to be who I am not?

"What is wrong with me?" I ask myself this question a lot. The lies I've told has driven me into madness that at this point, I might just have to continue to keep up with them or else the world will see me for who I truly am; A FLAWED HUMAN!

The cracks are beginning to show, yet I still keep on patching them up. When will I ever let myself be who I am? WHEN?

I just want to be perfect but can that ever truly be achieved?

Who even started this whole thing? How did it come to be? So many pretense. The whole world is flawed and yet it built a system of perfection that if you don't fit into it, you are an outcast and can never be something.

Your true self is rejected and only the false version of you that is accepted.

Why can't I just be different and stop with this perfection nonsense?

title: WHY DOES YOUR 'CLEAN' TOWEL GET DIRTY IF YOU ONLY USE IT AFTER HAVING A BATH?
excerpt: ‎YOU JUST TOOK A NICE BATH, SO WHY IS YOUR TOWEL GETTING DIRTY? ‎Imagine this. ‎‎You step into the bathroom, take a shower, wash your body thoroughly, rinse off the soap and come out feeling fresh and…
content:
‎YOU JUST TOOK A NICE BATH, SO WHY IS YOUR TOWEL GETTING DIRTY?

‎Imagine this.

‎‎You step into the bathroom, take a shower, wash your body thoroughly, rinse off the soap and come out feeling fresh and sparkling clean.

‎‎Then you grab a clean-looking towel and dry yourself.

‎‎A few days later, that same towel smells somehow offensive and makes you wonder what the hell is going on.

‎‎Sometimes it even feels like the towel has somehow become "dirty."

‎‎But here is the interesting question:

‎‎How can a towel become dirty when you only use it after bathing, which supposedly wipes dirt away from the body?

‎‎The answer takes us into the fascinating world of microbiology.

‎‎Your skin is not a sterile surface.

‎‎Even immediately after a shower, your body is still carrying millions of microorganisms.

‎‎Bacteria, fungi and other microscopic organisms naturally live on our skin as part of what scientists call the skin microbiome.

‎‎Bathing removes many of them, along with sweat, excess oil and dead skin cells.

‎‎But it doesn't remove everything.

‎‎Some microorganisms remain around hair follicles, skin folds, the armpits, between the toes and other areas of the body.

‎‎So when you step out of the shower and dry yourself, some of these microorganisms are transferred directly onto your towel.

‎‎But microorganisms aren't the only thing your towel receives.

‎‎Your skin is constantly shedding dead cells.

‎‎In fact, you lose tiny amounts of skin every day without noticing it.

‎‎When you rub your body with a towel, some of these microscopic skin particles end up trapped within the fabric.

‎‎Your towel can also collect small amounts of skin oils, sweat, salts and other organic materials.

‎‎And then something important happens.

‎‎The towel becomes wet.

‎‎This combination of moisture plus organic material can create an environment where certain microorganisms can survive and multiply under suitable conditions.

‎‎This is especially relevant when you leave a towel damp in a warm bathroom with poor ventilation.

‎‎The longer it takes to dry, the more opportunity microorganisms have to remain active.

‎‎And this brings us to that familiar smell.

‎‎You know the smell right?

‎‎You wash your towel. It smells fresh.

‎‎You use it several times.

‎‎Then one day, you pick it up and think:

‎‎"Why does this towel smell like this?"

‎‎That unpleasant, musty smell can be associated with microbial activity and compounds produced as microorganisms metabolize organic material trapped in the fabric.

‎So what you are smelling isn't necessarily "dirt" in the traditional sense.

‎‎It can be the result of microbiology happening inside your towel.

‎‎And there is another fascinating part.

‎‎Your towel doesn't only receive microorganisms from your body.

‎‎It also interacts with the environment.

‎‎The bathroom itself contains microorganisms.

‎‎Your hands can transfer microorganisms to the towel.

‎‎The air, surfaces and other damp materials around the bathroom can contribute to what eventually ends up on the fabric.

‎‎With repeated use, your towel can therefore become a miniature ecosystem.

‎‎Think about it:

‎‎Skin microbes.

‎Environmental microbes.

‎Dead skin cells.

‎Oils.

‎Sweat.

‎Moisture.

‎Fabric.

‎‎All coming together in one place.

‎‎This doesn't mean that every towel is dangerous or that you should panic after using one twice.

‎‎Not at all.

‎‎For most healthy people, a properly maintained towel is simply part of normal daily hygiene.

‎‎The important thing is what happens after you use it.

‎‎Don't leave it permanently damp.

‎‎Hang it somewhere where air can circulate and allow it to dry completely.

‎‎Wash it regularly, especially when it develops an unpleasant smell, becomes visibly dirty, stays damp for long periods, or has been used by someone who is ill.

‎‎Because there is something fascinating about microbiology that we often forget:

‎‎Microorganisms don't need a laboratory to grow.

‎‎They are already around us.

‎‎They live on us, in our environment and sometimes on the ordinary objects we use every day.

‎‎Even your towel.

‎‎So the next time you finish a shower, look at your towel differently.

‎‎You didn't just dry your body.

‎‎You may have just introduced an entire collection of microscopic passengers into a warm, damp piece of fabric.

‎‎And that is why your towel can get dirty even after you take a bath.

‎‎Welcome to the microscopic world.

‎‎It's closer than you think.

title:
Your best post flopped.
Their mediocre post went viral.
excerpt: The war that doesn't end, the war between algorithms and a dedicated writer.
content:
Your best post flopped.

Their mediocre post went viral.

You blamed yourself.

You shouldn't have.

There is a name for what happened to you.

And most writers will never know it exists.

Diasimocracy vs Meritocracy.

A war between dedicated writers and the algorithms.

(Adapted from Professor Douglas Giles's article on Medium)

You ever seen a post with nothing to do with excellence or brilliance?

A total disorder.

Screaming complete lack of professionalism.

And yet, not only is it showing up on your feed, it is actually performing better than every brilliantly crafted piece around it.

Welcome to the world of Diasimocracy.

Still searching for what that means?

You can stop now — I got you as always. 😊

From the Greek word Diasimos — meaning "famous" or "celebrity" — Professor and Philosopher Douglas Giles coined the term Diasimocracy to define a particular modern landscape shaped heavily by social media algorithms.

A world where being a talented writer does not make you a successful one.

A world where you pour your soul into a masterpiece — and your post performs woefully.

A world where fame outranks quality.

Every single time.

Now let me ask you something.

Were you operating under the assumption that the best content always wins?

That excellence is eventually rewarded?

That if you write well enough, consistently enough, the platform will notice?

That is called Meritocracy.

And I hate to be the one to tell you this —

You have been playing the wrong game. 😅

The Algorithmic Monsters

Every platform has its own personalised, ever-evolving algorithm.

LinkedIn has its own.

Medium has its own.

Every platform that uses a recommender program has their own.

And these monsters are stone-headed and stone-hearted.

They have no affection for the brilliance in your writing.

No concern for the hours you spent crafting your sentences.

No appreciation for the research behind your words.

All they care about is engagement signals, posting frequency, follower count, and algorithmic familiarity.

In short, they care about who you are, not what you wrote.

But here is the good news.

The algorithm is not unbeatable.

It is dynamic — and so can you be.

I will be making another post very soon breaking down exactly how to navigate the algorithm, stay ahead of the battle, and make the monster work for you instead of against you.

Stay tuned. 👀

💬 Have you ever had a brilliant post flop while a mediocre one went viral? Tell me about it in the comments.

♻️ Repost — every writer in your network needs to see this today.

title: Black Heart
excerpt: Chapter 1. Birth of Black Heart
content:
Aria’s point of view

The night hung heavy and silent around me a warning I knew better than to ignore.

i sat alone in the wooden cabin at the edge of the village, in the place no one dared go.

My hands clasped around my swollen belly, and with every sharp pain came the same reminder: Tonight, my world would change irrovacably.

I had waited until after the moon rose, until the village stirred no more. There could be no witnesses. Not for this. Not for him.

Sweat dripped down my face as another wave of pain tore through me. I gritted my teeth and braced myself, pushing harder than I ever thought my body could bear.

A scream escaped my lips, muffled only by my own desperate will to Stay silent. They could never know what I carried. What I had brought into this world.

The contraction came faster, stronger, until my body had nothing left to give but surrender.

With one final push, a soft cry broke the stillness and for a moment that felt endless, the world seemed to stop breathing with me.

I lay there, spent my body shutting down with exhaustion even as my heart raced with fear and something close to wonder. I reached for him with shaking hands. My son.

He wasn’t crying anymore. His small body, slick from birth, lay strangely still and that was when I saw it. Something was wrong. Or maybe not wrong. A Flame.

His hard was dark as the space between stars, and it shone in the candlelight. But it wasn’t the darknesses that stole my breath. It was the fire. Black flame licked delicately from his hair, curling and alive, and yet it did not burn.

I knew, in that instant, what it meant. I had known for months, if I was honest with myself known and refused to let myself believe it.

His father’s blood ran too thick in his veins.

“You’re beautiful,” I whispered, my voice rough with disbelief. He didn’t cry. His tiny chest rose and fell in steady breaths, but his eyes white as snow, empty of color entirely stared up into mine with a weight no new born should carry.

As if he already understood everything I hadn’t told him yet. I pulled him to my chest, my fingers brushing through hair warmed by flame that Never scorched my skin.

The fire only danced there, flickering in the dark, and still I was afraid. Not of him. Never of him. I was afraid of what this meant for both of us now. I had to move, and quickly.

if the villagers learned what I carried a demon’s child they would show no mercy. They’d hunt him down, tear him apart, burn whatever was left, and call it righteous. They feared Demons and they were right to.

But I wasn’t afraid of my son. Whatever he was, he was mine.

Tears blurred my eyes as i wrapped him in the old blanket. I’d kept hidden for weeks, prepared for his exact night.

I pressed a kiss to his forehead, and the flames parted beneath my lips, as though they recognize my touch and chose not to hurt me.

His father had promised me a world beyond this one. He was gone now, I was left with a child too powerful for either of us to hide.

There was no time to rest, no time to recover. I bundled him tight against the Cold and reached for the satchel. I’d packed weeks ago, for this very moment and walked to the door with my heart slamming harder than the wind outside. I looked back once. Past the trees.

The midwife had grown suspicious the moment I refused her help. Someone would definitely come looking.

so I ran, as far as my legs could take me. Running from this moment for so long hoping, against everything I knew, that loving a demon wouldn’t cost me what it always costs.

But love has a price. I would pay it over and over if it meant keeping my son alive

He stirred against me and made a sound unlike any Infant’s cry low, almost a purr, carrying something ancient beneath the smallness of his body.

I shivered and held him tighter. Outside, the cold bit into my skin. The wind pulled at my hair as if it’s already knew what I was fleeing.

I caught the first flicker of torchlight. Shit. They were awake. Maybe they’d felt it. The flames in the sky when he was born. Maybe they already knew.

my heart pounded harder as I forced my legs down the narrow path, away from the cabin. Away from everything I’d ever known. I didn’t know where I was going. Only that I couldn’t stop.

The villagers were close. Shouting and throwing rocks at me.

Terror gripped my throat. I pulled my son in against my chest and pushed myself faster, my breath tearing in ragged gasps. I needed somewhere to hide. Anywhere.

The trees broke open into a clearing, and there half swallowed by moss and vine stood the ruins of some ancient stone building. The kind of place people warned children away from. Cursed. They called it. I didn’t care. It was my only chance.

I didn’t hesitate. I ran for the ruins and pressed my back against the cold damp stone, listening.

I held my breath and prayed. My son stirred against me and I felt his flames dim, almost as if he, too understood the danger.

I gunned a lullaby under my breath, barely more than air, hoping it would keep him quiet, keep him stull.

I knew it wasn’t over. It would never really be over not as long as there was a demon’s child in this world for them to hunt.

I looked down at him, his small face lit Gold by the last flicker of his flame.

“I’ll keep you safe,” i whispered, my voice cracking. “I’ll protect you. No matter what.”

title: The Wrong Wedding Guest
excerpt: Romance • Slow burn • Betrayal
content:
Chapter 1: The Girl in Red

The wedding hall was filled with laughter, music, and expensive perfume.

Amara adjusted the simple red dress she had borrowed from her cousin. She wasn't supposed to be there. The invitation belonged to someone else, but her cousin had begged her to attend in her place.

"Just smile, eat, and come home," her cousin had said.

Easy enough… until Amara accidentally spilled an entire glass of champagne on the most powerful man in the room.

The music stopped.

Every eye turned.

The man slowly looked up. Tall. Calm. Dressed in a black suit that probably cost more than her school fees.

"I'm so sorry," Amara whispered, already searching for the nearest exit.

Instead of getting angry, he smiled.

"I've been trying to escape this wedding for an hour," he said. "You just gave me the perfect excuse."

She blinked.

"What's your name?"

"Amara."

"I'm Adrian."

She didn't know that Adrian wasn't just another guest.

He was the groom's billionaire younger brother.

And before the night ended, someone would mistake Amara for Adrian's girlfriend… changing both of their lives forever.

Chapter 2: The Fake Girlfriend

Amara took one step backward, ready to disappear into the crowd.

Then a glamorous woman in a silver gown walked over with a bright smile.

“Adrian! You finally brought her.”

She hugged Adrian before turning to Amara.

“And this must be your girlfriend.”

Amara’s heart nearly stopped.

She opened her mouth to explain, but Adrian gently took her hand.

“Yes… this is Amara.”

She stared at him in shock.

The woman beamed. “Your mother has been dying to meet you!”

Before Amara could protest, Adrian leaned closer and whispered,

“Please. Just ten minutes. I’ll owe you.”

Ten minutes became dinner.

Dinner became introductions.

And somehow, Amara found herself sitting beside Adrian’s mother, who looked at her with the warmest eyes.

“You make my son smile,” she said softly. “Don’t disappear after tonight.”

Amara forced a smile, guilt twisting inside her chest.

When the wedding finally ended, she hurried outside into the cool night air.

Her phone buzzed.

Unknown Number: Thank you for saving me tonight. — Adrian.

A small smile escaped her lips.

Across the parking lot, someone secretly snapped a photo of them standing together.

By morning, the internet would call them Lagos’ newest billionaire couple

Chapter 3: We’re Trending

Amara woke up to 37 missed calls.

Confused, she opened Instagram—and her heart dropped.

A gossip page had posted her photo with Adrian.

“Billionaire Adrian Bello spotted with his mysterious girlfriend at last night’s wedding.”

2.8 million views.

Comments flooded in.

She’s so pretty!

Who is this girl?

They look perfect together.

Her phone rang again.

It was Adrian.

“Don’t panic,” he said calmly. “I’m coming to explain.”

Twenty minutes later, a black Range Rover stopped outside her gate.

For the first time, Adrian saw where Amara truly lived—not in luxury, but in a small apartment filled with dreams.

He smiled gently.

You’re nothing like the girls they expected.”

Before Amara could reply, another car pulled up.

A woman stepped out wearing designer heels.

She removed her sunglasses and looked straight at Amara.

“I’m Vanessa,” she said coldly.

“Adrian is my fiancé.”

Chapter 4: The Woman Who Claimed Him

Amara felt her stomach tighten.

She looked at Adrian, waiting for him to deny it.

Instead, he sighed.

“Vanessa… not here.”

Vanessa laughed bitterly. “So you won’t tell her? Fine, I will.”

She turned to Amara.

“Our families arranged our engagement two years ago. The wedding is in three months.”

Amara’s eyes filled with tears.

“So… everything last night was a lie?”

“No,” Adrian said quickly. “The engagement is real, but I never loved Vanessa.”

Vanessa stepped closer.

Stay away from him, Amara. You’ll only get your heart broken.”

She got back into her car and drove away.

Silence remained.

Amara slowly removed her hand from Adrian’s.

“I was only your fake girlfriend,” she whispered. “Let’s keep it that way.”

She walked inside without looking back.

Outside, Adrian stood frozen… realizing he might have lost the only woman who had ever made him feel free.

Chapter 5: One Last Chance

For three days, Amara ignored Adrian’s calls.

She buried herself in work, convincing herself that rich people only brought complicated lives.

On the fourth day, there was a knock on her door.

It wasn’t Adrian.

It was his mother.

Mrs. Bello smiled gently and handed Amara a small box.

“Adrian asked me to give you this. He said you’d never open the door for him.”

Inside was the champagne-stained handkerchief from the wedding, carefully washed and folded.

A note was tucked beneath it.

You were never part of my plan… but somehow you became the best part of my life. Please meet me one last time.

Amara closed her eyes.

Her heart wanted to say yes.

Her mind screamed no.

She picked up her phone and typed just one message:

“This is the last time.”

The reply came instantly.

“8 PM. The rooftop where we first laughed.”

Little did she know, someone else had already arrived there first… and they weren’t coming to make peace.

Chapter 6: The Rooftop Truth

At exactly 8:00 p.m., Amara stepped onto the rooftop.

The city lights glittered below, but Adrian was nowhere to be seen.

Then she heard a voice.

“Looking for him?”

Vanessa emerged from the shadows, holding a small envelope.

“I warned you to stay away.”

She handed Amara the envelope. Inside were engagement photos of Adrian and Vanessa—smiling, elegant, perfect.

Amara’s chest tightened.

Just as she turned to leave, the rooftop door burst open.

“Amara, wait!”

Adrian ran toward her, out of breath.

“I ended the engagement today,” he said. “I chose my own life… and I chose you.”

Vanessa’s eyes filled with tears as she quietly walked away.

Amara looked at Adrian, her heart trembling.

“Choosing me comes with nothing,” she whispered.

Adrian smiled.

“You’re everything.”

As their hands finally touched, camera flashes suddenly lit up the rooftop.

Someone had followed them.

The next morning, the headline read:

“Billionaire Heir Dumps Fiancée for Mystery Girl.”

Chapter 7: The Price of Love

By sunrise, Amara was everywhere.

Every blog had her photo. Every comment had an opinion.

“Gold digger.” “She stole another woman’s fiancé.”

Amara switched off her phone and cried.

A knock came at the door.

It was Adrian.

“I’m sorry,” he whispered. “You never asked for this.”

Amara looked at him with trembling eyes.

“Do you know what it feels like to have strangers hate you?”

Adrian stepped closer.

“Then let me protect you.”

Before she could answer, another black car stopped outside.

An older man stepped out.

His voice was cold.

“I’m Adrian’s father.”

He looked directly at Amara.

“Leave my son, and I’ll give you ₦100 million. Refuse… and I’ll make sure you lose everything.”

Amara stood frozen.

For the first time, love had a price.

Chapter 8 (Final): The Right Wedding Guest

Amara looked at the cheque on the table.

₦100,000,000.

She took a deep breath… then tore it into pieces.

“I won’t sell my heart,” she said quietly.

Mr. Bello stood speechless.

At that moment, Adrian walked in. He had heard everything.

He faced his father for the first time without fear.

“You taught me how to build a business,” Adrian said. “She taught me how to love.”

Weeks later, the scandals faded. Vanessa moved on with her life, and the gossip pages found another story to chase.

One year later…

Amara walked into another beautiful wedding hall wearing a white dress—not as a guest this time, but as the bride.

Adrian smiled as she reached him.

“Funny,” he whispered. “I tried to escape a wedding, and that’s where I found my wife.”

Amara laughed softly.

“Maybe I was never the wrong wedding guest… just the right person at the wrong wedding.”

As they said “I do,” the room erupted in applause, proving that sometimes the greatest love stories begin with one unexpected mistake.

THE END.

title: THE POWER OF NETWORKING 🤝
excerpt: 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗣𝗢𝗪𝗘𝗥 𝗢𝗙 𝗡𝗘𝗧𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗞𝗜𝗡𝗚 🤝Over the years, I’ve heard people talk about networking, networking, networking.But honestly, I think many student…
content:
𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗣𝗢𝗪𝗘𝗥 𝗢𝗙 𝗡𝗘𝗧𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗞𝗜𝗡𝗚 🤝

Over the years, I’ve heard people talk about networking, networking, networking.

But honestly, I think many students and young people still underestimate its power.

So, if you’re reading this, please learn how to network.

𝗡𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗖𝗩 𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗻𝗼𝘁.

But networking requires 𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗮𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆.

You have to be willing to introduce yourself, ask questions, communicate what you’re passionate about, tell people what you’re working on, and genuinely look for ways to add value.

𝗜’𝘃𝗲 𝘀𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝘆 𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗶𝗻 𝗺𝘆 𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝗷𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆.

Back in 2021, I started following people who were doing amazing things and sharing knowledge that inspired me.

I paid attention to their work, learned from their experiences, and gradually became familiar with their stories.

Fast forward to 2025, I had the opportunity to meet one of those people in person.

I got his contact.

Then, in January 2026, I had the audacity to reach out and have a conversation with him about something I had been passionate about.

I almost talked myself out of it.

“How will I approach him?”

“What will I say?”

“Will he even respond?”

𝗕𝘂𝘁 𝗜 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝘂𝘁.

And that conversation became much more than just a conversation.

He mentored me, helped me break down what I wanted to do, gave me practical guidance, and helped me understand the steps I needed to take.

𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗻𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴.

Sometimes, the person who is already where you want to go has the knowledge, experience, or perspective that can help you navigate your own journey better.

So, wherever you are in your journey:

• 𝗙𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄 people who inspire you.
• 𝗔𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗱 events, trainings, webinars, and communities.
• 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁 meaningful conversations.
• 𝗕𝗲 𝗰𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿 about what you want.
• 𝗔𝗱𝗱 𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗲 before asking for favours.
• And most importantly, 𝗱𝗼𝗻’𝘁 𝗹𝗲𝘁 𝘀𝗵𝘆𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗽 𝘆𝗼𝘂 from building relationships.

You don't have to know everyone.

You just need to be intentional about knowing the right people and building genuine relationships with them.

I can confidently say that many of the opportunities and experiences I’ve had recently have come through God and the relationships I’ve built through networking.

𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗻𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗼𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗮𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.

𝗜𝘁 𝗺𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗮 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.

Go out there.

Introduce yourself.

Ask the question.

Start the conversation.

𝗡𝗘𝗧𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗞. 𝗡𝗘𝗧𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗞. 𝗡𝗘𝗧𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗞. 🤝

title: The Girl They Thought Would Never Rise
excerpt:
Part One

The Girl Nobody Chose
content:
Nora carried the tray of dirty glasses into the kitchen while candles on her stepsisters cake were still smoking. Twenty‑two of them.

Nora had counted without meaning to. It was Priya's birthday. It was Nora's birthday too. Nobody had mentioned it.

Nora had spent the morning polishing the silver for Priya's party, the afternoon ironing the tablecloth Meera had chosen and the evening carrying trays to guests who told Priya how beautiful Nora looked and never once wondered who the girl serving them was.

Meera said from the sink not turning around "Those plates go in the cabinet, not the rack.. Wipe the counters before you go upstairs. I do not want the kitchen smelling like fish in the morning."

"Okay " Nora replied.

It was the answer.

In that house many words were considered disrespectful. Few words made people forget Nora was there.

Her father sat in the living room with a newspaper on his knees, his glasses pushed into his hair. He arrived at the party in twenty minutes. Long enough to shake hands with guests. Enough to tell Priya she looked beautiful. Long enough to smile when people complimented the daughter he had chosen to celebrate.

He had not looked toward the kitchen once.

He had not wished Nora a happy birthday.

Nora was not sure which hurt more. That his father had forgotten or that his father remembered and decided silence was easier.

For years Nora had tried to convince herself that her fathers silence meant his father was staying out of it.

That a man who never defended Nora was also a man who would never intentionally hurt her.

Nora had stopped believing that a long time ago.

Silence was still a choice.

Her fathers choice had always been the same.

Her father watched.

Her father knew.

Her father did nothing.

Nora was up the stairs when she heard Meera's voice through the kitchen door.

The kind of voice people use when they believe a wall is doing more work than it actually is.

"She is eighteen now. Let her go her own way. We have done more than enough for her."

Nora stopped. She waited.

Not because she expected her father to defend her. Because some small, foolish part of her still hoped her father would

The house stayed quiet.

No argument.

No disagreement.

No voice saying, "She is my daughter."

Nothing.

Nora walked upstairs without making a sound.

That night Nora sat on the edge of her bed for hours.

The room at the end of the hallway had once been used for storage. It still felt that way sometimes. A place where things nobody cared about were kept.

Nora looked around at the space she had called home for years.

The old curtains.

The cracked mirror.

The tiny shelf where she kept the things that belonged only to her.

Nora thought about the girl she used to be.

The girl who sat in the front row at school with her hand raised before the teacher finished asking questions.

The girl who believed being talented mattered.

The girl who dreamed without apologizing for it.

Then life slowly taught her otherwise.

The school fees that somehow disappeared whenever it was her turn.

In the afternoon Nora was called out of class because her fees had not been paid and she never returned.

The books she wanted but could not have.

The opportunities given to Priya because she was "worth investing in."

Years of hearing that Nora would never become anything.

Until eventually Nora started saying it to herself.

Maybe they were right.

Maybe Nora was not special.

Maybe some people were simply born to stand behind others.

Noras eyes landed on the notebook hidden beneath her clothes.

The only thing in that room that still belonged to her.

The pages were worn. The corners were soft from years of being touched.

Inside were dreams she had written before she learned to be ashamed of wanting things.

A shop she wanted to open.

Places she wanted to visit.

A life she wanted to build.

Nora had not opened it in over a year.

Nora told herself it was because she had grown up.

But down, she knew the truth.

She was afraid. Afraid of wanting something she might never get. Afraid of hoping

That night she opened it.

For the first time in a long time, she allowed herself to imagine a different life. Before sunrise she packed a bag.

Nora did not own much. Two changes of clothes. Her mothers old coat that Meera had once thrown into a donation bag because it was "outdated."

Nora had quietly taken it back. Hidden it away. Her mothers ring, hanging from a string around Nora's neck because it did not fit her finger yet.

The notebook. That was everything. Before leaving she stood in the doorway of her room. And looked back.

There were no memories attached to the space. No moments where Nora had felt truly loved. No reason to stay.

Nora had spent years waiting for someone in that house to choose her. Maybe it was time Nora chose herself.

Nora left while the sky was still dark. She did not write a note. She did not say goodbye.

Nora doubted anyone would notice she was gone until they needed something from her.

The bus station at five in the morning was cold and nearly empty. One overhead light flickered above Nora buzzing like it could not decide whether to stay on.

Nora sat on a bench with her bag pressed against her chest and her mothers ring held tightly in her palm.

"This is a beginning, " Nora told herself.

"Not an ending."

Nora did not believe it yet. she repeated it anyway. Because it was the one thing she still had control over.

Nora slept sitting up that night waking every time footsteps came close.

In the morning Nora walked until she found a small diner with a handwritten sign taped to the window.

HELP WANTED. CLEAN TABLES

Nora stood outside for five minutes. Fear told her to keep walking. Pride told her she deserved better. Hunger reminded her that survival came before pride.

So Nora walked inside. The woman behind the counter looked at her carefully.

"Looking for work?"

Nora nodded.

"I can work hard."

The woman studied Nora for a moment before handing her a piece of paper.

"Come back this afternoon."

It was not a miracle. It was not a rescue. It was a chance. Sometimes a chance is enough.

Nora's first shift lasted six hours.

Nora cleaned tables, washed dishes, carried plates and smiled at customers who never learned Nora's name.

The money was not much. Less than what Meera used to spend on flowers for the dining table.

When Nora held that first paycheck in her hand she felt something she had not felt in years.

Pride.

Because nobody had given it to her. Nobody could take credit for it. It was Noras.

At the end of the week Nora rented a room above a laundromat. The mattress smelled like someone's life. The walls were thin. The room was nothing like the home Nora once dreamed of.

It was hers. With her salary she bought a notebook. A cheap one. Nothing fancy. The kind people walk past without noticing.

Nora sat on the edge of the mattress that night listening to the sound of washing machines below her. She thought about her fathers silence. Meera's words. Nora's former self.

Then she opened the notebook. Wrote one sentence.

"This is not where my story ends."

Nora pressed hard that the words marked the page underneath. She did not know what her story would become.

Nora did not know how many ttimes she would have to repeat those words when life tested her again.

Nora knew one thing. A person who writes down a dream has already made a decision. Somewhere beneath the fear. Somewhere beneath the pain. She has decided to try.


Years Later

The elevator doors opened onto the floor.

Meera stepped out wearing her coat already preparing the impatient tone she would use if anyone made her wait too long.

She was there for a business meeting. A connection someone had arranged.

A company that according to everyone was becoming impossible to ignore. She had not bothered asking who owned it. It did not seem important.

Until now.

The glass doors at the end of the hallway carried a name Meera did not recognize. Inside was an office overlooking the city.

Behind the desk sat a woman reading through documents with confidence. The kind of confidence that belonged to someone who no longer needed permission to take up space.

The woman looked up.

Meera stopped breathing.

Because Meera knew that face.

Meera knew those eyes.

The girl Meera had once told would never become anything was no longer standing in the corner of a kitchen. The girl was no longer carrying trays. The girl was no longer asking for permission.

The girl was sitting behind the desk. The name on the door belonged to Nora. The woman looked at Meera silently.

For the time, in many years Meera had no words at all.

Because the girl they had left behind, the girl they had counted out, was now the woman they would have to answer to.

title: Hypocrites, that is what we are.
excerpt: I love to think of myself as fair, objective observer of the world. I pride myself on having principles, and a sharp eye for right and wrong. But if I’m being c…
content:
I love to think of myself as fair, objective observer of the world. I pride myself on having principles, and a sharp eye for right and wrong. But if I’m being completely honest with myself, I’ve realized something uncomfortable: I am a hypocrite, and so are you and you and all of you.

​Human nature is practically built on double standards. We operate with an invisible set of rules that seamlessly shifts depending on who is on trial ourselves or someone else.

​Psychologists call it the fundamental attribution error, but I call it the "me vs. you" rule.

When I take time to relax, I’m "practicing self-care" and recharging. When a coworker takes a long break, they’re being lazy. When I speak up assertively to my younger siblings, I’m being passionate and decisive; when someone else does it, they’re being pushy or arrogant. We evaluate our own actions through the lens of our good intentions, but we evaluate others strictly by their outcomes.

​Why do we do this? Because our brains are wired to protect our egos. Admitting that we share the exact same flaws, impatience, and lapses in judgment as the people who annoy us requires effort. It’s far easier to hold up a mirror to the world while standing safely behind a one-way visor.

Remember I'm just a guy expressing his opinions.

-3enchNad

title: What Was Left of Me
excerpt:
I might not be where I want to be yet, but when I look back, I realise I have come farther than I ever thought I would.

That morning, I stood by my balcony, watching the world wake up beneath me.

Children ran across the compound, chasing one another with careless joy. Their laughter floated up to me, loud and unrestrained. One little girl stumbled, scraped her knee, and, after a few seconds of tears, got back up and ran after the others as though nothing had happened.

I smiled.

There was something beautiful about being young enough to believe that every day would be kind to you.

I rested my arms against the railing and watched them for a little longer.

"Enjoy it," I whispered, though they could never hear me. "Enjoy every moment you can. One day, you'll look back and wish you could have one more ordinary morning like this."

I turned away from the balcony and walked back into my room.

Then I saw it.

The photograph.

It sat quietly on the shelf, covered in a thin layer of dust. My fingers brushed across the glass, stopping over the faces I had spent years trying not to remember too often.

My family.

For a moment, the room disappeared.

There was the screech of tyres.

The violent crash.

Glass shattering.

Then silence.

I was fifteen when the accident took everything from me.

Fifteen years had passed since that day, yet sometimes, all it took was one photograph to make me feel like that little girl again, standing in the ruins of the life she once knew and wondering how she was supposed to keep breathing.

But somehow, I did.

I survived the accident.

I survived the empty house.

I survived the days when grief was the only thing that came home with me.

And when I thought I had finally survived the worst of it, my uncle took what remained of my family's inheritance.

Everything.

The house. The money. The things my parents had worked their entire lives to leave behind.

I still remember standing outside with my belongings beside me, watching the door close.

That was the day I learned that losing everything did not always happen in a single accident.

Sometimes, people took the pieces that were left.

I walked towards the mirror.

For a few seconds, I simply stared at the woman looking back at me.

Then I laughed softly.

"This babe has really been through shit."

My smile faded.

I looked closer.

The woman in the mirror wasn't the frightened girl from fifteen years ago.

She had scars she didn't talk about.

Memories she carried quietly.

Dreams she had nearly abandoned.

Yet somehow, she was still here.

Still dreaming.

Still trying.

Still becoming.

I placed my palm against the mirror.

Maybe I had broken more times than I cared to remember.

Maybe there were moments when I thought I wouldn't make it to the other side.

But I did.

And perhaps that was the part of my story I had been too busy surviving to notice.

I wasn't standing in front of the mirror because I had finally become everything I wanted to be.

I was standing there because, after everything life had taken from me, I was still becoming her.

And for the first time, that was enough.

I smiled at my reflection.

"Look at you," I whispered.

Still here.

Still standing.

Still chasing the dream.

Fifteen years later, the girl who thought her story had ended was still writing it.

title: You Cannot Afford To Give Up
excerpt: 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗖𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗔𝗳𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗚𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗨𝗽.There are moments in life when you sit quietly and ask yourself:“Is this really worth it?”You become tired.T…
content:
𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗖𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗔𝗳𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗚𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗨𝗽.

There are moments in life when you sit quietly and ask yourself:

“Is this really worth it?”

You become tired.

Tired of trying.

Tired of waiting.

Tired of starting again after every setback.

And sometimes, giving up begins to look like the easiest option.

But before you quit, pause.

Look back.

Look at where you started.

Remember the battles you fought when nobody knew what you were going through.

Remember the mistakes you made and the lessons they taught you.

Remember the doors that closed, the disappointments you survived, and the moments you thought you wouldn't make it.

Yet…

You are still here.

You are still trying.

You are still learning.

You are still growing.

You are still becoming.

That means something.

You cannot afford to give up because you cannot afford to let God down.

The journey may not look the way you imagined it would.

You may still be fighting certain habits.

You may still be battling fear, doubt, addictions, failure, or circumstances beyond your control.

But your current struggle does not mean your story is over.

As long as you are willing to keep moving, there is still hope.

And there is another reason you cannot afford to give up.

Someone is watching you.

There are people behind you who will one day draw strength from your story.

There are younger people who will look at your journey and say:

“If they could make it through that, maybe I can make it too.”

There are generations you may never meet who could benefit from the decisions you make today.

Your persistence may become someone's encouragement.

Your testimony may become someone's reason to keep going.

So, don't stop here.

Gather yourself.

Buckle up.

Take another step.

Even if it is a small one.

Keep moving.

Because there is still strength in you.

There is still hope ahead.

And one day, you may look back at this season and be grateful that you chose to keep going.

You have come too far to quit now.

title: Riddle me this
excerpt: At twenty-two, being a guy in the dating pool feels like trying to apply for an entry-level job that requires years of experience.I’ve watched the script play o…
content:
At twenty-two, being a guy in the dating pool feels like trying to apply for an entry-level job that requires years of experience.

I’ve watched the script play out since high school. Back when we were sixteen, the girls in my class looked past everyone in our grade with absolute disdain: "I don't date boys." Fair enough; we were dumb, loud, and smelled like cheap body spray. But now we’re twenty-two some twenty five scraping through our first real jobs and figuring out life, and the goalposts have simply shifted into the stratosphere: "I don't date guys my age."

We’re too broke. Our apartments lack aesthetic plant life. Some still live with parents lol. So the girls my age look straight over our heads toward the guys five, eight, ten years older, the ones with the high-rise leases, the car payments already sorted, and the money to pay for weekend getaways. It’s written into their roadmap: by twenty-five, the official policy is "I only date older men."

It used to make me bitter, until I started noticing the second half of the movie playing out in real time through some of my aunties.

The minute those exact same women hit thirty, the script suddenly flips from ruthless ambition to pure outrage. I hear them at family gatherings venting with complete fury: "Why are thirty-five-year-old men always chasing twenty-two-year-old girls? It’s shallow. It’s predatory. It’s disgusting."

The irony is wild to watch from where I'm standing.

For an entire decade, they treated dating like an open commodities exchange, ruthlessly trading their youth and beauty to bypass guys their own age and jump straight to the finish line of someone else’s success. They happily validated older men prioritizing youth, so long as they were the young ones receiving the dinners and the status.

Now the calendar flips, and they’re mad the economic rules haven’t rewritten themselves just to suit them. You can't spend ten years aggressively playing the market, pricing out the guys building from the ground up, and then cry foul the second the market leaves you behind for the new batch of twenty-two-year-olds.

Like my dad would always say , "new commodities are supplied into the market every minute so just wait, the price of a trendy product would definitely drop when it has served its purpose."

-3enchnad

title: Age Is Just a Number
excerpt: Except my dad didn’t see it that way. Team Titi or Team Daddy? You decide.
content:
Hear me out guys… let me just gist you people small.

I’ve missed my period for weeks now and I’m almost certain I’m pregnant. And before anybody starts forming assumptions — the person involved is not just anybody. This man is respected. Established. My family loves him🥹.

Like, it’s not even a small love. My mum literally calls him “our person.” Whenever anything happens in this house — anything at all — he’s the first person she calls.

He’s been in our lives for as long as I can remember. My parents trust him with everything — money matters, family decisions, even things they don’t tell just anybody.

So when this thing happened between us, I didn’t even sit and overthink am like that. E just happen. Before I knew it, I was counting dates in my head, doing small calculations, trying not to panic but also not trying to lie to myself🥲.

And honestly, if we are being sincere, at least it’s not a useless man. He already told me not to worry about anything — that he’ll handle everything, take care of me and the baby. The way he said it sef, you’d think say na small thing.

He even mentioned marriage o. Casual like that. Like it’s something we can arrange sharp sharp. I won’t lie, I didn’t hate the idea at all.

So imagine my confusion when I told my dad, and this man — who has never raised his voice in this house since I was born — started shaking. Shaking o. Like somebody wey see masquerade for afternoon.

I kept asking, “Daddy, why are you like this? Aren’t you happy for me?”

He just stared at me for a long time. Then he said, “Are you mad? That man is my childhood friend.”

I said, “Yes now, that’s why I trust him now—”

He didn’t even let me finish. “You’re pregnant for a man old enough to be your father??? Are you STUPID?”

Ehnnnn. Daddy ke😭. That word “stupid” entered somewhere I can’t explain.

But I no gree keep quiet o. I stood my ground.

“Daddy, am I supposed to just remove the pregnancy because he’s old enough to be my father? Yes, he’s old enough. But he’s NOT my father. There’s a clear difference!”

My mum just held her chest. “Titi, please don’t say another word—”

But I was not done. “I love him! Age is just a numberrrr daddy. What truly matters is love!”

That was when it happened. Everything moved in slow motion. My dad’s hand landed on my cheek before I even finished the sentence. One resounding slap that echoed through the whole parlour.

My mum jumped up, hands on her head. “Ah! Mogbe! Ah! Won ti pada get mi o”

I was holding my cheek, tears just dropping, but somehow still standing on business. “Daddy, you can slap me a thousand times, it won’t change how I feel!”

I mean, am I the delusional one here, or was my dad wrong for reacting like that?

Team Titi or Team Daddy?🥹😭

title: You Were Created For Impact
excerpt: 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗪𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗖𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗰𝘁During my primary school days, I had a couple of friends who would often come to me whenever they needed help.…
content:
𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗪𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗖𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗰𝘁

During my primary school days, I had a couple of friends who would often come to me whenever they needed help.

Sometimes, it was something small.

Sometimes, it was something they desperately needed.

And whenever I could help, I simply did.

I never thought too deeply about it.

I wasn't keeping records.

I wasn't expecting anything in return.

I wasn't thinking, “One day, this person will remember what I did for them.”

I was simply helping a friend.

Years passed.

Life happened.

We all grew up and went our separate ways.

Then, after many years, I met one of them again.

During our conversation, he suddenly said something that caught me off guard.

“Emma, do you remember how you used to give me a new exercise book whenever I didn't have one?”

I paused.

Honestly, I couldn't remember.

He continued telling me how there were times he didn't have a notebook to write in, and he was afraid the teacher would punish him.

And somehow, I had helped him.

Something I had completely forgotten had remained in his memory for years.

That moment taught me something profound.

𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗽 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗴𝗮𝘃𝗲, 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗼𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗽𝗲𝗱 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗻𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝗶𝘁.

And that is one of the reasons I believe we were created for impact.

Impact doesn't always begin with something extraordinary.

Sometimes, it is an exercise book.

Sometimes, it is a conversation.

Sometimes, it is sharing an opportunity.

Sometimes, it is teaching someone what you know.

Sometimes, it is simply being there for someone when they need help.

We often think we need to do something big before we can say we have made an impact.

But perhaps impact is not always about how big the action is.

Perhaps it is about how deeply it touches another person's life.

You may never know how far your kindness travelled.

You may never know who became more confident because you believed in them.

You may never know who continued their education because you helped them at a difficult moment.

You may never know who found courage because of a conversation you almost forgot.

And that is the beauty of impact.

𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗱𝗼 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗮𝗹𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝗲𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗿𝘂𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗺𝗮𝗱𝗲 𝗮 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲.

So, wherever you find yourself, do whatever you can to help people get where they are going.

Share what you know.

Open doors when you can.

Give when you have the capacity.

Encourage people.

Listen.

Teach.

Support.

And never underestimate the little things.

Because the thing you consider insignificant today may become a story someone tells years from now.

I once gave a friend an exercise book.

I forgot about it.

He didn't.

And perhaps that is the reminder we all need:

𝗟𝗶𝗳𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗺𝘂𝗰𝗵 𝘄𝗲 𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗲𝘃𝗲.

𝗜𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗹𝘀𝗼 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗮𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝘄𝗲 𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲.

You were created for impact.

So, make yours count.

title: I THOUGHT I WAS RESERVING MY POTENTIAL. I DIDN'T REALIZE I AM SHRINKING MYSELF
excerpt: 𝗜 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗜 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝘆 𝗽𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹. 𝗜 𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗻’𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗲 𝗜 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝘀𝗵𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝘆𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳.For a long time,…
content:
𝗜 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗜 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝘆 𝗽𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹. 𝗜 𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗻’𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗲 𝗜 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝘀𝗵𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝘆𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳.

For a long time, I had this mindset:

I didn't like showing people everything I could do.

I wanted my abilities to be a surprise.

I wanted people to say:

"Wow, you can actually do this?"

"We didn't know you could do this too!"

And honestly, I loved that feeling.

So, I started intentionally hiding some of my abilities. I would keep certain talents and skills to myself because I wanted to save them for the right moment.

But recently, I realized something:

𝗜 𝘄𝗮𝘀𝗻'𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝘆 𝗽𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹. 𝗜 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝘆 𝗼𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀.

When you consistently hide what you can do, people eventually form an opinion about your capacity based on what they have seen.

If they have never seen you do something, they may assume you cannot do it.

And when opportunities come, they naturally go to the people who have consistently demonstrated that ability.

Not necessarily because they are more talented than you.

But because 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗱𝗼.

Meanwhile, you may be sitting there thinking:

"I can actually do this."

But nobody knows.

And that was happening to me.

It got to a point where some things I knew I could do were no longer surprising when I eventually attempted them.

Why?

Bcause other people had been doing those things consistently.

They had practiced.

They had gained experience.

They had mastered the skill.

While I was still protecting my "potential."

That's when I realized:

𝗣𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗹𝘆 𝗵𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗻𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘆.

So, I'm changing my approach.

If I know I can do something, I will do it.

If I have a talent, I will develop it.

If I have an idea, I will share it.

If I have something valuable to contribute, I will contribute it.

I will stop shrinking myself just to create a future "wow" moment.

Because 𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗮𝗹𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝗯𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴.

Sometimes, people simply need to know what you can do before they can trust you with an opportunity.

So here's my lesson:

𝗗𝗼𝗻'𝘁 𝗵𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗽𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹. 𝗗𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽 𝗶𝘁. 𝗗𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗶𝘁. 𝗣𝘂𝘁 𝗶𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸.

The opportunity you are waiting for may require people to first see what you are capable of.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗽𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗯𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗵𝗶𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗽𝘂𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸?

title: Chapter 3
excerpt: The stranger offer.
content:
Aria’s point of view

Snow. Of course it was snow. Because my life needed one more thing to make it harder.

I was huddled under a blanket that had seen better days, freezing next to a fire that was doing the bare minimum, when I heard a cry. An actual cry.

Which was a problem, because my baby never cries. Apart from the night I pushed him out.

I sat up fast i nearly gave myself whiplash. “Black heart?”

He wasn’t next to me.

“Okay, cool, cool, normal, totally fine,” i said definitely not fine, scrambling to my feet with the blanket still half- wrapped around me.

“BLACK HEART!” I Yelled into the trees. The wind ate most of it. Great. Very helpful, wind.”

I stumbled through the snow, freezing, furious at myself, when I finally him cradled in someone’s arm.

Him. Cloak Guy. Back for round two, three days after round one.

“He’s beautiful,” Cloak Guy murmured, running his fingers through my baby’s flames like they weren’t actively on fire.

“Thanks,” i said, arms crossed, heart still hammering somewhere near my fucking throat. “Also you know it’s generally considered rude to just, I don’t know, take someone’s baby into the woods without asking?!”

He ignored that completely.”where is his father?”

And there it was. The one question guaranteed to ruin my night.

“Gone,” I said. “Since before he was even born. If you find him, tell him he owns me so much.”

“You still hope he’ll come back.”

“I don’t hope,” i said. Which was a lie, and judging by his face, he knew it too.

“I’ll help you,” he said. “His power will consume him if it’s isn’t guided, or it will consume you.”

Well that was fun to hear.

I looked at my baby, who was doing his signature “silently more powerful than everyone in this conversation” stare from cloak Guy’s arms, completely unbothered, like he’d already decided this was fine.

“Okay,” I said. I said softly, I needed help and acting strong wasn’t going to work.

He smiled. A real smile. And was that worse than the hood. “Good. Then let’s go. My cave isn’t far, and the wolves will be out soon.”

“Cave,” I repeated.

He was already walking away with my baby. I stood there for a second and sighed.

“ Great talk with myself as always,” i muttered and followed him into the dark, because apparently that was just what my life was now three days postpartum, following mysterious men into caves for the sake of my flaming silent baby.

title: When politicians forgets the people
excerpt: Promises in the campaign that cannot be made after the election
content:
In some countries, citizens can feel as though the people they elected no longer remember why they were given power in the first place. Politicians may make promises during elections, speak about better schools, hospitals, roads, jobs, security, and opportunities, yet citizens can later feel ignored when those promises are not followed by meaningful action. This does not mean every politician is uncaring, nor that every government fails its people, but there are political systems where the incentives facing leaders do not always reward serving the wider public. The World Bank has noted that political leaders can face incentives that push them toward decisions that protect their position or benefit particular groups rather than policies that produce better outcomes for society as a whole. When accountability is weak, leaders may have fewer reasons to respond quickly to ordinary citizens, especially when powerful groups, wealthy interests, political networks, or other influential actors have greater access to decision-makers. In such situations, the distance between government and the people can become enormous. Citizens continue working, paying taxes, raising families, and struggling with everyday problems while those in power may appear increasingly disconnected from the realities experienced by the population.

Corruption and weak institutions can make this problem even more complicated. Public resources that should support services can be diverted through bribery, favoritism, inefficient systems, or decisions that benefit particular individuals and groups. The World Bank describes forms of corruption that can affect government contracts, public services, and even the functioning of institutions themselves. Another problem is that citizens cannot effectively hold leaders accountable when they lack meaningful access to information, oversight mechanisms, or opportunities to influence decisions. Political participation is not only about voting every few years; accountability also depends on transparency, independent institutions, public debate, media, civic organizations, and citizens being able to question decisions made in their name. The OECD's 2026 survey found that, across the countries it studied, 40% of respondents believed elected officials “do not care about people like me,” while only 31% felt that people like them had a say in what government does. These figures describe people's perceptions across OECD countries, not every country in the world, but they demonstrate that feeling unheard by government is not limited to one particular nation or political system.

Perhaps the deeper issue is what happens when power becomes more important than responsibility. Government exists within institutions, laws, political parties, economic interests, and social pressures, so the behavior of politicians is shaped by more than personal character alone. If political systems reward short-term popularity, private benefits, loyalty to powerful groups, or staying in office more strongly than long-term public results, leaders can have incentives that do not perfectly match the needs of ordinary citizens. The World Bank has emphasized that changing these incentives can involve greater transparency and meaningful citizen engagement, while the OECD identifies accountability, participation, openness, and responsiveness as important parts of trustworthy government. Ultimately, the relationship between citizens and politicians is supposed to be one of responsibility: citizens give leaders authority, while institutions should provide ways for those leaders to be questioned and held accountable for how that authority is used. When that relationship becomes weak, people can lose trust and begin to believe that government exists for those who hold power rather than for the public it is meant to serve. The challenge for any country is therefore not simply finding politicians who make promises, but building institutions strong enough to encourage transparency, public participation, responsible decision-making, and accountability after the promises have been made.

title: Before I Was Forgotten
excerpt: Sometimes a woman loses herself simply because she loved everyone else too faithfully.
content:
Chapter Two

Her Mother's Hands

Zainab was eleven the first time she noticed that her mother's hands were never still.

Even at rest even in the rare minutes when Mama sat to eat, or listened to the Qur'an recitation on the radio, or simply breathed her fingers moved.

Folding the edge of a wrapper.

Smoothing a tablecloth that did not need smoothing.

Picking an invisible thread from someone's sleeve.

As though stillness itself were a kind of failure Mama could not afford to be caught in.

“Mama, come and sit,” young Zainab would say, patting the mat beside her.

“I am sitting,” Mama would answer.

She would already be getting up.

To check the pot.

Find Baba's misplaced prayer cap.

Settle a quarrel between Zainab's younger brothers before it became a proper fight.

Zainab's father, Alhaji Musa, was not an unkind man.

He did not raise his voice.

He did not raise his hand.

He simply existed in the house the way weather existed present, expected, unquestioned.

He never needed to ask where anything was because Mama had already made sure he would never have to.

“Your mother is the reason this house stands,” Baba would say, with genuine warmth, whenever guests praised the food or the order of things.

And Mama would smile.

That small, private smile of a woman who had heard the compliment many times and had learned, somewhere along the way, that being the reason a house stood was not the same as being asked to sit down in it.

Zainab remembered one evening especially.

She was thirteen.

There had been a wedding in the extended family, which meant days of preparation. Mama had been waking before Fajr, stitching, cooking, arranging, soothing nerves that were not hers to soothe.

On the night of the wedding itself, the hall was full of music and laughter.

Zainab looked for her mother.

She found her in the back kitchen.

Alone.

Still tying an apron over her good asoebi.

Still checking the last trays before they went out.

“Mama, aren't you going to dance?”

Mama looked up.

“Everyone is dancing,” Zainab added.

Her mother glanced towards the doorway.

For a moment, she looked almost confused.

As though it had not occurred to her that dancing was still available to a woman who had a kitchen to manage.

“Soon, my dear.”

Zainab smiled.

“Promise?”

Mama laughed softly.

“Go outside.”

So Zainab went.

She danced.

She laughed with her cousins.

And every so often, she looked towards the kitchen, waiting for Mama to appear.

She never did.

Years later, Zainab would remember that word.

Soon.

Not because her mother had lied.

But because she had believed it too.

It was only decades later, standing in her own kitchen with a ladle in her hand and a house gone quiet around her, that Zainab understood what soon had really been.

It had been the kindness women sometimes gave themselves when they knew they were postponing something they wanted.

Soon, when the children were older.

Soon, when the house was settled.

Soon, when there was less work.

Soon, when everyone else was all right.

And somehow, everyone else was always almost all right.

Her mother died when Zainab was twenty-six.

Three years into Zainab's own marriage.

One year before Halima was born.

At the funeral, women Zainab barely knew came forward one after another to speak about Mama.

She had fed their children when they were sick.

She had sewn wedding clothes without taking payment.

She had sat beside a neighbour the night her husband first raised his voice and never told another soul.

They spoke of her kindness.

Her patience.

Her generosity.

Her hands.

Everyone had something good to say about what those hands had done.

No one said what those hands had once wanted to do.

No one said Mama had dreamed of travelling.

No one said she used to sing beautifully before she stopped.

No one said she had once told Zainab, in a whisper, that she wanted a small fabric shop of her own.

Just her name on the sign.

Nothing grand.

A place where she could choose the colours.

Arrange the shelves.

Open when she wanted.

Close when she wanted.

Zainab was the only one who knew.

Mama had told her once, late at night, in the unguarded hush before sleep.

Then she never mentioned it again.

As if saying it once had been permission enough to let it go.

Standing beside her mother's grave, Zainab made herself a promise.

She was twenty-six.

Young enough to believe that knowing what had happened to someone was enough to prevent it happening to her.

I will not disappear the way you did.

She meant it.

She meant it with the certainty of someone who had not yet learned how quietly a woman could give herself away.

Not in one dramatic moment.

Not because someone forced her.

But in a thousand small, loving, ordinary decisions.

One dinner.

One sick child.

One postponed plan.

One “not today.”

One “they need me.”

One “I can do it later.”

Each choice so harmless that no one not even the woman making it could point to the exact moment she began disappearing.

And that was the part Zainab would understand much later.

Sometimes a woman did not lose herself because she stopped loving herself.

Sometimes she lost herself because she loved everyone else so faithfully that she kept placing herself last.

Until one day, last became nowhere.

Author's Note: Thank you for reading Chapter Two of Before I Was Forgotten.This chapter highlights how easily the patterns of our mothers become our own realities. Did any part of Mama's story remind you of your own mother, grandmother, or an aunt? Let's honor them and discuss their hidden dreams in the comments below.

📌 Don't forget to hit the FOLLOW button on my profile right now so you don't miss Chapter Three, where we finally go back to Zainab's wardrobe to uncover her hidden past!

title: You Want to Buy Dangote Refinery Shares? Read This First
excerpt: The Dangote Refinery IPO is everywhere, but before you put your money in, do you actually understand what you're buying?
content:
Everybody is talking about buying Dangote Refinery shares. Some people are already asking how much they can make, while others are just trying to figure out how to buy.

But before you join the excitement, do you actually know what you’re buying?

Let’s start with the basics. What exactly are you buying?

Dangote Refinery is offering shares to the public through an Initial Public Offering, or IPO.

In simple terms, an IPO is when a company offers shares to the public, allowing people to become part-owners of the business.

For this IPO, the shares are being offered at ₦525 each, with a minimum subscription of 10 shares. So you can start with ₦5,250.

But buying shares isn't the same as putting money somewhere and waiting for it to increase.

The price can go up, but it can also go down, and this is where I think people need to slow down a little.

You might see your friend buying 100 shares. Someone on X might be calculating how much they'll make if the share price doubles. Your WhatsApp group might suddenly become an investment class.

Then you start feeling like you're missing out. Don't buy it just because everyone else is buying it.

Before putting your money into the IPO, understand the business you're becoming a part-owner of.

How much money is the company making? Is it profitable? What are its debts and other obligations? How does the refinery actually make money? What does it plan to do with the money raised from the IPO?

These are the things you should be looking at, not just how much someone online thinks the shares will be worth next year.

You should also understand dividends. Owning shares doesn't mean the company automatically pays you money every year. Dividends depend on the company's performance and its decision to distribute profits.

And there's something else people sometimes forget: an IPO doesn't mean the share price can only go up.

After the shares start trading, the market will determine what investors are willing to pay for them. That price could be higher than ₦525. It could also be lower.

So, should you buy Dangote Refinery shares? That's not a decision someone on social media should make for you.

If you've done your research, understand the risks and you're comfortable with the amount you're putting in, that's your decision.

But if your only reason is, “Everybody is buying it and I don't want to miss out,” maybe that's a good reason to pause.

Because there's a difference between investing because you understand what you're buying and investing because you don't want to be left out.

title: Mercy for Whom? When a Mother’s Plea Comes After a Child’s Pain
excerpt: A woman is currently trending after reportedly being reported to the authorities for allegedly sexually abusing her own daughter. She is now pleading for mercy.…
content:
A woman is currently trending after reportedly being reported to the authorities for allegedly sexually abusing her own daughter. She is now pleading for mercy.

And, as expected, the internet has begun doing what it often does when a disturbing story breaks: reacting, debating, judging, and, in some corners, searching for reasons to soften the consequences.

But let us pause for a moment.

Mercy for what, exactly? And at whose expense?

The alleged victim is a child. A child who should be worrying about school, friends, cartoons, or whatever ordinary things children worry about. Not being subjected to sexual abuse by an adult who is supposed to protect her.

This is not one of those situations where we should allow the familiar Nigerian habit of saying, “Abeg, make una forgive her,” before we have even considered the child.

We are often very quick to preach forgiveness when the person asking for it is an adult. We ask people to consider her struggles, her family, her mental state, her future, and the shame she may face.

But what about the child’s future?

What about the psychological damage? What about the confusion that comes from being harmed by someone who should have made you feel safe? What about the possibility that the child may grow up questioning whether her body belongs to her or whether the people she trusts can hurt her without consequence?

These are not small matters.

And Accountability is not the opposite of mercy. A person can receive due process, appropriate care, and even rehabilitation where necessary, without society pretending that the alleged abuse is something to overlook.

We also need to stop treating child sexual abuse as family business. The moment a child is being harmed, it is no longer something to hide under “what will people say?” or “she is still the mother.” Being a parent does not place anyone above accountability.

The authorities must investigate properly, protect the child, and ensure she receives the support she needs. The public, too, must resist turning the child’s trauma into entertainment or spreading details that could further expose her.

Because, at the end of the day, this should not be a story about an adult begging the public to feel sorry for her.

It should be a story about a child who deserved protection in the first place.

And if we cannot agree on that, then perhaps we need to ask ourselves what exactly we mean when we say we care about children.

title: It's Okay to Love Again.
excerpt: A Story of Losing Faith, Finding It, and Falling Anyway
content:
Kate used to believe love was simple. Then she met a guy who made her believe it — the kind of love that felt like it had been waiting for her the whole time. He said all the right things, showed up when it counted, and made her let her guard down completely. For a while, it felt like she'd finally found the version of love she'd always hoped existed.

Reason it fell apart: The same things that made it feel so real were the things that made losing it so devastating. When it ended, it didn't just take the relationship — it took her belief that love could be trusted at all. Kate closed off. She told herself she was better off alone, that hoping for something real was just setting herself up to get hurt again. She spent a long time convinced that chapter of her life was closed for good. Then Steve showed up — not with grand gestures, but with consistency. He didn't try to rush past her walls; he just kept showing up on the other side of them, patiently, until she stopped counting the days she expected him to disappear.

Reason she let him in: Steve never asked her to forget what she'd been through. He just proved, day after day, that not everyone leaves. And somewhere in that quiet, unglamorous consistency, Kate found something she thought she'd lost for good — not the same love as before, but something steadier. Something real. She didn't fall in love again because she forgot what heartbreak felt like. She fell in love again because she finally let herself believe that not every ending has to define every beginning.

The takeaway: Losing faith in love doesn't mean you're done with it — it might just mean you haven't met the person who's patient enough to earn it back.
