title: YOUR PHONE KNOWS HOW TO KEEP YOU DISTRACTED BETTER THAN YOU DO
excerpt: You Didn't Lose Focus. It Was Taken, On Purpose.
content:
You opened your phone to check one thing. Twenty minutes later, you are three unrelated videos deep, in a comment section arguing about something you don't even care about, and you genuinely cannot remember what the original thing was. This is not a willpower failure. It's the design working exactly as intended.

If you have ever felt like your own attention doesn't belong to you anymore, this is for you.

THE SCROLL THAT NEVER ASKS YOU TO DECIDE

Notice what short form content actually removed, the decision. You used to choose what to watch next, pick a channel, select a video, make a small deliberate choice. Now the next thing just arrives, already loaded, already moving, before you have finished processing the last one. There's no pause for you to ask "do I actually want this," because the app was built to make sure that question never has time to form. That missing pause is the whole business model. Decisions create friction. Friction gives your brain room to opt out. Remove the friction, and you stay.

WHY THIS FEELS LIKE A PERSONAL FAILING (It Isn't)

Most people blame themselves for this, "I have no discipline," "I'm just addicted to my phone." That framing puts the entire responsibility on you, as if you are competing on equal footing with a product built by teams of people whose only job is to make sure you don't leave. You're not weak willed. You are outmatched. The algorithm has more data on what keeps your specific brain hooked than you have self awareness about your own patterns. That's not a fair fight, and it was never supposed to be.

WHAT CONSTANT STIMULATION ACTUALLY DOES TO YOU

Here's the part that shows up later, quietly, after enough scrolling, slower things start to feel unbearable. A book feels sluggish. A long conversation feels like it's dragging. A task that requires twenty uninterrupted minutes feels almost physically uncomfortable. That's not you getting lazier. That's your attention span being recalibrated to expect a hit of novelty every few seconds and anything slower than that starts to register as boring, even when it isn't. You have experienced this most times but gave it no regard because you didn't know it had a cause.

THE UNCOMFORTABLE TRUTH

You have probably tried "just deleting the app for a bit" and gone back within a week. That's not because you lack commitment. It's because removing the app doesn't remove the discomfort underneath the boredom, the avoidance, the small anxious energy that the scrolling was numbing in the first place. The phone is not the root problem. It's just the easiest, fastest tool for escaping something you haven't looked at directly. Fixing your relationship with your phone without addressing what you're using it to avoid is like bailing water out of a boat with a hole still in it.

WHAT ACTUALLY HELPS

Not another 24-hour detox you'll abandon by evening. You need smaller, sharper interruptions to the automatic pattern:

- Add friction back in deliberately: Log out of the app instead of just closing it, so opening it again requires an actual decision, not a reflex.

- Notice what you're avoiding right before you reach for it: Is it boredom, an awkward feeling, or an unanswered message. The phone is rarely the actual target, just the nearest exit.

- Protect one deliberately slow activity a day: it could be reading, a walk without headphones, or a meal without a screen, not because it's productive, but because it retrains your tolerance for things that don't move fast.

None of this defeats the algorithm. Nothing fully will. But it puts a small decision back where a reflex used to be, and that's usually where change actually starts.

SO WHAT NOW?

The next time you reach for your phone without meaning to, don't judge yourself for it, just notice it. That single moment of noticing is the only thing the algorithm can't design around. Everything else, it already knows how to handle.

Don't let your attention be stolen from you completely. I'm rooting for you.

title: We have a Copycat killer already.
excerpt: When the public followed the trial of Lindsay Clancy, the narrative was quickly enveloped in a wave of clinical terminology, medical debates, and public sympath…
content:
When the public followed the trial of Lindsay Clancy, the narrative was quickly enveloped in a wave of clinical terminology, medical debates, and public sympathy. At the time, many worried this intense, sympathetic focus risked reframing maternal violence from an abhorrent crime into an almost inevitable medical failure. The case of Carrie Walsh shows exactly how dangerous that precedent can become.

​According to prosecutors in Frankfort, Illinois, Walsh was actively discussing Clancy’s murder trial in a group text mere hours before her two-year-old son, Barrett, was found asphyxiated in their basement. When responding officers arrived, she reportedly claimed she killed her child because he was "the devil" and "the anti-Christ". Predictably, the public defense mounted immediately: a statement claiming a severe psychotic episode, pointing to an unraveling mind rather than a deliberate, horrific choice.

​I cannot escape the reality of how these spectacles function. When high-profile trials offer a platform where extreme violence against children is deconstructed, rationalized, and met with institutional hesitation even resulting in hung juries it provides an unspoken blueprint. It signals that almost any claim of delusion, distress, or sudden psychological collapse can be offered as a post-hoc justification to blunt legal accountability.

​When taking the life of an innocent child can be paired with an immediate excuse whether calling a toddler demonic or invoking psychiatric despair society’s baseline of deterrence begins to break down. We risk creating a culture where tragedies are not treated as urgent warnings, but as copycat scripts for the next catastrophic act of violence.

I am trying to make common sense

- 3enchnad

title: ARCHITECTS OF OUR OWN CRISIS
excerpt: Rethinking Collective Responsibility for Antimicrobial Resistance
content:
PART ONE: THE CRISIS AND THE CULPRITS

What are Antimicrobials?

Antimicrobials are medicines or chemical agents used to kill microorganisms or inhibit their growth. They include antibacterial, antiviral, antifungal, and antiparasitic agents.

But when we fact-check this definition, one could say that it doesn’t hold on a large scale for the antimicrobials in circulation today.

Microorganisms have mastered the craft of neutralizing nearly every weapon that man has fashioned against it.

Let us take a quick trip through history, shall we?

In 1945, while delivering his Nobel Prize lecture for the discovery of penicillin, Alexander Fleming made a warning that one might argue to be a prophecy.

He said and I quote “The thoughtless person playing with penicillin treatment is morally responsible for the death of the man who succumbs to infection with the penicillin-resistant organism”.

I look at us today and I see the thoughtless people he was hinting at.

We are even much worse.

We have progressively reduced the effectiveness of many antibiotics through misuse, overuse, inappropriate prescribing, poor infection prevention, and inadequate antimicrobial stewardship.

And WHY are microorganisms able to do this?

There isn’t a habitat or environment in this world where microorganisms haven’t been isolated. They possess impressive adaptation potential that makes it easy for them to adjust to the situation in any environment they find themselves.

Microorganisms possess remarkable adaptability, but resistance is not simply a consequence of surviving extreme environments. In clinical settings, resistance is driven by:

1. Genetic change: The antibiotic has a key that opens the microorganism’s padlock, the microbe can decide to change this padlock so that key becomes useless.

2. Exchange of resistance genes: Through communication portals, microbes can share knowledge and resources such that resistance factors can be distributed.

3. Selective pressure: We constantly release wastes containing antibiotics or their residues into the environmental water bodies, this in turn roots out all the “God-fearing” and “naive” microorganisms leaving room, space and time for the resistant and "ungodly" ones to thrive.

HOW does the resistance manifest?

These marvels have taken different approaches over the years and very notable is what was seen against penicillin, that is, deactivating the active compound within the core of penicillin.

Let me bring you a little closer to the chemistry within this process.

A pharmacist produces his medicine using two major ingredients known as the API (Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient) and Excipients.

The excipients are those components of a medicine without which the medicine would still function and serve its intended purpose, e.g. preservatives and sweeteners.

But the API is or are the components without which the medicine won’t serve its intended purpose.

Let’s use this knowledge to understand how some bacteria resist treatment by penicillin.

By virtue of a beta-lactam ring present at the core of penicillin (likened to the API in the context of penicillin), it is able to indirectly stop some bacteria from making their cell wall.

And as a result, they end up taking up toxic substances in to their cell and eventually die.

And these bacteria, engineers and architects as they are, studied and learned to produce an enzyme that opens up (cleaves) this beta-lactam ring and rendered the antibiotic useless!

HOW did we get here??

Microorganisms didn’t just become resistant overnight; superbugs did not emerge overnight. It took years and years of thoughtlessness to get us where we are today.

To save us a long essay about how we got here, I would just summarize it to be the result of a “poor antimicrobial stewardship”.

Our negligence to conform to the standard practices of antimicrobial stewardship is to blame for this perilous situation the world is currently in as far as AMR is concerned.

Who is the culprit?

We have established the crime, but who is the culprit?

From where I stand, it is EVERYONE!!

Security, as they say, is a collective responsibility, so it is only natural if I say insecurity, is a collective retribution.

Remember the you that waited out malaria symptoms, you even blamed your incessant cough on the rain and didn’t give diagnosis the chance to confirm your claims.

You are the reason we are here today, because by the time you later went to the hospital for treatment, your situation couldn’t settle for a single card of antibiotic anymore.

That means you will be taking antibiotics for a little longer and risking the chance for the microbes to learn about the drug and outsmart it like penicillin.

As if that version of you isn’t diabolical enough, you decided to take it a step further....

If you are still with me, I truly appreciate and want you to drop a name of any antibiotic you have used over the years in the comment section and I will tell you if and how microorganisms resist it. Thank you so much as you do that.

....So, what did you do this time around.

Every time an antibiotic is discovered, a lot of time and energy is devoted to ascertaining the appropriate lethal dose that kills the pathogen or halt its growth.

This is communicated by the physician or pharmacist to the patient at the point of prescription.

But what did you do? You stopped the treatment at the first sign of relief. The fever dropped, the pain disappeared, and you declared yourself victorious.

You forgot one small detail: the disappearance of your symptoms does not always mean the complete disappearance of the infection.

Some microorganisms may still be present, quietly waiting for their opportunity.

And perhaps you made matters worse by keeping the remaining tablets for another illness, sharing them with a friend, or taking them later without a proper diagnosis.

In doing so, you may contribute to treatment failure and the spread of resistance.

The rule is simple: do not improvise with antibiotics. Take them exactly as prescribed, and seek professional advice before stopping, extending, borrowing, or sharing them.

Yes, this is a serious problem that has been escalating over the years but as with every problem, there is a solution and that will be discussed extensively in the concluding part.

Congratulations on making it this far!

Now, if you’re a healthcare provider reading this thinking you’ve escaped the blame allotment for AMR… don’t get too comfortable.

Little do you know, I am coming for you in Part 2

If there is a need to point fingers in this pandemic of AMR, who do you think should be the culprit?

Let’s talk about it in the comments.

title: Advanced TypeScript Patterns: Generics, Conditional Types, and Template Literals
excerpt: Level up your TypeScript skills with advanced type-level programming: mapped types, template literal types, infer keyword, and type guards.
content:
Advanced TypeScript Patterns: Generics, Conditional Types, and Template Literals

TypeScript has evolved far beyond simple interface annotations. Modern TypeScript provides a Turing-complete type system capable of validating complex business logic, building type-safe ORMs, and enforcing API contracts at compile time.

1. Conditional Types and the infer Keyword

Conditional types enable dynamic type resolution based on relational conditions:

type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;

// Extracting the unwrapped return type of an Async function
type AwaitType<T> = T extends Promise<infer U> ? U : T;

type UserPromise = Promise<{ id: string; name: string }>;
type ResolvedUser = AwaitType<UserPromise>; // { id: string; name: string }

2. Template Literal Types for Event Systems

type EventType = "user" | "post" | "comment";
type ActionType = "create" | "update" | "delete";

// Automatically generates "user:create" | "user:update" | ... etc.
type EventChannel = `${EventType}:${ActionType}`;

function subscribe(event: EventChannel, handler: () => void) {
  // Completely type-safe!
}

3. Exhaustive Pattern Matching with Discriminated Unions

Ensure that all possible union members are handled in your switch statements using the never type:

type ApiResponse = 
  | { status: "success"; data: any }
  | { status: "error"; error: string }
  | { status: "loading" };

function handleResponse(res: ApiResponse) {
  switch (res.status) {
    case "success": return res.data;
    case "error": return res.error;
    case "loading": return "Loading...";
    default:
      const _exhaustiveCheck: never = res;
      return _exhaustiveCheck;
  }
}

title: Family Is Not Always Family
excerpt: Contract Of Silence
content:
It's the sheer audacity of people who get mad at victims for finally speaking up.

Lately, people are finally coming forward to share the truth about their upbringing. They are laying out the reality of what it was like growing up under narcissism, emotional manipulation, or outright hostility. It's not for clout, they're doing it to heal, to find closure, and to let everyone else trapped in those dynamics know they aren't crazy.

Suddenly, everyone has an opinion on "family loyalty." Suddenly, you’re ungrateful, bitter, or doing it for attention.

And the outrage is about the child having the nerve to talk about it.

For generations, families operated on a contract of silence: Whatever happens in this house stays in this house. It didn't matter if a parent or relative was emotionally abusive, manipulative, or downright cruel, the child was expected to swallow the trauma and carry the shame because family is family.

Transparency is a threat to abusive dynamics. When you speak your truth, you disrupt the story they told themselves to feel comfortable. You force them to face accountability, and people who thrive on control will always prefer a lie that protects their comfort over a truth that requires them to change.

title: My Friend, June
excerpt: Everyone came looking for something
content:
EVERYBODY HAD A PLAN

KORA

The first time I walked into my department, I took a deep breath and tried not to look as nervous as I felt.

The smell of freshly printed papers filled the hallway, mixing with the faint scent of dust and perfume. Colorful posters covered the walls, announcing elections, departmental activities and events I knew nothing about.

Everyone seemed to know someone.

Everyone except me.

I was a fresher, just like most of them, but I had resumed late because of my acceptance fee. My mother and I had spent weeks trying to raise enough money for my school payments. While everyone else was settling into university life, I had been at home watching my mother struggle.

I walked into the classroom quietly and immediately noticed her.

She was fair, bubbly and effortlessly beautiful. She was surrounded by both boys and girls, all laughing at something she had said.

She didn’t have to announce herself.

You could tell she was the Queen Bee.

I quietly found an empty seat at the back and began filling in my details when a voice beside me interrupted my thoughts.

“Hi. My name is June.”

She stretched out her hand.

I looked up.

Her smile was the prettiest and most sincere smile I had ever seen.

It was the Queen Bee.

“I’m Kora.”

I nervously shook her hand.

A few girls nearby chuckled.

I immediately pulled my hand back and lowered my eyes.

“Don’t mind them,” June said, laughing. “They’re only jealous because I find you worthy.”

I smiled.

That was the beginning of our friendship.

June was everything I wasn’t.

She was beautiful. Fair. Confident. Wealthy.

She came from a functional family and never seemed to worry about money. She paid her school fees and departmental dues before anyone else. She always had everything she needed.

I had none of those things.

My family was the complete opposite.

I remembered one particular morning when my mother called me crying.

My father had thrown her out of the one-room apartment we were managing because he had brought one of his mistresses home.

My mother was a fragile woman. She had spent years enduring his insults and humiliation, using the little profit from her business to feed us and, sometimes, even my father.

That morning, I imagined her standing outside with nothing but the clothes on her body while another woman occupied the room she had called home.

The thought poisoned something inside me.

I envied June.

Not just her money.

Her life.

Academically, however, I was better than her. I helped her with assignments and quizzes, and she never hesitated to tell everyone that she couldn’t survive school without me.

One afternoon, while I was thinking about my family’s situation, June walked into the classroom.

“Where are you going for the holiday?” she asked.

I froze.

I had never told June much about my family.

I didn’t want to go home.

So I lied.

“My father is dead,” I said quietly. “And my mother is a drug addict. I don’t really want to go back.”

June’s face immediately softened.

“I’m so sorry.”

I shrugged as though it didn’t matter.

“You can come home with me,” she said. “My parents won’t mind.”

That holiday, I travelled with June to her family’s home in Nnewi.

I had thought June was rich.

I was wrong.

Her family was wealthy beyond anything I had ever imagined.

Their house looked like something from a movie. Beautiful furniture. Massive rooms. Expensive cars. Servants.

But what struck me most wasn’t the money.

It was the family.

Her father adored her mother. He respected her. They laughed together. They spoke gently to one another.

I watched them and wondered what it would feel like to belong to a family like that.

Then I realized something.

Maybe I could.

June and her mother were often at loggerheads. Nothing serious, but enough for me to notice the cracks.

I quietly stepped into them.

I became helpful.

I anticipated her mother’s needs. I helped around the house. I listened to her complaints. I became the daughter who was always available.

Soon, June’s mother began comparing us.

“Kora, see how responsible you are.”

“Why can’t you be more like Kora?”

June never seemed bothered.

She was too sweet.

Too trusting.

And I knew I had found my way into the family.

There was only one problem.

June was still in my way.

I had already started thinking about how to remove her when I met Ike.

One afternoon, I helped him after he fell into a gutter.

He looked at me with gratitude.

“Madam, na you try pass. People just dey pass since, nobody help me. See, anything you want, I go help you. If you get enemy, I go help you comot am.”

I looked at him carefully.

Maybe God had answered me.

I called him later and told him terrible lies about June.

I told him she had ruined my life. I told him her family had destroyed mine. I told him I wanted her dead.

Ike listened.

Then he suggested something better.

“We kidnap her first. Collect money from her people. Then we finish the job.”

I agreed.

I gave him information about June’s movements, her routines and places she usually visited.

Everything was planned.

On the day of the kidnapping, June disappeared exactly as we had arranged.

Her parents panicked.

They didn’t waste time paying the ransom.

Days later, a photograph arrived.

June was covered in blood.

Dead.

At least, that’s what it looked like.

I cried with her parents.

I held her mother when she collapsed.

I comforted her father.

I became exactly what they needed.

Their daughter.

Their family.

Their replacement for June.

One evening, after they returned from a meeting, June’s parents walked into the living room holding hands.

They looked at me.

“Kora,” her father said gently, “June told us about your family.”

My heart stopped.

He continued.

“We know things haven’t been easy for you.”

Her mother stepped closer.

“You are always welcome here. In fact, we’ve discussed it. We would like to adopt you as our daughter.”

I couldn’t believe my ears.

I hugged them tightly.

My dream was finally coming true.

Or so I thought.

I was already included in their plans. I had gained their trust completely.

Everything was falling into place.

All I needed was to execute the final part of the plan.

I texted Ike.

Everything is ready.

That night, I drugged my foster parents’ drinks.

I left the entrance door open and made sure the gateman was distracted.

Ike and his men entered easily.

They made it look like a robbery.

They took valuables.

They shot June’s parents.

Before leaving, I asked Ike to assault me.

It was disgusting.

But I knew the police would expect a victim if they came.

I needed to look like one.

Weeks passed.

The investigation went nowhere.

Ike and his gang disappeared.

Life became easier.

I stopped thinking about school.

Money was more interesting.

I brought my mother to the mansion. For the first time in her life, she had servants attending to her.

I had everything.

Money.

Security.

A beautiful house.

A future.

I even started working with the family’s lawyer concerning the inheritance.

Then one afternoon, I returned from shopping.

The moment I stepped into the living room, I saw police officers.

My heart dropped.

But that wasn’t what frightened me.

There was someone standing behind them.

Someone who shouldn’t have been alive.

She slowly stepped forward.

I couldn’t breathe.

June.

Alive.

She looked directly at me.

And smiled.

JUNE

I had always been a difficult child.

My parents called it stubbornness.

My mother called it irresponsibility.

My father called it being spoiled.

Maybe they were all right.

I grew up getting whatever I wanted. If I cried loudly enough, someone eventually gave in. If I broke something, someone replaced it.

I learned early that people were easier to control when you understood what they wanted from you.

By the time I met Kora, I had become very good at reading people.

But there was one person who understood me better than anyone.

Julius.

We had been together for almost two years.

My parents hated him.

They thought he was irresponsible and beneath our family. They wanted me to date someone from a “proper” background.

Julius didn’t care.

He loved me.

Long before Kora came into my life, Julius and I had already talked about my parents.

We wanted to leave.

We wanted a life of our own.

But there was a problem.

My parents controlled everything.

My inheritance was locked away in a trust, and I couldn’t access it until they believed I was mature enough to handle it.

My mother especially didn’t think I was ready.

Sometimes I hated her for that.

Other times, I understood why.

Still, Julius had always been patient.

He never told me what to do.

He listened.

He let me complain.

He let me dream.

And sometimes, when I was angry enough, he would ask questions that made me think.

What if they never changed their minds?

What if you never got your inheritance?

What would you do?

At first, I didn’t have an answer.

Then Kora appeared.

The first day she walked into the classroom, I noticed how she looked at me.

Not with admiration.

With hunger.

I recognized it because I had seen it before.

She wanted something.

I just didn’t know what.

A week before I invited her home, I accidentally overheard her talking to her mother.

She was telling her how she intended to get close to me, gain my family’s trust and eventually take their money.

I stood outside the room and smiled.

Suddenly, everything became clearer.

Kora didn’t want to be my friend.

She wanted my life.

And I realized something else.

Maybe she could be useful.

I didn’t immediately know how.

I simply watched her.

I watched how quickly she became attached to my mother.

I watched how she reacted whenever my parents praised her.

I watched the way she looked around the house when she thought nobody was watching.

She wasn’t hiding her envy very well.

Then she started asking questions.

About my parents.

About their movements.

About the family business.

About the people who worked for us.

I never answered too much.

I didn’t need to.

I only needed to let her believe I trusted her.

Eventually, she told me about her problems.

Or what she wanted me to believe were her problems.

I listened.

I comforted her.

I became the friend she thought she had finally found.

And somewhere along the way, Kora stopped being my friend and became something else.

An opportunity.

When she finally met Ike, I knew the plan had begun to move on its own.

I didn’t have to tell her to kill my parents.

I didn’t have to.

Kora had already convinced herself that their money belonged to her.

All I had to do was stay out of her way.

The kidnapping was part of our arrangement.

The fake death was necessary.

And Kora played her part beautifully.

She believed she had killed me.

She believed she was grieving with my parents.

She believed she had won.

Then she killed them.

Just like that.

My parents were dead.

And Kora thought she had done it for herself.

She hadn’t.

She had done it for me.

After everything was over, I waited.

I let her settle into the house.

I let her become comfortable.

I let her begin thinking about the inheritance.

Then I went to the police.

I had saved the messages.

The conversations.

The evidence.

Enough to put Kora away.

I told them I had escaped.

I told them one of the kidnappers had helped me.

I told them I was too traumatized to report immediately.

It was a convincing story.

And Kora had already given me everything I needed.

So when I walked into that living room with the police officers, I watched her face collapse.

She looked at me like I was a ghost.

I smiled.

“You cannot outplay the player.”

The police handcuffed her.

She didn’t resist.

She just stared at me.

I had won.

My parents were dead.

The inheritance would finally be mine.

And Julius and I could finally leave.

For the first time in years, I allowed myself to imagine our future.

A new country.

A new apartment.

No parents.

No rules.

No pretending.

Just Julius and me.

I thought about him as I drove home that evening.

I couldn’t wait to tell him.

But when I got there, something felt wrong.

His phone was switched off.

I called again.

Nothing.

I went to his apartment.

The door was unlocked.

The place was empty.

Not abandoned.

Empty.

His clothes were gone.

His suitcase was gone.

His passport was gone.

I laughed nervously.

Maybe he was planning something.

Maybe he was surprising me.

Then I noticed the envelope on the table.

My name was written on it.

My hands trembled as I opened it.

There was no letter.

Just a photograph.

A photograph of Julius sitting in an airport lounge.

And beside him was a suitcase.

My suitcase.

The one I had packed for our new life.

I stared at the photograph.

Then my phone buzzed.

One message.

From an unknown number.

You were always the clever one, June.

Another message arrived.

But clever isn’t the same as careful.

My blood ran cold.

I rushed to the bank.

The inheritance account had been emptied.

Every transfer.

Every investment.

Everything.

Gone.

I stood there staring at the screen, unable to breathe.

Then another message.

Thank you for everything.

That was when I finally understood.

Kora had wanted my life.

I had wanted my parents’ money.

But Julius…

Julius had wanted everything.

And somehow, he was the only one who got it.

JULIUS

June always thought she was the smartest person in the room.

That was one of the things I loved about her.

She was beautiful, spoiled, reckless and clever enough to be dangerous.

But clever people have one weakness.

They hate believing they can be fooled.

I knew about her parents long before Kora arrived.

I knew about the trust fund.

I knew about the conditions.

I knew how badly June wanted freedom.

And I knew exactly what she was willing to do for it.

When she first told me about Kora, I didn’t think much of her.

Just another desperate girl.

But June kept talking about her.

How easily Kora trusted her.

How badly she wanted to belong.

How jealous she was.

I listened.

Then I realized June had found something better than an accomplice.

She had found a scapegoat.

I didn’t tell June to use Kora.

That was her idea.

I simply encouraged her.

I asked questions.

I let her believe she was coming up with everything herself.

That’s the easiest way to control someone.

Make them think the idea was theirs.

Kora did exactly what we expected.

She arranged her own downfall.

June got what she wanted.

Her parents died.

Kora took the blame.

And June inherited everything.

There was only one thing June didn’t know.

I had never planned to stay.

Not with her.

Not forever.

I loved June, in my own way.

But love had never been the reason I stayed.

Money was.

And now I had it.

The moment June’s parents died, I started moving things.

Accounts.

Documents.

Passports.

Transfers.

Quietly.

Carefully.

By the time she thought she had finally won, I was already gone.

She would blame Kora first.

Then the police.

Then herself.

Eventually, she would blame me.

It didn’t matter.

I was already on the other side of the world.

I looked out through the airport window as the plane prepared for boarding.

My phone buzzed.

June.

I ignored it.

Then I smiled.

She had always wanted a life where nobody could control her.

I had simply given her exactly that.

No parents.

No boyfriend.

No money.

No one left to control.

I picked up my suitcase and walked toward the gate.

For the first time in years, I was completely free.

And so was she.

Just not in the way she had imagined.

Every dad, every man should read Patrick Clancy’s 911 call transcript.

Dawson was his first son. The first son to a father is an incredible bond that only God can accurately explain.

My gut is wrenching and I cannot stop thinking about it.

𝗣𝗮𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸: My wife tried to commit suicide. 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗿: Stay awake. How old is she? 𝗣𝗮𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸: 31–33. 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗿: Is she awake? 𝗣𝗮𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸: Yes. 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗿: Is she breathing? 𝗣𝗮𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸: Yeah. Lindsay, what did you do to your neck? She’s talking. 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗿: When did this happen? 𝗣𝗮𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸: Last half hour. 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗿: How far did she fall? 𝗣𝗮𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸: 20 feet. 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗿: Is she responding normally? 𝗣𝗮𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸: A little bit. Wake up! 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗿: What part of the body was injured? 𝗣𝗮𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸: Her neck. She’s breathing. Lindsay, look at me. Look at me. 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗿: Are there weapons? 𝗣𝗮𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸: I don’t see any. Where are the kids? 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗿: Do not move her. 𝗣𝗮𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸: Open your eyes. Lindsay, look at me. Open your eyes. Say my name. 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗿: I’m going to tell you how to stop the bleeding. 𝗣𝗮𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸: It’s not really bleeding… open wounds. She’s in the backyard. 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗿: Is there something on her neck? Can you put pressure on it? 𝗣𝗮𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸: No. Lindsay, wake up. They’re coming. Look at me. 𝗦𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘀. First responders arrive. 𝗣𝗮𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸: I need you to stay with her. I have to go check on my kids.

𝗜𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘀𝗲 / 𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗙𝗼𝗼𝘁𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽𝘀. 𝗣𝗮𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸: Guys? Guys? Cora? Cora? Dawson? Oh no. Oh no! Wake up! Then screaming and gasping for an extended stretch. 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗿: What’s going on? Hello? 𝗣𝗮𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸: Basement! Basement! Oh my God! I need help in the basement right now. 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗿: Hello? Hello? 𝗣𝗮𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸: Dawson! My buddy! My little boy! My buddy! AHHHHH, SHE KILLED THE KIDS!!! Oh my God!

Now tell me who would fall into Postpartum psychosis?

title: How to Prepare for Jobs That Requires AI
excerpt: Preparing for AI Interviews: Skills, Tips and Sample Questions
content:
You may not be applying for an AI job, but AI could still show up in your next interview.

A marketing role might ask how you use generative AI. An executive assistant position might ask how you would automate repetitive tasks. A content job could test your ability to work with AI without sacrificing accuracy or originality.

The question is no longer simply, "Do you know AI?"

It is increasingly becoming:

"Do you know how to work with AI?"

That shift matters because artificial intelligence is changing the skills employers need across different industries.

LinkedIn's 2025 Work Change Report estimated that 70% of the skills used in most jobs could change by 2030, with AI acting as a major catalyst. LinkedIn also identified AI literacy as one of the fastest-growing skills across regions and job functions.

The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 similarly found that employers expect 39% of workers' core skills to change by 2030, with AI and big data among the fastest-growing skill areas. At the same time, skills such as creative thinking, analytical thinking, resilience and leadership remain important.

So if you are preparing for your next job interview, learning how to use AI is worth considering even if the job description doesn't explicitly say "AI."

Why AI Skills Matter in Today's Job Market

AI is already being used across businesses.

Stanford's 2025 AI Index reported that 78% of surveyed organizations said they were using AI in 2024, up from 55% in 2023. The percentage reporting generative-AI use in at least one business function more than doubled, from 33% to 71%.

That does not mean every company expects employees to become AI engineers.

It means more employees are likely to encounter AI somewhere in their workflow.

Think about a typical working day.

You might use AI to:

Summarize a long document

Research a topic

Draft an email

Analyze information

Generate ideas

Organize notes

Create a first draft

Automate repetitive tasks

Prepare a presentation

Extract action items from a meeting

The valuable skill isn't simply knowing which button to press.

It is knowing when AI is appropriate, how to use it effectively, and how to check its work.

PwC's 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer found that jobs requiring specific AI skills were growing 69% faster than the overall jobs market, while AI skills carried an average 62% wage premium in its analysis. It also found that AI-exposed entry-level roles were seven times more likely to require traditionally senior skills such as judgment and leadership.

That last finding is particularly interesting for people entering the workforce.

As AI takes over more routine work, employers can place greater value on what humans bring to the process: judgment, communication, problem-solving and decision-making.

What Skills Should You Prepare for an AI Interview?

You don't need to learn everything about artificial intelligence.

Focus on the skills most relevant to the role you want.

1. AI Literacy

Start with the basics.

You should understand terms such as:

Artificial intelligence

Generative AI

Machine learning

Large language models

AI agents

Automation

Prompt engineering

AI hallucinations

AI bias

Data privacy

You don't necessarily need to explain these concepts like a computer scientist.

You should simply understand what they mean and how they relate to your work.

For example, if an interviewer asks, "What is generative AI?", you should be able to explain that it refers to AI systems capable of generating content such as text, images, audio, video or code based on learned patterns.

LinkedIn's 2025 Skills on the Rise report identified AI literacy as one of the fastest-growing skills, while proficiency with large language models was also emerging as a fast-growing skill.

2. Prompting

You don't have to become a prompt engineer.

But you should know how to communicate effectively with AI tools.

Compare these two prompts:

Weak:

Write an email to a client.

Better:

Write a concise follow-up email to a potential client who attended a product demonstration yesterday. Keep the tone professional and friendly, mention the agreed next step, and keep the email below 120 words.

The second prompt gives AI more context and clearer instructions.

Good prompting usually involves some combination of:

Context + objective + instructions + constraints + desired format

You may even be asked to improve a poor prompt during an interview.

Your goal is to demonstrate that you can turn an unclear request into a clear task.

3. Critical Thinking

This may be one of the most important AI interview skills.

AI can give you an answer in seconds.

That doesn't mean the answer is correct.

Generative AI can produce inaccurate information, outdated claims, fabricated sources or convincing explanations that contain errors.

So don't tell an interviewer:

"I trust AI to give me the right answer."

Instead, demonstrate that you know how to verify AI output.

A good workflow is:

AI generates → Human reviews → Information is verified → Output is improved → Final decision

This is particularly important when dealing with financial information, legal information, customer data, research or business decisions.

Indeed Hiring Lab's 2025 research found that 46% of skills in a typical U.S. job posting fall into categories where GenAI could significantly transform the way the work is performed while human oversight remains important.

That is an important distinction.

AI transformation does not automatically mean human involvement disappears.

4. Problem-Solving

Don't focus only on the AI tools you know.

Focus on the problems you can solve with them.

Suppose you are applying for an executive assistant position.

Instead of saying:

"I know how to use ChatGPT."

You could explain:

"I could use AI to summarize meeting notes, identify potential action items and prepare a first draft of a follow-up message, while reviewing the output before anything is sent."

Now you're demonstrating application, not just tool knowledge.

The same principle applies to marketing, sales, administration, research, customer service and content creation.

Ask yourself:

What repetitive or time-consuming problem could AI help me solve?

That is a much better interview question than:

What AI tool should I learn next?

5. Workflow Thinking

One of the biggest differences between an AI user and an AI-enabled professional is the ability to think in workflows.

Consider a meeting.

A traditional process might be:

Meeting → take notes → organize notes → identify tasks → create task list → write follow-up email

An AI-assisted process could be:

Meeting transcript → AI summary → AI-generated action items → human verification → task-management system → human-approved follow-up

The AI isn't necessarily replacing the employee.

It is reducing repetitive work.

Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index, based on research involving 31,000 workers across 31 countries, found that 81% of leaders expected AI agents to be moderately or extensively integrated into their organization's AI strategy within the following 12–18 months.

This suggests that understanding how AI fits into a workflow not simply knowing how to use a chatbot will become increasingly useful.

6. Data Privacy and Responsible AI

Knowing when not to use AI is also an AI skill.

Imagine your employer gives you confidential customer information.

Should you immediately copy everything into an AI chatbot?

No.

Before using AI with sensitive information, consider:

Company AI policies

Data privacy requirements

The tool's security controls

Confidentiality agreements

Personal information

Customer information

Whether human approval is required

An interviewer may ask:

"What would you do if you wanted to use AI but the information was confidential?"

A good answer should demonstrate caution.

Explain that you would check company policy, determine whether the tool is approved for the information involved, and avoid exposing confidential data unnecessarily.

7. Human Skills

Here's something important:

AI skills do not make human skills irrelevant.

In many cases, they make them more valuable.

The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 identified creative thinking, analytical thinking, resilience and flexibility, curiosity and lifelong learning, and leadership and social influence among the skills expected to remain important as work changes.

PwC's 2026 research also found that AI-exposed entry-level roles were seven times more likely to require traditionally senior skills such as judgment and leadership.

So while you learn AI, continue developing:

Communication

Creativity

Leadership

Emotional intelligence

Decision-making

Collaboration

Adaptability

Problem-solving

The strongest candidate may not be the person who knows the most AI tools.

It may be the person who knows how to combine AI with good judgment.

How to Prepare for an AI Interview

Knowing the skills is one thing.

Being able to demonstrate them during an interview is another.

Here are practical steps you can take.

1. Research the Company

Before your interview, study the organization.

Understand:

What it sells

Who its customers are

How it operates

Its industry

Its major challenges

The technology it uses

Then ask yourself:

Where could AI realistically help this company?

Maybe it could improve customer service.

Maybe it could speed up research.

Maybe it could help organize information.

Maybe it could reduce repetitive administrative work.

You don't need to arrive with a 50-page AI strategy.

One thoughtful example can demonstrate that you understand how technology connects to business.

2. Study the Job Description

Look carefully at the responsibilities.

If the job involves research, think about AI-assisted research.

If it involves content, think about ideation, drafting and editing.

If it involves administration, think about workflow automation, documentation and information management.

If it involves customer service, think about response drafting, knowledge retrieval and ticket classification.

The goal is to connect AI to the actual job, not to force AI into every task.

3. Prepare Three AI Stories

Before the interview, prepare three examples.

Story 1: Productivity

Explain how you used AI to save time.

Story 2: Problem-solving

Explain how you used AI to tackle a difficult or repetitive task.

Story 3: Verification

Explain how you identified, corrected or checked AI-generated information.

Use the STAR method:

Situation → Task → Action → Result

If you haven't used AI professionally, don't pretend that you have.

You can talk about personal projects, training exercises, mock projects or experiments.

Just be transparent about the context.

12 AI Interview Questions to Practice

Here are questions you should prepare for.

General AI Questions

What is artificial intelligence?

What is generative AI?

What AI tools have you used?

How do you keep up with developments in AI?

Practical AI Questions

How have you used AI to improve your productivity?

How would you use AI in this role?

What tasks would you automate with AI?

What tasks should remain under human control?

Critical-Thinking Questions

What would you do if AI gave you incorrect information?

How do you verify AI-generated information?

Responsible AI Questions

What are the risks of using AI at work?

How would you protect confidential information while using AI?

Don't memorize answers word-for-word.

Instead, prepare your own examples.

How to Answer AI Interview Questions Naturally

One common mistake is trying to sound like an AI expert.

You don't have to.

If you are asked:

"How do you use AI?"

Don't simply list five tools.

Explain what you actually do with them.

For example:

"I use AI mainly for research, brainstorming, drafting and repetitive tasks. I provide the context and instructions, review the output, verify important information and then adapt it to the specific situation."

That answer is simple, but it demonstrates several valuable skills:

AI literacy + prompting + critical thinking + human judgment.

If you're asked:

"What would you do if AI gave you incorrect information?"

You could explain:

"I wouldn't rely on the output automatically. For important information, I would cross-check it against reliable sources, investigate inconsistencies and correct the response before using it."

Again, the point isn't to sound impressive.

It is to demonstrate sound judgment.

Don't Just Learn AI Tools Build AI Workflows

There is a difference between knowing AI tools and knowing how to work with AI.

You could know ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot and several other platforms and still struggle to explain how AI could improve a business process.

Instead, practice building simple workflows.

For example:

Problem: An executive spends hours processing meeting notes.

AI workflow:

Meeting transcript → AI summary → action items extracted → human review → tasks added to project-management system → follow-up drafted → human approval.

That demonstrates much more than simply saying:

"I use AI."

It shows that you understand process, automation, human oversight and business value.

What Employers Are Really Looking For

An AI interview isn't always testing how much technical knowledge you have.

In many roles, employers want to know whether you can:

Identify opportunities — Where can AI genuinely improve the work?

Use AI effectively — Can you provide clear instructions?

Evaluate outputs — Can you spot errors and weaknesses?

Protect information — Do you understand privacy and confidentiality?

Solve problems — Can you turn AI capabilities into useful outcomes?

Exercise judgment — Do you know when a human needs to take over?

Keep learning — Can you adapt as the technology changes?

That combination is becoming increasingly valuable.

Final Thoughts

Preparing for an AI interview doesn't mean becoming an AI engineer overnight.

It means becoming comfortable with the technology and understanding how it can be applied to real work.

Learn the fundamentals.

Practice prompting.

Experiment with AI tools.

Build simple workflows.

Learn how to verify information.

Understand responsible AI use.

And don't neglect the human skills that make AI useful in the first place.

The evidence points toward a workplace where AI is becoming increasingly embedded in everyday work. LinkedIn expects substantial changes in job skills by 2030. Stanford's research shows that organizational AI adoption has risen sharply. Microsoft reports growing interest in AI agents, while PwC's latest research shows strong demand and wage premiums for AI skills.

But perhaps the most important lesson is this:

Your goal shouldn't be to compete with AI.

Your goal should be to become someone who knows how to work with it.

So before your next interview, don't ask only:

"What AI tools should I learn?"

Ask:

"What problems can I solve better because I know how to work with AI?"

That is a much more useful question and a much stronger place to start preparing for the future of work.

What are your thoughts on this? Kindly put it in the comments.

title: Could It Be the Electra/Oedipus Complex?
excerpt: Or are we just uncomfortable admitting that some parents compete with their own children?
content:
There is something we don’t like to admit about mothers.

We have made motherhood almost sacred.

The mother is supposed to be the first home. The first person who loves you without conditions. The woman who sees her daughter and thinks, that’s my girl.

So when a daughter says,

“I think my mother hates me,”

people become uncomfortable.

They tell her she’s being dramatic.

“She’s your mother.”

“Maybe that’s just how she shows love.”

“You’ll understand when you’re older.”

But what if the daughter is not imagining it?

What if some mothers really do dislike their daughters?

Not necessarily in the dramatic, “I hate you” kind of way.

Something quieter.

A constant criticism.

A strange coldness.

A tendency to compete.

A preference for the son.

A need to remind the daughter that she isn’t as beautiful, as desirable, as successful, or as important as she thinks she is.

And maybe the most disturbing part is that sometimes the mother doesn’t seem to realise she’s doing it.

Freud had a strange idea about this

Long before TikTok therapists started explaining family trauma in sixty-second videos, Sigmund Freud had already given us one of the strangest theories about family relationships.

The Oedipus complex proposed that a young boy develops an unconscious attachment to his mother and sees his father as a rival for her affection.

The corresponding idea concerning girls later became known as the Electra complex.

These theories are heavily debated today and aren’t accepted as established scientific explanations of child development.

Still, there is something about the basic image that refuses to completely disappear:

Love can create rivalry.

A child wants the parent’s attention.

Someone else appears to have it.

And suddenly, affection becomes something that can be competed for.

Of course, I’m not suggesting that mothers are secretly sexually attracted to their sons or fathers to their daughters.

That’s not the point.

The more interesting question is what happens when that emotional closeness becomes enmeshment.

When a mother is excessively attached to her son.

When a father idealizes his daughter.

When a parent creates a special relationship with one child that leaves another child feeling like an intruder.

Because maybe the problem isn’t always who the parent loves.

Maybe it’s who the parent needs.

The son who can do no wrong

We’ve all seen it.

The son is grown.

He can barely cook.

He doesn’t clean.

He speaks disrespectfully to his mother.

He comes home whenever he wants.

He gets a woman pregnant.

And somehow, there is always an explanation.

“He’s a man.”

“That’s how boys are.”

“He’ll change.”

“Leave him alone.”

Then the daughter does something half as offensive.

Suddenly, she’s disrespectful.

Ungrateful.

Stubborn.

Too proud.

A bad example to her siblings.

The difference isn’t subtle.

The son is allowed to be human.

The daughter is expected to be good.

And perhaps this is where gender enters the conversation.

In some cultures, daughters are raised with the understanding that they are temporary members of the family.

They will marry.

They will leave.

Their husbands will become their primary families.

But sons?

Sons stay.

Sons carry the name.

Sons inherit.

Sons are expected to provide.

So perhaps some parents don’t consciously think, I love my son more.

Perhaps they simply invest more in the child they believe will eventually invest in them.

Which sounds practical.

Until you realise what it teaches the daughter.

You are temporary.

Your brother is the future.

Imagine hearing that message often enough.

Eventually, you stop asking whether your mother loves you.

You start wondering whether she ever really needed you.

But then something stranger happens

The daughter grows up.

And suddenly she becomes a woman.

She becomes beautiful.

She becomes independent.

She starts earning her own money.

She develops opinions.

She dresses differently.

Men notice her.

She doesn’t need permission for everything anymore.

And sometimes, something shifts.

The relationship becomes tense.

A compliment becomes criticism.

A conversation becomes a comparison.

The mother’s appearance is compared to the daughter’s.

The daughter’s body becomes a subject of commentary.

Her relationships become opportunities for judgment.

Her achievements are minimized.

Her confidence becomes arrogance.

Her boundaries become disrespect.

And you start wondering:

Why does this feel like competition?

Why does a mother need to remind her daughter that she’s prettier?

Or younger?

Or more desirable?

Why does a daughter’s success sometimes seem to make her mother uncomfortable?

Why does a daughter becoming independent feel, to some mothers, almost like betrayal?

Perhaps it isn’t always jealousy.

Perhaps it’s insecurity.

Perhaps it’s unresolved trauma.

Perhaps the mother never learned how to see another woman without measuring herself against her.

And perhaps, sometimes, the daughter is simply the closest mirror the mother has.

That can be difficult to look into.

A daughter can become her mother’s mirror

There is something uniquely confronting about watching your daughter become a woman.

She may have your face.

Your body.

Your mannerisms.

The things you like about yourself might appear in her.

So might the things you spent your entire life trying to escape.

And perhaps that’s why the mother-daughter relationship can become complicated in a way the mother-son relationship isn’t.

A son becomes a man.

But a daughter becomes a woman in the same world that taught her mother what it meant to be one.

She becomes younger where her mother is getting older.

She may receive attention her mother once received.

She may have opportunities her mother never had.

She may be more educated.

More financially independent.

More confident.

More sexually liberated.

And if the mother hasn’t made peace with her own life, her daughter’s freedom can feel less like a celebration and more like an accusation.

Look at everything you could have been.

Even when the daughter never said it.

And then there is the daughter who fights back

This is where things get particularly interesting.

Because the daughter who feels constantly criticized eventually develops a spine.

She says no.

She asks questions.

She doesn’t accept every family tradition.

She refuses to be used.

She earns her own money.

She leaves.

And suddenly she’s called difficult.

Disrespectful.

Proud.

Too independent.

A “modern girl.”

But maybe what the family calls rebellion is sometimes just a woman refusing to participate in her own erasure.

Of course, daughters can be wrong.

They can be selfish.

They can be disrespectful.

Mothers can be wrong too.

Both things can exist at the same time.

The problem is that families often give parents a level of moral immunity that they don’t give children.

If a daughter hurts her mother, everyone asks:

“How could you do that to your mother?”

But when a mother hurts her daughter, everyone asks:

“What did you do to make your mother behave that way?”

Interesting.

Very interesting.

So, do mothers hate their daughters?

I don’t know.

And perhaps “hate” is too easy a word.

Maybe what some daughters experience isn’t hatred at all.

Maybe it’s favoritism.

Maybe it’s emotional immaturity.

Maybe it’s misogyny that has been passed from one generation of women to another.

Maybe it’s a mother who never learned how to love a daughter without controlling her.

Maybe it’s a mother who sees her son’s dependence as affection but her daughter’s independence as rejection.

Maybe it’s competition.

Maybe it’s projection.

Maybe it’s simply a woman who has never confronted her own wounds and therefore doesn’t know how to raise another woman without passing those wounds down.

Or maybe sometimes…

A mother really does dislike her daughter.

And we’re so uncomfortable with that possibility that we’d rather invent a hundred explanations than admit it.

The most painful part

A daughter doesn’t need her mother to be perfect.

She doesn’t even need her mother to agree with everything she does.

She just wants to feel like her mother is happy to see her become a woman.

Not threatened by it.

Not competing with it.

Not constantly trying to shrink it.

She wants to be able to say, “Mummy, I love you,” and actually feel the words when they leave her mouth.

She wants to know that if her brother succeeds, her mother will celebrate him.

And if she succeeds, her mother will celebrate her too.

Not because she’s a daughter.

Not because she’s a son.

Not because of what she will eventually give back.

Just because she is hers.

Maybe that’s the part we don’t talk about enough.

Children don’t only remember the things their parents gave them.

They remember how it felt to be their child.

And perhaps there are grown women walking around today who have spent years wondering why they never felt like their mother’s daughter.

Not because they weren’t loved.

But because, somehow, they always felt like they were competing for the right to be.

And I wonder how many of them are still asking the same question:

Was my mother ever actually proud to have a daughter like me?

title: Demystifying Zero Trust Architecture: Principles, Implementation, & Best Practices
excerpt: Why the traditional perimeter-based security model is dead, and how Zero Trust implements 'never trust, always verify' across identities, devices, and microservices.
content:
Demystifying Zero Trust Architecture: Principles, Implementation, & Best Practices

The traditional "castle-and-moat" security model assumed that everything inside a corporate network perimeter was trustworthy. In today's landscape of remote work, cloud workloads, and sophisticated supply-chain attacks, perimeter security is obsolete. Zero Trust establishes a modern paradigm: Never Trust, Always Verify.

The Three Core Tenets of Zero Trust (NIST SP 800-207)

  1. Explicit Verification: Authenticate and authorize based on all available data points—including user identity, location, device health, service or workload, data classification, and anomalies.
  2. Least Privilege Access: Limit user access with Just-In-Time and Just-Enough-Access (JIT/JEA), risk-based adaptive policies, and data protection to safeguard both data and productivity.
  3. Assume Breach: Minimize blast radius by segmenting access by network, user, devices, and application awareness. Encrypt all sessions end-to-end and utilize automated analytics to detect threats.

Implementing Micro-Segmentation in Cloud Workloads

In containerized and Kubernetes environments, micro-segmentation prevents an attacker who compromises a single web pod from pivoting laterally across your entire cluster.

  • Mutual TLS (mTLS): Enforce cryptographic identity verification for all service-to-service communication using service meshes like Istio or Linkerd.
  • Network Policies: Restrict database ingress so that only dedicated backend worker services can establish connections on port 5432.

Continuous Monitoring and Telemetry

Zero Trust is not a single product you purchase—it is an ongoing operational posture. Centralize audit logs, API access events, and anomaly telemetry into unified Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) pipelines to detect credential misuse in real time.

title: Interstellar
excerpt: 3 Reasons Why "Interstellar " Remains Sci-Fi's Modern Masterpiece.
content:
​​It has been over a decade since Christopher Nolan released Interstellar, yet sci-fi movies are still trying to match its impact. Beyond the space travel and massive black holes, the film stands out for three core reasons:​A Human Story at Its Core: Strip away the space suits and physics, and the movie is simply about a father trying to keep a promise to his daughter. That emotional heart keeps you invested through every tense scene.​Real Visual Effects over Pure CGI: Nolan used physical sets and massive projection screens instead of relying entirely on green screens. When the actors look out a spaceship window, they are looking at real footage, making their reactions far more believable. Hans Zimmer’s Unforgettable Score: The music does not just sit in the background; it drives the entire movie. The heavy organ notes create an intense sense of urgency that makes space feel genuinely massive and dangerous.​If you haven't rewatched it recently, it holds up better than almost any modern sci-fi film in recent memory.

title: A Heart of Flesh, A Mind Renewed
excerpt: There is a direct connection between a renewed mind and a heart of flesh. When God gives you a heart of flesh, He gets access to work in you and through you. Th…
content:
There is a direct connection between a renewed mind and a heart of flesh.

When God gives you a heart of flesh, He gets access to work in you and through you. This was His promise to Israel:

“I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit in you; I will remove from you your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh.”— Ezekiel 36:26

A heart of flesh is soft, responsive, and teachable. It is a heart that can be renewed, shaped, and transformed by God.

Why the Word Sometimes Doesn’t Take Root

Most times, the reason the Word of God does not take deep root in us is not because the Word lacks power. It’s because the heart receiving it has not been transformed.

And transformation begins with the renewing of the mind.

“Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” — Romans 12:2

A hardened heart resists. A renewed mind receives.

When your mind is renewed, your heart becomes fertile ground. And when your heart is renewed, intimacy with your Creator becomes natural, not forced.

A Prayer for the Week:

As you step into this new week, ask God for a heart of flesh.

Ask Him to remove every hardness, every distraction, every resistance.

With a heart of flesh you will:

1. See Him more clearly – because your eyes are no longer clouded

2. Love Him more dearly – because your affections are aligned

3. Follow Him more closely – because your steps are guided

God is still in the business of working on hearts. Will you let Him?

May this week bring you closer to Him than ever before.

title: THE SILENT GENERATION
excerpt: The Battles Behind the Smile
content:
There is something about teenagers that society often misunderstands.

They can be hurting and still laugh.

They can be angry and still say nothing.

They can feel lonely while surrounded by hundreds of people.

They can be struggling and still show up to school every morning.

That is why looking at a teenager and saying, "You look fine," doesn't necessarily mean they are fine.

Sometimes, the person who makes everyone laugh is the person who goes home and cries alone.

The pressure to fit in

Teenagers want to belong.

They want friends.

They want to feel accepted.

They want to feel like they matter.

And sometimes, that desire to belong can push them into situations they aren't ready for.

They may start dressing differently because their friends do.

They may change the way they speak.

They may pretend to like things they don't actually like.

They may engage in things they know are wrong simply because they don't want to be called boring, childish or different.

Nobody wants to be the person left out.

But the pressure to fit in can become dangerous when a teenager begins losing themselves just to be accepted.

Teenage relationships

There is also pressure surrounding relationships.

Teenagers are constantly exposed to romantic relationships online.

They see couples showing expensive gifts, surprise dates, matching outfits and endless declarations of love.

It can create the idea that being in a relationship means you are finally important to someone.

So some teenagers rush into relationships because they don't want to feel left behind.

Others tolerate disrespect because they are afraid of losing the person they love.

Some confuse attention with love.

Some accept unhealthy behavior because they think, "At least someone wants me."

But teenagers need to understand that being loved should never require them to lose their dignity, safety or sense of self.

Body image and insecurity

Then there is the battle with appearance.

A teenager can wake up feeling comfortable with themselves and spend ten minutes scrolling through social media before suddenly feeling inadequate.

Too fat.

Too skinny.

Too dark.

Too light.

Too short.

Too tall.

Not curvy enough.

Too curvy.

Not attractive enough.

There always seems to be something society wants young people to change about themselves.

And filters have made the problem even worse.

People are comparing real faces to edited faces.

Real bodies to altered bodies.

Real lives to carefully selected moments.

A teenager should not have to hate their reflection because the internet taught them that beauty has only one definition.

The pressure to make money

There is also nothing wrong with wanting to be financially successful at a young age.

But the internet has created another kind of pressure.

Teenagers constantly see people their age claiming to make huge amounts of money.

They see expensive cars.

Luxury apartments.

Designer clothes.

Foreign trips.

Businesses.

And suddenly, simply being a teenager isn't enough anymore.

They feel like they must already have everything figured out.

But everyone has a different starting point.

Someone else's success should not become evidence of your failure.

When home doesn't feel like home

Perhaps one of the hardest battles is family problems.

Some teenagers have parents who love them but don't know how to communicate with them.

Some are constantly being compared to their siblings.

"Why can't you be like your brother?"

"Look at your classmate."

"You're disappointing me."

Words can stay with a person for years.

A teenager may forget the punishment, but remember the humiliation.

They may forget the argument, but remember how it made them feel.

This is why adults need to be careful with their words.

Discipline is important.

Boundaries are important.

But teenagers also need to know that making a mistake does not make them a failure.

The teenager who needs someone to listen

Maybe the solution isn't always complicated.

Sometimes, teenagers simply need someone safe enough to talk to.

Someone who won't immediately judge them.

Someone who won't turn every conversation into a lecture.

Someone who can say:

"I don't agree with what you did, but I still want to understand why you did it."

That sentence can open a door that shouting never could.

Teenagers don't need adults who pretend they were perfect at that age.

They need adults who remember what it felt like to be confused, insecure and afraid of disappointing everyone.

Because sometimes, the teenager who looks difficult isn't asking for more punishment.

They are asking to be understood.

AI Ethics, Governance, and Compliance in the Enterprise Era

As organizations integrate generative AI into core workflows, establishing clear governance frameworks is vital for risk mitigation, regulatory compliance (such as the EU AI Act), and user trust.

Key Pillars of Responsible AI Governance

  • Data Privacy & PII Scrubbing: Ensure confidential customer information is never transmitted to unvetted third-party LLM training pipelines.
  • Algorithmic Bias & Fairness Audits: Continuously monitor classification and recommendation outputs for demographic skew.
  • Explainability & Human-in-the-Loop Oversight: Require human sign-off for high-stakes automated decisions in healthcare, financial credit, and legal domains.
