title: IF I COULD GO BACK TO THE VERY FIRST DAY I MET YOU…
excerpt: The Life He Hid. The name I knew wasn’t his real name.
content:
“Which one?”

I didn’t understand the question.

“What do you mean, which one?”

She sighed.

“The name you know him by.”

My heart started beating faster.

“Kunle?”

“Yes.”

“What about it?”

“That’s not the name he used when I knew him.”

I sat down.

“Then what name did he use?”

“Daniel.”

I laughed.

Not because it was funny.

I just didn’t know what else to do.

“You’re lying.”

“I’m not.”

“I’ve known this man for years.”

“No, Bola.”

Her voice became softer.

“You’ve known Kunle for years. I knew him as Daniel.”

I didn’t say anything.

“That’s the problem.”

My hands started shaking.

“How do you know him?”

“Because I was married to him.”

I froze.

“Your… husband?”

“Yes.”

“Then why did he tell me you were his ex?”

She gave a short laugh.

“Because that’s easier to explain.”

I couldn’t speak.

“Bola, I didn’t call you because I wanted him back.”

“Then why did you call me?”

She took a breath.

“Because you need to know what you’re dealing with.”

“What exactly am I dealing with?”

“A man who has been lying about more than one thing.”

My chest tightened.

“What else did he lie about?”

“I can’t tell you everything.”

“Why?”

“Because you won’t believe me.”

“Try me.”

She was quiet for a moment.

Then she said,

“Ask him where he lived before he met you.”

I frowned.

“I know where he lived.”

“Do you?”

“Yes.”

“Then ask him.”

The call ended.

I stared at my phone.

Before I could even decide what to do, a message from Kunle came in.

Kunle: Have you eaten? ❤️

I stared at the message for a few seconds.

Of course.

Even now.

Somehow, this man could make me feel cared for at the exact moment I was questioning everything about him.

I typed a reply.

Then deleted it.

Instead, I called him.

He picked up almost immediately.

“Hey, babe.”

“Where did you live before you met me?”

Silence.

A long one.

“Why are you asking?”

“Just answer me.”

“I told you. I lived in Ibadan.”

“Which area?”

Another silence.

“Bola, what’s going on?”

“Which area, Kunle?”

He sighed.

“Why are you doing this?”

“Because someone just told me your name isn’t even Kunle.”

Silence.

This time, I knew.

Something was wrong.

“Who told you that?”

I didn’t answer.

“Bola.”

“What’s your real name?”

He breathed out slowly.

Then he said something I wasn’t prepared for.

“My name is Kunle.”

I almost laughed.

“That’s not what I asked.”

He went quiet.

Then, finally:

“Daniel.”

My heart dropped.

Not because of the name.

Because he had just confirmed it himself.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“It’s complicated.”

“No. It’s not.”

“Bola—”

“Who is Teni?”

Silence.

And that silence told me everything.

She wasn’t lying.

But there was still one thing I didn’t understand.

Why had a married man with another name walked into my life at my friend’s wedding?

And more importantly…

how did he know who I was?

To be continued…

title: How Nigerians Are Using AI to Find Jobs in 2026.
excerpt: How Nigerians Are Using AI to Find Jobs in 2026Job hunting in Nigeria can feel like a full-time job that refuses to pay you.You search.You rewrite your CV.You a…
content:
How Nigerians Are Using AI to Find Jobs in 2026

Job hunting in Nigeria can feel like a full-time job that refuses to pay you.

You search.

You rewrite your CV.

You apply.

You wait.

Then you apply again.

Now AI has entered the process.

For some Nigerian job seekers, artificial intelligence is no longer something they hear about in technology conversations. It is becoming part of how they search for opportunities, improve applications, prepare for interviews, learn new skills and even discover jobs they might not have found otherwise.

The interesting part is that AI is not only changing the jobs themselves.

It is changing how people look for them.

AI Has Entered the Nigerian Job Search

The Nigerian employment market has always been competitive.

There are graduates looking for their first opportunity, experienced workers trying to move to better jobs, freelancers looking for international clients and young people trying to turn digital skills into income.

At the same time, employers are increasingly asking for digital and AI-related capabilities.

Current job listings in Nigeria include roles around artificial intelligence, automation, AI agents and machine learning. Indeed's Nigeria listings, for example, currently show dozens of AI-related openings, while separate listings for AI-agent roles include both technical positions and jobs that require much more basic digital skills.

That creates an interesting situation.

The Nigerian job seeker is now facing two different questions:

What jobs are available?

And:

How can I become the kind of person those jobs are looking for?

AI can help with both

So What Are Nigerians Actually Using AI For?

The obvious answer is CVs.

But that is only the beginning.

1. Rewriting CVs

A job seeker can take an old CV and ask an AI system to identify weak sections, improve the wording and reorganize the document around a particular role.

That can be useful.

But there is a difference between asking AI to make your CV sound impressive and asking it to help you communicate what you have actually done.

The second is much more valuable.

AI cannot invent the experience you need.

It can only help you present what you have.

2. Understanding Job Descriptions

Job descriptions can sometimes look like another language.

"Experience with workflow automation."

"Knowledge of CRM systems."

"Strong analytical capabilities."

"Experience with generative AI."

"Excellent stakeholder management."

A job seeker can paste the description into an AI tool and ask:

What does this employer actually want?

That simple question can turn a confusing vacancy into a checklist.

You can identify the skills you already have.

You can identify the skills you lack.

And you can decide whether the job is worth applying for.

3. Preparing for Interviews

AI can also become a practice interviewer.

Give it the job description.

Give it your CV.

Ask it to interview you.

Then answer the questions yourself.

You can ask it to challenge weak answers, identify vague claims and generate follow-up questions.

For a young Nigerian who may not have access to expensive career coaching, that can be surprisingly useful.

But there is a catch.

The goal is not to memorize AI-generated answers.

The goal is to become better at answering questions yourself.

4. Learning the Skills You Are Missing

This may actually be the most important use.

Imagine you find a job you want.

You meet 70 percent of the requirements.

Instead of immediately deciding that you are unqualified, you can use AI to break down the remaining 30 percent.

What is a CRM?

How does a sales funnel work?

What is SQL?

What does an AI evaluation specialist do?

How does workflow automation work?

What should I learn first?

AI can become a personal tutor while you close the gap.

And this matters because the Nigerian labour market is not only dealing with unemployment.

It is also dealing with a skills problem.

In 2026, Nigerian employers and policymakers have continued to emphasize AI and digital skills as part of improving employability and workforce readiness.

But There Is a Problem With AI Job Hunting

AI can make you look more qualified than you actually are.

That is dangerous.

A person who has never written a proper report can ask AI to produce one.

Someone who barely understands Excel can ask AI to describe them as "highly proficient in data analysis."

Someone who has never built anything can generate a portfolio full of polished descriptions.

The application looks better.

The person has not necessarily become better.

And eventually, the interview comes.

Then the work begins.

This is where the AI advantage disappears if there is no real skill behind it.

There is already evidence of another problem emerging in Nigeria: authorities have warned about fake and AI-generated employment letters being used in recruitment scams.

So AI is creating a strange new environment.

It can help legitimate job seekers compete.

It can also make deception easier.

That means knowing how to use AI is not enough.

You need to know when not to use it.

The CV Is No Longer Enough

There is another shift happening underneath all of this.

For a long time, the CV was the main document through which a young person introduced themselves to an employer.

But increasingly, employers want evidence.

Can you actually do the work?

Can you show what you have built?

Can you explain what you learned?

Can you solve a problem?

Can you communicate?

Can you work with modern tools?

This is particularly important as AI lowers the barrier to producing certain kinds of work.

If everyone can generate a polished paragraph, the paragraph becomes less impressive.

If everyone can create a basic presentation, the presentation becomes less impressive.

If everyone can generate a generic CV, the CV becomes less distinctive.

The advantage moves somewhere else.

Proof.

The People Who Win May Not Be the People Who Use AI the Most

They may be the people who use it best.

There is a difference.

Someone can spend five hours asking ChatGPT to write things for them.

Another person can spend one hour using AI to research a problem, understand a market, build a prototype and improve their own work.

The second person is building capability.

That distinction will matter more as AI becomes normal.

Nigeria is already seeing this transition in the labour market.

There are now AI-related opportunities ranging from engineering and automation to AI training, evaluation and data work. Some current remote listings available to Nigerians even include entry-level AI evaluation and data roles.

The opportunity is therefore not simply:

"Learn AI."

It is:

"Learn something useful, then learn how AI can make you better at it."

You Do Not Have to Become an AI Engineer

This is where many young people get confused.

They hear about artificial intelligence and immediately think they need to learn Python, machine learning, mathematics and computer science.

Those skills are valuable.

But AI is becoming relevant far beyond engineering.

A marketer can use AI.

A researcher can use AI.

A designer can use AI.

A teacher can use AI.

A salesperson can use AI.

A writer can use AI.

A business owner can use AI.

An accountant can use AI.

A lawyer can use AI.

The valuable combination is increasingly domain knowledge + AI capability.

That is much more accessible than trying to become an AI engineer overnight.

The Nigerian Advantage

There is something else worth noticing.

Nigeria has a huge population of young people trying to enter the labour market at the same time that AI is changing the global economy.

That sounds like a problem.

It is.

But it can also become an opportunity.

A young Nigerian does not necessarily need to compete only for Nigerian jobs.

Remote work has already opened access to international companies and clients, while new AI-related work can be performed across borders.

Current platforms are already listing remote AI training, evaluation, annotation and data-related opportunities open to people in Nigeria and elsewhere.

The competition is global.

But so is the opportunity.

That changes the question.

Instead of asking:

"What job can I get in Nigeria?"

A young person can increasingly ask:

"What problem can I become good enough to solve that someone, somewhere, will pay me for?"

That is a much bigger question.

What Nigerian Job Seekers Should Learn Now

If you are looking for work in 2026, I would not make "prompt engineering" your entire career plan.

Learn how to think.

Learn how to research.

Learn how to communicate.

Learn one valuable professional skill deeply.

Then learn how AI can multiply that skill.

If you are interested in marketing, learn marketing and use AI to accelerate research, content and analysis.

If you are interested in software, learn software development and use AI to build and test faster.

If you are interested in research, learn how to investigate questions properly and use AI to organize and analyze information.

If you are a writer, become a better writer instead of simply becoming better at prompting a machine to write.

The machine is becoming easier to use.

That means the human skill behind the machine becomes more important.

AI Will Not Automatically Get You a Job

This may be the most important thing to understand.

AI can help you find the vacancy.

It can help you understand the requirements.

It can improve your CV.

It can prepare you for the interview.

It can teach you a missing skill.

It can even help you build something you can put in your portfolio.

But it cannot walk into the interview for you.

It cannot build your character.

It cannot give you five years of experience overnight.

And it cannot turn an empty portfolio into a meaningful career.

You still have to become useful.

The Nigerian Job Seeker Is Entering a Different Labour Market

The old formula was relatively simple:

Get a degree.

Write a CV.

Apply for jobs.

Wait.

That formula is becoming less reliable.

The new formula looks more like:

Learn.

Build.

Show your work.

Use technology intelligently.

Make yourself discoverable.

Keep improving.

And AI sits somewhere in the middle of that process.

Not as a magic shortcut.

As leverage.

The biggest opportunity may therefore not belong to the Nigerian who knows the most AI tools.

It may belong to the Nigerian who combines real skill, good judgment and AI better than everyone else.

Because eventually, employers do not pay you because you know how to use ChatGPT.

They pay you because you can solve a problem.

AI just changes how quickly you can get there.

The real question

The question for Nigerian young people is no longer simply whether AI will take jobs.

The better question is:

What can you become unusually good at because AI exists?

That is where the opportunity begins.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can AI help me find a job in Nigeria?

Yes. AI can help you understand job descriptions, identify relevant vacancies, improve applications, prepare for interviews and learn skills. It should support your job search rather than replace your own judgment.

How can I use AI to improve my CV?

Give an AI tool your real experience and the job description, then ask it to identify gaps, improve clarity and help you present relevant achievements. Do not allow it to invent experience, qualifications or achievements.

Will AI take jobs in Nigeria?

AI will change many jobs, and some tasks will become automated. At the same time, new AI-related roles and new ways of working are emerging. The effect will vary significantly by industry and occupation.

Do I need to become a programmer to work in AI?

No. AI is increasingly used across marketing, research, design, education, sales, finance, customer service and many other fields. Technical AI careers do require deeper technical skills, but using AI effectively does not necessarily require becoming an AI engineer.

What skills should young Nigerians learn for the AI era?

Strong communication, research, critical thinking, digital literacy, adaptability and domain-specific expertise are valuable foundations. AI skills become more powerful when combined with an actual profession or area of knowledge.

Let's talk.

If you’re Nigerian and you’re looking for work right now, how are you using AI?

Or do you think AI is actually making the job market harder?

Tell me your honest take in the comments. I want to hear the real experiences, not the polished LinkedIn answers.

And follow me if you want writing that goes beyond the headlines, exploring AI, Africa, young people, technology, work and the changes happening around us before everyone starts talking about them.

title: Sometimes, Life Rewards the Person Who Hurt You
excerpt: Do you know that some people can eat their cake and still have it?I just finished watching SISTA, and honestly, I am filled with clusters of emotions. Anger. Fr…
content:
Do you know that some people can eat their cake and still have it?

I just finished watching SISTA, and honestly, I am filled with clusters of emotions. Anger. Frustration. Disbelief. Maybe even a little resentment.

A 21-year-old man abandoned his 19-year-old pregnant girlfriend and their two-year-old son. He left her a letter asking her to move on, as though their entire relationship was a chapter he could simply close.

This was a woman who had supported him through school. A woman who, despite being young herself, became financially responsible for their little family. A woman who had to figure out how to raise two children while building a life from almost nothing.

Nineteen years later, she was still working as a cleaner when she crossed paths with him.

And guess what? He was rich.

He had returned from abroad with his wife. He recognized her. He wanted to be part of his children’s lives. He bought them expensive things, introduced them to possibilities their mother could only dream of, and suddenly became the father they were excited to know.

The children welcomed him.

And I understand why. They were meeting their father. They were excited. They saw someone who could offer them a different kind of life.

But me? I was angry.

Because this man abandoned his responsibility, lived his life, became successful, and then returned to enjoy the family he had left behind.

He ate his cake and still had it.

For 19 years, did it never cross his mind that there might be a young woman somewhere struggling with two children? His children? Did he never wonder how they were surviving? Did he never try to find them?

And what if that cleaning job had never happened? What if she had not been the person contacted? What if fate had not brought them together?

Would he ever looked for them?

That is the part that unsettles me.

Because sometimes, life does not reward people according to what they deserve. The person who hurt you may go on to prosper. The person who abandoned you may return years later with money, charm, and gifts. And the person who stayed may be left wondering why all her sacrifices seem so easy for everyone to forget.

The children forgiving him does not mean their mother did not suffer.

And accepting him as their father does not mean she has to accept him as her husband again. Those are two very different things.

His wife, thankfully, was supportive throughout. A good woman. And I think that distinction matters too. Not every woman who enters a complicated family story has to become an enemy. Sometimes, women can recognize one another’s humanity.

But beyond the movie, this got me thinking about something else.

We often tell women, “Just be good. Do the right thing. Stay faithful. Sacrifice. One day, people will realize your worth.”

But what if they don’t?

What if the person who did you wrong never apologizes? What if he never comes back? What if he comes back only when life has become comfortable for him? What if he gets to enjoy the rewards of a family you struggled to build?

Life does not always favor you because you have been a good person.

And I think women need to understand that.

You cannot build your entire life around the expectation that someone who hurt you will eventually return to make everything right.

Sometimes, they return. Sometimes, they don’t.

Either way, you have to choose yourself.

title: A Trap Called "Desire" (Part One)
excerpt: True wealth is not having an abundance of worldly goods. It is having a soul that cannot be bought in a store.
content:
We live in a world that never stops selling us an upgrade.

A better phone. A flashier car. A more expensive lifestyle. A vacation we can only afford if we don't check our bank account for the next three months.

We scroll, we see the "soft life," and a quiet voice inside us whispers: I want that too.

So we chase it. We stretch our budgets to the breaking point and pay the price.

But here's the truth nobody tells you until you're already stuck:

The things you think you own will eventually own you.

You walked right into a trap. A trap called desire.

The Illusion of the Next Best Thing

The trap works because it promises an ending it never delivers.

It tells you: *Once you buy this phone, you'll be satisfied.*

It tells you: Once you buy this shoe, you'll feel successful.

So you sacrifice your savings and you buy it.

For the first three days, the high is incredible. You place it where everyone can see it. You feel like you've finally arrived.

Then the high fades. The new item becomes normal.

And just like that, the next model drops. A slightly better screen. A minor camera upgrade. Your satisfaction vanishes overnight.

You're no longer happy with what you have you're consumed by what you lack. A treadmill where the finish line keeps moving backward.

Impressing People Who Don't Even Notice

Once you're caught in this trap, spending stops being about comfort. It becomes about validation.

You buy clothes you can't afford, to impress people who are too busy managing their own image to notice yours.

You become a slave to appearance trading your peace of mind for applause, stressing over bills because you're terrified of what people will say if you step down a level.

True wealth was never about how much you own. It's contentment the quiet ability to be satisfied with what you have.

Lose that contentment, and desire becomes a bottomless pit. No amount of money fills it.

The True Cost of a False Lifestyle

The most dangerous part of this trap isn't what it does to your bank account. It's what it does to your freedom.

To fund a lifestyle built on desire, people make compromises they swore they never would.

Some take on debt that keeps them awake at night.

Some abandon their ethics, chasing money fast enough to fund tastes that honest work can't.

Some quietly look down on family or partners living honestly within their means.

You think you're chasing luxury. You're building a cage.

Breaking the Trap

Getting free of it starts with one uncomfortable question, asked honestly, every time you feel the pull to buy something that stretches you thin:

Am I buying this because it adds real value to my life or because I'm using it to fill something empty inside me?

Worldly things are meant to be used, not worshipped.

Build a life sized to your actual budget. Protect your peace. Refuse to let a screen decide your worth.

Because true success is sleeping soundly at night owing no one, compromising nothing, knowing your value was never for sale.

title: He’s Her Father — What Could He Possibly Do?
excerpt: There's a conversation happening in comment sections right now that tears parents into two camps. Both sides are right about something real.
content:
Camp One says: there are certain ages, certain stages, certain kinds of closeness a girl should never share with her father unsupervised. Not because he's a monster. Just because.

Camp Two says: he's her father. The man who carried her on his shoulders, who paced the hospital hallway the night she was born, who would burn the world down to keep her safe. What exactly are you accusing him of?

Both women are talking past each other. Both are convinced the other one is either paranoid or naive. And here's the part that makes this so hard to settle: both of them are right about something real.

Let's slow down and actually sit in this, instead of picking a side in thirty seconds like everyone online seems to want us to.

Camp Two's Argument And Why It Feels So Obvious

Put yourself in her shoes for a second.

She watches her husband change diapers at 3am without being asked twice. She watches him learn to braid hair badly, patiently, over and over, because his daughter wanted him to do it, not her mother. She watches him check the locks twice before bed, not because he's paranoid, but because something in him rearranged the day she was born and now everything he does is filtered through keeping her safe.

So when someone online tells her to be "careful" about how much time her husband spends with his own daughter, it doesn't land as caution. It lands as an insult. It lands as: we don't trust the man you know better than anyone else on earth. We're treating your household like a crime scene waiting to happen.

And honestly? If you've lived inside a genuinely safe, genuinely loving home, that reaction makes complete sense. You're not naive. You're describing something true — because it's true for you.

This is Camp Two's real point, even if they don't phrase it this cleanly: suspicion is not the same as safety. A daughter who grows up watched, monitored, flinched-at even by people who mean well absorbs a message too: closeness to men, even the safest man in your life, is inherently risky. That belief doesn't protect her. It just teaches her fear before she's old enough to know what she's afraid of.

Camp One's Argument And Why It Refuses to Go Away

Now Sit In The Other Chair.

She's not making this up. She's not scrolling for drama. Somewhere maybe close, maybe not she has heard a story. A cousin. A classmate. A woman twice her age who finally said the thing out loud at 35 that she couldn't say at 9, because nobody had given her the words for it yet, and even if she'd had the words, nobody would have believed her over a man everyone called "such a good father."

That's the story Camp One is haunted by. And here's the part that makes it so hard to argue with: it is often not a stranger. Across cultures, across religions, across income levels the uncomfortable, repeated finding is that harm to children is frequently caused by someone inside the trust circle. Not the man lurking outside the school gate. The uncle who always volunteers to drop her home. The family friend who's "practically a father to her." Sometimes, devastatingly, an actual father.

This is not an accusation against fathers as a category. It's not even mostly about fathers most fathers are exactly what Camp Two describes. But Camp One isn't arguing about most fathers. They're arguing about the fact that from the outside, a safe household and a dangerous one can look identical. Same warmth. Same nicknames. Same family photos. You cannot tell by vibes. You cannot tell by how much a man clearly loves his daughter love and self-control are not the same muscle, and some men have built one and never been asked to build the other.

So when Camp One says "be careful," they are not necessarily accusing your husband. They are refusing to build a safety rule around a feeling. Because feelings "he would never" are exactly what families in situations like this may have believed, right up until they discovered they were wrong.

The Blind Spot on Both Sides

Here's what nobody in this argument wants to admit: they're each solving for a different failure mode, and treating the other camp's failure mode as if it doesn't exist.

Camp Two is solving for: don't let suspicion poison a genuinely safe home.

Camp One is solving for: don't let love become the reason nobody was watching.

Both failure modes are real. Both can ruin real families — just in opposite directions. A woman drowning her daughter in suspicion of a good man is a real tragedy. A woman staying silent because "he's her father" while something goes wrong under her own roof is also a real tragedy.

Neither camp is choosing the fake problem. They're just each staring at the real problem the other one hasn't experienced yet.

What Changes the Whole Conversation?

Here's the reframe that actually resolves this.

The guidance was never: watch fathers because fathers are suspects.

The better principle is: build the house with boundaries as its architecture, applied to everyone, regardless of how much you trust them.

Children even with their own parents can be taught to knock before entering a room. Privacy doesn't switch off because you share blood. Private space, private body, private moments belong to the child even inside the safest home in the world.

This isn't a rule invented because someone assumed the worst. It's a rule that exists so nobody has to guess who deserves the benefit of the doubt and who doesn't.

Notice what that does.

It removes the accusation from the room entirely.

Nobody is being called a suspect. Nobody has to defend their character before bedtime.

The boundary isn't: "I don't trust you."

It's: "This is simply how our home works, for everyone."

That's the piece both camps are missing. Camp Two hears "boundaries" and translates it to "accusation." Camp One sometimes does mean it as an accusation, aimed at a specific man, based on a bad feeling.

Neither has to be true. A boundary that exists structurally before there's ever a reason to suspect anyone protects the child without putting a single father on trial.

So Which Woman Is Right?

Neither one needs to win. And honestly, neither one should try to.

The mother who trusts her husband completely is not naive she can also teach her daughter to knock, to have appropriate privacy as she grows, and to know her body is hers. None of that requires her to distrust him. It simply means she's not betting her daughter's safety on a feeling, even a well-earned one.

The mother who's cautious is not paranoid but caution that curdles into fear, into a daughter flinching from her own father's ordinary affection, into a man quietly grieving the closeness he's not allowed to have with his own child that's not protection anymore.

That's a different wound wearing protection's clothes.

The house that gets this right doesn't ask "is this man dangerous?" It never even reaches that question. It simply asks: What does dignity require, from everyone, all the time?

And builds the answer into the walls before anyone needs to wonder who to worry about. That's the only version of safety that doesn't cost a daughter her closeness with her father to get it. And it's the only version of trust that doesn't require anyone to gamble.

Let's Settle This in the Comments

Let’s stop talking past each other.

Camp One or Camp Two: Which side of this argument did you naturally fall into when you started reading?

Do structural privacy rules (like knocking and private changing) protect a child, or do they poison a safe home with unnecessary suspicion?

Be honest, keep it respectful, and drop your thoughts below.

title: 𝐃𝐎 𝐍𝐎𝐓 𝐂𝐇𝐀𝐒𝐄 𝐑𝐎𝐎𝐌𝐒. 𝐁𝐔𝐈𝐋𝐃 𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐕𝐀𝐋𝐔𝐄 𝐓𝐇𝐀𝐓 𝐌𝐀𝐊𝐄𝐒 𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐑𝐎𝐎𝐌 𝐖𝐀𝐍𝐓 𝐘𝐎𝐔 𝐈𝐍 𝐈𝐓.
excerpt: 𝐃𝐎 𝐍𝐎𝐓 𝐂𝐇𝐀𝐒𝐄 𝐑𝐎𝐎𝐌𝐒. 𝐁𝐔𝐈𝐋𝐃 𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐕𝐀𝐋𝐔𝐄 𝐓𝐇𝐀𝐓 𝐌𝐀𝐊𝐄𝐒 𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐑𝐎𝐎𝐌 𝐖𝐀𝐍𝐓 𝐘𝐎𝐔 𝐈𝐍 𝐈𝐓. These days, it seems like everyone wants to be “in the room.” The room wi…
content:
𝐃𝐎 𝐍𝐎𝐓 𝐂𝐇𝐀𝐒𝐄 𝐑𝐎𝐎𝐌𝐒. 𝐁𝐔𝐈𝐋𝐃 𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐕𝐀𝐋𝐔𝐄 𝐓𝐇𝐀𝐓 𝐌𝐀𝐊𝐄𝐒 𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐑𝐎𝐎𝐌 𝐖𝐀𝐍𝐓 𝐘𝐎𝐔 𝐈𝐍 𝐈𝐓.

These days, it seems like everyone wants to be “in the room.”

The room with the right people.

The room where important conversations are happening.

The room with the decision-makers.

The room where opportunities are being created.

And honestly, being in the right room can matter.

But there is something I have come to realize over time:

𝐃𝐨𝐧’𝐭 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐬 𝐨𝐧 𝐠𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐨𝐨𝐦. 𝐅𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐬 𝐨𝐧 𝐛𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐬𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐨𝐨𝐦 𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐬.

I’ve had the privilege of speaking with and connecting with people I once thought I could never have a conversation with.

And one thing keeps standing out to me:

People want to know what you are bringing.

What are you trying to solve?

What do you know?

What can you contribute?

What problem can you help solve?

What value do you add?

Even organizations don’t bring people in simply because they want to be there.

𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐛𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐩𝐞𝐨𝐩𝐥𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐛𝐞𝐜𝐚𝐮𝐬𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐛𝐮𝐭𝐞.

So, while you are applying for one opportunity after another, attending events, networking, and trying to get into different spaces, pause for a moment.

Ask yourself:

👉🏽 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐞 𝐚𝐦 𝐈 𝐛𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠?

👉🏽 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐦 𝐚𝐦 𝐈 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐨 𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐯𝐞?

👉🏽 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐈 𝐛𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞?

Because getting into the room is only one part of the journey.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐝𝐨 𝐨𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐠𝐞𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞.

Don’t chase every room simply because someone told you that you need to be there.

Be strategic.

Build your knowledge.

Build your skills.

Build your character.

Build your experience.

Build your capacity.

Build something meaningful.

𝐁𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐦𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐨𝐨𝐦 𝐰𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐢𝐧 𝐢𝐭. 🚪

title: Relieved but caged
excerpt: What happens when the only thing standing in your way is you?
content:
I wish there was a name for the ability to watch yourself go through your own life.

To sit back and observe your routines.
To watch yourself waste time.
To grieve the days that have passed and will never come again.

Every epiphany only lasts a few days.
Then it fades, leaving behind the bitter taste of a version of you that once squeezed everything out of life.

Doom scrolling has become the norm.

Now, when you come across something that could actually help you find your way,
you swipe past it at the speed of light.

Not because it’s useless,
but because it triggers something in you.

And when you’re not on your screen,
your eyes are shut.

Not resting,
but escaping.

In that world, you take advantage of every opportunity.
You even create your own doors.

You move with clarity.
You become everything you know you could be.

And that’s the problem.

Because in reality, that same understanding doesn’t excite you.

It torments you.

You hear people talk about their struggles, their obstacles, the things holding them back.

And instead of feeling sorry for them,
you feel something else.

Relief.

Because at least they have a reason.

Something to point at.
Something to blame.

But what happens when you know
that the only thing standing in your way is you?

Knowing all of this, having the awareness, having the ability to think and even articulate it like this…

and still doing nothing,

feels like being trapped in a machine
where you are both the victim
and the one operating it.

And the craziest part is,

you don’t even have compassion for yourself.

You just keep pushing the machine further.

You’ve gotten used to the pain.
Maybe you even appreciate it.

Because it’s the only thing that reminds you
that not all of you is gone.

That tight, gut-twisting feeling…

it’s proof you’re still here.

But there’s something darker underneath it.

The fear that the moment you stop feeling it,
the moment it all goes quiet,

is the moment you’ve completely lost.

And maybe that’s your version of hell.

Not fire.
Not punishment.

Just awareness without action.

Maybe you need help.

Or maybe…

title: Local LLM Deployment: Running DeepSeek, Llama 3, and Mistral on Your Own Hardware

content:
Local LLM Deployment: Running DeepSeek, Llama 3, and Mistral on Your Own Hardware

Open-source AI models have achieved near-parity with proprietary cloud APIs across coding, summarization, and reasoning tasks. Running models locally guarantees 100% data confidentiality, zero per-token billing, and offline functionality.

Key Inference Frameworks

  • Ollama: The simplest way to get started with local LLMs on macOS, Windows, and Linux with a clean CLI and REST API.
  • vLLM: An industrial-strength inference engine featuring PagedAttention for maximum throughput and multi-GPU server deployments.
  • llama.cpp: Highly optimized C/C++ inference engine supporting 4-bit and 8-bit quantized GGUF models on consumer hardware.

Getting Started with Ollama & LangChain in Node.js

// Interacting with a local Llama 3 or DeepSeek instance
import { ChatOllama } from "@langchain/community/chat_models/ollama";

const model = new ChatOllama({
  baseUrl: "http://localhost:11434",
  model: "llama3:8b",
  temperature: 0.2,
});

const response = await model.invoke("Explain the CAP theorem in simple terms.");
console.log(response.content);

title: THE PRICE OF US
excerpt:
CHAPTER 1

Kael is accused of murdering the merchant's son in the market square. As the crowd turns hostile, Elara, a girl from one of the Seven Families, steps forward to speak for him, breaking the ancient Pact. Her action triggers a chain of consequences, and she is arrested alongside Kael. They are taken to the High Court for a joint trial.
content:
“I didn’t kill anyone.”

Kael’s voice cracked as he said it, but the crowd didn’t care. They had made up their minds the moment they saw the blood on his hands—his own blood, from the broken glass he’d stepped on that morning. But no one asked about that. The Pact of the Seven Families forbade anyone from speaking for an accused unless they were blood, and Kael had no family left. He was a street sweeper, a nobody with a torn shirt and a hollow belly. And now he was accused of murdering the merchant’s son.

The cobblestones of Cinder Street were slick with rain, and the morning light cast long shadows through the press of bodies. Guards surrounded him, their spears lowered, but the crowd was the real threat—their shouts grew louder, their fists clenched. Kael backed up until his shoulders hit the rough wall of the bakery, and he knew there was nowhere to run.

“Please,” he said, but the word was lost in the noise.

Then a voice cut through—sharp, clear, and utterly defiant.

“He didn’t do it.”

The crowd turned. A girl stepped forward, her dark hair braided with silver ribbons that matched the crest on her coat—the Oakwood Crest, woven in thread so fine it shimmered. She was from one of the Seven Families. Elara was her name, and she had seen Kael every morning for the past month, sweeping the street outside the bakery while she ordered her father’s pastries. She had never spoken to him, but she had noticed the way he always nodded at her, a small gesture of thanks for the extra bread she sometimes left on the step.

“Elara, step back,” her father growled from behind her, his hand gripping her arm. But she shook him off.

“I saw him this morning,” she said, her voice steady. “At the bell of the first hour. He was sweeping Cinder Street. He couldn’t have been at the docks when the merchant’s son was killed.”

The captain of the guard eyed her. “And you would swear this under the Pact?”

“I would.”

Kael stared at her, disbelieving. He had seen her too, but only from a distance. Why would she risk her name for a stranger? He opened his mouth to speak, but the crowd erupted. Some cheered Elara’s courage, others jeered at the lie they believed it to be. The captain raised his hand for silence.

“The law is clear,” he said. “Elara of the Oakwood family has spoken for the accused. By the terms of the Pact, she now stands as his witness and surety. If he is found guilty, she shares his sentence.”

Her father’s face went pale. “This is madness. She is just a girl. She doesn’t understand.”

“I understand that an innocent man is about to be torn apart,” Elara said, and she looked directly at Kael. Her gaze held no doubt. He felt something twist inside him—a strange warmth that wasn’t fear.

Then the captain signaled, and the guards moved. One grabbed Kael, another took Elara by the arm. Her father tried to intervene, but the crowd pushed him back. Kael and Elara were marched through the market square, past stalls and stares, toward the High Court at the top of the hill.

Kael’s heart pounded. He didn’t know what came next—only that this girl had just tied her fate to his. As they walked, he risked a whisper: “Why?”

“Because someone had to,” she replied, not looking at him. “And because the truth doesn’t stop being true just because everyone wants it to be a lie.”

The gates of the High Court loomed ahead, iron and oak, bound with silver hinges that gleamed in the sun. The guards pulled them through, and the door slammed shut behind them.

The trial would begin at noon.

title: Apple Finally Has a Foldable iPhone. Should Samsung Be Worried?
excerpt: Apple has finally joined the foldable-phone party.
content:
Okay, Apple… we see you. 😂

For years, Samsung has been out here folding phones while the rest of us watched from the sidelines wondering whether we actually wanted a phone that could fold.

Now Apple has finally decided to join the party.

On September 9, 2026, Apple introduced the iPhone Duo, its first-ever foldable iPhone. And honestly, it feels a little funny seeing Apple enter a market Samsung has been playing in for years.

So naturally, we have to ask:

Should Samsung be worried?

Apple finally folded. Literally.

The iPhone Duo is basically Apple saying, “What if your iPhone could become a mini tablet?”

When closed, it has a 5.4-inch outer display. Open it up and you get a much larger 7.6-inch screen for watching videos, gaming, browsing and multitasking.

And Apple isn't treating this like some random experiment.

The Duo comes with Apple's A20 Pro chip, a redesigned iOS 27 experience and a dual-battery setup. Apple also says the phone has a precision hinge designed for durability and a special inner display finish that helps reduce glare.

Basically, Apple didn't just fold an iPhone and call it a day.

But… Samsung was here first 👀

This is where things get interesting.

Samsung has been making foldable phones for years. The company has now reached its eighth-generation Galaxy Z lineup, including the Galaxy Z Fold8 and the new Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra.

So while Apple is entering the foldable-phone market with a shiny new product, Samsung is already sitting at the table like:

“Oh, so you finally came?” 😂

Samsung has had years to figure out what works, what doesn't and what people actually want from a foldable phone.

Its latest Fold8 has a 7.6-inch main display, while the Fold8 Ultra is designed more heavily around productivity and multitasking.

So Apple may have arrived late, but it definitely didn't arrive quietly.

And then we get to the price…

Ah.

This is where some people's excitement might suddenly disappear. 😭

The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 in the US.

Yes.

One thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine dollars.

At that price, your phone better greet you in the morning and ask how your day is going. 😂

Apple is clearly positioning the Duo as a premium device, and it's counting on the iPhone name, its ecosystem and the appeal of finally having a foldable iPhone to convince people to pay for it.

So, is Samsung finished?

Absolutely not.

At least, not because Apple released one foldable phone.

Samsung already has experience in this category, multiple foldable models and a whole ecosystem built around Galaxy devices.

But Apple doesn't necessarily need to destroy Samsung to make an impact.

Apple has something powerful on its side: people who already love Apple.

There are people who will look at the Duo and say:

“Finally! A foldable iPhone.” example Samsung's popular line "Well, well, well....Look who folded"😂

And let's be honest, some people would probably buy an Apple-branded brick if it came in Space Black and had an Apple logo. 😂

But here's why this is actually exciting

Apple entering the foldable market could make things much more interesting for everyone.

Samsung now has even more pressure to keep improving.

Apple has to prove that its first attempt was worth the wait.

And other smartphone companies have even more reason to compete.

At the end of the day, we—the consumers—might be the biggest winners.

Because when two massive companies are fighting for our attention, they have to give us better reasons to spend our money.

So, is Samsung worried?

Maybe a little.

But should we be excited?

Definitely.

Samsung may have been folding phones long before Apple joined the conversation.

But now that Apple has finally unfolded its hand, the real competition might just be getting started. And honestly…

We are here for it. 👀
