title: How I started my writing journey
excerpt: All it took was a single book, a short story and a review from my sister
content:
All it took was a single book, “The famished road”, a book by Ben Okri: it was about Azaro, a spirt child gifted with power to see the African spirit world”

It was the first book I ever read that made me wanna become a writer. I don’t know how to describe it, but it made me feel as I was present in the world the book was set in, so I told myself I wanna be as a great writer as Ben. So I started reading.

I read as much book as I could get my hands on. My mom was a teacher so there was no shortage of books at home. I read English text books, novels, plays and poem books. Honestly I couldn’t get enough of them because mum had an array to choose from.

I officially wrote my first short story when I was 13, and gave it to my eldest sister cos she was the one who always take me serious. Well, let’s say she admired my effort but wasn’t as impressed as I had planned. And rightfully so because what I wrote then was really shitty. But the admiration all was the push I needed, so I keep on writing.

I’m not gonna lie, there are times whereby I felt inadequate but anytime I feel that way, I remembered what my sis said, ‘I love your work and I believe in you”, and that has kept me going every single time.

Here I am today, I’ve recently collaborated with some authors for a fantasy novella, which will be out soon. I’ve also recently rejected a publishing deal for my first book (creative difference), and funny enough I got another offer from another publishing house almost immediately. So I basically got two books on the way now. Aside from the other three that I’m still working on.

I’ve made more progress than I ever dreamt of. And I’m this close to achieving my dreams.

title: My first arrest as a grave robber
excerpt: I never thought I’d be arrested on the charges of grave robbing. Well, here I am.
content:
"She was a Muslim. She was buried with no precious objects so why were you digging out her grave" ‎The police officer asked. He was rather gentle with me. A normal Nigerian policeman would have slapped me by now.

‎"Grave robbing is a serious crime you know but I’m really curious about your motives. Grave robbers only exhume a corpse thought to have been buried with worthwhile possessions so what’s your motive” he asked but I still kept mute

‎I didn’t wanna say a word.I don't even know what to say. The detective kept badgering me with questions but I didn’t answer.

‎My mind zoned off….

‎"Why do Muslims bury their dead so quick? I mean, leave something for the rest of us”. That was what came to my mind at Anty Amina’s burial. She had died after falling off the roof of her house. What was she doing there you might ask. Well, all she had to do was wait for her husband to come back from work to fix the leaking roof but she had complained to him many times about it but he did nothing so she decided to fix it herself. And here we are, at her funeral."

Why was I exhuming the body, you might ask.

‎I was a normal human being a couple of months ago until I decided to travel the continent. My plan was to try as much African cuisine as I could, so I cleared my savings and set on my journey. I travelled to Ghana, and had Banku, I had Ibiharage in Burundi, and Nsima in Malawi.

Oh it was fun until I got to a restaurant in a small town in Uganda. I requested for Matoke, their national food but the chef offered me a steak instead.

“No I want the Matoke, I’ve read all about it” I refused

The chef obliged but brought the steak as a side dish. The Matoke was delicious but the steak stole my taste bud. It was flipping delicious. I went back there the second day for the steak, and the next day and the next and the next.

I got addicted until one day I got there and found the restaurant has been sealed off by police strips. I asked a passer-by if he knew what was wrong “They cooked and sell human beings” was the reply I got.

I lost all feelings in that moment. The next day I was back in Nigeria. I don’t even remember booking the flight. All I know was I’m back and I’m now affected with a variation of the retrovirus “HK2”. Now I crave that particular steak.

One thing led to another, and here I am at the police station, being questioned for grave robbing. No way in hell I’m telling them I was exhuming Anty Amina’s corpse to eat her

So, I’m just gonna keep staring at this stupid detective and hope he doesn’t torture me.

Note: No AI involved

title: AI Is Moving Too Fast: Tech Leaders Call for a Slowdown
excerpt: The race to develop increasingly powerful artificial intelligence systems is facing renewed scrutiny after some of the technology industry's biggest names calle…
content:
The race to develop increasingly powerful artificial intelligence systems is facing renewed scrutiny after some of the technology industry's biggest names called for a slower approach to AI development.

Dario Amodei, CEO of AI company Anthropic, has urged technology companies to reduce the pace at which they develop increasingly capable AI models, arguing that safety measures need more time to catch up with the technology.

In an essay published on Saturday, Amodei warned that more advanced AI systems could create serious risks if their capabilities continue to increase faster than safety controls. He proposed stronger independent evaluations of AI systems, common safety standards among major AI companies and greater international cooperation.

The proposal has received support from other major figures in the AI industry. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman agreed that companies need to “pace the frontier” of AI development, while Elon Musk also backed Amodei's position. Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis has also expressed support for slowing the pace of development.

The debate comes as concerns grow over what increasingly autonomous AI systems could eventually do. Recent incidents involving AI systems carrying out activities such as hacking have added to calls for stronger safeguards and independent oversight.

However, not everyone supports slowing the technology's development.

U.S. President Donald Trump has rejected calls for a broad slowdown, arguing that the United States needs to maintain its lead over China in the global AI race. Trump said the U.S. must remain ahead because of the strategic importance of artificial intelligence.He said concerns about AI are being exaggerated while acknowledging that some safeguards may be necessary.

So the debate is basically:

AI companies: "We need to move carefully because AI is becoming extremely powerful."

U.S. government: "We can't slow down so much that China overtakes us."

And that's what makes this story particularly interesting.

Why this matters to Nigeria 🇳🇬

This isn't just an American or Silicon Valley issue. AI is increasingly affecting Nigerian students, writers, businesses, developers and job seekers.

The question Nigeria needs to ask is not simply "Should we use AI?" but:

How do we benefit from AI without becoming completely dependent on it?

For someone working in content and writing, this is especially relevant. AI can make research, brainstorming and editing faster, but employers are increasingly concerned about whether people can still produce original thinking and human-quality work.

The disagreement highlights a growing challenge for governments and technology companies: how to continue benefiting from AI while preventing increasingly powerful systems from creating serious risks.

For now, the global AI race shows no sign of stopping. But with some of the industry's leading figures calling for greater caution, the debate over how fast AI should develop is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

title: The pressure to have Your life figured out in your 20s
excerpt: Everyone seems to have a plan. But what happens when you don’t ?
content:
There is a strange pressure that comes with being in your 20s. Somehow, it feels like everyone around you is moving forward while you are still trying to understand where you are going. One person has graduated, another has a good job, someone is starting a business, and another is already talking about marriage and the future. Then you look at your own life and quietly ask yourself, “Am I falling behind?”

Social media can make this feeling even worse. Every day, we see people announcing new jobs, businesses, achievements, relationships and big plans. We rarely see the months or years of uncertainty that came before those moments. We only see the result, so it becomes easy to compare our unfinished story with someone else's highlight reel.

The truth is that being in your 20s does not mean you should have everything figured out. It is a period of learning, making mistakes, changing your mind and discovering what actually matters to you. Yet, there is an invisible timeline that makes many young people feel as if they are already late.

Sometimes the pressure comes from family. Sometimes it comes from friends. Other times, it comes from ourselves. You start thinking about what you should have achieved by a certain age, where you should be working, how much money you should have saved or what your future should look like. Before you realise it, you are no longer enjoying your journey because you are constantly measuring it against someone else's.

One of the hardest things to accept is that people do not start from the same place. Two people can be the same age and have completely different opportunities, responsibilities and circumstances. One person may have support that another person does not. Someone may know exactly what they want, while another person is still trying different things to find their direction.

And there is nothing wrong with that.

Not having everything figured out does not mean you are failing. It can simply mean that you are still figuring yourself out. Sometimes the path becomes clearer only after you try something, realise it is not for you, and move in another direction.

We also need to stop treating other people's timelines as deadlines for our own lives. Someone getting a job at 21 does not mean you have failed because you got yours later. Someone starting a successful business at 23 does not mean you are behind because you are still learning. Life is not a race where everyone is expected to reach the same destination at the same time.

What matters is that you keep moving.

You can learn a new skill, try something different, make mistakes, start again and take small steps toward the person you want to become. Those steps may not look impressive from the outside, but they still count.

Maybe the goal of your 20s is not to have all the answers. Maybe it is to become comfortable with asking questions, trying new things and growing along the way.

So if you are in your 20s and you feel like you are behind, take a breath. You are not necessarily behind. You may simply be on a different path.

You do not need to have your entire life planned out today. You just need to keep learning, keep moving and give yourself permission to grow at your own pace.

title: How It All Started
excerpt: Before social media became what it is today, I was just a JSS3 girl trying not to miss out.
content:
The pressure was real. Almost all my classmates were on Facebook. And no, Yahoo or online fraud wasn't the trend back then.

I had just entered JSS3, and I remember almost everyone around me already had an account. It felt like I was the only one still living in the dark while everyone else had stepped into a new world.

That pressure, not having anything to contribute to the trending conversations pushed me to create my very first Facebook account using my mum's Itel phone. After all, no one was going to buy me a phone in junior secondary school.

Social media wasn't something you needed lessons to understand. I found my way around it quickly and started doing what almost everyone did then—chatting with strangers. Some became friends. Some I never heard from again.

I sent friend requests to people simply because they looked interesting or because my classmates said they were fun.

Somehow, I loved it.

Imagine being able to tell people about your favourite things, your likes and dislikes. My age didn't seem like a big deal, so I shared a lot about myself with people I'd never met.

For the first time, it felt like I had a place to talk... a place to belong.

And that was only the beginning.

title: The Spiritual Struggle Nobody Talks About
excerpt: The goal was never to look like a righteous person online. It is to become one when nobody is watching.
content:
The Spiritual Struggle Nobody Talks About

You post reminders about Fajr.

You share a verse about tawakkul.

You remind people about sabr.

People see your status and think, “MashaAllah, she must really have her deen together.”

But they don't see what happens after you put your phone down.

You know you have been struggling too.

Maybe your prayers have become rushed.

Maybe Qur'an hasn't felt the same lately.

Maybe you keep falling into the same sin you promised yourself you were done with.

Maybe you're constantly reminding other people about Allah while privately wondering why your own heart feels so far away.

And that can leave you feeling like a fraud.

But listen carefully.

Struggling does not mean you have to stop reminding people.

You don't have to become perfect before you can say something true.

A person can remind others about Fajr and still struggle to wake up for it.

A person can speak about sabr and still lose their temper sometimes.

A person can remind people to trust Allah while fighting their own fear about tomorrow.

That doesn't make the reminder false.

But there is something you must be careful about:

Don't let your public reminders become a substitute for private obedience.

Posting about salah is not the same as praying.

Sharing Qur'an is not the same as reading it.

Reminding people about tawakkul is not the same as actually trusting Allah when your own life becomes difficult.

The reminder should eventually turn back towards you too.

And when it does, don't run from Allah because you're ashamed of yourself.

That's another trap.

You missed Fajr?

Pray the next salah.

You fell into a sin?

Repent.

Your iman feels low?

Keep going.

You haven't opened the Qur'an in days?

Open it today.

You made a mistake again?

Turn back again.

Don't wait until you feel worthy to return to Allah.

You never became worthy by being perfect in the first place.

Allah says:

«“Do not despair of the mercy of Allah.”

— Qur'an 39:53»

And the Prophet ﷺ taught us that faith has periods of enthusiasm and periods of weakness.

So perhaps what you need right now isn't another beautifully designed reminder for everyone else.

Perhaps you need ten quiet minutes with Allah.

No status.

No audience.

No trying to look spiritually impressive.

Just you.

Make wudu.

Stand on the prayer mat.

Tell Allah honestly:

“Ya Allah, I know I am struggling. I know I am not where I should be. But I don't want to stay here. Help me come back to You.”

Then take the next step.

Not twenty steps.

The next one.

And keep reminding others too but let those reminders remind you first.

Because the goal isn't to look like a righteous person online.

The goal is to become one when nobody is watching.

One Honest Question

Have you ever gone through a period where your public Islamic reminders looked stronger than your private worship?

If you have, you don't need to explain everything.

Just leave a “I understand” in the comments.

Someone reading it may realise they're not the only one struggling.

And if this spoke to you, share it with someone who may need the reminder too.

title: Dealing With Jealousy Without Becoming a Bitter Person
excerpt: Understanding Jealousy: The Feeling We Don’t Like to Admit Jealousy is one of those emotions people experience but rarely want to admit to. We talk about happiness. We talk about sadness, anger, heart…
content:
Understanding Jealousy: The Feeling We Don’t Like to Admit

Jealousy is one of those emotions people experience but rarely want to admit to.

We talk about happiness. We talk about sadness, anger, heartbreak, disappointment and even loneliness. But jealousy seems to occupy a different space. It is an emotion many people feel privately while trying very hard not to be seen feeling it.

Why?

Because we have attached so much shame and guilt to it.

To admit that you are jealous can feel like admitting that you are a bad person.

Someone tells you that they got the job you both applied for, and you congratulate them. You smile. You tell them how happy you are.

But somewhere inside you, there is another feeling.

Why them?

Why wasn’t it me?

And immediately, you feel guilty for thinking it.

Perhaps your friend gets into a beautiful relationship with someone who adores her. You genuinely love your friend and want her to be happy, but you also go home and wonder when you will experience that kind of love yourself.

Perhaps someone you know buys a house, starts a successful business, travels frequently, gets married, has a child, loses weight, gets a promotion or simply seems to be living the kind of life you wish you were living.

You can be happy for them and still feel something uncomfortable inside yourself.

That uncomfortable feeling is often jealousy.

And perhaps one of the reasons we struggle with jealousy so much is because we have misunderstood what the emotion actually means.

What is jealousy?

Jealousy is an emotional response that can arise when we perceive that someone else has something we want, value or fear losing.

It can involve comparison, insecurity, fear, resentment, sadness or inadequacy.

Sometimes it is about another person.

Sometimes it has very little to do with them.

A friend getting a job does not necessarily make you jealous because you dislike your friend. You may simply be disappointed that you didn’t get the opportunity you wanted.

Someone being in a loving relationship does not necessarily make you jealous because you don’t want them to be happy. You may simply be longing for that kind of love yourself.

This is why jealousy can be complicated.

It isn’t always saying:

“I don’t want you to have this.”

Sometimes it is saying:

“I wish I had this too.”

Those are not the same thing.

More people experience jealousy than they admit

One of the most interesting things about jealousy is how private it can be.

People often learn to hide it because they are afraid of how they will be perceived.

We don’t want our friends to think we are secretly competing with them.

We don’t want our families to think we are envious.

We don’t want people to believe we are unhappy about their success.

So we learn how to perform happiness.

We say congratulations.

We celebrate.

We post the pictures.

We comment, “So happy for you!”

And sometimes we genuinely mean it.

But genuine happiness for someone does not automatically erase every other emotion we may be experiencing.

Human beings are capable of holding contradictory emotions at the same time.

You can love someone and be jealous of them.

You can be proud of someone and wish you were in their position.

You can want someone to succeed and still feel disappointed that their success highlights something you are struggling with.

That doesn’t necessarily make you dishonest.

It makes you human.

Why are we ashamed of jealousy?

Perhaps because jealousy is often associated with ugliness.

When we describe someone as jealous, we sometimes imagine a person who wants to bring others down, cannot stand seeing others succeed and is secretly hoping for their failure.

That kind of jealousy certainly exists.

But that is not the only form jealousy can take.

There is a difference between feeling an emotion and choosing what to do with that emotion.

You may not always be able to control the first feeling that appears inside you.

You can control what you do afterward.

Imagine two friends who have spent months applying for jobs.

They attend interviews.

They rewrite their CVs.

They encourage each other.

Eventually, one friend gets an offer.

The other friend is genuinely happy.

She hugs her friend.

She congratulates her.

She means it.

But later, when she gets home, she cries.

Not because she wants her friend to lose the job.

Because she wanted one too.

She is disappointed.

She is tired.

She is wondering when her own opportunity will come.

Is she jealous?

Perhaps.

Does that automatically make her a bad friend?

No.

The emotion itself is not the problem.

What matters is what she does with it.

You can be happy for someone and still hurt for yourself

I think this is one of the hardest things for people to accept.

We sometimes think that if we are truly happy for someone, we shouldn’t feel any discomfort about their success.

But real emotions don’t always work that neatly.

You can watch your friend get engaged and genuinely be excited for her while also thinking about your own desire to be loved.

You can celebrate your sibling’s new job while worrying about your own financial situation.

You can admire someone’s beauty while struggling with your own insecurities.

You can be proud of someone’s business while wishing yours was doing better.

The presence of one emotion doesn’t automatically cancel out another.

Your friend’s success does not have to become your failure.

But sometimes it can remind you of what you are still waiting for.

And that reminder can hurt.

Sometimes jealousy tells us something about ourselves

This is where jealousy can become useful.

Not pleasant.

Not comfortable.

But useful.

Instead of immediately asking yourself,

“Why am I jealous of this person?”

you can ask:

“What exactly am I jealous of?”

The answer might surprise you.

Maybe you aren’t jealous of your friend’s entire life.

Maybe you’re jealous of her financial freedom.

Maybe you’re jealous of the confidence she has.

Maybe you’re jealous of the affection she receives.

Maybe you’re jealous of the opportunity he got

Maybe you’re jealous because he is doing something you have always wanted to do but haven’t had the courage, resources or opportunity to pursue.

Sometimes jealousy points directly toward an unmet desire.

It can reveal what we want.

It can reveal what we feel we are missing.

It can even reveal areas of our lives that need attention.

The problem begins when we refuse to examine the feeling and instead allow it to turn into resentment.

When jealousy becomes unhealthy

There is nothing particularly dangerous about thinking,

“I wish I had that too.”

The problem comes when that thought becomes:

“I don’t want them to have it.”

And then becomes:

“I need to make sure they don’t have it.”

This is where jealousy can become destructive.

Someone who feels jealous may begin comparing themselves constantly.

They may start looking for flaws in the other person.

They may minimize another person’s achievements.

They may secretly enjoy their failures.

They may gossip about them.

They may become cold or hostile.

They may even try to sabotage them.

At that point, jealousy is no longer simply an emotion being experienced.

It is becoming behaviour.

And that behaviour can damage friendships, relationships, families and even our own sense of self.

You don’t have to turn jealousy into shame

Perhaps one of the worst things we can do when we feel jealous is immediately attack ourselves for feeling it.

“I’m a terrible person.”

“Why can’t I just be happy for people?”

“What’s wrong with me?”

Shame doesn’t necessarily make the feeling disappear.

Sometimes it simply makes us better at hiding it.

Instead, we can acknowledge it honestly.

“I am happy for this person, but I also wish I had what they have.”

“I love my friend, but seeing her relationship made me realize how lonely I feel.”

“I’m proud of her achievement, but I’m disappointed in where I am right now.”

There is something powerful about being able to tell yourself the truth without immediately judging yourself for it.

Once you understand what you’re feeling, you can decide what to do with it.

So, how do we handle jealousy?

First, acknowledge it.

You don’t have to announce it to everyone around you.

But be honest with yourself.

If you are jealous, admit it privately.

Then ask yourself why.

What exactly triggered the feeling?

What does this person have that you wish you had?

Is the feeling about them, or is it about something missing in your own life?

Are you actually angry with them, or are you disappointed with yourself?

These questions matter because sometimes the person we are jealous of isn’t really the problem. They are simply the person who happened to remind us of something we desperately want.

Then, separate your feelings from your behaviour. You may not be able to prevent the first flash of jealousy but you can decide not to turn it into cruelty.

You can feel jealous without gossiping.

You can feel jealous without undermining someone.

You can feel jealous without hoping they fail.

You can feel jealous and still congratulate them.

And you can feel jealous while also deciding that their success will not stop you from pursuing your own.

Your jealousy does not have to become your identity

I think we sometimes make the mistake of turning temporary emotions into permanent descriptions of ourselves.

You feel jealous once and think:

“Maybe I’m just a jealous person.”

But you are not one emotion.

You are a person experiencing an emotion.

There is a difference.

The goal isn’t to become someone who never envies anyone.

That may not even be realistic.

There will always be someone who has something you want.

Someone will earn more.

Someone will get married before you.

Someone will have children before you.

Someone will travel more.

Someone will become successful in an area where you are struggling.

Someone will receive an opportunity you desperately wanted.

The question isn’t whether you will ever feel jealousy.

The question is what you will do when you do.

Will you allow it to make you bitter?

Will you allow it to make you cruel?

Or will you allow it to show you something about yourself?

Maybe the feeling is telling you that you want more.

Maybe it is telling you that you are tired.

Maybe it is telling you that you need to stop comparing your life to everyone else’s.

Maybe it is telling you that there is a dream you have neglected.

Maybe it is simply reminding you that you are human.

Jealousy does not have to be something we are ashamed of.

But neither should we use “it’s normal” as an excuse to hurt people.

Feeling jealousy is human.

What we choose to do with it is where our character begins to show.

And perhaps the healthiest response is not to pretend we never feel it.

Perhaps it is to be honest enough to say:

“I’m happy for you. And I’m also hoping that one day, it will be my turn.”

Both can be true.

title: Magical Bedtime Story for Kids: The Girl Who Found a Door Under Her Bed
excerpt: Looking for a magical bedtime story for kids that will spark imagination and keep little readers wondering what happens next? Meet Amara, a curious girl who discovers a mysterious door beneath her bed and steps into a magical world where the moon has disappeared.
content:
The Girl Who Found a Door Under Her Bed

At exactly 12:03 a.m., Amara heard someone knock under her bed.

Knock.

She froze.

Knock. Knock.

Amara pulled her blanket up to her nose.

“Mummy?” she whispered.

No answer.

She listened carefully.

The house was quiet.

The fan hummed above her. Rain tapped gently against the window. Somewhere outside, a dog barked once and went silent.

Then—

KNOCK. KNOCK. KNOCK.

This time, Amara knew.

The sound was coming from under her bed.

She slowly sat up.

“Okay,” she whispered to herself. “Maybe it is just a rat.”

Then something under the bed giggled.

Amara's eyes widened.

Rats did not giggle.

She reached for her flashlight.

One foot.

Then the other.

She leaned over the edge of the mattress and shone the light underneath.

Nothing.

Just dust.

Her old school bag.

And…

Amara blinked.

There was a tiny blue door underneath her bed.

She had never seen it before.

It was barely as tall as her hand.

A golden handle sparkled in the middle.

And something was written across it:

AMARA, PLEASE OPEN.

She almost screamed.

Instead, she whispered, “How does it know my name?”

The door knocked again.

Knock. Knock.

Amara should have run to her parents' room.

She knew that.

But curiosity tugged at her like an invisible string.

She reached down.

Her fingers touched the golden handle.

The moment she turned it—

WHOOSH!

A bright blue light exploded from the little doorway.

Amara fell backward.

And the tiny door suddenly became enormous.

It grew.

And grew.

And grew.

Until it was taller than her.

Behind it was not the dusty floor.

It was a forest.

A glowing forest.

Purple flowers floated in the air. Tiny stars danced between the trees. Fireflies formed little golden roads through the darkness.

And standing at the entrance was a rabbit wearing spectacles.

The rabbit looked at Amara.

Amara looked at the rabbit.

The rabbit sighed.

“Finally.”

“You… you can talk?”

“Obviously.”

The rabbit adjusted his spectacles.

“We have been waiting for you for three hundred and twelve years.”

Amara swallowed.

“Why?”

The rabbit pointed deep into the forest.

“Because someone stole the moon.”

Amara stared at him.

“The moon?”

“Yes.”

“The actual moon?”

“The actual moon.”

“But it's outside!”

The rabbit looked embarrassed.

“It was.”

Amara stepped through the door.

Behind her, the bedroom disappeared.

The door slammed shut.

Suddenly, the forest went completely dark.

Something enormous moved between the trees.

The rabbit grabbed Amara's hand.

“Don't make a sound.”

“What is that?”

“I don't know.”

“That doesn't make me feel better!”

A deep growl rolled through the forest.

Then two enormous yellow eyes appeared between the trees.

Amara held her breath.

The creature stepped forward.

It was huge.

Its fur was black as midnight, its ears were longer than Amara's arms, and around its neck hung a necklace made of tiny silver bells.

The rabbit trembled.

“The Moon Keeper.”

The creature stared at Amara.

Then it spoke.

“Why have you come?”

Amara opened her mouth.

Nothing came out.

The Moon Keeper stepped closer.

“You were invited.”

Amara looked at the rabbit.

The rabbit looked away.

“Invited to do what?”

The creature reached into its fur and pulled out a small golden box.

“To return what you took.”

Amara frowned.

“I haven't taken anything!”

The Moon Keeper opened the box.

Inside was a tiny glowing marble.

Amara gasped.

She knew that marble.

She had found it three nights ago behind her grandmother's old cupboard.

She had put it in her pocket.

The rabbit whispered:

“The moon's heart.”

Amara stared at the glowing marble.

“I thought it was just a toy.”

The Moon Keeper nodded.

“That is how the moon disappeared.”

Amara carefully took the marble.

“Where do I put it?”

The creature pointed upward.

There was a giant empty space in the sky.

Amara understood.

She held the moon's heart above her head.

Nothing happened.

She tried again.

Still nothing.

“It's not working!”

The Moon Keeper said quietly,

“Because you are holding it too tightly.”

Amara looked at her hand.

She was squeezing the marble.

She slowly opened her fingers.

The marble floated upward.

Higher.

Higher.

Then.....

BOOM!

A silver light exploded across the sky.

The trees lit up.

The flowers opened.

The fireflies danced.

And far above them, the moon returned.

Whole.

Bright.

Beautiful.

The rabbit cheered.

The Moon Keeper smiled.

“You have learned something important tonight.”

Amara nodded.

“Don't take things that don't belong to me?”

“Partly.”

“Then… what?”

The Moon Keeper pointed toward the glowing moon.

“Sometimes, when you are afraid of losing something, you hold it so tightly that you stop it from becoming what it was meant to be.”

Amara looked at the moon.

She thought about all the things she tried to control.

Her friends.

Her toys.

Her little brother.

Even her parents.

Maybe not everything needed to be held so tightly.

The rabbit cleared his throat.

“Well, that was lovely and emotional.”

Amara smiled.

Then she heard her mother's voice.

“Amara!”

She jumped.

The forest disappeared.

She was back in her bedroom.

Morning sunlight poured through the curtains.

Her mother stood at the doorway.

“Why are you sleeping on the floor?”

Amara looked under her bed.

There was no door.

No forest.

No rabbit.

Nothing.

She laughed nervously.

“I… had a strange dream.”

Her mother smiled.

“Come and eat breakfast.”

Amara climbed onto her bed.

Then she stopped.

Something was sitting on her pillow.

A tiny golden marble.

And beside it was a folded piece of paper.

Amara opened it.

Only four words were written inside:

“See you next moon.”

Amara stared at the message.

Then.....

from underneath her bed

Knock. Knock.

She smiled.

“I'm coming.”

The End… or is it?

title: 5 AI Tools Nigerians Can Use to Start Making Money Online in 2026
excerpt: You don’t need to be an AI expert. Here’s how to turn everyday AI tools into services people will actually pay for.
content:
Artificial intelligence is no longer something that only belongs to big technology companies.

Today, a student with a smartphone and an internet connection can use AI to write content, create designs, produce videos, research ideas and offer digital services to clients.

But there is one important thing to understand:

AI itself does not make you money. What you do with AI can.

Instead of looking for a magical AI app that promises easy money, the smarter approach is to use AI to provide a service that people already need.

Here are five AI tools you can start exploring in 2026.

1. ChatGPT — For Writing, Research and Digital Services

ChatGPT can help with writing, rewriting, brainstorming, research, explanations and many other everyday tasks. It can also work with images and uploaded files, depending on the features available to your account. (OpenAI Help Center⁠)

For Nigerians trying to earn online, this makes it useful for services such as:

  • Blog and article writing

  • Social-media captions

  • Product descriptions

  • CV and resume improvement

  • Research assistance

  • Email writing

  • Content ideas

  • Script writing

How can you make money with it?

Don’t simply tell a client, “I use ChatGPT.”

Instead, sell the finished result.

For example, instead of advertising:

“I use AI to write articles.”

Offer:

“I will write a 1,500-word SEO article for your website.”

AI can help you work faster, but your job is still to check the information, improve the writing and make the final product useful.

2. Canva — Turn AI Into a Design Service

You don’t necessarily need years of graphic-design experience to start learning digital design.

Canva’s Magic Studio includes AI-powered features designed to help people create and work with designs more easily. (Canva⁠)

You can use Canva to create:

  • Social-media posts

  • Flyers

  • YouTube thumbnails

  • Business adverts

  • Event invitations

  • Simple presentations

  • Ebook covers

  • Promotional graphics

Who can pay you?

Small businesses are a good place to start.

A restaurant might need social-media graphics.

A fashion seller might need promotional posts.

An author might need a book cover.

A small business owner might need a flyer for WhatsApp.

Instead of waiting for a big company to hire you, you can start by offering simple design packages to small businesses and individuals.

3. AI Image Generation — Create Visual Content

AI image-generation tools have become much more capable.

For example, ChatGPT Images can now create and edit images from natural-language instructions, including designs with different aspect ratios. (OpenAI Help Center⁠)

That creates opportunities for people who need visual content but don’t know how to create it themselves.

You could offer:

  • Social-media artwork

  • Promotional images

  • Product concepts

  • Posters

  • Blog illustrations

  • YouTube thumbnails

  • Creative advertisements

The key is to remember that clients aren’t paying you because you pressed an AI button.

They’re paying you because you solved a visual problem for them.

4. AI Video Tools — Help Businesses Create Short Videos

Short-form video has become an important part of online marketing.

Many small businesses want videos for TikTok, Instagram Reels and other platforms but don’t have the time or skills to create them consistently.

This creates an opportunity.

You can learn AI-assisted video editing and offer services such as:

  • Short promotional videos

  • TikTok videos

  • Instagram Reels

  • Product videos

  • Captioned videos

  • Simple educational videos

You don’t need to start by offering complicated cinematic productions.

Start with something simple:

“I will create 5 short promotional videos for your business.”

Then build your skills as you get clients.

5. AI + Your Existing Skill

This may actually be the most important one.

You don’t have to become an “AI expert.”

Instead, take something you already know and use AI to make yourself more productive.

For example:

Writer + AI = faster content production

Designer + AI = faster design concepts

Video editor + AI = faster editing workflow

Social-media manager + AI = faster content planning

Student + AI = better research and study assistance

This is where the real opportunity is.

AI becomes your assistant rather than your entire business.

How to Actually Start

Don’t download 30 AI apps and spend three months watching tutorials.

Pick one service.

For example:

“I create social-media posts for small businesses.”

Learn the tools you need.

Create 3–5 sample pieces.

Put those samples somewhere potential clients can see them.

Then start contacting businesses, creators, authors and entrepreneurs who might need your service.

Your first goal shouldn’t be:

“How can I make ₦1 million with AI?”

Your first goal should be:

“How can I get one person to pay me for a useful service?”

Once you can do that repeatedly, you have something you can build on.

The Bottom Line

AI is creating new opportunities, but it isn’t a shortcut to effortless money.

The people most likely to benefit are those who combine AI with something valuable: writing, design, video, research, marketing, customer service or another practical skill.

So don’t chase every new AI tool that appears.

Learn one. Pick one service. Create examples. Find people who need it. Start selling.

That is a much more realistic way for a Nigerian beginner to turn AI into an income-generating skill.

title: My Mirror Reflection
excerpt: I stood before the mirror again today. It said nothing, but somehow it knew. The road has been longer than they promised. The applause never came, the doors did not open on time, and somewhere between…
content:
I stood before the mirror again today. It said nothing, but somehow it knew.

The road has been longer than they promised. The applause never came, the doors did not open on time, and somewhere between trying and surviving, I learned how quietly things can fall apart. Piece by piece. Not enough to make a sound. Just enough to notice.

Still, I keep gathering what remains, pretending I remember where everything belongs. There have been days when silence felt heavier than failure, when rejection arrived so often it began to feel familiar. Yet somehow, I am still here, worn, uncertain, but not gone.

So I told the reflection what I have been telling myself for a while now: This is only a season. Maybe that is faith. Maybe it is denial. Maybe, for now, there is no difference.

I do not know where the good days went, or if they are simply taking the longer road back to me. But I want to believe life has not shown me all its cards yet. That somewhere beyond this tired version of myself, there is still something waiting with my name on it.

Until then, I will keep rebuilding in silence. And if the mirror meets me here again tomorrow, perhaps it will understand.

I was never asking for an easy road.

I was only hoping the road was leading somewhere.

title: The Feeling of Rejection Can Feel Like a Monster
excerpt: You know how it feels to get rejected or betrayed by those you put your full trust in.Betrayals can come from either family or friends. Rejection is heartbreaki…
content:
You know how it feels to get rejected or betrayed by those you put your full trust in.

Betrayals can come from either family or friends. Rejection is heartbreaking when it comes from someone you trust, so does rejection really mean that the person is tired of you or doesn’t want you?

In our everyday lives, we get to hear “no” as an answer. The ability to take that “no” and move on means you’re strong enough.

Rejection doesn’t always mean you’re not good enough. Sometimes, it simply means you’re not the right fit for that particular situation.

Not every rejection is meant to destroy you. Some are simply meant to redirect you.

title: The Daughter of nature
excerpt: Discover the story of a young girl whose deep connection with nature hints at a mysterious destiny. As she grows up hearing tales of the great goddess Ani, her love for the earth, animals, and flowers…
content:
The Mother of Nature, the great goddess Ani, had always wanted to protect the beauty of the earth.

The beauty of the sunset and the sunrise. The trees that danced with the wind. The rivers that carried life, and the animals that roamed freely beneath the open sky.

History has it that she fought so hard to preserve them, even as technology advanced, buildings rose higher and pollution spread across the land.

Some say she disappeared while protecting nature. Others believe she became one with the earth she had spent her life protecting.

But whatever happened to her, her story remained.

And it has always been my favourite.

I do not care how many times my mother tells it or how boring my other siblings find it. I always want to hear it again.

Sometimes, I close my eyes and picture the world Ani once knew.

A world without tall buildings blocking the sunset. A world where trees stood freely, where animals ran across the land and where the sky stretched endlessly above the earth.

I picture it every morning after my devotions, when I stand by my window and watch the sunlight touch the buildings outside.

And at night, before bedtime, I return to the same world in my imagination.

Most times, I take out my picture storybook and compare the animals in its pages with the world I have created in my mind.

I imagine giraffes walking beneath the golden sky, zebras moving across the grasslands and birds flying freely above the trees.

I wonder what it must have been like to live in a world so beautiful.

One day, while helping my mother in the kitchen, I finally asked her.

“Mummy, can you take us to the zoo? I want to see what nature looks like.”

My mother smiled.

“Onwa, you are nature herself. That is why I called you the moon.”

I looked at her.

“The moon?”

“Yes, my child.”

She wiped her hands on her wrapper and turned towards me.

“You were born on the day of the eclipse. The day the moon and the sun seemed to battle for the sky.”

I laughed.

“Mummy, the moon and the sun do not battle.”

“Perhaps not,” she said, smiling. “But I knew there would be something extraordinary about you.”

I did not understand what she meant then.

I was only a child who wanted to see animals outside the pages of a picture book.

But my mother had always told me that I was different.

When I was three, I brought a wounded bird home from school. I had found it lying helplessly on the ground, its little wings unable to carry it into the sky.

I refused to leave it.

I fed it, cared for it and watched over it until it was strong enough to fly again.

My mother said I had cried when it finally left.

I do not remember crying.

But I remember how happy I felt when I saw it spread its wings.

My room looks like a little garden.

I gather flowers, plant them in pots and water them every morning. I love watching new leaves appear and tiny buds open into flowers.

Sometimes, I sit beside my plants and imagine that I am in Ani's world.

A world where nature is not fighting for space.

A world where the earth is allowed to breathe.

I do not know why everything about nature feels so familiar to me.

Why the sunset makes me feel as though I am remembering something I have never seen.

Why the sound of birds makes me want to follow them.

Why I sometimes look at the trees and wonder if they know something I do not.

But perhaps my mother was right.

Perhaps I am nature herself.

Or perhaps, somewhere beneath the stories of the great goddess Ani, there is a part of her that has always lived in me.

title: HOW TO STAY ORGANISED
excerpt: It can get quite overwhelming in our day-to-day activities, with a lot of things fighting for your attention. Staying organised can be a whole job on its own.Yo…
content:
It can get quite overwhelming in our day-to-day activities, with a lot of things fighting for your attention. Staying organised can be a whole job on its own.

You lose track of where things are, stuff gets strewn all over the place and you miss important dates and meetups.

So how do you keep things organised and stay on top of on everything?

Check out these tips to go from scatterbrain to PA precision.

1. Have a place for everything - Clothes, jewellery, books, files, shoes etc. should have their designated place. It's easier to locate them when you need them.

2. Put things back immediately - When you use something, put it back where it's supposed to be. Leaving them about makes your place really scattered.

3. Use digital calendars - Birthdays, anniversaries, lunch/dinner dates, appointments etc. should be scheduled in the Google calendar app or similar.

4. Prepare before hand - Whether you're going to work, Church, interview or a meeting, putting things together a day before, avoids delays in looking for items you'll need for the day.

5. Stick to a routine - Following a daily, weekly or monthly routine can help in maintaining an organised schedule. Repeated patterns often stay in your subconscious and become part of your life.

An organised life is a stress-free life. You stay on top of your game and have things under control. Incorporate these tips and you'll never have to remember where you kept things or if you forgot an important date.

title: The sky was never the problem
excerpt: The Sky Is Big Enough for Two Birds to FlyWhen Funke first started making clothes, she had no customers.Neither did Tomi.They met at a fashion training program,…
content:
The Sky Is Big Enough for Two Birds to Fly

When Funke first started making clothes, she had no customers.

Neither did Tomi.

They met at a fashion training program, became friends almost immediately, and spent hours talking about the businesses they would build someday.

“We’ll both blow,” Tomi would always say.

Funke believed her.

For the first two years, they were genuinely happy for each other.

If Tomi got a big order, Funke will celebrate.

If Funke got featured on someone’s page, Tomi was the first person to repost it.

They shared vendors, referred customers to each other and even complained about the same things.

Then things changed.

Funke’s business started growing faster.

She got more customers. Her page became more popular. People began mentioning her name more often.

And slowly, Tomi stopped celebrating.

Not openly.

She simply became quieter.

She stopped reposting Funke’s work.

When people complimented Funke, she found a way to mention something she was doing better.

“You’re lucky your location is better.”

“Your customers probably have more money.”

“Instagram just favours some people.”

Funke noticed.

But she ignored it.

Until one afternoon, a mutual friend told Funke something Tomi had said.

“She feels like you’re taking all the customers.”

Funke laughed when she heard it.

Taking customers? From who?

But later that night, she couldn't stop thinking about it.

Then she realized something.

Tomi wasn't angry because Funke had done something wrong.

She was angry because Funke’s success had become a mirror.

Every time Funke moved forward, Tomi saw where she thought she should have been.

And perhaps that was the saddest part.

They had started together, but somewhere along the way, friendship had quietly turned into a race.

A few months later, Tomi finally got her big break.

A major client placed a huge order with her.

The kind of order they had both dreamed about when they were starting.

Funke saw the announcement.

She smiled.

Then she sent one message.

“I’m so happy for you. You deserve this.”

Tomi stared at the message for a long time.

Because suddenly, she remembered something they used to say when they were younger.

“The sky is big enough for two birds to fly.”

Maybe it had never been about who would fly higher.

Maybe they had simply forgotten that they could both fly.

There was never a shortage of sky.

Only a shortage of belief that there was enough room for both of them.

title: Man Utd hits new revenue high of £677.6m despite missing European football
excerpt: Manchester United turned in its strongest top-line performance yet for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2026, pulling in £677.6 million in revenue even without a single European fixture on the calendar…
content:
Manchester United turned in its strongest top-line performance yet for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2026, pulling in £677.6 million in revenue even without a single European fixture on the calendar. The club credited disciplined cost-cutting including redundancies among non-football staff and tighter spending controls for flipping last year's operating loss into a £22.6 million operating profit, while adjusted EBITDA rose 18.4% to a record £216.4 million. A third-place Premier League finish helped broadcasting income surge nearly 20%, offsetting softer commercial and matchday numbers tied to fewer home fixtures.

Despite those operational gains, the bottom line still slipped further into the red, with the net loss widening to £43 million as finance costs bit harder. CEO Omar Berrada framed the results as proof the club's business model can hold up even in a down year on the pitch, pointing to fresh sponsorships and the return to Champions League football as tailwinds. Looking ahead, United is guiding for £740-760 million in revenue next season, banking on European competition, continued stadium redevelopment plans, and sustained commercial momentum to close the gap between growing revenue and persistent losses.

title: Before I Was Forgotten
excerpt: Some promises are sincere when they are made and still get lost in the years that follow.
content:
Chapter Three

The Proposal

Before she was anyone's wife, Zainab was a girl who filled notebooks.

She wrote badly, by her own admission long, breathless entries about nothing in particular: the taste of suya from the corner stand, an argument she'd had with her cousin, a line from a khutbah that had stayed with her all week.

But she wrote every day, in a small, round hand, in a green notebook she kept hidden beneath her mattress, not out of shame, but out of a private, fierce sense that it was hers the one thing in the house that belonged to no one else's needs.

She had told Mama, once, that she wanted to teach. Not just any kind of teaching she wanted to teach girls in the village schools who had no one telling them their notebooks mattered.

“Insha'Allah,” Mama had said, in the tone of a woman who had learned not to promise her daughter anything the world hadn't yet promised her.

Ahmad came into her life the ordinary way through an aunt, a suggestion, a visit arranged with tea and careful silences.

He was twenty-eight, soft-spoken, recently returned from his engineering studies, with the kind of seriousness that made him seem older than he was and kinder than most men his age bothered to be.

At their first proper meeting chaperoned, brief, everyone pretending not to listen from the next room he had asked her, unprompted, what she liked to do.

No one had asked Zainab that in a long time.

Suitors asked about cooking, about her family, about how many siblings she had and whether she could manage a household.

Ahmad asked what she liked to do, as though the answer might matter beyond what it could offer him.

“I write,” she said, surprising herself with how quickly it came out, how much she wanted him to know it. “Nothing serious. Just thoughts. And I want to teach, one day. Small girls, the ones nobody expects much from.”

She braced, out of habit, for the polite deflection that usually followed the that's nice that meant that's irrelevant.

Instead, Ahmad nodded slowly, as if turning the idea over with real attention.

“My mother wanted to be a nurse,” he said. “She never got the chance. I used to think, if I ever married, I wouldn't want my wife's chance to disappear the way my mother's did.”

Zainab remembered that sentence for years.

She would return to it later much later the way a person returns to a photograph of themselves happy, trying to locate the exact moment things had begun, so quietly, to change.

He proposed within three months, with her father's blessing and her own eager, unguarded yes.

On their wedding night, after the guests had gone and the henna was still dark on her palms, Ahmad had held her hand and said, “I want you to keep writing, Zainab. Whatever else happens in this life, don't let this house make you forget you had a mind before it.”

She had believed him completely.

She had no reason not to.

What neither of them understood yet—what no one tells a new bride, because perhaps no one fully understands it themselves was that a house doesn't take anything from a woman all at once.

It asks for small things, reasonable things, one at a time:

just this week, just until the baby sleeps through the night, just until things settle, just until.

And a good wife, a loving wife, a woman who has watched her own mother give in the same reasonable way, says yes to each small thing without ever once feeling herself say no to the larger one.

Zainab did not stop writing on her wedding night, or the week after, or even the year after.

The green notebook came with her to Ahmad's house, tucked into the same corner of a drawer, still hers.

She simply, slowly, stopped finding the time.

Some promises get lost, but the story continues.If Zainab's journey resonated with you, please leave a Like and hit Follow to stay with her as Chapter Four unfolds.

title: Valediction at Dusk
excerpt: The fire has burned down to soft ashes,and I’ve worn through the soles of my favorite shoes.Looking back at the messy, beautiful road we took,I can honestly say…
content:
The fire has burned down to soft ashes,

and I’ve worn through the soles of my favorite shoes.

Looking back at the messy, beautiful road we took,

I can honestly say it was fun while it lasted.

There is a quiet car waiting out in the driveway,

its engine humming beneath a heavy sky.

Soon I would take my leave,

slipping through the hall without making a scene.

Please don't wait up or keep the porch lamp on.

Just keep telling our stories to the open room,

and carry a bit of my warmth into tomorrow.

title: THE DREAM BEYOND THE HOOP
excerpt: I may not know everything about basketball, but I know that every dream has a story, and every story deserves to be told.
content:
The basketball hoop stood against the evening sky, its net swaying gently in the breeze.

Liam rested his hands on his hips and watched the sun sink behind the trees. The sky had turned the colour of an old photograph, soft orange fading into pink.

For a moment, he could almost hear the sound of a bouncing basketball.

“Liam! Liam! Take that uniform off before you start playing!”

His mother’s voice.

The laughter of six boys.

The familiar thud of a ball hitting the ground.

He smiled.

“Good old days,” he whispered.

He had been eighteen when those days came to an end.

Before school, after school, and sometimes when they were supposed to be doing their homework, Liam and his friends could always be found with a basketball.

Jade, Ted, Benny, Tommy, Blake, Jack, and Liam.

Seven boys who believed the world belonged to them.

They played on the road outside their homes, on dusty patches of ground, and anywhere they could find a suitable place to throw a ball. A hole in a fence could become a basket. A rusty ring could become a basketball hoop. All they needed was a ball, a little space, and one another.

“Pass it here!” Benny would shout.

“Not if you can't catch it!” Tommy would yell back.

The ball would fly through the air, followed by a chorus of laughter.

Liam could still remember his mother standing at the doorway, shaking her head as he ran past in his school uniform.

“Liam, are you going to play basketball in those clothes again?”

“Just one more game, Mum!”

“One more game? You said that an hour ago!”

He would laugh and run off before she could catch him.

They played as though their lives depended on it.

Perhaps, in a way, they did.

Basketball was more than a game to them. It was the dream that kept them together.

One day, they would become professional players. One day, people would know their names. One day, they would stand on a real court, wearing matching jerseys, with thousands of people cheering for them.

And Tommy always believed they would get there.

“Listen,” he would say whenever one of them complained about losing. “No matter what happens, never give up on your dream. Don't let anyone or anything stop you from succeeding.”

Tommy was the oldest among them, only a year older than the rest, but they treated him like their big brother.

He was the one who knew how to bring everyone together after a bad game. The one who could turn a quarrel into laughter. The one who reminded them why they had started playing in the first place.

And when their dreams finally came within reach, he was the one they needed most.

It was a Sunday morning.

The final tournament was only a few hours away.

The winning team would qualify for the state team, bringing them one step closer to becoming professional basketball players.

Liam stood outside the house, his basketball tucked beneath his arm, while Jack paced beside him.

“Where is Tommy?” Jack asked.

“Still not here,” Liam replied, checking his phone.

Benny called him again.

“Tommy, where are you? We're leaving soon!”

His voice came through the phone, faint but cheerful.

“I'm coming, I'm coming. Give me a few minutes.”

“Your few minutes are always thirty minutes,” Benny complained.

Tommy laughed.

“Relax. I'll see you soon.”

That was the last time they heard his voice.

A few minutes later, Liam's phone rang.

He answered without looking at the screen.

“Hello?”

The voice on the other end was not Tommy's.

“Are you one of Tommy's friends?”

Liam straightened.

“Yes. Who is this?”

There was a pause.

“I'm sorry, but Tommy has been involved in a car accident.”

The basketball slipped from Liam's arm and rolled across the ground.

For a moment, he heard nothing.

Not Jack asking what had happened. Not Benny calling his name. Not the sound of the ball rolling to a stop.

Nothing.

Then he heard himself ask, “Is he okay?”

The answer came quietly.

“He has been taken to the hospital.”

Tommy did not survive.

The news settled over them like a heavy blanket.

They sat together outside the hospital, their jerseys folded beside them, their basketball resting against the wall.

Nobody spoke.

Jack stared at his shoes.

Benny kept rubbing his palms against his trousers.

Liam watched a nurse walk past the doors, hoping she would turn around and tell them they had made a mistake.

They had spent years dreaming about this day.

The final tournament.

The scouts.

The chance to join the state team and take their first real step towards becoming professional basketball players.

Now, none of it mattered.

“What is the point?” Jack whispered.

Liam looked at him.

“What?”

“What's the point of playing without Tommy?”

Nobody answered.

Because they were all thinking the same thing.

They had lost more than a teammate.

They had lost the person who held them together.

By the time Coach Charles arrived at the hospital, the tournament officials had already agreed to postpone the final until the following day.

The other team had been informed.

The boys would have one day to grieve before returning to the court.

Coach Charles found them sitting together, their heads lowered.

He stood in front of them for a long moment.

“Are you boys planning to play tomorrow?”

Nobody responded.

Jack lowered his head.

“We can't, Coach.”

“Why not?”

“Because Tommy is gone.”

Coach Charles sat beside them.

For a while, he said nothing.

Then he looked at Liam.

“Do you remember what Tommy used to say whenever you lost a game?”

Liam swallowed.

His voice came out barely above a whisper.

“Never give up on your dream.”

Coach Charles nodded.

“And do you think he would be happy seeing you give up now?”

Liam looked away.

“He might be watching you tomorrow,” the coach continued. “He might be wishing you would make him proud.”

Benny wiped his face with the back of his hand.

Coach Charles leaned forward.

“You cannot bring Tommy back. But you can carry what he gave you. You can carry his courage, his dedication, and his belief in this team.”

He looked at each of them.

“So, what are you going to do?”

Liam stared at the basketball resting beside his foot.

Then he picked it up.

“We're going to play.”

The next afternoon, the court was loud.

The final tournament had arrived.

The crowd cheered as the teams walked in.

Liam looked at the empty space beside him where Tommy should have been standing.

For a moment, his chest tightened.

Then he looked at his teammates.

Jade.

Ted.

Benny.

Jack.

Blake.

They were all there.

And Tommy was with them in the only way he could be.

The whistle blew.

The game began.

The ball moved from one player to another.

Liam ran across the court, his trainers squeaking against the floor. His heart hammered against his ribs.

“Pass!” Benny shouted.

Liam threw the ball.

Benny caught it and shot.

The ball struck the rim.

The crowd gasped.

Then it dropped through the net.

“YES!”

They shouted together.

Liam smiled, but there was no time to celebrate.

The opposing team came charging towards them.

They defended.

They ran.

They passed.

They fell.

And every time one of them stumbled, another reached out a hand.

“Get up!” Jack shouted.

“We've got this!”

“Come on, boys!”

The final minutes were the hardest.

Their opponents were close behind.

Liam could hear Coach Charles shouting from the sidelines.

“Keep moving! Keep your eyes on the ball!”

The scoreboard showed only a few seconds remaining.

Liam held the ball.

He looked at the hoop.

Then he heard Tommy's voice in his memory.

No matter what happens, never give up on your dream.

Liam took the shot.

The ball rose into the air.

For one breath, the entire court went silent.

Then it dropped through the net.

The final whistle blew.

They had won.

The boys rushed towards one another, shouting and laughing, tears running down their faces.

They had qualified for the state team.

They had taken the first step towards the dream they had shared with Tommy.

Liam looked up at the sky.

“That's for you, Tommy.”

Years passed.

The boys grew older.

The dusty road outside their homes became a distant memory. The little holes they once used as baskets were replaced by real courts, real hoops, and real games.

And the dream they had once whispered about became their reality.

The boys had grown into the players they once dreamed of becoming. They travelled together, played in tournaments and stood on real courts wearing the jersey they had once imagined

But no matter how many games they won, they never forgot the boy who had once thrown a ball to them on a dusty road.

“Dad?”

Liam blinked.

His son stood beside him, holding a basketball.

“Dad, why are you staring at the hoop like that? Aren't we playing today?”

Liam looked down at him.

Then he smiled.

“We are.”

His son grinned.

“Then come on!”

“Give me a minute.”

His son sighed dramatically.

“You always say that.”

Liam laughed.

The words took him back to a Sunday morning, to a boy who had once said the same thing.

He looked at the hoop again.

“Tommy,” he whispered.

“Dad?”

“Have I ever told you about Tommy?”

His son rolled his eyes.

“A thousand times.”

“A thousand?”

“Maybe more.”

Liam chuckled.

“And you're not tired of hearing it?”

His son shook his head.

“No. I like hearing about him.”

“Why?”

“Because whenever you tell me about Tommy, you smile differently.”

Liam looked at his son.

The boy continued.

“He must have been a really good friend.”

“He was.”

“Was he the reason you became a basketball player?”

Liam glanced at the hoop.

“He was one of the reasons.”

His son bounced the ball once.

“Then I want to hear the story again.”

Liam laughed softly.

“Again?”

“Again.”

He looked towards the fading sunlight.

For years, he had wondered what Tommy would have thought if he could see the life they had built.

Would he have cheered from the sidelines?

Would he have shouted at them to keep moving?

Would he have smiled when they finally won?

Liam would never know.

But perhaps that was all right.

Some people leave before we are ready.

Some dreams are achieved without the people who first believed in them.

And some memories never grow old.

Liam reached for the basketball.

“Come on, son.”

His son smiled.

“Race you to the court!”

He ran ahead.

Liam followed, laughing.

Above them, the basketball hoop stood against the evening sky.

And for a moment, Liam could almost hear seven boys laughing again.

One of them was missing.

But his dream was still alive.

And it was being passed on.

title: Are Smart Glasses Finally Replacing Our Phone Addiction?
excerpt: For over a decade, consumer technology has demanded one physical concession from us: tilting our necks down and staring into an illuminated glass rectangle. When tech giants first attempted to break t…
content:
For over a decade, consumer technology has demanded one physical concession from us: tilting our necks down and staring into an illuminated glass rectangle. When tech giants first attempted to break that habit, their solution was immersion—bulky virtual reality headsets and heavy augmented-reality goggles. Instead of freeing people from screens, those early devices strapped screens directly over their eyes.

Today, a quiet pivot is reshaping ambient computing. Instead of clunky visors, the hardware looks nearly indistinguishable from classic designer eyewear. Driven by the explosive adoption of camera-equipped frames and lightweight voice interfaces, "screenless" smart glasses are establishing themselves not as futuristic novelties, but as the first practical alternative to the smartphone interface.

Stripping the Screen to Fix the Habit

The most radical design choice behind recent smart glasses is what manufacturers chose to leave out: an actual display.

Early iterations like Google Glass flopped partly because floating digital prisms felt intrusive, dorky, and visually exhausting. Modern audio-and-vision frames—pioneered at scale by Meta’s partnership with EssilorLuxottica (Ray-Ban and Oakley) and followed by players across Google's Android XR ecosystem—swap optics for multimodal sensors:

  • Micro-Cameras: Miniature sensors embedded in the hinge capture high-resolution photos and video from your natural perspective.

  • Open-Ear Spatial Speakers: Directional audio drives sound directly into your ear canals without sealing off the outside world, eliminating the social isolation of noise-canceling earbuds.

  • Multimodal AI Processors: An onboard assistant that doesn't just listen, but "sees" what you see in real time.

By removing the display entirely, hardware makers eliminated thermal throttling, solved the terrible battery drain of micro-OLEDs, and preserved lightweight, all-day aesthetics. Most importantly, it dismantled the trap of the infinite scroll.

Everyday Relatability: Ambient Utility over Endless Feeds

Smartphones are friction-heavy paradoxes. You unlock your phone to set a cooking timer, see an unread badge on Instagram, and emerge twenty minutes later wondering what you originally intended to do. Screenless smart glasses operate on the opposite premise: low-latency ambient utility.

  • Hands-Free Cooking & Tasks: Instead of smearing garlic sauce over a glass screen to read a recipe, you look at ingredients on your counter and ask the assistant to walk you through prep steps verbally.

  • Real-World Translation: Walking through an unfamiliar neighborhood abroad, you can look at street signs or train timetables and hear live, whisper-level translations without breaking stride.

  • Preserving Moments Naturally: Traditional smartphones force you to view birthdays, concerts, and family gatherings through a phone viewfinder. Tap a frame button or speak a command, and the glasses record the memory while you remain fully present with your eyes on the moment.

The Friction Ahead: Privacy and Social Etiquette

Despite their convenience, the road to replacing smartphones isn't without significant hurdles. Societal trust remains a massive barrier.

Subtle recording indicator LEDs are intended to warn bystanders, yet privacy advocates and casual observers continue to express unease about cameras constantly facing the public. Venues ranging from gyms to intimate venues have introduced bans on smart eyewear to curb involuntary surveillance.

Furthermore, voice is inherently public. Dictating sensitive work emails or managing banking details on a crowded commuter train exposes personal data to anyone sitting next to you, which means phones will still serve as the secure transaction hub for the foreseeable future.

Looking Up Instead of Down

Smart glasses might not wipe smartphones off the map overnight, but they are succeeding where bulky headsets failed: nudging our attention back outward. By offloading mundane interactions—capturing a photo, asking for directions, reading a quick text—to a voice-driven frame, we reclaim the simple habit of keeping our heads up. In an era characterized by chronic screen fatigue, that shift alone might make them the defining wearable of the decade.

title: YOUR JOB IS NOT SUPPOSED TO BE YOUR ENTIRE PERSONALITY
excerpt: Who Are You When the Job Title Is Removed?
content:
Someone asks "so, what do you do?" and you answer instantly, easily, maybe even proudly. Then someone asks "so, what do you do for fun?" and there's a pause. A slightly too long pause. You mention something you used to enjoy, in past tense, before you can stop yourself.

If that pause felt uncomfortably familiar, this is for you. Ride with me.

THE COMPLIMENT THAT BECAME A CAGE

At some point, being "hardworking" and "dedicated" stopped being a description of your effort and started becoming the entire description of you. People praised the long hours. The promotions validated the exhaustion. Somewhere in there, the job stopped being something you do and became the main thing you are, the answer to every question about your identity, your worth, your Sunday night mood. Nobody forces this shift directly. It happens gradually, through every time your value at work got mistaken for your value as a person, and you let the mistake stand because it felt good in the moment.

WHY THIS FEELS SAFER THAN IT ACTUALLY IS

Work is measurable in a way that most of life is not. You get a title, a salary, a performance review, a clear "yes, you're doing well" or "no, you need to improve." Relationships, hobbies, rest, none of that comes with a scorecard. So it's tempting to pour your identity into the one area that gives you clean, regular feedback, even if that area was never built to hold your entire sense of self. The problem is that anything measured that precisely can also be taken away that precisely, a layoff, a bad quarter, a company restructuring and if that's where your whole identity lived, it goes down with it.

WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THE JOB BECOMES THE WHOLE PERSON

Watch what occurs when someone whose entire personality is their career loses the job, or even just goes on leave. The silence is unbearable. The identity crisis is real, not dramatic because there genuinely is not much else there to fall back on. Not because they are shallow people, but because every other part of them got quietly deprioritized for years in favour of the one that paid. That's the actual cost of letting a job become your whole personality, not burnout alone, but a self that is dangerously thin outside of one context.

THE UNCOMFORTABLE TRUTH YOU'RE RUNNING FROM

Some of the people most praised for their work ethic are, underneath it, avoiding something, a relationship that needs attention, a hobby they are scared they have lost the ability to enjoy, a version of themselves that only exists in unstructured time they don't know how to fill anymore. Overworking can look like ambition from the outside while functioning as a hiding place on the inside.

It's worth asking, honestly: is the job the thing you love, or is it the thing you retreated into because it was easier to master than everything else?

WHAT REBUILDING AN IDENTIFY OUTSIDE WORK ACTUALLY LOOKS LIKE

Not a five step "work life balance" plan. Smaller and more specific than that:

- Reclaim one interest with no productivity attached to it: Something you're allowed to be mediocre at, purely because it's enjoyable, not because it builds a skill or a brand.

- Notice what you talk about when you are not talking about work.: If the honest answer is "nothing, really," that's the actual gap to look at.

- Let rest be unproductive on purpose: Not recovery so you can perform better at work tomorrow, rest as its own point, with no return expected.

None of this makes you less driven. It just means your drive stops being the only room you live in.

SO WHO ARE YOU, REALLY?

Try answering the "what do you do for fun" question again, slowly, without mentioning work at all. If the answer still doesn't come easily, that's not a personal failure, it's just useful information about where the rebuilding actually needs to start.

Don't forget to share your thoughts with us in the comments.
