title: Things Nobody Warns You About When You Turn 20
excerpt: Growing up sounded a lot more exciting when we were 15.
content:
Turning 20 sounds like a big deal.

You've officially left your teenage years behind, so naturally, you expect to become this mature, organized adult who knows exactly what they're doing.

Then you turn 20.

And somehow, you're still calling your mum to ask what to cook. 😭

Nobody really tells you that your twenties aren't going to feel as glamorous as they looked when you were younger. There's no magical moment where you suddenly understand life, become financially stable and stop making questionable decisions.

If anything, you just get better at saying, “I'll figure it out.” 😂

Here are a few things nobody warns you about.

1. You don't actually feel like an adult

Remember when you were 15 and thought people in their twenties had everything figured out?

Yeah... whoever lied to us deserves an explanation.

You turn 20 and realize you're still trying to understand yourself, your emotions, your career, your finances and why your phone battery disappears so quickly.

You're technically an adult, but sometimes you still need someone to tell you, “Don't worry, you'll be fine.”

And that's okay.

Being 20 doesn't mean having all the answers. It just means you're old enough to start discovering them.

2. Everyone suddenly looks like they're doing better than you

This one is dangerous.

You open Instagram and someone is travelling.

You check WhatsApp and someone just got engaged.

You go on TikTok and someone your age is making enough money to buy a house.

Meanwhile, you're calculating whether you can afford shawarma this week. 😭

And suddenly you're wondering:

“Am I doing something wrong?”

Probably not.

You're just comparing your everyday life to everybody else's highlight reel.

Someone else's progress doesn't mean you're behind.

Sometimes you're exactly where you're supposed to be—you just wish your bank account would get the memo. 😂

3. You suddenly want to travel everywhere

You enter your twenties thinking, “This is my time! I'm going to travel, go on vacations, take cute pictures and make unforgettable memories.” ✈️🌴

And honestly? You should!

The only small problem is that your bank account did not receive the same memo. 😭

You want to visit Dubai, Cape Town, Zanzibar, London... meanwhile, you open your banking app and see ₦2,847.36 staring back at you.

At this point, even Google Maps is judging you.

You start saving vacation pictures on Pinterest like you're planning a world tour, but your actual travel itinerary is:

Home → School → Home. 😂

Nobody warns you that your twenties come with big dreams and very questionable finances.

And that's okay. You don't have to have the money for every dream right now.

Just don't let the pressure to “live your best life” make you spend money you don't have trying to prove that you're living it.

The vacation can wait. Your bank account is already on life support. 😭

4. Friendships start changing

Nobody warns you that some friendships will simply... expire.

One day you're talking every single day.

Then university gets busy. Life happens. Someone moves away. Someone gets a new relationship. Someone becomes distant.

And before you know it, you're staring at their contact thinking:

“Wait... when did we stop being friends?”

Sometimes there's no dramatic fight.

You just grow into different people.

And honestly, that's one of the hardest parts of growing up—learning that loving someone doesn't always mean they'll remain part of your life forever.

5. Money becomes painfully real

When you were younger, getting ₦5,000 felt like winning the lottery.

Now?

₦5,000 can disappear before you even leave the house. 😭

Transport.

Food.

Data.

School expenses.

Something you suddenly “need.”

And somehow your money is gone.

Nobody really prepares you for the reality of becoming financially responsible.

You start realizing that being an adult is basically looking at your account balance and asking:

“What happened here?” 😭

6. You might start questioning everything you're doing

You can be in university and still wonder if you chose the right course.

You can love what you're studying and still worry about your future.

You can have a career plan today and completely rethink it next month.

And that's normal.

You're allowed to change your mind.

You're allowed to discover that the dream you had at 16 isn't the dream you want at 20.

You don't have to have your entire life mapped out just because you turned 20.

7. Relationships start looking different

When you're younger, love can seem very simple.

I like you. You like me. Great. Let's date.

Then adulthood enters the chat. 😭

Suddenly you're thinking about communication, emotional maturity, compatibility, finances, boundaries, trust and whether this person actually brings peace into your life.

You start realizing that being in love isn't the same thing as being in a healthy relationship.

And you also realize that being single isn't the tragedy social media sometimes makes it look like.

Sometimes you're not lonely.

You're just enjoying your peace.

8. You start caring less about impressing everyone

This one sneaks up on you.

You start realizing you don't actually have the energy to explain yourself to everybody.

You don't want to attend every event.

You don't want to maintain every friendship.

You don't want to dress a certain way just because everyone else is doing it.

You slowly start asking:

“Do I actually like this, or do I just want people to like me?”

And honestly, that's a beautiful question to start asking.

Because your twenties are not just about building a career or making money.

They're also about figuring out who you are when nobody is watching.

9. You will have days when you feel completely lost

And this is probably the one nobody tells you enough.

Some days you'll feel like you're doing amazing.

Other days you'll wonder whether you're wasting your life.

You'll have moments where you feel confident about your future and other moments where you have absolutely no idea what you're doing.

You might cry.

You might change your plans.

You might make mistakes.

You might start over.

That's life.

You're not supposed to have everything figured out at 20.

You're supposed to be figuring it out.

So if you're 20 and you're currently wondering whether everybody else received an adulthood instruction manual that somehow didn't reach you...

Don't worry.

They didn't. 😭😂

We're all just out here paying bills, making mistakes, falling in love, losing friends, chasing dreams and occasionally pretending we know what we're doing.

And maybe that's what your twenties are really about.

Not having everything figured out.

Just slowly becoming someone you're proud to be.

So, what's one thing nobody warned you about before you turned 20? 👀

title: The Roadmap to Senior Software Engineer: Beyond Writing Code
excerpt: What truly separates senior engineers from junior and mid-level developers: system design intuition, trade-off analysis, technical writing, and team leverage.
content:
The Roadmap to Senior Software Engineer: Beyond Writing Code

Early in a software engineering career, advancement is driven by technical proficiency: learning syntax, mastering frameworks, and closing tickets rapidly. However, reaching Senior, Staff, and Principal levels requires a fundamental shift in perspective from individual execution to organizational leverage and strategic impact.

1. Mastering the Art of Trade-Off Analysis

Junior engineers look for the "perfect" solution; senior engineers understand that in software architecture, there are no solutions—only trade-offs. Every technical decision balances speed, scalability, maintainability, cost, and developer experience.

When proposing a new technology or architecture, senior engineers always articulate:

  • What are the operational costs of maintaining this service in 3 years?
  • How will this impact deployment complexity and onboarding time for new team members?
  • What is the failure mode when this system undergoes a 10x traffic spike?

2. High-Impact Technical Writing (RFCs & ADRs)

Code is read far more often than it is written, and architectural consensus is forged through clear written communication. Senior engineers author Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) and Request for Comments (RFCs) that align cross-functional teams before writing a single line of production code.

3. Mentorship and Force Multiplication

Your impact as an engineer is capped if you only measure the code you personally commit. Senior engineers act as force multipliers by:

  • Conducting empathetic, educational code reviews that elevate team standards.
  • Refactoring brittle CI/CD pipelines and developer tooling to save hundreds of collective engineering hours.
  • Mentoring junior engineers into confident, independent problem solvers.

4. Managing Technical Debt Pragmatically

Not all technical debt is bad; strategic debt allows startups to validate product-market fit quickly. Senior engineers know when to move fast with pragmatic compromises and when to pause feature velocity to refactor mission-critical core abstractions.

title: Why Does Social Media Know What I’m Thinking About?
excerpt: Did My Phone Hear Me, or Am I Just Being Paranoid?
content:
I don't know if it's just me, but sometimes social media feels like it's inside my head.

I'll be thinking about something completely random, and later I'm seeing it on Instagram or TikTok. Sometimes it's so specific that I start wondering if I somehow searched for it without remembering.

It can feel creepy, but there are a few reasons this happens.

Social media platforms learn from almost everything we do on them. What we search for, the videos we watch till the end, the posts we like, the accounts we visit, what we skip, and even how long we pause on something can help shape what appears on our feed.

So maybe you didn't search for that particular thing today. Maybe the app already had enough clues from your previous activity to know you'd probably be interested in it.

There's also the “frequency illusion.” Once something is on your mind, you start noticing it everywhere. You might have scrolled past the same type of content several times before and barely noticed. But because you were just thinking about it, suddenly it feels like the internet is following your thoughts.

And then there's the question everyone asks: "But what if my phone was listening?”

Phones and apps can use microphones when you give them permission, but seeing an ad or video about something you just talked about isn't proof that your microphone was listening to that conversation.

Honestly, I think the more unsettling explanation is simpler: we've given social media so much information about ourselves that sometimes it doesn't need to listen. It can already make a pretty good guess.

And somehow, that's still a little creepy.

title: I Was Told I Was A Girl
excerpt: # The Day I Was Told I Was a GirlI was sixteen the year I started watching Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala.I don't remember exactly when it started. I just remember not bei…
content:
# The Day I Was Told I Was a Girl

I was sixteen the year I started watching Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala.

I don't remember exactly when it started. I just remember not being able to stop. Here was a woman standing in rooms full of men, moving through global finance like it belonged to her, and something in me rose up to meet that. I was thrilled in a way I didn't have words for yet. I wanted to be part of whatever she was part of. Not finance necessarily, not her exact path, just that momentum, that refusal to shrink. Honestly, I still do. Even now.

Then came that Sunday.

It was a beautiful evening, the kind Ogidi gives you sometimes like an apology for the rest of the week. Chilly, with the mango tree outside our house swaying a little. My aunt had come visiting and was sitting across from my father in our sitting room. I wasn't part of their conversation. I was just close enough to hear it.

*Are you preparing your daughters for marriage?* she asked him.

My father gave that awkward laugh people give when a question catches them off guard, and said no, they wanted to go to university.

*University,* she said, almost like the word itself offended her. *You are training them for another man. Marry them off. For now. If they reach their husband's house, they can go to school if they want.*

I heard all of it. And somehow I understood, in that way you understand things said past you and not to you, that this wasn't really about university. It was about what my father actually believed. That women couldn't be trusted with ambition. That whatever brilliance existed in his daughters was nice to have but not something to build a future on. I was the most brilliant of my siblings. It didn't matter. He had already decided, somewhere deep down, that women were restless, unserious, up to no good if left unsupervised by marriage. No report card was undoing that.

I don't remember arguing back. I don't think I even had the words yet for what I would have been arguing for. I just remember standing there while something in the house quietly rearranged itself without asking me.

My aunt wasn't saying anything new that evening, honestly. She was just saying out loud what a lot of people around me already believed and hadn't bothered saying to my face yet. That a girl's education came with conditions. That ambition was something to pause, not something to chase. That the real destination — the "for now" — was someone else's house, someone else's name, someone else's permission to become anything more.

I still think about Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala a lot, and I think those two moments live side by side in me for a reason. One woman showing me what was possible. One conversation, on one ordinary Sunday, trying to convince me it wasn't possible for someone like me. I didn't choose between them on purpose. But looking back, I know which one I held onto tighter.

I want to be clear about something. I'm not writing this as a feminist making some grand statement. And I'm not writing this against marriage either — I don't think there's anything small about the life my aunt was describing. I'm writing it as a young woman who was told, plainly, in her own sitting room, that she had no right to dream because she was only but a girl — and who has spent every year since trying to prove that wrong.

I'm still proving it. Every degree I've earned is, in some way, a receipt. Proof I keep collecting to put out there — to myself, to anyone who still needs convincing — that I actually have a spot in the grand scheme of things. Every essay I write, every naira I earn from my own words, every choice I make on my own terms is part of that same proof. My father laughed that Sunday, unsure, caught somewhere between what his sister expected of him and what I might actually become. I still think about that laugh sometimes. How it held both. How it hadn't decided yet.

I'd like to think I'm still deciding it for him.

title: The Developer's Guide to Systematic Prompt Engineering & LLM Orchestration
excerpt: Learn how to structure deterministic prompts, utilize few-shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, and implement structured JSON output enforcement in production.
content:
The Developer's Guide to Systematic Prompt Engineering & LLM Orchestration

Prompt engineering is often misunderstood as casual guesswork. In software engineering, prompt design is a disciplined interface specification between probabilistic models and deterministic codebases.

Core Principles of Robust Prompt Architecture

1. Clear Role, Context, and Delimited Constraints

LLMs attend heavily to structural boundaries. Use XML or Markdown tags to cleanly separate instructions, background context, reference data, and user input:

<system_instructions>
You are an expert PostgreSQL DBA reviewing SQL queries for security and indexing optimizations.
Analyze the provided SQL query and output only a structured JSON object.
</system_instructions>

<constraints>
- Never output explanatory conversational markdown outside the JSON block.
- Validate that all table joins have corresponding foreign key index recommendations.
</constraints>

<user_input>
{{QUERY_INPUT}}
</user_input>

2. Few-Shot Demonstration

Providing 2–3 high-quality input/output pairs dramatically reduces variance and guides the model toward the exact schema format you expect:

Input: "Fix broken button in mobile Safari" -> Category: "Bug", Severity: "High", Area: "Frontend"
Input: "Update privacy policy date" -> Category: "Chore", Severity: "Low", Area: "Compliance"

3. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Reasoning

For complex logic, arithmetic, or code analysis, instruct the model to think through steps inside a scratchpad tag before generating the final output. This significantly boosts reasoning accuracy on multi-step problems.

Enforcing Structured JSON Outputs

Modern LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini) offer native Structured Outputs with JSON Schema enforcement. Always provide an explicit schema definition to guarantee that your backend JSON parser never throws runtime syntax errors.

title: Web Security Fundamentals: Hardening Modern Full-Stack Applications Against Attacks
excerpt: A practical guide to mitigating the OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities: Content Security Policy (CSP), Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), SQL Injection, and secure session management.
content:
Web Security Fundamentals: Hardening Modern Full-Stack Applications Against Attacks

Security is not an afterthought to bolt on before release; it is a fundamental architectural requirement. Understanding modern threat vectors and defense-in-depth methodologies ensures your applications withstand automated scanners and determined adversaries.

1. Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Prevention

XSS occurs when malicious actors inject arbitrary JavaScript into web pages viewed by other users, allowing attackers to steal session cookies, capture keystrokes, or perform actions on behalf of the victim.

Defenses:

  • Context-Aware Output Encoding: Never inject unsanitized HTML directly via dangerouslySetInnerHTML or v-html. Always pass user input through verified sanitizers like DOMPurify.
  • Robust Content Security Policy (CSP): Restrict which script sources and inline scripts the browser is permitted to execute:
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://trusted-cdn.com; object-src 'none';

2. SQL Injection (SQLi) Elimination

SQL Injection remains among the most destructive vulnerabilities, allowing attackers to bypass authentication, read confidential tables, or destroy databases. The remedy is absolute: never concatenate user strings into SQL queries. Always use parameterized queries or trusted ORMs.

// ❌ DANGEROUS: Susceptible to SQL Injection
const query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + req.body.email + "'";

// ✅ SECURE: Parameterized query ensures input is treated purely as data
const query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1";
await pool.query(query, [req.body.email]);

3. Secure Cookie and Session Management

Authentication tokens stored in localStorage are completely exposed to any XSS payload. Secure your sessions using HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies:

// Setting hardened authentication cookies in Next.js / Express
cookies().set({
  name: "session_token",
  value: token,
  httpOnly: true, // Prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie
  secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production", // Transmitted only over HTTPS
  sameSite: "lax", // Protects against Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
  path: "/",
  maxAge: 60 * 60 * 24 * 7, // 7 days
});

4. Rate Limiting and Brute-Force Protection

Protect public authentication endpoints (login, password reset, OTP verification) with IP-based and user-based token bucket rate limiters (e.g. Upstash Redis or memory-cache limiters) to thwart automated credential stuffing attacks.

title: The Girl Who Borrowed Five Minutes From Tomorrow | Magical Bedtime Story for Kids
excerpt:
The Girl Who Borrowed Five Minutes From Tomorrow is a magical bedtime story for kids about Maya, a curious girl who discovers that borrowing five minutes from the future comes with a price. Her journey takes her into a mysterious world of clocks, lost time, and an unexpected friendship.

The story gently reminds children that time is precious. Instead of always wishing for more time, we should learn to appreciate the moments we already have, especially the moments we share with the people we love.

Key takeaway: Sometimes, five ordinary minutes with someone we love can become a memory we treasure forever.
content:
The Girl Who Borrowed Five Minutes From Tomorrow

Maya was always late.

Not a little late.

Very late.

Late for school.

Late for breakfast.

Late for church.

Late even when her mother told her, “Maya, we are leaving in five minutes,” and she replied, “Okay!” while still looking for the other half of her shoe.

One Tuesday morning, she was sitting on her bed, trying to finish a drawing.

It was a picture of her and her grandmother sitting under the old mango tree behind their house.

Maya had been drawing it for days.

She wanted to give it to Grandma before she left for her trip the next morning.

But the clock was moving too quickly.

7:41.

Her school bus came at 7:45.

Maya looked at the drawing.

One corner was still unfinished.

“Just five more minutes,” she whispered.

From the hallway, her mother shouted,

“Maya!”

“I'm coming!”

“Maya!”

“I said I'm coming!”

She looked at the clock again.

7:43.

Her heart sank.

“I just need five minutes.”

She squeezed her eyes shut.

“I wish I could borrow five minutes from tomorrow.”

The room went quiet.

Maya opened one eye.

Nothing.

She laughed at herself.

“See? Even my wishes are late.”

She picked up her pencil.

Then she heard a tiny tick.

Not from the wall clock.

From underneath her bed.

Maya slowly leaned down.

There, hidden in the darkness, was a small silver alarm clock.

She had never seen it before.

Its hands were spinning backward.

Then it stopped.

The clock displayed:

TOMORROW — 7:43

Maya stared at it.

“What?”

The little clock gave a soft ding.

A piece of paper popped out of its side.

Maya picked it up.

There were only five words written on it:

YOU MAY HAVE FIVE MINUTES.

Maya's mouth dropped open.

“Seriously?”

The clock ticked once.

Maya grabbed her pencil.

And suddenly, everything around her stopped.

The fan froze.

The curtains stopped moving.

Even the sound of her mother's voice disappeared.

Maya looked at the clock.

Five minutes.

She smiled.

She finished the drawing.

She added the mango tree.

Grandma's earrings.

Her yellow dress.

And a tiny bird sitting on one of the branches.

Then she signed her name.

MAYA.

The moment she finished, everything started moving again.

The fan spun.

The curtains moved.

Her mother's voice returned.

“MAYA! THE BUS IS HERE!”

Maya grabbed her bag and ran.

She made it onto the bus just in time.

She smiled all the way to school.

She had done it.

She had borrowed five minutes from tomorrow.

Easy.

Or so she thought.

The next morning, Maya woke up feeling strange.

She looked at the clock.

7:40.

She jumped out of bed.

“I'm early!”

She brushed her teeth.

She got dressed.

She even found both shoes without crying.

Then she remembered.

Today was the day Grandma was leaving.

Maya ran downstairs.

Grandma was sitting at the dining table, drinking tea.

Maya handed her the drawing.

Grandma looked at it.

For a moment, she didn't say anything.

Then her eyes became shiny.

“Oh, Maya.”

She pulled Maya into a hug.

“This is beautiful.”

Maya smiled.

“I made it for you.”

Grandma kissed her forehead.

“I'll keep it forever.”

Maya hugged her tighter.

Then she noticed something strange.

Grandma was staring at the clock.

Her smile disappeared.

“What is it?” Maya asked.

Grandma pointed at the wall clock.

7:43.

Maya's stomach dropped.

“What?”

Grandma whispered,

“It's 7:43.”

“So?”

Grandma looked at her.

“I've been seeing that time everywhere this morning.”

Maya said nothing.

Grandma stood up.

She walked toward the window.

Then she suddenly stopped.

“Maya…”

“Yes?”

“Did you ask tomorrow for something?”

Maya's heart began beating faster.

“How do you know?”

Grandma turned around.

Because she wasn't smiling anymore.

“Because,” she said quietly, “tomorrow doesn't like lending things.”

Before Maya could answer, the lights went out.

The house became silent.

Then the little silver clock under Maya's bed began ringing.

DING.

DING.

DING.

Maya ran upstairs.

She pulled the clock out.

The screen had changed.

It no longer said:

TOMORROW — 7:43

It said:

DEBT DUE.

Maya's fingers went cold.

“What debt?”

A tiny piece of paper slipped out.

She opened it.

This time, there were six words.

You borrowed five minutes. Someone must lose them.

Maya stared at the message.

“No.”

The clock ticked.

“No, no, no.”

She grabbed it.

“Give them back!”

Nothing happened.

She shook it.

“Give them back!”

Suddenly, the clock began glowing.

A bright light filled the room.

And Maya heard a voice.

Not her mother's.

Not Grandma's.

A voice that sounded like hundreds of clocks ticking at once.

“Five minutes cannot disappear.”

Maya whispered,

“Then where did they go?”

The voice answered:

“Tomorrow.”

That night, Maya couldn't sleep.

She kept thinking about the message.

Someone must lose them.

At exactly midnight, she heard footsteps in the hallway.

She opened her bedroom door.

Grandma was standing there.

But something was wrong.

Grandma looked confused.

“Maya?”

“Yes?”

“What day is it?”

“Wednesday.”

Grandma frowned.

“No.”

She looked at her hands.

“I was supposed to leave yesterday.”

Maya's heart stopped.

“What?”

Grandma looked at her.

“I already said goodbye to you.”

Maya shook her head.

“No, Grandma. You haven't left yet.”

Grandma stared at her.

Then she smiled sadly.

“I think I know what happened.”

Maya's eyes filled with tears.

“What?”

“You borrowed five minutes from tomorrow.”

Grandma touched her cheek.

“And now tomorrow is missing five minutes.”

Maya swallowed.

“Can we give them back?”

Grandma nodded.

“But you have to find them.”

“Where?”

Grandma pointed toward the window.

“Where else would lost time go?”

Outside, the moon was shining.

And somewhere beyond the clouds, a clock was ticking.

Maya climbed onto the roof.

She had no idea how she got there.

She only knew she had to fix what she had done.

Above her was a sky filled with stars.

Then she saw it.

A tiny golden door floating in the air.

Maya reached for it.

The door opened.

Behind it was tomorrow.

Not a place.

Not a day.

A strange, endless hallway filled with clocks.

Hundreds of them.

Thousands.

Some were moving forward.

Some were moving backward.

Some had no hands at all.

At the end of the hallway stood a little boy.

He looked about Maya's age.

He was holding a broken clock.

“You took my five minutes,” he said.

Maya's eyes widened.

“I didn't know.”

“I know.”

“I'm sorry.”

The boy looked at her.

“I waited for you.”

“For me?”

He nodded.

“I needed those five minutes to say goodbye to someone.”

Maya's heart sank.

“Who?”

“My grandmother.”

Maya looked at the floor.

“I'm really sorry.”

The boy smiled a little.

“Then give them back.”

Maya held out her hands.

“I don't have them.”

The boy pointed at her.

“You do.”

Maya looked down.

The drawing.

She was still holding it.

The picture of her and Grandma under the mango tree.

The boy smiled.

“You used the five minutes to make that.”

Maya understood.

The five minutes weren't inside the clock.

They were inside the memory she had created.

She held the drawing out.

The little boy touched it.

The picture began to glow.

Five tiny golden sparks floated out of the paper.

One.

Two.

Three.

Four.

Five.

They flew into the hallway.

Every clock stopped.

Then....

TICK.

Everything started again.

The boy smiled.

“Thank you.”

Maya smiled back.

Then the golden door began closing.

“Wait!” Maya shouted.

The boy waved.

“Don't borrow time again.”

Maya laughed.

“I won't.”

The door disappeared.

The next morning, Grandma left for her trip.

Maya hugged her tightly.

“Come back soon.”

“I will.”

Grandma kissed her forehead.

“And Maya?”

“Yes?”

“Thank you for the picture.”

Maya smiled.

This time, she wasn't thinking about five extra minutes.

She was thinking about the five minutes she already had.

Because sometimes, we spend so much time wishing for more that we forget to love the little time sitting right in front of us.

Maya watched Grandma's car disappear down the road.

Then she looked at the clock.

7:43.

She smiled.

And for once…

she wasn't late.

The End.

title: The Debt She Couldn't Fold
excerpt:
Ngozi was in her second year at UNILAG. Accounting.

Her school fees was ₦120,000. Her father, a driver in Benin, had sent it in two transfers with a note: _"Don't disappoint me, my daughter. Make us proud."_

She paid the first ₦40,000 for registration. Then her roommate showed her a betting app.

"₦1,000 can turn to ₦50,000 in one game," the girl said, eyes bright. "People are paying fees with it."

Ngozi tried it with ₦2,000. She won ₦8,000.

Her heart jumped. That was easy.

The next week she put in ₦20,000. Lost it.
The week after, ₦40,000. Lost it.

Panic set in when she checked her balance. ₦20,000 left. Deadline was in 10 days.

She couldn't tell her dad. He'd just borrowed the money.
So she chased it.

She sold her laptop. ₦35,000. Put it all on one "sure odd." Lost.

She borrowed from 3 friends. ₦60,000. Lost it trying to recover the first loss.

Now she had ₦0, and people were asking for their money.

Someone in a Telegram group told her about "quick loans."

"Just meet my boss," he said. "He helps students. No paperwork."

She was desperate. She went.

The address was a duplex in Ajah. The man who opened the door was smiling, gold chain,

title: Modern React State Management in 2026: Zustand, TanStack Query, and Context
excerpt: Why Redux is no longer the default, how to separate Server State from Client State, and when to use Zustand vs. React Context.
content:
Modern React State Management in 2026: Zustand, TanStack Query, and Context

State management in React has matured significantly. The modern consensus cleanly separates Server State (asynchronous API data, caching, revalidation) from Client State (UI toggles, modals, draft inputs).

Server State: TanStack Query (React Query)

TanStack Query manages data fetching, background polling, automatic caching, and optimistic UI updates with zero boilerplate.

Client State: Zustand

Zustand provides a minimal, boilerplate-free state store using external hooks without the context provider nesting hell.

import { create } from 'zustand';

interface ThemeState {
  isDark: boolean;
  toggleTheme: () => void;
}

export const useThemeStore = create<ThemeState>((set) => ({
  isDark: false,
  toggleTheme: () => set((state) => ({ isDark: !state.isDark })),
}));

title: 24 Feared Dead in Ondo State After Suspected Poisoning Linked to Local Herbal Drinks
excerpt: At least 24 people have died and several others have been hospitalized following a suspected mass poisoning incident across three communities in Odigbo Local Go…
content:
At least 24 people have died and several others have been hospitalized following a suspected mass poisoning incident across three communities in Odigbo Local Government Area of Ondo State, Nigeria. The deaths occurred over the weekend in Araromi-Obu, Odigbo, and Orita New Town, according to reports.

Eight deaths were recorded in Araromi-Obu, while sixteen were recorded in Odigbo town. Victims reportedly developed health complications after consuming suspected contaminated food or substances, though the precise source of the poisoning has not yet been officially established.

Sources suggest the fatalities may be linked to poisonous substances contained in sachet herbal concoctions, with some victims dying in their homes and others in their sleep. In response, the Odigbo Local Government Chairman imposed a one-month ban on the sale and consumption of locally brewed herbal drinks in the area as a precautionary measure, warning that anyone caught selling or distributing the banned drinks would face arrest and prosecution.

Ondo State's Commissioner for Health, Dr. Banji Ajaka, confirmed the incident and said government had launched an urgent and comprehensive investigation, working alongside officials from NAFDAC and the World Health Organization. He cautioned against speculation, stressing it would be premature to attribute the deaths to any particular substance until laboratory analyses and medical investigations are concluded.

The Ondo State Police Command has also launched an investigation, working with state health authorities to determine the exact number of casualties and cause of death.

The tragedy has triggered anger in the affected communities, with youths marching to the palace of the traditional ruler of Araromi Obu to demand urgent action.

As of this report, the exact substance responsible for the deaths remains unconfirmed, and investigations by state and federal health authorities are ongoing.

Sources: Vanguard News, National Agency for Government (NAN via The Eagle Online), The Guild NG, Roving Reporters NGR

title: Micro-Interactions & Cognitive Psychology in Modern Product Design
excerpt: How subtle animations, feedback loops, and cognitive psychology principles (Hick's Law, Fitts's Law) transform functional tools into delightful products.
content:
Micro-Interactions & Cognitive Psychology in Modern Product Design

Great software products do not just work correctly; they feel intuitive, responsive, and tactile. The difference between an ordinary product and an unforgettable one frequently lies in micro-interactions: subtle, single-purpose visual and tactile feedback loops that guide user behavior.

The Four Stages of a Micro-Interaction

  1. Trigger: The initiating condition—such as a user clicking a bookmark icon, or a system threshold like battery reaching 20%.
  2. Rules: What happens when the trigger is activated (e.g. save article ID to local cache and increment like count).
  3. Feedback: The immediate sensory response (e.g. button scale animation with a slight bounce and heart fill transition).
  4. Loops & Modes: Meta-rules governing state over time (e.g. changing the icon to an active state permanently).

Core Cognitive Laws in Interface Design

  • Hick's Law: The time it takes to make a decision increases logarithmically with the number and complexity of choices. Simplify menus and avoid cognitive overload.
  • Fitts's Law: The time required to rapidly move to a target area is a function of the ratio between distance to the target and width of the target. Make primary action buttons prominent and easy to hit on mobile screens.
  • Peak-End Rule: Humans judge an experience largely based on how they felt at its peak (intense point) and at its end. Celebrate achievements (like publishing an article or completing a task) with rewarding animations.

title: A COLD NIGHT IN LONDON (2)
excerpt: Four strangers. One empty chair. And someone watching from inside.
content:
Part Two: THE FOUR

The black Mercedes moved through South London without a word from either of them.

Daniel sat in the back seat, watching the city slide past the window.

Rain crawled down the glass in thin, crooked lines. Red buses passed in the opposite direction. People hurried beneath umbrellas, unaware that somewhere behind them, four strangers were being assembled for a job none of them understood.

Daniel looked at the woman beside him.

Mara.

She had introduced herself as though they were meeting for drinks.

No surname.

No explanation.

Just Mara.

She was dressed simply: black coat, dark trousers, boots. Nothing about her suggested twenty thousand pounds was enough money to impress her.

Daniel cleared his throat.

“So.”

Mara looked at him.

“So?”

“Are you going to tell me where we’re going?”

“No.”

“Right.”

He looked back through the window.

“Are you at least going to tell me who you are?”

“No.”

Daniel nodded slowly.

“Excellent conversation.”

For the first time, she smiled.

“You’re funnier than I expected.”

“I wasn’t trying to be funny.”

“That makes it better.”

The driver said nothing.

Daniel noticed something then.

There was no partition between the front and back seats, but the driver hadn’t spoken once.

Not when Daniel entered.

Not when Mara gave directions.

Not even when Daniel had asked him, fifteen minutes earlier, whether the heating was broken.

That bothered him.

He looked at Mara again.

“Who is he?”

“Our driver.”

“I gathered that.”

“Then why ask?”

Daniel sighed.

He was beginning to understand that Mara enjoyed making people uncomfortable.

His phone vibrated.

UNKNOWN NUMBER

One message.

YOU SHOULD HAVE STAYED HOME.

Daniel stared at it.

Mara noticed.

“What did you get?”

“Nothing.”

She held out her hand.

“Give me the phone.”

Daniel hesitated.

Then handed it over.

She read the message.

For the first time that night, the smile disappeared from her face.

“Interesting.”

“What?”

She handed the phone back.

“You weren’t supposed to receive that yet.”

Daniel felt the temperature inside the car change.

“Yet?”

Mara looked out the window.

“We’re almost there.”

Twenty minutes later, the Mercedes stopped outside an old building in Bermondsey.

It looked abandoned.

Three floors.

Brick walls blackened by years of London weather.

One broken window.

No sign.

No security.

Nothing that suggested twenty thousand pounds was waiting inside.

Mara stepped out.

Daniel followed.

The driver remained in the car.

Daniel looked back.

“You’re not coming?”

The driver didn’t answer.

Mara was already walking toward the building.

Daniel hurried after her.

“Is he staying there?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“He doesn’t come inside.”

“Why?”

She stopped.

“Daniel.”

He stopped too.

“You ask too many questions.”

“I’ve noticed you answer too few.”

She smiled.

“That’s why you’re here.”

Inside, the building was warmer than it looked from outside.

A narrow hallway led to a staircase.

Mara climbed.

Daniel followed.

Second floor.

Third.

At the top was a single door.

Mara knocked twice.

Waited.

Knocked once more.

The door opened.

A woman stood behind it.

Elegant.

Tall.

Dark hair pulled neatly behind her head.

She looked at Daniel.

Then at Mara.

Then back at Daniel.

“You’re late.”

Mara glanced at her watch.

“We’re early.”

The woman smiled faintly.

“I wasn’t talking about the time.”

Daniel didn’t like her.

He couldn’t explain why.

She stepped aside.

“Come in.”

Inside were two other people.

A man sat on a battered sofa, eating crisps from a packet.

He looked up.

“Is that him?”

Daniel stopped.

“Who?”

The man pointed at him.

“Daniel.”

Daniel looked at Mara.

Mara said nothing.

The man grinned.

“Well, that’s awkward.”

“What’s awkward?”

“You’re the last one.”

Daniel looked around the room.

There were four chairs arranged around a table.

Four folders.

Four glasses of water.

Four names.

He recognized his own.

DANIEL CROSS

Across from it:

MARA VALE

Beside hers:

LEO MERCER

And the final folder:

EVELYN REED

Daniel looked at the woman who had opened the door.

“You’re Evelyn.”

“Yes.”

He looked at the man eating crisps.

“And you’re Leo.”

Leo raised the packet.

“Guilty.”

Daniel looked back at Mara.

“You knew all of them?”

“Not exactly.”

Leo laughed.

“That means yes.”

Nobody laughed except him.

He stopped.

“Right.”

Daniel walked toward the table.

Something was wrong.

He could feel it.

Four people.

Four folders.

Four glasses.

Four chairs.

But there was something else.

A fifth chair.

It sat against the wall.

Empty.

Daniel pointed at it.

“What’s that for?”

Silence.

Mara looked at Evelyn.

Evelyn looked at Leo.

Leo stopped eating.

Daniel felt his stomach tighten.

“What’s the fifth chair for?”

Evelyn finally answered.

“It isn’t for anyone.”

Daniel stared at her.

“Then why is it here?”

Nobody answered.

His phone vibrated again.

Everyone looked at him.

Daniel slowly pulled it from his pocket.

Another message.

YOU’RE ALL FINALLY TOGETHER.

He looked up.

Mara was no longer smiling.

Leo put down the crisps.

Evelyn’s face had gone completely still.

Daniel’s phone vibrated again.

This time, there was an image.

He opened it.

It was a photograph of the four of them.

Taken from above.

Taken inside the room.

Daniel looked toward the ceiling.

There was no camera.

Another message appeared.

NOW WE CAN BEGIN.

And beneath it, one final line:

DON’T TRUST THE FIFTH PERSON.

title: Building Modern Design Systems: Tokens, Components, and Scalable Architecture
excerpt: How to bridge the gap between Figma and production code using Design Tokens, headless UI primitives, and cohesive typography scales.
content:
Building Modern Design Systems: Tokens, Components, and Scalable Architecture

A design system is much more than a component library; it is a shared visual and functional language connecting product designers, frontend engineers, and product managers. When executed well, design systems accelerate feature shipping velocity by 3x while ensuring consistent brand quality across platforms.

1. The Design Token Foundation

Design tokens are the atomic visual attributes of your design system—colors, spacing scales, typography rules, border radii, shadows, and animation curves—stored in a platform-agnostic format (JSON) and compiled to CSS variables, iOS Swift tokens, and Android XML resources.

/* Root design tokens in CSS */
:root {
  --color-brand-primary: #1a8917;
  --color-surface-bg: #ffffff;
  --color-text-main: #242424;
  --space-xs: 4px;
  --space-sm: 8px;
  --space-md: 16px;
  --space-lg: 24px;
  --radius-sm: 4px;
  --radius-md: 8px;
  --font-sans: 'Inter', system-ui, sans-serif;
}

[data-theme='dark'] {
  --color-surface-bg: #121212;
  --color-text-main: #f0f0f0;
}

2. Component Hierarchy: Atomic Design

  • Atoms: Fundamental building blocks that cannot be broken down further (Buttons, Inputs, Badges, Icons).
  • Molecules: Combinations of atoms functioning together (Search Input with Clear Button, Form Field with Label and Error Text).
  • Organisms: Distinct UI sections assembled from molecules (Navbar, Story Card, Comment Thread).
  • Templates / Pages: Layout structures populated with real dynamic content.

3. Accessibility (a11y) as a First-Class Citizen

A world-class design system embeds accessibility directly into core components: ensuring minimum 4.5:1 WCAG contrast ratios, complete keyboard navigation focus rings, and proper ARIA semantic roles on interactive modals and dropdowns.

title: WHY YOU KEEP STARTING OVER EVERY MONDAY AND HOW TO FINALLY STOP
excerpt: Why you're just treating every setback like a reason to start over.
content:
Every Monday, you become a new person.You wake up determined. This week will be different. You'll exercise every morning, eat better, stop procrastinating, read every night, save money, wake up early and finally become the person you've been promising yourself you would become for over five years now.

By Wednesday, the motivation has started fading. By Friday, you are negotiating with yourself. By Sunday night, you are disappointed. Then Monday comes again and somehow, you are back at the beginning. If this sounds familiar, your problem probably is not that you lack discipline. You may simply be trying to build a completely different life in seven days.

YOU'RE NOT STARTING OVER BECAUSE YOU DON'T CARE

Most people don't repeatedly abandon their goals because they don't want them badly enough. They start over because their expectations are impossible to maintain. You decide you are going to work out six days a week when you have barely exercised once a week. You plan to read 30 pages every night when you currently struggle to read five. You create a strict morning routine that requires waking up two hours earlier, exercising, journaling, meditating and planning your entire day.

It feels exciting on Sunday night because you're imagining the result. But eventually, real life shows up. You're tired. Something unexpected happens. You miss a workout. You sleep late and suddenly, your brain tells you the entire plan is ruined, so you wait for Monday.That's the trap.

Missing a Day Isn't the Same as Failing. One of the biggest reasons people keep restarting is an all-or-nothing mindset. You miss Monday's workout, so you decide the week is already ruined. You eat something unhealthy at lunch, so you abandon your diet for the rest of the day. You procrastinate for three hours, so you decide you'll "start properly tomorrow." But a missed day is just a missed day. It doesn't need a dramatic comeback.

If you planned to exercise five times this week and exercised four times, you didn't fail. You exercised four times.The goal is not to never fall off. The goal is to stop turning every small setback into a full reset.

BUILD HABITS YOU CAN REPEAT ON BAD DAYS

A sustainable habit is not one you can perform only when you are motivated. It's one you can still manage when you're tired, busy or having a terrible day. Instead of telling yourself you will read 30 pages every night, start with five. Instead of promising to exercise for an hour, start with 15 minutes. Instead of completely changing your diet overnight, improve one meal. This might feel too small. That's the point. Small habits are easier to repeat and repetition matters more than intensity when you're trying to build a lifestyle.

You don't need a routine that impresses you on Monday. You need one that still works on Thursday. Stop making Monday responsible for your discipline. Monday has become a psychological reset button. New week. New goals. New version of me. But here's the uncomfortable truth:

Monday is not going to save you.

Neither is January.

Neither is your birthday.

Neither is the first day of next month. You don't need a perfect starting point. You need the ability to continue from where you are.

If you missed yesterday, continue today. If you ate badly at lunch, make a better dinner. If you didn't study in the morning, study in the evening. If you wasted three hours, don't waste the remaining five because the day is "already ruined."

Your life doesn't reset at midnight.

You don't have to either.

MAKE YOUR GOALS SMALLER, NOT YOUR STANDARDS

This does not mean you should stop challenging yourself. It means you should separate ambition from unrealistic expectations. If your goal is to become healthier, the first goal doesn't have to be a six day workout schedule. If you want to write consistently, you don't have to publish every day. If you want to save money, you don't need to save a huge amount immediately.

Give yourself a minimum.

Something so manageable that you can do it even on an ordinary day. Then, when you have more energy, do more.The minimum keeps the habit alive.The extra is a bonus. Learn to continue without feeling motivated. Motivation is useful for starting. It is terrible as a long term strategy.You won't always feel inspired to study.You won't always want to exercise.You won't always feel like working on your goals. That's normal.

The goal is not to become someone who is permanently motivated. It's to become someone who knows what to do even when motivation disappears. Some days, you'll do the full workout. Some days, you'll take a 15 minute walk. Some days, you'll write 1,000 words. Some days, you'll write 100. It still counts because you are teaching yourself something more valuable than perfection which is, I can keep going.

Stop Asking, "When Can I Start Again?"

Start asking, "What's the next thing I can do?"

That question changes everything.

You don't need another Monday. You need another decision. Another meal. Another workout. Another page. Another hour of focused work. Another attempt.

Your goal is not to create a perfect week. It's to create enough ordinary days where you keep showing up. Eventually, you stop needing the dramatic feeling of a fresh start because you realize something,

you were never supposed to start over. You were supposed to continue.

What's your Monday reset experience, tell us in the comments.

Like. Comment. Follow. Share

title: PART THREE — THE FINAL FIGHT
excerpt: We fought to keep him alive. We lost everything trying. But in the end, we lost him too.”
content:
We sold almost everything trying to save him. But some battles cannot be won with money.

For a long time, her father was the kind of man people looked up to.

He was hardworking. He owned cars, lands, shops and properties. He had built something for himself from the ground up, and by the time she was growing up, their family was known in the community.

Her grandfather had married two wives, and after his death, her father became one of the men who carried the weight of the family on his shoulders.

He was not a perfect man.

But he was a strong man.

He tried.

He provided.

And in his own way, he made sure the children around him experienced life.

There were children from different mothers, but they shared the same father. Despite the complicated family structure, they respected him deeply.

To them, he was their father first.

And then, everything changed.

THE SICKNESS

Her father became sick.

At first, they believed it was something they could treat.

So they treated it.

Then they treated it again.

And again.

They spent money.

They looked for solutions.

They went from one place to another, hoping that the next treatment would finally bring him back to the strong man they knew.

But the sickness refused to leave.

The family began spending the money they had worked so hard to make.

Land was sold.

Properties were sold.

Things that had taken years to build disappeared one after another.

Millions were spent trying to save one man.

And nobody complained.

Because when the person you are trying to save is your father, you don’t count the cost.

You simply keep trying.

She remembered how her father had once celebrated her birthday.

It was only one birthday, but she never forgot it.

He had also spoken about her future. He promised that she would go to university. He even talked about sending her to boarding school.

Those promises became memories she would later hold onto.

Because there are some promises you don’t understand the value of until the person who made them is no longer there to fulfill them.

THE LAND

But there was another problem.

A problem that had been sitting quietly inside the family for years.

It was about land.

The compound where they lived was connected to land that had originally come through her grandfather’s family.

When her grandfather divided his properties between his families, that particular land eventually came into her father’s hands.

And that was where the trouble began.

The family from the other side believed the land still belonged to them.

There was jealousy.

There were disagreements.

There were things left unsaid.

And there were people watching every decision her father made concerning the land.

Ironically, her father wasn’t even benefiting from everything that land produced.

The other side still collected fruits from it.

They still did things there.

Yet when her father decided he wanted to give part of the land to a man whose wife was pregnant, everything changed.

Her father had always been a generous man.

He could go without eating just to make sure one of his workers had something.

The man he wanted to help had a pregnant wife.

Her father wanted him to stay on the land, manage it, do his mechanic work and use the opportunity to feed his family.

To her father, it was simply an act of kindness.

But someone else saw it differently.

One of his brothers from the other side of the family confronted him.

He questioned why her father wanted to give the land away.

He warned him to stay alive and watch what would happen to the land.

Her father didn’t argue.

He even rejected things brought from the land.

He wanted nothing from it.

He simply wanted the man to stay there and work.

But from that moment, the atmosphere around the land changed.

THE SNAIL

Then one night, something strange happened.

It was around midnight when they were closing the shop.

A snail appeared inside.

Not an ordinary sight.

The family was familiar with traditional beliefs surrounding certain things, and to them, the particular type of snail they saw was considered a bad sign.

They removed it.

But her father couldn’t ignore what had happened.

The following morning, because he was a man who believed strongly in tradition, he went to ask questions.

He explained what they had seen.

And what he was told frightened the family.

They were told that someone had been invoking the spirit of his late father against him.

The claim was that his father had not been properly buried or settled spiritually and that someone was allegedly going to his grave, pouring drinks and calling on his spirit to harm him.

Whether it was true or not, the fear became real.

And from that period, everything seemed to become worse.

His sickness intensified.

The family searched for answers everywhere.

They prayed.

They treated him.

They spent money.

They sold what they could.

They refused to give up.

THE LAST FIGHT

Her father fought.

That was the kind of man he was.

Even when his body became weak, the family kept believing that he would survive.

They had already sacrificed almost everything.

Land.

Properties.

Money.

Time.

Hope.

But sometimes, no matter how much a family fights, there comes a moment when there is nothing more they can do.

The man who had once been strong became weak.

The man who had taken them to different places could no longer move the way he used to.

The man who had provided for others now needed everyone to provide for him.

And eventually…

the iroko tree fell.

In that community, her father was a known and respected man.

People knew him.

People looked up to him.

His presence carried weight.

So when he died, it did not feel like an ordinary death.

It felt like something enormous had fallen.

And the family was left standing beneath the shadow of it.

She kept thinking about everything he had promised her.

The university.

The boarding school.

The birthdays.

The places he had taken them.

The life he had built.

Everything they had sold trying to save him.

And then one painful thought remained:

If her father were still alive, would all these things happening to the family now even be happening?

She didn’t know.

All she knew was that the man who had held the family together was gone.

And after his death, the real battle over everything he left behind was only beginning.

To be continued…

title: 7 Digital Skills That Can Get You Remote Work in 2026
excerpt: You don’t need to leave Nigeria to build a global career. These digital skills can help you work with clients and companies from anywhere.
content:
The internet has changed what it means to have a job.

Today, someone sitting in Nigeria can write for a company in the United States, manage social media for a business in the UK, design content for a startup in Canada, or provide customer support for a company thousands of kilometres away.

But there is one important requirement: you need a skill that people are willing to pay for.

If you’re a Nigerian youth looking to start earning online or build a remote career in 2026, here are seven digital skills worth learning.

1. Content Writing

Every online business needs content.

Websites need articles. Companies need blog posts. Brands need social media captions. Newsletters need emails, and businesses need people who can explain their products clearly.

If you can research a topic, write clearly, understand an audience, and create useful content, you can potentially work with clients remotely.

What you can learn:

  • Blog writing

  • SEO writing

  • Copywriting

  • Email writing

  • Social media writing

  • Ghostwriting

Beginner tools: Google Docs, Grammarly, ChatGPT, Canva

The important thing is not simply knowing how to use AI to generate text. Learn how to research, edit, fact-check and make the content sound human.

2. Social Media Management

Businesses don’t just need social media accounts—they need someone to manage them.

A social media manager can help a business plan posts, write captions, respond to comments, monitor performance and create content.

You can start by learning how platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, Facebook and LinkedIn work.

Skills to develop:

  • Content planning

  • Caption writing

  • Basic graphic design

  • Community management

  • Analytics

  • Short-form video strategy

You can even create sample posts for imaginary businesses to build a portfolio before getting your first client.

3. Graphic Design

You don’t have to become a professional Photoshop expert before you can start designing.

Tools such as Canva have made basic graphic design much more accessible.

Businesses constantly need:

  • Social media graphics

  • YouTube thumbnails

  • Flyers

  • Presentations

  • Advertisements

  • E-book covers

  • Business documents

Start with the fundamentals—layout, typography, spacing, hierarchy and visual consistency.

Then create several sample designs and put them into a simple portfolio.

4. Video Editing

Short-form video is everywhere.

TikTok, Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts have created huge demand for people who can turn raw footage into engaging videos.

You can learn:

  • Cutting and arranging clips

  • Captions and subtitles

  • Transitions

  • Basic sound editing

  • Storytelling

  • Short-form video pacing

You can start learning with mobile-friendly tools such as CapCut or other editing apps.

And you don’t necessarily need an expensive computer to begin. Your first goal should be to become good at editing, not to own expensive equipment.

5. Virtual Assistance

A virtual assistant helps businesses and individuals handle tasks remotely.

Depending on the client, this can include:

  • Managing emails

  • Scheduling appointments

  • Data entry

  • Internet research

  • Organising documents

  • Customer communication

  • Social media assistance

This can be a good starting point for someone who is organised, communicates well and is comfortable using basic online tools.

You can begin by learning tools such as Google Workspace, Microsoft Office and project-management platforms.

6. AI Skills

Artificial intelligence is changing the way people work.

But learning AI doesn’t necessarily mean becoming a programmer.

There is growing value in knowing how to use AI tools effectively for tasks such as research, content creation, brainstorming, data analysis and workflow automation.

You can learn:

  • AI-assisted writing

  • Prompting

  • AI research

  • AI content workflows

  • AI automation

  • Using AI tools for business tasks

The strongest approach is to combine AI with another skill.

For example:

Writing + AI = faster content production

Design + AI = faster creative workflows

Marketing + AI = faster research and content planning

AI should make you more productive, not replace your ability to think.

7. Customer Support

Not every remote job requires advanced technical skills.

Companies also need people who can communicate with customers through email, chat and other support channels.

If you are patient, professional and good at solving problems, customer support can be worth exploring.

Useful skills include:

  • Clear written communication

  • Problem-solving

  • Customer service

  • Email etiquette

  • Basic computer skills

  • CRM software

Good English communication can be a major advantage when working with international customers.

Which Skill Should You Learn First?

Don’t try to learn all seven at once.

That’s one of the biggest mistakes beginners make.

Instead, choose one skill, spend several weeks learning it, practise by creating real examples, and build a small portfolio.

For example:

Writing → 5 sample articles

Graphic design → 10 sample designs

Video editing → 5 edited videos

Social media management → 2 sample content calendars

Your portfolio doesn’t have to be perfect.

It simply needs to show potential clients what you can actually do.

Can Nigerians Really Get Remote Work?

Yes—but learning a skill is only the first step.

You also need to learn how to:

  • Build a portfolio

  • Find legitimate opportunities

  • Write good proposals

  • Communicate professionally

  • Price your services

  • Avoid online scams

  • Deliver work on time

Don’t believe anyone promising that you will make huge amounts of money overnight.

Remote work is still work.

You are competing in a global market, so your advantage should be your skill, reliability and ability to solve problems.

Start Small, Think Global

You don’t need to wait until you have a perfect laptop, expensive software or years of experience.

Start with what you have.

Learn one skill.

Practise it.

Create proof of your ability.

Then start looking for opportunities.

The goal isn’t simply to “make money online.”

The goal is to develop a valuable skill that someone anywhere in the world is willing to pay you for.

Your location may be Nigeria, but your potential clients don’t have to be.

title: How to Ace the System Design Interview: A Framework for Modern Distributed Systems
excerpt: A battle-tested step-by-step framework to navigate system design interview rounds with confidence, structured calculations, and deep architectural trade-offs.
content:
How to Ace the System Design Interview: A Framework for Modern Distributed Systems

The System Design interview is often the most decisive factor in determining engineering leveling (Mid-level, Senior, or Staff) at top tech companies. Unlike LeetCode coding rounds, system design questions are intentionally open-ended, evaluating your ability to architect scalable, fault-tolerant systems under ambiguity.

The 4-Step System Design Framework (45-Minute Breakdown)

Step 1: Requirements Clarification (5–7 mins)

Never jump immediately into drawing database boxes. First establish functional and non-functional requirements:

  • Functional Requirements: What are the top 2–3 features the user can perform? (e.g. Post a tweet, follow users, view home timeline).
  • Non-Functional Requirements: High availability vs. strong consistency (CAP theorem), latency constraints (<100ms p99 read latency), global distribution.
  • Back-of-the-Envelope Math: Estimate Daily Active Users (DAU), read/write ratios, QPS (Queries Per Second), and 5-year storage projections.

Step 2: High-Level Architecture (10–12 mins)

Design the end-to-end data flow from client devices to edge load balancers, API gateways, application microservices, and primary databases.

Client -> DNS/CDN -> API Gateway -> Load Balancer -> Stateless App Servers -> Primary DB + Cache Cluster

Step 3: Deep Dive into Core Bottlenecks (15–20 mins)

Identify the most challenging component of the design. For a timeline feed system, discuss the tradeoffs between Fan-out-on-Write (Push Model) vs. Fan-out-on-Read (Pull Model) for high-follower celebrity accounts.

Step 4: Reliability, Monitoring, and Edge Cases (5 mins)

Conclude by addressing single points of failure (SPOFs), database replication lag, circuit breaker patterns, and telemetry monitoring.

title: The sky she never flew
excerpt: Part 3 continue They tried to get an okada. No one would ride in the rain.By the time Alhaji's friend came with his car, Amina was barely conscious. Yusuf was h…
content:
Part 3 continue

They tried to get an okada. No one would ride in the rain.

By the time Alhaji's friend came with his car, Amina was barely conscious. Yusuf was holding her hand, crying. At Murtala Muhammed Specialist Hospital, the nurses were running. Eclampsia. Severe pre-eclampsia. We've lost too much blood. They moved fast. Too fast.

Amina opened her eyes once. The lights above her were bright and white. For a second, they looked like runway lights.

She could hear a sound. Waa-waa-waa. An ambulance in the distance. To her, it sounded exactly like a plane taking off. She smiled. Just a little,Then she let go. They buried her on Wednesday. The rain had stopped. Alhaji did not remarry for a long time.

The baby, a girl, survived. They named her Hadiza, after Amina's grandmother. Yusuf was the one who raised her, He finished school and got a job at the airport. Not as a pilot but As ground staff. But every Friday he brought Hadiza to the fence near the runway.

"See that one?" he'd say, pointing. "That's an A320. See how it climbs?" When Hadiza turned 5, Yusuf gave her a gift. A small frame. Inside it was a yellowed paper plane, folded small. Under it, in fading blue ink, were words Amina had written years ago:

The sky is not the limit.

Hadiza didn't understand it then. But every evening, she would stand on their small balcony, arms stretched wide, face to the wind, And somewhere above her, a plane would roar past, heading for the clouds.

The End.

title: WHEN MOTHERHOOD DOESN'T FEEL LIKE HAPPINESS
excerpt:
The silent struggle of postpartum depression in Nigeria

 [FATIMA TAHIR]

The baby is finally asleep, but the mother is wide awake.

Her body is still recovering from childbirth. She is exhausted, yet her mind refuses to rest.

Around her, people see a new mother who should be grateful, happy and completely in love with her baby.

But behind that picture of motherhood, she may be struggling with sadness, anxiety, guilt or an overwhelming sense of isolation.

For some women, these feelings do not simply disappear. They can develop into postpartum depression — a serious but treatable mental-health condition that can affect a mother's wellbeing, her ability to function and her relationship with her baby.

In Nigeria, recognising that struggle can be particularly difficult when motherhood is surrounded by strong expectations about how a woman should behave.

Research involving Nigerian women and their families has found that cultural expectations, family relationships, stigma and ideas about mental illness can influence how postpartum distress is understood and whether women seek help.

---

MORE THAN THE “BABY BLUES”

Not every difficult emotion after childbirth is postpartum depression.

The “baby blues” are common and may involve mood changes, crying, anxiety and difficulty sleeping during the first days after delivery. They generally improve within about two weeks. Postpartum depression is more severe and persistent and can interfere with a mother's daily life and ability to care for herself or her baby.

Recent Nigerian research shows why the condition deserves attention.

A 2026 study of 374 postpartum women attending six primary healthcare centres in Ilorin, Kwara State, found that 33.7% screened positive for probable postpartum depression using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. The researchers identified previous depression and marital violence as independent predictors.

That figure should not be interpreted as meaning that 33.7% of all Nigerian mothers have postpartum depression. The study was conducted among women attending selected primary healthcare centres in Ilorin, and screening positive is not the same as receiving a clinical diagnosis.

But it does provide evidence that postpartum depression can be a substantial problem in some Nigerian populations.

Another study published in 2024 followed women who had recently given birth in Kano and found a cumulative incidence of postpartum depression of 15.32% among participants followed in the study.

The researchers found insufficient evidence that postpartum haemorrhage itself significantly increased the risk of postpartum depression. They also examined factors including perceived stress and social support.

Together, these studies point to an important reality: there is no single number that can describe every Nigerian mother's experience, but postpartum depression is a problem that deserves recognition, research and appropriate care.

---

WHEN THE SADNESS DOESN'T GO AWAY

Postpartum depression does not always look like a mother who is visibly crying all day.

A woman may continue feeding her baby, attending to household responsibilities and smiling around other people while privately feeling overwhelmed.

Symptoms can include persistent sadness, loss of interest or pleasure, intense guilt or worthlessness, exhaustion, anxiety, difficulty sleeping, changes in appetite, difficulty concentrating and problems bonding with the baby. In serious cases, thoughts of suicide or harming oneself or the baby can occur.

The World Health Organization notes that maternal mental-health disorders after birth can affect both mothers and infants. Severe or prolonged mental illness can interfere with mother-infant attachment, breastfeeding and infant care.

That is why postpartum depression should not simply be dismissed as a woman being tired, ungrateful or unable to cope.

It is a health condition that deserves attention.

And sometimes the first step is simply recognising that what a mother is experiencing has a name — and that she does not have to face it alone.

---

WHY IS THIS HAPPENING?

When motherhood comes with more than a new baby

There is no single reason a woman develops postpartum depression.

Risk can be influenced by a combination of psychological, social, physical and environmental factors. The WHO identifies factors including extreme stress, exposure to violence and low social support as risks for mental disorders during pregnancy and after childbirth.

The 2026 Ilorin study provides a Nigerian example.

Among the 374 women studied, previous depression and marital violence remained independently associated with probable postpartum depression after the researchers adjusted for other variables. Women with a history of depression had more than four times the odds of screening positive, while exposure to marital violence was associated with about three times the odds.

The researchers also found associations involving factors such as younger age, lower education, having four or more children, inadequate social support, Caesarean delivery and non-exclusive breastfeeding. However, these did not all remain independent predictors after adjustment.

The Kano research also points toward the importance of stress and social support in understanding postpartum depression among women studied there.

For some Nigerian mothers, these pressures exist alongside expectations to care for a newborn, recover physically, manage the household and appear happy.

That can make it difficult to say:

“I am not okay.”

---

WHY DON'T WOMEN ASK FOR HELP?

When asking for help isn't so simple

Recognising that something is wrong is only the beginning.

Research on help-seeking for perinatal depression in southwestern Nigeria found that women and their families often had to negotiate when, where and how treatment would be sought. Family caregivers could play an important role in those decisions.

The same research found that concerns about stigma could encourage families to keep the illness and treatment process private. Participants described stereotypes surrounding mental illness, including portrayals of affected women as aggressive, irrational or cursed.

Earlier Nigerian research similarly found that explanations for perinatal depression could include relationship problems, inadequate care from a husband, family difficulties, spiritual beliefs and insufficient rest after childbirth.

This matters because the way a family understands a mother's distress can influence what happens next.

If her symptoms are understood as a medical problem, she may be taken for professional care.

If they are interpreted as weakness, bad behaviour or a spiritual problem, professional mental-health care may be delayed or avoided.

The 2023 Nigerian qualitative research found that help-seeking could depend on the help immediately available, how the problem was interpreted within the family, concerns about stigma and perceptions of immediate risk.

So telling a struggling mother to “just ask for help” can overlook the reality around her.

She may first have to understand what is happening to her, overcome fear of judgment, convince people around her that she needs help and find a service capable of providing it.

The question is therefore not only whether Nigerian mothers need help.

It is whether the people and systems around them make it safe and possible to ask for it.

---

IT CAN BE TREATED

Postpartum depression is serious, but it is treatable.

Treatment can include psychological therapies, social support and, when clinically appropriate, medication. The WHO also recommends integrating maternal mental-health care into general health services, including maternal and child-health services, and notes that non-specialist and community health providers can play a role.

Nigerian researchers are exploring what culturally appropriate treatment can look like.

A 2025 pilot randomised controlled trial in Jos tested a 12-session programme combining Learning Through Play with culturally adapted Cognitive Behavioural Therapy among mothers experiencing postnatal depression. The study involved 66 mother-child pairs across three centres.

The researchers reported high participation and satisfaction with the intervention, along with preliminary evidence of reductions in postnatal depression and anxiety. However, they stressed that a larger, fully powered trial is needed to establish clinical and cost-effectiveness.

That distinction matters.

The Jos study provides promising preliminary evidence. It does not mean that the intervention has already been proven effective for every Nigerian mother.

Another Nigerian study looked at whether bringing postpartum-depression interventions closer to mothers could improve access.

Researchers worked with mothers screened at National Programme on Immunization clinics in Lagos and Enugu and brought intervention services into primary healthcare settings. They reported that 95.2% of mothers in the intervention-access study continued to access services through the final follow-up, compared with 33.7% in an earlier referral model where mothers had been asked to visit a mental-health facility.

The finding suggests that where care is offered can matter.

For mothers who already visit health facilities for their babies' immunisations and other services, bringing appropriate mental-health support into those settings may reduce some of the barriers associated with referral to a separate specialist facility.

---

WHAT NEEDS TO CHANGE?

Postpartum depression cannot be addressed simply by telling mothers to “be strong.”

Families need better awareness of the signs.

Healthcare workers need to recognise women who may be struggling.

Mental-health support needs to become easier to access, particularly through services mothers already use.

And mothers need to know that asking for help does not make them bad mothers.

WHO guidance supports integrating maternal mental-health care into general healthcare, including maternal and child-health services, while Nigerian research suggests that culturally appropriate and community-based approaches may help improve access.

The challenge is therefore not only treating women once they become severely unwell.

It is recognising the problem earlier, reducing stigma and making appropriate support easier to reach.

---

SHE DOES NOT HAVE TO SUFFER IN SILENCE

For a woman struggling with postpartum depression, recovery may begin with something that sounds simple but can be difficult to find:

Someone who listens.

That person could be a partner, family member, community health worker, doctor or mental-health professional.

What matters is that her distress is taken seriously.

The research from Nigeria offers reasons for hope. The 2025 Jos trial found that a culturally adapted psychological intervention was acceptable to participating mothers and showed preliminary evidence of reducing depression and anxiety, while earlier Nigerian research demonstrated that bringing intervention services into primary healthcare settings could improve access.

But research also shows why the conversation cannot stop at treatment.

Stigma, family decision-making, social expectations and access to services can all shape whether a woman receives care in the first place.

The birth of a baby is often described as one of life's happiest moments.

But for some mothers, it can also mark the beginning of a difficult and lonely period that other people cannot see.

Postpartum depression does not make a woman a bad mother.

Sometimes, she is simply a mother who needs someone to notice that she is struggling — and help her find her way back.
