title: MTN vs. The Nigerian Who Refused to Let It Slide
excerpt: For a while now, a lot of MTN users have quietly complained about data disappearing faster than it should you buy a plan, barely touch your phone, and somehow i…
content:
For a while now, a lot of MTN users have quietly complained about data disappearing faster than it should you buy a plan, barely touch your phone, and somehow it's gone. Most people shrugged it off, assumed it was "just how data works" in Nigeria, and moved on. Nobody really pushed back until now.

A lawyer, Zaenab Olawunmi Adams (@yettydlaw_), decided she wasn't going to let it slide. She formally challenged MTN over the depletion of her 800GB annual data plan, demanding a detailed breakdown of her usage down to the date, time, and volume of every deduction. And instead of stopping at her own case, she's now collecting reports from other subscribers experiencing the same unexplained, excessive, or disputed data usage, turning one woman's frustration into what could become a real, collective case against MTN.

What makes this different is that it's not just noise online it's backed by an actual legal team and a real demand for accountability. And that's exactly why it matters. Nigerians are used to venting and moving on the next day, while the companies involved wait it out, knowing the outrage will fade.

We just hope this doesn't end up like every other online "protest" trending for a week, then forgotten. This time, we hope it actually gets a result.

title: CHAPTER 3: THE SCALES OF CINDER
excerpt: The High Chamber was a cavernous hall of white granite, built to make men feel small and the law feel eternal. Tiered gallery seats rose toward vaulted ceilings, packed tight with spectators—nobles dr…
content:
The High Chamber was a cavernous hall of white granite, built to make men feel small and the law feel eternal. Tiered gallery seats rose toward vaulted ceilings, packed tight with spectators—nobles draped in velvet and silk on one side, and wealthy merchants on the other. Below them sat the seven High Magistrates, wrapped in robes of crimson and obsidian.

At the center stood the High Chancellor, his silver hair gleaming under the skylight like a crown.

Kael and Elara were led to the center ring, surrounded by double-walled iron railings. The heavy chains clanked against the stone floor with every step. Thousands of eyes bore down on them, but Kael kept his head held high—not out of pride, but because he refused to give the crowd the satisfaction of seeing him cower.

"Silence in the Court," the Chancellor’s voice echoed off the white walls.

The room fell deathly quiet, save for the patter of rain against the glass roof high above.

"We assemble under the ancient laws of Cinder to judge the murder of Lord Thomas Vane," the Chancellor announced. He looked down at Kael. "Kael of Cinder Street, you stand accused of cold-blooded murder. How do you plead?"

"Not guilty, Your Honor," Kael said, his voice ringing clearer than he expected. "I was sweeping Cinder Street when Lord Vane was slain."

Laughter erupted from the Vane family's box in the gallery. Lord Vance Vane—the victim’s father—stood up, his face flushed with rage. "He lies! Three witnesses saw a man in rag-stitched clothes fleeing the docks with blood on his wrists!"

"Blood from broken glass, my Lord!" Kael shouted back, holding up his bandaged hand. "I cut myself on Cinder Street!"

The Chancellor struck his heavy brass gavel. "Order! Blood evidence is not conclusive without magical verification. However..." He turned his sharp, icy gaze onto Elara. "We have an unprecedented complication. Lady Elara of House Oakwood has invoked the ancient Pact of Surety."

A collective murmur rippled through the gallery.

"Lady Elara," the Chancellor said, leaning forward. "Your father has petitioned this court, claiming you acted under emotional distress. If you retract your statement now, you will be escorted home without penalty, and the court will proceed with the execution of the accused."

Every eye in the room turned to Elara. Kael looked at her, too. He felt a sudden, terrifying pang of guilt. If she walked away now, she would be safe. She would return to her gilded life, and he would face the rope. It was the sensible choice. The only logical choice.

Elara adjusted her silver-braided coat, stepped to the front of the iron cage, and looked the High Chancellor dead in the eye.

"I will not retract," she said, her tone as hard as diamond. "My mind is clear. At the first bell of dawn, Kael was on Cinder Street. He could not have committed the murder at the docks."

A gasp went through the noble gallery. Lord Oakwood put his head in his hands, while Vance Vane glared at her as if she had personally stabbed his son.

"So be it," the Chancellor said, his face hardening. "By the authority of the Pact, Lady Elara of House Oakwood is now bound to the accused. Should he be proven guilty, her life, her titles, and her bloodline share his punishment."

"Then let us present the truth!" Elara demanded, resting her hands on the iron rail. "If Lord Vane was murdered at the docks at the first bell, call the harbor master! Call the dockworkers! Examine the wound! The Vane guards sealed the docks before any independent magistrate could inspect the body!"

Vance Vane sneered from the gallery. "The body was inspected by the Vane House Physician. We need no third-party meddling for a street rat's execution!"

"And there lies the lie!" Elara countered, her voice rising to fill the grand hall. "A murder on royal docklands requires a High Court coroner, not a family physician. You broke procedure because you wanted a quick hanging, not justice!"

The gallery broke into heated chatter. Magistrates whispered among themselves, nodding at her point. Lord Vane’s jaw clenched.

"Enough!" the Chancellor roared, slamming the gavel three times. "The court recognizes a procedural conflict. Under the Pact, when surety is invoked and evidence remains disputed, the court cannot order immediate execution."

Kael felt a faint glimmer of hope spark in his chest.

"However," the Chancellor continued, his voice cold and ominous, "the law does not permit an accused murderer of noble blood to walk free during investigation. By unanimous decree of the Magistrates, Kael of Cinder Street and Lady Elara of House Oakwood are hereby sentenced to The Black Reach."

A collective gasp echoed across the court. Elara’s breath hitched.

"The Black Reach?" Kael whispered. "What is that?"

"The southern penal exile," Elara murmured, her confidence wavering for the first time. "A wasteland of sulfur mines and lawless outlaws. Nobody returns from the Reach."

"You shall be stripped of your titles, your possessions, and your names," the Chancellor declared, raising a glowing parchment seal. "You are exiled to the Reach until such a time as absolute proof of innocence—or guilt—is brought before this bench. Guards! Take them!"

Heavy hands grabbed Kael’s shoulders. As he was shoved toward the side exit, he caught sight of Vance Vane in the upper gallery. The grieving father wasn't crying. He was smiling—a thin, cruel smirk.

Vane didn't just want Kael dead; he wanted Elara ruined, and the Oakwood influence destroyed. The murder was never about Kael. It was a political trap from the very start.

Kael looked back at Elara as the guards forced them down the dark stairway toward the transport wagons. Her noble life was gone. Her family had abandoned her. She had lost everything because she chose to speak the truth for a street sweeper.

They think they're sending us to die in the dirt, Kael thought, his hands clenching into tight fists until his cuts burned. They think the Reach will swallow us whole.

He leaned toward Elara as they were thrust into the back of an iron-barred wagon.

"They took your name, Elara," Kael swore, his voice low and dangerous. "They took your home. But I swear on my life... we are coming back for Cinder. And when we do, we won't just ask for justice. We'll buy the whole damn city and tear it down."

title: IF I COULD GO BACK TO THE VERY FIRST DAY I MET YOU…
excerpt: The Answer He Couldn’t Give
content:
“Who is Teni, Kunle?”

Silence.

I checked my phone to be sure the call hadn’t ended.

“Kunle?”

“I’m here.”

“Then talk to me.”

He sighed.

“Bola, this is not something I can explain over the phone.”

“Okay. Come home and explain it.”

“I’m on my way.”

He ended the call.

And just like that, I was left alone with a thousand questions and a husband who suddenly had nothing to say.

⸻

By the time Kunle got home, I had replayed that conversation so many times in my head that I was beginning to hate the sound of his voice.

He walked in, dropped his keys on the table and came towards me.

“Bola.”

I didn’t answer.

He sat beside me.

“Can I explain?”

I turned to look at him.

“I’m listening.”

He took a breath.

“Teni and I were together a long time ago.”

“Together how?”

He hesitated.

“We were married.”

For a moment, I genuinely thought I had heard him wrong.

“Married?”

“Yes.”

I stared at him.

“And you thought to tell me this when exactly?”

“Bola, it’s not what you think.”

I almost laughed.

“Kunle, I don’t even know what to think. That’s the problem.”

He rubbed his palms together.

“That marriage was over before I met you.”

“Then why did she call herself your ex like there was something you were hiding?”

“Because she’s my ex.”

“Kunle.”

“Bola, we had been separated for a long time.”

I looked away from him, trying to make sense of what I was hearing.

Separated.

Married.

Teni.

Daniel.

The names and pieces of my own life were beginning to feel like somebody else’s story.

“Were you divorced when you married me?”

He didn’t answer.

I looked back at him.

“Kunle. Were you divorced?”

He leaned forward, elbows on his knees.

“No.”

I blinked.

“What do you mean, no?”

“The divorce wasn’t final.”

I stared at him, waiting for him to say something else. Something that would make the sentence less terrible.

He didn’t.

“So you were still married to her when you married me?”

“We were separated, Bola.”

“That is not what I asked you.”

“I was going to sort everything out.”

“When?”

He looked at me.

“I didn’t want to lose you.”

And there it was.

The explanation that was supposed to make everything better.

I shook my head slowly.

“So you decided I didn’t deserve to know?”

“I was scared. I knew how it would sound.”

“How it would sound?” I repeated. “You let me marry you without telling me you were still married to someone else.”

“I love you, Bola.”

I looked at him, and for the first time that night, I didn’t know what to do with those words.

Because this was Kunle.

The same man who checked if I’d eaten. Who noticed when I was quiet. Who could tell when something was bothering me before I said a word.

And now he was sitting in front of me, telling me he had hidden something this big because he loved me.

I got up from the sofa.

“Does your family know?”

He looked up sharply.

“Why are you bringing my family into this?”

“Because I’m asking a question.”

“Bola, please. Let’s deal with what’s between us first.”

I paused.

That answer bothered me more than I wanted to admit.

“Did your family know you were still married when you married me?”

He stood up.

“I said I was going to sort it out.”

“And I’m asking if they knew.”

He looked away.

I waited.

But he didn’t answer.

My phone buzzed on the table.

A message from Teni.

Teni: Has he told you the truth about why our marriage ended?

I read it once.

Then again.

Kunle looked at my phone.

And the expression on his face changed.

Not confusion.

Not surprise.

Fear.

I picked up the phone.

“What else is there, Kunle?”

He opened his mouth.

Nothing came out.

And suddenly, I wasn’t sure the truth about Teni was the only thing he’d been hiding from me.

To be continued…

title: CHAPTER 4: THE ASH AND THE IRON
excerpt: The transport wagon rattled violently over rutted roads, its iron bars vibrating against Kael’s spine with every turn of the wheel. Outside, the lush green pine forests surrounding Cinder gradually ga…
content:
The transport wagon rattled violently over rutted roads, its iron bars vibrating against Kael’s spine with every turn of the wheel. Outside, the lush green pine forests surrounding Cinder gradually gave way to a stark, dead landscape—bleached grass, shattered grey rocks, and distant plumes of yellow sulfur rising against a bruised sky.

For three days, they had traveled south. Three days of stale water, hard bread, and complete silence from the four armed guards riding escort on horseback.

Elara sat opposite Kael, her knees pulled tight against her chest. The silver-braided coat—her last remnant of noble status—was now stained with mud and road dust. Yet, despite the grime, she sat with a quiet, rigid poise that the iron cage could not strip away.

"You haven't slept," Kael said, his voice raspy from the dust.

Elara shifted her gaze from the iron bars to him. "Neither have you."

"I'm used to sleeping on stone," Kael said, offering a faint, self-deprecating smile. "Though usually without guards."

Elara looked down at her hands. The fine leather gloves she had worn in the market square were long gone, confiscated by the court guards along with her family ring. Her fingernails were dark with dirt, her skin raw.

"They won't let us live long enough to reach the sulfur pits, will they?" she asked quietly. Her voice didn't tremble, but the question was bare, honest. "Vance Vane wouldn't leave two loose ends to rot in a mine."

Kael leaned forward, the heavy chains binding his wrists clinking against the wooden floorboards. "Vane didn't just want me blamed. He wanted your house disgraced. If we die in an 'unfortunate accident' on the road, he gets his revenge without paying the court a copper."

"Which means the guards aren't just escorts," Elara murmured, glancing through the rear bars at the mounted men behind them. "They're executioners waiting for the right stretch of road."

"Exactly," Kael said. He raised his hands, subtly tapping his thumb against the iron ring of his shackles. "Which means we don't wait for them to pick the spot."

Elara’s eyes narrowed slightly, a sharp intelligence flashing behind her exhaustion. "What are you proposing, sweeper?"

"Back on Cinder Street, I used to clean the lockboxes outside the merchant shops," Kael whispered, angling his body so the guards couldn't see his movement. He reached into the tear in his boot lining and slipped out a thin, rusted iron nail he had palmed from the holding cell back at the High Court. "Ancient iron mechanisms are all built the same way. Heavy, crude, and easy to trick if you know where the tumbler sits."

Elara watched as Kael worked the nail into the keyhole of his wrist shackles. His hands were calloused and scarred, but his fingers moved with a practiced, light precision. A soft click echoed over the rumble of the wagon wheels.

The left cuff sprang open.

Elara’s breath caught in her throat. "Where did you learn to do that?"

"You learn a lot of useful things when you spend six years dodging dock wardens and city guards," Kael said, keeping the open cuff resting on his wrist so it appeared still locked. He looked up, his dark eyes locking onto hers with an intensity she hadn't seen in him before. "The Reach isn't a prison, Elara. It's a grave. If we let them take us there, we die. If we break now, we have a chance."

"A chance at what?" she asked. "We're two fugitives with no money, no names, and the most powerful families in Cinder hunting us down."

"A chance to build something they can't touch," Kael said, his voice dropping into a low, firm promise. "They think wealth is made in comfortable courts and gold mines. But wealth starts in the mud. The dead trade routes, the black markets, the places the Seven Families are too soft to rule. I know how those streets work."

Elara studied him for a long moment. The street sweeper who had nodded to her outside the bakery was gone. In his place stood someone forged by desperation—a boy who was looking at a death sentence and seeing an empire.

"First," Elara said, holding out her bound wrists toward him, "you pick my lock."

Kael grinned—a raw, sharp edge of a smile. "Hold still, My Lady."

Outside, the lead guard raised a hand, bringing the convoy to a halt near the edge of a jagged ravine known as Deadman’s Pass. The sun was dipping below the horizon, casting blood-red light across the barren rocks.

"Rest the horses!" the lead guard shouted, dismounting and unfastening the heavy iron sword at his hip. He turned toward the wagon, a cold, ruthless smirk spreading across his face as he met the eye of the guard beside him. "Time to settle the High Chancellor's account."

Inside the dark wagon, Kael felt the second lock click open under his touch. He slipped the iron cuff off Elara’s wrist and looked at the shadows gathering outside the bars.

"When I open this gate," Kael whispered, his fingers tightening around the heavy wooden latch of the wagon, "run for the rocks. Don't look back."

"I don't run alone," Elara said, her hand reaching out to grip his arm. "We're bound by the Pact, remember? Where you go, I go."

Kael nodded once, feeling a strange, solid warmth ground him against the cold dusk air.

"Then let's go take what's ours."

title: The Princess Who Found Freedom
excerpt: I saw the small crown and wondered about the heart beneath it. A crown may look small, simple or luxurious from the outside, but the person wearing it may carry something far greater than what the wor…
content:
Everyone thinks they know what it means to be a princess.

They see the crown.

The jewels.

The silk robes that sweep across polished palace floors.

They see servants bowing as I pass, maidens waiting for my command, and guards standing outside my chamber as though I were the most precious thing in the kingdom.

Perhaps that was exactly what my father wanted them to see.

A beautiful princess.

A fortunate daughter.

A girl who had everything she could ever desire.

But no one ever asked what it felt like to belong to an entire kingdom.

My life had never truly been mine.

Every hour had a rule. Every decision had a consequence. Even my future had been written long before I was old enough to understand what the word future meant.

I still remembered something my mother once told me.

“My dear, this is the fate of a princess. You do not make every choice for yourself. You follow the rules. Sometimes, the kingdom decides your fate.”

At the time, I had stared at her.

“And what if I don't want the fate they choose?”

Her expression had softened, but she had not answered.

Years later, I finally understood why.

Some questions were dangerous in a palace.

Especially when you were the princess.

The sound of trumpets pulled me back to the present.

I stood at the entrance of the grand hall, my fingers curled tightly around the folds of my robe.

Red.

I had chosen red.

Not because this was supposed to be a celebration of love.

Not because my betrothed was finally visiting the kingdom before our wedding.

I wore red because, beneath the jewels and gold embroidery, my heart was mourning.

Ahead of me, the people of Cebian had gathered.

My parents sat upon their thrones, surrounded by members of the royal court. The moment I stepped forward, whispers rose from the crowd.

“How lucky she is.”

“She looks beautiful.”

“What a fortunate princess.”

I kept walking.

My crown rested heavily upon my head.

My jewellery glittered beneath the palace lights.

And with every step, I felt less like a princess and more like a prisoner dressed beautifully for the world to admire.

No one could see the heart beating beneath the silk.

No one could see the fear hidden behind my smile.

They saw a princess.

They did not see Roseline.

Sometimes, I imagined running away.

I would leave the palace before sunrise, disappear beyond the mountains, and keep running until no one knew my name.

No crown.

No guards.

No kingdom deciding whom I would marry.

Just me.

But fantasies were easy.

Reality was waiting for me at the end of the aisle.

And his name was Dalton.

I had met him only once.

Once.

That was all the time I had been given to look into the eyes of the man I was expected to marry.

Our wedding had been arranged for the following week.

After our first meeting, I was not even allowed to see him again.

My parents had already made their decision.

And apparently, that was supposed to be enough.

I hated him before I even knew him.

Not because Dalton had done anything to me.

But because he represented everything I had spent my life trying to escape.

Another rule.

Another decision.

Another door closing before I even had the chance to choose what was on the other side.

So, on our wedding night, when the palace doors finally closed and we were left alone, I made one decision for myself.

I refused to let him touch me.

Dalton stood a few feet away from me.

For several seconds, neither of us spoke.

I waited.

I expected anger.

Disappointment.

Perhaps even the cold reminder that I was now his wife and that my wishes no longer mattered.

Instead, he took a step back.

“Roseline,” he said quietly.

I looked at him.

“I won't push you.”

The words caught me off guard.

His gaze remained on mine.

“I won't force myself on you either.”

Something inside me shifted, but I refused to let him see it.

He continued.

“Allow me to prove that I am worthy of your love.”

My breath caught.

Dalton lowered his eyes briefly before looking back at me.

“I know you never agreed to this marriage.”

My fingers tightened around the fabric of my nightdress.

“Then why did you?”

The question slipped out before I could stop it.

For a moment, he was silent.

Then he smiled.

“Because on the first day we met, I fell in love with the woman wearing the red robe.”

I stared at him.

Of all the things I had expected him to say, that was not one of them.

“And if you are not ready to love me,” he continued, “then I will wait.”

I should have known then.

Perhaps my heart already knew.

But I had spent too many years protecting myself from disappointment to trust something as fragile as hope.

So, I turned away.

I went to bed.

And Dalton kept his promise.

Days became weeks.

Then weeks became months.

He never forced his way into my heart.

Instead, he stood patiently at its door.

Whenever my parents questioned why I seemed distant, Dalton would find a way to protect me.

“She is still adjusting,” he would say.

“She has had a long day.”

“Roseline needs time.”

He never allowed me to be humiliated for not being the wife everyone expected me to become.

And slowly, without realising it, I began to watch him.

I watched the way he listened when others spoke.

The way he treated the servants as though they were people rather than shadows in the palace.

The way his guards respected him without fearing him.

And when I visited his kingdom, I discovered something that changed everything.

Dalton ruled differently.

He listened to his people.

He questioned traditions that caused suffering.

He believed that a ruler was not meant to control every breath of the people, but to protect their right to live their own lives.

One evening, I found him standing alone on the palace balcony.

Below us, the lights of the kingdom glowed beneath the night sky.

“You would change the rules, wouldn't you?” I asked.

He turned towards me.

“If the rules are wrong, yes.”

My heart beat harder.

“What if the people disagree?”

“Then we listen to them.”

“And what if tradition stands in the way?”

Dalton stepped closer.

“Roseline, tradition should serve the people. The people should not spend their lives suffering just to serve tradition.”

For the first time, I looked at him and did not see the man my parents had chosen for me.

I saw a man I could choose for myself.

That night, something inside me finally broke.

Not my heart.

The walls around it.

I had spent my life believing that love would arrive with freedom.

I never expected that freedom itself would arrive through love.

When I finally embraced Dalton, there was no command behind his touch.

No expectation.

No reminder of duty.

Only a question in his eyes.

And for the first time in my life, the answer was mine to give.

I chose him.

Three weeks later, I discovered I was carrying his child.

I stood alone in my chamber, staring at the confirmation in my trembling hands.

Then I laughed.

A strange, breathless laugh.

And before I knew it, tears were running down my cheeks.

For years, I had prayed for happiness.

I had begged the gods to take me away from the life that had been chosen for me.

But when my answer finally came, I almost pushed it away.

I thought Dalton was another chain.

I thought marriage would be another prison.

I thought the crown would become heavier.

Instead, I found a man who looked at the princess everyone admired and asked to know the woman beneath the crown.

Years later, I would stand in the same palace hall where I had once walked towards a future I feared.

But this time, I was not alone.

My child stood beside me.

And when the time came for them to make their own choices, I remembered the promise I had made to myself as a frightened young princess.

I would never allow my children to live as prisoners of tradition.

I kept that promise.

My child would be free to choose who to love.

Free to choose their own path.

Free to say no.

And free to say yes.

As for me?

I was still a princess.

I still wore the crown.

I still carried responsibilities that could never be ignored.

But the crown no longer felt like a chain around my life.

Because I had finally learned something my younger self could never have imagined.

Sometimes, freedom is not running away from the life you were given.

Sometimes, it is finding the courage to change it.

And sometimes, the person standing at the end of the path you fear the most is not there to imprison you.

Sometimes, they are there to take your hand.

And show you that, for the first time in your life, you are free to choose.

Dalton was the choice I never wanted.

Until he became the love I never knew I had been waiting for.

title: The Night We Played Truth or Dare
excerpt: It was supposed to be just a game
content:
It was a few minutes past 10 p.m. My eyes were still wide open despite having a stressful day in school. I'd finished all my chores so I could use my mum's phone without interruption.

I got chatting with my stranger friend, and everything was going smoothly until he asked if we could play Truth or Dare. I agreed because I'd always heard my friends talk about their funny dare experiences.

After all, I wanted the experience too.

We started with truth. The questions were harmless.

"What's your favourite colour?"

"Who's your celebrity crush?"

"Have you ever had a boyfriend?"

We laughed through every answer, and somehow it made us even more comfortable with each other.

Then we switched to dares.

"Change your profile picture for five minutes."

"Send a random emoji."

Easy enough.

But as the game went on, the dares became more personal.

He asked me to send a picture. At first, it sounded innocent, so I did. Then another. Then another.

Before I knew it, the requests became uncomfortable.

He kept saying things like, "Come on, it's just a game," or, "Don't you trust me?"

I remember staring at my screen, wondering why I suddenly felt uneasy. I didn't want to seem rude or boring, but deep down, I knew I didn't want to do what he was asking.

So...

I refused.

The atmosphere changed almost immediately.

The friendly guy I'd spent weeks talking to suddenly felt like someone else. His replies became cold. The jokes disappeared. The warmth I'd grown used to was gone.

I kept wondering what I'd done wrong.

Was I overreacting?

Had I ruined the friendship over a simple game?

For the next few days, our conversations were never the same. The excitement faded, and so did the person I thought I knew.

I couldn't explain it, but I had a feeling that the game we'd just played had changed something between us.

I was right.

I just didn't know how much it would change.

To be continued...

title: CHAPTER 5: DEADMAN'S PASS
excerpt: The rear door of the wagon burst outward as Kael threw his weight against the iron latch, slamming the heavy wooden frame directly into the face of the first guard. The man stumbled back into the dust…
content:
The rear door of the wagon burst outward as Kael threw his weight against the iron latch, slamming the heavy wooden frame directly into the face of the first guard. The man stumbled back into the dust, clutching his bloody nose, his sword clattering against the gravel.

"Go!" Kael shouted.

Elara didn't hesitate. She scrambled out of the wagon, her skirt hitched up in one hand as she bolted toward the maze of jagged obsidian boulders lining Deadman’s Pass.

"Traitorous rats!" the lead guard bellowed, drawing his broadsword with a sharp ring of steel. "Kill the boy, take the girl's head!"

Kael leaped from the wagon bed, sweeping up the fallen guard's dropped sword. The blade was heavy, ill-balanced in his untrained grip, but he didn't need master swordsmanship—he needed raw momentum. As the second guard lunged at him with a spear, Kael ducked under the point, slammed his shoulder into the guard's midsection, and sent both of them tumbling over the embankment into the dirt.

Dust exploded around them. Kael kicked wildly, catching the guard in the knee before scrambling up the steep incline toward the shadow of the rocks.

Behind him, two horses neighed in panic as crossbow bolts were loaded.

"Elara!" Kael yelled, weaving through the stone pillars.

"Over here!" her voice echoed from a narrow crevice between two towering granite spires.

He slid between the tight rock walls just as a steel bolt struck the outer stone with a shower of sparks. Elara reached out, grabbing his arm and pulling him deeper into the shadowy, sulfur-scented gorge.

Outside, shouting guards echoed off the stone, but the pass was a labyrinth of dead drops and ancient dried riverbeds. The dusk light faded rapidly into ink-black night, and within minutes, the heavy boots of the guards grew distant, their frantic curses swallowed by the howling desert wind.

Hours later, the pair collapsed against a shelf of sandstone deep within the badlands. The air here was bitter and thin, smelling of roasted iron and ash. Below them, stretching across the vast desert valley, lay the low, flickering crimson lights of The Rust Sinks—the border hub of the southern outlaw territories.

Kael sat breathing heavily, resting his hand on the hilt of the stole broadsword. His palms were raw, his clothes ruined, but for the first time in his life, no noble or city warden stood over him.

Elara sat beside him, pulling her knees to her chest against the desert chill. She looked at the sprawling, lawless settlement below—a city built of rusted shipping containers, canvas tents, and salvaged timber.

"We made it out," she whispered, her voice a mix of awe and quiet terror. "We're dead to Cinder now."

"No," Kael said, his gaze fixed on the glowing sea of campfires below. "In Cinder, we were dead. Here, we're unknown."

He turned to look at her. In the moonlight, the silver ribbons in her hair were frayed and covered in dust, but her eyes held a fiercely sharp light.

"Down there, money doesn't care about bloodlines," Kael continued, leaning forward. "The men in the Sinks trade in weapons, stolen ore, and secrets. You know the legal loopholes, the noble trade routes, and how the Seven Families move their gold. I know how to navigate the gutters, read a liar, and survive on nothing."

Elara looked down at the rough town, then back at Kael. The gap between a highborn lady and a street sweeper had burned away back in the High Court. What remained were two survivors tied together by blood, law, and revenge.

"If we build something down there, Kael," Elara said softly, holding out her hand, "we build it together. No masters. No families."

Kael took her hand, his rough fingers closing firmly around hers.

"Together," Kael agreed. "We make them pay for every copper they took."

Below them, the Rust Sinks hummed with the sound of iron hammers and low laughter—a city of monsters and outlaws, waiting for its new masters.

title: CHAPTER 6: THE RUST SINKS
excerpt: The smell hit them before the noise did—a suffocating mix of burnt grease, cheap grain spirit, and the sour tang of damp iron. Kael and Elara descended into the valley as dawn bled across the jagged p…
content:
The smell hit them before the noise did—a suffocating mix of burnt grease, cheap grain spirit, and the sour tang of damp iron.

Kael and Elara descended into the valley as dawn bled across the jagged peaks behind them. The Rust Sinks was a sprawling sprawl of mud lanes, scrap-iron hovels, and towering structures built from sunken barges dragged inland from the river. There were no guards at the perimeter, only men leaning against rotted fence posts with crossbows resting casually across their knees.

Kael kept his stole broadsword sheathed at his hip, his hand resting lightly on the pommel. Elara pulled a frayed woolen cowl over her dark braids, keeping her face shadowed.

"We need shelter, weapons, and information," Kael whispered as they threaded through a crowded alley of stall keepers selling rusted nails, gray meat, and contraband silk. "And in a town like this, you don't look for work—you look for the man who owns the floor everyone stands on."

"That would be the Smelter," Elara replied quietly, her eyes darting across the street, taking in every sign, brand, and whisper. "I recognized the iron crest on the gate wagon back at the pass. It belongs to the Ironhead Syndicate. Down here, they control the ore trade and the black market routes into Cinder."

They turned a corner into a wide, muddy plaza dominated by The Slag Pit, a cavernous saloon built inside the hollow hull of an ancient iron warship. Smoke billowed from twin chimneys welded to the deck, and the rumble of bass-heavy lute music vibrated through the mud.

"Keep close," Kael said.

Inside, the heat was stifling. Dozens of heavily armed mercenaries, prospectors, and smugglers sat at long timber tables, dicing, drinking, and shouting over the din. At the far end of the hall, elevated on a platform carved from a massive boiler, sat a man broad as a furnace, his bare arms covered in dark, soot-stained tattoos.

That was Gharon "The Smelter" Vane—though he shared no blood with the noble Vanes of Cinder, he ruled the Rust Sinks with the same ruthless iron fist.

Two hulking enforcers stepped into Kael and Elara’s path before they reached the steps of the platform.

"State your name or turn around, rat," the taller enforcer growled, placing a massive hand against Kael's chest.

Kael didn't flinch. He reached up, grabbed the man's thumb, and twisted just enough to break the pressure, stepping into the guard's space. "Tell Gharon that two dead souls from Cinder have come to make him rich."

The saloon grew noticeably quieter around them. Gharon leaned forward on his iron throne, his small, dark eyes glinting with amusement beneath heavy brows. He raised a massive hand, waving his guards back.

"Dead souls from Cinder, you say?" Gharon's voice sounded like stones grinding together in a mill. He looked Kael up and down, then let his gaze fall on Elara, narrowing as he noticed the silver-threaded trim showing beneath her frayed cowl. "You wear fine silver under that dirt, girl. And the boy carries a High Court guard's standard broadsword. You aren't prospectors."

"We're the reason the High Court sealed the southern trade roads yesterday," Elara said, taking a step forward and throwing back her cowl. Her voice was cool, precise, and held the command of a noble raised to give orders. "I am Elara of House Oakwood. Or rather, I was."

A murmur ran through the tavern patrons nearby.

Gharon’s laughter boomed through the hull, deep and mocking. "A noble bird flew out of her golden cage and landed in my mud! The High Chancellor offered two hundred gold sovereigns for your heads this morning, My Lady. Why shouldn't I cut your throats and collect the bounty?"

"Because two hundred gold is pocket change for a man running a broken smuggling ring," Kael interjected, his voice carrying clearly across the room.

Gharon stopped laughing. His eyes locked onto Kael. "Watch your tongue, sweeper."

"It's the truth," Kael said, stepping onto the first wooden stair of the platform. "Your wagons are being raided at the Deadman's Pass by Vane House mercenaries. Your ore shipments are down thirty percent this month because you're using the old riverbeds. You have the men and the iron, but you don't know the High Court's patrol schedules."

Kael looked at Elara, who gave him a sharp nod.

"My father designed Cinder's southern trade defenses," Elara said evenly. "I know every shift change, every blind spot in the mountain forts, and every corrupt tax collector on the riverway. Hand us over for two hundred gold, and you stay a small-time boss in a mud hole. Give us ten percent of your shipping operations, and we will double your intake before the full moon."

Gharon stared at them in tense silence. The entire saloon seemed to hold its breath. A single wrong word would draw twenty blades.

Slowly, the crime lord leaned back into his throne, resting his chin on his bruised knuckles.

"Ten percent?" Gharon sneered softly. "You've got nerve for two dead kids in rags."

"We have nothing left to lose," Kael said, his hand remaining steady on his sword pommel. "And those are the most dangerous people you'll ever meet."

A long, agonizing moment passed before a brutal grin spread across Gharon’s soot-stained face. He picked up a wooden tankard and slammed it against his armrest.

"Bring them two plates of salt pork and a bottle of rye," Gharon barked to the barkeep. He pointed a thick, scarred finger at Kael and Elara. "You have until the full moon to show me my double. If you fail... I sell your bones back to Cinder by the pound."

Kael met the crime lord's stare without blinking. "Deal."

As they were shown to a table near the back, Elara looked at Kael, a faint, dark smile touching her lips. "That was reckless."

"It worked," Kael whispered back, sitting down across from her. "This is where it begins, Elara. We take his network, we take this town, and then we go back for Cinder."

title: CHAPTER 7: THE BLOOD IRON AMBUSH
excerpt: The rain in the high mountain pass did not fall—it whipped sideways, freezing as it hit the black rocks of Deadman’s Pass. Kael crouched behind a ridge of shattered granite, his leather coat soaked th…
content:
The rain in the high mountain pass did not fall—it whipped sideways, freezing as it hit the black rocks of Deadman’s Pass.

Kael crouched behind a ridge of shattered granite, his leather coat soaked through, his eyes fixed on the narrow mountain road below. Across the gorge, hidden beneath a canopy of pine branches and grey wool cloaks, Elara signaled with two sharp raises of her lantern—a faint red gleam obscured from the valley floor.

"Three wagons," Kael muttered to Jarek, the scarred Ironhead lieutenant sitting beside him. "Heavy escort. Twelve mounted guards carrying Vane repeating crossbows."

Jarek spat into the mud, wiping rain from his beard. "Too many, kid. Gharon sent us with eight men. We hit that convoy head-on, and Vane's guards will butcher us before we touch a single bar of raw silver."

"We're not hitting them head-on," Kael said, his voice quiet, steady, and cold as the rain. "We're going to let them destroy themselves."

He checked the heavy iron wrench tucked into his belt, alongside two black-powder charges Elara had prepared using sulfur from the Sinks and saltpeter stolen from the court's outer supply sheds.

For three weeks, Elara had analyzed the Vane House shipping manifests she had memorized from her father’s ledgers. She knew precisely which day the high-grade silver-iron ore left the mountain mines, which guard captain led the patrol, and—most importantly—where the wagon axles were prone to cracking under heavy loads.

Below, the heavy rumble of wooden wheels echoed through the canyon.

The Vane convoy appeared through the mist. At the center rode Captain Torvan—the same man who had locked Kael’s wrist cuffs on Cinder Street three weeks ago. He sat proudly atop a grey warhorse, wrapped in a blue mantle bearing the silver ship crest of House Vane.

Kael’s grip tightened around his weapon. The burn of the memory made his blood run hot, but he kept his breathing slow. Recklessness had almost gotten him hanged in Cinder; strategy would make him rich here.

He raised his hand. "Wait for it..."

The lead wagon crested the narrow wooden bridge spanning the Devil’s Teeth—a hundred-foot drop into jagged river rocks. The bridge was ancient, reinforced with Vane iron, but built on wood that had rotted from decades of mountain damp.

Elara’s lantern flashed twice more.

"Now," Kael whispered.

Jarek pulled the pin on a heavy timber log rigged to the rockface above. The log swung out over the gorge, smashing not into the guards, but into the support beams beneath the far side of the wooden bridge.

The timber groaned, splinters flying like shrapnel. The lead wagon’s front wheel dropped through the fractured planking, locking the entire convoy in place midway across the narrow bridge. Horses reared in panic; guards shouted, drawing their blades into the blinding rain.

"Guns up!" Captain Torvan bellowed, drawing his broadsword. "Protect the silver!"

Before the guards could form a perimeter, a sudden crack split the air—not thunder, but Elara’s black-powder charge blowing out the rear rock wall of the pass behind them. A rain of heavy gravel and boulders tumbled down, completely sealing the convoy's retreat.

They were trapped.

"Ironheads! Forward!" Kael roared, leaping over the ridge.

He slid down the muddy bank, dropping directly onto the driver’s bench of the second wagon. Before the driver could raise his whip, Kael struck him with the flat of his stolen sword, shoving him into the mud.

Torvan turned his warhorse, eyes wide with recognition as he saw Kael charging through the rain and smoke. "You? The sweeper?!"

"I told you I'd pay back my debts, Captain!" Kael yelled.

Torvan lunged with his broadsword, but Kael didn't try to parry the heavier blade. He ducked low, letting the steel slide past his shoulder, and jammed his iron wrench into the spokes of Torvan’s horse harness. The horse stumbled, throwing the captain heavily onto the slick cobblestones.

Kael was on him in an instant. He planted his boot on Torvan’s throat, holding the point of the stolen sword against the captain's visor.

Around them, the remaining Vane guards, surrounded by Ironhead men and cut off from escape, threw down their crossbows.

Torvan gasped for air under Kael’s boot, his eyes wide with disbelief and terror. "The... the court... will hunt you to the ends of the earth..."

Kael leaned down, his dark hair plastered to his forehead by the rain, his eyes gleaming with ruthless clarity.

"Tell Vance Vane that his silver didn't make it to Cinder," Kael whispered so only Torvan could hear. "And tell him the street sweeper he tried to hang is coming to buy his house."

He kicked Torvan’s helmet, knocking him unconscious, then turned to the wagons.

Jarek pried open the wooden crate on the second wagon with a crowbar. Inside lay row upon row of unrefined silver-iron ingots, gleaming dimly under the rain—worth at least five thousand gold sovereigns on the black market.

Jarek looked at the treasure, then at Kael, a new look of sheer respect in his eyes. "By the gods, kid... you actually did it."

Up on the ridge, Elara stepped out from the shelter of the pine trees, lowering her cowl. Their eyes met across the misty gorge. She gave him a slow, decisive nod.

They had their first fortune. And the rise of the untouchable had officially begun.

title: CHAPTER 8:  The Price of Power
excerpt: The high-grade silver-iron ore from Deadman’s Pass didn't go to Gharon’s smelters. It went straight into hidden mountain vaults that Elara had mapped out weeks before—vaults known only to her, Kael, a…
content:
The high-grade silver-iron ore from Deadman’s Pass didn't go to Gharon’s smelters. It went straight into hidden mountain vaults that Elara had mapped out weeks before—vaults known only to her, Kael, and a handpicked handful of Ironhead men whose loyalty had been bought with double wages and promises of a future beyond the mud.

For six months, Kael played the loyal lieutenant. Every haul brought back to The Slag Pit was generous enough to keep Gharon fat, drunk, and unsuspecting, but the true wealth—the high-purity silver ingots, the stolen court documents, the rare black-powder recipes—was quietly diverted.

While Gharon spent his coin on spirits, silver-gilded armor, and gaudy velvet coats, Elara turned their hidden stash into an invisible empire. She established a shadow ledger, buying up the debts of every tavern keeper, blacksmith, and smuggler captain in the Rust Sinks. Kael, meanwhile, walked the mud streets every night, learning the names of every miner, orphan, and discarded mercenary. Where Gharon ruled through beatings and extortion, Kael offered fair cuts, protection, and respect.

By autumn, the tide had turned. Gharon still wore the crown, but Kael held the kingdom.

The confrontation came on a night when the sulfur fogs rolled thick off the valley floor, blanketing the Rust Sinks in an eerie yellow gloom.

Inside The Slag Pit, the air was warm and loud. Gharon sat on his iron throne atop the hollow boiler, gnawing on a roasted pig leg, surrounded by his six personal bodyguards.

The heavy iron doors swung open with a slow, deliberate groan.

Kael walked in first. He wore a fitted coat of boiled leather lined with wolf fur, two fine-steel broadswords strapped to his back. Behind him came Elara, her dark hair braided with thin silver wire, clad in a sleek dark blue coat that mimicked the noble cuts of House Oakwood—not as a captive, but as an equal. Behind them marched thirty Ironhead fighters, including Jarek, all carrying loaded repeating crossbows.

The music died instantly. The clatter of dice ceased. The patrons scrambled toward the walls, leaving a wide, empty clearing in the center of the hall.

Gharon lowered his food, wiping grease from his beard with the back of a scarred hand. His small eyes narrowed as he took in the sight of Jarek and the armed men behind Kael.

"What is this, sweeper?" Gharon rumbled, his voice echoing off the iron hull. "You bring weapons into my hall?"

"Not your hall, Gharon," Kael said, stopping at the base of the iron stairs. His voice was calm, almost conversational, but it carried to every corner of the room. "Not anymore."

Gharon let out a harsh, bark-like laugh, though his eyes darted nervously toward his guards. "You think because you pulled off a few wagon raids you can stand on my floor and challenge me? I made you! I gave you a roof when Cinder threw you in the dirt!"

"You didn't make us," Elara said, stepping forward beside Kael, her voice cutting through the hall like chilled steel. "You charged us seventy percent interest on stale bread and let us do the work you were too cowardly to attempt yourself." She drew a thick leather ledger from beneath her coat and held it high. "This is the master ledger of the Rust Sinks. As of midnight, every mine owner, forge master, and mercenary guild in this valley owes their debt to us, not you. We bought your contracts, Gharon. You own nothing."

Gharon’s face flushed purple with rage. He slammed his fist onto his armrest, shaking the boiler frame. "Guards! Kill them! Kill them both!"

None of his six bodyguards moved.

One of them—a towering brute named Bram—stepped away from Gharon’s throne and lowered his sword tip to the floor. "Kael paid off my sister's debt to the medical house in Cinder last week, Gharon. He paid Jarek's men double for the pass raid. You haven't paid us in two months."

"Traitor!" Gharon roared. He lunged to his feet, pulling a massive war hammer from the rack behind his throne. "I’ll break your skull myself!"

Gharon charged down the iron steps, swinging the massive hammer with terrifying force.

Kael didn't draw a sword. He waited until the last second, stepping inside the hammer’s arc as the heavy iron head smashed into the wooden floorboards. Kael drove a sharp elbow into Gharon’s nose, feeling the cartilage break, followed by a sweeping kick to the back of Gharon’s knee.

The hulking crime lord hit the ground hard, rolling onto his back, gasping for breath. Before he could recover, Kael drew his right broadsword and pressed the cold, gleaming steel directly against Gharon’s throat.

The room was deathly quiet.

Gharon stared up into Kael’s dark, unyielding eyes. For the first time, he saw no street boy, no frightened fugitive. He saw a man who had looked death in the face and decided to conquer it.

"You have two choices, Gharon," Kael whispered, leaning down so only the fallen boss could hear. "You can take ten thousand silver sovereigns, walk out of this valley tonight, and never return. Or I can let Jarek and the men settle their old accounts with you right here."

Gharon swallowed heavily against the sharp edge of the blade. Sweat beaded on his forehead. "Ten thousand?" he rasped.

"Ten thousand," Kael repeated. "Consider it your pension."

Gharon’s shoulders slumped in defeat. "I'll take the coin."

Kael stepped back, sheathing his sword in one smooth motion. Two of Jarek’s men grabbed Gharon by his collar, dragging him off the platform toward the back doors to collect his payoff and his exile.

Kael walked up the iron steps and turned to face the crowded saloon. He mounted the high platform, looking out over the faces of outlaws, prospectors, and mercenaries who had once viewed him as a ragged nobody.

Elara joined him on the platform, standing at his right side.

"The Ironhead Syndicate is finished!" Kael announced, his voice ringing loud and clear through the iron hall. "Starting tonight, this town operates under The Black Pact. No more extortion. No more starving workers. You fight for us, you get paid fair, and you get protected!"

A cheer erupted from the crowd—first from Jarek and his men, then spreading like wildfire through the tavern until the whole ship shook with the roar of a hundred voices.

Elara looked at Kael, a rare, genuine smile gracing her lips. "So, Lord of the Sinks... what is the first decree of the Black Pact?"

Kael turned his gaze northward, toward the distant, cloud-shrouded peaks where Cinder lay in its comfortable, arrogant peace.

"We build," Kael said, his eyes burning with cold ambition. "We build mines, we build foundries, and we build an army. In two years, Elara, Cinder won't just hear our name—they will pay us for their very survival."

title: CHAPTER 9: The Shadow Empire
excerpt: Three years passed in the sulfur-choked valleys of the south, but to Cinder, the Black Reach remained nothing more than a graveyard for the damned. They did not know that the graveyard had blossomed i…
content:
Three years passed in the sulfur-choked valleys of the south, but to Cinder, the Black Reach remained nothing more than a graveyard for the damned.

They did not know that the graveyard had blossomed into a fortress.

Where rusted hovels once leaned against muddy alleys, stone foundries now rose six stories high, their massive chimneys pouring dark smoke into the grey sky day and night. The Rust Sinks was no longer a squalid outlaw camp; it was Vane-Reach, a booming industrial stronghold governed not by brute force, but by cold, calculated commerce.

Down in the lower vaults, water-driven hammers pounded raw iron and silver into ingots, weapons, and heavy machinery. Above them, high in a tower carved into the cliff face, sat the heart of the operation.

Elara unrolled a massive leather map across a polished oak table. Her dark hair was neatly styled, bound by silver filigree pins, and she wore a tailored coat of dark blue velvet lined with black sable. Across the table sat Kael.

The ragged, starved sweeper of Cinder Street was gone, replaced by a man broad of shoulder and sharp of eye. He wore a dark wool coat over fine chainmail, his dark hair cut short, and a heavy silver ring—engraved with an oak leaf entangled in iron chains—shining on his right hand.

"The northern reports came in this morning," Elara said, tapping a quill against a ledger. "House Vane’s iron mines in the Shattered Peaks are failing. Their yields dropped forty percent this quarter because of deep water flooding."

"And they can't afford the pumping engines from the Eastern Guilds," Kael said, leaning over the map, his fingers tracing the trade routes leading north to Cinder.

"Because we bought all the eastern Guild contracts last month through our puppet merchants in the capital," Elara replied, a faint smirk touching her lips. "Vance Vane is desperate. He’s taking loans from the High Court treasury just to keep his docks open."

"And what of your father?" Kael asked softly, his tone softening slightly.

Elara’s eyes flickered, but her voice remained steady. "House Oakwood is isolated. Without my marriage to Julian Vane, the alliance broke. My father refused to align with the Vanes after they humiliated him in court, and now Vance Vane is squeezing Oakwood trade routes out of spite. House Oakwood is on the brink of bankruptcy."

Kael studied her face. "Do you want me to crush them, or save them?"

"I want them to realize that the girl they discarded was the only thing keeping their house standing," Elara said, looking up at him. "My father threw me to the wolves to save his reputation. Now, he will have to bow to the wolves to buy his bread."

Before Kael could answer, a heavy knock sounded at the chamber door. Jarek stepped inside, his chest plate polished to a high sheen, holding a sealed parchment stamped with a royal wax emblem.

"Message from the capital, Chief," Jarek said, handing the letter to Kael. "Brought by a royal courier who looks like he hasn't slept in three days."

Kael broke the black wax seal and scanned the fine calligraphy. A dark, dangerous smile slowly spread across his face.

"What is it?" Elara asked, stepping beside him.

"The High Court of Cinder is hosting the Grand Winter Conclave in two weeks," Kael said, reading aloud. "Every noble house, master merchant, and foreign ambassador is required to attend. And because Cinder is facing an unprecedented iron shortage..." He turned the letter toward her. "...the High Chancellor has sent an official invitation to the mysterious 'Master of the Black Reach' to negotiate a royal supply contract."

Elara’s breath hitched. "They don't know who you are."

"They think I'm a ruthless warlord who took over the southern mines," Kael laughed softly, a low, cold sound. "They think they're inviting a wealthy barbarian to save their economy."

"If we go back..." Elara murmured, her hand coming to rest on his shoulder, "...the moment we step into that High Chamber, Vance Vane will recognize us. They will call for our execution."

Kael stood up, turning to face her. He reached out and gently took her hand, his thumb tracing the silver ring on her finger.

"Let them call for it," Kael said, his dark eyes burning with fierce conviction. "Three years ago, we left that court in chains, bleeding and nameless. This time, we enter with the entire city's wealth in our pockets. We own their debts, we own their iron, and we own their guards."

Elara looked into his eyes, feeling the pulse of absolute certainty radiating from him. The street boy who had once nodded to her over a pastry was now the most formidable man in the realm—and he belonged to her just as she belonged to him.

"When do we ride?" she asked.

Kael smiled—a sharp, deadly edge of white teeth.

"Prepare the gold carriages, Elara. It's time to go home."

title: CHAPTER 10: THE WINTER CONCLAVE
excerpt: The Great Keep of Cinder stood wrapped in mountain ice, its tall granite spires piercing the gray winter sky. High above the cobbles of Cinder Street—where snow now covered the cracks and gutter grime…
content:
The Great Keep of Cinder stood wrapped in mountain ice, its tall granite spires piercing the gray winter sky. High above the cobbles of Cinder Street—where snow now covered the cracks and gutter grime—carriages bearing the crests of the Seven Families rolled up the winding stone avenue toward the High Chamber.

Inside the grand hall, fires roared in massive marble hearths. Tables groaned under roast boar, sweet wines, and silver platters of spiced fowl. Nobles in velvet and ermine mingled with wealthy guild masters, their voices buzzing with anxious chatter. Beneath the laughter, panic hung thick in the air. The Vane iron mines were dry, the city’s treasury was empty, and rumors of a mysterious power in the south had reached every corner of the capital.

At the head table sat Lord Vance Vane, his face lined with age and stress, sipping dark wine beside Lord Oakwood, whose graying hair and frayed silk cuffs betrayed his family’s dwindling fortune.

"He won't come," Vance Vane muttered, slamming his goblet down. "This 'Master of the Reach' is an outlaw, a savage who lives in the mud. He won't risk coming north."

"He holds eighty percent of the realm's silver-iron, Vance," Lord Oakwood said quietly, his voice tired. "If he doesn't sell to us tonight, the city's foundries go cold by nightfall."

Before Vane could answer, the heavy iron-and-oak doors at the back of the chamber swung wide.

The hall fell dead silent.

A company of thirty heavy guards marched in first—not in the royal crimson of Cinder, but in polished black steel inlaid with gold filigree. They formed a double line, their halberds striking the marble floor in perfect unison.

Behind them walked a man and a woman.

The man was tall, broad-shouldered, and striking. He wore a coat of midnight-black velvet lined with silver fox fur, over a tunic stitched with gold thread. At his side hung a sword with an obsidian pommel—a weapon fit for a king. Beside him walked a woman of breathtaking elegance, her dark hair braided with diamonds and silver ribbons, her sapphire-blue dress sweeping the polished stone behind her.

A gasp echoed across the high gallery.

Lord Oakwood’s wine glass slipped from his fingers, shattering on the stone floor. Vance Vane stood up so violently his chair crashed backward.

"It... it can't be," Vane breathed, his face draining of all color.

Kael walked to the center of the hall, stopping right on the circular bronze crest where he had stood three years ago in heavy iron chains. Elara stepped up beside him, her posture flawless, her gaze sweeping over the frozen faces of the nobility with cool indifference.

The High Chancellor stumbled forward from his dais, clutching his golden chain of office. "Who... who are you? Guards! Who permitted—"

"You sent the invitation, High Chancellor," Kael said. His voice was deep, smooth, and commanded every ear in the room without raised volume. "I am the Master of the Black Reach. Owner of the Southern Foundries, Lord of Vane-Reach, and keeper of Cinder's iron."

He paused, a dark, sharp smile touching his lips.

"Though three years ago, when you sentenced me on this very stone, you called me Kael the sweeper."

Shouts burst out across the gallery.

"Traitor!" Vance Vane roared, pointing a trembling, ink-stained finger. "He is an escaped convict! A murderer! Guards, seize him! Seize them both!"

Not a single black-clad guard moved. Even the royal court guards hesitated, looking nervously at the thirty heavily armed men standing behind Kael.

"On what charge, Lord Vane?" Elara asked smoothly, taking a single step forward. Her voice echoed off the white granite walls. "Murder? The same murder you framed him for to hide your illegal trade deals with the Eastern Guilds?"

"Lies!" Vane shouted, though sweat had broken out across his forehead. "You were exiled under the Pact!"

"And under the Pact," Elara countered, drawing a thick stack of parchment sealed with royal wax from her coat, "an exiled party who returns bearing proof of innocence and holding title to royal trade land may demand immediate review by the High Magistrates."

She tossed the documents onto the Chancellor's podium.

"Inside those pages," Elara continued, her hazel eyes locking onto her father, who stared at her as if looking at a ghost, "are the original manifests signed by Vance Vane's private clerk, dated three days before Thomas Vane's death. He killed his own son for the insurance payout from the Merchant Guild when his mines began to fail."

The chamber erupted into chaos. Magistrates scrambled toward the podium to inspect the seals; nobles whispered frantically; Lord Vane’s jaw worked silently as he backed toward his seat.

"This court is a farce!" Vane bellowed, reaching for his dagger. "I am a Lord of the Seven Families!"

Before Vane could draw his weapon, Kael moved. In a blur of motion, he crossed the distance, grabbed Vane by the wrist, and twisted it until the dagger clattered to the floor. Kael slammed the noble down onto his knees in front of the high bench.

"You took my freedom, Vane," Kael whispered into the old lord's ear, his hand gripping the man's neck with crushing force. "You took her name. You thought we were dirt under your boots."

Kael looked up, addressing the entire court—the Magistrates, the nobles, and the silent guards.

"As of this morning," Kael declared, "I have purchased every debt note held by House Vane and House Oakwood. The mines, the docks, the ships, and this very hall are secured under my name. Cinder belongs to the Reach now."

The High Chancellor looked at the verified documents in his hands, his fingers shaking, then looked down at the kneeling, sobbing Vance Vane.

"Lord Vance Vane," the Chancellor said, his voice trembling. "By order of the High Court... you are stripped of your title and placed under arrest for murder and high treason."

Royal guards finally moved, dragging the screaming Vane away through the side doors—the very doors Kael and Elara had been dragged through three years prior.

Silence returned to the High Chamber.

Lord Oakwood stepped down from his bench, looking at Elara with eyes full of sorrow, shame, and awe. "Elara... my daughter..."

Elara looked at her father. There was no hatred in her face, only the quiet distance of someone who had outgrown the smallness of noble politics.

"House Oakwood will retain its manor, Father," she said softly. "The debts are cleared. But my home is in the south now."

She turned back to Kael. He reached out his hand, and she took it—their fingers intertwining, the silver ring on his hand touching hers.

Together, they turned their backs on the Seven Families and walked out of the High Chamber, not as fugitives escaping into the night, but as the new rulers of the realm.

title: Why Most Nigerians Struggle to Save Money — Even When They Earn
excerpt: Your income may not be the only problem—here’s why your money disappears before you get the chance to save.
content:
The problem isn’t always how much you earn. Sometimes, it’s what happens to your money after payday.

You receive your salary, freelance payment, business income, or side-hustle earnings.

For a moment, you feel comfortable.

Then you pay for food.

Data.

Transport.

Bills.

A few unexpected expenses.

Maybe you send some money to family.

Then suddenly, you check your account and wonder:

“Where did all my money go?”

If this sounds familiar, you’re not necessarily bad with money. But you may have a system that makes saving almost impossible.

Here are some of the biggest reasons Nigerians struggle to save — and what you can do about them.

1. You Try to Save What’s Left Over

This is one of the biggest mistakes.

The thinking usually goes:

“I’ll spend what I need to spend, then save whatever remains.”

The problem?

There may be nothing left.

Instead, try reversing the process.

When money enters your account, decide on a small amount to save before you start spending.

It doesn’t have to be ₦50,000.

Even ₦1,000 or ₦2,000 is a starting point.

The important thing is creating the habit.

2. Small Expenses Don’t Feel Like Expenses

₦500 doesn’t seem like much.

Neither does ₦1,000.

But repeated spending can become significant.

Maybe you buy snacks several times a week.

You subscribe to services you barely use.

You order food when you could have prepared something cheaper.

You make frequent impulse purchases.

None of these expenses necessarily looks serious on its own.

The problem is what happens when you add them together over a month.

That’s why tracking your spending can be eye-opening.

For one month, write down every naira you spend.

You might discover that some of your money isn’t disappearing mysteriously.

You’re simply spending it in places you weren’t paying attention to.

3. Lifestyle Inflation Can Eat Your Extra Income

Imagine you start earning more money.

Instead of saving some of the increase, your lifestyle immediately becomes more expensive.

Better phone.

More expensive meals.

More subscriptions.

More outings.

More unnecessary purchases.

Your income increases, but your savings don’t.

This is called lifestyle inflation.

There’s nothing wrong with enjoying your money.

The problem is when every increase in income automatically creates an increase in expenses.

When your income rises, consider increasing your savings before increasing your lifestyle.

4. You Don’t Have an Emergency Fund

One unexpected expense can completely destroy months of saving.

A medical bill.

A broken phone.

An urgent trip.

A family emergency.

A sudden school expense.

Without emergency savings, you may have to borrow money or empty the money you were saving for another goal.

You don’t need to build a huge emergency fund immediately.

Start small.

Your first goal could simply be building enough money to handle one unexpected expense without completely emptying your account.

Then gradually increase it.

5. You Treat Savings Like Spending Money

You receive money and keep everything in the same account.

Then you see the balance.

You think:

“I have ₦80,000.”

But perhaps ₦20,000 of that is supposed to be savings.

If you don’t separate the money mentally — or physically — it becomes much easier to spend.

Consider creating separate places for:

Daily spending

Savings

Emergency money

Specific goals

When money has a purpose, you’re less likely to treat every naira as available spending money.

6. You Think You Need a Huge Income Before You Can Save

This is another trap.

Someone earning ₦100,000 might say:

“I can’t save because I don’t earn enough.”

Someone earning ₦300,000 might say exactly the same thing.

Of course, low income can genuinely make saving difficult. If most of your income is already going toward basic needs, there may not be much room to save.

But whenever you have some flexibility, developing the habit of saving something can still be useful.

The amount matters.

But consistency matters too.

Saving ₦1,000 regularly is better than repeatedly planning to save ₦20,000 and never doing it.

Try the “Save First” Method

Here’s a simple experiment.

The next time you receive money, immediately set aside a small percentage or fixed amount.

For example:

Income: ₦50,000

Savings: ₦5,000

Available to spend: ₦45,000

Don’t wait until the end of the month.

Save first.

Then build your spending around what’s left.

If ₦5,000 isn’t realistic, start with ₦1,000.

If your income changes every month, use a percentage instead of a fixed amount.

The goal isn’t to copy someone else’s number.

The goal is to create a system that works with your actual income and expenses.

Don’t Forget Your Real-Life Responsibilities

Personal finance advice sometimes makes saving sound ridiculously easy.

“Just save half your income.”

For many Nigerians, that’s simply unrealistic.

People may have rent, school expenses, transportation, food, family responsibilities, healthcare costs, and other obligations.

So don’t compare your financial situation to someone posting their savings journey online.

Look at your own numbers.

Ask:

What comes in?

What must go out?

What can I reduce?

What can I save consistently?

What financial goal am I working toward?

That’s a much more useful starting point.

Your Goal Isn’t Just to Save — It’s to Build Financial Breathing Room

Saving money isn’t about refusing to enjoy your life.

It’s about giving yourself options.

When you have some money set aside, an unexpected expense doesn’t have to become a disaster.

When you save toward a specific goal, you don’t necessarily have to rely on debt when the time comes.

And when you consistently keep part of your income, you begin to develop something more valuable than a bigger bank balance:

financial discipline.

Final Thought

You don’t have to become rich before you start managing money properly.

Start with what you have.

Track where your money goes.

Save before spending when possible.

Separate your savings from everyday spending.

Build an emergency cushion gradually.

And whenever your income increases, try not to increase your expenses at exactly the same speed.

Because sometimes, earning more isn’t the first solution.

Learning to keep more of what you earn can be just as important.

title: Why Your Online Side Hustle Isn’t Making You Money — 6 Mistakes Nigerians Keep Making
excerpt: You’re signing up, applying, and trying—but your online income still isn’t growing. Here’s what might be holding you back.
content:
Getting started online is easy. Turning it into consistent income is where most people get stuck.

You’ve probably seen people online saying they make money from freelancing, testing websites, writing, content creation, remote jobs, or other online side hustles.

So you try it.

You create an account, complete your profile, maybe even pass a few tests — and then…

Nothing.

No clients. No tasks. No meaningful income.

Before you conclude that online work is a scam or that you simply “aren’t lucky,” check whether you’re making one of these common mistakes.

1. You’re Trying Too Many Platforms at Once

One of the biggest mistakes beginners make is signing up for everything they see.

Today it’s freelance writing. Tomorrow it’s surveys. The next day it’s website testing. Then voice recording. Then another app promising easy money.

The problem?

You end up spending your time creating accounts instead of developing a skill or actually earning.

Instead of joining 20 platforms, choose 2–4 opportunities that genuinely match your skills and learn how they work.

If you’re a writer, for example, concentrate on writing-related opportunities rather than constantly jumping between unrelated platforms.

2. You Don’t Check How You’ll Get Paid

This is especially important for Nigerians.

A platform can have hundreds of tasks available, but that doesn’t automatically mean it’s useful to you.

Before spending hours working on a platform, check:

  • What is the minimum withdrawal?

  • What payment methods are available?

  • Does it support Nigerians?

  • How long do withdrawals take?

  • Are there verification requirements?

  • Are there fees?

Imagine completing ₦20,000 worth of work only to discover that you can’t withdraw the money using a payment method available to you.

Always investigate the payment system first.

3. You Expect Money Immediately

Another problem is unrealistic expectations.

You sign up today and expect your first ₦50,000 tomorrow.

Sometimes that happens, but it’s not the normal experience for most beginners.

Building an online income can involve creating a portfolio, learning a platform, applying for opportunities, getting rejected, improving your work, and eventually getting your first client or payment.

Your first goal shouldn’t necessarily be:

“How can I make ₦100,000 this week?”

A better first goal might be:

“How can I earn my first ₦5,000 and understand exactly how I earned it?”

Once you understand the process, you can work on increasing it.

4. You Have No Proof That You Can Do the Work

If you’re offering writing, graphic design, video editing, voice-over, social media management, or another service, simply saying “I can do it” may not be enough.

Clients want to see evidence.

That’s where a portfolio comes in.

And you don’t necessarily need previous clients to create one.

For example, if you want to become a copywriter, create:

  • A sample advertisement

  • A sample email campaign

  • A social media post

  • A product description

  • A landing-page section

Put your best examples somewhere potential clients can easily see them.

Show people what you can do instead of only telling them.

5. You Keep Doing Free Work Without a Strategy

Free work can sometimes help you gain experience, but there’s a difference between building experience and continuously working for free.

If you’ve already created several samples, you should start looking for opportunities where your work can generate income.

Don’t fall into the cycle of:

“I’ll work for free until someone notices me.”

Instead, use free samples to demonstrate your ability, then start pitching your services.

Even your first paid job doesn’t have to be huge.

A ₦5,000 job is still a paid job.

The goal is to move from practice → proof → paid work → repeat clients.

6. You Stop Too Early

This might be the biggest one.

You apply to five opportunities.

Nothing happens.

You conclude:

“Online work doesn’t work.”

But five applications aren’t enough data to make that conclusion.

You may need to apply to dozens of opportunities before finding the right one.

You may also discover that your profile needs improvement, your portfolio isn’t strong enough, or you’re targeting the wrong type of client.

Instead of quitting after rejection, ask:

What can I improve before my next application?

That’s how the process becomes easier.

The Real Secret: Stop Chasing Every Opportunity

Making money online isn’t necessarily about finding a magical website that pays everyone.

It’s about finding something that matches your skills, location, payment options, and available time — then getting better at it.

For Nigerians, payment compatibility and platform availability matter just as much as the advertised earning potential.

So before joining another “easy money” platform, pause and ask yourself:

What skill am I actually building?

Who would pay me for it?

How will I receive the money?

And what proof do I have that I can deliver?

The internet has created thousands of ways to work and earn.

But the people who make progress aren’t necessarily the ones who discover the most platforms.

They’re often the ones who pick a direction, build something valuable, and keep improving.

Your next ₦10,000 might not come from finding another app.

It might come from getting better at something you can already do.

title: Why Does Everyone on LinkedIn Have Something to Celebrate?
excerpt: Scroll through LinkedIn for five minutes and you might start wondering if you’re the only person who hasn’t achieved something.If someone hasn’t gotten a new jo…
content:
Scroll through LinkedIn for five minutes and you might start wondering if you’re the only person who hasn’t achieved something.

If someone hasn’t gotten a new job, they just got promoted, if not they completed another certification or just hit 10,000 followers, another person won an award, landed their dream opportunity or is celebrating a career milestone.

Of course, we’re expected to clap for everyone and celebrate with them because you won’t grow if you don’t engage with posts, but that’s all the post your feed is showing you 🫠.

But it got me wondering when LinkedIn became a place where almost every post is a celebration of achievement. I thought we’re there to connect professionally and to get jobs/clients.

There’s nothing wrong with celebrating your wins. In fact, people should be proud of their progress.

But when your entire feed consists of other people’s achievements, it can create a strange impression that everyone is constantly moving forward while you’re standing still.

So, is this simply what professional networking looks like now, or have we turned LinkedIn into a scoreboard where everyone is trying to prove they’re winning?

What’s an AI Inference Engine, Anyway?

You hear about AI “training” that’s when a model is fed massive amounts of data to learn patterns. But once the model is trained, it needs to actually do something. That’s where the inference engine comes in.

Think of training like learning to ride a bike. You wobble, fall, practice, and eventually your brain figures out how to balance. Inference is the moment you a bike and just ride no thinking, just doing. It takes the trained model, real-world data. You type a question into a chatbot, and the inference engine runs the model to predict the most likely helpful answer.

Inference is everywhere. When Netflix suggests your next binge, when your phone autocompletes a text, or when a camera spots a pedestrian that’s inference in action. It’s the whole point of AI: making smart decisions right now, not just during training.

But there’s a catch. Inference needs to be fast and efficient. Training can churn away for days on massive server farms, but inference often happens on your phone or a tiny sensor. And for bigger AI models, even the most powerful devices struggle. That’s where GMI Cloud comes in.

GMI Cloud provides the infrastructure that makes inference engines actually usable at scale. Instead of buying and maintaining your own expensive GPU servers, you can rent them through GMI Cloud.
