title: Poor people are better off than middle class.
excerpt: NEPO VS LAPO VS MIDDLE CLASS
content:
People who were born poor are better off than people who were born middle class.

Hear me out.

Let me rephrase, life favors NEPO babies and LAPO babies more than those who fall somewhere in between.

NEPO babies have life mostly figured out for them. They don’t necessarily have to worry about money while chasing their dreams, no matter how bizarre those dreams might be.

They can say, “I want to be an artist,” or “I want to start this weird business,” and actually give it a shot without worrying about how they’ll pay their bills next month.

Then you have LAPO babies, the people who were born poor. They have to fight their way out of poverty. And because of that, they often become strong-willed, motivated and extremely determined to change their circumstances.

Most times, they put their dreams on hold and chase money with everything they’ve got and guess what?, many of them eventually break through.

That’s why we hear so many “grass to grace” stories.

But then there’s the middle class child, the ones who didn’t grow up rich, but they also didn’t grow up poor.

There was food on the table, clothes on their backs, their school fees were paid and most of all, they were comfortable.

However, that can make leaving their comfort zone very hard because what exactly are they running from?

They have enough to survive, there’s no need for dreaming big. They just need a safe job with a great retirement plan and health insurance. If they have a business idea, they postpone it and tell themselves that they’ll pursue that dream “when things are better.”

Before you know it, years have passed and they have nothing substantial to show for it.

So, if you had to choose, would you rather be born rich, poor, or middle class? And why?

title: My first Deal with a Devil
excerpt: ‘Him who makes a deal with the devil usually gets what he wants but might never enjoy what he gets.’ That was what my grandmother told me when I was young.
content:
I woke up early this morning with a lot of zeal. I had a nice cold shower. Washing myself was 10% less stressful than usual, but I couldn’t quite put my finger on it. I dressed up in my best suit. I looked damn fabulous. For some reason,  walking down the road to take a bus to my new place of work was quite easier than usual. While on the bus, I was also way more comfortable than usual. I still couldn’t put my finger on it.

AYOCORP is the biggest law firm in my State. I’m replacing the old manager today. That horny old bastard was let go on multiple charges of sexual harassment .

The pay was good, too good, my PA was sexy as hell too. Oh, life’s good, real good.

“Oh, I gotta pee”. Shouldn’t have taken all that coffee this morning, I thought as I went into the rest room. I unbuckled my belt, zipped down my trouser, and then it dawned on me: I can’t put my finger on it ‘Literally’.

“Where the fuck is my Penis, and my bloody balls”. I panicked and tried to scream, but someone or something covered my mouth and whispered into my ears

“Yeah, about that. Remember when you made a deal with us for this new job you have? Exactly, this is the price to pay. Don’t panic too much, you have a little pee hole down there to use. You just gotta kiss any other attachments goodbye”

 

 

 

Note: No AI was used in the writing of this short story

title: Stop Trying To Kill The Version of You That's Just Hurting
excerpt: The hardest war to win is the one you wage against your own self.
content:
There is a version of you living in the back of your mind that you are constantly at war with.

It’s the version that stays awake at 2:00 AM, counting every mistake, every awkward thing you've said to people, and every reason why you aren't enough. You look in the mirror and treat yourself like an intruder, picking apart your face, your choices, and the space you take up, wondering why you can't just be better, enough or different.

You spend so much energy trying to evict your own inner self. You split yourself in two: the person you pretend to be for the world, and the person you punish in private for not measuring up to the standards of the world.

But the reality is that you cannot hate yourself into a healing process. Every time you tear yourself down to please someone else or punish yourself for being human, you are just handing weapons to the people who want to break you.

At some point, you have to stop fighting your own inner self. You have to look at that exhausted, complicated person in the mirror and drop the weapons, even if you're messy and even if you're broken. Because nobody else can save you from yourself until you decide you are worth defending.

When was the last time you forgave yourself for just trying to figure life out?

title: Modern Cryptography Essentials for Web Developers: Hashes, Signatures, and Public Keys
excerpt: Understand how cryptographic hashing (Argon2, bcrypt), asymmetric keypairs (RSA, Ed25519), and JWT digital signatures protect web applications.
content:
Modern Cryptography Essentials for Web Developers: Hashes, Signatures, and Public Keys

Cryptography is the bedrock of online trust, authentication, and secure communications. Developers must understand the fundamental difference between encoding, symmetric encryption, asymmetric encryption, and cryptographic hashing.

1. Secure Password Storage: Why SHA-256 is Inadequate

General-purpose hash algorithms (like MD5, SHA-1, and SHA-256) are designed to be fast. Because GPUs can compute billions of SHA-256 hashes per second, they are vulnerable to brute-force dictionary attacks. Always use slow, memory-hard key derivation functions: Argon2id or bcrypt with salt rounds ≥ 10.

2. Asymmetric Cryptography & Public Key Signatures

Asymmetric cryptography uses mathematical keypairs: a Private Key (kept secret by the server) and a Public Key (distributed freely). Signatures generated with the private key can be mathematically verified by anyone using the public key (e.g. RS256 / EdDSA JWT tokens).

title: Mastering Redis: Caching Strategies, Distributed Locks, and Cache Invalidation
excerpt: A deep dive into caching patterns: Cache-Aside, Write-Through, Cache Stampede prevention with probabilistic early expiration, and distributed Redlock mechanics.
content:
Mastering Redis: Caching Strategies, Distributed Locks, and Cache Invalidation

Redis (Remote Dictionary Server) is the industry standard for in-memory data storage, sub-millisecond caching, session management, and distributed coordination. Understanding caching topologies is critical to preventing database stampedes during traffic surges.

1. The Cache-Aside (Lazy-Loading) Pattern

In Cache-Aside, the application first queries Redis. On a cache hit, data is returned instantly. On a cache miss, the application loads the data from PostgreSQL, populates Redis with an expiration TTL, and returns the result.

2. Preventing Cache Stampedes (Dog-Piling)

When a popular cached item expires, thousands of concurrent requests can simultaneously query the underlying database, overwhelming it. Mitigate this with Probabilistic Early Expiration (XFetch algorithm) or mutex locks:

async function getCachedPostWithLock(slug: string) {
  const cached = await redis.get(`post:${slug}`);
  if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached);

  // Acquire distributed mutex lock so only 1 worker hits the DB
  const lock = await redis.set(`lock:post:${slug}`, "1", "NX", "EX", 5);
  if (lock) {
    const post = await db.fetchPostBySlug(slug);
    await redis.set(`post:${slug}`, JSON.stringify(post), "EX", 3600);
    await redis.del(`lock:post:${slug}`);
    return post;
  } else {
    // Wait 50ms and retry from cache
    await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 50));
    return getCachedPostWithLock(slug);
  }
}

title: As AI Becomes Better at Thinking, What Should We Be Learning?
excerpt: Influence of Ai on human behaviour
content:
There was a time when being “smart” meant knowing things.

You were the person who remembered the formula.

You knew the definition.

You could write a well-structured essay without checking Google.

You could solve the problem on the board while everyone else was still copying the question.

Knowing things gave you an advantage.

Then the internet arrived.

Suddenly, information became cheap.

You didn't have to memorize everything. You could search for it.

Then came Google.

Then YouTube.

Then online courses.

And now, AI.

Today, you can ask a machine to explain quantum physics like you're five, write a business proposal, analyze a spreadsheet, generate ten marketing angles, debug your code, summarize a 50-page report, or help you plan your next career move.

And it can do it in seconds.

So we're entering an interesting period.

The things we spent years learning are becoming things machines can increasingly do for us.

That should change what we teach.

It should change what we practice.

And, more importantly, it should change what we consider valuable.

Because if AI keeps getting better at thinking, what exactly should humans be learning?

I have a few strong opinions about this.

---

First, we need to stop treating information as intelligence.

This distinction matters.

Information is knowing what.

Intelligence, at least in the human sense, involves knowing what to do with it.

Imagine two people are given the same research report.

One can summarize every page.

The other asks:

“What does this mean for our business?”

Then:

“What are we not seeing?”

Then:

“What decision should we make based on this?”

The first person knows the information.

The second person knows how to use it.

AI is becoming extraordinarily good at the first part.

That means the second part becomes more important.

Don't just learn facts.

Learn how to interpret them.

Don't just collect information.

Learn how to make decisions from it.

Don't just know more.

Learn to see better.

---

1. Learn how to ask better questions

This may sound simple.

It isn't.

A lot of people think prompting AI means learning the right collection of magic words.

“Act as an expert…”

“Give me 10…”

“Make it professional…”

“Use a conversational tone…”

That's useful, but it misses the bigger skill.

The real advantage is understanding what you actually need to ask.

Imagine you're a founder whose sales have dropped.

A weak question is:

> “How do I increase sales?”

A better question is:

> “Our traffic has increased by 30%, but conversions have dropped. What possible explanations should I investigate?”

Now you've given the problem structure.

You're no longer asking for random advice.

You're directing the investigation.

This is why curiosity matters.

People who ask better questions will often get better results from the same AI tools.

AI doesn't eliminate the need for thinking. It raises the standard for thinking.

---

2. Learn critical thinking, because AI can be confidently wrong

Here's one of the most dangerous things about AI:

It can give you a terrible answer in a very convincing voice.

No hesitation.

No awkward pause.

No “I'm not sure.”

Just:

Here are five reasons why…

And you're sitting there thinking:

“Wow. This thing knows what it's talking about.”

Except it doesn't.

Sometimes.

That's why blindly trusting AI is not intelligence.

It's outsourcing your brain.

If AI gives you an answer, you should be able to ask:

How do we know this is true?

What evidence supports it?

What could make this wrong?

What information is missing?

What would change the conclusion?

These questions are not becoming obsolete.

They're becoming survival skills.

The better AI gets at producing convincing answers, the better humans need to become at evaluating them.

---

3. Learn judgment

This is different from knowledge.

And I think we're going to underestimate its value.

Imagine AI gives you three possible strategies for your company.

Strategy A is cheap and fast.

Strategy B is expensive but potentially transformative.

Strategy C is safe but unlikely to create significant growth.

AI can compare them.

It can calculate.

It can create projections.

It can even recommend one.

But somebody still has to decide.

And that decision isn't purely mathematical.

You have to consider your risk tolerance.

Your people.

Your values.

Your timing.

Your customers.

Your resources.

Your reputation.

Sometimes the “best” decision on paper isn't the best decision for you.

That's judgment.

AI can give you options. Humans still have to live with the consequences.

So learn to make decisions.

Not just gather recommendations.

---

4. Learn creativity, but don't confuse creativity with generating ideas

This one is especially important for writers and marketers.

AI can generate 100 headlines in seconds.

100 business ideas.

100 social media posts.

100 names for your new company.

So if your definition of creativity is:

> “I can come up with lots of ideas.”

We're in trouble.

Because machines are very good at that.

Real creativity is more complicated.

It's noticing something other people overlooked.

It's combining two unrelated ideas.

It's understanding a person's experience deeply enough to describe it in a way that makes them say:

“I've never heard anyone put it like that.”

It's knowing that the obvious idea isn't always the interesting one.

A machine can give you possibilities.

You need taste to choose the possibility worth pursuing.

That's why I believe taste will become one of the most underrated skills of the AI era.

When everyone can produce content, design, images and ideas quickly, the differentiator won't simply be production.

It will be:

“Do you know what's actually good?”

---

5. Learn storytelling

This is where humans have a serious advantage.

Think about the difference between these two statements:

> “Our product increased productivity by 40%.”

And:

> “Every Monday morning, our team spent nearly two hours trying to figure out what everyone was working on. By Friday, we were still chasing updates. We built the product because we were tired of working like that.”

Same basic idea.

Completely different experience.

Facts inform.

Stories make people care.

AI can help you structure a story.

It can suggest a hook.

It can identify an emotional arc.

But storytelling isn't just arranging sentences.

It's understanding people.

It's understanding tension.

It's knowing what detail to reveal and what to leave out.

It's knowing that sometimes the most powerful sentence isn't the cleverest one.

It's the most honest one.

And as AI-generated content becomes everywhere, human experiences will become more valuable, not less.

Your mistakes.

Your observations.

Your weird experiences.

Your perspective.

Your story.

That's material a machine cannot authentically live for you.

---

6. Learn communication

We often think communication means speaking well.

It doesn't.

Good communication means making another person understand what you mean.

That sounds obvious.

Yet watch how often smart people explain simple ideas in complicated language.

They know the subject.

They just can't make you understand it.

That's a problem.

In an AI-heavy world, the ability to simplify complexity will become incredibly valuable.

Can you explain a complicated business problem to a customer?

Can you explain a technical concept to a non-technical executive?

Can you persuade without manipulating?

Can you disagree without turning the conversation into a war?

Can you write something that sounds like a human being actually wrote it?

Those aren't minor skills.

They're career skills.

The smartest person in the room isn't always the most valuable person in the room. Sometimes it's the person who can make everyone else understand what the smartest person was trying to say.

---

7. Learn emotional intelligence

Here's another uncomfortable truth:

AI may become extremely good at understanding human language.

That doesn't mean humans are becoming better at understanding humans.

We still struggle to listen.

We interrupt.

We assume.

We react emotionally.

We misunderstand tone.

We send angry messages we later regret.

We confuse being right with being effective.

Technology doesn't fix those problems.

People do.

And the more digital our lives become, the more valuable genuine human connection may become.

People will still want to work with people they trust.

Buy from people they like.

Follow people they believe.

Hire people who understand them.

Leadership will still require empathy.

Sales will still require trust.

Management will still require emotional intelligence.

You cannot automate your way out of being human.

---

8. Learn how to learn

This might be the biggest one.

Because the problem with the AI era isn't simply that AI can do more.

It's that the definition of valuable skills will keep changing.

The skill that makes you employable today might not be the skill that makes you valuable five years from now.

So don't build your identity around one tool.

Learn the principles behind the tools.

Don't just learn one writing software.

Learn how to write.

Don't just learn one AI platform.

Learn how to research, evaluate, experiment and adapt.

Don't just memorize a process.

Understand why the process works.

Because tools change.

Platforms disappear.

Algorithms change.

Job descriptions change.

But the ability to learn survives all of them.

---

And here's where I disagree with a lot of AI advice

We keep telling people:

“Learn AI or you'll be left behind.”

I think that's incomplete.

Yes, learn AI.

Understand it.

Use it.

Experiment with it.

But don't spend all your energy learning how to make machines do everything for you while neglecting the abilities that make you valuable.

If AI writes your emails, can you still communicate?

If AI gives you ideas, can you still think?

If AI researches the market, can you still question its conclusions?

If AI makes your presentation, can you still tell the story?

If AI gives you five options, can you still make the decision?

If AI does your first draft, can you still recognize bad writing?

That is the real test.

---

The future isn't humans vs. AI

I don't think the most useful question is:

“What can humans do that AI can't?”

Because that question assumes the list will remain fixed.

It won't.

AI will probably continue crossing boundaries we once considered uniquely human.

So instead, ask:

“What kind of human do I need to become in a world where machines can do more?”

For me, the answer looks something like this:

Learn to question, not just answer.

Learn to think, not just retrieve.

Learn to judge, not just recommend.

Learn to create, not just generate.

Learn to communicate, not just produce words.

Learn to connect, not just engage.

Learn to adapt, not just specialize.

And perhaps most importantly:

Learn to remain curious.

Because I don't think AI makes learning less important.

I think it makes learning more important.

The difference is that we're moving from a world where your value often came from what you knew to one where your value increasingly comes from what you can do with what you know.

AI can help you get the information.

It can help you process it.

It can even help you think through it.

But you still have to decide what matters.

You still have to choose.

You still have to care.

You still have to create meaning.

And you still have to be responsible for what you do with the tools in your hands.

Maybe the future isn't asking us to become more like machines.

Maybe it's forcing us to become better humans.

title: Why do your eyes and nose ache when you’re about to cry? 😭👃
excerpt:
Have you ever noticed that your nose starts hurting when you're about to cry?

Your nose isn't being dramatic. 😂 There is actually a fascinating reason your eyes, nose and emotions seem to gang up on…
content:
It’s not actually your tears “hurting” you!!!

When you’re about to cry, your brain activates the lacrimal glands to produce tears. At the same time, your nose and the tissues around your eyes are closely connected through the same facial nerves and blood vessels. Your tear drainage system also sends some of those tears into your nose.

That’s why you may experience:

A strange pressure or ache around your eyes

A tingling/burning sensation in your nose

A blocked or runny nose

That funny feeling in your throat...

You can drop other fun fact questions,answers,and/or conversations in the comments...

Follow,like,share for more fun facts convo.

#funfacts

title: THE PRICE OF US Chapter 2
excerpt: Chapter 2: the iron and the oak
content:
The cell beneath the High Court smelled of damp saltpeter and old iron. A single high window, narrow as a dagger's blade, let in a slice of gray rain light that cut through the darkness.

Kael sat on the cold stone floor, his back pressed against the weeping wall. He held his hands out before him, staring at his palms. The blood on his skin had dried into dark, flaking crusts. It wasn't the merchant's son's blood. It was his own, sliced open by broken cider bottles in the dark alley behind the tavern at dawn. But to the crowd, blood was blood, and guilt was whatever was easiest to believe.

Opposite him, sitting on a low wooden bench with her skirts gathered neatly around her knees, was Elara.

Her silver-braided coat was spotless despite the march up the hill, but her knuckles were white where her fingers clasped her knees. She had not spoken a word since the heavy oak doors had slammed shut behind them.

"You shouldn't have done that," Kael said. His voice was raspy, dry as chaff.

Elara didn't look up immediately. "Done what?"

"Spoken for me. The Pact... I know what the Pact is. Every street boy in Cinder knows it. If they find me guilty, they hang us both." He pulled his knees to his chest, suddenly hyper-aware of his torn sleeves and the dirt caked under his nails. "I'm a sweeper, Elara. My life was worth half a copper before this morning. Now yours is worth the same."

Elara lifted her gaze. Her eyes were a striking, clear hazel, steady and unblinking. "My name is Lady Elara of House Oakwood. And my life was already spoken for, long before this morning."

"What does that mean?"

"It means my father intends to marry me to Julian Vane next month," she said softly, a flicker of bitterness touching her lips. "To seal a trade treaty for the ironworks. If I stayed silent, I would have lived a long, golden life in a cage. Today, I chose my own path—even if it leads to a gallows." She leaned forward slightly. "Besides, you were sweeping outside Master Torv's bakery at the first bell. I watched you put out the milk bowl for the feral ginger cat. The merchant's son was killed at the South Docks at the same hour. You couldn't have been in two places at once unless you can fly."

Kael swallowed hard. "They won't care about the truth. The Vanes own the docks. The merchant was their man. They want someone to swing for it by nightfall so the harbor reopens."

"Then we make them care," Elara said firmly.

Before Kael could answer, heavy iron bolts scraped outside. The door groaned open, revealing two court guards in polished breastplates, flanked by an older man in rich midnight-blue robes embroidered with silver oak leaves.

Lord Oakwood.

His face was drawn and pale, his eyes burning with fury as he stared past the guards into the dim cell.

"Elara," her father commanded, his voice tight. "Stand up. The High Chancellor has agreed to set aside your testimony on account of... emotional distress. You will sign a recantation, and you will come home."

Elara slowly stood, drawing herself up to her full height. Though half her father's size, she looked entirely unyielding. "I suffered no distress, Father. I gave true witness under the Pact of the Seven Families. The law is invoked."

"The law was written for nobles, not street rats!" Lord Oakwood stepped into the room, his boots clicking hard on the flags. "Do you realize what you've done? The Vanes are demanding blood. If you stand as his surety, you bind House Oakwood's honor to a common murderer!"

"He is not a murderer," Elara said, her voice dropping into a dangerous, calm register. "And if you break the Pact to save me, you prove to all Seven Families that Oakwood honor is a lie."

Lord Oakwood looked as if he had been struck. He glared at Kael with a hatred so pure it made Kael's blood run cold.

"You," Lord Oakwood hissed at Kael. "You miserable leach. You've dragged my daughter into your grave."

"I didn't ask her to—" Kael began, but the lead guard stepped forward and slammed the butt of his spear into Kael's chest, knocking the air out of his lungs. Kael collapsed back against the wall, gasping.

"Silence, dog," the guard barked.

"Noon approaches," Lord Oakwood said, turning his back on Kael completely. He looked at Elara, his eyes shining with desperate anger. "If you do not recant before the High Court, Elara, I cannot save you. The Vanes will have their trial, and they will have a conviction."

"Then let them try," Elara said.

The heavy bell at the top of the High Court tower began to toll. One. Two. Three.

Noon had arrived.

The lead guard gestured with his spear. "Up. Both of you. The High Chancellor awaits."

Kael forced himself to his feet, clutching his sore ribs. He looked at Elara, whose face had gone pale, though her chin remained high. As they were led out into the torchlit corridor, Kael fell into step beside her.

"If we survive this," Kael whispered under his breath, watching the shadows dance on the damp stone walls, "I will pay you back for this day. Every bit of it."

Elara didn't turn her head, but he caught the small, tight nod she gave. "Worry about surviving noon first, sweeper. Then we'll talk about debts."

title: Dangote Is Selling Shares to Nigerians. But What Does That Actually Mean?
excerpt: The Dangote Refinery IPO explained without all the confusing stock-market language.
content:
So apparently, Dangote wants us to own a tiny piece of his refinery. 😂

And judging by the chaos happening online, a lot of Nigerians are interested.

On September 14, Dangote Petroleum Refinery opened its Initial Public Offering (IPO), giving members of the public an opportunity to buy shares in the company. The shares are being offered at ₦525 each, with a minimum purchase of 10 shares, meaning you can start with ₦5,250. The offer is expected to raise up to about ₦2.15 trillion and is scheduled to close on October 13.

But if you're sitting there thinking, “Okay... but what exactly am I buying?”

Let's talk about it.

So, what is an IPO?

IPO simply means Initial Public Offering.

In normal human language, it means a private company is offering some of its ownership to the public by selling shares.

Think of it like this:

Imagine you own a very expensive cake.

Instead of keeping the entire cake to yourself, you decide to cut it into millions of tiny pieces and sell some of those pieces to other people.

You still own most of the cake.

But now, other people can own a small piece too.

That's basically what Dangote is doing with the refinery.

And no, buying one share does not mean you can walk into the refinery and tell the security guard, “I'm part owner. Open the gate.” 😭

So how much can you actually buy?

The offer price is ₦525 per share, and the minimum subscription is 10 shares.

That means the minimum starting amount is ₦5,250. So technically, you don't need millions of naira to participate.

That relatively low entry point is one reason the IPO has attracted so much attention from everyday Nigerians and first-time investors.

And Nigerians have definitely noticed. The demand has reportedly been so high that several digital investment platforms experienced outages as people rushed to subscribe. Reuters reported that one platform, Bamboo, saw traffic increase roughly tenfold within half an hour. 😭

Apparently, everybody suddenly remembered they wanted to be an investor.

But wait... does buying shares mean you're going to make money?

No.And this is probably the most important part.

Buying a share doesn't come with a guarantee that its value will increase.

If you buy shares for ₦525 and the market later values them at ₦700, your investment has increased in value.

But if the market price falls to ₦400, your investment is worth less.

That's the basic idea of investing in shares.

So please don't see “₦5,250” and immediately start planning your Dubai vacation. 😭

Your shares still have to perform.

And Dangote is still very much Dangote

Opening the refinery to public investors doesn't mean Dangote is handing over the refinery.

The IPO is offering roughly a 3% stake to the public, while Dangote is expected to retain about 87% ownership after the offering. So yes, you can own a little piece of the refinery.

But let's manage our excitement.

If you buy 10 shares, you're not suddenly becoming Aliko Dangote's business partner. 😂

You're simply becoming a shareholder with a very small ownership stake.

So why is everybody talking about it?

Because this isn't just another company selling shares.

The Dangote Refinery is one of the biggest industrial projects in Nigeria, and this IPO is being described as Africa's largest-ever share sale.

It is also being marketed as a “people's IPO,” because the offering is designed to allow ordinary investors to participate with a relatively low minimum investment.

For people who have never invested in the stock market before, this could be their first experience owning shares in a major Nigerian company.

And that is probably one of the most interesting parts of the whole thing.

But before you rush...

Please remember that investing isn't the same thing as saving money.

You can lose money.

You should understand what you're buying, read the official offer information and consider whether the investment makes sense for your own financial situation.

And because the IPO has generated so much excitement, there have also been warnings about scams and impersonation. Reuters reported that regulators have cautioned investors about phishing and fraudulent schemes surrounding the offering.

So if somebody messages you saying:

“Send ₦20,000 to this random account and I'll help you buy Dangote shares.”

Please.

Run. 😂

So, what does this actually mean?

It means that for the first time, ordinary Nigerians can buy a small ownership stake in one of the country's biggest industrial businesses through a public share offering.

You don't need to be a billionaire.

You don't need ₦100 million sitting in your account.

But you do need to understand what you're getting into.

Because at the end of the day, buying shares isn't about saying:

“I own Dangote.”

It's about saying:

“I own a tiny piece of this company.”

And honestly, that's pretty interesting.

Imagine telling your children one day:

“You know Dangote Refinery? I actually owned some of it.” 😂

Whether you choose to participate or simply watch from the sidelines, one thing is already clear:

Nigerians are paying attention.

And for once, the conversation isn't just about how much Dangote owns.

It's about whether ordinary Nigerians can own a piece of it too.

title: IF I COULD GO BACK TO THE VERY FIRST DAY I MET YOU…
excerpt: THE WOMAN WHO KNEW TOO MUCH
content:
“Bola, you really don’t know who your husband is.”

The call ended.

I stood there with my phone in my hand, staring at the screen.

What the hell did that mean?

I called the number back.

It rang once.

Then went off.

I tried again.

Same thing.

At this point, I was getting angry.

Who was this woman?

And why was she talking like she knew my husband better than I did?

I almost called my husband immediately.

But something stopped me.

I remembered what he had told me three weeks earlier.

She wants me back.

She’s trying to cause a problem.

What if this was just another attempt to make me doubt him?

So I decided not to say anything.

At least, not yet.

That evening, when my husband got home, everything was normal.

He kissed me.

Asked how my day went.

Complained about traffic.

Then he walked into the kitchen to see what we were having for dinner.

I watched him.

And for the first time since I met him, I was studying him.

His face.

His voice.

The way he moved.

Everything suddenly felt unfamiliar.

Who exactly did I marry?

“Bola?”

I snapped out of it.

“Hmm?”

“Are you okay?”

I forced a smile.

“I’m fine.”

He came closer.

“You sure?”

“Yes.”

He kissed my forehead.

Normally, that would have melted me.

That night, it just made me more confused.

⸻

I didn’t sleep much that night.

The woman’s voice kept playing in my head.

You really don’t know who your husband is.

By 2 AM, I picked up his phone.

I opened the messages I had seen three weeks earlier.

I read them again.

This time, I wasn’t looking at them as a jealous wife.

I was looking for something I had missed.

I scrolled.

And scrolled.

Then I saw it.

A message from my husband.

Him: You know I can’t let her find out.

I froze.

Let me find out what?

I kept scrolling.

Another message.

Him: Give me time. I’ll sort everything out.

My heart started beating faster.

This wasn’t sounding like a woman who was simply trying to get her ex back.

There was something else.

Something they weren’t telling me.

⸻

The next morning, I started looking.

Nothing dramatic.

I wasn’t breaking into anything.

I just started paying attention.

I checked the things I had never bothered to question because…

why would I?

I knew where he worked.

I knew where he grew up.

I knew his friends.

I knew his family.

Or at least…

I thought I did.

I started with his social media.

Everything looked normal.

Photos with me.

Photos with family.

Work.

Friends.

Nothing.

Then I remembered something.

A name.

A woman’s name.

I had seen it somewhere before.

I couldn’t remember where.

I searched for it on Instagram.

The account came up almost immediately.

I opened it.

And my heart dropped.

Because I knew the woman in the profile picture.

I had met her before.

Not once.

Not online.

In person.

She had been at our wedding.

I remembered her now.

She had hugged me.

She had smiled at me.

She had even taken pictures with us.

I remember my husband introducing her.

He had said,

“She’s an old family friend.”

I stared at the screen.

Then I looked at the pictures on her page.

There were pictures of her with my husband.

Not recent pictures.

Old pictures.

Very old.

Pictures from before I met him.

I zoomed in on one.

My hands went cold.

Because the caption said:

“Some people will never understand what we survived together.”

I kept scrolling.

Another picture.

Another caption.

Then I saw one that made me sit up straight.

It was a picture of my husband.

But the name tagged in the picture…

wasn’t his name.

I stared at it.

Then I checked the date.

Seven years ago.

I checked another picture.

Same man.

Different name.

Another one.

Same man.

Same different name.

My hands were shaking now.

I went back to the woman’s profile.

And suddenly, I understood why she had called me.

She wasn’t trying to get my husband back.

She was trying to warn me.

I immediately called her.

This time, she answered.

“Hello?”

Her voice was calm.

Mine wasn’t.

“What is my husband’s name?”

Silence.

Then she asked,

“Which one?”

I couldn’t breathe.

And that was when I knew…

I had only just started finding out who I married.

title: Building Passwordless Authentication with Passkeys (WebAuthn) and FIDO2
excerpt: Step-by-step implementation guide to building biometric passwordless authentication using WebAuthn Passkeys in modern web applications.
content:
Building Passwordless Authentication with Passkeys (WebAuthn) and FIDO2

Passwords are notoriously vulnerable to phishing, credential stuffing, and data breaches. Passkeys utilize public-key cryptography and device biometrics (Face ID, Touch ID, Windows Hello) to deliver seamless, phishing-resistant authentication.

How WebAuthn Registration Works

  1. The server generates a cryptographic challenge and sends it to the browser.
  2. The browser prompts the user for biometric authorization and generates a public/private keypair inside the hardware security enclave.
  3. The browser returns the public key and signed challenge back to the server to store in PostgreSQL.

title: How to Make Social Media Algorithms Work for You Without Paying for Ads
excerpt: Understanding how social media algorithms work and how to use them to grow without relying entirely on paid ads.
content:
How to Make Social Media Algorithms Work for You Without Paying for Ads

You don't always need a big advertising budget to get people to notice your content.

Sometimes, the difference between a post that reaches 100 people and one that reaches thousands comes down to something less complicated than money: relevance, usefulness and how people respond to the content.

This is where social media algorithms come in.

Many creators and businesses see the algorithm as an invisible system working against them. When a post performs poorly, they blame the algorithm. When another post suddenly takes off, they assume they have discovered a secret.

But algorithms are not necessarily designed to stop you from being seen.

They are designed to help platforms decide what content to show to which people.

If you understand that, you can start creating content that has a better chance of being discovered organically even when you aren't paying for ads.

So, how does the algorithm actually work?

First, forget the idea that there is one single “social media algorithm.”

Instagram, LinkedIn, TikTok, Facebook and YouTube all use different systems. They also consider different signals depending on what people are doing on each platform.

Instagram, for example, uses different ranking systems for Feed, Stories, Explore and Reels.

LinkedIn is also changing how it recommends content.

In March 2026, LinkedIn announced a new AI-powered Feed ranking system designed to better understand what a post is about and match it with members who may be interested in that subject. The system uses large language models and other AI technologies to understand content and users' changing interests.

The important lesson is simple:

The algorithm is trying to understand content and decide who is most likely to care about it.

Your job is to make that decision easier.

Your audience helps teach the algorithm

Imagine you regularly post about:

  • Artificial intelligence

  • Executive productivity

  • Social media

  • Virtual assistance

  • Leadership

  • Digital tools

You are creating a clear pattern.

Your audience starts to recognize what you talk about, but the platform is also collecting signals about your content and the people interacting with it.

LinkedIn says its Feed uses information about a member, their activity, the content they engage with and other signals to personalize their Feed.

This is one reason consistency matters.

If you talk about everything under the sun today and something completely unrelated tomorrow, it becomes harder to build a clear professional identity.

You don't need to talk about one subject forever.

But you should have a few clear areas you want people to associate with you.

For example, if you are a social media professional who also works with executives, your content might consistently revolve around social media, productivity, AI and better ways of working.

You are not just building an audience.

You are helping the platform understand who your content is for.

Engagement is a signal, not the whole strategy

You've probably heard people say:

“Get lots of likes in the first hour and the algorithm will push your post.”

That's an oversimplification.

There is no single engagement number that guarantees success.

LinkedIn says its Feed ranking considers hundreds of signals when deciding what individual members see.

Instagram has also highlighted watch time, likes and sends as important signals for ranking content. Instagram Head Adam Mosseri has encouraged creators to pay attention to metrics such as average watch time, likes per reach and sends per reach.

This tells us something important.

Don't create content simply to collect likes.

Create content that makes people want to:

  • Read to the end

  • Watch the video

  • Save the information

  • Share it

  • Send it to someone

  • Visit your profile

  • Follow you

  • Come back for more

These actions tell the platform that your content has some level of relevance to its users.

Stop asking, “What will go viral?”

Instead, ask:

“Who would find this useful or valuable enough to share?”

That small change can completely improve the way you create content.

For example, instead of posting:

“5 productivity tips for busy professionals.”

Try:

“Your calendar is full, but your most important work keeps getting pushed back. Here's what might be wrong.”

The second version starts with a real problem.

It gives someone a reason to stop scrolling.

This doesn't guarantee that the post will go viral. But it creates a stronger reason for the right person to pay attention.

And that is what good organic content should do.

Create content people actually need

One of the simplest ways to improve your content is to stop asking:

“What should I post today?”

Ask:

“What problem can I help my audience solve today?”

For an executive audience, you could create content about:

  • Managing an overloaded inbox

  • Organizing a busy calendar

  • Preparing for important meetings

  • Using AI to save time

  • Delegating tasks

  • Reducing unnecessary meetings

  • Managing travel and appointments

For a business owner, you could talk about:

  • Building a social media workflow

  • Managing customer enquiries

  • Organizing leads

  • Creating a content calendar

  • Using analytics

  • Improving customer communication

The goal is not to sound intelligent.

The goal is to be useful.

When people consistently find your content useful, they have a reason to follow you.

Originality matters more than copying trends

Social media is full of recycled content.

The same hooks appear everywhere:

“5 things you need to know…”

“Stop doing this…”

“Here's what nobody tells you…”

“AI will change everything…”

There is nothing inherently wrong with these formats. The problem comes when everyone says the same thing.

LinkedIn announced in 2026 that it was taking action against automated comments, engagement pods, engagement bait and other forms of inauthentic activity. The company said it wanted to give more visibility to genuine professional conversations and useful content.

That is an important shift.

You don't have to invent a completely new topic.

You can take a familiar topic and add your experience, observation, opinion or example.

For instance, thousands of people talk about AI.

Instead of writing:

“AI is changing the workplace.”

You could write:

“I used AI to organize a week's worth of executive tasks. Here's what it handled well and what still needed human judgment.”

Now you have a personal experience.

That is harder to copy.

Give people a reason to stop scrolling

Before someone can engage with your content, you first have to earn their attention.

This is especially important with short-form video.

Instagram has identified watch time as one of the important signals creators should monitor.

That means your opening matters.

Don't spend the first 15 seconds introducing yourself before explaining why someone should care.

Get to the point.

Instead of:

“Hello everyone, my name is Dennis and today I want to talk about…”

Try:

“If your calendar is always full but your important work keeps getting delayed, your problem may not be time management.”

Now the viewer has a reason to continue.

The same principle applies to LinkedIn posts, articles and carousels.

Your first sentence should create enough interest for someone to keep reading.

Organic growth is about consistency, not constant posting

Another common misconception is that you must post several times a day to grow.

More content does not automatically mean better results.

Sprout Social's 2026 research analyzed nearly 2 billion engagements across approximately 307,000 social profiles and found that engagement patterns differ across platforms and audiences. The research emphasizes adapting your publishing strategy rather than simply producing more content.

So consistency doesn't mean:

“I must post every day no matter what.”

It means giving your audience something valuable on a regular basis.

Three useful posts can be more valuable than seven posts created just to fill a content calendar.

Let your analytics teach you

If you want to improve your organic reach, don't guess forever.

Look at your analytics.

Ask:

  • Which topics get the most meaningful engagement?

  • Which posts are being shared?

  • Which videos have the longest watch time?

  • Which posts bring people to your profile?

  • What questions keep appearing in your comments?

  • Which topics attract the audience you actually want?

Then use those answers to improve your next piece of content.

This creates a simple cycle:

Create → Measure → Learn → Improve → Create again.

That is much more useful than constantly searching for an “algorithm hack.”

Organic reach doesn't mean you should never pay for ads

There is an important distinction here.

I'm not suggesting that paid advertising is useless.

It isn't.

Advertising can be valuable when you want predictable distribution, lead generation, product sales or a targeted campaign.

In fact, social advertising remains a huge industry. Sprout Social's 2026 social media statistics report estimates that global social media advertising spending will reach roughly $317 billion in 2026.

The point is not:

“Never pay for advertising.”

The point is:

“Don't assume advertising is the only way to get attention.”

Paid advertising can buy exposure.

Good organic content can help you build trust, authority and relationships.

The two can work together.

So, how can you make the algorithm work in your favour?

Here are five practical principles to remember:

1. Know who you're talking to

Be clear about your audience and the problems you want to help them solve.

2. Create useful content

Answer questions. Solve problems. Explain complicated things simply. Give people something they can use.

3. Make your content easy to understand

Use strong openings, simple language and clear structure.

4. Give people something worth sharing

Don't ask people to share just because you want more reach. Create something they naturally want to send to someone else.

5. Study your results

Your analytics can tell you what your audience responds to. Pay attention and adjust.

You don't have to beat the algorithm

The biggest mistake you can make is treating the algorithm like an enemy.

You don't need to trick it.

You don't need to find a secret formula.

And you certainly don't need to believe that every successful post has discovered some hidden hack.

Social media platforms are becoming increasingly sophisticated at understanding content and predicting what individual users may find relevant. LinkedIn's latest Feed system is a good example of this shift toward AI-powered content understanding and personalization.

That means your strategy should be simple:

Create something useful for a specific audience.

Make it easy to understand.

Give people a reason to stop.

Give them something worth sharing.

Then study what happens and improve your next post.

You may eventually decide to invest in advertising. That's perfectly fine.

But you shouldn't have to pay for every piece of attention you receive.

The goal isn't simply to go viral.

The goal is to become relevant enough to be discovered, useful enough to be remembered and valuable enough to be shared.

And when you can do that consistently, the algorithm isn't something you have to fight.

It can become part of your distribution strategy.

title: The Future Of Agriculture In Africa

content:
🌱 Sustainable agriculture does not have to begin with vast farmland or huge capital.

Sometimes, we make agriculture look like something that requires hectares of land, expensive machinery, and massive investment before you can make an impact.

But sustainability starts with something much simpler: how well you manage the resources available to you.

It can begin with a small piece of land.

A backyard garden.

Efficient use of water.

Proper waste management.

Recycling farm residues.

Choosing practices that protect the soil.

And adapting farming decisions to changing climate and environmental conditions.

The goal is not always to start big.

The goal is to start wisely.

With proper planning, good farm management, efficient resource utilization, and consistency, a small farming system can gradually become more productive and profitable.

For young people interested in agriculture, don't let the size of the farm or the amount of capital you have discourage you.

Start with what you have. Manage it well. Learn. Improve. Scale gradually.

Because sustainable agriculture is not simply about how much land you own.

It is about how responsibly and efficiently you use what you have. 🌍🌱
