title: Olu Jacobs Is Gone. Will Gen Z Ever Understand the Nollywood We Grew Up With?
excerpt: Olu Jacobs’ death brought back memories of the Nollywood some of us grew up watching
content:
I saw the news about Olu Jacobs and started thinking about old Nollywood. Not the Nollywood we have now.

I'm talking about the one with VCDs, dramatic family meetings, village scenes, questionable wigs and movies that somehow had part one, part two and sometimes part three.

And then I started wondering: can Gen Z even relate to that Nollywood anymore?

Because some of us caught the last part of it. We remember when you could go to a shop and spend money on a VCD because the cover looked interesting.

You didn't have Netflix telling you what to watch, or have TikTok reviews, and didn't even have to know the name of the director.

Sometimes you just saw Olu Jacobs, Pete Edochie, Patience Ozokwor or Nkem Owoh on the cover and you already knew you were probably getting a good movie.

Olu Jacobs died at 84 on September 16, 2026, after a career that lasted more than five decades.

But for people who didn't grow up watching that era, I don't think they can completely understand what these actors meant to us.

Imagine telling someone who grew up with Netflix that there was a time when the same Nigerian movie could play on your TV so many times that you practically knew the dialogue.

And you still watched it. There was no “I'll watch something else.”

That was what was available, and honestly, some of those movies were unserious.

A man would wake up from a coma and suddenly remember he had a twin. Somebody would go to the village and meet a mysterious old woman.

One family would spend the entire movie fighting over a piece of land, and somehow, we were invested.

But the actors made those stories work. Olu Jacobs had that kind of presence.

You didn't need social media to know him. You knew him because you kept seeing him.

That's probably one of the biggest differences between that Nollywood and the one Gen Z is growing up with now.

Today, an actor can become popular from TikTok before you have even watched their movie.

A movie can trend for three days and disappear. People watch films on Netflix, rate them online, make memes about them and move on.

The industry has obviously improved in many ways.

The cameras are better. The stories are more varied. The productions are bigger.

Nigerian actors are getting opportunities that weren't as common before, but something else has changed too.

The way we remember people.

Olu Jacobs wasn't just somebody whose movie you watched. He was one of those faces that kept showing up while you were growing up.

That's why his death hits differently for people who grew up with that Nollywood, and maybe that's something Gen Z won't completely understand.

Not because they're doing anything wrong. They simply grew up in a different time.

For them, nostalgia might be a Netflix series they watched during lockdown, a TikTok trend from secondary school or an artist they discovered online.

For some of us, it's a VCD, a crowded sitting room and somebody shouting, “Who has the remote?”

Olu Jacobs is gone, and with him, we're slowly saying goodbye to a Nollywood that many of us didn't realise we were going to miss this much.

title: What Dangote Refinery Going public Could mean for ordinary Nigerians
excerpt: Africa’s biggest refinery is opening its ownership to the public. But what could that actually mean for everyday Nigerians?
content:
For years, the Dangote Refinery has been one of the biggest business stories in Nigeria. Now, something different is happening: ordinary investors are being given an opportunity to own a small part of it.

The refinery's Initial Public Offering, commonly called an IPO, opened on September 14, 2026. The company is offering 4.1 billion shares at ₦525 per share, with a minimum subscription of 10 shares, or ₦5,250.

That means this is no longer simply a story about a massive refinery owned by one of Africa's richest businessmen. It is also a story about Nigerians potentially becoming shareholders in one of the country's most important industrial projects.

But what does that really mean?

First, it is important to understand what an IPO is.

An IPO is when a company offers shares to members of the public. If your application is successful and shares are allocated to you, you become a shareholder. In simple terms, you own a small piece of the company.

That does not mean you suddenly have control over the refinery. It simply means you have a financial interest in the company through the shares you own.

The minimum entry point for this IPO is ₦5,250. That makes the opportunity more accessible than many people might expect. However, affordable does not mean risk-free.

A share can increase in value, but it can also fall.

The Dangote Refinery itself has ambitious plans. The company currently operates at around 700,000 barrels of crude oil per day and plans to expand its capacity to 1.4 million barrels per day.

The money raised from the IPO is expected to help fund that expansion.

If the expansion goes well, the refinery could become even more significant to Nigeria and the wider African energy market. It could produce more refined petroleum products, serve more markets and potentially strengthen Nigeria's position as a major refining hub.

There is also a bigger question for ordinary Nigerians.

Can a refinery this large actually change everyday life?

The answer is not as simple as yes or no.

The refinery has already changed the conversation around fuel refining in Nigeria. For decades, Nigeria exported crude oil and depended heavily on imported refined petroleum products. Having a large modern refinery operating locally creates the possibility of reducing some of that dependence.

But Nigerians should not expect the IPO itself to immediately make fuel cheaper or make everyone richer.

Owning shares is an investment, not a guaranteed source of income.

The official IPO information makes this clear: dividends are not guaranteed, and the value of shares can rise or fall after listing.

That is why the excitement surrounding the IPO needs to be balanced with careful thinking.

It is easy to see ₦5,250 and think, "I can afford that."

The more important question is, "Do I understand what I am buying?"

That question matters because investing should not simply be about following what everyone else is doing.

The Dangote Refinery IPO is significant because it gives ordinary investors an opportunity to participate in the ownership of a major Nigerian industrial asset.

Whether that opportunity becomes a good investment will depend on what happens after the IPO: the company's performance, its expansion plans, profits, the wider economy and the future demand for its products.

For Nigeria, however, there is something bigger to watch.

This could be another step toward a culture where ordinary Nigerians participate more actively in the ownership of major businesses instead of only watching them from the outside.

The refinery may belong to one of Africa's biggest business empires today, but through the public offering, thousands or even millions of investors could potentially own a small piece of it.

And perhaps that is the most interesting part of this story.

The question is no longer only, "What is Dangote building?"

It is also:

"Who gets to own a piece of what he has built?"

title: If I Could Go Back to the Very First Day I Met You…
excerpt: The First Lie
content:
The first thing I did was check the time.

It was 2:17 PM.

I remember because I had just finished lunch and was about to get back to work when I saw the message.

I read it again. And again.

Unknown: Are you sure she doesn’t know?

My heart started beating faster.

Who was she?

And what exactly was I supposed to know?

I stared at the message for a few seconds before opening the chat.

There wasn’t much.

But there was enough to make me uncomfortable.

They had clearly spoken before.

A lot.

I scrolled up slowly, reading through the messages.

Then I saw one that made my stomach drop.

Her: So you’re just going to pretend nothing happened?

I stopped scrolling.

Nothing happened?

What did that mean?

I kept reading.

Her: After everything between us?

My hands suddenly felt cold.

I locked the phone.

Then unlocked it again.

I don’t know why.

Maybe I was hoping I had misunderstood something.

Maybe I was hoping there was some perfectly innocent explanation hiding somewhere in those messages.

And honestly, that was the annoying thing.

He had given me no reason to suspect him.

None.

This was the same man who told me everything.

At least, I thought he did.

I knew his password.

He knew mine.

He had never acted secretive about his phone.

Sometimes he’d leave it beside me while he went to shower.

Sometimes he’d ask me to help him reply to a message.

He had never made me feel like there was something I wasn’t allowed to see.

So why was my heart telling me something was wrong?

I decided I was going to ask him.

When he got home that evening, I waited until we had eaten.

I didn’t want to start a conversation when either of us was hungry or tired.

So while we were sitting on the couch, I turned to him.

“Can I ask you something?”

He looked at me.

“Of course.”

I picked up his phone.

“Who is this?”

The smile on his face disappeared.

He looked at the screen.

Then looked at me.

“Where did you see that?”

“I saw it on your phone.”

He was quiet.

I waited.

Finally, he sighed.

“Bola…”

“Who is she?”

He rubbed his forehead.

“She’s someone I used to know.”

I frowned.

“Used to know?”

“Yes.”

“So why is she asking if I know?”

He looked at me for a few seconds.

Then he said,

“Because she wants to cause a problem.”

I blinked.

“What?”

“She wants me back.”

I stared at him.

“You’re saying your ex is trying to get you back?”

“Yes.”

“And you’ve been talking to her?”

He nodded.

“A little.”

“A little?”

“I should have told you.”

I didn’t say anything.

He moved closer to me.

“Bola, I know how this looks.”

“Do you?”

“Yes.”

“Because it doesn’t look good.”

“I know.”

He took a deep breath.

“But nothing happened.”

I looked at him.

“Nothing?”

“Nothing.”

“You didn’t sleep with her?”

“No.”

“You didn’t kiss her?”

“No.”

“You didn’t meet her?”

“No.”

He answered every question without hesitation.

Then he said,

“I told her I’m married. I told her I love my wife. I told her whatever we had is over.”

I wanted to believe him.

But that message was still sitting in my head.

After everything between us?

“So what happened between you two?”

He looked down.

“We dated before I met you.”

I already knew that part now.

“But after we broke up, she kept trying to come back.”

“And you kept responding?”

“I was trying to handle it without being cruel.”

I almost laughed.

“Being too nice is what got you here?”

He smiled slightly.

“I guess.”

I didn’t smile.

He noticed.

Then his expression changed.

“Bola, look at me.”

I looked at him.

“I am telling you the truth.”

And somehow…

I believed him.

Not because everything made perfect sense.

It didn’t.

But because he was him.

The man who had been there for me.

The man who had supported me.

The man who had never made me feel like I had to compete for his attention.

The man I had trusted with everything.

He took my hand.

“I should have told you about her. That was my mistake.”

I swallowed.

“I don’t like secrets.”

“I know.”

“Then don’t keep things from me.”

“I won’t.”

He pulled me into his arms.

And I let him.

Maybe that was my mistake.

Because I forgave him that night.

I didn’t know that I had just forgiven a lie.

And I definitely didn’t know that three weeks later, the same woman would call me herself.

My phone rang while I was in the kitchen.

I looked at the screen.

It was an unknown number.

I almost ignored it.

Then I answered.

“Hello?”

A woman’s voice came through.

“Is this Bola?”

“Yes. Who is this?”

She was quiet for a moment.

Then she said,

“So he finally told you?”

My heart sank.

“Told me what?”

There was a pause.

Then she laughed.

“You actually believe him?”

I froze.

And before I could ask another question, she said,

“Bola, you really don’t know who your husband is.”

Then the call ended.

title: Accelerate Africa Is Coaching Founders Who Later Built Andela, Flutterwave and Moove And It's Still Taking Applications
excerpt: If you're an early-stage founder in Africa trying to get your business investor-ready, this is worth your attention. Accelerate Africa Startup Program 2026 is a…
content:
If you're an early-stage founder in Africa trying to get your business investor-ready, this is worth your attention. Accelerate Africa Startup Program 2026 is an 8-week accelerator run by operators from Future Africa; the same network that advised founding teams behind Andela, Flutterwave, Moove and DukaConnect before those companies became billion-dollar businesses.

What You Actually Get

The programme runs for 8 weeks, working with a small cohort of around 10 founders at a time. Instead of a generic curriculum, founders get hands-on coaching built around three things: telling their story clearly, fixing how their business runs day to day, and getting ready to raise money.

Here's what makes this one different from a typical accelerator:

  • No equity taken. Accelerate Africa doesn't ask for a stake in your company just to join the programme.

  • One-on-one mentorship, not group lectures, from founders and investors who've actually built companies at scale.

  • A real path to funding after the programme — participants get access to Accelerate Africa's investor network, with potential post-programme funding between $250,000 and $500,000 through partner funds, subject to due diligence.

That last point matters: the programme itself doesn't guarantee you funding. What it gives you is the positioning and the network to actually go raise it.

Who Should Apply

You need:

  • A founding team — solo founders aren't eligible

  • A business operating in an African country

  • Early traction or a working prototype (not just an idea on paper)

  • A real, scalable problem you're solving — there's no sector restriction, so fintech, agritech, healthtech, logistics, whatever you're building can qualify, as long as it's genuinely solving something

There's no long list of technical requirements beyond that. What the programme is actually screening for is whether your business has real potential to scale, and whether you're the kind of founder who'll put in the work over 8 weeks.

How to Apply

Applications are open now, with no fixed closing date published — but multiple sources tracking the programme note that cohort spots fill on a rolling basis, so applying early is genuinely better than waiting. Apply directly through Accelerate Africa's official programme page.

Why This One's Worth Your Time

A lot of accelerators promise mentorship and deliver a slideshow. This one is run by people with a decade-plus track record actually building African startups into global businesses — some acquired by companies like Mastercard, some now processing serious revenue at scale. For a founder who's past the idea stage and needs real structure to get investor-ready, that kind of hands-on experience is the harder-to-find part of this deal, not just the funding number at the end.

title: There are million of things that we don't know but we don't actually care
excerpt: There are countless things surrounding us every day that we see, hear, touch, and experience without truly understanding them. We wake up beneath a sky that has…
content:
There are countless things surrounding us every day that we see, hear, touch, and experience without truly understanding them. We wake up beneath a sky that has existed long before any of us were born, surrounded by forces we cannot see and systems we barely understand. Air moves around us, invisible but essential. Gravity holds everything to the ground, yet we cannot see it with our eyes. Our bodies perform thousands of complicated processes while we sleep, most of which happen without us consciously controlling them. Even the world beneath our feet contains mysteries that humanity is still discovering. We have explored only a small portion of the deepest parts of our oceans, and there are countless organisms, environments, and natural processes that remain unknown to us. When we look at the stars at night, we are seeing light that may have traveled enormous distances before reaching our eyes. Somewhere beyond what we can observe, there may be things we have not yet imagined—not because we have proof of them, but because the universe is far larger and more complicated than our individual experiences can reveal.

The unknown also exists within things that seem completely familiar. Every person we pass on the street has an entire story inside them that we may never know. Someone can smile while carrying worries nobody else can see. A stranger can influence our future through one brief conversation, a decision, or an event that seems insignificant at the time. Even our own minds contain mysteries. We do not completely understand consciousness, memory, dreams, or why certain thoughts and emotions appear when they do. Science has answered enormous questions, but every discovery seems to create new questions waiting to be explored. We once believed certain things were impossible until someone discovered a way to understand them. Diseases that were once mysterious became subjects of scientific study. Distant worlds that were once only points of light became places we could observe in extraordinary detail. The history of humanity is, in many ways, the history of discovering that reality is much more complicated than we originally believed. What we know today may eventually become only a small part of what future generations understand.

Perhaps the most humbling truth about the unknown is that not knowing something does not automatically make it supernatural, impossible, or frightening. Sometimes it simply means we have not discovered the answer yet. There is a difference between mystery and evidence, and being curious does not require us to turn every unanswered question into a definite conclusion. The unknown should encourage us to ask better questions, investigate carefully, remain open-minded, and accept that our knowledge has limits. There will always be things beyond our current understanding, no matter how advanced humanity becomes. Somewhere in the depths of the ocean, in the vastness of space, inside the complexity of the human brain, and even within the ordinary world we walk through every day, there are questions waiting for answers. Maybe that is part of what makes existence so fascinating: we are living inside a reality that is still revealing itself to us. We may never discover everything, but every honest question, every experiment, every observation, and every new discovery brings us a little closer to understanding the enormous world we are fortunate enough to exist within.

title: MAKE HAY WHILE THE SUN SHINES
excerpt: Opportunities are temporary; wisdom is knowing when to act
content:
Life rarely announces its greatest opportunities. Sometimes they come disguised as an ordinary day, a small chance, a new skill to learn, or a door that opens for only a moment. That is the meaning behind the timeless proverb: Make hay while the sun shines.

Long ago, farmers knew they had to dry and gather their hay while the weather was sunny. If they delayed until the rain came, the hay would spoil and their hard work could be wasted. Our lives work the same way. The “sunshine” represents the moments when we have the strength, time, resources, and opportunity to move forward. The question is: Will we use them, or will we wait until it is too late?

Many people dream of success, but dreams alone change nothing. The student who studies before exams, the entrepreneur who starts with the little they have, and the young person who learns valuable skills instead of wasting every free hour are all making hay while the sun shines. They understand that today's discipline becomes tomorrow's reward.

One of the biggest mistakes we make is believing there will always be another chance. Sometimes there will be—but sometimes there won't. Opportunities expire, time passes, and habits become harder to change. That is why growth begins with action, not excuses.

So if today you have a chance to learn, create, apologize, save money, apply for that job, or begin the project you've been postponing, do it now. Don't wait for the “perfect” moment. The perfect moment is often the one you already have.

title: You're Not Behind. Don't Let Social Media Fool You
excerpt: So if you're 24, 27, 30 or whatever age you are, and you don't have everything figured out yet, relax.
content:
I opened Instagram one morning and, within five minutes, I had seen someone's engagement, someone's new job, someone's trip abroad and someone's new business.

I dropped my phone and just stared at the ceiling. Everybody is moving. What am I doing?

Maybe you've had that moment too. It's funny how you can be perfectly fine with your life until you start scrolling. Suddenly, the job you're working towards doesn't feel like enough. Your plans feel slow. Even the things you're proud of start looking small.

But social media is showing you everybody's moments at once.

You're seeing the person who finally got the job, not the months they spent applying. You're seeing the new apartment, not the struggle it took to afford it. You're seeing the announcement, not everything that happened before it.

And that's what makes comparison so exhausting. You're comparing your everyday life with somebody else's biggest moments.

So if you're 24, 27, 30 or whatever age you are, and you don't have everything figured out yet, relax.

You are not behind.

Don't let social media give you a deadline for your life.

title: The Islamic Advice I Wish Young Muslims Heard Before Marriage
excerpt: Before you say “Qubool,” look beyond how religious someone appears. Pay attention to how they handle anger, money, and responsibility.
content:
When young Muslims talk about marriage, the advice often sounds the same.

“Marry someone righteous.”

“Make sure they pray five times a day.”

“Look for someone with good deen.”

And yes, all of that matters.

But here is something we don't talk about enough:

Someone can know how to look religious and still not know how to treat a spouse.

Prayer is essential. Deen is essential. Character is essential too.

Marriage will eventually put you in situations where someone's real habits become difficult to hide when money is tight, when tempers rise, when families disagree, when one person is exhausted and when neither of you gets exactly what you want.

So before you say “Qubool,” there are conversations and observations you should not skip.

1. Watch Their Character Under Pressure

Anyone can appear patient when everything is going their way.

Pay attention when it isn't.

How do they speak when they are frustrated?

How do they react when someone disagrees with them?

How do they treat people who cannot benefit them?

What happens when they are corrected?

A person doesn't suddenly develop good character because they got married.

The Prophet ﷺ said:

«“The best of you are those who are best to their wives.”»

(Jamiʿ at-Tirmidhi)

Marriage gives character a place to show itself every day.

Don't only observe how someone treats you when they are trying to win you.

Observe how they treat people when they have nothing to gain.

2. Talk About Money Before Money Becomes a Problem

Money is one of those subjects people love to postpone until after marriage.

Don't.

Islam establishes financial rights and responsibilities between spouses, but couples still need to discuss how those responsibilities will work in their actual lives.

Ask uncomfortable questions.

What happens if the husband loses his job?

What are your expectations about the wife's income?

Will either of you be supporting parents or relatives?

What does “living within our means” actually mean to each of you?

What debts or major financial obligations already exist?

What does halal income and responsible spending mean to both of you?

You don't need to marry a wealthy person.

But you should understand the financial habits and expectations of the person you are marrying.

Love does not make financial incompatibility disappear.

3. Pay Attention to Anger

You will disagree in marriage.

That is not automatically a sign that the marriage is failing.

The question is how you disagree.

When this person is angry, do they insult?

Threaten?

Shout?

Humiliate?

Give prolonged silent treatment to punish you?

Bring up private information you trusted them with?

Or do they know how to step away, calm down and return to the conversation without trying to destroy the other person's dignity?

The Prophet ﷺ taught that true strength is not merely physical strength, but the ability to control oneself wohen angry.

(Sahih al-Bukhari; Sahih Muslim)

A person who repeatedly becomes cruel when angry should not be excused simply because they are loving when calm.

You are not marrying only someone's gentle side.

4. Discuss Family Boundaries

Marriage does not erase your responsibilities toward your parents.

But marriage also does not mean every relative gets access to every part of your household.

Before marriage, discuss this.

Will private disagreements remain private?

How will decisions involving the couple be handled?

What happens when a parent strongly disagrees with a spouse?

Will either family be allowed to control the marriage?

How will you respond if your family is wrong?

These conversations are uncomfortable.

Have them anyway.

Honouring parents is part of Islam. So are justice, trust, privacy and fulfilling the rights of your spouse.

Don't wait until there is a family crisis to discover what your spouse believes about these things.

5. Look Beyond Religious Appearance — Check for Religious Compatibility

You can agree on how you dress and still disagree on the kind of home you want to build.

Talk about the things that actually matter.

How do you want to raise your children?

What role will Qur'an have in your home?

How do you respond when one of you makes a religious mistake?

Are you willing to accept sincere correction?

What happens when you disagree about an Islamic matter?

Are you both trying to grow, or is one person constantly dragging the other?

Religious compatibility isn't about finding someone who is perfect.

It is about knowing whether you are moving in the same direction.

Someone may look deeply religious while having completely different expectations about what married life should look like.

Don't confuse religious appearance with shared religious values.

6. Stop Assuming You'll “Figure It Out Later”

This is where many people deceive themselves.

“I'll know when we get married.”

“We'll adjust.”

“They'll probably change.”

“She'll understand later.”

“He'll become more responsible after marriage.”

Maybe.

But you should not build a marriage around potential you have no evidence for.

Discuss everyday life before everyday life arrives.

Who expects to work?

What are the expectations around household responsibilities?

How will major decisions be made?

How will childcare be handled?

How much involvement will extended family have?

What does each person expect from the other emotionally?

You don't need identical answers to everything.

You need enough honesty to know where the differences are.

Marriage Is Not a Reward for Finding the “Right Person”

There is a dangerous idea that once you find “the one,” everything else will somehow work itself out.

Islam does not teach that marriage becomes effortless simply because you chose a good spouse.

Marriage requires taqwa, patience, responsibility, mercy, communication and the willingness to do what is right even when your emotions are telling you to do otherwise.

So don't only ask:

“Do I love this person?”

Ask:

“Can this person handle responsibility?”

“Can they control themselves when angry?”

“Will they be just when nobody is watching?”

“Do our expectations about marriage actually match?”

And perhaps most importantly:

“If the excitement disappears tomorrow, is there enough character and deen here to build a life with?”

Because marriage is not simply about finding someone you enjoy loving.

It is about choosing someone with whom you can seek Allah while navigating the ordinary, difficult and beautiful reality of life together.

Choose character.

Choose responsibility.

Choose deen.

And before you say “Qubool,” make sure you have actually looked at the person you are saying it to.

What's one question you think every Muslim should ask before marriage? Share it in the comments and pass this along to someone who needs to read it before they say “Qubool.”

title: PART TWO: NAVIGATING A DIASIMOCRATIC WORLD
excerpt: 6 things you need to do to seduce the algorithms.
content:
Your best post last week got 12 likes.

A celebrity's lunch photo got 4,000.

That's not bad luck. That's a system.

And systems have rules.

Here are the 6 that matter 👇

In Part 1, I called this world a Diasimocracy.

Today, I'm handing you the map.

The algorithm isn't unbeatable. It's a machine. Machines have patterns. Learn them and stop being its victim.

Here's how 👇

1. Engineer your first 60 minutes

The moment you post, the platform gives your content a small test audience.

Engage — it pushes further.

Don't — it buries you.

Your first hour is everything.

Do this immediately after posting:

→ Reply to every comment within minutes

→ Like every reaction personally

→ Comment meaningfully on 5 other posts (signals activity)

→ Send your post to 5 people and ask for genuine thoughts

Engagement in the first hour tells the platform:

"This post is alive. Push it."

2. Never put links in your post body

Platforms suppress posts with external links.

Why? they want you to stay on their platform.

And what platform wants you to ever leave, check Tiktok and thank me later.

The fix:

Post without the link.

Drop it in the first comment.

Write "Link in the comments 👇" in the post.

3. Hook or nothing

Platforms measure one thing above all else in the first second:

Did they stop scrolling?

Your first line decides your post's fate.

Not your second line.

Not your headline.

Your first line.

Weak first line → they scroll → algorithm buries you.

Strong first line → they stop → algorithm pushes you.

Study your best posts. The first line is almost always why they worked.

4. Comments beat likes. Always.

The algorithm ranks engagement like this:

💬 Comments — highest value

🔄 Reposts — second

👍 Likes — lowest

10 genuine comments outperform 100 likes.

Stop asking for likes.

Start asking questions people want to answer.

5. Consistency signals credibility

The algorithm has a memory.

It tracks how often you post.

How often people engage.

How long they've followed you.

Three posts a week for three months builds momentum a viral one-off can't buy.

Show up consistently, not perfectly.

Three good posts a week beats one perfect post a month. Every time.

6. Speak the algorithm's language

Platforms currently reward:

→ Text posts with line breaks, like this one

→ Posts that spark debate

→ Personal stories using first-person language gets boosted

→ Native documents and carousels

→ Posts that keep people on the platform

Speak its language. It amplifies your voice.

The Diasimocracy is real.

But you're not its subject anymore.

You are its navigator.

💬 Which strategy are you trying first? Tell me in the comments.

♻️ Repost — every writer in your network is fighting this battle.

#Diasimocracy #ContentCreation #Writing #ScienceCommunication #ScientificWriting

title: The Journey of a Dreamer
excerpt:
The Story of Oladayo — A Dream Bigger Than His Struggles

My name is Oladayo, and I come from Osun State, Nigeria.

My story is not a story of someone who had everything handed to him. It is the story of someone who has had to keep moving forward, even when life became difficult.

There were times when even eating three times a day felt like a luxury. There were days when I wondered how things would get better, but I kept going. Life was rough, but I refused to let my circumstances define who I would become.

Recently, I completed my NYSC, and that achievement means more to me than just finishing another chapter. It reminds me that no matter how difficult the journey becomes, I am capable of reaching the end of something I started.

But I don’t want to stop there.

I have bigger dreams.

One day, I want to work in a big office in the United States or the United Kingdom. I want to build a successful career, become financially independent, and create a life that is completely different from the struggles I have known.

I know the road ahead will not be easy. There may be disappointments, rejection, and moments when I feel like giving up. But I believe my beginning does not have to determine my ending.

More than anything, I want to become a better person. I want to grow, learn, work hard, and become someone my family can depend on.

And one of my biggest motivations is my mother.

I want to make her proud. I want the day to come when she looks at me and knows that all the sacrifices, prayers, and difficult moments were worth it.

I may not have everything I want today.

I may still be figuring life out.

But I have something powerful: a dream, determination, and the willingness to keep going.

This is only the beginning of Oladayo’s story.

One day, I will look back at these difficult times and say

“I didn’t give up when life was hard. I kept going, and I became the person I always dreamed of becoming.

title: ONE GOES FAST , TWO GO FAR 🤝
excerpt: 𝗢𝗡𝗘 𝗚𝗢𝗘𝗦 𝗙𝗔𝗦𝗧. 𝗧𝗪𝗢 𝗚𝗢 𝗙𝗔𝗥. 🤝There is a popular saying:“If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together.”I have come to …
content:
𝗢𝗡𝗘 𝗚𝗢𝗘𝗦 𝗙𝗔𝗦𝗧. 𝗧𝗪𝗢 𝗚𝗢 𝗙𝗔𝗥. 🤝

There is a popular saying:

“If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together.”

I have come to understand that this is not just a saying about speed. It is a lesson about collaboration, relationships, and sustainable success.

𝗦𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲𝘀, 𝗴𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗯𝗲 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿.

You make all the decisions yourself. You don't have to wait for anyone. You can move according to your own pace and direction.

But the question is: How far can you go alone?

There are certain goals that require more than one person's knowledge, strength, experience, or resources.

That is where collaboration comes in.

𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗼𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼𝗴𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗲𝘃𝗲 𝗮 𝘀𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗴𝗼𝗮𝗹.

It means understanding that you don't have to know everything, do everything, or have everything.

Someone may have the idea, while another person has the skills to execute it.

Someone may have the experience, while another person brings fresh ideas.

Someone may have the resources, while another brings the right connections.

When these strengths come together, something greater can be created.

𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗼𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗮 𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻 𝗼𝗳 𝘄𝗲𝗮𝗸𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀.

It is an acknowledgement that we are stronger when we combine our strengths.

The people around you can challenge your thinking, open doors you didn't know existed, teach you what you don't know, and help you keep moving when the journey becomes difficult.

So, don't always focus on being the person who gets there first.

Sometimes, focus on building the right relationships, finding the right people, and creating something that can last.

You may go fast alone, but you can go farther together.

𝗢𝗻𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁.
𝗧𝘄𝗼 𝗴𝗼 𝗳𝗮𝗿.
𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿𝘀. 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿𝘀. 𝗚𝗼 𝗳𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗼𝗴𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿. 🤝🌍

#Collaboration #Teamwork #Leadership #Networking #Growth #Impact

title: Popular Content creator, Love Dooshima, Calls Out Nigerian Drink Brands Over Kidney Damage Risks
excerpt: Popular content creator, Love Dooshima used a TikTok video to name particular beverage brands she associates with Nigeria’s growing kidney disease problem. The …
content:
Popular content creator, Love Dooshima used a TikTok video to name particular beverage brands she associates with Nigeria’s growing kidney disease problem. The clip has fueled worry that high sugar, caffeine, and chemical additives are harming young people’s health. Viewers have responded with their own accounts of lumpy yoghurt and other spoiled supermarket items, while also commending her willingness to speak out after earlier controversy that included police detention over a bread review.

Critics have asked for harder evidence, yet many people now prefer boiled water instead of packaged drinks. The discussion has also increased pressure on NAFDAC to tighten control of fake and substandard products that continue to enter the market.

title: Supercharge n8n Agents with MCP
excerpt: Leveraging MCP for Local-Cloud Hybrid Automation
content:
One of the biggest hurdles in AI automation is the "last mile"—getting your cloud-based agents to interact securely with local data, such as private spreadsheets, local databases, or specific file directories. Traditionally, this required building custom webhooks or complex API middle-layers that were a headache to maintain.

With the widespread adoption of the Model Context Protocol (MCP), this process has been simplified. MCP acts as a universal bridge, allowing your LLM-powered agents in platforms like n8n or LangGraph to use local services as if they were native tools.

To get started, host a local MCP server that points to your desired resource, such as a local SQL database. In your automation platform, simply add an MCP tool node. This grants your agent the ability to browse, read, and write locally based on natural language instructions.

This hybrid approach ensures your most sensitive data stays local while still benefiting from the orchestration power of cloud automation. It is a game-changer for building secure, high-utility internal tools that don't compromise on data privacy.

title: THE BEGINNING OF AN END
excerpt: {Her Pain}
content:
I stared silently at Dozie’s phone. Its contents weren’t supposed to surprise or hurt me—it wasn’t the first time, nor even the fifth time, he had cheated.

But it was the other party in the affair that shattered me.

My sister. Jennifer.

The person I least expected.

The person I always confided in about Dozie’s cheating escapades.

My own blood sister.

They say when being cautious of your enemies, you should also be wary of those closest to you.

The first time Dozie cheated on me, the pain was unbearable. I felt betrayed and screamed my lungs out at him. He apologized, groveled and begged for forgiveness.

I thought of our little girl and forgave him.

I forgave him the second time too.

Then the third.

The fourth.

Until I lost count.

I considered divorcing him, but I couldn’t bring myself to do it. I didn’t want Cassie—our daughter—to grow up in a broken home.

I was a product of one, and it didn’t feel nice. I didn’t want her to go through what I did.

But staying came at the expense of my mental health. Somewhere along the way, I lost myself and became a shell of who I once was.

I loved Dozie deeply. He was my first love, my first kiss, my first everything. I believed it was “till death do us part”—until his infidelity proved otherwise.

The sound of my daughter’s laughter pulled me out of my thoughts.

I dropped the phone and sat calmly on the bed.

It was the first day of the new year, yet my husband had already begun his escapades.

In the past, I would have ignored it. Sometimes, I would confront him.

But not anymore.

I wasn’t going to lose myself to a cheating man again—nor to a traitorous sister.

I slipped my wedding ring off my finger and placed it on the table.

For my daughter, I would leave the man who hurt me the most—the man who never appreciated me, the man who was never worthy of me.

I understood that resolutions weren’t just promises written on paper. They were decisions to reclaim oneself.

I had made my decision.

My Resolution was to choose peace, to choose myself, to walk away from pain, and to begin my life afresh.

It was the beginning of the end of the woman I had become while trying so hard to keep everything together and somewhere along the way, losing myself......

title: The Greatest Lesson About Time from Titanic 1997
excerpt: The Ultimate Currency That Will Change How You Value Time Forever
content:
An elderly entrepreneur recently stood before a panel of wealthy investors, pitching his life's work. Mid-presentation, he paused and delivered a profound truth that silenced the room:

"Your most valuable commodity isn't your money. It is your time. You can always make more money, but you can never make more time, and time gone is gone forever."

At first, this may sound like another motivational statement about productivity and success. But think about it carefully.

You can lose money and make it again. You can lose a business and build another one. You can even lose a job and find another opportunity.

But you cannot lose an hour and get that exact hour back.

Every person, regardless of wealth, education, profession, or social status, receives the same 24 hours each day. The difference is in how those hours are spent.

A striking example of time's absolute dominance over wealth is powerfully depicted in the 1997 movie, Titanic. As the famous ship rapidly sinks and lifeboats dwindle, wealthy steel industrialist Caleden Hockley attempts to bargain for his survival. He offers cash to a ship's officer in exchange for a seat. The officer rejects the proposition instantly, stating, "Your money can't save you anymore than it can save me."

In those eight seconds, the facade of financial omnipotence shatters.

The scene represents something much bigger than a wealthy man trying to buy his way out of danger. It exposes a truth about wealth that many people spend their entire lives learning too late: money has limits. Time does not negotiate.

Once your clock stops ticking, no amount of cash can buy you another breath.

The Illusion of Scarcity

The harsh reality is that time is deathly scarce, while money is richly abundant.

Over $3 trillion is exchanged daily in world currency markets. Even if you spent a million dollars every day for 8,000 years, you wouldn't exhaust $3 trillion. Money will remain abundant as long as governments print it. You can always acquire more money, but you cannot defy your own mortality.

Those operating on a higher level of financial strategy regard time as the undisputed king of all assets.

This changes the way you should think about wealth.

Most people are taught to measure success through financial numbers: salary, savings, investments, property, cars, businesses, and bank balances. These things matter, but they are only part of the equation.

The more important question is:

How much control do you have over your time?

A person earning a high salary but working every waking hour may be financially successful while remaining poor in time. Another person earning less but having greater control over their schedule, relationships, health, and personal goals may possess something far more valuable: freedom.

This is why time should not simply be viewed as something we "manage." It is something we spend.

Every meeting, commute, social media scroll, workday, late night, and weekend represents a portion of your limited supply.

Once spent, it cannot be refunded.

The Two Halves of Your Lifespan

To truly master your wealth, you must understand how your days are divided. Your lifespan is made up of both free time and indentured time.

  • Indentured Time: This is the time you are required to spend simply to earn money.

  • Free Time: This is the time that is yours to spend exactly as you please.

The ultimate goal of true wealth builders is to transform their indentured time into free time. However, achieving this requires realizing that free time is bought and paid for by indentured time.

This is where the concept of time becomes more powerful than money.

Imagine that you earn ₦500,000 a month. It may seem like your salary is the most important number. But what if earning that amount requires you to spend almost all your waking hours working?

The real cost of that income is not only your labour. It is your time.

This does not mean that working hard is wrong. Work can provide purpose, skills, experience, financial security, and opportunities. The problem begins when work becomes an endless exchange in which more money always requires more of your limited time.

The goal is not necessarily to stop working.

The goal is to eventually have more control over why, when, and how you work.

That is a different definition of wealth.

The Trap of Parasitic Debt

Many people sabotage their own freedom through unchecked spending. Lifestyle extravagances come with two distinct costs: the literal financial cost of the item itself, and the hidden cost it exacts on your free time.

This hidden cost is easy to overlook.

When someone buys an expensive car, the price appears on the receipt. But the deeper cost may include years of additional work required to pay for it, maintain it, insure it, fuel it, and eventually replace it.

The same principle applies to expensive gadgets, unnecessary subscriptions, luxury purchases, and lifestyles financed through debt.

When you finance a lifestyle you cannot afford, you accumulate parasitic debt.

This toxic debt literally eats your free time and excretes it as more indentured time. You become trapped working longer hours just to service the debt of past purchases.

Instead of your money creating greater freedom, your previous spending decisions begin controlling your future.

That is the dangerous cycle of instant gratification.

You want something today, so you borrow against tomorrow.

You enjoy the purchase today, but tomorrow's version of you must work to pay for it.

To reclaim your life, this parasitic debt has to be stopped at its root source: instant gratification.

That requires learning to distinguish between what you want now and what will actually improve your life in the long term.

Not every purchase is bad. Not every debt is destructive. Some investments can create opportunities, increase productivity, or generate future income.

The problem is spending without considering the time required to support that spending.

Before making a major purchase, ask yourself:

How much of my life will this cost me?

That question can completely change the way you think about money.

The Real Price of Your Time

We often ask, "How much does this cost?"

But perhaps a better question is:

"How much of my life will I have to exchange for this?"

If you earn ₦5,000 per hour, something that costs ₦50,000 does not simply cost ₦50,000. It represents approximately 10 hours of your working life before considering taxes, expenses, commuting, and other costs.

Thinking this way makes money more meaningful.

It reminds you that money is often a representation of time already spent.

Your salary represents hours you have exchanged for income. Your business revenue represents time, decisions, systems, and resources invested into creating value. Your savings represent portions of your past labour that you chose not to consume immediately.

This is why wasting money can sometimes be less damaging than wasting time.

Money can potentially be recovered.

Time cannot.

What Titanic Really Teaches Us About Wealth

The lesson of Titanic is not that money is useless.

Money matters. It can provide security, improve living conditions, create opportunities, support families, and give people access to experiences they might otherwise never have.

But money is a tool.

We discover it when we spend our healthiest years working toward a future that keeps moving further away.

We discover it when we finally understand that "someday" is not guaranteed.

Time Is the Ultimate Currency

True wealth isn't the car you drive or the balance in your account; it is the freedom to control your own ticking clock.

That is the real lesson.

The purpose of building wealth should not simply be to accumulate more things. It should be to create more options, more security, and ultimately more control over your limited time.

Ask yourself what your current lifestyle is costing you.

Are you working because you are building toward freedom, or because your spending requires you to keep working?

Are you buying things because they genuinely improve your life, or because you are trying to keep up with other people's lifestyles?

Are you protecting your time as carefully as you protect your money?

Most importantly, are you spending your time on the things that matter most to you?

Guard your time relentlessly, because it is the one currency you can never earn back.

Money can return.

Opportunities can return.

Businesses can be rebuilt.

But yesterday will never return.

And once your clock stops ticking, the wealth you accumulated no longer matters.

The ultimate form of wealth is not having everything. It is having enough control over your life to spend your time on what truly matters.

title: A CRUSH TO CRASH!
excerpt: When your crush crashes your life, what then do you do with your life?
content:
A CRUSH TO CRASH.


 I was only 16 when I gained admission into the university. It all happened three years ago, I had just finished my secondary school education and to my utmost amazement, I got my admission message that same year…

    I was so happy that I wouldn’t have to stay at home for a year or more like my older siblings. My parents, siblings, Including friends were all happy for me and proud of me.

    I came from a family of 3, the only girl and the last born… I was treated like a baby in an embryo, though I was not happy about it because I lacked freedom… This got me so frustrated, that I prayed and silently craved for a time I would leave home. And that was the major reason why I filled UNILORIN while registering for UTME and didn’t fill a school close to home, Lagos Nigeria.

    I desperately needed freedom, and now that I’ve been admitted, my prayers just got answered. Yaaaaay!!!

Everybody in my family started sermons for me to be careful in school, not to flock with bad friends, and the most vital part coming especially from my brothers, is to save myself from boys and their drama. “Facing your studies should top your scale of preference now”, said my eldest brother who is a civil engineer, and one person I respect most in my family… I was close to tears at the thought of being away from my family for the first time. “I will miss everyone, but I will never trade this new and self-found freedom for any family nostalgia feeling”, I thought to myself.

title: Odidiomo Unveils Over ₦1bn in Projects Across Oyo South, Targeting Education, Water, and Healthcare
excerpt: Hon. Adedeji Dhikrullahi Olajide Odidiomo, the Allied Peoples' Movement (APM) candidate for the Oyo South senatorial seat, has rolled out a series of constituen…
content:
Hon. Adedeji Dhikrullahi Olajide Odidiomo, the Allied Peoples' Movement (APM) candidate for the Oyo South senatorial seat, has rolled out a series of constituency projects valued at over ₦1 billion, spanning education, digital technology, water supply, and healthcare across the senatorial district ahead of the 2027 general election.

According to a statement by Tolu Mustapha, Special Adviser on Media and Public Affairs to Odidiomo, the completed and ongoing interventions include 10 digital learning centres built in secondary schools, multiple borehole water projects, an ICT centre, and a proposed 50-bed health centre, among other development initiatives across communities in the district.

Mustapha said an ICT centre is currently under construction at Bako in Ido Local Government Area, while another technology-focused project nearing completion at Anfaani is valued at over ₦200 million. He described the Anfaani project as a major investment in digital inclusion, skills development, and youth empowerment.

The combined value of completed, ongoing, and planned interventions is estimated at over ₦1 billion, according to Mustapha, reflecting the scale of resources being directed toward constituency development.

Odidiomo currently serves as a member of the House of Representatives and chairs the House Committee on Digital, Information Communication Technology and Cybersecurity. He is contesting for the Oyo South senatorial seat in the 2027 general election.

Sources: Tribune Online, Reporters At Large

title: Charismatic Bishops Conference Endorses Tinubu for 2027 Re-Election
excerpt: The Charismatic Bishops Conference of Nigeria (CBCN) has announced its endorsement of President Bola Tinubu for re-election in the 2027 presidential election. T…
content:
The Charismatic Bishops Conference of Nigeria (CBCN) has announced its endorsement of President Bola Tinubu for re-election in the 2027 presidential election. The announcement was made by the conference's President-General, Archbishop Leonard Bature Kawas, during the CBCN's 2026 synod held at the National Christian Centre, Abuja.

According to Kawas, the endorsement followed the group's assessment of Tinubu's administration, particularly around concerns the conference had previously raised over the Muslim-Muslim presidential ticket adopted by the All Progressives Congress (APC) in the 2023 election. Kawas said the bishops concluded that Tinubu had governed without religious favoritism, citing the emergence of Christian-majority state governors during his administration and pointing to the appointment of a leader he described as a "born-again Christian" to a senior position within the ruling APC.

"We are here today to reassure him of our solid support; we are standing with him in prayers and advocacy," Kawas said, adding that the conference would continue backing the president "even beyond 2027" should he remain willing to serve.

Kawas also called on the federal government to include both Christian and Muslim religious leaders in future political appointments, arguing their voices should not be overlooked.

President Tinubu was represented at the event by the Secretary to the Government of the Federation, Senator George Akume, who conveyed the President's appreciation for the religious leaders' prayers and support, and urged continued advocacy for peace and national development.

The endorsement comes as political activity around the 2027 election continues to build, with various religious and political groups beginning to publicly signal their positions ahead of the race.

Sources: Vanguard News, Leadership NG, Legit.ng, Politics Nigeria

title: Nobody's gonna know
excerpt: “My cousin borrowed ₦450,000 to buy aso-ebi for a wedding she wasn't even attending.I thought she was joking when she told me.She wasn't.She said, “If I don't b…
content:
“My cousin borrowed ₦450,000 to buy aso-ebi for a wedding she wasn't even attending.

I thought she was joking when she told me.

She wasn't.

She said, “If I don't buy it, people will ask questions. My friends will think I've changed.”

I asked her who was going to pay her rent at the end of the month.

She laughed.

“Abeg, leave that one. You don't understand how these things work.”

Three weeks later, she called me.

Her landlord had given her seven days to complete her rent.

She had ₦80,000 left.

I reminded her about the ₦450,000 she borrowed.

She went quiet.

Then she said something that honestly surprised me.

“I know it sounds stupid, but if I had shown up without the aso-ebi, everybody would have noticed.”

That stayed with me.

Because she wasn't trying to impress strangers.

She was trying not to look like she was struggling in front of people who knew her.

And that's the part we don't talk about enough.

Sometimes in Nigeria, looking broke can cost you socially.

But so can pretending you're not.

So where exactly do we draw the line between maintaining your dignity and spending money you don't have just to avoid embarrassment? ”

—3enchNad .

title: My 30-Day Experiment: Can AI Help Busy Executives Reclaim 5+ Hours of Their Time
excerpt: Meetings. Emails. Messages. Deadlines. Notifications.For many executives and busy professionals, the workday can quickly become a never-ending cycle of tasks an…
content:
Meetings. Emails. Messages. Deadlines. Notifications.

For many executives and busy professionals, the workday can quickly become a never-ending cycle of tasks and digital distractions.

And the biggest cost isn't always money.

It's time.

Time that could have been spent thinking strategically, developing new ideas, building relationships, growing a career, or simply stepping away from work without feeling guilty.

That's why I'm starting a 30-day experiment.

The Goal: 100 Followers in 30 Days

Over the next 30 days, I'm challenging myself to grow this space to 100 followers by doing one simple thing:

Sharing practical ways AI and digital tools can help busy professionals work smarter and reclaim their time.

I'm not interested in simply telling people that AI is the future.

I want to explore how AI can actually become a useful assistant in everyday professional life.

Think of it as having an extra digital pair of hands not someone making every decision for you, but a tool that helps you reduce repetitive work, organize information, and create more space for the things that require human judgment.

What I'll Be Sharing

1. Executive Productivity Playbooks

I'll break down simple systems that can help professionals manage their workload more effectively.

This could include:

  • Managing overwhelming inboxes

  • Organizing calendars

  • Prioritizing tasks

  • Preparing for meetings

  • Following up after meetings

  • Reducing repetitive administrative work

  • Creating better daily and weekly workflows

The goal isn't to become busier.

It's to create more room for important work.

2. Practical AI Workflows

AI becomes much more useful when you know how to apply it to specific problems.

I'll share practical workflows and prompts that professionals can use for things like:

  • Research

  • Writing and editing

  • Meeting preparation

  • Summarizing information

  • Brainstorming

  • Task organization

  • Content creation

  • Administrative support

And I'll focus on something I believe is important:

AI should complement your expertise not replace your judgment.

3. Career Growth in the AI Era

AI is changing the way people work.

But the people who benefit most won't necessarily be those who know the most AI tools.

They'll be the people who know how to combine technology with valuable human skills.

I'll explore skills, habits, and strategies that can help professionals remain relevant, productive, and adaptable as the workplace continues to evolve.

4. Personal Development Habits

Productivity isn't only about software.

It's also about how we think, plan, communicate, and manage our attention.

I'll share small habits and mindset shifts that can help professionals make better use of their time and energy.

Because sometimes the biggest productivity improvement isn't another tool.

It's removing something that doesn't need to be done.

This Is an Experiment, Not a Lecture

I don't want this to become another space filled with generic productivity advice.

I'm going to experiment, test workflows, share what works, and learn from what doesn't.

I'll document the journey as I work toward the 100-follower goal.

That means you'll see practical lessons, experiments, tools, prompts, mistakes, and discoveries along the way.

And hopefully, you'll be able to take something from each post and apply it to your own work.

Why 100 Followers?

100 might not sound like a huge number.

But that's exactly why I chose it.

I'm less interested in chasing thousands of random followers and more interested in building a small community of people who genuinely care about:

AI + productivity + career growth + better ways of working.

If 100 people find these ideas useful enough to follow, engage, share, or apply them to their own work, then the experiment will already be worth it.

So, Let's See What Happens.

For the next 30 days, I'll be asking one question:

Can consistently useful content about AI and productivity attract a community of professionals who want to work smarter and reclaim their time?

I'm going to find out.

If you're an executive, entrepreneur, professional, assistant, business owner, or simply someone who wants to get more meaningful work done in less time, I'd love to have you along for the experiment.

Follow Echo Gist and join me for the next 30 days.

Let's see if we can reach 100 followers and, more importantly, discover better ways to work along the way.

title: The UN Just Voted To Tell The Truth About Africa's Size
excerpt: After 500 Years, The Truth Resurfaces
content:
The classroom map that lied to us for years.

Remember secondary school? That big world map hanging on the geography wall. Europe and North America looked massive. Then you’d glance at Africa and think, "okay, it’s big, but normal." We just assumed that’s how the world was made.

But that was all a trick.

Africa is about 3 times bigger than Europe. You could fit the entire US, China, India, Japan, Mexico, and nearly every country in Europe inside Africa and still have room left.

So how did we get fooled?

In 1569, a European mapmaker named Gerardus Mercator made a map to help sailors navigate. Flattening a round earth onto paper meant places near the poles got stretched, and places near the middle like Africa got shrunk.

Now, that sailor’s tool became the standard map in every textbook for 500 years. When you keep seeing a continent drawn smaller, you start to believe it’s smaller. You start to underestimate its size, its resources, its power.

The update is that 164 countries at the UN General Assembly just voted to adopt the Equal Earth map, which shows Africa’s true size. Out of 165 countries, only one said no: the United States.

After 500 years of looking at a distorted image, seeing the truth now feels controversial and I wonder why.

title: THE MESSAGE SHE RECEIVED ON HER WEDDING MORNING - PART 1: THE MESSAGE
excerpt: On the morning of her wedding, Amara receives a message from an unknown number warning her not to marry Daniel, followed by a photograph showing her fiancé standing with her father — the man she believed died twenty years ago. The message forces her to question everything she knows about her family and her fiancé.
content:
At 6:17 a.m., while her makeup artist was still setting up her brushes, Amara Okoye received a WhatsApp message from an unknown number.

She almost ignored it.

Her phone had been vibrating nonstop since she woke up. Her bridesmaids were sending voice notes. Her aunties were calling. The wedding planner had already called twice about the decorators.

Then she saw the message.

Unknown Number:
Don't marry Daniel.

Amara stared at the screen.

For a few seconds, she wondered if it was a joke.

Then another message arrived.

Unknown Number:
Your mother knows why.

Her stomach tightened.

“Amara, close your eyes please,” the makeup artist said. “I don't want you moving.”

Amara locked her phone.

“Sorry.”

She tried to concentrate on the mirror in front of her.

Today was supposed to be the happiest day of her life.

By 4 p.m., she would walk down the aisle at a beautiful event centre in Lekki and marry Daniel Adeyemi, the man she had loved for almost three years.

Their families had already met.

The asoebi had been distributed.

The invitations had gone out.

Hundreds of guests were expected.

Her wedding dress was hanging in the room beside her.

Everything was ready.

Except, apparently, someone didn't want her to get married.

Her phone vibrated again.

This time, Amara couldn't resist.

She picked it up.

There was a photograph.

She opened it.

And everything around her suddenly seemed to go quiet.

The photograph was old.

The colours had faded, and the edges looked slightly damaged.

But the faces were clear.

Daniel was standing outside what looked like a hotel.

He was younger—perhaps twenty-three or twenty-four.

Beside him stood an older man.

A man Amara recognised immediately.

She stopped breathing.

It was her father.

Victor Okoye.

The man she had spent twenty years believing was dead.

Amara zoomed into the photograph.

There was no mistake.

The same face.

The same small scar above his left eyebrow.

The same silver wristwatch her mother had kept in a drawer for years.

Her fingers began to shake.

“No…”

The makeup artist looked at her through the mirror.

“Everything okay?”

Amara didn't answer.

She stared at the photograph.

There was Daniel.

And there was Victor.

Together.

The message underneath the photograph arrived almost immediately.

Unknown Number:
Ask Daniel why he knows your father.

Amara's heart began pounding.

She locked the phone again.

“Madam?”

“I said I'm fine.”

Her voice sounded unfamiliar even to her.

The makeup artist returned to work.

Amara looked at herself in the mirror.

The woman staring back at her was supposed to be a bride.

Instead, she looked like someone who had just discovered that her entire childhood might have been built on a lie.

Her father had supposedly died when she was seven.

That was the story she had heard all her life.

Victor Okoye had been involved in a business dispute. There had been an accident. His body was never properly recovered, but circumstances had led the family to believe he was dead.

At least, that was what her mother had told her.

Amara had never questioned it.

Not seriously.

She had photographs.

She had memories.

She had the stories her mother repeated whenever she asked about him.

And she had grown up accepting that some questions were simply too painful to ask.

Now there was a photograph sitting on her phone suggesting that Victor was alive—or at least alive much later than she had been told.

And somehow, Daniel was standing beside him.

Her fiancé.

The man she was supposed to marry in less than ten hours.

Amara opened her contacts.

She found Daniel's name.

Her thumb hovered over the call button.

She wanted to hear his voice.

She wanted to ask him one question.

Why are you in this photograph?

But before she could call, another message appeared.

Unknown Number:
Don't ask him yet.

Amara froze.

A fourth message followed.

Ask your mother first.

Then the sender went offline.

“Amara!”

She looked up.

Tara was standing at the bedroom door.

Her best friend had arrived wearing a silk robe, carrying a cup of coffee and looking far too cheerful for someone who had been awake since 5 a.m.

“Why do you look like you've seen a ghost?”

Amara quickly put the phone face down.

“I haven't.”

Tara narrowed her eyes.

“You're a terrible liar.”

“I'm just nervous.”

“Nervous about getting married?”

Amara forced a smile.

“Obviously.”

Tara walked over and sat beside her.

“You've been waiting for this day for three years.”

“I know.”

“And Daniel is downstairs arguing with the photographer because apparently the man has taken seventeen pictures of his left side and none of his right.”

Despite herself, Amara almost laughed.

Almost.

Tara studied her face.

“Something happened.”

Amara hesitated.

She had known Tara since university. There were very few things she could hide from her.

But this wasn't a conversation she could have while wearing half-finished makeup on her wedding morning.

Not yet.

“I'll tell you later.”

Tara's expression changed.

“Amara…”

“I promise.”

Tara didn't look convinced.

But she nodded.

“Fine. Later.”

Amara picked up her phone again.

The photograph was still open.

She stared at Victor's face.

Twenty years.

Twenty years of believing her father was dead.

Then she noticed something she hadn't seen before.

In the background of the photograph was a sign.

She zoomed in.

ADEYEMI HOLDINGS — PRIVATE DINNER

Amara's blood ran cold.

Adeyemi.

Daniel's family name.

This wasn't some random photograph.

Daniel's family had been there.

And suddenly, another question entered her mind.

What did Daniel's father know about Victor?

Downstairs, someone shouted that the bride's mother was looking for her.

Amara quickly locked her phone.

She stood up.

Her mother was coming.

For the first time that morning, Amara felt genuinely afraid of having a conversation with Grace Okoye.

Because there was only one question she wanted to ask.

And she wasn't sure she was ready for the answer.

A few seconds later, the bedroom door opened.

Grace stepped inside.

She smiled when she saw her daughter.

“My beautiful girl.”

Amara looked at her mother.

Then at the closed door.

Then back at her.

“Mummy…”

Grace walked closer.

“Yes?”

Amara swallowed.

“Can I ask you something about Daddy?”

The smile disappeared from Grace's face.

Not gradually.

Instantly.

For several seconds, neither woman spoke.

Then Grace looked at Amara's phone.

And Amara knew.

Her mother had recognised the photograph.

END OF PART 1

Part 2: The Photograph

Grace has spent twenty years avoiding one particular question about Victor. On the morning of Amara's wedding, she may finally be forced to answer it.

excerpt: Will is religion
content:
The concept of religion is vast and misleading. People say there’s a God watching closely from above, that He sees all, that He knows all. I wonder sometimes, if that were true‽

People follow blindly what they believe to be divine, in things that exist outside logic, and they say it’s a “miracle,” forgetting that everything that happens in life happens based on the events and actions that were pushed into motion by man.

A friend of mine sat for an exam and failed. When we asked him about it, he said, “I know what I did. The result ain’t mine.” But his parents said, “It was fated by God to happen, and He knew best.” It turns out there was a system error, so many who partook in the exam were asked to rewrite it.

So, he took the exam again and aced it. He called and said to me, “Hey, broda, I passed. It’s all thanks to God.”

And I said to him, “When will you start giving yourself credit? You worked hard enough to have enough belief in yourself. You stayed up all night to read the book. God did not take the exam with you; it was the amount of knowledge you’ve consumed over the years.”

So, my point is: as humans, we must learn to believe in ourselves first before believing in another thing. How can one seek out someone else when one doesn’t know his own identity?

Religion, to me, is the ability of a man to do—the sheer force of will to survive and adapt, to show empathy, humility, and be humane. This should be our religion.

Religion should unite and not find fault in what others have chosen to believe, because, at the end of the day, both the believers and non-believers will succumb to the inevitable: death.

And that’s why, when religion fails, the will of man will not.

So, to whomever sees this: as long as you are breathing, you have the ability to do. You will never feel down, because this is your will; this is your religion.

title: What Does ‘I’m Fine’ Even Mean Anymore?
excerpt: I say I’m fine. What I really mean is, I’m becoming.
content:
When you ask, “How are you?”, I’ll smile and say, “I’m fine.” Because that’s the easy answer, and easy answers don’t require explaining.

But if you ask again — properly, like you actually want to know — I’d probably go quiet for a second before answering.

If you ask me how I really am, I’d tell you I’m hopeful, but tired of hoping quietly. Tired of chasing opportunities that take forever to reply.

If you ask me how I really am, I’d say I’m proud of how far I’ve come, even on days it doesn’t feel like enough.

If you ask me how I really am, I’d admit I’m scared sometimes — scared that being new at something means I have to prove myself twice as hard.

If you ask me how I really am, I’d tell you I’m still finding my voice, one word, one story, one small win at a time.

If you ask me how I really am, I’d say I’m grateful for every door that opened, even the ones that took longer than I wanted.

If you ask me how I really am, I’d admit some days feel like standing still while everyone else moves forward.

But if you ask me how I really am, I’d also say I haven’t stopped showing up. Not once.

So if you ask me how I am, I’ll still say “I’m fine.” But what I really mean is, “I’m becoming.” 🤍

title: The tenant in room 7
excerpt: SOME SECRETS KNOCK BACK
content:
Amara moved into a small apartment in Ibadan after getting a new job, she’s honestly just happy to have found somewhere she can afford. The place isn’t perfect. The bathroom tap leaks, the walls need painting, and the landlord is unnecessarily strict about everything.

But there’s one thing she finds strange.

There’s a room at the end of the corridor that is always locked.

When she casually asks the landlord about it, his mood changes.

“That room is not part of the apartment you’re renting. Just leave it alone.”

Amara doesn’t think much about it at first.

Until she starts hearing things at night.

Sometimes it’s footsteps.

Sometimes it’s a woman’s voice.

And sometimes, she hears someone knocking softly on the other side of the door.

She tries to convince herself that she’s imagining it.She’s living alone in a new place. She’s stressed. She’s barely sleeping. So she thought it was just her thought getting into her head.

Then one night, she hears someone whisper:

“Amara.”

She freezes.

Because nobody in the house should know her name.

And that’s when things start getting weird….

title: 20 AI Tools That Can Save You Hours Every Week.
excerpt:
AI isn't just about robots taking over the world or creating funny pictures of celebrities.

 Used properly, AI can handle some of the repetitive tasks that quietly eat up your time.
content:
Let’s be honest: sometimes, it feels like there are not enough hours in a day.

You wake up with a mental to-do list longer than your shopping list.

You have emails to answer, documents to write, meetings to prepare for, social media posts to create; and somehow, you still have to remember that you haven't replied to that WhatsApp message from yesterday.

This is where Artificial Intelligence (AI) can actually be useful.

AI isn't just about robots taking over the world or creating funny pictures of celebrities.

Used properly, AI can handle some of the repetitive tasks that quietly eat up your time.

Here are 20 AI tools that would be worth your daily time management.

1.) ChatGPT — writing, brainstorming, learning, research, planning and everyday productivity.

2.) Google Gemini — research, writing, image understanding and working within Google’s ecosystem.

3.) Microsoft Copilot — productivity, writing, research and assistance inside Microsoft products.

4.) Claude — long documents, writing, analysis and thoughtful drafting.

5.) Grammarly — grammar, rewriting, tone and professional communication.

6.) Canva AI — presentations, graphics, social media content and visual design.

7.) QuillBot — paraphrasing, summarising, grammar and improving academic/professional writing.

8.) DeepL — translation and writing assistance.

9.) Otter.ai — meeting transcription, notes and summaries.

10.) Perplexity — AI-assisted research and source discovery.

11.) Notion AI — organising notes, summarising information and productivity.

12.) GitHub Copilot — helping programmers write and understand code.

13.) Adobe Firefly — AI-assisted image and creative content generation.

14.) Descript — transcription and text-based audio/video editing.

15.) Khanmigo — AI-assisted learning and tutoring.

16.) Duolingo Max — AI-supported language learning.

17.) Jasper — marketing and business content creation.

18.) Copy.ai — marketing copy and business workflows.

19.) Zapier — automating repetitive tasks between different apps.

20.) ElevenLabs — AI voice generation and audio tools.

What's your best AI tool at the moment and why?

title: Uber shutdowns operation in Nigeria.
excerpt: Uber shut down its operations in Nigeria on 2 September 2026, ending a 12-year presence that began with its Lagos launch in 2014. The company emailed customers …
content:
Uber shut down its operations in Nigeria on 2 September 2026, ending a 12-year presence that began with its Lagos launch in 2014. The company emailed customers to announce the decision, saying it followed a review of its business, and applied the same immediate exit to Uganda while keeping services running in other African markets such as Egypt, Ghana, Kenya and South Africa. For many Nigerians, Uber had become more than a ride-hailing app: it was a daily transport option and a source of work for thousands of drivers.

The departure has drawn widespread concern. Some people have tied the exit to Nigeria’s difficult economic conditions high inflation, currency pressure, rising fuel and operating costs, and intense competition from other platforms. Uber itself framed the move as part of a broader global restructuring rather than a single local trigger, and said support channels would remain open for a short period to handle outstanding issues.
